text: This is, without a single doubt, the best open world shooter game I have ever played. It has everything that made Far Cry 1 and Far Cry 2 great. The graphics, color, and the area itself is beautiful. Everywhere you look could be another potential painting. The gameplay is fun, immersive, and addictive. Every action you do feels real. When you go down a sloped hill, you'll slide, when you fall off of a ledge you'll tumble and have to relocate your finger. The coolest part is the games ecology. There's a whole ecosystem built into the game of animals and plants. You can see tigers chasing deer in the jungle, crabs scuttling across beaches, komodo dragons eating pirates. And the gunplay is spot on. Aside from the gameplay, the story is also great. One of my biggest gripes with Far Cry 2 was the♥♥♥♥♥♥poor voice acting, but this game... this game did it right. Vass is as intimidating as a Batman villian and just as twisted. This game puts all other open world shooters to shame. The best thing to happen to games since Red Dead Redemption.
One word.WOW

It's time for a super serious review guys
A Herd of Cassowaries rampaging through a pirate outpost. Sneaking through the jungle until a tiger decides to try to make you its lunch. Ramming a car bomb into a base and setting it off. A hot pink 1911.
If any of those sounded appealing, then you’ll probably like Far Cry 3. To put it simply, Far Cry 3 is what Far Cry 2 should have been. Almost every aspect of it is improved. No more are there infinitely respawning checkpoints or enemies that can spot you out of nowhere. Far Cry 3 takes what was bad about Far Cry 2 out, improves on what it did right, and then sprinkles some komodo dragons and magic mushrooms on top.
The plot starts with you, Jason Brody, and your fellow spoiled-white-kid friends getting captured by Vaas Montenegro, leader of the pirates on the unnamed island you have decided to visit. After escaping, you set out to save your friends, and get off the island. While your character, and the slice of the 1% that you came to the island with, are often insufferable, virtually every other character is fantastic. Vaas is a psychopath, and absolutely drips of crazy; Dr. Earndhart is fantastically creepy; and Willis Huntley may very well be my favourite character of 2012.
But there’s far more to Far Cry 3 than the story. It’s set in an open world, letting you wander off and ignore the plot completely in favour of hunting animals, taking outposts and climbing radio towers if you’d like. There’s a crafting system, allowing you to upgrade how many guns you can have on hand, how many syringes you can carry, etc. You’ll get most of the upgrades quickly, though, since there’s plenty of animals to hunt and skin, and while the final upgrades for most things are part of hunting sidequests that unlock at conquered outposts, they’re all available on the first island. There’s also a skill system, giving you new abilities and upgrades. XP is easy to come by, but some skills are locked behind missions and won’t be available until a ways into the game.
While the gameplay is a lot of fun, I was sometimes left wanting more. The one downside to having outposts not respawn is that you can clear out an entire island of enemies and then have nothing left to do but hunt cassowaries and mop up sidequests. If you’re lucky you’ll run across the occasional firefight between a washed up group of pirates and your native allies, but those are often over before you figure out where the gunfire is coming from.
Side missions are a mixed bag, all of them are fun the first few times, but they rarely stray from their formula. Assassination missions make you kill a guy with a knife, supply drop missions make you drive through some checkpoints, et cetera. Fortunately the hunting missions have at least some variety in what kind of weapons and animals you are using or going after. Using an RPG to hunt down a pack of rabid dogs is a lot of fun, I assure you.
While there is a finite limit to the content, it’s not like this is a short game. There’s PLENTY to do in the story missions alone, and if you add general island dicking around time to that you have a very substantial experience. Even the formulaic side missions are good for a change of scenery every few hours.
Speaking of scenery, this game looks good. Really goddamn good. and getting a very smooth frame rate with some amazing visuals. The first island is mostly jungles, but there are plenty of beaches, rivers, bunkers and so on and so forth. The game is also really colourful. In a world if grey and brown shooters, it’s great to see a game set on a tropical island that feels, well, tropical. There are bright birds and plants everywhere, and with the wildlife system the game world feels alive.

Now, I don't know if I actually recommend this, or not. I feel like I should, but at the same time, there is alot of small issues, not bugs, that really spoil the experience. Maybe it's better for you, I don't know, but here goes.
Being an Ubisoft game, it REQUIRES you to run it through Uplay, which is basically the same thing that Origin is. Another unecessary program to run games through.
The tutorial is very long, tedious, and boring. The main character is a whiny, rich white kid, and so are his friends. Even after the hour-long tutorial, mini tutorials pop up for everything, and do not disappear until you hit escape to view it.
Animal skinning is required for you to do anything at all in the game, but it's also tedious, and unlike another game that did hunting extemely well *COUGHREDDEADREDEMPTIONCOUGH*, there's nothing that shows you where the bodies are, most times just getting lost in the grass, forcing you to search for a while, unless you memorized the exact location of where they died.
Melee stealth kills are extremely hard to do, because enemies are stuck inside each others ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, basically, and it only rewards you with 30 xp as well, when a headshot gives you 25 xp. Plus, dogs ♥♥♥♥ you over, because they can't be stealth killed, and immobilize you for about 5 seconds. You can throw rocks as distractions, but that really does not help, unless it's a very small group of enemies.
The menus are a hassle to go through as well, and when you pick up any sort of item, if you hit escape for about 5 seconds afterwards, it takes you directly to that page, which would be nice, if you then didn't have to scroll back through every page you would normally go through.
Like I said, these are all small issues, in the grand scheme of things, but put together, it spoils the experience. That, and the fact I continuously run into a bug where the "Saving" icon NEVER GOES AWAY, until I completely exit out, and start the game up again. It's happened multiple times, so it will no doubt happen more, unless that is patched. Nothing else is a bug, it's all design choice. Bad ones, but design choices nonetheless.
If all of that sounds fine and dandy with you, enjoy the game. It's not bad by any means, and I am going to play more of it, but those are things that people should be aware of before buying it, just in case.

I can't remember the last time I've had this much fun with a game. It is like this perfect blend of some of my favorite games and at least one I've always wanted to play. It seems like a hybrid of Far Cry 1, Borderlands, F.E.A.R, and Red Dead Redemption.
The controls are extremely fluid, that was one thing I was worried about. When you start the game, you have no unlocks and your character doesn't move very well, give yourself 10 hours with the game and make your way through part of the skill tree's. You will notice yourself becoming better and better at traversing the environment and taking down enemies efficiently and it doesn't only become more comfortable, it eventually becomes a superior FPS control scheme.
Everything from the ability to slide into cover/sprint to the simple and effective way the cover mechanic itself is handled, there was a lot of attention paid to the movement, that is why it is sad that there were certain basic keys that you cannot bind like either return keys, and you come across the occasional bug like gliders reverting back to WASD even after you changed the controls, one time there was a cinematic part where you are supposed to get out of a vehicle driven by someone else and you HAVE to press "E" even if you bound something else. The story is surprisingly good, and while I am less than half way through the game's actual story, I have already invested 16 hours. That is another beauty, you can take on the game any way you like.
There is also a great crafting system where you have to hunt animals to create the things you need to survive like extra ammo pouches, a larger wallet for carrying more money, a larger backpack for carrying more loot, etc. There are huge radio towers you can climb and disable, revealing more of the map and new places to explore. You can loot dead bodies and find everything from meth pipes to gold chains and then sell it all at a store. There is even a fast travel system that you can use at any time. The characters are also very interesting, especially Vaas the pirate. This keeps you invested in the world as you play outside of the main story missions.
FC3 comes with a very long campaign, as mentioned I have invested 16 hours and I am only on mission 13/38 and have not even reached the second Island yet. I'm guessing it will take be 40-50 hours if I continue at the rate I'm going, and it is quite lkely I will play through the game again. I've been told the ending is great. Besides that, theres a separate co-op campaign which I've been told is like 30 hours in itself, then there is the obligatory PvP multiplayer modes like capture the boring and team deathsnore, but you really don't want to buy this game for that. I believe it only allows like 16 players and it uses the typical matchmaking system like COD does now. Finally, it comes with a map editor allowing you to create single player maps to run around in or multiplayer maps (not co-op). You are able to add AI opponents and allies, and even wild life to the single player maps, but you can't export them as a multiplayer map with those assets for some reason. I'm guessing people will figure out a way around that with mods in the coming months, as well as how to make co-op maps.

People seem to have a love-it-or-hate-it kind of relation with the Far Cry games. I still think the first part is one of the forgotten open-world FPS gems, mutants withstanding. But I also think that the second part was a total trainwreck with nausea-inducing "body awareness" and endlessly respawning enemies.
Therefore I find Far Cry 3 to be a very pleasant surprise; A game that I don't think many people will find much at all to complain about. Everything from stealth to action just works here, which is a small miracle considering the number of different mechanics at play. Satisfying on so many levels, Far Cry 3 is the new yardstick for open-world shooters.

Co-ops are pretty entertaining and so is a bit grindy multiplayer.(It does encourage sticking together as a team though.)
Despite a few drawbacks the game possesses. I can still say that the game does many things tastefully. I can say this is my GOTY of 2012.

This game is going sraight to my "Best of the best" category. You have 2 huuuuuuuge islands to explore!!! And there is a looooooooot to do!
1. Outposts. Each outpost designed as a small puzzle with at least 2-3 possible solutions. Feel free to do whatever you like with those filfy pirates! Stealth is highly recommended on first outposts. You'll train your takedowns, takedowns chains and save some ammo.
2. Relics. If you haven't tried Uncharted - you're an idiot for starters :D Go and try that awesome game. Second - FC3 place relics in such places which Naughty Dog have to copy paste in Uncharted 4 :D There are also letters from japaneese solgiers. They are totally sepparate story! Awesome story btw!
3. Characters. They are magnificent in this game. Vaas and everyone you'll meet - A+ for voice acting!
4. Movement mechanics. One of the best I've ever seen. Sliding, falling, diving, swiming, running - everything is perfect!
5. Shooting and the rest of stuff. My issue is that there are not much weapons and I'm afraid that Ubi is going to sell weapons DLCs. But you can always get bow! Bow + explosive arrows = bad-assary!
6. Balance. Tbh it's crap if you finish as much as possible before continue to next mission. In final third of the game I had sooooooo many money and nothing to buy/upgrade...

It's kind of like Skyrim with guns.
Add in a little bit Red Dead Redemption and Assassins Creed, and you have probably the best Singleplayer EgoShooter in 2012!

I chose to buy the Steam Controller over an XBO Controller or a DS4 mainly due to the fact that I don't have either of those consoles. I bought this when it was on sale, so it was about the same price as buying an XBO Controller. But the customization freely and easily available to you for any game that supports this controller is amazing. Almost every customization option has a description that allows you to understand what it is trying to do. I feel the Steam Controller can have a foothold in any style of game from FPS to RTS, racing or adventure. The battery life is decent too, with low haptics my controller has lasted over 65 hours. For those who say it feels cheap, I guess it is not as textured for grip as it should be or that it is rather light, but I think the lightness is a plus for when you are using the gyroscope function as the controller will not flop arround in a loose grip. As for storage, I keep it in the box it came in, as it has good packaging and looks nice. Overall, I would recommend this if you want a good controller with a lot of features and want to play games the way most naturally for you, with your own controls, but I would wait for it to be on sale. If you have an XBO Controller or a DS4, and/or you are fine with any preset controls with games you would use a controller on, I think you would be fine with a different controller than this.

I got a 90% discount coupon from crafting and decided to give the game a go since it was basically free, in a sense. Hunter's Grimm is an old-school RPG where two heroes you control embark on a journey to kill the Emperor Behemoth, the final boss apparently. There aren't many good points about this game other than its decently-drawn sprites. However, there is an overwhelming number of bad points in this game which resulted in me not recommending the game.
1. The title screen is absolutely atrocious. Most of the UI options and button selection is handled by F-keys on your keyboard. Other than the girl artwork, everything else about the title screen simply screams "no effort".
2. The story is bland, dull and uninteresting. It is rather predictable, but at least the characters follow a plot, which I guess isn't too bad. The story won't keep you playing though, for obvious reasons.
3. There is a lack of proper tutorial. Although some may enjoy the joy of discovering every element of the game by trial and error, I can guarantee there is absolutely no joy in doing so. While most controls and mechanics are easy to grasp, there will be certain parts of the story where the lack of direction can be annoyingly frustrating since to progress through the plot, you can required to perform certain actions at a certain place. But since the game doesn't tell you that, you wouldn't know unless you button-mashed your "Interact" key everywhere and happen to chance upon that. Moreover, the currency on screen is indicated as "G", which one may assume is gold. For some odd reason, when you pick up money from the ground, it is called "Silver Keys". Very confusing indeed.
4. Battles are rather lame. I got through most of the battles by button-mashing "Action" or "Attack". There does not seem to be any strategy involved nor do you need to plan your moves for each encounter.
5. The achievements are senseless and pointless. They do not relate to the game at all. You get one achievement every one second you are playing the game; nothing related to completing tasks, reaching goals or progressing through the game. Nothing. If you just want free 695 achievements to increase your achievement count on your profile or be able to use emojis as your achievements, you can pick this game up and just leave it running for ~12 minutes to get all of them.
Overall, I would not recommend getting this game at all. The game is not completely unplayable or downright horrible, but there is a lot of room for improvement and much to be desired. I did not finish the game; my patience ran dry at a certain point and just stopped playing. Honestly, the money you spend on this game just isn't worth it, imo. The only reason why one would even willingly purchase the game is to farm the easy achievements and trading cards.

Valkyrius Prime is a cool shoot'em up with nice gameplay elements!

+ The gameplay is LOADS of fun. One of the best shooter's I've played in a very long time. The levels are short but are filled with so much fast paced action with tons of enemies and projectiles flooding the screen.
+ Visually the game looks excellent and is simply a great addition to the genre. Lots of detail, color, weather effects, explosions, etc.
+ The boss fights are all unique, and very challenging!
+ Weapon power ups / pick ups are something that really helps this game shine. You have two guns (left and right), and you can pickup a different gun for both sides. Including things like machine gun, cannon, spread shot, missiles etc. This allows you to strategize a bit, perhaps having a spread shot to deal with small fast enemies, while a cannon could do heavy damage to larger enemies.
+ A warp mechanic allows you to blink or teleport a short distance away. This allows you to avoid otherwise fatal instances where bullets or enemies don't leave any room for escape.
+ The level variety and pacing is excellent! Some of the backgrounds have 3D environments with a sense of depth. One level feels like you are falling down a hole with enemies coming up and around. It's pretty unique.
+ Fantastic soundtrack that really helps intensify the action and fits the game so well!
+ You get rewarded at the end of each run with credits that you can spend on a variety of upgrades that you can use on your next play. Things like extra continues which are vital if you hope to make it far on harder difficulty levels.
+ This is a minor note, but you can toggle your weapons on and off. This is just such a nice addition which keeps you from having to hold the button / trigger constantly.
- A bit short in length. There are 6 stages total which should take under 40mins to complete on easy. Although there are multiple difficulty levels to challenge yourself.
- Not enough resolution options. I would have liked to see a borderless window option, and support for resolutions higher than 1080p.

Invicta Beam is a great-looking, very frustrating, somewhat cumbersome FPS experience. While everything you will see and hear have a sleek style to them that is undeniably impressive, the gameplay includes an annoying, unforgiving system of one-hit deaths, cluttered screens, ineffective player weapons / powerups and a host of other issues which make the game great to see and enticing to want to play more of, but very cumbersome to get through at times.
The overall design of Invicta Beam strikes a great tone with colorful neon lights blazing in the distance amidst futuristic structures and great-looking enemies including spider-like mechs launching rockets which buzz around you in circles of smoke trails or boss characters such as a humongous Triceratops skeleton looming overhead with a ton of guns under its shell. This all looks awesome, and at times the combat can be a rewarding experience as you dodge their attacks while delivering your own.
Unfortunately, it seems some of the enemy turrets, such as the laser enemy are bound to hit you no matter what you do, with their LOS being immediate, direct shots to the player.
Other unforgiving and "cluttered" feeling moments of the game include the player waiting to progress to the next area just outside of a green laser gate. While these gates will block all of the enemies incoming shots until you decide to step through, if they have littered the gate with bullets already, you will just be standing there waiting to enter until the shots have deflected enough, giving you enough space to proceed.
If you dare to step through a hair to the left or right of one of the yellow stacked up bullets, however, thank you for playing, Game Over, reload and run through the laser gate as soon as the game loads before the enemies have stacked up any bullets to try your hand at the arena ahead.
This gives the game a challenging difficulty and an interesting skew of "having to plan ahead your next move and clear the room accordingly" that is unique when compared to other First Person Shooters, and it can be fun at times. Unfortunately, with enemies such as the aforementioned laser turrets being so incredibly accurate, and the player needing to receive little more than 2-3 hits from enemies to be killed, your own shots begin to feel very underpowered. Save for a sparse rocket pickup you occassionally find and an invaluable shield which deflects enemy bullets, the player powerups are few and far between. You dump tons of ammo into enemies hoping for them to finally keel over while your own vitality is somewhere between dry twig on the bed of a forest and fruitfly caught in a hurricane.
Invicta Beam's recent (Oct 30 2017) update resolves some of these issues with the game, by allowing more of the game to be experienced, by side-stepping its prohibitive difficulty via unlocking all of its levels to everyone from the get go.
Whereas in other titles I have found having all levels unlocked from the start to kill my interest in the game, I'm glad this is present in Invicta Beam, as I wanted to see more of the game somehow but found its difficulty and combat design to be taxing. While the update doesn't address these issues overall, I hope that in a future update the disparity between player damage / abilities and enemies damage / life total is balanced out a little more, to allow more of the game to be experienced.  Although I think Invicta Beam can be an annoying player experience due to its difficulty and some issues with its pacing, thanks to its awesome visual design and immersive effects, I still enjoy Invicta Beam as more of a "first person experience" than fluid-functioning "First Person Shooter."
I would highly recommend checking out the demo to Invicta Beam before deciding whether or not to purchase it, as it will give you a general idea of how it looks and feels, and whether its steep difficulty is something you want to bother trudging through or not.

This is a perfect example of a game that was not properly playtested. Of course there are plenty of junk games on Steam that have that problem, but Invicta Beam is not a junk game - there was clearly a lot of effort made by the developer here, as seen in the nice visuals and overall level of polish.
But it's a giant pain to play. For a quick demonstration of why, watch this brief clip (not my video) from the final room of the very first non-tutorial level of the game (skip to 7:41 if your browser doesn't do it for you):
Note that the player in that video enters the room with 3 lives at full health and finishes with 1 life remaining (the health bar is in the upper-left corner). Did you spot the moments where they take damage? In this game your health just seems to suddenly drop with no audio or visual indication of what is happening, other than a little "beep" when you lose a life. This lack of feedback is the #1 problem.
So how are they being damaged? The first bit of health gets taken off from the green turrets that pop up early. It looks like the turrets are just sitting there doing nothing, but they are actually firing from a little machine gun near the top. The bullets are invisible and seemingly impossible to avoid.
The next chunk of damage comes from the rockets being fired by the blue turrets towards the end of the clip. They are definitely making contact since the health bar is dropping, but on-screen the rockets look like they are either passing right through the player, circling around them, or flying into the walls, again with no feedback for any of it.
Another problem shown In that clip - The player has a secondary rocket launcher weapon that they fire numerous times. Half the time the rocket reaches the target, while the rest of the time the rockets immediately blow up in their face. Why does that happen? I have no idea. It was constantly happening to me also, which makes the rocket launcher useless (the other secondary weapon is a shield, which also suffers a lack of feedback on whether it is working or not).
This is all just in the first level. I only made it to the end of the second level, after dying about 20 times in just 30 minutes of playing, before giving up. The problems got much worse in a very short amount of time.
I think it's great that the developer provided a demo, but you probably won't need it - You will know well before the 2 hour mark whether or not you will enjoy the rest of the game. I requested a refund, but I will keep following it to see if any additional gameplay updates are made.

Let me be specific here: I do NOT recommend the game, but there is a demo and I DO recommend trying that first.
I have very little playtime for a very specific reason: I do not like the gameplay mechanics. Concept and aesthetics are fantastic and right up my alley, but the way the game feels to play is just so off-putting. Let me describe to you from FPS gamer to FPS gamer: There is no inertia. Any change in movement input is enacted instantly with no respect for momentum. Aiming while moving becomes jittery and impercise to the point one must retrain how they aim in an FPS for this one game.
But wait; there's more! Graphical options are a simple A/B setting. Now I don't mean individual options are either high or low, no I mean the whole set is either high or low. Add to that various cinematography effects like motion blur and while you have a great game for screenshots; it just looks and feels horrible to play. Jittery lack of inertia in the aiming while moving with having to aim through motion blur is on a level of annoyance it made my skin crawl.
The same may not be true for you though. So please! Try the demo~
P.S: You can't change options while in-game. You have to reload the main menu, wait for the animation pan to finish, change w/e options, restart the level you were on, wait for the un-skippable description sequence to end, then it begins loading the level, and press any key to begin so you can test your changes; such as aiming sensitivity. My biggest nitpicks are a few glitches, and a menu problem:
The worst annoyance is the menu and the lack of being able to save a game. I played this game for a while man, and I got pretty far. Then I went to start the game up and it was lagging, so I started spamming enter (which is exactly what people do when they get impatient, what gamer doesnt?) and when the game actually loaded, the cursor started on the "new game" button. Long story short, it erased my game and I had to start over just because there's the capacity for one playthrough. There's not even an option to go back to a certain level if you've been there before. One small mistake and hours of gameplay are gone with no hope of getting them back, seriously dumb.
In the game there are mobs that drop weapons, which you can then pick up, and throw them as a secondary attack. It's kind of cool because these dropped weapons are essentially a resource to use, and they are needed in many cases to pass the levels. There is a glitch when you kill two mobs with the same weapon (you should be getting two of the same weapon at this point) and they land in the same area. When you go to pick one of them up, it just picks them both up and you can only use one. They morph together or something. So basically depending on the rng of where the weapon drops, you have sporadic amounts of resources. It never was the determining factor of whether or not I passed a level, but it was still super annoying.
Another glitch has to do with the time ticks for damage. I'm supposed to be able to throw these weapons at mobs, and it damages them, but somtimes if I throw two in a row very fast it only registers that one hits them. This can't be because of a mechanic that they can only be hit in a specific time frame, because you can throw a weapon and then smack it with your sword super fast. So basically you miss out on hitting them just because you are trying to be efficient (Which is super annoying) In fact, this glitch definitely made me not pass levels a lot, it was really frustrating.

Keeping this short:
Pros:

Cons:
>Collectathon (for quests, alchemical skills, rewards, etc.) with some quest specific collectables appearing only after initiating the quest in previous dungeons and a decent chunk of secret paths/hidden collectibles with zero context clues
>Level-up system only increasing HP and MP, leaving stat increases at the mercy of stat-boosting items and equipment.
>Story being your generic adventure anime complete with trope characters of ditzy, young, swordswoman, nerd-boy alchemist, grumpy old-man berserker, and sexy witch/cleric, stopping a big bad defeated long ago from reviving as they bumble through the world as adventurers for hire.
>Terrible comedy/engaging character writing to barely keep you engaged if at all.
>Combat being an abyssmal, broken mess, with equipment quickly making you under or overpowered, useless magic attacks (not enemy magic attacks on your party, those work just fine) and elemental weakness/resistance system (just go for basic attacks, it will always hit higher even for the mages if they were to hit an enemy with it's elemental weakness while the character is buffed), buffs/debuffs are OP as hell all of which you have no real counter for as the silence you can use on old-man berserker is a VERY low accuracy single target silence, the equipment reliance on stat boosting creates a massive difference between enemy difficulty, being absurdly underpowered in early game, to absurdly tanky/overpowered late game.
>Bugs, save the glaring issue I'll save for next, just chewy bread healing the alchemist for 50% instead of the 25% it should as it does for all the other party members
Note, GAME BREAKING BUG: After getting to the ship segment, when you square off against your rival and either win or lose, you are taken to the brig, where some plot unfolds.  A bit into this, you get to the point Sarai, the protagonist, has a character arc and "doesn't know what to do next", however, as soon as this dialogue is advanced, you are brought to the title screen, and forced to resume from the last point saved (note, I have both won and lost the fight against the rival once, and this bug has occured twice), making play beyond this point (save community/fan patches for a fix), impossible.
Overall score and conclusion, 2/10, if you have $2 and have to decide to choose between this game and a bag of potato chips, get the potato chips (unless you desperately want the achievements), it's far more satisfying and a much better use of your time.

Port of a classic War3/SC2/Dota2 arcade map to mobile, ported back to PC. While this contains much of the original combinations, the PC version really needs multiplayer to compete with other titles. That said, it's good if you just want to try different builds without pressure from opponents.

While this game looks extremely basic and seems like it's design was too, the history behind it actually dates back about a decade, starting off as a custom map or mod to Warcraft 3, and since then it's come to both Starcraft 2 and DOTA 2; it's fair to say many great ideas from the custom games made in and through Warcraft 3 are thankfully making their way in one form or another as stand alone titles be it Gem TD, Legion TD, DOTA 2, etc.
That said, many of these games have started out in very basic forms but over time were polished in becoming the legendary titles they are today, and while this game might still be in it's early stages; it is however being made from the original dev crew...
So we can both expect a faithful dedication to it fufilling every expectation in due time of previous known modifications and their awesomeness... as well as a dev crew that won't abandon their game but keep to it untill it's well worth over what you pay for it. Don't let it's current state decieve you, it will most assuredly get better.
While this game is basically an app store game ported to Steam, expect it to grow into something much greater, as for things I'm waiting for besides the obvious such as harder difficulty, better UI and PC controls, bug fixes and polishing/balances, improved animations/graphics, etc.
I also look forward to in the future seeing things like multiplayer and co-op, and hoping further development and experimentation such as maybe a new element like "wind" or "controller support"... These people no doubt will make this game into something worth easily $10 or more, but in it's current state is worth the small price tag it's currently sitting at.
It's expected from devs like this with 10+ years of not being EA games, that they will do their best to make this both a great game on the app store and an even greater game on Steam, and I'm willing to support these devs as much as I have (bought it twice, and in app purchases through the free version on app store) because they intend on not abandoning their title and seeing it through just as they did with all the other iterations of the game.
So, I'm a bit of a fanboy now seeing how the devs have responded to everyone so far on the reviews, and can't help but think that's worth recognition... so buy it! be a supporter to the WC3 legends, be a supporter of good development, be someone who supports indie stuff/games. :D
TL;DR? Recommended both for a stable build and a promising future... and because I've been waiting for all my favorite WC3 mods to be made... it's fun and lives up to it's price point, though I feel once polished would be a steal buying at current price due to this game's history/other-iterations.

This has slowly but surely, become my favorite controller. It's not perfect but it does everything advertised and more. It is definitely the PC Gamer's controller. I want to make a disclaimer. Do not write a review or write off this controller until you've put some hours into it. You've used traditional controllers for hundreds of hours and it's only right you allow an acclimation period for this one. After passing around 500 hours of use on this I think I'm qualified to write a review for it.
Pros:
- Comfortable
- Lots of buttons
- Even more customization
- Controller profiles on games
- Wireless/Wired operation
- Versatile
- Can play Mouse/Keyboard games and even be used as a mouse/keyboard for other apps
Cons:
- It DOES feel cheap when you first get it. It's not heavy but as I've used it I've started to like that fact
- Can't be used as a "normal" controller outside of steam*
- Batteries can be a pain to remove
* It CAN be used on non steam games. But if you want to use it on like an Emulator, some can't be launched with steam so that's my issue.
My main game time comes from Rocket League but I've played everything from Morrowind to Doom to Cities Skylines on this. You still get the FPS disadvantage (expected) but it's far better because you get the touchpad which is more precise than a second stick.
Overall, I love the Xbox One controller but this is still my favorite. It's also the PERFECT pairing with the Steam Link. Get them both, you'll not regret it.

It is a pretty game, but you see some of the same rooms and hallways and stairs over and over again (I do realize some of this is part of the story) but it does get tedious. The nice visuals are overwhelmed by the convoluted stories and jarring philosophy. Honestly, the game takes itself way too seriously and that detracts from a enjoyable experience that could have been so much more than a 14-year old's ponderings.
If you enjoy reading and interpreting the not-very veiled stories of Jonah, Soloman, Abraham and Jezebel, intertwined with the philosophical basics of postmodern melodrama (skeptical reinterpretations), epistemology (the theory of knowledge), and ontology (the nature of existence) that you learned in high school, then this game is for you.

The Old City: Leviathan is possibly my favourite indie game of all time. The graphics, controls and music are all AAA quality, but even if they weren’t, I’m not sure it would bother me. The heart of this game is it’s willingness to deeply explore the human condition in a way that few other games ever have. From religion and philosophy to the frailty of the human mind, The Old City immerses you in a state of quiet contemplation like I’ve never experienced in any other game.
Sounds pretentious? Well, possibly. And I guess this is Leviathan’s only real shortcoming. It’s not a game for everyone. I’d even argue it’s not a game for most people. If the term ‘walking simulator’ sends a chill down your spine.. Well. Beyond the lush and beautifully realised environments, the game is text heavy. And that’s not even including the optional novella scattered throughout the world. There’s no hand holding to be found, and the game is far more adept at throwing up questions than providing answers. There is no certainty. But as with most things in The Old City, that fits quite nicely.
If you have an interest in religion, philosophy or divergent schools of thought and feel like spending a few days in a beautifully realised world, I can’t recommend this highly enough. The voice acting is brilliant, Atrium Carceri’s soundtrack is stunning, and the entire experience continues to linger with me years after my first playthrough.
It’s worth noting there were numerous concepts and terms referenced in the game I wasn’t initially familiar with. Some Googling didn’t hurt the experience. If anything, it enriched it.

It's kinda cool, I guess. The little that it actually does is really well done. Minimal interaction, like a Myst without puzzles that you just kinda walk through. Some of it is a little creepy, but it's not quite horror. A lot of it is vaguely existential and depressing but in such an impersonal and emotionless way that it's not even nicely melancholy. It's kinda metaphorical and referential, again like an artsy friend who just read A Book and wants to make sure you know it.
Maybe it's deep - some of it sounds like it could mean something. By the end I was definitely ready tp set sail for a new adventure - I guess that's the point; SPOILERS: by the end of the game, the truth doesn't really matter anymore because the important thing is that you'lre stagnating and you need something new.
You could just skip playing the game and play something else new instead. Same result, less protracted backstory.

The current version of the game (played in this review) is a mobile port of the game (which means it was made available on PC platforms but is the exact same as the mobile/tablet app). On the phone I found it a bit too fiddly as the screen is smaller but still entertaining, it works very well on tablet.
The game itself comes from an established history of success in both the Starcraft 2 Arcade and DOTA2 as games within games. I will now break it down into pros/cons/summary.
Pros:
- It's got a multiplayer scoreboard which is great for trying to beat the others, finding the best combination of towers.
- It's simple to play and understand.
- It's cheap. Seriously, for the kind of entertainment you get thinking of different tower combinations and then trying to put it all in the correct order so you can get a high score it has tonnes of hours play time.
Cons:
- It's literally the mobile version, no changes.
- It's limited to 1680x1050 when windowed which means that due to being a port the buttons and graphical interface seems a bit 'IN-YOUR-FACE', ALL UP IN YOUR FACE WITH THE HUGE BUTTONS.
- No mulitplayer. Other versions of the game on Starcraft 2 or DOTA2 had the option for multiplayer. It was nice to have someone there with you so you can laugh at their demise. Not having that reduces it's replayability.
- Tower descriptions require you to hover over the icons individually to get stats and descriptions. On PC this would be better served if they were in a different format (top to bottom) or in a spreadsheet system due to the large monitor being able to display more information.
- Selecting squares to place towers requires selection then de-selection which can lead to accidentally buying many towers at the same time without realising it. Or upgrading many towers at the same time. (A little annoying for me, but I could get used to it)
- The Graphical User Interface. I just can't get it out of my mind (or face). It would have been better not being ported as a whole and designed for the PC audience.
Summary:
Yes I would buy it, but on the tablet not on the PC. It's just horrible to see such a wasted opportunity on a lazy port.

So, this is my first review, and I had to write it because this game is FANTASTIC. I am a huge fan of JRPG's, it's what I grew up on, and still continue to play to this day. Tales of Vesperia is my favorite JRPG of all time, but Legend of Heroes has taken a firm number two spot.
What the game does right:
Characters - The characters are diverse and well written. I find myself liking a majority of the characters they introduce, and find myself LOVING a select few. Very few characters are poorly written, and although you may hate a few characters in the beginning, the more you learn about them, the more you understand. With 9 main characters, they do a great job of talking about all of them and showing the type of person they are.
Story - Super enthralling. I played 12 hours straight my first night with this game. I couldn't put it down because I had to keep playing
Music - OH THIS SOUNDTRACK. It's incredible, so pleaseeeeeee play with volume up and don't have anything in the background
Combat - Incredible single-player JRPG strategy combat. I think its unique and enjoyable.
Things this game does wrong:
Traveling - Sadly, this game puts HUGE restrictions on traveling, limiting you to small areas for quite a while, and keeping you stuck in that one area until you finish your job.
Quests - The quests ALWAYS end the same way for each zone, which leads to a lack on unique gameplay and a predictable ending to the chapter.
Overall, 9/10. Buy this game on sale or full price, it is worth it no matter what,

Soooo with the Christmas holidays, I was able to sit down and put  in (easily) 100+hours into this game just over the past two weeks - completing it just today.  I've played Legends of Heroes: Tails in the Sky 1 & 2 (SC) -  and both of those were great games in my opinion.... but the experience of playing Trails of Cold Steel is on a whole other level - I think probably due to the graphics and voice acting.  I found the experience to be very immersive - and the characters, relations and writing were amazing.
The only caveats that I'll point out are that like most of the JRPGS that I've played, the story in this is pretty linear - and some of the story elements may at times require to suspend your disbelief or overlook details (but as someone who is usually fairly critical, I'll be the first to admit that the enjoyment of this game made it easy to do so...).
I'd wholeheartedly recommend purchasing this game and treating yourself to a very enjoyable "experience"  - though be prepared to invest a substantial amount of your time to complete it. (I purchased and played through the game over the holidays and literally played well over 100+ hours over two weeks - and that was on "Easy" as I wanted to focus on the story).
Good luck and have fun!

Now when I first found this in my inventory after pre-ordering FM16 I thought it was going to be a silly fan project but it turns out its much more than that. It’s a very interesting documentary that even includes real managers such as former Manchester United legend Ole Gunnar Solskjær and how he uses it to scout players and create tactics using the game, there’s also cameos from professional players such as Tottenham’s
Andros Townsend and Will Hughes who play the game to waste time on trips and joke about buying themselves on their saves. You can also learn about some of the history of the game like when they originally had the idea way back then and pitched it to Electronic Arts but they declined as they felt this game wouldn't succeed and how Sega bought the rights to the game and how the developers transitioned from Championship Manager to Football Manager and took the engine with them, It also talks about the tech in the game and how you needed a lot of imagination back then since what was happening was only written as text and then the graphics evolved from dots to 3D graphics. It also talks about the transition from handmade animations to motion capture after the transition to 3d and shows you how motion capture works with some AFC Wimbledon players. One of my favorite topics is probably the large database and how many clubs use it due to the large number of people that scout and get information for Sports Interactive games. One topic that many long time Football manager players might enjoy is about some of the In-game legends such as Freddy adu and how some of them were fan favorites in the game but haven't had the same success in real life.
This is a brilliant documentary with a lot of variety that all types of FM fans will enjoy. It’s very good for a 70 minute documentary and it has excellent flow and transition. There’s a great variety of people getting interviewed such as players of the game, developers, players, commentators, scouts and even professional football managers! What's great about this documentary is that it’s good enough to get people who have never played the game interested but there's also some very interesting information for hardcore fans and I feel many of the experiences shared by the fans can be relatable to hardcore fans though some moments are too cringe worthy and forced. The most wonderful thing about this documentary is how it’s able to connect the game to many real life experiences. There’s a fan who plays with a national team in Europe and one day travels there with his wife to watch a 2nd division game, to former football manager Alex McLeish of Glasgow Rangers, inquiring Barcelona if he could get Lionel Messi on loan because his son saw his stats in Football Manager and told him "This youngster will become the greatest player in the world" and almost ended up with current Barcelona captain Iniesta! It's these stories that make it charming and relate-able to many fans.
So in short, you should definitely looks into this if you're a FM fan as it’s a brilliant insight on the game and its history. If you haven't played it before but want to get into it, it’s a wonderful way to learn about the game and its community and how it's even used by many professionals in the sport. The price is a bit too high in my opinion but you can get it for free if you pre-order FM16 but if you aren't planning to pre-order it I’d recommend waiting as I feel it’s a little high.

The Old City falls squarely into the genre of “walking simulator” - the first-person, story-driven, exploration-based style popularized by the likes of Gone Home, Dear Esther, and The Stanley Parable. But while it delivers some beautiful environments to gawk at, it simply doesn’t deliver on the story.
A plot synopsis? Well, the game is set in a desolate, abandoned city. Throughout, you read diary entries by someone named Jonah, heavily alluding to the Biblical story of Jonah and the whale. There are references to some sort of past apocalypse, and the survivors splitting into three camps, overseen (I think?) by a group called the Minotaurs. And throughout, you hear unbearably pretentious narration from your unseen protagonist, musing on the nature of existence and so forth. Oh, and tying into the story of Jonah, there’s also a giant whale involved (the titular Leviathan), which probably doesn’t literally exist but maybe I’m wrong. I don’t really care.
And that’s why it’s so hard to recommend this game: I don’t care about any of it. There’s simply no human, relatable element to the story, like piecing together your sister’s journey of self-discovery in Gone Home. All this game has to offer are pretentious philosophical musings and frankly boring exposition dumps, mixed with a dose of largely unsuccessful mind♥♥♥♥ery (remember the whale I mentioned)?
It sure is pretty, though.

Mostly good!  If you prefer a controller to a mouse and keyboard, I'd recommend this with a few suggestions to tweak.
First, BUTTONS.  I honestly just spent a while (too long) clicking all the buttons and enjoying the little power-up jingle I could customize.  Sitting in my hands, it's a little on the big side, so reaching the ABXY buttons will take some muscle training before it's committed to memory.  I can see this being very handy if paired with something like Joy-to-Key since there are more programming options available than on a standard PC controller.
Second, the haptic feedback.  It's weird to feel for sure, but oddly pleasing?  Maybe it's a kind of ASMR thing, but I dunno because I don't have a degree in that field to say for (more) certain.  It's good, though, since it gives a more solid connection between your brain and the controller without that weird blank space in between because you're moving your finger over a smooth surface.
My biggest gripe has to be the right-hand trackpad.  The placement right above the buttons feels awkward after being used to an 360 controller (again, I'll probably get used to it with more playtime).  Something I wish was an option was the ability to make a deadzone on the outer edge of the trackpad; already had a few instances of reaching for the buttons, only to have the edge of my thumb JUST graze the trackpad and have my field of view careen to the side.
Gripe part 2; the default setting has you swipe your finger over the circle like a mouse.  Fun for navigating a menu or surfing the web, not fun for Skyrim, ESPECIALLY LOCKPICKING.  After looking up a template and spending about 2 hours going through the settings (there are many), I think I've made a satisfying simulacra for a joystick without having a physical stick.
I can post a pair of screenshots of my settings if requested; I'm aware this won't be great for everyone, but heck, it's a starting point.  If anything, I wish this would be the default (or at least a secondary default) for that right pad.
I could give a solid recommendation to controller-users, like I said.  If you prefer mouse and keyboard, not only would I be less likely to suggest it, but let's be honest and say you would be better off just investing in a nice gaming mouse and keyboard.  For folks like me, though, that can't comfortably use a keyboard (cough-laptop-cough), I'd say give it a shot!  Maybe wait until a sale like I did to get it at a discount if you're not sure.  (it comes in a snazzy box)

I've had the steam controller for around 2 weeks now and I've come to the conclusion that it's the best gamepad style controller I've ever used and this includes console controllers going all the way back to before the original NES.
The thing about the steam controller is that it's sort of deceptive in just how good it is when you first encounter it. The packaging and the controller design (from an aesthetics point of view) are not particularly special. There are even some minor annoyances with it like the fact that it doesn't come with a rechargeable battery pack (although the battery life is incredible; haven't had to change them yet), or that the handles are perhaps a tad too thick, or that the glossy plastic on the controller face is perhaps not the best choice, or even that the plastic materials in general feel a little on the cheap side.
But once you get to using it, and once you've become accustomed to the interface, it's just on another level entirely compared to other controllers like the xbox one or ps4.
The reason for this is the accuracy that is afforded by using the touchpads in combination with the built-in gyroscope for an additional axis of control. It's so good that, when properly configured, it is actually competitive with a high quality mouse and keyboard combo for FPS games.
Before trying the controller, when I'd see people talk about that I thought it was mostly a gimmick. Even after trying it for like the first 15 minutes I really wasn't sure it was true. But after a few hours I changed my mind. I was playing through DOOM and I realized that after a few hours I was able to control the camera just as accurate as I had with a mouse and it felt really natural. Things like jumping from platform to platform while and spinning the camera 180 degrees and getting mid-air headshots just worked. I could never get that kind of accuracy with a standard gamepad.
Then there's the customizability which is just phenomenal. Valve has opened a lot of this up to other controllers now so it's perhaps not as special of a thing as it was originally, but I feel that the flexibility is more important for the steam controller than other standard gamepads just due to the extreme versatility of the trackpad design.
Specifically, the trackpads allow the steam controller to be usable for games which just aren't designed for gamepads originally. Almost anything that would normally require a mouse can probably be adapted to suit the controller with a proper configuration. And due to the haptic motors in the controller, the trackpads can be made to actually feel a lot like trackballs when you slide your thumb across them. So it still feels pretty natural, especially if you've ever used a trackball device.
There's more I could say about this thing but I think that's probably enough. It really is great. It's not perfect of course, and I would like to see a future version that was a bit slimmer and with a rechargeable design, but it's still better than the alternatives by a huge margin in my mind.
I see that there's a lot of mixed feelings about the controller in general, which I honestly find a little bit surprising. My impression is that perhaps not everyone is able or willing to adapt to the different feeling of using this type of interface versus more standard gamepad designs. I think some people try it, get a little bit frustrated, and then write it off before they have a chance to really figure it out.
I've seen one person describe their very first experience with the controller (playing counterstrike; not a good first choice IMO) as making them feel "helpless" compared to what they were used to. Don't expect to be perfectly proficient with this thing on the very first try and realize you need to pay attention to configurations. Like I said, it takes some getting used to.
But it's so worth it. In fact, I often prefer playing on this thing instead of keyboard and mouse just because it's more comfortable for me to sit on the couch after a long day rather than spending more time at the desk. Valve nailed it in that regard.
If you need a gamepad and you want something that is precise and usable for genres likes FPS then give this a try.

The Tribes games are still unmatched in terms of movement, and high-speed combat.
It's hard to describe the feeling of it, but I'll try.
Every downslope is your friend, if you come in at the right angle you can increase your precious speed.
Rocks, trees, sudden gullies are your enemies, always an inch or two away from a broken ankle or 'SPLAT'.
Health is speed. Every perfectly-placed disc- or nitron-jump can give you a boost of acceleration, but costing a chunk of your limited health pool. Spend your health early and give it time to recharge as you traverse the battlefield.
Now, you gotta go fast, you start your run, give a "VFF" for good measure, and tell your friends you are 30 seconds out.
Leap, Jetpack, up, up, up, good.
Drop. Feather the jets a tiny fraction, and...
Skiing, picking up speed, now!
First disc aimed at feet, acceleration surging out of control, now airborne and about to hit the....
Second disc, bouncing off a mountain peak and soaring off into the sky at full jetpack and - 5 HP - guess that was cutting it close.
No time to think about that, start curving around to hit that slope at just the right direction... "5 seconds to flag!"
and managed to NOT break an ankle this time, that's good, HP is regenerating now, and full, just in time for the...
Final nitron, lined up just right for the perfect flag grab, coming in at... 420 KPH
VFF, VFF, VFF!!!
PROS: Gotta go fast. Meaningful skill-based high speed combat.
CONS: Game got run into the ground by developers, despite their final efforts to repair the damage, it was too little too late. RIP meaningful skill-based high speed combat.
Maybe someday...

This game is so amazing I legit feel guilty for buying during the winter sale. Absolutely worth price.
I'll start off with the good then hit up the couple of slightly more annoying bits at the end
The good:
-The amount of effort that must have gone in to giving every single NPC new locations and new dialogue during every single transition from morning to noon to night must have been staggering. No NPC will ever tell you the same thing twice if the time of day has changed. From the annoying Patrick Hyarms to the janitor. They all move throughout the day with new lines each and every time. Makes talking to NPC's in the game amazing. (Talk to Beryl or vivi whenever you can for good laughs.)
-World building is nuts as well in this game. Every chapter you visit a new location and find out more and more about political climate of the hot mess of a country that is Erebonia. The zones themselves range from snoozer to oh♥♥♥♥♥♥I wouldn't mind living here. Nord is gorgeous with great music, legram is hauntingly beautiful little town.
-The ending. Yeah thats right. I'm putting this under good. I won't spoil anything. But anyone who Played FC and had to wait for SC knows exactly what kind of cliffhanger falcom like to give it's fans. If you end the game with anything other then "WHERE THE ♥♥♥♥ IS THE REST OF THIS GAME" you're weird. but its in a good way. You will spend the next 3 days of your life googling "WHEN DOES TRAILS OF COLD STEEL 2 RELEASE ON PC" in all caps, of course. Love you folks at XSEED!
-So many other good points to this game. It's a slow burner. Don't rush things even when you get impatient, you will cheat yourselves out of so many little breadcrumbs. Take your time and enjoy the ride. It's worth it.
The barely bad:
-Voiced parts of the game can be a bit patchy at times. One scene will be fully voiced followed by the next being not. Not too big a deal though and takes very little away from an otherwise amazing game.
-The way they handle character movement during cutscenes can be a little underwhelming at times. Outside of a few headpats and a couple other instances, everyone stands the same or poses the same during scenes making things feel a little robotic at times. I will say you will only notice this for the first few hours or so before you get used to it and no longer care. Given the enormity of the game and the smallish size of the company that makes the game however this totally gets a pass in my book.

I'm not sure why people are so negative on the forums about this documentary, because it's quite good. To be clear; this is not some crappy fan project, it is very well shot, has good narration and has been edited professionally. If you are complaining about the price, that's fair. But I will get to that later.
At first I thought this would be a documentary about fans and their experiences with Football Manager. Turns out it's about
more than that. It is about pretty much everything regarding the game. From actual football managers (like Ole Gunnar Solskjær and Demetrio Albertini) using data from the game to scout players and create tactics, football players (like Andros Townsend and Will Hughes) who play the game and desperately try to buy themselves. It's about how the developers had to transition from Championship Manager to Football Manager, how Electronic Arts rejected their initial pitch for Championship Manager.  It's about the motion capture involved with the game now it features a 3D engine, how there are a lot of people from all over the world working for Sports Interactive to help them put data in the game. It's about hidden gems in the older FM games and how their actual real life career turned out. I can go on and on, but you get the idea.
Yes! I really like how much variety there is in this documentary. They never get stuck on one subject and it's got a nice flow. For a 70 minutes long documentary I think that's quite impressive. It also has a nice variety in the people getting interviewed. There's the fans obviously, but also football players, commentators, developers, researchers, etc. This documentary can be watched by people who don't know anything about Football Manager while still being interesting enough for the hardcore fans. It won't bury you in statistics, but the experiences the fans share will be very recognizable for people who play the game. Talking about the fans, I have to say there are some cringeworthy scenes from people supposedly playing the game and reacting to it which seem a little exaggerated and feel forced. What I like most about the documentary is the stories people share and how it all connects to Football Manager. From a guy who one day decides to start playing with a Bulgarian squad and ends up going there on his honeymoon, to Alex Mcleish asking Barcelona if he could loan Messi when he was coach at Rangers at 2002 because his son saw his stats in Football Manager (and almost ending up with Andrés Iniesta!). It's all these stories that give it character and make it worth watching. It's very recognizable for me personally as well. It reminds me of the time my friend was really into Football Manager. He was always playing with Yeovil Town, he knew all the players and was leading them to the Premier League each year. When I was on holiday in England I decided to go and visit Yeovil and was teasing him about it, posting pictures and such. He couldn't be more jealous. It's amazing how a simple videogame can help create all these great experiences.
If you're a Football Manager fan, you should buy this. It gives you a great insight in your favorite game and it might surprise you along the way. You might be thinking that the price is too high right now and I would agree. I bought it during the launch sale with a 30% discount which I think is worth it, but I don't think it's worth the full price. I would have liked to see a big discount for people who own a Football Manager game on Steam to give something back to the loyal fans, which there are a lot of. Ultimately it's up to you if you think it's worth it.

Hunter's Grimm is a typical RPG Maker game that claims inspiration from a slew of JRPGs that tug at your heartstrings and make you wish for the days where you stayed up late playing Dragon Warrior or Chrono Trigger.
The problem is, it is nothing like any of the games it wants to take inspiration from, the sole thing they have in common is the fact that they're old school RPGs. Hunter's Grimm has a lot of problems, but I'll begin by listing the few positives it does have.
Unlike a lot of RPG Maker games, the assets feel like they have a different touch to them. Unless it's the actual game interface, it feels like some work was put into either having someone else create the assets, or the dev found non-default assets to make their game. The base story of the game is not a bad story, I enjoyed the "detective work" in some quests.
The issues with this game lie with it's dialogue, interface, and a few "oopsies" that were never ironed out. Your quest begins and it feels fairly obvious where to go. You are not introduced to a world map until you are struggling to find your second quest, which your quest log explains is "north of your manor". Since there was no world map before, I figured I would just try to go north outside of the manor, as the quest said. It didn't work, you have to go south, completely out of the manor's map to get onto the world map. On the world map, towns are not marked as FF-esque town sprites, instead you have half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥sparkles showing you where to go. The sparkles in lieu of sprites are embarrassing in any RPG Maker game, because I know how easy it is to make a world map on there, no clue why the developer didn't take a couple seconds to make the world map aesthetically pleasing.
After the second quest line, you are told to go to another town, Omber or something (everything in this game gets forgettable after the first fifteen minutes) - on the way to this town, you are introduced to a mountain maze. The level design is completely shoddy and angered me so much that after I got to Omber, I had to put the game down. It's not that it was hard, it was tediously long, and on the way there was nothing to look at. There was a patch of the maze that was literally nothing but grass, and this part can go on for up to 15-20 minutes if you have trouble navigating the maze. It was poorly developed and probably will reduce you to a ragequitting mess.
Oh yeah, there are enemy battles. They are initiated a-la Earthbound style, except the enemies are much slower on here and you can easily ignore them. I fought three enemies in the entire time I played - two quest battles, and the first monster I encountered. The battles are dull, and the sprites don't mash up with what you actually fight, so the ghost you have to fight in a quest turns out to be a headless masquerade villain?? It's just typical, default RPG Maker combat with nothing added in to spice you up.
Overall, an okay story and cohesive graphical design (except the fact that your main heroine's portrait looks absolutely nothing like her sprite) doesn't save this game from being a mess in what matters, the gameplay. The towns become forgettable as you begin to realize everything looks and feels the same. As the towns feel the same and battles get boring, you realize you're not playing a Square classic, or even a good RPG Maker indie like labyronia - instead, it feels like you're playing your younger sibling's RPG Maker creation and it loses it's appeal quickly. Sadly, Hunter's Grimm is a predictable, "Grimm" experience.

Hunter's Grimm is an old-school RPG, which in my shallow game history is closest to be compared to Final Fantasy 4 in both its good aspects, and bad. You're inevitably going to fight
, just because you're wanting to teach him a lesson on how to name himself, because
is surely not to be taken seriously.
Realistically,
kicked a lot of♥♥♥♥♥back in the day, but when he eventually got beaten, the four Hokage separated his armor in the four corners of their evidently flat world. I'm assuming, somehow, the armor got reunited, and these poor teenagers you'll be dropping in the story as, will have to try and de-throne the Emperor. It's worth nothing that the Sarai and Nicholas' parents both went to the store a year ago for milk and haven't been seen since. Unfortunate.
A fun fact, also, is that this game was released back in October of 2013 by a different developer. The publisher and developer acknowledged on the community board that this is an updated re-release featuring new art and some other stuff. You can still find the older version of this game, albeit much more expensive, on some corners of the Internet.
Enough of the formal introductions, let's see the good, the bad, and the score.
: For coming straight out of RPG Maker, almost four years ago this year, the updated character and monster arts are pretty decent. This is including the sprites. However, the title screen is horrendous.
: In my Steam Redlight time, I always find games that have either an unfitting sound-track, no sound-track at all, or something that could only be related to drinking bleach, but with your ears. This game is unique in the way that I didn't want to take a sander to my ears after a reasonable period of time.
: If you've played one RPG Maker game, you've played quite a few of them. This game doesn't introduce any cool mechanics or core competencies, and thus the gameplay is bland and uneventful. Not only this, but the game doesn't share certain information. For example. there's a part in the game where to continue, your character has to jump over a river. There's no indication that you know your character can do this, and they haven't done this in the past. You likely wouldn't find this out until you decided to walk around and press the action button on every square pixel in every cardinal direction, leaving a frustrating experience for players.
Also, I paid little to no attention to the battles. I have a tendency to grind through each mob that I can see just so I don't risk falling behind, and because of that, all mobs I encountered I eventually found myself browsing my phone while tapping the action button repeatedly. Perhaps my own fault, but there was simply no need for any additional mechanics or attention.
: RPGs are generally lore-rich adventures, but I found this game's universe to be pretty bland. The characters were intolerable due to upholding their tropes and the story-writer's love to play a joke out until it's dead. I couldn't be arsed to play the game past my initial 3.5 hour time limit I gave myself to decide if I wanted to play it, and because it couldn't keep my interest, I stopped.
: I don't particularly care for achievements, but I was able to get all 695 by leaving my game on for an extra hour after I decided to stop playing. I did it as a test to see if it actually happened, and it did. So if you decide you want to pay $2.00 for 695 achievements, here you go.

First thing's first. This is not truly a game, more of an atmospheric, immersive experience. There's minimal interaction.
Also, if you don't have a good grasp of philosophy and the like, you may want to move on. It goes into some fairly deep territory into the nature of belief and being human. There's a lot of imagery you'll miss if you're not interested in this sort of content.
If you love this sort of stuff, you'll also love this. If you like nice aesthetics, this is also good. If you're after doing something besides enjoy an environment and read a ton of text on the walls, maybe skip. This is indeed a niche game and it will not appeal to everyone.
But, for the record, I really enjoyed it. I also think that it's a very professionally done game. My only quibbles were occasionally getting stuck on things when I was walking. The walking is also somewhat slow but you *can* run by holding down SHIFT.
It's also fairly short, but it packs a lot of stuff into its time. It feels a lot longer somehow.

TLDR:
An atmospheric, dystopian walking simulator with excellent visuals and decent pacing, held back by an heavily esoteric narrative. But given the modest price, I believe it to be a solid acquisition for the exploration enthusiast.
Review:
Old City: Leviathan is what I'm starting to refer to as a "mood game," in that it's primary purpose appears to be to establish a mood for the user for the purpose of expressing an idea or ideas for consideration. That is, there isn't any real game play here: no puzzles, no combat, no strategy, not even a mystery to solve. You explore what is a fairly linear reality that has the trappings of a story, but is really a vehicle to discuss ideas about existence.
Now, not being a philosophy major, I can't begin to explain the ideas being bandied about here - another review refers to them as "pseudo-philosophy," and I have confess that there were plenty of moments where my eyes started to roll to the back of my head - but I imagine that there are far deeper thinkers than I, who would enjoy digesting the meaty narrative. If you've played the game, "Everyone's Gone to the Rapture," to completion, the I would liken the themes of this game to the narrative of Rapture's final chapter (the observatory area); if you liked that, odds are you'll like this.
For me, the highlight of Leviathan is its visuals, as it's an attractive game. But then, so was Rapture, which I did not recommend except to the hardcore walking sim enthusiast. So what did Leviathan do better? For that I think you have to look at both the level design and the movement mechanics:
- smaller exploration areas per chapter, with a lot of labyrinthine twists and turns that keeps the user from plodding along in a straight line. Even if all you're doing is walking, it is more interactive to be turning and navigating than setting a focus on a point far away and walking straight towards it.
- faster base walking pace and a jog mode for faster travel (although admittedly, the jog mode was barely faster than walking).
- more things to draw the eye while walking, causing you to look this way and that, taking your mind off the actual walking part of the process. I think this also helps the experience feel more like exploring than merely traveling.
I will also allow that I'm a fan of dystopian fantasy and found the surroundings both surreal and visually interesting, which helped keep me immersed.
A couple key flaws you should be aware of:
- there's a LOT of reading in this game. Some of it comes in the form of small notes you find tacked up here and there, but a significant portion of it is a rather lengthy journal that also happens to be very dry and esoteric. To me it felt disruptive to stop playing in favor of trying to struggle through the reading portions, when you're reading the same paragraph two or three times to try to understand what the journalist was trying to say.
- the spoken narrative is of the same dry, esoteric nature, to the point where I had to stop moving and focus on what was being said to have any hope of understanding it (and that's with the subtitles turned on). Now, it could just be that I'm a moron; YMMV. But as a middle-aged player with a post-grad degree in the sciences, I can't imagine your average player is going to do a lot better with it.
- you cannot save progress on demand. Saving is done automatically at the end of each chapter. I found this to be a minor annoyance, since the chapters are small enough that you aren't rushing to catch up to where you left off, but it's a curious design decision nonetheless.
As for value for your money, I bought this at the full-price of $6 and got almost 5.5 hours of gameplay out of it; in my book, that's good value, and superlative value if you can get it half off.

While the game is literally stacked against you, that doesn't actually make it more challenging or interesting.
The basic mechanics are familiar to anyone who has played a TCG before. This particular game uses the "stationary blockers" approach, where you play units that will attack whatever unit is in front of them, or the player if they are unopposed. There is no mulligan and you are entirely at the mercy of the energy cards you draw (slightly mitigated by the fact you can discard a card to draw a replacement each turn).
The UI is weak. Aside from the popup display settings when you start the game, all you can do is adjust the volume. You can only click to view cards when it is your turn to act, which means you may not know what the opponent actually did to cause something to happen. Also, viewing cards tend to get stuck on the screen until blind clicking eventually closes them. A lot of game information could be better displayed, as well as including tooltips to say what given abilities do.

I want to get one thing out of the way first.   This is a beautiful looking game, and it is clear that a lot of work went into polishing the environments and building a stunning world to play in.  Unfortunately, that may be part of its downfall.  As I played through this game, I could not help but get the feeling that the developers wanted to make sure that I knew they put a lot of work into making their game look good.  The first thing that made me think this was that your movement speed seemed very slow, and navigating some of the bigger areas started to become a chore.  This may seem like a small complaint, but as there is no substantial gameplay, walking is front and center.  I know that there are many other games that fit this formula, to the point that there is beginning to be a whole genre of these ‘walking simulators’ but many of those either allow you to move everything along at your own pace by having the story be entirely in context clues, or give you something to keep yourself occupied while the story unfolds.
This is where The Old City seems to fall the hardest.  There is nearly no interaction at all, and none of the story was there to find.  You simply walk through the environments and listen to the narrator piece the story together as you go.  The walking seems to be so slow as to keep you from triggering the next dialog before the current one is complete.  This makes every area seem like a long trudge to get to the next, and while the environments are beautiful to look at, they start to feel boring after you have been walking through it for so long.  The worst part is when it is all said and done, this can hurt the story’s delivery.  I have no doubt that the developers have crafted a wonderful and interesting story for this game, but sadly in my case, I don’t remember any of it.  I have played through the entire game, and cannot recall any of the story. All I can remember is how the slow and frankly boring pace made me want the game to be over, and when it finally was, I did not want to play it again.
This game has a lot of potential and it is clear that the developers put a lot of care into the environments and story, but it is pacing and lack of player engagement leave the overall experience boring and forgettable.   This is only more apparent when other similar games such as Gone Home, Only If, and Layers of Fear have shown that even with virtually no interactivity a game can still be engaging and well-paced to deliver a good story.
