There's a saying in creative writing circles: show, don't tell. With the obvious exception of interactive novels and text adventures, which one evidently enters into expecting truckloads of reading, the "show, don't tell" principle surely applies all the more to video games. Unless you're the makers of The Old City: Leviathan, who have chosen to scatter not just bog-standard "notes" but entire SHORT STORIES throughout their game! The good news for those of us who DON'T wish to stop playing for a full twenty minutes to read backstory is that the voice-over narrative and shorter notes posted intermittently on the walls provide enough context for us to follow the story, which, as it turns out, is a pretty good one indeed.
Tonally and narrative-wise, I'm actually tempted to compare it to the slightly superior Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs, a game which took an awful beating over its minimal mechanics but excelled - in my opinion, at least - in the area of storytelling. The Old City and Machine certainly share a very nihilistic, almost borderline misanthropic view of humanity: feel-good this ain't, so if you're only into the more "relaxing" end of the "walking simulator" spectrum, might be best to give this one a miss (though it does harbour a tiny bit of hope towards the end). That said, it's a great game for those of you who enjoy a dark atmosphere without being constantly harassed by monsters and other dangers, as there's none of that here. Just reflections on the monstrous nature of humankind, and the horrible things we are all-too-capable of.
Technically-speaking, it's a minor gem. The sound design and voice acting are very good, and the graphics are simply luscious, with some quite gob-smacking sights on offer. Presuming this is the debut of PostMod Softworks (terrible name!), it's quite the debut indeed.
Strongly recommended to all "walking simulator" fans, especially those who are up for a bit of reading; though as I said above, it is kinda optional. The atmosphere alone is worth the price of admission, and six bucks is a pretty small asking price for what you're getting here. I'd also recommend this to anyone who's been curious about the whole "walking simulator" phenomenon: you could do far, far worse than to start here, as this is by far one of the best specimens of the genre to date. Sure, it's a tad pretentious, but I'll take that over lack of ambition any day.
Full kudos to the devs for their unashamed effort to make not just a game, but a fully-fledged work of "art". They pretty much pulled it off, too.
Verdict: 9/10.
(PS You know, I enjoyed this game so much by the end that I think I may put aside the time to read all those super-long passages on a second playthrough. I suspect they may be worth it. But I still say it's questionable video game design to plonk a twenty minute read in the player's lap in the first fifteen minutes of play, haha.)

Excellent environment and engrossing story. Definitely not a game for everyone, but I enjoyed it. The game delivers its narrative exceedingly well, given the lack of actual characters with which to intereact in real time. Solomon's notes can be a little long to read, but not worse than the volumes of lore you'd find in games like Skyrim. I'd consider it a feat that the devs managed to make a game where it made some sense that there are people wandering around a post-calamity sort of place while discussing philosophy. I can mostly empathize with the narrator's concluding thoughts. The philosophical ideas are pretty straight forward. Doesn't delve too deeply into jargon, and sticks with issues that many people have, no doubt, grappled with at least a little during their lives (I hope). I can best describe this as an existential crisis in game form. Can't say I think about the metaphysical much these days. Though the game's heavy on ideas, the reoccurring characters were appropriately developed. I can't help but feel bad for Solomon and Belle.
According to the website, this is intended to be the first of a series of games. I hope that the devs successfully continue the series, and we can eventually explore the Old City!

THIS IS WHERE IT ALL STARTS!
If you want to start making games in Unity with no prior knowledge this is where you should start.
Not only does GTGD S1 teach the basics of unity but it also teaches you a way to order your games when building them.
(eg. enabling multiplayer then applying damage to enemy players).
The game you end up with at the end is pretty good (depending on how you change it). You might even get to play with friends and have fun with it (I know I did).
Please note GTGD is a series of videos and unity project files and Unity scripts. It's not a game creation tool like RPGmaker or GameMaker.
At my pace it took me about a month to make (there's about 30 videos and I was doing about 1 a day).
But one thing this game gave me is memories.
I will never forget the pain I suffered when trying to hide the mouse cursor through scripting and the ♥♥♥♥ing amazing feeling I had when it finally worked.
And most of all I will never forget fighting back the tears as I finally got my friends to play this game. One thought went through my head that day. "They're playing a game I made!" "They're playing my game!" "They played MY game!" "They downloaded my game".
Or maybe that's just me.
Remember
You are more than a gamer.

Let me just first state that I tried very very hard to give this a recommendation but I just can't. As I play and discuss the game more, I will try to give it a recommendation.
Pros:

Mediocre:
~The Orcs are inconsistently consistent. It appears that they will sometimes swing at you from say 6 pixels away and sometimes only when you're 4 pixels away. I don't know if this was meant to be but it makes it much more difficult to defeat them.
~The GUI could be a little more developed
~Level design. Somewhat unique, but they can also be long and repetitive.
~The story is alright, just enough to make it enjoyable IMO but could be more.
Cons:
-Soundtrack ;( gets repetitive and very basic.. but it's so-so
-Not a lot of "menu" type options, more focused on gameplay
-When you die, for example, it instantly respawns you at the start with no message, I think at least something would be nice
-Archers and Wizards-- unfortunately, these two will kill you before you can even see them. What I mean by this is say you're jumping up a cliff- as soon as you get to the top, an archer will one shot you. With Wizards, the same situation sometimes happens or oftentimes they'll kill you when you havent even seen one on the screen yet. Very annoying when you're trying to progress long levels.
-Inconsistent knockback as well as some other things.. you'll hit an archer back and sometimes you can instantly swing again and kill it, other times you have to move towards it and swing again. This results in you inconsistently getting hit in this manner.
-Several hitboxes are not precise. Additionally, sometimes your character will be floating above a block or your feet halfway into the block.
-The aforementioned cons just make it frustrating to play overall without it appearing to be simply another "challenge" :/
-I would like to see some more items/weapons/powerups
-It seems sort of like an Early Access game, or even possibly a Flash game in this state.
---Update: I accidentally pressed New Game instead of Load Game once and it reset all my progress. No confirmation or multiple saves? That's a big problem, especially when the game launches on the "New Game" menu option.---
///In Conclusion///
This game definitely has potential but I'd really like to see more out of it.
A few things on these lists could be intentional to make the game harder, simpler, etc. by the Dev, but I just can't leave a recommendation. I will continue playing it and seeing if I like it more, I believe I'm about halfway through. I hate to leave negative reviews, and this is my first, so hopefully something the developer does will change my mind. Clarifications on anything from the Dev would help as well.
Well, this is a very long review for a $0.49 game. Thanks for reading and I hope I was helpful!
Edit: After accidentally pressing A on my controller twice when launching, it reset all my progress. That's pretty bad, so I don't feel bad leaving a negative review anymore.

The Steam Controller; to grab one, or to pass on?
Whilst initially disheartened by the lack of out of the box, plug and play Xinput drivers; What you do get in terms of hardware and customisation with a steam controller is very generous, and most definately unrivaled on the PC platform. Sure, it's certainly not for Tech illiterates, but with some time, patience and config tweaking; I was able to run everything i would usually play rather nicely with just this one device (Regardless of whether I'd usually play Mouse/KBD or Gamepad). Moreover, if you point steam to an emulator, or any other non-steam game or application, you can use all of it's tweakable features just as easily, creating per game controller configurations for every single entry in your library.
What you get;
Features include 2 touchpads (each with 8 way directional input, five bindable physical buttons. configurable deadzones and a seperate bind inside of said deadzone! w/ optional touch sensative controls and the choice for the right pad to act as either a mouse cursor or xinput right stick), 2 Bumpers, 2 triggers (soft andd full depress as optional seperate bindings), an analogue stick, standardized xbox style face buttons, 2 Rear grips (additional physical buttons), Gyro / Accelerometer (perfect for games that can utilise motion input, or even those that don't!) and adjustable Haptic (vibration) feedback per control element, per profile.

Overview;
Whilst any other standard xbox controller is instantly supported by most of Steam's more reputable games; The Steam Controller is compatible with ANYTHING that you chose to run via steam, whether that's an emulator, a game you may have on UPlay, Origin or battlenet, or a game with no controller support at all.
Now I have to be honest, I do big up Vavle wherever possible and I already own a number of wired and wireless xbox & xbo controllers for my pc; but the fact that i can navigate my desktop, play mouse / kbd games, play Xinput Games and play my Wii / Wiiu games (with motion controls!) on one controller., It blows my mind and it's genuinely totally incredible.
'One Device for any and every game'
What an ambitious goal, and the Steam Controller truly delivers.
~ Rob Lefevre  / 31/12/17

Without a doubt, the Steam Controller is the best controller out there. Sure, it will take a lot of getting used to but when you really nail the button placement and the touchpad down, it is very satisfying to use and is a lot of fun! The controller has your generic A, X, B, Y buttons like on most controllers, a massive D-Pad, a Steam Home button for Big Picture Mode, a Start and Back button and four triggers at the top, and there are also two paddles on the back which you can bind to an action in game! Strangely enough, no second stick. This is because the Steam Controller uses a touchpad for camera movement, which is actually a lot better than it sounds! The Steam Controller comes in a box that also comes with a Wireless USB and two batteries for Wireless gaming! You put the batteries in by sliding the little slider-thing on the bottom of the controller, inbetween the two handgrips, and putting the batteries in the sides. There is also a carrying case that you pay another $20 for but it doesn't seem very useful as you already have a box that's portable enough. It is also compatible with, I believe, every game on Steam, (take this with a grain of salt, I'm not 100% sure if it is) all with their own control scheme so you don'ty have to mess around with custom configs! Not to mention that it is frequently on sale!
The Steam Controller is a great purchase if you need a good controller, if you can tolerate the steep learning curve. It's worked wonders in every game that I have tested it in, and is often on sale making the purchase even more tempting! I love this controller to bits, think about buying it!

I went into The Legend of Heroes: Trails of Cold Steel without expectations, and left with it as one of my favorite games of all time. This game sucked me in and didn't let go for over 80 hours. I've never really clicked with a JRPG before, though I am a pretty avid anime/manga fan, so finally finding my game in the genre is amazing.
Frankly speaking, The Legend of Heroes: Trails of Cold Steel is a steal at $40, the sheer volume of quality gameplay and story you're getting for your money blows most Western RPGs out of the water. It isn't an amazing looking game (it was originally made for the PS3 and PS Vita, after all), but the graphics are consistent and the game runs at a buttery-smooth 60 FPS.
The plot slowly unfurls to reveal one of the most intriguing video game storylines I've ever had the pleasure of playing. The characters are all memorable and rapidly endear themselves to the player, while shadowy political entities duke it out behind the scenes and create more than a little mystery. There are two other released Trails of Cold Steel games that are direct sequels to this, and another one is on the way - II should be on Steam by mid-2018, while III may take much longer; IV will release in Japan in Fall 2018 so that game may not show up in the West until 2020. You should be prepared for the long haul with this series.

This would best be summarized as a classical strategy game that belongs in the 90s. It's pretty amusing. It kept me entertained for 4.5 hours. It's decent if you're looking to buy this for under $5.00 USD. It's certainly not worth much more. It's a slight bit outdated.
Starting off, you make a selection of 3 possible races, 4 magical paths, 3 map choices, any start location desired, and a lot of buildings to choose from.
Each unit has an upkeep. You either build toward military or economy. Early game I focused on defensive builds, spammed range units. Mid game, focus economy and magic. Late game, military and rush the enemy.
Want to break the game and win a lot? Just get archers or wizards. Upgrade them for better range. They can win against all melee units in total disregard of being outnumbered 2 to 1. They will suffer against cavalries. The AI will run past your frontline to hit your archers and wizards first. Simply sit your own cavalry or melee units next to your flanks and counter-attack the enemy or defend the middle of the map as your range units chip away at the enemy.
The rebellions will become so hazardous that even the AI struggles to keep the peace. I simply just held key choke points, controlled a large chunk of land at a time, and just blitz'd the life out of the enemy. You don't need to control every single area to win the game. Sack the enemy, and vacate the area. When that stack is weakened from blitz tactics, split them into single units and attack every surrounding territory, some of which will be empty if AI owned. Guerilla and Blitz tactics combined makes winning easy.
Remember children... No matter what strategy game you play... Either Run and Shoot or Blitz :)

Decently enjoyable game which seems to be a modern attempt to ape Master of Magic.  While the art itself is well-made, it seems largely to be poorly implemented.  Lack of visibility options (colorblind, heavy region borders, etc.) would be appreciated, but it's servicible without them.  Nothing particularly poor in the game, but too, nothing that's exciting.
Some quality of life and ease-of-use methods would be nice, such as universal development queues (setting up a "basic" method for all towns to follow after having at least X in the coffers, and similar), and some automation ability therein.  I'd also love to have arrows on mouse-over in-battle so I can tell which way a unit is facing for flanking.
The AI does seem to  be somewhat aggressive, overall, but unit-wise in combat it loses match-ups that it shouldn't, which is frustrating at higher levels.  Would also like to note that kiting a group of melee units with a horseman and Wrack wins battles, and probably shouldn't; perhaps the AI should handle disenchanting better?  Or lean more towards having balanced units (more healers/rangers)?
I picked up the game for $0.13 USD, and it's certainly worth more than that, at the least.  Would love to see it pick up some nuance, and correct typos (such as "Thorn" instead of "Throne" in the ending text), and the like.  A bit more development or care and I'd gladly recommend this, but as it is, I'd recommend picking up Master of Magic on GoG, or Enemy Nations from its own site before paying for this.

The game play in this iteration of Doom is very much like its early predecessors. You have to run and gun in this game. It’s all about dodging, double jumping, and frantic shooting in a room full of demons. If you stand still, you die. Yet, as hectic as it is, the game makes you feel tougher than most other games. It’s a horror game in which you terrorize the horrors. The little bit of narration that exists tells the story of a legendary character, and that character is you! For what little story there is, it is a very cool story.
It’s quite metal. There’s tons of gore. The environments, enemies, and weapons are all very well varied and fun to experience. I couldn’t wait to discover the next level. There’s also a surprising level of RPG elements in which you can choose certain strengths in your suit’s effects and attachments for your weapons. These level ups come about through your performance and your discovery of secrets. I missed quite a few secrets, so there’s some replability there.
The controls are very smooth. The visuals have a lot of depth and wonder. The sounds and music pound into you. Everything is highly polished. I experienced no technical issues.
This is as far from stealth and slow paced games as it gets, and I usually prefer those slower types of games, but I also found a sort of mindless enjoyment in this and highly recommend it for the carefree guilty pleasure that it is. My only complaint was that I would've liked there to have been more. This is about running lines between start/end nodes on a grid. You have a certain number of 3x3 square blocks to place on the board to redirect the lines towards their destinations. There are only three types of block in the entire game: 90 degree, 180 degree and bounce (only in later levels).
There are six Worlds that are each unlocked when a set number of levels are completed on the previous level, so there is always a good supply of levels to attempt - you never get to a bottleneck with only a small number of levels available. There are also a few Bonus levels branching off the main Worlds with a small number of levels where you must use all blocks, that's the only difference. 100+ levels total.
Graphics are minimal/functional. With this said, I think there is room for improvement. Everything is blue or white, and it can sometimes make it hard to see what's happening when you run a line on the more complex levels. One suggestion is to make highlighting of the start/finish nodes (and/or the line itself) of a successful route more prominent, perhaps red or purple.
There are in-game screen resolution settings which are entirely redundant because you can drag the window to any size you like and it stretches to fit.
Music is a synthesised electro affair which became annoying to me after a while and I switched it off.
Now let's talk about the sound effects. When I mouseover a starting node it highlights the corresponding exit node so I can see where that particular route needs to go. I need to keep it highlighted while I think about my solution. While I do this, I'm subjected to the most rage-inducing noise I've ever heard. It makes me want to murder someone. I bet they use this noise in North Korean torture chambers. The only way to get rid of it is to disable the SFX entirely. You have been warned.
There are a few unexpectedly easy levels scattered around later worlds but on the whole the difficulty progression is excellent. Easy World 1, and steady increase to hard-as-nails. There are no new mechanics, you have the same three types of block throughout the game, but the level layout restricts your placement in all kinds of devious ways. There never seems to be enough space or enough blocks. It's very satisfying to watch all your convoluted lines filling the board like spaghetti and then "Success!"
Players like to have options so I would like to see some kind of hint system (for casual players you understand, not for me, God forbid). Perhaps allow for auto-placement of a single block every few minutes?
Another suggestion: there could be a specific world containing 'red herring' blocks. You wouldn't know which ones to use. Or perhaps unlimited blocks. Just an idea.
14 achievements all related to general gameplay, nothing that makes you play differently than you normally would. 6 Trading Cards available. Level editor with workshop support. Steam Cloud is supposedly included, but it does not sync between my Windows/Linux partitions on the same computer. You may (or may not) have better luck between Windows/Windows.
$13? Really? I have more than my fair share of minimal puzzlers in my Steam library and in my opinion this is a $3 game, $5 tops. Nobody is going to pay $13 and it's a shame because it's a worthwhile puzzler and more people need to be allowed to enjoy it.
There is a level editor and workshop so you can, in theory, get some extra play value from custom levels. However, considering the price I question whether there will be much produced by the few players who fork out that much cash.
Putting aside the overpricing and the odd UI quirk, the core gameplay is solid and challenging. A worthy addition to the large puzzler category in my Steam library. And thanks for Linux!

Operator Overload has that most desirable quality of puzzle games; after trying every possible combination on a level and thinking it is impossible, you feel a real rush of elation when you finally spot the solution! It's almost like beating a boss on Dark Souls.
The game has 100 levels to keep you solving puzzles all night long. New magnets are introduced at a good pace, to keep the worlds fresh, whilst not overwhelming the player with mechanics. The soundtrack is perfect to chill to and deserves a special mention.
Disclaimer: The creator of this game Benn Powell is my brother-in-law :) I stand by what I wrote above.

"You are about to inhabit a broken mind. Not everything you hear or see is trustworthy."
From the opening to the end, this game is drop-dead beautiful, well worth the very modest price. It is a pure walking simulator with narration, no puzzles, just walking and narration, relevant to your current location or some event that happens. The visuals are absolutely stunning, very fitting and with lots of detail in the background, making this game an absolute amazing time to take screenshots in certain locations.
For 2-3 hours, you can exist in a completely different world in a way no AAA title can ever hope to convey, alone, in a dead, decaying world, with nothing but your and your broken, half-rambling thoughts to keep you company. There are so many questions I want to ask about the past and present of the setting, and of the character too. The game answers very little of them, but that somehow seems... fitting. You're a broken man, in a broken world, possibly the last one alive. Your past, present and future don't matter much, all that's left is just to recount what was important to you, be reminded of this and that for the last time, and maybe take a leap of faith. Maybe you'll go to some magical place... or maybe the madness will finally stop.

The stunning environments (which even my integrated graphics chip can handle somehow) and wonderfully tense atmosphere are really held back by the writing, which ranges from decent to terribly preachy and incomprehensible. The first 90% of the game is worth your time, but much of the voiceover sounds like it was taken from a freshman philosophy final paper written at 3 am the night before it's due. Which is a real shame--I enjoyed basically everything about this game aside from the writing. Overall, I'd recommend the game (especially for the price, $6 at time of writing), on the basis of the first ~8 chapters being great.

I can't make sense of some of the other reviews here - I think this game is a lot of fun. I thought the graphics overall were very nice, gameplay smooth and the AI reasonable. Even if it didn't have great visuals, its a card game, what matters most is the game mechanics. That said, there are a few issues, although, they're nothing that I am going to hold against the game.
1 - Some of the reviews have mentioned that its almost pay to win. Look, the developers have to make money somehow and if the cards that are for sale aren't good, then people aren't going to buy them. However, not everyone is going to do this. Most people aren't going to bother paying, and when you face off against these people, its all fine. Honestly, even by purchasing the special decks, its not a guaranteed win. The problem is that there aren't a lot of people playing. If there were hundreds upon hundreds of people playing this game, this wouldn't be an issue. If you only have like 20-30 people playing then its a bit more of a problem. Because the game is free to play, I think it should attract more new players. The devs definitely have a very viable path to success that they're on now.
2 - The biggest challenge with this game is the balancing. This is going to make or break the game. Its still in development, so there are a few issues at the time that I am writing this. I think this will sort itself out over time, and that's why I am not holding it against the game right now.  I would say that the different factions aren't all equal but I feel like this is something the devs can easily resolve if they listen to their community since the foundation for the game is already there.
Overall, I would recommend this game.

There's a lot of mixed reviews, but I quite like Forgotten Myths.
Unlike other games like MtG or Hearthstone, Forgotten Myths plays fast, but doesn't have the potential for first- or second-turn winning decks, at least not that i've seen so far.
I don't think it's worse than similar games, just different in a good way.
Pros:
Lots of interesting mechanics such as
-lanes each creature must fight through
-fortresses which boost creatures in the lanes they watch over
-No HP cap on creatures (if you heal a card that has taken no damage, it's health will increase by 3)
-Garrison (a personal favourite, creatures can enter fortresses and deal damage to opposing creatures before combat starts)
-Ways to combat fortresses and garrsion (I haven't yet had a fully set up field of fortresses blasted to smithereens, but it will happen at some point)
Very well executed game design
Seems fairly balanced
Possible to aquire Gems and Cards through tournaments, not just pay-to-win
Absolutely free, so you may as well give it a try if you like card games
The devs have responded to a lot of what was mentioned in previous reviews in recent updates
Neutral:
Energy cards used to be unbalanced, but a recent update removed that. If a previous review cites +3 energy cards as being overpowered, they now have a chance of discarding another card in your hand.
Cons:
F***ing elephants. I hate elephants now.
Also Rhevan Pheonix
The Single-player campaign starts off fairly easy, but gets much more difficult as you progress, due to how the A.I. decks work. It has no card limits on decks, and combined with the certain cards mentioned above, this can become annoying.
Althought this isn't the devs' fault, there's a small player base, making it difficult to find a match for duels. Again, this isn't the devs' fault.
Three factions aren't imediately accessible at the beginning of the game, as they came in later expansions.
In conclusion, I like the game, although I understand how others can be put off. It's free, and a very small download, so I suggest you at least give it a shot. It might just impress you.

Created and published by Vextro, Welcome To Heaven is a free game on steam that is an attempt by the creator to voice his disillusion with the idea of heaven.
A rather touchy subject given the poor quality of writing and ham fisted way the game portrays the subject I believe it lacked the type of subtlety that these types of games require to succeed at delivering their messages. This feels like one persons angry lashing out at religion presented in a very dismissive manner, it is not trying to debate or educate but simply state "You Are Wrong".
It was actually the sheer negativity of the reviews that drew my interest to the free game along with its concept, the curiosity of just why this had so much dislike drew me in. After playing I can really see why its been highlighted as not only a bad game but as an example of the Holier than Thou or I am Very Smart attitudes can be just as likely to be put forward by those dismissing religion as those defending it.
Seemingly random elements, such as the Assassin's Creed reference and the four strange identical men in blue shirts are out of place and are neither humorous or useful to its message, the sprites were created from images taken from a costume selling website so there is a lack of variation between the various characters making it difficult to remember who you have spoken to and the general layout feels designed to purposely drag out the gameplay and be obstructive.
However placing the player in charge of judging those in purgatory is quite the unique twist. Will you condemn a woman to an eternity in hell for cyberbullying even though she stopped engaging in this activity and is apologetic of her actions before her death?
Hopefully someone else will take the idea of a  game that focused around judging those in purgatory or attempting to redeem souls would be interesting, the thought of a "Papers Please' approach to the game popped into my mind and almost made me spit tea from giggling.

This software is about to undergo a massive overhaul.  Buying it at the moment will give you a once-useful tutorial that, while informative, applies to Unity 4 and contains outdated/incompatible information.  You may not get much use out of this at the moment, but GTGD is currently reworking this with a remade season based on a modern version of Unity 5.  Hang in there!
==
If you want the videos themselves for free, they're on the youtube channel
.
Why would you buy it on Steam?  For starters, it's an offline and downloadable version of the season with project files included, but usefulness may vary there.  Why did I buy it?  Well, why do you leave a tip for your waiter?  It's a great series and it's easily understandable, plus it's designed using the free edition of Unity 4 for maximum accessibility-- a quality tutorial made entirely to assist others.  It's absolutely commendable.
I'd recommend this to anyone who wants to learn the Unity engine.  Why Unity?  It's actually a great engine, and you shouldn't associate it with Air Control or any of that nonsense because if you look closely, you can see just how little effort was put into those shovelware titles.  Countless exceptional titles have been made on the engine, ranging from Virtual Reality based shooters (H3VR, BAM) to visually stunning platformers (Ori, ReCore).  The technology behind this engine is highly capable, despite a rather user-friendly interface, and great things can be accomplished with the engine if you set your mind to it.
While I'd say you should watch these videos on YouTube and decide for yourself whether you actually need the Steam version, GTGD certainly deserves every donation made from this.
These videos teach you Unity's interface, basic knowledge of C#, and more; arguably, they're more helpful than the actual Unity Technologies tutorial series.
If you truly wanted to know why this is on Steam, have a quote from the series creator himself...

This game deserves to be in the pantheon of incredible jRPGs along with the Trails in the Sky games, Persona games, Earthbound, and others. I love the structure of it, how slow it is yet how interesting it always continues to be, I was never bored throughout the 90ish hours I played the game which is astounding.
Every character has their moment, through their relationship with the main character or with each other. This game does social links better than the modern Persona games ever did and it weaves them brilliantly into the main story. The combat is always entertaining (even when you absolutely break it with powerful quartz and abilities towards the end of the game). The cliffhanger ending isn't quite as good as the first Trails in the Sky game, but it makes me super hype for the sequel to come out on steam. I kind of wish it didn't look like a PS2 game, but even with its rudimentary visuals it shows off some impressive world design and cities throughout.
Just a note regarding how I played the game: I've heard the dub in this game is quite good, but I played it with modded files to use JP voice acting since that is how I prefer to play these type of games. This worked fine, the only lines that are missing translation are the battle voices  (including the very short dialog from the bosses as you beat them up). Unfortunately I also had some performance issues that seemed to be related to the fact that running the game in fullscreen puts it in borderless fullscreen. I've had this issue in other games where running in window mode kinda messes up the framerate, which is why I run games in exclusive fullscreen. Turns out the only way to run this game in exclusive fullscreen is to edit the xml file directly, and when you do that it doesn't have any alt-tab support or the game crashes. Other than the alt-tab issue, running the game in exclusive fullscreen fixed my framerate issue completely.

The first game in the series for Trails of Cold Steel, part of the larger universe of "The Legend of Heroes". This game is a PC port of the original game launched back in 2013.
When i initially saw this game on steam in August 2017, I was interested. The second the game release  I brought it, and never regretted it. This is my second foray into JRPG, my first being my aborted attempted at one of the Tales Of series, that had real time battle sequences, apart from the turn based the majority of JRPG's use.
I personally, now after completing my first run through of this game 70 hours in, prefer the turn base.
The story commences, and you are immeditately hit with a large group that will evantually grow into your team. Each, yes, it could be said with its "torpe" characters, and some sequences which basically almost ever anime has used at least once :)
But, for someone coming into "The Legend of Heroes" series, this game is a great introduction, though technically in the teamline it is in the latter part of the universe. The visuals, yeah are not excellent 3D hyper resourced required models, but that doesnt take away from the beauty of the game, its sequences, action scenes, and the universe you start to explore.
The music is beautiful, especially in the later part of the game where there are some truly majestic boss pieces that play in the background as you face some truly formiable foes. Also, during the quieter periods, the soft music that plays in the background could easy be used for a nice relaxing day in the real world.
As i said, the charaters do have their torpes, but each is unique as you explore and learn more about them. The story unfolds slowly, which might annoy some people who want every question answered straight away. But the slow unfolding story allows you to take in what is occurring, and what might occur.
The PC Port has been brillantly done and created, so much so you wouldnt even realize once you are ingame, that it was created for consoles. Additionally, the settings and options you can configure, will make it easy for many PC gamers to configure the game and tweak it to your hearts content.
With this being the first game of four games for this story, there are still many unanswered questions, and the ending of this game has left me pumped for the next game to be released ported to PC in early 2018.
While this game might not be flashy, its storyline, characters, music, universe, scenes and those little moments are something you rarely find packaged within a single game. If you are looking for a great JRPG, that has a expanding story and universe that will keep you exploring for hundreds of hours, I truly recommend you give "The Legend of Heroes: Trails of Cold Steel" a go

This is a decent casual 4x fantasy game.
Choose one of three factions and one of three maps to conquer.  Every space has about a dozen pre-determined buildings that you can place, which will generate gold or mana or let you create more powerful units.
To slow you down, after conquering a territory you will need to garrison a large army there for a few turns or there will be a revolt.... losing you the territory and spawning a large neutral army.  On balance, it is easier to conquer slowly and not deal with the rebels.
And that is the whole thing.  The art isn't great but it isn't terrible.  The sound effects work.  I liked the music, but that will be to taste.  The UI is a little rough, and the game was clearly done in flash, including getting flash memory errors and the like while playing.
More maps, more armies, and more of a reason to play the different factions differently is what this game needs to go to the next level.  I found the same strategy worked no matter which army I picked, and the differences in the stats faction to faction were too minor to create unique playstyles.  At which point choosing the armies is mostly a reskin.  Once you figure out how to slowly roll forward on any map with any faction.... well there is not much more to the game.
I beat it twice in 5 hours, including once on the hardest difficulty.  There are no achievements, and not much replay value beyond that.  All that being said, I did enjoy the 5 hours I spent with it.  Be aware that what you are getting is 4x light.  The 5 hours I played were fun, and I would like to see an expansion or sequel that did more.

Nice game...I grew up with the first version of DOOM.

1 – GENERAL
I do not know if I should classify DOOM as a FPS or a run and gun. Probably both should be the correct answer.
When you start playing, and after a short and easy demon killing spree, the Doom Guy is presented with the first burst of storytelling. You immediately think that the game is ruined, but you are wrong. Doom Guy almost always ignores all the information and help, he's there to kill demons, and that's also, what you want. So it's a win-win, right?
Despite that, the story is there if you want to know it, and it's quite good tbh. I assume I was one of those searching and reading parts of the story, it's interesting enough to keep me motivated to search for it. It's not shallow also. Thumbs up Bethesda.
We have quite a set of sounds to talk about in this game. The guns have nothing remarkable to speak about, but also nothing wrong about them. That's good, do not get me wrong, but not at the same level as the demons sounds, that are mostly flawless and very different between them. And I cannot forget the soundtrack. That heavy metal... what a joy to listen. Probably the best soundtrack of a game from this genre.
This game is not a visual novel, and if you are searching for top quality graphics probably this is not your game, but it does the job quite well, and both Mars and Hell are quite well designed, and they are very immersive. The game as tons of platforming, so most levels evolve around that concept. The ledges have to be distinguishable so we know where to grab, that's enough for a surprisingly atmospheric game, but not enough to be as beautiful as the Witcher 3. But believe me, you will not notice that.
2 – GAMEPLAY
Brace yourself because you will spend some time dashing and shooting in this game. And you will have to do this at quite a fast pace. That's positive stuff in my book, but at some point, this starts to get a bit repetitive, and you will ask for more. At that point, you will start to sense the endgame, and your excitement starts to grow again. OFC the very intensive boss battles give a little help to that excitement, even if the bosses are a bit of bullet sponges with not much of intelligence to go with it, but believe me when I say that you will only think about that after the battle is over.
Glory kills are a blast and you will not get sick of those. Nothing better than a demon dismemberment to start the day, right? And also, those are very important for you, since they provide valuable health and armour pickups. Without those, you would not last long.
Are you getting short of ammo? Worry not, just grab your chainsaw and saw some demon in half. He will give you that much needed ammo refill in form of massive ammo drops. Does this make the game significantly easier? Yes, but who cares? Just give me that chainsaw kill!!
You can upgrade all your weapons for an increased amount of fun. You just have to find the correct pickups and buy an upgrade. Simple as that.
That game is packed full of secrets to find and places to explore. Just prepare yourself to do some platforming puzzles and you are good to go. I admit that my main focus was always the killing part, but at some point, I started to take joy in finding those secrets also.
You also have a multiplayer mode. I've tried to understand with the community the reason for so much criticism around this game mode, and it seems a complex theme, so I'll just leave my opinion. It's an unconventional arena shooter, with tons of unlockable and where you can play the demon also. This last part is the best thing about multiplayer modes. The mode is OK, but just very far from the fun I have in campaign mode. There's a lot of people still playing it, so if that's your thing, you will enjoy this one also.
3 – CONCLUSION
I usually play older games, and I'm always complaining that the games are not what they used to be. DOOM is what games used to be when I was younger, and at the same time, it gives me hope for some other older games like Duke Nukem or so.
It's a very good game, very fast paced, very straightforward, very linear and very fun.
It worth every penny.
Just go buy it!

Edit: One honorable mention despite this being a positive review: Many users seem to have trouble with corrupt autosaves after a crash. Luckily this didn't happen to me, but I can see why developing a game with only ONE single automatic save slot and no way of manually saving the game is a terrible idea. Since you can only "continue" your campaign, if that save is gone, then the campaign is also gone.
Perhaps the best shooter since Wolfenstein. Period. DOOM takes us back to the good old days of running, gunning and jumping. Gameplay could probably best be compared to Unreal Tournament/Quake with hordes of monsters. The monster design is phenomenal, graphics are slick and every demon has a purpose in this game. Couple that with sprawling maps that can be fully explored (though there are some annoying points of no return and some of them aren't telegraphed) and a wide array of weapons, which can be upgraded with not one but TWO alternative firing modes, which can then further be upgraded and THEN after that be "mastered" to become even better, and you have yourself a really enjoyable kill fest for every difficulty. Speaking of upgrades: You can also get upgrades for your suit of armor and unlock specific runes from rune trials that further enhance and customize your playstyle. This game is just full of upgrades everywhere. Whether you simply find them, unlock them or complete challenges to get them, there's plenty to do. And when you're done with that there are also lore items and collectible toy DOOM marines to find, as well as secret classic Doom levels to uncover (these are quite hard to find). Rarely did I have so much fun just looking at a 3D map to find the next stuff to collect.
If there was one weakness then that there barely is any story. The 3 characters you meet on your journey don't have much substance and it's always pretty much the same, plus there's hope for a sequel. But you don't play this game for the story anyway. I just wanted to mention it. Wolfenstein is still overall the far superior FPS in my opinion, but if you just want to shoot stuff and explore beautiful maps to get unlocks and complete challenges, then DOOM is a perfect fit. Got this on a bargain sale for under 10 bucks and had 15 hours of pure fun with it.

A last minute purchase during the Winter Steam sale, The Old City: Leviathan is a beautiful, albeit strange, walking simulator of a game.
For those wondering: this is not a horror game, but it makes use of its atmosphere brilliantly, to the point where I was walking around looking at the ground/with my volume way down low, because I wasn't sure if anything was going to jump out at me. Nothing did, thankfully, so never fear. From the grungy, post-apocalyptic over/underworld to the startlingly gorgeous dreamscapes this game has you walk through, atmosphere is something Leviathan does So Well.
Unfortunately, that's about all the good I can say, because the actual story of this game is impossible to follow.
I tried, I really did! I'm someone who really enjoys reading and understanding the lore of the world I'm in. But the story was extremely muddled and bogged down in unnecessary writing. I'm talking pages and pages of writing found in journals and posters found throughout the game. A lot of the writing should have been streamlined and, honestly, made simpler for the player to understand.
I know this game has some biblical undertones, to say the least, but pretty much every journal I picked up in-game felt like I was talking to one of those 2Edgy4U atheist guys who tried to mansplain a thing to me. Too much talking, not enough explanation, just A LOT of words. The first journal I found was at least five full-length pages of a dead guy writing his thoughts down about his room.
It was not good, to say the least.
(Which is honestly a shame, because there were some really interesting concepts in this game! Especially the Minotaurs!)
Once I decided to ignore the journals after a few failed attempts to get through them, I had a much better time of it.
If we're being honest, the only reason I'm recommending this game is because of the cool environments and pretty decent voice acting. Ignoring the story completely, you're a person walking through a post-apocalyptic world who comes across giant creatures from time to time, which was really cool (and at times, properly scary!) It's worth getting through the world if you do it just for that.
So if you have a few bucks to spend and don't know what to get, buy this during a Steam Sale! But don't expect too much from this game. It's a very pretty walking simulator with some creative level designs, but that's about the long and short of it.

A game that, like others in this new 'Walking Simulator' genre, explores how far one can go with the extremely simple mechanics of walking and looking. This one goes further than most - your movement is intentionally very slow, and is slowed further by a smattering of large chunks of text that are crucial to filling in the details of the story. To top it all off, the game refuses to convey a straighforward story. Instead it contains a mix of exploring a post apocalyptic reality with several concrete main characters as well as a very metaphorical and philosophical layer of meaning that is harder to interpret (but becomes rather clear by the end).
A great many people can no doubt already know from the above description that this game is not for them, but I am not one of those people. I liked the slow speed, the glacial unraveling of the story, and even its philosophical explorations. My main criticism would have to be that even if I appreciated the story and the philosophical ranting, by the end it all feels quite verbose. I am not sure if having this many layers, this much interacting stuff to unravel, actually make for a more compelling experience or just a more complicated one. But, I do know I enjoyed my first play through and understood what I would guess are the main details to be uncovered. So, be warned that this game is what it is, and if you think you may like that I definitely recommend playing through it.

You begin in a city sewer or something and end up exploring by walking/running (both at a snail's pace) in different corridors until you find the right one, after which, the game instantly hurls you into the next chapter.
10 minutes pass and I arrive in an outside area; here there are three doors you can go through - each go somewhere different.  I entered one and the path kept on going and going so I turned back worried that I missed out on the other places outside. Look, I'm sorry, I
to like this game. I really did. The seeds of a good game are here and I did my best to stick with it as long as I could. But I honestly just couldn't like this game because, well, it's really,
badly-made.
That's it in a nutshell: the game's mechanics are decent, but the overall package is just the most amateurish thing I think I've ever seen in a digital CCG. From the horrible-looking and awfully unwieldy full 3D rotational main menu, low-rez card art and crude-looking Unity assets, to the appallingly clunky in-game interface and impenetrable gameplay stemming from the
tutorial and complete lack of tooltips, the game just looks like a student project, or an early alpha. Never have I seen a game this carelessly user-unfriendly- after playing dozens of games, I
had absolutely no idea what half the mechanics did because they weren't explained in the tutorial, the game completely lacks tooltips to explain them (I never realised how vital these are until I actually played a game that lacks them) and there's no in-game documentation explaining them either. I questioned a few people in the chat channel and managed to get a few answers (ones COMPLETELY different to my best guess, which shows how unintuitive these mechanics are) and was basically told that I should have looked up the rulebook on the developers' website. Now why the hell isn't there actually anything
telling me that? Why should I even
to do something so clunky and counterintuitive just to
That aside, the mechanics really are rather simplistic. You play Energy cards to increase, well, your Energy pool then use them to throw creatures down onto your attack line, structures down behind them, or play actions in your actions phase. You can't move or dismiss your own creatures once you've played them and who goes first in each phase toggles each turn, so a lot of important strategic decisions have to be made basically blind, reducing a lot of the gameplay to guesswork. The Energy system really bites hard- Energy comes in +1, +2 and ultra-rare +3 variants and, while you get a number of +2 Energy cards as you level up your account, the only other way to get them is by buying expensive Energy Boosters, packs that contain nothing but Energy cards. This system is painfully crude, the game is borderline unplayable until you get enough +2 Energys to replace you starting mess of useless +1s, and you're very prone to getting Energy screwed. The player who draws more energy will usually just win outright. The system is far cruder than Magic's Land system, and far less elegant than Spellweaver's Shrine system (which contains MULTIPLE mechanics to prevent you from getting Shrine screwed) and it's a serious flaw in the game.
While the array of cards available for you to use are interesting, there's big problems with a lot of them. The game uses the same 5 colours of card as Magic, black, white, blue, green and red, as well as a neutral faction. Deck construction is limited solely by which colours are willing to work together- you can put black and red cards in a deck, for example, but not black and white. While I didn't experiment enormously with deck design (since the interface for deck construction is atrocious even by the standards of the rest of the game), there don't seem to be any limitations to how you build your deck. The problem is there are WAY too many card interdependancies. A LOT of cards gain bonuses from being played not only with specific
of card, but even specific
themselves! This means if you don't actually
the card that provides the synergy, the card is more or less useless, or at least drastically underpowered. There's way too much of this sort of thing in the card set, and the difficulty of acquiring new cards makes it even worse.
I need to give special mention to the tutorial as absolutely the
I have ever suffered through. It didn't so much handhold me as hand
me, giving me my starter deck and forcing me to play through a number of boring mini-matches to learn basic mechanics in the most excrutiating way possible, every single action restricted to the letter, even if I could see an obviously better one available. After that, I was forced to play through the first 5 missions of the game's
expansive PvE campaign before I was even given access to the rest of the menu options, including my Inventory or the Store- that's right, I couldn't even
my own deck until I'd beaten the first leg of the campaign! And these weren't simple formality cakewalk opponents either, my starting deck was so rubbish that some of them were actually quite difficult because they simply had better decks! It was so terrible I almost quit before I even cleared the tutorial. Apparently the devs heard the massive outcry about this and improved it quickly, but I can't speak about that since you can never replay the tutorial, so I have no idea what it's like now.
You might see a number of other reviewers rubbishing the idea that the game is "Pay to Win". Now firstly, don't be absurd, ALL CCGs since the invention of Magic: the Gathering have been, by definition, P2W, or at least pay to get better cards which will increase your odds of winning. But I do have to contradict anyone who calls this game "generous" by CCG standards. To be honest, the game is EXTREMELY stingy. Packs are extremely expensive (3-4k gold when you get only couple of hundred for winning a game) and initially the all-important Energy Boosters were Emerald (real money currency) exclusive! Fortunately the devs realised what a
idea this was and made them simply cost more gold than normal boosters, but it still stings. You
earn Emeralds by doing a few daily missions as well as a couple when you level up, but they trickle in at a pittance. I've played a LOT of F2P CCGs and I've compared the free stuff they give you, and Forgotten Myths is definitely among the stingiest of the lot- where games like Spellweaver or Infinity Wars will regularly give you free
Forgotten Myths will toss you a few Emeralds and tell you to appreciate it. Oh, and there are special promo cards that can only be bought individually with Emeralds, playable in all modes. And you can't buy them until you've spent real money at least once. The devs justify this with "they're not especially OP". Um, that's called "selling power" guys, that IS P2W and it's inexcusable.
Technically the game is ugly as sin. The 3D 1st person rotational main menu is just plain annoying (you don't have to go out of your way to be special, guys) and the rest of the interface really shows its Unity base. Some of the card art is pretty good, but even on maximum settings it's jarringly blurry and low-resolution. There are almost no sound effects and in-game animations are extremely sparse. The music is initially OK, but rapidly becomes irritating in its intrusiveness until you want to turn it off.
Oh and the PvP is so counterintuitive I was barely able to play a single match. There doesn't appear to be any matchmaking system
you have to host a game and wait for someone to challenge you, or challenge someone who's hosting. Maybe there's more to it than that, but once again, absolutely
was explained at all and I was sick of messing around with trial and error.
Like I said at the start, I
to like this game. The devs seem to be trying and I can see the core of a decent game here. Unfortunately the game wrapped around that core is just really shoddy. I'm sorry to post such a negative review, but I can't be anything other than honest, and Forgotten Myths is just one of the least-impressive free CCGs I've ever tried.

Don't judge a book by it's cover!
I say this because originally I didnt like this game. Like some of the other reviewers here, I spent very little time in the game and formed an opinion after seeing just the surface.
I admit that the tutorial needs some work and there are some gameplay mechanics that aren't obvious. I've chatted and emailed with devs and have seen them make changes and fix issues pretty much immediately.
There are still things to fix however they know about them and are working on it.
So, to the game review!
This is somewhat similar to other CCG games where you create your deck with cards and then play against an opponent (2v2 and guild wars coming soon).
You start with one of three starter decks and quickly get a booster pack. I was very frustrated in my first hour because I was struggling in the single player missions (there are a LOT of them). That being said, as soon as I leveled up a few times I gained +2 energy cards which made a HUGE difference.
Coins (the free in game currency) come fast enough that I was buying extra booster packs and even individual cards to strenghten my deck.
One interesting aspect of this that is different from MtG and Hearthstone is Fortifications. They are back-row units that offer bonuses and can garison some other units for added firepower.
Community is very good, I haven't seen a single troll in game and only 2 spammers (which get shut down right away due to the anti-spam feature of the chat).
I suggest you give this game a try and have patience enough to get past the first few levels, it really opens up after that.
The game has a referral system which confused me at first. Basically when you start it asks for a referral code which is the case-sensitive username of another player. As soon as you put in a code, you are rewarded with 2000 coins and some free cards (no need to purchase, just make sure you put in a real referral code). If you end up buying emeralds then the person you entered as referral gets a bonus just on your first purchase.

I will give you free cards if you end up buying any emeralds as a thank you. Please note that you need to reach level 10 to access the auction house which is how we can trade cards back and forth.
Even if you don't purchase anything or even use my referral code, feel free to chat me up in game and ask any questions or even play a game against me.
Hope to see you in game!

I have 1 year of formal C# instruction under my belt, and about 5 hours of Unity and GIMP experience combined (mostly just navigating the windows and learning the controls). I've made a few 1-2 (imported) texture landscapes without any objects or anything. I have a good grasp on what each of the different softwares used in this tutorials series does, but very little experience actually using them first-hand (besides c# programming).
I'm on video 4 of the series (So take my review with a grain of salt, I may update after I finish the series) and I've just completed creating a projectile object which can be fired from the user as if it were a bullet of some kind. The video is very easy to follow, even using a never version of Unity (not reccommended).
I would warn buyers that the video series does not aim to teach you how to code in c# or how to use the different technologies showcased. It's more about following along, monkey-see-monkey-do style so you can see what goes on behind the scenes in game making. You will still need to learn more on your own to understand how everything works (especially the code).
For people who have never coded, or used any sort of game development technology, this will be hard to understand - easy to follow. By that I mean. You won't learn a ton about how the C# language works, you might not understand how Unity keeps track of all the objects or how it applies materials, and you might not become a GIMP artist, but you will be opened to a wonderful world of possibilities.
I highly suggest anyone without any programming or gamedevelopment experience consider buying this series and following every spoken word to the letter (most important when coding so you can keep track of the variables he's referring to). If you are a parent of gamer children, this would be a good series to get them into so they can get an idea of how games are made.
For those with programming experience, you will get the most out of this series if you take a look at the documentation to expand on

I quite enjoyed this game for what it was. Sure, there are some things about it that aren't perfect mechanically, and it could certainly use some work. I bought this with the intention of wanting to support an indy developer as I am attempting to go through the same process.
I played this game through to the end taking a little less than two hours, plus some time just messing around inside the game for fun.
Pros:
- Price.
- Some entertaining, though at times, awkwardly written dialogue.
- A variety of challenges from level to level; each level introducing something new.
- Retro-esque graphics, if you're into that sort of thing.
- A few hilarious references, my favourite being Mortal Kombat's Sub-Zero reference.
- A short game; doesn't overstay it's welcome.
- Appears to be easy, but looks are deceiving. Can be quite challenging!
- Good for a few chuckles.
- Addictive with a dash of charm.
Cons:
- Minor mechanical game issues:
- At times I would push the thumb-stick one way and suddenly face the opposite direction when attacking.
- Clipping into the side of moving platforms and floating for a bit.
- If two weapons are on the ground and on top of each other, it reads as one pickup, destroying the second weapon.
- Rendering issue where, at odd times, a frame would go completely black.
- Enemy projectiles seem to continue through walls. (Died in a spectacularly hilarious way because of this)
- Fairly repetitive combat as you can really only swing your sword or throw the item in hand. (Found that just running past enemies and dodging was the easiest way to power through this game).
- Some parts are frustrating and annoying due to stacked enemy placement. This being different from a difficult situation, as some of these places you had no choice but to take a hit.
I would say that this is a great prototype that doubles as a game. There are certainly a lot of things that the dev could do to improve upon what's already there and build this into something larger and more refined. It's clear that the dev was passionate about what he/she was doing and I have to congratulate them on releasing their game.
Keep up the great work!

I do not think reviews do justice to this device: it is much better than I expected from reading them. After reading reviews, I was hesitant to buy it, but now I am really glad I did, totally worth the money.
The touch controls provide much higher accuracy than regular sticks and relieve your thumbs from strain, which is a huge win.
Also, it works out of the box as a replacement for the desktop mouse, and a proper usable replacement, much better than a regular gamepad in the same role.
Does not feel "elite" or expensive, but does not feel particularly cheap either, despite what many reviews say.
Previously I used Razer Sabertooth and Logitech F710. Steam Controller blows them out of the water.
It requires getting used to, of course, but so is any new input device. Also requires tuning in games, which is easy and flexible, and that tuning is not a chore, but rather a set of additional possibilities that I did not have with a regular gamepad.
There may be a problem with imperfect support in some games, which do not support mouse and gamepad simultaneously, but it is never worse than a regular gamepad anyway.

It really takes some time to get used to, but the high level of customization/remapping makes it worth it.
It's also pretty large, even for someone with large hands.
The touch pad clicks are annoyingly loud and, it really does look and feel cheap.
But, for the level of customization you can do, it's worth buying on sale, between $30 and $40.
Valve really should bring the price down to $30, so a sale price can dip down to $20 or $25.
It's a great concept but needs a better design to warrant the typical $49.99 price.

At the end of the day, this controller mostly comes down to personal preference, but it definitely brings something new to the table.
P.S. A little trick I'm sure others have mentioned: if the controller feels too light or "cheap", just leave batteries in, even if you're not using it wirelessly. It's a pretty nice weight with batteries, but feels just a little off without them.

I've been playing JRPG's for a long time and love them, however a lot of them have a similar formula that is pretty predictable and can be stale at times, while Trails of Cold Steel doesn't reinvent the wheel it does a fantastic job at taking the core elements of what makes a good JRPG and builds on them.
The combat is fun and flashy and can at times be challenging, sometimes there's a random difficulty spike but I never found myself being forced to grind all that much compared to some of the other JRPGs out there. The game is also pretty forgiving if you lose a battle. The characters and story are one of the best parts of the game. The characters really grew on me and I found myself wanting to do all the little side missions just to find out more about them. This game also has a few plot twist moments that will leave you speechless. The voice acting is pretty impressive as well.
Some of the cons for the game though would be that the music didn't really blow me away. There are some tracks that stand out more than others but sometimes I found the music to just be lacking. The story also ends on a massive cliffhanger; there is a sequel on Ps3 that is coming to PC in 2018 but with no exact date yet it's hard to wait patiently. If that wasn't bad enough the game is part of a 4 part game series with parts 3 and 4 not being confirmed for the west yet. While steam only recorded about 40 hours the game took me about 65 hours to complete so like most JRPG's a decent amount of time needs to be invested.
Tl:DR: If you like JRPGs and haven't played this one yet you're doing yourself a disservice and should pick it up.

This is a short game that suffered from a lack of interesting plot or interactivity. I normally enjoy games that are jokingly referred to as walking simulators, but this one doesn't require any engagement at all.
If you enjoy disturbing games with routine rambling narration you might enjoy this game more than I could.

What I liked:
The Old City: Leviathan is an interesting and highly abstract story with gorgeous and surreal environments. I've been searching for quite a while for a game that makes me feel similar to the way I felt playing Dear Esther for the first time, and this is it.
What I didn't like:
-Player movement speed is very, very slow. There's a "sprint" function, but it's barely any quicker than walking.
-By default, Mouse 1 zooms up on objects, a feature which is honestly pretty useless. Seems to me that it'd make more sense to have Mouse 1 as the use key (as opposed to having a separate use key), then let the player bind a "HUD Zoom" key if they wanted one.
-Sometimes you get hitched on geometry and will need to jump or walk slightly to the side (small staircases are especially bad for this).
Overall:
I'd recommend The Old City: Leviathan to anyone who enjoys a slow, intriguing walking similar with amazing visuals. Don't play this expecting a fast-paced game or really any interaction with the world. The game essentially consists of walking between points of interest, interpreting voiceovers, reading notes, opening doors, and
. As well, some general familiarity with the biblical story of Jonah is very valuable in understanding this game.

In a word: inchorerent.
I can't recommend this game. It plays like the designers stitched random unassociated demo projects together and then slapped a story on at the last minute. The 'levels' are disconnected visually and thematically, and the notes and collectibles are more obfuscating than illuminating. Just as Star Trek archetyped the term "techno-babble," games like The Old City: Leviathon archetype what I would call "mystery-babble." It's the illusion that there is a deeper more rewarding mystery behind the scenes. The appearance of any mystery is facade.
That may be unfair, there may actually be an intentional commentary/story lurking behind the game. If that's true though, then my criticism would be that the post-modern story-telling style is too self-indulgent.

I bought this game (with a few others) as an introduction to the walking sim genre, excited and apprehensive about exploring a narrative primarily through environment and visuals, but this game does not deliver that experience at all.
While the visuals are beautiful, and the sound wonderfully atmospheric, there would be no narrative at all without the barrage of words ceaselessly interrupting the artistic aspects of this game.
The description boasts of exploration, but mere minutes of "exploration" reveal the maps to be merely corridors, with the amount of narration requiring a large area, slow pace, counterintuitive layout, or some combination thereof, to force enough time on players to read and hear all the plot and philosophizing inserted into the experience.
The gameplay itself does not communicate an experience. The visuals themselves do not communicate an experience. Even combined, it is too ephemeral to convey what PostMod presents through the text.
I think the game's aims fail on their own terms because there are two very different stories being told without enough synthesis between them. The soundscapes and environment suggest only that a milieu has passed and that the player exists in its ruins, with, perhaps, a struggle of perception common to any lone survivor. The narration and text tell an entirely different story that concretizes and informs the visuals, but could stand on their own, without being in a game at all.
How, for example, would a walking sim communicate the idea of subjectivity? Wouldn't the environment itself need to be ceaselessly changing? The jump physics or movement speeds inconsistent even during movement? There was an attempt at this, but it was unbelievably typical, and did not at all, I feel, measure up to the extreme that, again, the notes and the narration explore.
This game feels not at all like a walking sim and much, much more like a travelator through some gorgeous places, interrupted, constantly, by a drone of deliberately obtuse intellectualization.

You spend most of your time exploring abandoned sewers and subway stations, wandering around aimlessly until you find the one door in the area that loads the next chapter.  Your exploration is results in minor rewards with a small number of collectibles and some notes left behind by previous inhabitants of the abandoned passageways.   The environments are extremely detailed but, sadly, the gorgeous environments are about all this game has going for it.
The game is advertised as having significant depth and meaning, but ultimately the story is a convoluted mess that just leaves you confused when the game suddenly and unexpectedly ends. The game gives just enough story elements for you to know that
is going on, but not enough information for you to actually know
is happening (or happened).  There's something about a catastrophic event, contaminated water supply, three factions of idealist, and some parasite...? I never really understood.  Story elements are presented piecemeal through fragmented dialogue and scarcely placed text, which results in the  vast majority of the story content being missable if you don't discover all the hidden writings.  I consider this an unforgivable failure in a walking simulator considering the story
the game.
Other quibbles:
The default movement speed is unbearably slow and the run speed provides an almost imperceptible increase, so still unbearably slow.  I held the run button the entire game and felt like I was crawling.  There are also a few audio glitches in the game that cause multiple audio tracks to play simultaneously, resulting in the narrator talking over himself.
I actually really enjoyed this, some solid ideas in a gorgeous world - worth it.

GTGD is the akronym of "gamer to game developer".
It's a tutorial series which teaches the basics of developing a game in the Unity 3D engine (you can do 2D games as well, don't worry) by creating a simple multiplayer shooter.
It also includes some awesome feature programming like placing blocks.
This tutorial series has a very high production value. Both the sound and the resolution of the videos are very good and all the project files and scripts for the finished project are included in the download.
The tutor does a good job of explaining all the steps and tasks, not to slow or to fast and with a good amount of detail. Most importantly he does not skip anything, so you won't feel left alone.
A big part of this tutorial is coding. Make no mistake there is no way around that if you want to make your own games.
That said, even if you are a complete beginner at coding you should be able to follow the tutorial, though I would encourage you to at least read up on some basics (What is a class? What is a function? What is a variable?).
You will need them sooner or later anyway no matter what engine or programming language you use.
If you are intermediate the scripting won't bore you either. From a software development standpoint the scripts are very well structured, both in the way they interact and in and of themselves.
The scripts are kept simple and make no mistake, that is a big endorsement.
(If you don't know what I mean google the KISS principle.)
Still the tutor does not miss out on important elements of Unity coding and I was very happy to see some co-routine programming included where appropriate.
The tutor does an awesome job of commenting everything he writes and explaining what everything does, which makes it very easy to follow his train of thought.
If you are an aspiring gamedeveloper, beginner or intermediate, this tutorial series is well worth your money.
You do not need to buy any other software since both the game engine Unity 3D and the script editor MonoDevelop are free.
Yes, Unity has a commercial "Unity Pro" version but you don't need to worry about that at this point. The extra features included there are very specific and well beyond what you need to make most games, not to speak of just getting started in game development.
So all you need besides this tutorial is patience and time.
Learning takes effort and anyone who tells you otherwise is a charlatan and a liar.
But while there is no fast way to become a cometent developer, as far as learning effectiveness, pacing of content and completeness are concerned this is the best you will find.
So good luck and many squeals of delight ;).

+ Offers an incentive to play and do well in ranked (Gems are awarded at the end of the month based on rank.)
+ Offers strategic lane-based gameplay that is very interesting.
+ Allows both players play the game simultaneously with alternating phases and initiative changes every round.
+ Allows players to buy Common/Uncommon singles of all factions and to sell unwanted cards.
+ Functioning Auction House.
What FM does wrong:
- Offers exclusive promo cards behind a paywall (which you can't buy with Gems earned for free unless you make an initial purchase of Gems.)
- Tiers newer faction boosters (Green, Blue, Forgers) behind a level restriction (6, 8, and 10 respectively), unless you buy them for Gems, which is a bit much and can easily be misconstrued as P2W.
Overall, Forgotten Myths is still very much a diamond in the rough, but if you give it a chance, you will find it to be a very rewarding and enjoyable experience. =)

Okay, let me preface this by saying it's not awesome, just pretty good I guess.
Pros:
- Extremely customizable; has basically all of the features that I've been wanting out of button-mapping wrappers for years, including the ability to map inputs to a specific mouse-click area on screen, and the recognition of input groupings (face buttons, either of the two touch pads, joystick) so that they can all serve a similar function such as camera or character movement (rather than just getting locked in 8 directional control), and the ability to toggle or hold other input profiles with a button
- Grip buttons are a welcome feature that no console's default controller has - will greatly reduce the amount of situations you'll need to take your thumbs off the pads or joystick in.
- If you're too lazy to spend a lot of time carefully crafting the optimal mapping that will suit your style perfectly, chances are someone has already made it, so you can just download it and get to using it instantly.
- Mouse movements are pretty precise. Infinitely better than trying to aim with a right-stick on FPS games, for example.
- Pretty ergonomic, all things considered.
- The price is pretty fair compared to is competition, especialy on sale.
- Definitely better than some small cheapsh## wired logitech controller, for example.
Cons:
- It feels cheap. Everything is made out of either that matte hard plastic or the glossy fingerprint-kind, and it has no significant weight to it.
- You have to use a (pretty sizable) dongle; no bluetooth. Although, MINI-PRO: if you get one without a dongle (like I did because I bought used off Amazon), just tell valve you didn't get one, and they'll be light "aight" and ship it for free, no questions asked. It's extremely helpful and it happened to both my friend and I.
- The mapping software is not graceful in any capacity. It's clunky, and it tries+fails at trying to be user-friendly. You need to go to Big Picture to access it (bet you forgot that exists) and the way profiles work is so broken, and, dare I say, glitched. I made an Overwatch mapping as the first thing I ever did with my controller, and somehow I ended up with a profile that said "Overwatch" for like a year, no matter how many times I thought I deleted it and made a new napping or deleted it or changed it, it annoyed me, which brings me to...
- Barely compatible with non-steam properties. I still barely understand how to even get it to work outside of big picture. Don't expect to be having fun on Origin,
, or Dolphin any time soon if you buy.
- The face buttons are kinda small and awkwardly placed. It sounds picky, but it's important to me.
- Is still absolutely no replacement for aiming with a mouse, even if it is more ergonomic.
- DualShock 4 or frankly any [good] gamepad is better in just about every aspect except price, customizability (kinda), and mouse precision, but those are pretty important in PC gaming, so...
I know, I'm too wordy.
