Highly recommmend. Nihon Falcom strikes again with a killer, memorable, original, and thoroughly polished RPG!
First star goes to the original storyline. Rather, the deft handling of the storyline. One can spot a mile a way the many tropes that Falcom used to convey the story. As with most Falcom fans, the attention is given to the characters and how they react to the story. Nihon Falcom really takes to heart the writer's adage of "a simple story about complex characters". Once again, these NPCs are the most stand out characters in RPG history. The English voice acting is fun to hear. In my mind's eye (in addition to being predisposed), the actors sound exactly how I envision the characters to sound. I couldn't escape from hearing their specific voices in my mind when I was reading the silent dialogue.
One of the main complaints about Falcom's games is that they tend to have a slow beginning. I completely agree. The beginning ten hours are a labor of love when I play each game and I kinda doubt the game will go anywhere. By about the 12th hour, everything is set up so brilliantly and convincingly, that you must see things through as a play to the very end, even if that end is yet another 60 hours down the line.
With that in mind, make sure you play this game during a month off of responsibilities; because it will eat up about 60 hours of your life. You'll be very content after that. Not an hour of those 60 wasted!
Next star goes to the killer soundtrack! The Falcom sound team outdoes itself with the best ambience, fight, boss, cinematic music ever! If you do not buy this game, at least purchase the soundtrack or listen to it online in order to get a taste of how epic the music is. Every city, character, sentiment is given a specific music piece, which means that when that music plays out of the blue, you know exactly what will happen. That's a great narrative technique. Nihon Falcom has had over umpteen games to perfect this winning formula.
I'd highly recommend playing the first Trails in the Sky games before playing the Cold Steel, because not only do some characters make a triumphant return, but also the combat system is the same from the Sky trilogy only refined and polished further. I admit it took about three Sky games to really perfect that combat system, and to pick up the small adjustments in this series for me as a veteran player went swimmingly. The next star goes to the game's polished mechanics. When I thought this series could not become more original or polished, out comes Cold Steel.
The graphics one could say is a bit dated even for when this game came out originally, back in 2013 I believe. But again, to play this game is not about the graphics; it's about immersing oneself into Falcom's world. The character models are a bit simple. But the simple designs lend themselves to doing nuanced actions. Characters blush, flirt, cry, dance, shutter, glare, and really convince you that they come alive with their actions. These NPCs again are much more alive than other games from this same era with more complicated graphics.
The final star goes to how the previous factors came together, which was a brilliant result.
5/5 Stars. One of my favorites. Seriously, other corporations need to figure out what Nihon Falcom has been doing for the past coupla decades and crank out games like them. Each one is a serious hit in Japan and in the US. I hope our fanbase grows by the day! Send your love to X Seed to get CS II published!

I CHALLENGE YOU AND YOUR MAGICAL TALKING CAT TO A DUEL! GIANT ROBOTS AT ONE HUNDRED PACES!!!

While I’d otherwise be willing to give the game a thumbs up, this just… Wow. The ending was such a resounding symphony of stupid I’m kind of reeling. I know that in JRPGs, a lot of tropes are to be expected. Oftentimes even appreciated. But, rather than having them highlighted throughout the game, worked in and established as part of the world, this just piled them on full force in the last couple scenes. Imagine if the Lion King ended in a pie fight - that’s how this game’s ending” feels.
Not to mention the final fight was all new nonsense mechanics you’d never encountered before - any game that pulls that immediately loses immense points. Not that the game was perfect - there were way, WAY too many instances of the always infuriating, never excusable “oh, you thought you beat the badguy, but WAIT they were JUST HOLDING BACK!!!” where your hard fought victories amount to nothing. This includes a literal instance where the enemy in question goes “guess I don’t have to hold back!” It’s ridiculous. Victory blue balls.
Including, once again, the “ending”.
Ultimately, while I enjoyed playing this, the “end” was such a rushed, crazy, stupid cliffhanger of holes, logical lapses, and obnoxiousness I have to give it a thumbs down. This just squandered all its promise, and failed completely to deliver.

DOOM is the reboot of the classic first person shooter video game that came out in 1993. DOOM (2016) takes the best parts of the original game and updates them to today's standards. This game is incredibly fun and brutal.
You play as the Doom Marine, or Doomguy, as you wake up in the UAC, a company using Mars and Hell for resources. You are trying to figure out what happened, but mainly rip and tear through some demons. This game has been criticized for its apparent flat story that lacks all the fullness that other games like Wolfenstein: The New Order possess. This game does indeed have a story that isn't as strong as other games, but DOOM is not a story-drived game. The Doom franchise has always been an action driven franchise with the original having hardly any story. The story that this game has meets the middle grounds where it isn't too much story that it can take away from your gameplay experience, and it isn't too little that you have no idea what is going on and why.
As stated before DOOM is an action driven game, and it delivers incredible action gameplay. Right away you are thrown into a room of demons and given a shotgun and you immediatly have to kill them all and stay alive. This game has some of the best action of any first person shooter. It also is insanely fun to run around with the vast variety of weapons killing demons.
Another amazing part of this game is the world. The design of the UAC, Mars, and Hell is so well done. The UAC looks destroyed as it should, Mars looks like a hellish version of Mars, and Hell is frightning and intimidating. Along with the world design, the character design of Doomguy, the demons, and the UAC members you see are also fantastic. The demons have great diversity and look realistic. The bosses are also great examples of fantastic design, all looking like boss characters. And Doomguy looks epic as Hell.
DOOM also has a multiplayer mode, which yes isn't the greatest, but has improved since launch. Has it improved to a state where it is now great? No, maybe just good, or okay. It is probably much more fun just to stick to the excellent campaign. The most annoying part of the multiplayer however, is all the annoying achievements included that completionists would have to achieve. The other feature DOOM includes is a SnapMap mode which allows the player to create their own maps, and this feature is awesome.
One part of this game that cannot go without mention is the soundtrack. Mick Gordon's sountrack for DOOM is the audio incarnation of Hell being ripped in two. It is without a doubt the greatest soundtrack created for a game to date, and the only thing that might top it is the inevitable sequel. Playing the game without this soundtrack would be similar to playing the game without guns, it would feel like something is missing.
DOOM also pays off to the people who grew up playing the original. With secret classic maps hidden throughout, to returning demons, bosses and characters, DOOM offers nostalgia everywhere and without a doubt acknowledges and praises the original two.
In the end, DOOM is an amazing game. It is the perfect way to reboot a game franchise and one of the bests first person shooters there is, just like the original at the time. It is full of non-stop fun and the story is so balanced it doesn't pull you into a cutscene and take you away from the action. The campaign is full of fantastic world design but additionally, aside from the campaign, DOOM offers both multiplayer and SnapMap (which can be played with friends) modes. The soundtrack is awesome and can be bought for only $10 on iTunes so go buy that it is worth it. This game is highly recommended, buy it and play it.

Short and Sweet: "Forgotten Myths is Free2Play Mid-Level dTCG that will appeal to players looking for a card game which is much easier to access for normal players - while diehard players can get into exceptionally high skill ceilings, a new dTCG player will still feel comfortable playing this."
(Note: The "Pay 2 Win" accusation in one review is silliness - out of the dozens of dTCGs I've tried, this is one of the 3 least pay-2-win of the genre, it's by far the cheapest to get into, and one of the two easiest to get a full playset in without spending a dime)
Disclosure:
- I first got directed to look at Forgotten Myths in 2013, in its early alpha stages. Gave my critique then, and forgot about it for the most part (though I did cover the initial starter decks as well, as I am prone to do, being known for TCG coverage)
- A few weeks ago, several active members of the Forgotten Myths community started popping up on my old coverage saying the game was coming to steam and I should come look at all the changes (several of which were things that I mentioned and that they fixed :D)
I will post a video at the end of this review where you can watch the game in action, the first half covers the user interface, costs, etc. and the second half covers gameplay (you can click an annotation to skip straight to the gameplay) - if you don't feel like reading, that will be your best option.
Main Bullet Points:
Pros:
:: Affordable "F2P dTCG" - It is free to play, and it is possible to get a very respectable collection fairly easily wtihout spending real money (in fact, in terms of dTCGs, this is undercosted - it's cheaper than almost every other dTCG out there, and paying money is not required to advance - doing the Single Player campaign alone will net you enough for a few decks, without spending a dime). Community is also fairly active at helping people get the rarer cards they may have trouble getting. You don't need to break the bank or spend months grinding hardcore to get a full playset (unlike Hearthstone/Duelyst/MtG/Hex)
:: Good Entry or Mid-level dTCG - It is an accessible dTCG, simpler than some, but still enough depth of strategy to be enjoyable - diehard MtG enthusiasts probably won't be impressed by its depth, but fans of games like SolForge and the such, will find its got several layers of strategy and a number of nice features.
:: Good Community - the community has always been nice, sure with the surge of Steam players that may change, but there's a strong friendly community that's been there for 3 years, and will help you out. If you see a DoW member, you can usually ask them for help.
Cons:
:: User Interface still a little unpolished - being honest, it could use a little bit of work, it's still fairly rough looking, though it has improved - the gameplay is all there, but there's a few things they could do to make it 'feel' more satisfying (without changing the mechanics, the actual game is fun)
:: Prices are "weird numbers" - this is likely where the "Pay 2 Win" comment is coming from, the crystals are bought in weird amounts, and the costs are weird amounts, making the 'quick math' a little more annoying. They are planning to fix this though and adjust bought emeralds to match this. They were very open to the discussion on it, and took my experience with the genre into account during the discussion.
I can go on further, and if you have any questions about the game, I'm more than willing to answer them myself - as I've gotten nice crash courses in many of the things I missed as a new player.

I'm a huge fan of Magic: The Gathering, and own most of the duels games they have put out, but the last few entries have been pretty disapointing.  Thus, when I see new CCG games come out I rush to give them a try.  Forgotten Myths is one such game and I really wanted to like it, as it seems to have a pretty good combat system and during my play time was bug free, but I found one huge thorn in the otherwise level playing field that forced me to give this game a not-recommended rating.
Pros:
Solid CCG, has what seems to be quite a few cards, factions (colors), and game modes.
Good graphics, smooth animations for the most part, though watching my energy (mana) card animations got old fast.
No game breaker bugs found like crashes, dissconects, etc.
Cons:
Really only one, and that is the huge paywall that is rather transparent at first but once you start trying to earn coins (the grindable free currency) and diamonds (the much less grindable real money currency) it becomes apparent.  Your energy cards come in 3 rarities and add 1, 2, or 3 to your pool when played.  You start with all 1 energy cards, but the computer controlled starting quest enemies soon start throwing down 2 and 3 energy cards, forcing you to play against someone with 2-3 times the resources very quickly.  This is especially apparent because you can be unlucky and not draw an energy card to use every turn.  You computer controlled enemies do not seem have this drawback, as in roughly 50 games I never saw an AI opponent not have an energy card to play untill it had exausted its hand at turn 5-6.  They also seemed to have a 2 energy card (if it was in their deck) about 1/3 of the time in their starting hand.  The ONLY way to get 2 and 3 energy cards is to use diamonds (you dont have enough at the start to even afford one) to buy "energy card" booster packs.  Yup, they shoot you in the foot before you even get started.
TL;DR: This particular free to play game is sadly not free to play.

The Old City: Leviathan is, more than everything, a niche game.
It's basically an atmospheric walking simulator. You drink in the dialogue, the sounds, the things you see and read. But there's barely anything that you can do to cause change in this game. You're more of a passive observer than anything. That's not bad, for certain types of people; but for many it will be.
I personally took joy in piecing together the story of this world. The stories of Jonah and of Solomon.
However there is the issue that both these characters, the ones that are present the most in the story, speak in such a way that it becomes incomprehensible (not only the meaning of their words, but the points they are trying to make). I can't tell if I didn't really get their philosophy because of a failure in comprehending it due to the speech used or for some other reason. And while yes I do recommend to search the references they make to names of mythology and religion if you don't get them at first; I'm not going to pause in the middle of Jonah's ramblings to grab a dictionary. This is not something that you can really do in a conversation and while I understand that it is somewhat fitting of the character, I also believe that this aspect of his speech goes a bit too far.
On Solomon I do not mind it half as much because he's writing it to a reader that is indeed meant to hold his dictionary and use it to "learn about the old world".
But other than this I enjoyed the game a lot, and some of its concepts will stick to me for sure. The environments were great, the ambience given by both sfx and music was unsettling in a lot of parts, putting me on edge even when knowing I should be safe.... Until Jonah started talking loud and clear and pretty much jumpscared me. I'm not joking, this happened a handful of times when inside the deepest parts of Leviathan's belly.
Optimisation-wise... I didn't really had noticeable framerate issues most of the time. The last chapter's particle effects were a killer tho. A framerate killer. Also some textures and parts of the geometry seem to load on the corner of the eye throughout the whole game and motion blur was unable to hide it.
Movement was slow. Very. I know Jonah it taking a stroll here but please, if the man can sprint, let him do so at a decent speed, especially when you may want to backtrack a lot in a chapter. The jump is a laughable one, and imo mostly to use in case you get stuck in a weird corner of geometry.
Long story short: if just wanting to see and explore the areas you see in the store page pictures is exciting for you and you like listening to weird ideas, then this game is probably a good idea for you. It's not even expensive, and given all the visual and auditory detail it has, it's well worth the money despite its shortness.

This game really deserves a thumbs up. There's so much to enjoy about it; impressive scenery, poignant music and enticing narration. But be warned: you will be disapointed. Not in what this game is - afterall it is still quite enjoyable - but at what it could have been.
The game's biggest flaw is the poor writing and it's clear disconnect with visuals. The writing attempts to deliver a mysterious and intruiging narrative but the result is pretentiously wrapped inane babbling. I'm not hating on the narrator. He actually does a great job considering the writing he's working from. His tone and emphasis really manage to produce good product built from crap material.
Another issue is that the level design leaves you with the sense of having missed out on content. It's often unclear which path is the route of progression and backtracking is slow and awkward. The result is you're left with the feeling that you might have missed something cool through the door you didn't open or around the corner of the path you didn't take.
But don't let those two issues detract you from the great expierence still to be had here. There's a lot to appreciate in the effort that went into delivering the gorgeous scenery present throughout the game. Treat this as an explorative game and simply go for a wander and enjoy the sights and sounds. You've been warned though.. There is no interesting story to be found here.

As is common with these sorts of games, the more you bring into it, the more you get out of it. Another aspect of a text-heavy game with a propensity for intellectual musings is how much you engage with the actual content of the game. Whether or not I was capable of engaging or extracting something from this experience is not immediately clear, and naturally it would require some effort through reflection.
At its core, or at least by what the initial impression of Old City: Leviathan intimates, the game is strictly Schopenhauerian. Pessimism is the constant underlining thought, in virtue of the misanthropy of the quotes, the anger in regards to stupidity and lightheartedness, the refusal of people in general to engage with what is morally deemed as “intellectually more important”, and so on. “You will never be content”, the game proclaims. The cynical disgust of this game is one that I know personally, and have tried hard to distance myself from. Old City: Leviathan seem to carry with it the same amount of ambiguity. At the one hand, a rat should be allowed to be a rat, it is its nature to be a rat, to rat. But the human being, with its rationality and faculties of mind is held to a higher standard. Suicide is said to be caused by weak-mindedness (depression), whereas the utilitarian argument is seen as a higher form of reason to commit suicide. Being useless, or thinking you are useless, serves, according to this game's narrator/main character, as a reason to not exist as a functioning human being. The utilitarian argument, however, needs to be limited to the act itself of killing oneself, and derive from the idea of being of as much use or happiness to as many people possible. Any such idea where suicide is seen as the ultimate response to a problem of uselessness, can be solved through means altogether distant from event of death. Hopefully that can be understood well enough, since its elaboration has no real place in a “review”.
A story seems to be connected, but is far from conspicuous or intelligible. It's fragmented, like games of this ilk normally are. Story elements come piecemeal and give you just enough to intrigue you until the next point of exposition. But many of them point to a distinct Nietzschean bent, existential philosophy in general may be applied to a multitude of points in this game, with ease. The game speaks of drinking from the common pools of water, and being released from the confines of these waters by experimenting with other bodies of water, observing their toxicity levels and finding that they are harmless, that they are liberating. What other metaphor could this serve as than the one of State and individual? Of State-philosophy in regards to the nomadic philosophy? The conventional ideas as the obverse of the thinker in solitude? Institution against uninhibited expression and creation of concepts? “I would rather die than to continue to exist with the same unchanging fruits of an undiscovered tree”, I would rather die than to continue to exist with the same unchanging facts of an undiscovered source of ground for its existence. Perhaps it is simply what I take from this, which is likely, but I see in it the individual's frustration with the Other, with the outside, with the constructed, with the disingenuous and spurious, with the mindlessness of everyday life and its routines. A frustration so powerful that it feels the urge to maim, crush and stab every notion that may be interpreted as being a mode of that Other, of that conformist thinking. Perhaps even a frustration in regards to shame, an attempt at self-preservation, maintaining one's form, conatus, as Spinoza would call it.
At the same time, there is an aspect of the game that praises discovery. The game in itself is discovery. Albeit a somewhat reduced version of discovery. You choose which way to go, get transported back to where you started and choose a different path. Perhaps that diminishes the idea of free choice here, but discovery is at the core what you do. You do not walk as much as you see and think and read, at least not when reduced to what is remembered and thought about regarding the game. A game like this, to be satisfying, does not need to give you something all the time, it does not need to talk all the time, give you the most exciting things to look at, but it needs to be atmospheric with a proper amount of thickness. It needs to understand sound-design and well-crafted scenes, it needs to understand visual composition and the manipulations coupled with both visuals and sounds. I do believe this game understands this to a large extent. Some scenes were genuinely shocking, to the point where my stomach turned a bit, and I felt truly uncomfortable. That, I felt, was the combination of the writing, the visuals and the audio. Where the music sets the tone, with perfect drones that give this ambiance of discomfort through uneasy rumblings, through distorted singing-tones and even more so: with silence. This is not to say that the entire experience was filled to the brim with highlights, but they are there, and they are solid.
It is always interesting when something creative propounds to stand for something destructive. Where one has yet reached the constructive phase of development. It is easy to tear down the constructs of the former mind, society or whatever, but to rebuild is an entirely different matter. What kind of positivity can be brought, or is there, after the destruction? If one searches for truth, is that truth not then a point of stagnation? What then becomes of the dream of progress? Is progress linear, is it eschatological? Is it always reaching for entelechy? Creativity seems to be entirely different from those endeavors, different than meaning and dreams and fulfillment. Creativity seems to be in itself and for itself, thus making all writing for its own sake, not for the sake of expression or giving, even finding truth, but to create and form structures that are only held up by the strength of their seams. It is pure activity, positive constructionism.
The above view is more of the one found in schizophrenic laughter, as Deleuze and Guattari would have it. Meaninglessness to the point of meaninglessness and pointlessness being moot points, or just nonsensical. A thetic theism in the guise of existentialism, the struggle of privation, the Lack of some kind of God or universal meaning. As there are physical means of obtaining a hidden truth of the world, as if existence changes through insight. Loneliness does nothing but make you alone, and that is the true pain of it. In one of Solomon's notes we can see the classic view of loneliness being the key to finding truth, to gaining the scientific unbiasedness that is so pathetically craved. Despite loneliness, we only have so many ideals to find, and the ones immediately available are the ones we generally associate with intelligence. Science! Mankind! Humanity! Functionality! They are wonderfully revered, even in the lonely. But even this area of thought lies in contiguity with conformity, with conventionalism, with Method, with prescription. Even a lonely person cannot shake their ideals, the ones formed in sociality. What they find is only the arbitrariness of it all, and mistake it for meaninglessness, instead of trying to perceive it for what it is.
The game goes a different direction and finds itself in Cartesian waters, while entirely misunderstanding his grounds for knowledge. There is always an answer to nihilism, and to progression and the Spirit of humanity, and that is the perpetual cycle of pointless argumentation. The circumventions are what are interesting. We find it in Bergson and Deleuze and originally in Spinoza. No matter what counters there are to the existential philosophy of this game, the conversation and core of it is very enjoyable to live through, to think through.

The Old City: Leviathan is  an exploration game in the vein of Dear Esther, albeit with more intellectual depth and more text within a loosely Continental philosophical framework.
The game takes place in an unidentified broken Western city, where among things the water supply has been contaminated. The surrounding civilisation have collapsed. We play a more or less insane sewer dwelling isolationist and get quite a bit of insight into one other isolationist - Solomon through finding his journal entries. Besides the surrounding environment.
The game invites us to piece together an ambiguous and murky story as the plot unfolds.
Nice mystery atmospheric narrated exploration game.

'Mixed' sums up my feelings the best.
Superficially, the game looks fantastic, has wonderful art direction and really nails that dreamlike feeling, and the OST only matches or exceeds that in quality. Production wise I have absolutely zero complaints, so well done on that front.
It's the story where things get mixed. The atmosphere and general questions about the presented world are interesting and throughout playing I continually wanted more, but in terms of writing there could be some improvement. The game follows two protagonists, one being the avatar you control and another whose letters you find throughout the game. It's a simple enough format, but the prose throughout is needlessly complicated. I get artistic expression and language as art etc. etc., but once it sounds or reads like a college student trying to pad an essay, a line has been crossed. I suppose in some way it fits with the (heavily used in the game) concept of a minotaur and the attempt to navigate the maze that is the mind... but when the philosophy behind it all is neither groundbreaking nor detailed, the whole thing comes off as pretentious.
Not to say that's an entirely bad thing. Yes, the concepts presented aren't actually new. Yes, much of the initial confusion is due to the developer's love of surface level symbolism. Nevertheless, the player is encouraged towards making their own thought, and while you likely have already considered questions such as 'is cruelty necessary?' in Critical Thought 101, is a revisit such a terrible thing?

The Steam controller is a failed experiment. Others have already given in depth hardware reviews, so I will just tell you a little story of the last time I tried to use it.
So, I decided to be lazy and play KOTOR (an RPG) from my couch. This should be an ideal job for the Steam controller right? KOTOR is a slow paced mouse and keyboard game without Xinput support. I spent a little time configuring the controller, then started up the game. After playing the tutorial area and further refining my control scheme, I came up with a setup that worked. It felt awkward, unnatural, and slow but I could certainly play the game with the Steam controller with some effort.
Then I realized I was hungry and that I would start a new game another time now that the controller is sorted out. So, I picked up my budget priced wireless mini-keyboard to exit the game and put my computer to sleep. The mini-keyboard is just a $10 cell phone sized bar with keys and a laptop style mouse track pad. It's very handy for casually operating my PC from across the room. Then I realized something...
It was far easier to play the game with that little piece of junk that it was with the controller andd it required zero effort to set up. I absolutely do not recommend the Steam controller for any purpose as there is always a better, and cheaper, tool for the job.

By Mike Walter, the author of "Life of a Wizard" and "The Lost Heir" trilogy. Three works that has a lot of point in common, quality being one of those point. Well-written, well thought, a lot of statistics taken in account and a lot of specific event tied to how you developped your character.
Some negative point being : 1.despite the numerous choices, in the end the outcome might seem similar 2.I think Mike Walter is a great plot and story writing author but each time he doesn't make fleshing out his character a priority, in those stories (which are great) you barely have the time to get to know the protagonists like the romance or the main side-kicks. It's not that there is nothing about them, it's just the minimum. 3.the end always seems to come a little too fast, especially in life of a mobster, there is not much said on the consequences and it's a little like "okay, finished, done"
I had a lot of fun testing the different way you can experience the story but once you did a few run-through you pretty much saw 90% of the game and there is just a few text changes here and there. So I think all those choices are like a big storyline with variations and not really a novel that gives clear different path. That's not really a problem though, just a fact.
Overall Mike Walter is one of my favourite CYOA so far and Life of a Mobster didn't disappoint me. You're not forced to play a character you don't recognize yourself into, the story is believable and you read through it easily. Sometime you're overtaken by the "meta" side of the title, but I actually think it's positive. Just take a break and dip in again later, the story still has some lenght to it.

Wow, this truly was an experience!
If you are the kind of person who are completely sold on neat graphics and extreme sound, this maybe wont give you much, as this completely builds on intellectual construction and the ability to imagine.
Think of it as reading an interactive book, where you direct the narrative to a certain degree in order to better suit your own liking.
The more you are able to 'read between the lines' the better and more giving this will get.
And if you are gifted with some stable second sight this will be even more satisfying as you will be in for a 'ride'.
The story is extremely well written in easy to understand language. It incorporates all the necessary jargon for this particular genre to make it immersive and 'alive'.
I really did not know what I was getting into when I bought this, but this will completely blow your mind if you are open minded. As the layering in the story is really great, the patterning and subtle and obvious red lines are lovely.
I write this as I have made my first run, the most 'innocent' and honest one, as I could not rely on any experience in the patterns or what was to be expected.
If you wish to experience something that is not totally built to be visually and auditory stimulating, then this is for you.
Get your favorite music playlist running and immerse yourself.
The only tip I can give to you as a player is to be honest, see it as a kind of personality test. Think metaphorically and what you truly would do in such situation and go on in the choices. The outcome will be actually pretty spot on, in metaphor, one way or another.
The only remark I would like to make to the developers is that it would be nice to have the option to get a dark background with white text, as it is much more soothing for the eyes, and also helps with easing the distraction from the mental imagery.
All in all, I am pleasantly surprised, this went far above my expectations!

Anguished is a game made in RPG Maker MV. And it shows. Forrest Keel uses a lot of the game's default assets, including tilesets and music, and used the built-in character creator for his characters. But enough about the assets, let's talk about the gameplay. The story is really shallow -- or at least, what little I've seen of it, since there's this chase scene literally two minutes into the game that is near-impossible to get past. Furthermore, there's a very limited range of view that makes the whole thing really tedious. It's like playing Mario Kart in near pitch-black with a steamroller on your tail. And the worst part is, they completely removed any way to close the game normally, forcing you to use ALT+F4.
Long story short, don't buy this game, not for $0.99, not for 50 cents, not even for a single dime. It's a wonder how Anguished even got greenlit in the first place...

Due to my love for Dear Esther, I had nabbed this walking sim during a sale as it seemed equally promising. Sadly, it's not even close. Just as a forward, I'm going to be making several comparisons to DE, because I do think this game was inspired by DE and wanted to reach the same sort of audience.
To start, the story--or lack thereof. Through notes posted about, we discover that this is a post-apoc world, there a three warring factions, with "Minotaurs" (aka you) being a semi-fourth. The factions fight over ideologies, while Minotaurs remain as loners. Our narrator waxes on about ideas and dreams, but it's mainly a bunch of truisms. Nothing of inherit interest. Like no duh, you have to take that risky first step to get anywhere. But the biggest fault is that I. Don't. Care. There is no heart or emotion. Even when you witness death, there is no personal connection. Contrast this with DE, where the story revolves around one man dealing with the grief of a lost loved one; the poor sod is sharing these emotions and letters with you, and you come to understand what he's feeling.
Also, the game up front informs you that the narrator is unreliable, as if I'm too dumb to figure that out. Sorry to break it to the devs, but the unreliable narrator trope is extremely old. Anyone who has read a few dozen books will have encountered it.
I do give the voice actor a lot credit, because he tried. It's just a shame that the material was so lacking in heart.
If you collect all of Solomon's notes, you get the equivalent of a novella in-game. However, I found the writing too "fluffy", again lacking in substance. You need to get to the damn point if you want to keep your reader around.
The environments are nice and varied, although too often the textures are low-res. I thought DE looked better.
There is more exploration than DE, but too often you're backtracking which adds to the tedium. A couple times the split paths looped around, which I appreciated, it just didn't happen often enough.
Music is excellent, adds much to the atmosphere.
So yeah, I can't recommend. There's potential, but the writer went way overboard and forgot why we read stories in the first place: to be entertained. And I wasn't entertained.

A walking sim. That about says it all for those who have no interest in walking sims. But for those who like walking sims, I believe you will like this one for several reasons: 1) graphics are good;  and 2) story, while overwrought philosophically and psychologically, has a positive message (no sophmoric nihilism or political correctness here such as ruined the mod Enderal for me). Cons: 1) self-taught life lessons passed off as a kind of neo-existentialism (very boring); 2) Should have taken a page from Milton and written it as poetry (much easier to accept without understanding); and 3) voice acting and narration done in such a way that was grating; and 4) too much meaningless meaning, which could have been mitigated by better voice acting and writing.
All in all I recommend the game to those who like walking sims. I also recommend it to those who can tolerate, even forgive,  poorly written philosophical angst.
In short, this is my opinion. I liked it.

The Old City: Leviathan is a surreal, walking simulator from PostMod Softworks. Let’s get rocking.
The Good
Easily the best thing about TOC:L is the soundtrack. The soundtrack for this game is done by Atrium Carceri (a Swedish musical project by the talented Simon Heath). If you’re not familiar with his work, you should make yourself familiar with it. It’s hard to find better dark ambient music than Atrium Carceri. That being said, the soundtrack for TOC:L is easily on par with his other work.
This game looks beautiful. The city is intriguing. There’s nothing really lacking in the graphics department here.
The Bad
For whatever reason, the monologue that you are forced to hear as you wander through the city is not good. I, personally, felt that it sounded pretentious; plenty of useless, big words were thrown in to make the story feel smarter than it actually is. Whoever did the writing, did this game a real disservice.
The Meh
As I stated above, the monologue is, at best, the ramblings of a middle school student trying to get a C+ on an essay for English class. If the devs had chosen to only tell the story through written and/or visual clues, that would have been so much better.
Verdict: Nay
If you can get this one for dirt cheap, or free, yeah, it’s probably worth a playthrough. Honestly, though, your money would be better spent by just buying the OST.

I'm pretty surprised at all of the positivity in the reviews. The pay off you get compared to the time you spend clicking & stat building & quick saving is not enough. In my opinion there is hardly any pay off at all. Maybe it just feels this way because of how long it is between moments with the characters, but you barely even talk to them other than the little bits at home. & those little bits get repetitive very, very quickly. I realized after a few hours that I wasn't really having fun, & I wasn't really enjoying the stories of the routes either. It doesn't feel like there's any chemistry between the boys + Heejung, & when there is it feels forced which is unfortunate because this takes place over the course of a year, so it should feel more natural than other games. In games like these you want the player to feel invested, so that when good / bad / romantic - anything happens - the player will feel something. If a player isn't invested, they're not going to give a crap about what happens in a story or to a character. Which is why I'm surprised so many people loved this. I'm the type of person to easily get sucked into stories & care about it's environment & it's people, but during this I just felt like I was going through the motions, which NEVER happens to me. It was to the point that when I reached the endings I was like "k next".
I didn't HATE the game, & it was well made (other than translation - typos galore. there was one place where something important was happening & it was spelled wrong & had :.}} after it... really takes you out of the environment which was already lacking). The voice acting was great, & music was okay, most of the drawings were really good. I can see there was effort but for me it just didn't add up unfortunately.
I don't know, I liked Nameless & Mystic Messenger, but this really fell flat for me. This is probably my least favorite VN I've ever played. I understand that it was their first game, though, & I'm glad Cheritz has gone on to make (imo) better things.

NARUTO SHIPPUDEN: Ultimate Ninja STORM 4 is a fun, 3D arena fighter that while being simplistic in design can take a while to master. It has its flaws but is still worth playing and is a must have if you like the Naruto Manga or anime. STORM 4 continues where STORM 3 left off (STORM Revolution being ignored other than one or two fights), and focuses on the last arc of the 4th Great Ninja War, including Obito’s decent into darkness and why he became the masked man, Sasuke reviving the previous Hokage, the 10 tails battles, Kabuto’s redemption, the final battle against Kaguya and the final battle
between Naruto and Saskue.
There are now forks in the story progression, which allows for you to break up the story of who you are using (eg Naruto or Sasuke). You still have to do all of the battles in the arc to move onto the next chapter, but it lets you mix it up if you are getting bored of using certain characters.  I found this time around a lot of the battles are a lot harder - the enemies have four health bars to your two, and there are a lot of interactive battles (press a button at a certain time). To get an S rank you also need to finish with over 90% health and there are no recovery items (no ninja tools)- this makes getting a S rank a matter of grinding some missions (there’s only one mission that had me screaming at the screen- whoever made the Might Guy vs Madara fight needs to be taken out back and beaten.  You can just select the Movies and stills to watch (once you have beaten the corresponding fight), so it’s nice that you can re-watch the game at a later date.
The game is animated very well, and the main game is voiced all the way through. For some strange reason, some missions have a full cut scene while some are just stills with a voice over. It does distract from the experience, luckily not many missions have the stills/voice over so it’s like playing the Anime. I found that this game focused a lot on the villain’s, you play a fair chuck of the game as Tobi, the masked man, Obito, Kubuto. It was interesting to do the some of the fights from previous games from a different perspective, but that does seem to be a lot of what Naruto is about. As with the previous games, most of the fights devolve into a spamming combo’s, ninja attacks, and ultimate’s. Since they all have different ranges and ways of connecting, it does turn into a game of rock paper scissors until you have a good take on the opposition. The music sounds like it has in all the other STORM games, likely it has been reused, which isn’t a bad thing as I’m sure some of it comes from the Anime.
There are plenty of customization that can be done, some things unlock from playing the game and DLC’s, other things have to be purchased in “the store” (Naurto’s in game store where you trade money and items you have picked up from battles for title cards, pictures ect)
Adventure mode plays much like STORM Revolution, you have your town, places to visit and people that need help. There are plenty of grindy quests to be done in all of them, but they are much easier (Ninja tools).  A trial of the gales plays like Sakura’s dating service, trying to set Naurto and Hinata up together- it has its moments of humor and is obviously set before the Naruto: The Last movie. There are a few DLC packs that can be purchased, Shikamura’s DLC focuses on Shikamura and the other ninjas of the hidden leaf, following their progress after the final battle. It is heavily tied onto Gaara’s DLC, as they follow the same meeting between the Hokage and the Kazekage, but from different viewpoints. It’s also fun watch Ino try and set Shikamura and Temari up before turning her attention towards Sai. After the meeting with the Hokage, Gaara leans what is means to be the Kazekage from the other Kage. A lot of the battles use different characters other than those used in the main story, and since the cast is very large it’s a good way get players to use some of the less used characters. One of the features that I thought was missing was ring outs, but they do appear (infrequently) in the adventure mode.
Boruto’s tale follows the plot of the Boruto movie, but plays much the same as above.  Majority of adventure mode is just stills with voice over the top instead of being fully animated- I thought this was a shame and let adventure mode down compared to the main game.
There is a fair choice of stages to select, and some of the stages have destructible backgrounds (Konoha village is a great example. I thought this was a very nice touch, and I don’t remember seeing it in the previous games). There are other stages that have some obstacles on the course, which can help/hinder depending on your character.
The survival and tournament league make a return- for more grindy achievement fun.
If you are chasing 100% achievements then it’s possible, but be prepared to grind some of them out. At least there’s no RNG so once you know what you are doing, it’s just a matter of putting it into practice.

Well, I lost my previous review that I was typing, so let me break it into points:
1) Tribes has never been an easy game to learn, and spinfusors have existed since day one. They are not overpowered, as they are one of the slowest projectiles. With practice you can learn to reduce and even avoid their impact on you once you learn the Game's mechanics.
2) I understand that some players like to earn their equipment and weapons through experience and practice. Planetside 2 does this well. However, the original Tribes games did not require this, as all equipment was unlocked right out of the box to allow more customization for players. Hi-Rez doing so was a better move for all players, but especially Tribes Veterans.
3) I know the tutorials in T:A suck. Hi-Rez failed the newbies miserably with that, as the original games (including Tribes: Vengeance, the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child of the series) had much more extensive and helpful tutorials geared for new players joining the universe for the first time.
4) My biggest complaint for the current state of the game is the absolute absence of two major tribes the CotP (Children of the Phoenix) and SW (Star Wolf) and the lore behind the Diamond Sword and Blood Eagle. There is NO lore with T:A, which was one of the things that got many players introduced and interested when the first games came out. Sure, by T:A, it would be ancient history, but the history was extensive, and interesting. The special edition of the Starsiege pack included instruction booklets with stories written by the devs and players, as well as the Starsiege Compendium, which was essentially the wookieepedia (Star Wars wiki) for the Tribes universe, in printed format with some fantastic art. I would give a lore breakdown here, but this is a review unfortunately, so that would have to wait.
But, if this piques your interest, try google, and start searching for information with the title "Earthsiege".
5) I have loved this game since it first came out. While it lacks the lore and explanation of the universe you are fighting in, it does well preserving the gameplay of the older entries in the series. The game has a learning curve, but once you catch on, offers combat that I dont see in many other games, and I love it. (Next Closest games I can think of are the Section 8 games) The action is fast paced and brutal, I know. But that is why we Tribes veterans love it so much.
6) Look for me (Talamaeus) or others in game and you might find that many, many veterans would eagerly help you learn the mechanics of the game. Just ask around when you enter a match, or before the actual match starts. The tribes community, once thriving and fairly large, is indeed dwindling, but we would gladly help newbies with the game if you just ask. We want Tribes to live on, so just give the game a shot, make some friends, and maybe you can get the time learn why so many of us love Tribes.
TL:DR
This game is not as broken as it appears, but the lack of tutorial and guidance left by Hi-Rez is likely why you are having issues with the game. Give it a chance and ask around. Maybe some of the veteran players would help you learn the game so that you too can enjoy it.
As for it's "random existance" among shooters, The universe in Tribes has actually existed since the 90s with the Earthsiege games, but the universe as a whole kinda disappeared after 2003.
For more information on the universe you are fighting in, go to google, and start with a search for "Earthsiege".

This is a "middle thumb" game. At the point of writing this, I've done somewhere between a third and half of the puzzles, and I do plan on finishing the rest of them. It's not bad, it's just no where near as good as it could (and for $10, really should) be.
The art for each puzzle is fine, but a bit generic. It doesn't really feel representative of the diversity that anime has to offer. Most of it would be at home in shoujo manga. A few of the puzzles have a bit of a cyberpunk flair, but that's about it.
There are some significant shortcomings to the gameplay. Let's get the worst out of the way first. When I played Ocarina of Time as a kid, I was never annoyed by Navi. The fairy in this game, however, is the WORST. Her lines are terrible. You can hide her, true, but she reappears at the start of every new puzzle. The game doesn't remember your "fairy setting." Not only that, but turning off the fairy turns off your ability to use the hint powers that the game offers. You would think that the game would still fill the hint meter with or without the fairy visible (or more importantly audible), but it doesn't. If the game doesn't show the animation for the fairy granting your your hint power, you just don't get it.
Second, I don't know what is up with the jigsaw shapes in these puzzles, but they can be pretty bad. Like, I'm embarrassed for them, bad. I'd much rather play with "boring," normal-shaped jigsaw pieces than with pieces that have little dragon cut-outs or other awkward shapes.
Next, why are my jigsaw pieces moving? The pieces that aren't on your board constantly float and bounce around in the background, making any kind of sorting impossible, unless you fill up the whole board, and usually overlap the part of the puzzle you've already completed. The game offers a "tray" that you can pull out or put away, where you can store pieces without putting them on the board, but it's really too small to be useful for much.
The "snap" radius of the puzzle pieces seems way too high. If you set a piece down in the right general area (facing the right direction), the piece will snap to the part of the board that it is meant to go on. That would be fine, but I've seen some pieces jump as far as the piece is wide. It can feel like the game is solving itself.
Finally (and this is perhaps my biggest complaint), why can't I lock two fitting pieces together without knowing exactly where on the board to put them? If I've found a pair of peices that go together, I should be able to snap them together and treat them as a unit, just as I would do if I were solving a physical jigsaw puzzle. Discovering that two pieces go together in this game is pretty much useless unless one of them has already been snapped to the board.
Overall, I would rather be able to zoom and pan, and solve the puzzle anywhere, than have a specific "magnetic" board where every piece has a predetermined spot that it will snap to. Microsoft Jigsaw on Windows 10 does a good job at replicating a jigsaw puzzle experience in this way, however, that game doesn't require you to rotate your pieces—they are always facing the right direction. I do like how this game makes me figure that out. Another thing that this game could have done is offer multiple difficulties for every picture, rather than just one size of puzzle per image. Some images are 60-piece puzzles, while others are 220-piece, with other sizes between, but there's really no reason why each image couldn't have an option for any size.
I'm mostly enjoying this game, even if I find some of the mechanics frustrating, but I did recieve it for free as a gift. Unless you're really into jigsaw puzzles, or don't think that the things that I don't like would bother you, I don't recommend buying it, at least not at full price.

With this Anime-themed one specifically, it more or less just appeals to those who are attracted to anything that looks anime since every image in the game look like original work; if they're from somewhere, then I don't know where. For every other random piece you magnetize on the mat and for every few minutes or so, you get "pixel dust". Depending on how much of that you have, you can use one of three abilities–like in the previous game–to possibly help you put pieces in the right location somewhat faster.
The pixel dust comes from this little floating fairy thing that gets in the way of a small part of where the puzzle pieces float around. She's a nuisance even though she's meant to be helpful. She'll randomly talk while you're doing a puzzle and her "humor" is just something I couldn't bear a minute of. You can press DELETE while doing a puzzle to get rid of her entirely but you'll no longer get the advantageous pixel dust until you go back to the main menu to bring her back. You also can't mute her without muting the entire game since the only audio option you get is a "sound" slider.
Once more, getting interested in this game is just going to be based on the attraction to the theme of a Pixel Puzzles game and/or actually getting into the premise of the franchise. I never found these kinds of games to be "relaxing" or anything in any way and this particular one felt more like an incredible slog to go through. $10 base price is already too high for something like this.

Cover mechanics are predominant in modern, single-player FPS games these days. You grab a gun, find a wall, and pop bad guys while letting your environment absorb damage for you. Not so in DOOM. This game takes you back to the old days where cover wasn't a thing and quick dispatch of enemies and even quicker evasion were paramount to success. It is hard to imagine this working with a modern game, but it absolutely feels amazing here. You control an unstoppable killing machine who doesn't know the meaning of hide and shoot, blasting demons and tearing them apart as you rip through a series of well designed and gorgeous levels. The action is fluid and satisfying and the visuals are amazing (not to mention superbly optimized, meaning you will get eye candy despite running on a mid-tier and somewhat old gaming rig such as mine). The lore is interesting and kept me yearning for more. Collectibles and achievements exist, but they grant perks that provide you with even more ways to destroy your enemies which just adds to the fun. I would venture to say any FPS fan should play this game. It grants such a departure from what has become the tradition and the execution is near flawless. My only gripes with the game are some very minor annoying bugs that had to do with the notification system on the collectibles screen. Other than that, I did not run into any game-crashing bugs or anything that hindered my overall enjoyment of the game. Absolutely recommend.

Bonus note: Nominate this for the award for the villian that just needs a hug. You are a heartless penguin murdering innocent dinosaurs trying to evolve in peace or eat (looking at you hungrysaurous).
Played every level on the first gamemode, may update this as I complete other modes too.
Gameplay: I had fun playing archaeologist mode where you pick up bones from dinosaurs you defeat to charge up your "ultimate" - a powerful single use ability that comes from a large shotgun blast of bones to a dinosaur friend that kills enemy dinosaurs for a short period. There is also the weapon: your main attack that has a short reloading time, your potion: a recharging potion that is throw to umlease powers to affect dinosaurs or yourself and finally a technique: a recharging abilty to help you in battle (e.g. a knife that drops a heart on kill or a charge).
Controls: Movement is standard WASD. The addition of both a potion and technique can be confusing and I often mix up the two buttons (right mouse and space by default) and after overwatch I think of q as ultimate. The controls can be changed in the options so you can make them suit you better.
Enemies: Dinosaurs have clear roles. Yellow and red ones appear lots but can only attack close up, black one armours up other dinosaurs to have more health, blue and purple have lots of health and can move fast either generally or in bursts causing the player to have to deal with them. Their health is easy to remember when using one particular weapon (e.g. with the first weapon yellows are 1 shot and reds are 2).
Levels: Nearly all levels have unique twists or dinosaurs to them. They have various layouts, settings and spawnpoints for dinosaurs. Some of them can be repetitive with a central area and a couple of walls around it or a large open area with small bits of cover but they are still fun and genrally the levels are different.
Graphics and art style: The art style is cartoonish and simple making the dinosaurs and map clear. The dinosaurs are easily distinguised from one another from each of their unique colours, shapes and sizes although a couple of dinosaurs are a similar shade of green and are harder to distinguish as colour is the easiest to do so quickly. The special parts of maps such as lockboxes and water and easy to spot. The fog is one block colour and could be detailed more (although this isn't a huge issue).
Music: Music is nice, I quite like the tracks particually the one in the trailer video: I would probably have chosen that one for it too if I had too. It's not really loud or distracting to the gameplay.
Menu: Lettering and boxes look great and the how to play is very simple yet informative. Could be more graphical options (e.g. more resolution options) but the simple cartoonish artstyle doesn't need loads of options for this.
Ui: Contains necessary information (health, kills, rank, equiped items, recharge times) however the items and recharge times in the bottom-left are small and looking at them can distract you from the rest of the game. There is lots of empty space on the sides that isn't used and this could easily be enlargened and stuck there. Here is an idea for it:
It would make the recharge bars and item icons a lot bigger and easier to see my using empty space at the side of the screen and also make your health in a more central position. Effects on the dinosaurs and player are shown by small icons making it clear they have been effect but it isn't very clear what some of them do.
Bugs: Twice while playing I got stuck at the very top of the level and could only move side to side but I haven't encountered any other ones.
Conclusion: Really like this game: it had good gameplay, art style and is very clear. Haven't seen many bugs but there is room for improvement in some areas. Get this game, it isn't very well known and I think it deserves to get some more publicity.

Alchemist Penguin is an action, omniscient (overhead, in-case I needed to clarify) shooter game that places you in the feathers of a penguin, who has guns, potions, and knives that he can use at his disposal to kill dinosaurs. There are different stages and gamemodes to play, as well as many different weapons and abilities to unlock. Yet overall, the fact that you're a penguin with a gun (BOOMSTICK!!!) already sounds downright sick because penguins with guns is already on the market here.
So, this game actually resembles some type of shooter-arcade game, and so when I looked at it and first started playing it, I had the expectations of that of an arcade game. Playing it for about an hour, it just
like an arcade game: one has their simple controls and weapons, and you basically run and kill enemies and dodge projectiles. Turns out, I was very blown away by the content and integrity of the game. Each enemy being different, each stage having their own unique dynamics and obstacles, and overall, it seems like a Binding of Isaac that mated with a Zelda: The Minish Cap because of the gameplay and how the game actually functions as an overhead-shooter.
Now, the game itself is fun, and when I first started playing it, I had some unconcious nostalgia because this game reminded me of an old arcade game I used to play as a kid, but I couldn't remember the name of it. Anyway, buying this game for $1.99, it was
worth the price because there is so much one can do in this game. Once one finishes almost the entirety of the game, one can level all their weapons, potions, and special abilities to max levels, and try to go for the highest tier ranking for each level, all of which makes the player play more and more, and better enjoy the achievement and progress the game provides. The game urges one to progress more by playing more, and I told myself I'd play only an hour before reviewing this game, which I managed to do successfully without getting carried away.
In addition, the game itself is not all that easy, nor is it too easy, or too hard, but just in-between. As one prolongs their stay in a particular stage, different dinosaurs with more health and utility begin appearing, and that creates challenge. While I appreciate challenge, if it is impossible, it isn't fun. However, the way the Devs created the game and the AI, the challenges are possible to overcome, and if completed, makes the game more fun and "meaningful" (yes, I'm serious) to the player. Speaking of AI, they are intelligent AI, particularly with the ones that shoot projectiles; they make the game fun because of dodging.
The music in this game is... okay. It was not the best type of music in a videogame, where it might be good for a medieval setting, but for an arcade-esque game, the music is
better than others. The graphics are slightly pixel-lated and geometric (by geometric, I mean large usage of simplistic shapes like squares and triangles, combined or sliced to create a figure), so if expecations included HD or some form of realistic texture, one won't find it here.

Ultimately, this is going to be a very subjective review, because ultimately, your experience with this game is going to depend heavily on how you feel about some very specific details. The Great Whale Road is a fresh take on the Banner Saga formula, using the Banner Saga engine. If either of those things has already put you off, you're probably not going to have a good time playing this. On the other hand, if you adore everything about Banner Saga, this might still not be what you're looking for. Let's dig a bit deeper, and I'll show you what I mean by that.
The Great Whale Road is largely an economic sim, but one that plays out slowly and is punctuated by battles. You have a village that generates resources for you, you have a ship that takes them out to trade with other villages, and you have a warband for when those trades go poorly. Your village is made up of several different meters, measuring population, happiness, and food supply. It also provides a range of bonuses to your warband, enhances your ship, and farms different kind of resources depending on what you upgrade and where you assign your population. Of course, to upgrade your village, you need specific goods, which come from trading. Meanwhile, your warband relies on equipment, which must be purchased by liquidating goods into hacksilver. These three elements of gameplay, taken together, make for a really engaging experience, where you're juggling your warband's ability to keep pace with the story fights vs your village's economic growth vs. your trading party's profitability.
Unfortunately, that's only about an eighth of the game.
And this is where the Great Whale Road falls flat.
90% of gameplay is watching a little boat sail for a few minutes, maybe clicking a response on a timed random event, then pulling into port, browsing several shops, assigning some people to hunt, selling the meat you get, and leaving. And if that sounds boring, yes. Yes it is.
The actual plots of the three campaigns (all of which are pretty long, but would be much shorter without the boring filler of sailing to fifty bland identical villages just to complete a single quest) are pretty good, and it's possible that the choices you make in them even matter. I can't be too certain about that, since a lot of your choices feel like Telltale decisions, but the writing is immersive and well-researched regardless, and I found myself liking even the characters that got only a few lines of dialog.
Like Banner Saga, the art here is pretty good--although not quite as breathtaking. It makes the samey oceans and samey villages more tolerable, and visiting a town for the first time is even kind of cool.
Unfortunately, here's where the game takes another dive.
Combat is boring. On top of that, combat is broken. Once you figure out how to play, you will never lose a fight.
Battles take place on a hex grid, Banner Saga's Armor and Strength system has been replaced with a more complex, more RNG-based health and armor system, and attacks have three damage types. Weapons have multiple hits, and the more hits the better a weapon is. Weapons also have different ranges, and units can go into counter-attack mode, striking out at the first person to wander into their range. Each hit has a chance of landing based on your unit's accuracy and your enemy's evade, but there's also a block chance on top of that. If your attack isn't evaded, it might still be blocked, dealing its damage to armor instead of health. Weapons have three types of damage, slashing, bashing, and piercing. Slashing glances off of armor, bashing deals a point of extra armor damage, and piercing deals both armor and health damage. If you whittle down a target's armor, you can swing straight at their health without a block chance, which usually results in a kill.
So, the way the game was designed, you're supposed to use bashing to create an opening, and then lay in with slashing for the kill. Or, alternately, pick away slowly at an enemy with piercing.
Which would work fine, if spears didn't exist.
The thing is, spears have two tiles of range, they have the highest damage output, they match the next best class for number of hits, and nearly all of them have the coveted peircing damage type. On top of that, the spear-using class, the Heavy, has an early special ability that pours on a bunch more hits. Taken all together, this means that building a good combat party is mostly about taking every Heavy you have, with a few Assault classes taken to fill in the gaps. By early midgame, combat is usually wrapped up in a turn or two, although even so, the cumbersome combat interface means it drags.
If that weren't enough to make this a diamond in the rough, the whole economy element is trivialized by the way food works. Both your town and your trading party need food to survive, so it should be a thing that you'd want to conserve, but each town has a hunting spot where you can just haul billions of rabbits out of the bushes, field-dress them, and pack them instantly into what I can only assume are Nordic MREs. This makes provisioning for journies a matter of taking as little as possible, so that your burly warriors can go out into the trees and come back with armfuls of stoats. You then sell your food at a premium, go through an obnoxious screen transition, and go hunting again.
Midway through your first quest, if you're doing things right, you're rolling in hacksilver.
And that's without doing the hunting dogs glitch.
(Did you know that when you send one dog out to hunt, sometimes you get dozens back? The Viking erra was a strange time indeed.)
So, where does all of this leave us?
At a very unfortunate conclusion.
I enjoyed this game. Unsanded edges and all, I liked what it had to offer, I enjoyed its setting and story, and I suffered through all its sub-optimal design decisions to get more of what it had to offer. It's not going to be everyone's preferred brew, but it's got a definite flavor to it.
If you're looking for something quick and polished, this isn't for you. But if you got really excited about any of the elements I mentioned, this is worth a try. I would advise picking it up on 50% sale, but I think the devs are worth supporting, and I would dearly like to see what they have in the pipeline next.

On the plus side, the atmosphere is incredible and I love the sailing gameplay. The artwork and the story are great. The game feels really nice despite a few object clicking issues where you need to move the mouse around but not a big deal.
I love the village management aspect and the story-based decision making parts (very reminiscent of Banner Saga if you're familiar.)
On the bad side of things is the initial combat in the first few hours.
I didn't know how it felt to chew five-gum until I played the combat in this game.
I get 4 guys for the first few hours and I just had to fight 7 enemies. All of them hit for 8 damage every turn. I am lucky to hit for 2-3 damage every 4 attempts.
I love a challenge and tactical combat games are usually a piece of cake for me but this is different. I had to take a break after 2.5 hours cos I felt like smashing my head through the monitor.
Basically I love everything about this game but the combat would drive a man insane. Not saying nerf it, but maybe don't let the player get abused before they've even started the game properly.
I recommend it regardless of my own issues with the combat.

This is a story-driven game involving watching/building stats for various things in your Viking village, while your warriors go on seafaring quests to defeat enemies in turn-based combat and return with the spoils.
You start the game in your home village and learn that all the best warriors have been killed by the Saxons on a voyage to England. You've been (half-heartedly) voted in as the new chief and it's your responsibility to restore the fortunes of the village and ultimately avenge the deaths of your friends.
First of all you have to manage your village by assigning points to various aspects such as farming, diplomacy, craftsmanship etc. Then it's time to set off on a quest. You select which warriors you want to take with you and stock up on enough supplies, repair tools and trading items to sustain you on however long the voyage is due to last, and then off you go. As you sail along, multi-choice dialogs pop up with various scenarios and you have to decide on options such as attack, investigate, trade etc. which have positive/negative/neutral outcomes. Occasionally you have the option to stop off at various villages where you can replenish your strength by doing some trading, hunting, resting and perhaps upgrade your weapons. At this point there is usually some kind of challenge to invite you for some combat. It's possible to decline one way or another, but of course this will incur penalties.
Once you're done with the side-village it's on to the next one, or else you can keep sailing on to the main destination. As you visit villages they are revealed on the main map, and the overall story unfolds.
It's turn-based combat on a hex board. It uses the common style whereby you place your fighters at one end of the board and then move them within a range that's lit up. Depending on the type of weapon, you sometimes have a choice of two types of attack - blunt attacks are best for lowering defence before the penetrating slash/pierce attacks - or you can choose to defend. Weapons have various stats, some have longer reach, others are better for specific types of attack etc. You also have a certain number of 'Warcry' points you can use to boost your fighers for one turn - you get extra Warcry points when you defeat an enemy, and lose them when your own crew members die.
Call me a philistine if you like, but I'm a modern gamer who has come to expect games to teach me how to play by example, being shown what to do, and starting off gently. Here we have the old-school philosophy of reading instructions and then applying them afterwards. And these are pretty complex instructions, especially for someone not familiar with this genre. I was about to say I forgot most of it each time I had to scroll through several dialogs explaining the small details of what I was about to do next, but then I realised that was not entirely true. The fact of the matter is that those instructions might as well have not existed at all. Not a single item of information penetrated my cranium. I found myself performing the usual procedure of clicking everything to see what options were available, using my experience from other games, and generally playing it by ear. This is the normal way of doing things, isn't it?
Nobody enjoys reading instructions and user manuals at the best of times, even for flat-pack furniture and stuff like that, but this is a GAME. It's not 1990 any more, I really shouldn't be forced to do that.
Due to the tutorial methods being so awful, this makes the learning curve unacceptably steep. The game starts with a one-day quest which I managed to win, but it was nothing more than a quick test. The first proper 12-day quest I attempted was a failure. I seemed to be outnumbered in every battle. Lost them all. Lost a warrior each time, making the next battles even more one-sided. My whole party was soon dead and I was offered the option of either reverting to my last auto-save point or starting again from scratch. I have to admit, neither option was very appealing.
There are no overall difficulty settings. It looks like you have to just keep replaying until you get the hang of it, or else study the text-based tutorials to improve your understanding and make better progress. I'm sure there must be ways to defeat enemies with superior numbers on their side, but the methods to reach that stage of competence seem like drudgery to me.
Graphics are pleasant enough with some nice watercolour scenes but the game is more focused on function rather than form. Animations are sparse and basic, but do the job well enough. Music and effects are what you would expect, not much to report.
Trading cards have already been added and achievements have been promised although they haven't appeared yet. Steam Cloud support has not been mentioned, and I would very much like to see this added. It would be very useful for dual-booters like myself, since the game is fully cross-platform.
It's a fair price for the amount of content and complexity of the game. There's no fancy presentation but the underlying game is solid and plentiful.
I suspect there's a worthwhile game here if you have the patience and willpower to persevere with it. All the proper ingredients are included: village building/management stats; unfolding storyline; dialog choices; turn-based combat. But the final product doesn't excite me, I'm just not 'feeling it'. The 'RTFM' style of tutorial is a particular annoyance that in my opinion doesn't belong in modern gaming, except in games like TIS-100 (look it up and you'll see my point). Combine that with throwing you in at the deep end with no easy levels to get you into the swing of it, and this is a recipe for frustration.
I always try to 'get over the hump' with games like this that block me from further progress in the early stages. In this case I wanted to experience some more of the storyline, but after several hard attempts I just couldn't get past the difficult combat.

This is definitely not for everybody. If you want something that will do what your Xbox or Playstation controllers do, you don't need this thing.
The Steam controller can play controller-centric games fine. But you don't need it to do that; you already have controllers for that. What you need this thing for is:
1. Playing first person games better than a typical controller. You probably still won't want to use this in multiplayer vs. people using keyboard & mouse, but the right touchpad is so much better than an analog stick it's a wonder nobody has done this before.
2. Playing games with control schemes that regular controllers can't handle.
The beauty of this thing is the insane degree to which you can customize it. Unfortunately this is also sort of a con: the fact that you can customize it so much means that to really make good use of it, you have to.
But hey. You probably built a computer to play games, right? How hard is changing some controller settings?
