All Jettomero wants when he woke up was to help the humans out. The last thing he wants is to wipe them out on each and every planet that he happens to visit. Destroying one building is bad enough! Unfortunately, the way he was designed goes against his wishes. And well, being pelted by the humans doesn't help much when it can send your foot flying through a building. Surely the humans can't understand him, after all Jettomero's size brings in a lot of misunderstanding to his true intentions of landing on their planet.
Jettomero is not just a small robot, but a towering one. One that when he lands on the planet, created dents in the planet. Walking around may not create prints, but certainly has enough power to kick buildings out of the atmosphere. Even the moon has no chance as it will shatter into pieces if you run into it. Asteroids and comets liters each galaxy, but one direct hit and the shatter as well, while storm clouds in space can suck out his fuel. Each planet does generally look the same, as there are only two variations, but there are some extra things to do. If you like customization, each planet has at least two signals that when stomp on will show you which part you unlocked. There are also some random events that can happen. There can be a forest fire, a building set ablaze, a nasty storm happening, or a pile of rubble that suspiciously looks like someone may be trapped under it. Though as you can guess, brings in even more destruction even if Jettomero’s intentions were good. In addition, one planet will have an enemy that he will go face to face against in a QTE fashion. The difficulty of these do adjust to how you're doing in them, so the timer might get a little bit faster or require you to push more buttons if you previously did well. Once you defeat it, you will be able to explore the other planets if you haven't already, go through the wormhole, or decode a message. Just make sure to gather some fuel so you can lift off or find a volcano to help you.
With Jettomero having no memory of where or why he was created, each time you finish off an enemy, it unlocks a back issue that you have to decode. This serves as the driving force to continue for both the player and Jettomero. Of course, the twist the story has can be predictable if you pay close enough attention to the humans and who they attack. Once you find out the truth, you can choose between two endings. I do recommend going for both as one ending is shorter than the other, which does give you more story and even more satisfying ending.
Even when Jettomero has its own story and personality, the player also has their own hands in Jettomero. In turn this tells something about you in this situation. There is no penalty to kicking and stomping buildings, but at the same time there are no rewards if you don’t. All the planets, with the exception of the one Jettomero wakes up on, are armed and will not hesitate to attack Jettomero the second you land. The question is, are you someone that can see the misunderstanding and avoid the buildings or are you one that due to this, see it as fair and stomp through? Do you change your mind as you visit more planets? Whatever you choose, Jettomero will still say sorry but will you bring meaning to it.
The controls are incredibly smooth. When you’re flying, it’s as smooth as butter and feels just as good. While on a planet, you get the feel of being clumsy, just like Jettomero, as careful steps can easily turn into disaster for the humans. The only part that does have the controls a little bit more sensitive in the decoding minigame as you can easily go past the letters you want right before you test it out.
The visuals are absolutely great as it gives off the feel that it’s in a comic book. With the more cutscenes for the story you unlock bringing this more into mind as it is set up like a comic book page. With the galaxies bringing in a unique look as the Sun can vary in color but still look great. WIth planets from afar looking more like the sun with its atmosphere giving off millions of dots and once you get closer, getting more in detail as you can see the buildings and weather it might have at that point. With Jettomero looking as the cute robot he is no matter what customization you choose. You also have a variety of filters to choose from when you enter into photo mode, giving you a bunch of opportunities to make appealing screenshots or you can play in a specific filter if you choose to. The soundtrack brings this all in full circle as it does feel like you're traveling through the universe and stumbling on planets.
There are really only two weaknesses this game has, however it’s ones that many people dislike. The first is the length. Exploring every planet is not mandatory by any means, only finishing the enemy battle in every galaxy, so you will be in situations where the enemy is in the first planet you visit. Though the length may be due to the second weakness, the repetitiveness. As throughout you do just go through wormholes, visit planets till you find the enemy, do the enemy battle, and continue on to do the same thing to the next galaxy. Making this a weird balance that the weaknesses are good but bad at the same time.
Jettomero: Hero of the Universe is a very sweet and charming story. A too short of a story with some negatives that does cause this game to become repetitive. I sadly do not see that many people getting this game due to the length, specifically, as it can really be finished when you have a free afternoon. Nice chill game. I love the soundtrack, the visuals, the little cosmetics you can put on Jettomero, it's a charming way to spend a little while to zone out and explore. The story itself is quick, fun and a bit silly.
The only complaints I really have are that every time I've reloaded the game sends me back to the fifth story entry (post-tutorial I think). Once you collect all the cosmetics you just scour planets in each system until you find the one with a monster, and losing progress, while not bad at all to recover from, didn't help with the already repetitive core of the game. You do retain all cosmetics you've found, so it isn't an issue of not saving I don't think, but yeah the story seems to reset while other aspects of the game are saved, even after finishing the story mode I resumed to test it and I was back at the fifth story entry. A bit weird, the game really seems meant to be done in one sitting, but if you take breaks you may find yourself booted back a ways.
The other issue is really minor, but once you reach a certain point near the end a new wormhole appears, but using the signal button guided me to the normal wormhole, sending me to another system to do the same quest step over and over again. There really should only be the one wormhole to take you to the finale, for sake of not getting confused; I did see the second wormholes but I kept following my sensors figuring they were taking me to the right spot to progress. Maybe I misread some dialogue, but the choice seems unnecessary.
Otherwise, I really enjoyed my time with Jettomero, he's a cute giant clumsy destructive robot and the hero our universe needs! Or deserves? Or wants, or doesn't or... Well, he's some kind of hero anyways.

A great jrpg with a fantastic port, featuring additional quality of life options, pc enhancements, and tons of additional, high quality voice acting.
Quality of life includes:
Turbo mode - for speeding through animations you've seen before and wringing every last piece of dialogue out of npcs
Autosaves - comes in 1, 5, and 15 minute varieties
Button prompts for both Xbox and Dualshock controllers
PC enhancements include, but not limited to:
Graphical options including unlimited draw distance, (high quality) depth of field options, 60 fps and unlocked frame rate,
"High" preset graphic options set runs great on older pcs.
KB/M control (I play exclusively with controllers, but the option is there for those who want it)
The game itself is fun to play, but recommended for those who enjoy long stretches of story segments interspersed with combat/exploration segments. The story has a nice, positive tone with the occasional moments of melodrama that really makes you root for the protagonists. Cast list is full of varied and quirky characters, and that includes the npcs as well. NPCs often have little side stories that makes the game world feel more alive than the average rpg. Talk to everyone (twice)!
Combat is fast paced and regular usage of special abilites and magic is expected. The paradigm is focused on taking immediate control of battles and keeping control - doing everything right tends to make combat feel a little too easy, but screw up and even random encounters can wipe you out. As the game goes on the lethality of random encounters is reduced (due to having more options in battle and equipment), but bosses will always happily take control of battle from you should you give them a chance. I played on Hard, those who are experienced with rpg combat may want to play NIghtmare.
A fine game and an excellent pc port.
After having finished the game, I can fully recommend this to anyone who likes a good jrpg story.

This game is obviously not meant for adults, it should be common sense to anyone that looks at it. It's a time waster and a baysitter. I like coloring, but the pictures were a little simple which is fine. I have young nieces and nephews that would get enjoyment out of this game, keeping them occupied while I'm busy doing something else. I got it in a bundle, I think, so I really only spent pennies on this, if anything, and it's not bad for that price. However, don't spend $3 on this, because it's not worth that.
While the game is meant to be simple because it's meant for children, I did find a couple issues with it. There should be an undo button somewhere, just in case you color in the wrong spot or just want to undo a couple brush strokes. The only way to "undo" anyhting is to clear the whole picture, which I don't appreciate too much, and I don't think a kid would either since kids are prone to making mistakes.
Another issue I have with it is that you don't control which letter you're going to. The game automatically takes you to the next hut, where you have to click on the door to enter. It would be more fun and interesting if you were able to explore the path yourself and go to whatever letter you want to go to.
It would be nice if you were able to mix colors or something to create a bigger color palette with custom colors. OR just have access to a color wheel. I don't know how much use a toddler would get out fo the feature but a kid slightly older could use it, and they would be entertained as well.
Some of the pictures were also set up in such a way that if you colored one area of the background, it would automatically color the whole thing. Instead of separating the sea water from the sky, for example, if you use the paint bucket, you would color both the same, and then you'd have to go in with the brush tool to fix it.
Lastly, There could've been a couple more songs added to the soundtrack. There's just one song that repeats over and over and over again. That would drive any parent nuts. It is a cute song and I liked it for a while, but there needs to be other music available too.
Overall, I like the huts, seeing all the different houses with letters was cool, the music was cute, and the pictures were interesting, since after the first round they change. I'm not sure how many unique pictures are in there, but there's at least 2 rounds worth of pictures. I would pick this up for really young/toddler aged kids, but nobody older than maybe 6.

TGWR is a great game for the right people.

It's not an open-world and it isn't really that much of a freeform RPG.
Instead it's a story. A story in which you might be able to make choices that change some of the outcome, but the general way the plot goes stays the same.
For now, there is only one arc of the in total three promissed storys available, but, the one that is there, is very much satisfying and interesting enough.
The gameplay itself is a mix of choose-your-own-adventure style textwindows, in which you decide how to act in the storysetting and a rather simple but rewarding economy-simulation. You're the theign of a small village and you allocate your villages population to certain tasks.

-
-

Then there is the obligatory combat, realized by a two action movement/attack-action turn- and tilebased system. It's serviceable. While sometimes challangeing, espescially early, you gather up skills quickly and find yourself quite often useing the same tactics over and over again. I'll be honest, I think they would've had a more rounded game if they focused more on the trade/economy aspect and ditched the combat all together. Maybe made it into a "preparation-phase" and cardbased "choose-your-tactic" minigame.
As it is now, it's oftentimes a way too worthwhile option while at the same time being a slog, due to the limited unit-variety mixed with the shallow way to "interact" with the enemy. CC, for example, is in my honest opinion allmost useless, when you can simply outdps allmost every enemy-composition, while the somewhat limited AI (codeing a competent AI is pretty much one of the hardest jobs, without resorteing to flat out cheating) is easily tricked into takeing unfortunate positions.
What do I mean by that? Well, for example, there is the random event of you sailing past a ship which lies heavy in the water with no guards to be seen. The outcomes if you take the opportunity to loot are at best free very worthwhile loot, worthwhile loot after a easy fight (bonus warrior-XP) or just a fight. Unless you're fully loaded, there is no sittuation in which you shouldn't simply go and take their stuff.
There is also a barebones "loyalty"-system in place, which decides on which turn you can put your units into the fight, but it's mostly rendered pointless, since
1. the enemy allmost never start directly upon you, so you got plenty of time to wait and even kite them around
and
2. you allmost allways have 1 or 2 other units ready with a imidiate summon.
_____________________________________
Well, the game in itself is however still very satisfying to play. It catches you in a somewhat cliche but still very enjoyable plot and while some things are not as well rounded or fleshed out as I personally would like them to be, they never pull you out of the experience.
I personally, had no real bugs or crashes to speak off, despite maybe the fact that I sometimes couldn't choose an item to drop from my longboat to accomodate a lootitem I got during a landside-event.
If you like storyfocused games that have more gameplay than just "hold W and point your mouse at things", go for it. It's basically a different no-fantasy take on "Banner Saga" set in our history.

If you expect a openworld RPG where you go about being a fantasy raider-godking, you might want to look into other games, like Expedition: Vikings
.

I'm enjoying this game a lot. I see some people comparing it to Mount & Blade: Viking Conquest or Expeditions: Vikings, and I can totally see why - the viking theme, the strategic combat etc... But to me the game has much more in common with The Banner Saga or King Of Dragon Pass. It has a fantastic art style, and features a broadly linear storyline, although you are given multiple "choose-your-own-adventure" style options to respond or make choices throughout, with varying consequences. Combined with this is turn-based combat, with different classes, abilities, and equipment to choose. I found this challenging at first, but as I upgraded my characters it has become slightly repetitive and simple. Hopefully there will be a little more variety in the upcoming further storylines. At the start of each year you are also given a light management screen, where you assign people to farm, or trade, or train for warfare, and can make upgrades to your village depending on resources you pick up during quests. If you've played King Of Dragon Pass, it's pretty similar. These 3 elements essentially make up the gameplay - story + choices, turn-based combat, and village management. If you're looking for a sandbox to rampage around in freely, this may not be the game for you.
+ Beautiful art style and music
+ A well-told story, with interesting characters and choices to make
+ Further storylines and updates on the way!
+/- Combat can get repetitive once you figure out the 'winning formula' but still enjoyable

- Random events can also get a bit repetitive when sailing - you quickly learn the "correct" answers
UPDATE: The few bugs I encountered have all been fixed with the latest patches!
Overall:
I definitely recommend this game, especially for fans of The Banner Saga. I know some other reviewers have criticised the RNG in terms of combat or trading for resources, but this hasn't been my experience at all. I found it challenging but fair, and a lot of fun, and have been completely charmed by the game.

If you're seeking out a somewhat laid back atmosphere, (somewhat cliche) romance, and a relaxing art style, I would recommend buying this game, especially on sale.
Critiques:
The stories, aye, are quite cliche. Plottwists are predictable, and anything you might assume to happen in a romance novel happens in this game. I might have adored this in the past, when I was infatuated with anime and romance and I was six years younger. Now, many years later, I've found that I'm not as easily entertained by a "sexy anime boy." Therefore, if you do plan to buy this game, understand that the intended audience ranges between 12 to 17 years old; don't expect complexities and don't expect a different type of romance.
The heroine is incredibly dim-witted, despite her education. I understand that it's somewhat "cute" to have a rather naive protagonist, but this again falls under a rather boring cliche. Body language, atmospheric language, and just verbal language seem to be lost to her. It's a tiresome role to play in a romance, quite honestly.
There isn't much variety in dialogue. You usually only have one or two lines to choose from, and you can never escape your naive personality.
The stat bars are tedious and feel unnecessary. The activities themselves are designed to stretch out the story, but, at the same time, they do ground you in the reality of the heroine's position; she has work to do and other things to think about besides boys. Therefore, I suppose it's not too much of a critique. It has no great impact on the story, which is my only gripe.
Praises:
The art style is easy on the eyes, elegant, and clean. Each romantic interest has his own aesthetic, and they differ in fashion and appearance to make for a variety of choices. From an artist's stance, I am, at the very least, envious. It makes for a gorgeous game.
The voice acting is phenomenal. Of course, I can't understand the language, but each voice has their own tenor and tone that perfectly fits their character. Even the protagonist has a sweet, honey-silk voice.
The stories last longer than I expected. You get your money's worth when you pay the full $30 on Steam; I've only completed 1 route, and it lasted an average of 6 hours. I still have 4 more to try, and I know I'll have a good deal of content to read and play.
The soundtrack is relaxing and I never found it to be repetative. Others have, which is understandable, but it simply assisted in my focus in the story and the emotion invested in the story.
-
Overall, it's a great game for young, female anime fans who have a thirst for romance. If you sit outside of this demographic, I still encourage you to try it out, but aim for a lower price when Steam has a sale. If you're not wholly interested in it, it won't be worth your $30.

Now here's a game I'm definitely on the fence on. I don't dislike it, but I don't think it's anywhere as amazing as the vast majority would say it was. There were aspects I thought were great and showed potential, other areas that were initially good but could have been better, other areas I thought were just flat out bad.
Things I loved was was it's fast paced action as well as it's setting. From the UAC facility set in the rocky plains of Mars all the way to hell and back it really felt you were raging a war against hell with every shot and that was cool. Plus I loved much of the voice acting, just how some of the voices sounded were just flat out out awesome, let alone the great effort made by the actors, well except that of one or two actual talking demons. There were parts where you got exposition from certain stones around the game and the voice talking, which I can only assume was a demon doing this, was kinda meh.
The parts I was on the fence on was monster design and story implementation. I get they were trying to go old school doom by having as little story as possible while still having a narrative, but my issue was that if you're going to go minimalist, then go all the way. This game seemed to have an issue with being sure if it wanted to tell a story or not. It seemed like it wanted to stay away from tedious story bits, all the while locking you in a room listening to people talk in addition to optional story bits. Now, I'm all for a great story, but if you're going to try and avoid it, then avoid it (as the original doom did with having most of its story either in the manual or at the end of each episode). If you're going to have us be in a room having conversations with characters, then give us something substantial. It felt like the game was sorta flipflopping around in terms of what it wanted to do about presenting it's story.
Monster design was questional at times I felt too. Some of the demons looked awesome, and I especially liked the look of the Mancubus, Pinky, Hell Knights (which looked a lot like the Doom 3 versions), and cacodemons. But others were just downright awful (such as the Imps) or looked dumb (I'm looking at you Cyberdemon, you weren't even a fun monster to fight). It felt like the designers were trying to do something new, of course, but other areas they were being faithful and made me wonder that if they were going to be THAT faithful to some demons, why not others?
Plus, I think hellguard was all around unnecessary, in terms of both design and battle. They looked super cliche and played out like your steriotypical N64 boss battle.
The part I thought was completely bad, in addition to the Cyberdemon and Imps, however was the forced arena battle parts. They weren't bad, at first. But the fact that the vast majority of this game were parts where the room was locked down until you defeated the demon threat, then the lock down was lifted and you could proceed. One of the issues I consistantly had was that there was always that one Imp that would jump down when I jumped up, then jumped up when I jump down, prolonging the lockdown and killing the little bit of momentum I had built up for myself until that point.
I remember reading in a forum where someone stated that the Doom series was an arena shooter at heart. While I don't disagree that the series has had arena sections since the beginning, it wasn't anywhere at the level as this game and found myself just dreading them here, whereas in the other installments (even Doom 3), I would welcome them because they weren't constantly locking the room down.
I give this game a recommend rating, but with the preface of the fact that I didn't love the game. If they had reduced the amount of "lockdowns," had better creature designs in some areas, and actually making a decision on whether or not it wanted to tell a story, then it would have been a far better experience for me.
Now, I give the developers a LOT of kudos for avoiding the micro-transaction route. All added content is completely free and you will not be spending a single penny on the game after the initial pay price. I totoally applaude this, and makes me feel good that a recent AAA game actually went this route. It's rare these days.
So if you played all pre 2016 Dooms to death, and are looking to get more Doom in, then by all means buy this one. I would recommend getting it on sale. Just know that sometimes even post-release hype can be just as high as pre-release hype.

You have to know what to expect from the Steam Controller before buying it.
The Steam Controller is not a replacement for keyboard and mouse, and it's not a replacement for a more action-oriented controller like the ones that come with dedicated gaming consoles. It's a middle ground that allows you to play keyboard and mouse-based games from your couch. With that in mind, it's very good at what it does, though you might have to play with the settings to get it feeling just right. I have not yet messed with the sensitivty settings, but I'm sure I will have to.
When I opened the package I was surprised by how sturdy the controller felt. I had read a lot of negative review impressions about its build quality, but this is a solid piece of equipment. However, the various triggers (especially the two built into the cover of the battery port on the back) and the clickable touchpads on the face have a similar feeling to a clickable touchpad on a laptop. The triggers/pads require only a light touch, and just like a laptop there's a learning curve with a pad that can also be pressed in for a "click." In that sense the pads and triggers feel more delicate than those you would find on console controllers even though they appear to be pretty solid. That's where the "flimsy" complaints come from, I think.
As for the rest of the controller, the analog stick is high quality and so are the face buttons. The placement of the A,B, X, and Y face buttons will take some getting used to as they're in a slightly lower position than those on other controllers, but they're perfectly useable and responsive. The right thumbpad is a very poor replacement for a second analog stick, so you'll want an Xbox One controller or something similar for action-based games. (And keep in mind that without a dedicated wireless dongle, other controllers will need to be wired to the Link. For example, I use a lengthy microUSB cable to connect an Xox One controller to the Link.)
If you're wanting to play mouse-heavy games from your living room, the Steam Controller is a good solution paired with a Steam Link. I don't regret the purchase. But when you switch over to, say, platformers and FPSs, you'll be switching to a different controller.

Then came my issue. I went to upgrade my ship, but my parts to upgrade weren't there. I KNOW I had the parts, but they simply weren't there.

It's my opinion that this game is not really worth getting, and when compared to its predecessor, it falls flat. Very grindy in a way that gets old very fast. I really like grindy, but not having to play multiple runs just to get my ships upgraded. That's just foolish.

Many reviews quite thoroughly summarize the general gaming experience of Jettomero already. I’ll stick to the finer details of the game which I came to appreciate most. To describe my gameplay experience briefly, however, I would compare it to the satisfaction one gets popping a fistful of bubble wrap (when you're not supposed to). Everything is just so crisp and satisfying in Jettomero (even -read 'especially'- the destruction).
On the surface, Jettomero is a free-for-all one-bot rampage you’re leading, while simultaneously blurting absurdly courteous regrets like “Ack” and “Whoops”. No one but me says these things out loud IRL so I can’t help but identify with Jettomero. I am already a sucker for clumsy little Unity robots like B.U.D. from Grow Home (a character Jettomero’s dev @GhostTimeGames cites as a creative inspiration) so if you can relate, then Jettomero is for you.
Aesthetically (and sometimes philosophically) the game feels like one of Bill Waterson’s Calvin and Hobbes comic strips. Specifically, the colorful Sunday strips when Calvin daydreams of the adventures of one of his many alter-egos, Spaceman Spiff. Both Spaceman Spiff and Jettomero share classic sci-fi elements like laser blaster bolts, careening space ships and the feeling that every encounter is a life or death situation (though in both instances, there is little to no actual threat to the protagonist’s well-being). The inner-monologue being presented as narration within cartoony speech bubbles keeps the comic aesthetic alive throughout Jettomero. The cipher challenges (which actually reveal exposition via comic panels) are simple enough and are a unique take on short video game puzzles.
The design and gameplay seem extremely polished and despite Jettomero’s (intentional) clumsiness, I never encountered a gamebreaking glitch or “stuck” moment. Some of the best moments actually arise from Jettomero’s wonkiness. For instance, before a monster battle, Jettomero would occasionally point at his enemy with a cliché threat and accidentally smack a spaceship that had been hovering nearby and launch it out of frame into the depths of space. Pure gold. You’ll spend most of your time laughing, BTW.
If you note my gameplay time it should be acknowledged that I spent most of that time in Jettomero’s Photo Mode. This is a feature you rarely see in such a small title and it was very expertly implemented, IMO. With nearly two dozen filters (each of which can be tweaked and used as a playable filter) and impressively flexible camera movement with very long zoom range, Jettomero’s Photo Mode feature allows you to capture every nook and cranny of the gorgeous universe while playing director. The parts selector also lets you dress Jettomero up to set a certain tone if you like. The steam community screenshots are really impressive. I’ll include some of the favorite shots that I’ve taken as well.
I highly recommend that everyone load one of the funkier filters (like gridlock, contrast or chalkboard) then fly around space and stomp a few cities with this new perspective. It truly ups the replay value and encourages you to wander. I would also encourage players to take some time to marvel at the game’s details; especially for those who may get bored with the ‘explore a planet, fight a monster, repeat’ core of the game. Sometimes it’s fun just to put on a photo-mode filter and let Jettomero get bombarded by the mosquito-like alien military vehicles while you watch the scene play out. There are a number of beautiful textures, particle effects and kinetic surprises to discover. Volcanoes, lightning and comets all bring little beats of fun interaction along the way. Jettomero was clearly a passion project and I am still finding small details that make it stand out from other indie titles in the same genre/price range.
The OST has been stuck in my head for weeks and taking time to carefully frame a shot in Photo Mode can be quite enjoyable when you’re on a planet with one of your favorite tracks looping in the background. Also, when you’re floating around in space you will be hypnotized by what I can only describe as a refined and mellowed-out ode to the music in Super Mario Bros 3 when you fall from the airship with the wand in your hand
.
Minor gripes: *The L3 button control is pretty sensitive and it can be tricky to lock onto selected letters when using the Cipher. This gets easier with practice, however. *The monster battle button prompts do not align with PS4 controllers so there’s an extra challenge to it if that’s what you use *I lost some Jettomero parts and statistic numbers after beating the game. It seems like an odd bug not everyone encounters though. I didn’t lose achievements, which is the most important thing.
**More than my review above, I hope you take the time to read the updates for Jettomero's long-since-completed Kickstarter campaign. Most of the earliest posts are available to everyone (not just backers) and the game’s dev, Gabriel Koenig, speaks thoughtfully about what went into the game; from musical and visual inspirations, to his own story-telling philosophy and his perspectives on video games and art. It contains far more than the typical “Thanks for your support, don’t forget to retweet” updates many campaigns bombard their backers with. The updates are what truly connected me to the game and I think if there is anything in those updates you can appreciate either as a gamer, artist, dev or just a fan of robots, you will find something to appreciate in Jettomero. Those can be found here (scroll to the bottom for the earliest posts):

Jettomero is a short game, but a cute and quirky experience. You play as a clumsy robot, walking around planets, picking up energy crystals and trying to defeat kaijus who are apparently terrorising planet residents. It does get a bit repetitive, because you will be doing just that over and over again, but it's a fun distraction that's not very long, and the music is excellent. It's also a pleasure when a game looks this gorgeous. You can also search for customisable robot parts (like legs, torsos, heads) that can make Jettomero look as silly or as stylish as you like.
For a game that's cute and whimsical, there's a surprisingly profound backstory. You reveal snippets of it through solving cipher puzzles that can get trickier in the later levels. But overall, Jettomero is a lovely game to pass the time with, and I'll be purchasing that amazing soundtrack.

Jettomero: Hero of the Universe is a short and relaxing game about a robot doing its best to save what remains of humanity. You should expect your adventure to last around 3 hours or less depending on how much you engage with photo mode and the huge number of filters.
I’ll start with the game’s biggest weakness which is its repetitiveness. You’re not going to have any moves unlocked as you play. You can clumsily walk around, trying not to destroy innocent people, swatting away angry human spaceships, stomp the ground to collect new body parts or just for fun, and engage in a boss battle if the planet has one occupying it (followed by a decoder puzzle). Then you can take off and fly around space into a wormhole or so that you can land on another planet to explore. The lack of gameplay variety means Jettomero is best experienced in shorter sessions despite its already short playtime.
What kept me playing was the game’s continued delivery of a chill experience and my curiosity about the robot’s past. It’s backed by a soothing soundtrack filled with synths as I tried to avoid smashing into things… usually. I was heroic for the most part, I swear. The strong visual style and wonderful filters also kept me entertained, especially when I noticed filters carry over into the boss cutscenes. I definitely had my handful of favorite ones that I used regularly, but the default game already looks great.
The photo mode is also a good addition to this game as I probably spent way too much time tweaking filters, angles, and finding just the right position for that perfect or not-so-perfect shot. Here are some examples:
When it comes to the value proposition of the game, I think I received my money’s worth at $13. That’s very subjective though and dependent on your disposable income. If you’re on the fence, then definitely reconsider it during a sale. I do recommend picking the game up if you’re looking for a chill time and not overlooking the fun of photo mode.

There are a whole lot of fans for this series, which seems to have a growing following. But whether or not you'll like this game depends wholly on what you're looking to do. If you want a hack and slash RPG that has fast action and a quick pace, this game is not for you. If, on the other hand, you greatly enjoy a game that is heavy on the story, you may have just died and gone to Valhalla.
I've been a gamer forever, and have played hundreds of titles. I have never in my gaming history experienced a game that is so heavy on the storyline. You will be bombarded with cutscenes and dialog every literal step of the way. There is no skip option, so if you don't have time for all that, don't pick up this title. You've been warned.
That said, you're less likely to enjoy this game if you're an older gamer. Let's face it, we've heard all the basic scenarios before, and most of the dialog, though beautifully done, will probably come across as mundane to most older RPG fans. That, and also the fact that we have jobs, families, and lives to get to. It's really less like a gaming expeirence and more like watching an interactive anime. Which is cool, but I think it's been done way over the top in this title.
Aside from the storyline, the combat sequences are very good. There is a combo system, along with magic (functions like materia, ala FF7), leveling, etc. All the traditional things you would expect from an RPG are represented here. However, I have two gripes that are difficult to get my head around.
First, the game is nowhere near an open world experience (at least not at the point I am in the game). It is entirely linear, so much so that, upon completing a quest, you advance days of the calendar year. Each day represents a certain timeframe in the gameworld, and only during those timeframes can certain things be done. If you miss out on talking to someone, getting a hidden quest, or purchasing an item, you're screwed. That means that unless you're playing with a guide, this game takes far too long -- you literally have to revisit every area and talk to everyone again each time the storyline advances. It's an interesting dynamic, but serves to slow down the action even further. To it's credit though, I will say that it offers an immersive experience having to talk to everyone and revisit things over again....though for most people you will just click the mouse a hundred times to get past the mountains of dialog.
Second, the combat system is a lot of fun, but it is a bit slow. It is far more strategic than typical RPGs, but primarily because you can't power level to dominate your opponents. The experience you gain from battles diminishes each time you level -- and since this is not an open world environment, it's obvious the developers wanted you within a certain level range for each chapter of the story. Yes, you can sit there for hours to gain a few more levels, but its truthfully not worth it -- especially since the first battle you fight in the next chapter is going to automatically level your characters. The worst part of this system is that battles within chapters never really get any easier, either. You can pack on 5 levels by grinding for 3 hours, but you're probably only shaving a few seconds off each battle, which average out out to 1-2 minutes per.
Pros:
Visually stunning, even though the graphics are outdated
Incredibly good voiceovers, and a whole lot of them
Fantastic cutscenes
Story and Dialog are all extremely well done. They were paying attention to the details for this game
Great combat dynamics with all the essentials
Very immersive, with great character development
Cons:
Very slow paced (expect to dedicate a lot of time to progressing this game)
Linear
Combat gets repetitive
Money -- While you don't have to grind for levels, you do have to grind for money, and currency for essential upgrades
Not able to skip the numerous and lengthy cutscenes
Too much pointless dialog
OVerall:
Good game if you have the time to play it, love storyline and character development above combat, and want an immersive experience

I'm someone who played Trails in the Sky (a sort of unrelated prequel trilogy in the same world) and thought it was trash. Trails in the Sky actually got  one of the few negative reviews I've ever written. I thought it had potentially, but was let down in way too many ways, so I thought I'd give this game a go.
While Trials of Cold Steel doesn't fix every Issue trails in the sky had, it does enough in every area to turn it from a bad game into an increible one.
Random battle combat: Trails in the sky had unrewarding combat that you had to slog through. Every single fight whittled you down enough to cost the mana or item for a heal. In return for fighting, you got a little money ♥♥♥♥♥♥all) and very little exp. If you are 2 levels above the enemies in the area, you get 1 exp. This was my biggest complaint with the game.
In Cold steel, you can get through a lot of fights wihtout taking damage (think persona). The rewards still aren't great, but they are improved. You get moderate (maybe a little to the low side) experience, and a decent amount of money. Most fights you don't really need to think about, but things can get out of hand if you screw up too badly, so it keeps it relatively interesting. You have a tonne of spells that can be used by any character, and abilties that are character specific, meaning who you choose to have in your party matters and will change how you fight. I would say the combat is better than average for a turn based rpg.
Boss Battle Combat: The bosses are usually very well designed. Each character has an ability called an 'S break' (Basically a limit break in final fantasy). It's charged by taking damage, dealing damage, or using some spells or abilities. Random enemies will almost always be one hit by these abilities. Bosses however, can usually take well above 4 of these abilities to kill, which means that you can't just enter a fight and murder the bosses by using each characters S break (parties have a maximum of 4 units with a further 2 on standby). The battles feel epic, and though you get into a routine after you have worked out what to do in each battle (for example have main character use normal attacks, one person heal, one person buff and another using attack abilities or something to this effect) you will often have to change this up. Maybe a character gets KO'd or you take a bit more damage or you get a status effect or the enemy is using a stronger aoe ability. Boss battles are engaging and have you of the edge of your seat. You can't switch off your brain or you will lose. You almost always feel like an underdog against a boss, but they are always possible to win.
Story: Exactly the same problem as Trails in the Sky: There is a ♥♥♥♥ton of dialogue, but that doesnt amount to a ♥♥♥♥ton of story. Everyone talks so GODDAM MUCH, and very very little of it matters. I get that the designers want to create a world, but for goddsake, learn to show and not tell. It's the weakest part of the game BY FAR. The actual story is decent, it is just surrounded by so much ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that I can't find myself caring. Spend 20 minutes talking to everyone about who gives a♥♥♥♥♥♥what, and that 20 mins can by summarised by "there are bad people. stop the bad people." Really, the story isn't that bad, but the STORYTELLING is really awful.
Game flow: I don't really know what to call this. What I mean is that the game's chapters follow the exact same formula. Do missions around the school > Investigate old school (battle enemies) > Do teachers exam battle > Go on a train for a field trip > Do missions at new place > Beat a boss > Do more Missions at same place > have a section that is related to the story in the new place, usually ending in a terrorist fight > go back to school > repeat.
If this had happened once or twice it would be okay, but it happens every time. it just makes the formula for the story of the game so plain, which adds to why the story is the weakest part.
Music: Increible. Gets you hyped. Makes battles feel fun and engaging. You will find yourself humming it.
Character/Party Customisation: Very good. Every character has a role that is assigned by the devs: eg Luara is a high damage character, Fie is the fast one, Emma is the damage mage, etc. However, you can play any character however you want (to a degree). If you equip a character with the right spells, equipment, and base magic ability 'orbment', you can passably play any character how you want. You can afford to play a character sub optimally, because the spells that everyone can use cover for glaring weaknesses.
Characters: They are interesting and likeable. You can form bonds that give you bonuses like in Persona. You can form links in battle that do things like let your partner attack if you crit an enemy. They all feel unique and their skills match who they are. They 'show don't tell' much better with the characters than the rest of the story, and it pays off well.
'Side missions': There are a lot of optional side missions that are literally just go to point A, talk to someone, go to point B, talk, Point A, Point C, point A, mission complete. They suck. I used a guide to get through them. As I said earlier, the game has a dialogue fetish. It wants to build the world, but this is a♥♥♥♥♥♥poor way of doing it. Combat missions are better 100% of the time. Combat missions are more engaging 100% of the time.
Even worse, there are special 'hidden missions'. you get these by 'stumbling across the right person at the right time'. By that, I mean you follow a guide to find them, because it could literally be a little girl in the middle of a kitchen in an army base that you literally never need to go into. That mission was another 'go to point A then B then A then B then A'. If you don't do these hidden missions, even if they are a waste of time, you can't get an S rank for the chapter. If they werent in the game, the game would be better, because you get rewards based on your ranking for the chapter, so you want to do them.
Overall: I would say the combat carries this game, but it doesnt need to. There is more than enough good, and the combat just adds to it. I have said a lot of negatives here, but that's because other reviews will focus on the positives. The Combat is great. The world is great. The storytelling sucks♥♥♥♥♥ and the formula of the game is glaringly obvious. It's not a bad formula, but it would be better if it was shaken up more. This game is interesting, there are parts of the story that are awesome and keep you playing. I will be buying and playing the next game as soon as it comes out.

TL;DR Read Sophie's World instead.
The game environment is gorgeous. From the textures to the level design, each frame is a work of art. The subtle environment changes help inspire the tense atmosphere that underpins the entire game. This is a project of passion, and I would really recommend exploring the world thoroughly to make as much sense of the story as possible.
Sadly, the game has the philosophical subtlety of a sledgehammer. Perhaps Maslow was onto something. If it's not the overbearing symbolism, it's the infernal kettle logic scattered in notes throughout the world. For a game that explores existential issues, this proof by verbosity reeks of pseudophilosophical rambling. The underlying message is neither new nor profound, and it's presented in such a shoddy and pompous manner it feels like you've wandered into a student bar on a Sunday evening.
Perhaps there was a deeper satirism that flew completely over my head. Perhaps the game really is nothing more than vacuous truth. Perhaps, like the game's bitter Solomon, I'm psychoanalysing my own failure to psychoanalyse. Must be the water.
It's clear that the developer has put a lot of effort into researching and making the game. However, this has produced a game whose core message may be inaccessible to someone with no experience in philosophy. The developer acknowledges this, and I respect that. It takes guts to produce a game that doesn't hold players' hands.
Ultimately, this game explores some very deep existential issues. Unfortunately, it seldom strays past the populist trite you'd find in a teenager's bedroom.
Read Jostein Gaarder instead.

TL;DR: A short walking simulator with an engaging storyline that has a lot of room for interpretation. Taking place in a unique, post-apocalyptic world, Leviathan has a one-of-a-kind narrative that some may find very interesting while others might hate it for being (at times) boring. The game has excellent graphics, great accompanying music and it rewards you for exploring each section in its entirety. Of all the FPE (first person exploration) games out there the Old City is a must.
Leviathan belongs to those games that can be characterised as "first person exploration" games or simply "walking simulators". There are no enemies here, no levels to complete with a boss fight, no real challenges; the emphasis is on story immersion by walking and at the same time interacting with objects of the world is kept to a minimum. This also means that these games are rather short and a walkthrough means we've pretty much seen everything that is to be seen.
I have grown fond of these games in recent years. So much so that I enjoyed exploring all the different endings of "Stanley Parable" and I even completed a rather mediocre game called "The NADI Project". I also know that it's best to steer away from some of these games - let's just say they have reached the level of AAA games meaning the final product cannot always please everybody (yes, I'm looking at you, "Everybody's Gone to the Rapture"!).
Leviathan puts us into a unique world; a world which is first seen as an industrial complex. As we go through the storerooms full of boxes and tables littered with notes (messages meant for us to elaborate the history of the Old City) we may get bored but after a while we notice a change of scenery. Outside locales look refreshing but also equally confusing: What are these floating statues doing in the sky? Why is a dead whale ashore next to several dozens of huge containers? And while going towards the subway entrance we are mesmerised by the game's attention to detail - looking up we can see a highway and suddenly get stunned by the huge crab-like creature leisurely strolling on the road (I guess he did not need to pay the tool fee). We barely see it but we know it is there. And how come more than one level starts in a child's room only for us to see the sewers and the storerooms once more when exiting mentioned room?
This is an interesting ambiguity we are faced here. For once we expect to get an explanation for this world's post-apocalyptic nature but then we start questioning whether or not this is all going on in our mind. The "voice" that regularly (mainly at the beginning of each chapter) speaks pushes us forward so that we can find out more on the 3 factions (the Guild, the Order and the Unknowing) and makes us try to identify the people behind the names that all have biblical origins (Abraham, Jonah, etc.)
Completing Leviathan can happen pretty fast. Walking from point A to point B is easy - sometimes the door to the exit is right in front of us. Still, it's best to explore our periphery to see what the Old City holds for us. We may get some extra lines from our "voice", plus, hidden in various corners and alleyways we may bump into Solomon's notes, documents giving us further reading and helping understand the world that may just be in our imagination.
Beside the interesting story what stands out is Leviathan's graphics. Not as detailed as in the "Vanishing of Ethan Carter" (you really cannot top this one), still, in terms of atmosphere and attention to detail it is top-notch in every which way. Unlike "Gone Home" or "Dear Esther" for the first time I felt the need to replay a couple of chapters to see what more information the city could give me.
If you like the genre this game is a must. And if you have a hard time with the understanding join the discussion thread in the forum - there are some interesting theories as to what the game's message is.

The developer clearly wanted to do something thoughtful but went about it with a pseudo-story that ultimately felt unsatisfying and was needlessly gory.
Ironically, the developers have come across as hypocritical with the thoughts they wanted to share as the three relgious groups portrayed in the game, who are parodies of aetheists, spiritualists and nihilists, end up being embroiled in a violent conflict of hatred towards one another. The devs ultimately claim that 'stupid ideas, die with stupid people' while they also claiming that people should be free to think whatever they want. The contradiction is self-evident and the events in the game reveal more of this critical attitude towards anyone with a belief (the stupid people). You can see that the developer has done some theological study as there are many biblical references throughout the game but you can't help but feel that (despite claims to the contrary) the developer is clearly pushing an anti-religious egenda in how they say that beliefs are a cage, that any kind of faith or certainty in a belief is ultimately self-destructive. This idea is reinforced by the characters that belonged to one of the factions within the game ending up miserable and suicidal or dead as a result of the war. The survivor is the one who chose to reject all the other organisations and who held no fixed beliefs.
I would recommend this game for design purposes but simply cannot when the message it is trying to get across is a thinly veiled, hypocritical critisism of other people's beliefs. In a world already filled with intolerance we don't need more of this attitude.

Is this supposed to be the path of death?  Is he being pulled into hell or swimming out of it?  Is he dead or dying?

The Old City: Leviathan is a first-person adventure game with a pseudo-philosophical twist developed and published by PostMod Softworks. You explore through a decaying old city with a very ominous vibe to it and at times you also venture into what seem to be dreams that you explore. Throughout the game you will not encounter any enemies nor puzzles so The Old City really focuses on story and having to explore to piece the story together yourself rather than have it told to you. This sounds like a system that would work well with walking simulator type games and it does, for the most part, but since there isn't really that much of conrete story in the game it leaves a lot of it up to subjective discussion. Therefore this somewhat hurts the game as a whole since everyone seems to have their own interpretation and I really would have liked to have at least a forum post by the devs telling us some concrete points in the story.
Throughout your time in Th Old City: Leviathan you visit various environments and each one feels more interesting and different than the last while also maintaining a similar vibe with the game as a whole. The environments you pass through look absolutely stunning and really just pile on to the whole ominous overtone that the game seems to have. The environments usually have maybe one or two side doors with small areas you can explore but for the most part this is definitely not an exploration game. You can look around to find notes about the world and to help piece together the story and can also find small boxes called Solomon's notes that tell the story of a man named Solomon on his journey in the Old City. The problem with having a story that the player has to piece together themselves is that this means there are pages of notes that make the story easier to understand that the player can simply miss out on because they didn't explore a single side room. When you go to leave an area there's no forewarning and the doors you use to go to the next chapter look exactly like normal doors. This means sometimes you can be exploring the area and if you open the wrong door then you end up heading onwards to the next chapter instead of finding a side area. This gets really annoying towards the end of the game and almost discourages exploring since it feels more like walking through a minefield instead of hunting for extra bits of story.
I can't really talk much about the story itself since everything is connected so I couldn't discuss one object without having to talk about a certain character and so on. There's also the problem that while playing you may not completely understand the story since the game gives you just enough to really get you interested before it ends. While playing through The Old City I found there were a few interesting bible references that seemed to be woven into the story and instead of just being references they actually seemed to connect the stories told in the bible to the game itself, which I found very interesting. The Old City also has very heavy philosophical overtones such as the truth needing to be compatible with itself and other such lines. The Old city: Leviathan very much feels like it's proving that games can indeed be art and in that, I would say that it's succeeded.

So ... I conditionally recommend this game :)  Let me start by saying, it is very much not for everybody.
This is very much a "video game as art" sort of concept, along similar lines as Dear Ester.  You will spend most of your time holding down the 'shift' and 'W' keys as you move your slow butt thruogh a beautifully rendered world.  The voice-overs are more or less sync'd with your slow walking speed, so at least there feels like a reason for being so slow unlike a lot of walking game where the slowness just feels like an excuse to pad time.
Despite this, I found the game interesting and entertaining.  There are no enemies or puzzles, but there are a few ways through the game unlike what people say.  Usually there's a way to bee-line straight to the end without encountering anything and a way to go through something 'traumatizing' for each level.  You certainly get more out of the game if you explore and find the 'traumatizing' bits.
My biggest complaint with the game is that it is often really easy to accidentally skip through a level -- once you go to the next chapter, you can't go back, and there's no warning that you're about to move on.  I would have appreciated some sort of 'you are about to leave this sector and you cannot come back' sort of warning.  This lead to a lot of extra walking on my part as I wanted to make sure I thoroughly explored everything, and towards the end this made the game feel tedious for me.
However, if you like interactive art (this really isn't a game) and you don't mind reading -- totally worth a try.

I received this product for free and was not aware I was receiving it.
At the time of this review, I'm just under two hours of use. I know that is not very long to spend within a D.A.W., but I've come to say that my first impression hasn't been a good one. I decided to import some raw audio files from an old Reaper project of mine. Doing this saved me some time. I left out the drums and imported a midi of the drums to test out the included drum VSTi. I find mixing to be a pain in this program compared to the one to which I'm accustomed. The included VSTi's were decent. The drums and synth being my favorites. I like them more than the D.A.W. itself. The workspace is just a pain for me. I come at this very biased as I've been on Reaper as my primary D.A.W. for the last nine years, but there is not much about this program that has felt intuitive to me. It feels clunky. The Piano Roll works as expected and I don't have any complaints there. It supports third party VST plugins, but I can not for the life of me get mine to load. Thanks to this, I found the VST effect filters for guitar they have. I have not listened to them all, but I was surprised to find that they weren't terrible. Mind you; they were not good either. Plenty of free guitar amp modeling exists which sound better, but it's not terrible considering the sixty dollar price tag paired with the rest of the contents.  Despite them being better than I expected it just reminded me that I wasn't using BiasFx. I'm sure I'll get them to work eventually. I'm not positive what's wrong. During my short test, I did not hook up a midi controller. I don't often use it as I use a tablature program for most of my midi work. I export the midi file from there, import it into my D.A.W., and then make any further edits I need manually. It's likely I won't test the controller. Despite importing old audio files, I did check my inputs, and it worked just fine.  Hard to mess that up.  I haven't any interest in loops, so I left that terrain alone.
As I said earlier, my biggest problem with Music Maker 2017 Steam Edition is the workplace. I do not like interfacing with it, and I'm not sure whether it's because I'm too stuck in the programs I'm used to or if it's just indeed clunky. I haven't stepped out of my waters in a long time. If this is your first time getting a D.A.W., then this might work out for you. I still wouldn't recommend it, though. This program is the same price as what I usually use, but nowhere near as good. It comes with a fair amount of stuff to get you started making music with midi, but I would still steer newcomers to look elsewhere.  I've read people are having a lot of crashes, and I've not experienced this yet. Will update if it starts in future use.

*Note* This is going to be somehwhat of a Rant because I'm ticked off at the other reviewers who haven't done justice to the community by brutalizing the game for short sighted emotional reasons instead of judging the game on its actual merit.
SO this is my opinion on what happened....You have a Huge number of Mount and Blade warband fans, battle brothers fans and expeditions conquistador fans who bought the game not based on what it is and appreciating the aspects of the actual game. Instead they are beating it up for not being like the above mentioned titles. I know this because I too am a huge fan with lots of hours on the above titles so I understand what they are saying, yet thats total bogus because thats not what THIS title is about and its killing the game for a lot of people who might enjoy this game for what it actually is.
-Honestly the bad reviews kept me away despite having seen this game and followed it for a little bit while it was in early access. I saw a lot of reviews bashing the game for what it isn't and I saw one guy write a friggen book about what it is and I still didn't really understand what the hell anyone was talking about. SO I bought the game myself and tried it out and this is my attempt to cut through the drama and anger and garbage and tell you the real deal.
#1 Most of the negative reviews are based on people being angry about not being able to do this or that....The game is story driven and that's okay. Nothing wrong with that....The tragedy is people see so much potential and want so much more that instead of saying that, they focus on what isn't in the game like its a flaw instead of appreciating what is actually there......To say the game is broken because it's not an open world is rediculous. Is banner saga an open world? Is The oregon trail an open world? NO.....SO first thing first.....Its okay to enjoy a story and want more...So in concluion its a story based title Like banner saga. Judge it on what it is.
#2 The world is rich and looks good for a hand drawn game. You start out choosing who you are going to be taking over the tribe. While I personally would of liked more character options again lets be fair, in Banner Saga for example you get two choices. You get two choices here as well and then it goes into a combat tutorial. I'm not sure why they raised the difficulty of enemies recently and I hope they take a look at that again, its not needed.
#3 After this you go into the city tutorial screen, this gives you an overview of the choices you make for winter planning and what your little villiage will yield based on your choices of where to allocate your people for what task. This is actually a deeper system then banner saga and is more rewarding since you are building a settlement instead of just fleeing all the time like in Banner saga.

The basic summary of the story:
Pros:
1. I guess the drawings are pretty good. Some of the characters look awkward (body proportion wise), but pretty good anyway.
2. First MC I actually like from an otome game. She actually has a personality.
3. Some of the idea concept is interesting.
Cons:
1. The stat building is grueling, annoying, infuriating, and pointless in my opinion. Once you get the hang of it it is easy to do, but there is so damn much of it. It makes the game take forever just doing that part alone.
2. One feature I LIKE from otome games is dialogue options which can make other characters react or change their personality towards the MC in different ways. THERE IS BARELY ANY!!!! In fact, your success depends on stat building and interacting with other characters in the flow of rigid and set dialogue which you have little if any influence upon.
3. Due to those two above cons, combined, I feel as though there is really little story overall and rather misleading in fooling you that there is ample game play involved. Stat building is boring!
4. There are some bugs in this game. I got all those dumb stamps for every character, but for some reason, even though finishing those routes and getting a good ending, those stamps disappeared and cannot unlock those boring bonus? extra feature drawings?
5. I am not sure if I really like any of the characters to be honest. There are funny moments and boring moments.
6. Ending is abrupt. I know that could be a technique, but after all that terrible stat raising, little story in truth, I would expected a little more effort. Instead, my overall opinion is more like "meh" okay, well that passed the time.
If you like otome games and are bored waiting for more interesting ones to come out, sure. Now that I am finished I doubt I will play this game again. I just don't want to go through that click, click, click crap in the stat building.

Okay. This is a fantastic game. In fact, one of the couple of games that made me interested in getting a Steam account.
This was my first dating sim, and I have to say that I wasn't disappointed. I love visual novels (even ones that are more novel than game, Zero...) and this just amazed me. The five boys felt really realistic (minus the bunny ears) and although - especially early game - it seemed like a lot of comic relief was going to be involved, they really got serious. I admit, some characters I was looking forwards more to than others (Jiwoo and Jihae if you're curious) but I really wasn't disappointed by any of the stories. Jiyeon gave a lot of entertainment to my gaming club when I brought this in and Jisoo and Jieun kept me entertained for a time when I was bedridden. And the one bad ending I have seen (the chicken ending) is just as amazing (though I think the others are going to be very different).
But I feel like I'm rambling. The game is great. The characters are great. The stories are fantastic, each one making me cry for one reason or another. Until I found the bonus for getting all the good endings, it had the villain I loved to hate the most. Still love him after it, I just don't hate him as much now.
Upsides... Like I said, great characters and great stories. The art and music is fantastic (I'm legitamately considering picking up the OST) and there are nice bonuses if you're diligent with the game. Stamps are easy to collect (I got 45 and 50 for Jisoo and Jieun, once I found out how good eye drops are). You get really good rewards that I can't sing enough praise about. A fantastic experience.
Downsides of this game... It's a little pricey and there are some translation errors... A couple of times characters are misnamed and there are some spelling and grammatical errors... But it's easy enough to figure out what they mean and its pretty charming, but some people might find it a little off-putting. Oh, and there's a hint something at one small point with Jisoo I wish I could have found out more about (don't want to spoil anything, but alcohol was involved). But that's just something personal.
LOVE the intro music, LOVE the characters!!! It's very different from Nameless but still stands strong. My favorite is Jihae <3

I really wanted to recommend this. The voice acting is quite good, the CGs are lovely, and the stories can be quite interesting. I can understand why people have been putting this game on their lists for what defines the VN genre.
But it's horrifically buggy. You need to play through all storylines in order to unlock the final short stpryline, but after I played two routes, the game erased all the progress I made on the first route. And because there's a lot of micromanagement required to successfully complete a character route, it's not something I want to go back and do a second time.
Most of the 'day management' sim involves repeatedly quick-saving so as to fight against the RNG. I'd say a good 98% of my 28-hour playtime is just reloading the game over and over so that I wouldn't fail a task on a particular day. The game doesn't have a lot of polish, either. Fonts change randomly, music glitches out, and sometimes the whole game will just stutter to a halt. Not to mention that you have to have an internet connection to play this game, and the team is constantly apologizing for server maintenance issues.
It would be easier to overlook the flaws if not for the ridiculous price. There are VNs out there with way better polish that you can download for free, or at least a fraction of the price of this one. Go find those.

If you like games about the Civil War in the US, then this game is not for you. If you like turned-based strategic games, like those that Paradox does, then this game is not for you. If you like sims of naval actions, as in Total War, then this game is again not for you.
Buy this game only if you want to play a strategy and simulator of the Civil War at sea. In this role, the game reveals all its strengths. But do not demand much from her. It is deep enough and interesting for its price. And to make it clear that the game is very cheap, I will give an example of the prices of other games of this genre: Distant Guns $ 49.99, Jutland $ 49.99, War in the Pacific (Matrix Games) $89 ...
This game is a special category. Once upon a time I played similar games about sailing ships (Age of Sail Series). Then this genre died.
I consider myself an "old school" player. I remember the times when we played drums with desktop friends. Yes it was fun, but very long. Now all the boring or controversial moments are taken over by the computer. And I like it. For me, the "Clad in Iron: Gulf of Mexico 1864" - this is a good game.

Clad in Iron: Gulf of Mexico 1864 continues the proud Ironclads tradition of scalable simulations rich with gameplay functions and realism for hardcore naval games junkies but not for casual gamers. With good graphics, a standout dynamic campaign, and tons of thoughtful details throughout that add to the ambiance, Clad in Iron is a must-have for intrepid skippers everywhere. But keep in mind that to understand the game is not easy.

Everything in this game is not as easy as it seems from the screenshots and video. This game dumbfounds its uniqueness. This is both bad and good.
The bad thing is that all the previous gaming experience does not make sense. You look at the screen and do not understand what is happening and what you need to do. And in the game there is no training. Need to read the manual. It's not bad written, but you want to play, not read. Now for me this is not a problem. I bought Totem Games products and so I figured out the game rules.
On the other hand, this uniqueness almost perfectly realizes the mechanisms of naval warfare in the 19th century. Of course, there are complaints about the interface and the strange turned based system, but this does not spoil the pleasure of the game. You can plan a whole military operation. To lure or block the enemy fleet, then defeat the coastal forts (a nice novelty), destroy the ships protecting the port and land the soldiers. Or you can concentrate your efforts on destroying enemy supply ships and blockade.
I'm absolutely sure that this game is not for everyone. I see the development of the series and improvements. I hope to see the training. This is very necessary for beginners. It's hard for me to recommend this game, but I get pleasure from it.
P.S. Guys, I'm looking forward to the game about the Spanish-American war.

When I been playing Ironclads 2 War of the Pacific, I was thinking that number of ships is too low, it is too risky to lost ironclads (there are 2 maximum!) in first fight ... here we have a lot of ships, I like that, still it feels like Pacific or Caroline Island - you can't build ships or infantry, only repair or reinforce them, which is in my opinion is very close to a small conflict period.
I have to say that I played two times and I lose both) AI on map still pretty smart, on battle map I think it's improved. Lot of game moments are improved I think, most appreciated thing for me is a feature to leave battle, no more need to wait until time is over or all ships destroyed.
What I want from future games is a better infantry part, maybe it is a possible to expend harbor attacks and defences in this area.

Clad in Iron: Gulf of Mexico 1864 deserves praise, provides excellent entertainment, and is well worth its price. I admire both the design of the strategy and tactical layer. There is good balance between realistic and arcade elements. And the game's polished graphics makes playing a real pleasure. Clad in Iron: Gulf of Mexico 1864 distinguish itself with well-designed interface and game mechanics, historical accuracy (considering gameplay limitations). It seems to be a good choice for those interested in naval warfare history as it would not offend their intelligence and knowledge; and for those who just seek a nice game to sink ships. I recommend this game to all who are fascinated with American Civil War at sea, especially those who would like a taste of a bit of strategy in their naval action.

I've had mine for about 2 years now and I absolutely love it.  The customization, the form factor, the back paddle buttons, all fantastic.  There is a break in period, the dual touch pads are unlike any other controller.  But once you get used to it, and customize the controls to your liking, you will agree with me.
At first I really did not like this controler, it feels weird and diffrent from traditional controlers. But after a week I was in love with it. Ten times better thant a traditional controler!

The gyro... Look, if you play space sims a lot, and want a cheap setup, get this controller here or on ebay or something. It works like a charm for a heck of a lot less than some of the better joystick setups (on ebay the price is about 5-10 pounds... the value proposition is insane).
If you like using controllers for the relaxation, or for the added control they bring to movement but don't like the horrible aiming on the right stick, get this controller. It'll solve all your issues, the trackpad is simply that amazing a lot of the time.
If you like trying out new control methods, get this controller. It's cheap, and the largest innovation in recent history - that hit mainstream, anyway.
This controller is not without its flaws though. The bumpers are too stiff to use in rapid succession, and the triggers have a slightly low throw for things like race sims. Regardless, I feel like this is a worthy addition to anyones collection of game control methods, even for things like race sims as the trackpads offer a ridiculous amount of control over your steering -
those of you who use controllers will know that the tiny joysticks are just awful at times compared to wheels, this will more or less solve that issue, and be a lot better for arcade racing on top of that.
Don't buy this if you want a control method than keyboard and mouse that's better for fps games. Buy this to get a control method that's better than a controller for a lot of games, not just fps. I will probably forever fault some of the marketing for this device, prioritisng the comparison with keyboards rather than controllers, but in the end it was never meant to replace anything. It simply exists, alongside the competition, giving people a usable alternative to the extreme ends of the spectrum, with keyboard and mouse at the one end and controllers on the other.
Anyway, go get this, it's probably the best gamepad/controller out there.
Ah, one last thing: you'll probably want to take into the account of the rechargeable batteries when buying this controller, and if you feel it's too much then, don't buy it, as it's basically the cheapest way to use this controller wirelessly.
