An absolute gem of a game to play--Jettomero doesn't take long to dive into, nor is it too deep. You're a robot who is slightly confused on everything around it, blasted into a galaxy you don't know, and events taking place around you with the human civilization that you haven't quite caught up on yet. It's an adorable story that unfolds like a comic book, with super hero pacing that can only leave you feeling pumped up!
The gameplay is so imaginative, easy to pick up and wonderful to experience. You play as Jettomero--a clunky red robot who walks around like a drunken toddler. Not only is it cute to control, it's relatively easy too. There is a bit of a learning curve to Jettomero's general movements, but it really doesn't take long at all to figure it out. He's fun, full of personality, and you can't help but love him straight away. The sympathy he feels for a human race that is clearly scared of him is all too endearing to watch. They fly around, bomb him, shoot at him as he towers over buildings, but he can't help but stomp around fighting for them, and forgiving them for playing on their fear.
There's much to do to keep you busy, that which doesn't pit you in one type of gameplay. Mini puzzles of decrypting can be quite fun, and just challenging enough for accomplishment, but not heartache. Battles commence as you land from planet to planet and find individual Godzilla-like monsters threatening the humans. The fights work like a type-off, in which you have to literally type letters out to gain ground. It's simple and if sailing quietly through the Universe isn't your particular speed--it more than picks up the pace. You also run around stomping holes in the ground to collect appearance items--I have to say, it made me laugh how upfront the game was about the vanity of these collectibles too. For nothing more than looking the part of Hero of the Universe! D'aww!
Saving what I think is the best for last--Jettomero's art style is...well, stunningly gorgeous. It's a treat to look at and walk around in a lavish MS Painted universe. Bright and colourful, bold and unforgiving. And oh, so fluid! I suspect the developers knew what they had on their hands here, giving the player a specific mode to take photos in. It's an art style in a game that I've never seen, and could certainly see being imitated by future titles.
Asteroids to smash, little achievements to keep you going--it's so full of life and wonder, without being too deep. I found it all to be refreshing, and Jettomero's attitude always finding a way to paint a smile on my face. It's an absolute must-have if you generally enjoy exploring things with child-like wonder. I read a review in which someone put it best, "Is it too early to ask for a sequel?"

Now this one is absolutely gorgeous.
Jettomero is one of those rare games that managed to perform this magic trick-like thing. Most games need to grow on me. Jettomero didn't. Instead, it instantaneously made me feel home. I launched the game, saw, heard, read, clicked a little, and there I was, already in a state of euphoric cosiness.
Of course, this makes sense, since you can pretty much tell from its trailer how much it relies on seduction. Actually, a few seconds of its trailer were enough to conquer me.
Still, it's a thrill to let it bring me back to my late 90s /early 2000s, when the generic art student that I was was raving to the beautifully naive, silly and other-wordly melodies that kept popping out from record labels such as Warp, Planet Mu, Rephlex, or Tigerbeat.
Jettomero :
Hero of the Universe, like a few other space games out there (thinking of Nate Schmold's delightful Cosmochoria), has this particular mood, - both melancholic and good-humoured -, that was like the common emotional ground on which the aforementioned wacky, clicketty-clacking sci-fi scores were standing. When I did shut down the game, I felt an urge to dig my music library for some Bogdan Raczynski, Arovane and Jega tunes that I hadn't been listening to for a long time.
Naturally, special attention has been paid to Jettomero's soundtrack (which can be purchased on Steam as a DLC). It is deeply rooted in this electronica scene, and well, it's fine
. To put it simply, it's very
-ish, it works great, and you may well end up humming one of its tunes while doing housework.
So what is Jettomero like, gameplay-wise ? To be honest, I don't care much. It is very simple, in the sense that it is both easily understood and done, and humble. It is very probable that the people at Ghost Time Games didn't care that much either. The essential point is that they made it feel smooth. That's enough, because what I'm here for is to enjoy the audiovisual ride.
And it's a damn nice and fluent ride. Jettomero's comic book style truly works wonders. This clumsy, clueless giant robot is adorable.
Just peek at the community's screenshots page, and you'll see that the game's integrated photo mode (which lets you pause the game, choose your angle and apply filters to your images) can give quite impressive results illustration-wise, and that it might prove a fun toy to tinker with.
Thanks, Gabriel & others, that's great work!

I want to sing the praises of this game deeply, because on so many levels it is amazing; the visuals are awe inspiring, and for a UDK game better than some Unreal Engine 4 titles, and the premise is interesting. I love the ominous feeling you get walking around, and the way the environment evolves reminds me of Layers of Fear a little, which was a strong title as well.
But as much as I recommend trying this game, I also have a problem with one thing in particular: the delivery. I love to read, and I love writing for games as a means of expression. However, one thing that slightly bothers me about this particular instance is the fact that the game is somewhat built on the impression that the story should purely unveil itself throught text with complex wordplay and alliterations, hyperbole and allusions used correctly, but oftentimes unnecessarily. I exited the game when I ran into this instance while reading a note from a character in the game called Solomon (which counteracts Jonah, another character in the game, and obviously denotes some sort of biblical reference), where he actually asks the player, "Why should you be reading this?" and in my mind I began to realize how large the amount of text was that I was in the middle of, and that broke my immersion in a heavy handed way.
In the beginning you find notes with dates pinned up on the walls all over the place, and in those digestible bits, you can understand the gist of what is going on; the only problem is there are a lot of notes, and sometimes even notes within notes, which are a little bit much for even an enthusiastic reader and writer. All this information is given to you under the pretense that it is "optional," but reading a little about the game and feedback from other people stating otherwise, I feel this information is necessary to truly get a sense of what kind of world this is, and to understand the philosophy that the developers are getting at within the context of the story.
My hope is that with the next entry they spend more time conveying this story in some sort of *visual* way, rather than a *textual* way. If I were reading an interactive fiction, this would have been somewhat interesting, but it would have lost my attention thanks to the lofty wording. As much as it strives to sound intelligent, often comes across as somewhat pretentiously overthought, like they wrote it in a more basic manner and then converted it with an online thesaurus.
All of this to say from only 33 minutes of play. I'm a poet, don'tcha know it?

The game's art is pretty good and I loved the little details like the sunglare when the ship sets sail. The music is also pretty epic and I loved the mood and atmosphere the devs set up. However due to many reasons, I can't recommend this game to anyone in this present form, assuming its gonna get a decent overhaul anytime in the future.
Tutorial is Confusing:
The tutorial is in the form of multiple pages of text which you had to read through to understand the mechanics except that  you don't really understand much since many of the terms/jargon used in the tutorial text doesn't mean anything to you since they weren't explained. Telling the player that "Waylay" is pretty awesome isn't very informative when the player doesn't even know what Waylay is or looks like when it was mentioned. Too much text to read. Like this review.
Lack of Clarity in Winter Planning:
There are only 2 seasons that matters in the game. Summer and Winter. You plan activities for Winter on day 1 if i'm not wrong, and in summer you go out and do quests. 1 quest per year. The Winter planning screen is confusing because when players first see it, its hard to understand what "Warfare Bonus" is. After several in-game years I still don't know how much Warfare Bonus helps and if its even worth assigning anybody to that task. And why is Happiness a Bonus? If its a bonus, what is the base? I had 44% Happiness Bonus at the start. Is that bad? How bad is bad? The game doesn't tell you. The game also doesn't explain why when you had assigned people to Warfare and was expecting to get 47% but ended up with 18% somehow. No way to understand why that happened. Also, how much food is enough? There was a line at the end of the pages of tutorial text about Winter planning that says "1 food stock is enough for 5 people". For a day? For a week? A year? For how long? I assumed it was a day after playing the game for a bit more. So I had 1900 units of food as reserve. I also expect to make around 1400 units of food by winter. Does the game expect me to maintain an excel spreadsheet outside the game to calculate if I have enough food to last a year? A simple estimation in the game would help a great deal. Like tell us if I am going to have enough or not enough. Even King of Dragon Pass, which this game was clearly inspired by, did that.
Combat UI Needs Improvement:
At first glance the combat mode can be confusing. The avatars don't move at all. Not even when attacking. The only way to tell if a character is making a move is by looking at the top right at the active enemy portrait. Yes, top right. That's pulling the player's attention away from where the eyes tend to focus on, the characters in the center of the screen. You hear all these sounds of attacks missing and you realized that the glove icons appearing in the middle of the screen means missed shots. The concept of Defense Points were mentioned in the tutorial even before players had any idea what they meant or how they affect the combat. Elements such as health bars, defense points, and names of characters were hidden by default. They don't show even when someone was hit. I feel that the health bar should at least show up when a hit lands. You can show everything by clicking on this "eye" icon at the top right of the screen. I feel this should be on by default because you have to click on that every battle.
Narrative doesn't make sense:
The narrative is very confusing and unclear. Requiring players to read essays of text doesn't help. Its even worse when each random yearly event that pops up is another essay to read. It helps to have portraits of characters show up on the pop-up panel when you are in a dialogue with someone. There is a reason why many games do that. Because not all players have crazily good memory to be able to memorize all the names of every character in a game. It helps to have a visual reminder of who the characters mentioned in an essay of text are. Saxon and Danish names don't sound too different to someone who weren't from the region so when the narrative didn't specify, its hard to tell who is Saxon and who is Danish. There are also a lot of Danish words used that doesn't make sense unless you google it. Assuming that every one of your character knows what they mean just isn't right.
~ TLDR version ~
The bads:
- Bad tutorial system (walls of text)
- Confusing narrative (lots of danish words and jargon; essays of text to read)
- Economy system is confusing, doesn't make sense or not informative
- Combat UI poorly designed
The goods:
- Epic music
- Art is pretty good
- Combat can be fun if you can get past the bad UI

I had this game since it was released for EA and tried it on various ocasions.
This review is not a easy one.
What I love
- Atmosphere
- Art (all beautifuly hand drawn)
- Story (believable characters, also you can see that the developers invested a lot of their time to doing their homework regarding the setting)
- Writing (the writing is good, it is just about enough lenght and quality. It isnt by any chance too much overly complicated text that is long just for the sake of being long without being relevant to anything, so the people who are not native speakers struggle to not get lost in it - looking at you Torment: Tides of Numenera!!)
- Village customization and winter part of the game
- Events (will get to that later)
What I neither love nor hate
- Music (the tracks are ranging from iritating to absolutely forgetable to quite nice...)
What I dont like
- Events (While they generaly likeable, the problem is, that they are VERY repetitive. Some more than others (bloody trading ship trap and smoking hamlet). I played until the 13th year and still encounter new events. I really suggest the devs to put some script into game so events happen only once a year. I really dont want to encounter 6 smoking hamlets and 5 trade ship traps every year...)
What I HATE (not overeacting, really HATE)
- Combat (this is the most frustrating and experience breaking part of the game for me. Until you get your hands on better equipment and level up your characters, the combat basicaly goes by this scenario: ''You have 78% of hit and have 4 attack. The opponent has 15 HP. OK game, lets make it MISS, MISS, MISS, 1 DMG'' *REPEAT until turn 20*. This wouldnt be so frustrating and iritating if there was at least option to make the combat >FASTER<. It is extremely slow, boring and not challenging in the later stages of game. The combat basicaly make me save scum to avoid some radnom events (Looking at you, you damned ''unavoidable stucked trade ship trap'' which I for some reason encounter many times every summer... Did I mention I really hate the trade ship event?)
What is worth mentioning
- BUGS. This hame has them and LOTS of them. From black screen, load freezes, ship dissapearing while traveling, etc, etc. I could go on I've seen most of them. But I have to say that the devs are small studio and are actually VERY responsive and helpful, doing their best to fix them, given their limited resources. So I have to give them credit for that.
- VERDICT
I do recommend it. It needs more work on it  and I dont think that it was ready for full release. But I like it and dont regret buying it for the given price.
EDIT: I have to admit that on my second playthrough, I realized that I have been missing many combat related mechanics and that was what made it very frustrating for me. I was still used to the ''card deck'' combat back from the EA. I still dont like it to be honest but I cant say its THAT bad...

I feel really bad for downvoting Dandelion. I really wanted to love it, and I sank so much time into it so I can get the full story from all of the routes and the graphics that go with them. But the more I think about it, this game just wasn't all that fun and the story wasn't too great either. (Please don't think I hate this game either though, I just like to poke fun at it a little sometimes)
It's not a badly-made game for sure; the music is good, the art is beautiful, the voice acting is very well done, the English translation is solid, and the guys you get to date aren't too terrible. Unfortunately though, I think the place where this game is weakest is in its story and characters, which are the most important things in a visual novel. Every single character in this game ends up being shallow, bland, and forgettable --- some worse than others. I didn't feel particularly emotionally attached to any of them. Most of your interactions with them consist of...going out to places together once a week, giving them gifts, and watching some pre-set dialogue that mostly consists of small talk. That just seems like the shallowest way to develop characters and relationships in terms of a visual novel. There are also some routes where almost nothing at all happens, leading to a very empty experience overall. The romances aren't super well developed and you don't really spend much my time getting to know any of the characters. (Not helping is the fact that a lot of these guys' personalities are full of cliche tropes...I'm pretty sure Jihae's big character flaw was...being too pretty but thinking he was ugly??? which made sort of sense as a magical interdimensional rabbit but not as a human haha) I also personally didn't like the setup that
Plus most of the time, the guys that you aren't dating mostly get pushed to the side, which is weird because you all live in the same house! Keeping some friendly interactions with them or something would have been nice, because these dudes did have a lot of potential to be weird or funny.
Other reviewers have pointed out that some of these relationships would be considered unhealthy or dysfunctional and that the heroine overall comes across as being too weak and passive, and I can certainly see where they're coming from. I know that there's a level of cultural differences and personal likes/dislikes at play here, I know that a game can be enjoyable regardless of whether or not the relationships portrayed are 100% perfectly healthy (I thought Magical Diary and Hatoful Boyfriend were super great for crying out loud)...But, I still just didn't care for it and I can see why others wouldn't either, so it's worth pointing it out at least. I personally just found the heroine to be a rather bland character, though she definitely has a sense of relatability to her.  Then there's also the fact that
though at least Jieun's route (the young albino rabbit) didn't do that, so that was a nice change of pace.
So basically all of the routes are pretty much just angst, boredom, and frustration and not much else (which honestly could probably be fixed if the stat raising was toned down and the pacing wasn't so damned slow). I also didn't find the true ending to be anything special or compelling, just...weird? It was honestly sort of a letdown, like there wasn't really an overall story arc or anything that was worth completing all the routes for.
I will admit though that Jiwoo's route (the blonde rabbit guy) was probably the most interesting/enjoyable since both he and the heroine get some character development and have a bit more natural interactions. Plus he has the added benefit of being hilarious. Jiwoo is the real true ending :P
And of course, most of this game is stats management. The stats barely have an impact on the game, but they take up most of your time, so the game ends up feeling a lot like a chore. There's also the fact that it takes FOREVER for your regular ol' rabbits and cats to turn into dudes (Hell, I think their bonding with the heroine was more compelling when they WERE animals because of how much she brightened up and started to find joy and meaning in her sad and empty life through her pets, which is what many people do experience in real life). Even more frustrating is the fact that you have to start the game from the very beginning for each route if you want to unlock the character graphics, but at least you can start pressing the skip button then (I'm a filthy completionist lol)
My overall thoughts on Dandelion is that it's not a bad game, it's got its cute and heartwarming moments and its characters are decent, but it's not that great or fun of a game either. I honestly think this game way too overhyped; take away the art and the voice acting and you don't have much else left in this game that's worthwhile, especially for such a steep price tag (I understand why it's such a high price, obviously games take a lot of time, effort, and money to make, especially when there's gorgeous art, voice-acting, and multilingual translations, but the product still kinda felt like a waste of my time due to its overall shallow and boring content). By all means buy it if you're still interested, it's just that for me the game fell so short of the amazing and compelling game I thought it would be after hearing so many great things about it. It's got a lot of problems with pacing and bland characters.
You'd probably be better off just buying Cheritz's other game, Nameless, which still has the beautiful art and voice acting, but has a more compelling story and characters and basically avoids/remedies ALL of the pitfalls that I mentioned here for Dandelion. Or hell, maybe try Date Warp; that game has a pretty similar setup/premise but it's a lot cheaper and the characters are better developed (plus its sadly underrated and could use more love...)

Relationships Take Time, Some Skills, and Apparently a Really Bogus Twist Ending
While I'm recommending this game, I do want to point out the elephant in the room with the multiple endings (not just the "Bad End" where the school friend proposes to you out of nowhere). Without spoiling anything, I really didn't like them at all, and the game seemed to just end suddenly with them. It seemed unfinished, and really irked me considering how much time I had put into this game/the relationships involved. I've said my peace: I'm not a fan of it. There.
But as for the rest of the game itself, I found it mainly decent. The part I liked best was the skill-building mechanic, where you can choose to build up your skill level in multiple areas with one activity per day, and lower Stress and Pressure areas in order to stay healthy. I questioned whether Feminitity and Beauty were really the most important things she should be focusing on, but I didn't find anything really offensive about it either. The item collection mechanic that's secondary in it could use some work - going to the bookstore doesn't allow you to read any of the new books you purchase? That seems like it was meant to contribute to skill building at some point, but the developers didn't have time to finish it.
The characters, including our main, can be pretty one dimensional. Jisoo is the 'bad boy', Jihae is the pretty and shy older man, Jiyeon is the perpetual child, Jieun may be a literal child from how he looks and acts on first impression, and Jiwoo is the rich-boy a*hole. At least, that's all based on first impression, but the writers do try to develop them more depending on which relationship you pick. Some of the redeeming backstories work, while others seem out of place. Also, I didn't really like how Jisoo would often bully or try to intimidate Heejung if she didn't pick him, with pretty much every choice, and led to some awkward encounters. Even if it's in character for him, that made me uncomfortable and crosses the line from 'bad boy' to 'obsessive and abusive and borderline manipulative stalker who you should definitely stay the HELL away from'.
Heejung is not a bad character, but at times it feels like she has no autonomy over her decisions. Her mother's abuse may have led to her crippling insecurity and this would explain this, but I'd really rather she grew to have more confidence in herself and not really let herself be led around by men or overwhelmingly shy around Jihae, for example. Again, it wasn't an offensive thing to me or stopped me from enjoying the game, but I'm kind of a bit sick of the insecure girl trope. It'd be fun to have a protagonist who's direct, has her own opinions and knows what she wants, but that's just my opinion.
Overall, I really think the mechanics in this game hold up, but the long hours it takes to play, multiple character/writing problems, and the bad endings I know I'm gonna get even if I do everything right, really stop me from playing this all the time. I'd say it is a good sometimes-game, it's definitely good for a dating sim, and there are some cute moments with each of the characters. But the flaws are kind of too big to ignore.

The biggest downside of the Steam controller is that very few games really benefit from it. The games I like the most with it are Rocket League and driving games in genral, Resident Evil 4 and 5, and Spectale Fighters, specifcially Bayonetta and Devil May Cry 4. I like binding one of the 2 back battery cover buttons to the lock-on function in those games, It just feels way more natural to use those buttons when you need to hold a button down. 2D sidescrollers are pretty good for the most part. However, this controller is pretty awful for games that require constant control of the camera and/or precision aiming. Any twin-stick shooter or a game like Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons which implement some kind of twin-stick control scheme are basically unplayable on this controller. The Steam controller is not a replacement for an Xbox controller by any stretch of the imagination, but for certain games, the Steam controllers unique offerings are really nice.

I keep hearing people say that the Steam controller is a controller/mouse hybrid. It does a bit of both, but both not as good as the original. And it's kinda true, there are definately scenario's where I'd prefer a mouse or a normal controller. But there are also a lot of situations where the Steam controller really shines.
The Steam controller looks and feels a bit clumsy. It feels slightly too big and a bit too light for my taste. The touchpads need a lot of getting used to. I also feel like the steam controller isn't really meant for shooter games. Its touchpads feel way more accurate than joysticks, but the device still lacks the sensitivity and accuracy that a mouse offers and that shooters really need.
With that being said, the Steam controller offers some exiting new features to the world of controllers. The most usefull one by far are the back buttons, which offer a new layer of input. Moving your thumb from the A to the B button takes time, and if the A button is attack and the B button is dodge, you're gonna use both a lot. With the steam controller, you can reassign either or both to the back buttons. This really shaves off a few milliseconds of your reaction time.
Having a steam controller handy is also very usefull for when friends come by. The controller can behave like a xbox controller, which is very widely supported. And if you do come across a game that doesn't support it, you can make the steam controller behave like a keyboard. The biggest downside is that a game HAS to be launched through steam in order to make the steam controller work, but you can do this via the "add a non-steam game to my library" option.
So if you're looking into controllers to buy, take the steam controller into consideration. It takes some getting used to, it's slightly experimental, but not expensive (especially on a sale) and opens up a new world of gaming.
+ Back buttons are very usefull for quick response actions
+ Widely supported
+ Use with cable or with bluetooth
+/- Touchpads usefull for some situations but clumsy in others

I have owned a Steam Controller for almost two years and have used it exclulsively.  I can say, without doubt, that this is the best input device I have ever used.  For most games the keyboard is unnecessary and, combined with the Steam Link, this controller can be used on any display in the house.
Programming this device can be as simple or as complex as you like.  There is a long learning curve if you want to familiarize yourself with every, single, function.  In time, you will find how much power you have...literally in the palm of your hand.  Controller configs can be modified, saved, shared, and each Steam game has user-created, and recommended configs you can download in a snap and modify to your liking.  Altering configs during gameplay is as easy as the push of a button.
This device is larger than the standard console controller, and it's heavier and more durable, too.  The ergonomic design makes it a pleasure to hold for hours, and hours.  The Steam Controller is wireless by design, but can be used with a USB cable if you run out of battery power.
This controller has too many details to go over in one small review, but I have nothing but good things to say about each one.
Some important information:
Do's:
Do buy a set of rechargable AA batteries that come with a dedicated recharger.  I use Eneloop.
Do get a Steam Link if you want to be able to play games on other TVs in the house.
Do take your time to familiarize yourself with this controller's potential.
Dont's:
Don't expect to master all the intricacies over-night.  Programming configs is not for the faint of heart.
Don't get frustrated if you can't figure something out.  The Steam Community is always available for support.
Don't waste another minute deciding if you should get one.  Get one!

I really enjoyed the first Space Run game.  And I love this one even more!
Space Run Galaxy is a different animal than the original but the premise and gameplay is basically the same.  The original was more of a tower defense puzzle game.  Each level was a puzzle solved by tower selection, arrangement, and timing.  Galaxy is more like an RPG.  There's an extended map where you can repeat the same routes but with different cargo or missions.  You have to unlock and build the tower components, as well as your ship design, as you go along.  This makes every space an ever evolving challenge.  There isn't "one" solution like in the original.  It's more dependent on building up your ship and trying to make runs to progress the game than trying to solve each level.  As you can tell from other reviews some people don't like this style, but I really enjoy it.  It has much more replayability or continuous playability than the original.  I can see how some find it a little grindy, but it never stops being fun for me.  (And it's not any more grindy than the original - I remember replaying levels over and over until I figured out the "solution.")
It's still pretty early in the game for me.  Looking forward to finishing the game and many hours of play!
Another great feature is how the game lends itself to easily scale in difficulty according to your preference:  challenge to reach 3 stars each run, how much time you spend upgrading your ship, choice of routes to complete your mission, how many contracts you take for each route - all these allow you to increase or decrease the difficulty at any time during play - ingenious!
UPDATE: 3/4 way through and many hours of enjoyment!  Way better than the first one, and much longer.  Having a great time.

A good variation on tower defense gameplay, Space Run Galaxy is very similar to the first game in the series, almost identical in fact, a game I got from Good Old Games back when it originally released. Varied and powerful towers, emphasis on both fast and strategic construction, and a fun space western vibe that, otherwise, is among the most unabashedly grindtastic games I have ever played. If that does not bother you, by all means, keep reading.
As a rookie Space Runner working under legendary transporter Buck Mann, the player character of the first game, It will be your task to transport various valuable, sometimes dangerous cargoes between planets and space stations, quickly and safely. You'll be paid in credits and raw materials, and gradually open up new destinations and jobs as you progress. Completing jobs also rewards XP, with levels earned conferring new types of structures to use in the levels.
Your ship takes the form of a hex grid, with each structure taking up a certain number of hexes, with many having additional placement requirements- engines can only go on the left edge, for example, as you are always flying to the right. Many structures confer bonuses to any structures they are placed next to, such as the shield generators and upgraders. Structures are divided into four categories and color-coded accordingly: Red for offense, blue for defense, green for utility and yellow for the special "connectors", which transfer bonuses between all structures that touch them or any ultimately linked connector, enabling you to build up a power grid. Unlike the first game, where your ship was preconfigured in shape and you could build as many turrets of a type as you wished permitting you have enough hexnuts, the in-level currency, in this entry you can choose a ship, but you are limited to the structures you actually have in your posession and must craft more if you want to use more in a given level. To do so, you'll need credits and materials.
Here's where things get ugly. When you purchase or are awarded materials, they are stored at the station you're docked at when you recieve them. To build a new turret, you have to have the materials at that station to do so. To further complicate matters, a given station's merchant may not sell materials, said materials are outrageously expensive, and the local mechanic will almost never produce all four types of structures. Now for the kicker: you'll need to physically transport crafting materials between stations as you would with mission cargo.
Combine this with expontially increasing material costs for each structure built and the sheer time investment involved with not only personally shipping all this junk around but doing extra runs just for cash and experience in order to have powerful enough structures in sufficient quantities, and you have a recipe for a game that will wear out is welcome alarmingly quickly.
It's so grindy in fact that I cannot in good faith recommend this entry to others- unless you either have many hours to spend doing blue milk runs for cash and parts, or are willing to do a bit of messing with the files to bypass the grind. It's a shame, really, the game has great potential otherwise.

Sure, it adds "realism" you might think, but when the pieces have weird shapes, not to mention that some of them might consist of a single colour (with large parts of the puzzle being of that same colour), it gets annoying.
The "pixel fairy" can be helpful, with the different powerups she provides. The rotation power is somewhat useful, as well as the location one. However, the "ghost" powerup is not so good. Not because it isn't useful, but rather because the ability to see the image you're building is something you can easily do with real world puzzles. Also, the fairy can be sometimes annoying as she gets in the way of the pieces.
As far as the theme goes, when it says "anime" it means that the puzzle images are drawn in a style reminiscent of anime; don't go into the game expecting to see puzzles based around things like Dragonball or Rurouni Kenshin. Even then, I'd say the quality of the drawings is nice.
I guess I'll give this a thumbs down; not because it's a bad game, but because it has certain flaws that I can't ignore.

The Golden Age of J-RPGs has ended. No longer can we expect to see a plethora of J-RPGs coming every year. This time has come and past, and some people do not hesitate to state that J-RPG, as a genre, is dead. Do I agree? Not quite. While it is true that the genre is less represented than before, some developers are hell-bent to keep making this type of game, and they can be divided in two categories. Those that keep trying to make the genre evolve, like Square-Enix, and those that focus on the core aspects, like all the J-RPGs made with RPG-maker that strive to recreate that nostalgic feeling of the SNES era.
If I were to put Falcom in one of these two categories, it would definitely be in the second one, with the interesting particularity that it's a relatively big studio, which means they can afford to be more ambitious, graphically speaking, than little indie devs. This means that what they do, is keep making J-RPGs with a PS1/PS2/Dreamcast vibe. Unlike Square, they don't focus on beautiful graphics and real-time action, no, they put their focus on what they've done well for the past decade : writing, music, and turn-based combat design.
Why all these info, why not speak about the game directly? Well, because if you're a fan of good J-RPGs of the PS1/PS2/Dreamcast era, I'm sure you already frantically installed this game to see what all these good reviews are all about. And if you're not in that category, then I hope it will allow you to know what to expect, more than detailing the strengths and weaknesses of Trails of Cold Steel.
Some people like to point out how everything in Cold Steel feels generic and already seen. I won't argue, but I want to point out that while Falcom does heavily use tropes and clichés, such as child-characters, a school-setting in Cold Steel 1, and things like that...they use them in the right way : not as the "be all end all" of an idea, but as the starting point for writing it and giving it an interesting swing. This is what makes the characters lovable, the world believable, and the story interesting.
Finally, I want to put some perspective about this game. It's part of The Legend of Heroes series, comprised of J-RPGs that are set in the same universe, but are separated in arcs of 2 to 4 games. Each arc takes places in a different country of the main continent, and they are only separated by a couple years, or take place at the same time. As of now, there are three arcs : the Trails in the Sky arc, the Ao/Zero arc, and the Trails of Cold Steel are. The Sky arc has two games plus one side-story and is available on Steam, the Ao/Zero is not officially translated unfortunately (yet!), and Trails of Cold Steel will have four games, this one, the second should come out on Steam early 2018, the third one is out in Japan (count roughly 1-3 years for the translation), and the fourth one is in development. Falcom has also stated that they plan to do a fourth arc in the future.
This means that The Legend of Heroes, for how generic its name feels, is in fact the sole J-RPG series with so many games set in the same universe and that take place roughly at the same time. And Falcom does intend to keep making these games. Of course, if all the games are bad, or of diverse quality, it would not be that interesting, but Cold Steel 1 is considered one of the weakest entry in the series, a sentiment I kinda share, and it's still a damn awesome game.
For a J-RPG fan, this is something to follow : a whole ongoing series with an excellent average quality, that even at its lowest is still superior than the majority of the genre. So, is the J-RPG genre dead? Actually no, it may not be as flamboyant as before, but it's still very alive and kicking. Because, why fix what isn't broken?

I want to love this game. For most of it I do. The story is engaging and interesting, the exploration and choices are fun, if somewhat repetitive onboard the ship during travels, and the gear and loot gathering I find exciting. I also love building up my city and expanding my ship.
One area that frustrates me greatly is the complete lack of character choice other than male or female. I cannot pick my name, my class or skills, my appearance, or even the weapon I started with (I chose Flóki, the male “support-class” character which was one of two options at release.) I feel like he is the weakest character in my party most of the time, having poor armor and melee skills (though a fast attacking weapon is nice sometimes,) he's a support character which kills my interest in playing my own way (I'd enjoy being a front-line character, personally) and limits my weapons and skills to one default. It shatters my replay interest, and I imagine it's on the shelf until expansions come out someday as I don't want to be this same, relatively weak character with the same name, and backstory as my first playthrough.
So much is right with the game, but that huge design flaw hurts my enjoyment and severely limits the time I will put into this and my interest in recommending it to anyone.
There are some release-day technical flaws, which with character customization and more interest in the "hero character," I could overlook. The game does have some lock-ups, crash-to-desktop errors, inventory issues - an example being that food cannot go over 100 in your stock or it "rolls-over" and leaves only the digits after the one-hundred place (ex 114 becomes 14), often leading me to starve during travels, and when purchasing in stores sometimes you cannot buy items from the trader despite money and inventory space. I have also had random bandit events during winter where I fought off the entire bandit force except their lone archer. The archer had evasion so high you had sometimes less than zero percent chance to hit. Seriously, even when surrounded by five vikings they had 110% evasion. 10% below zero chance of being hit. I actually spent ten or twelve rounds sometimes trying to just hit them a single time using accuracy boosting skills. Something is wrong there.
All in all, I highly recommend the game for the story, city and ship building, exploration and freedom of choices, but the fact that the game is based around unchangeable characters and gives you zero option for customization beyond your limited armor/weapon preset, wrecks an otherwise fantastic game for me. If you don't care about being pigeon-holed into two lackluster characters and only want story in a Viking setting, this game is for you. If you care about who you play as and like to have some choice, this game is not for you.
I really want to love this game, I want this company to make a pile of money and to produce sequels. I just wish they would implement some form of character customization. I think they earned my purchase price, but I won't be buying DLC/Add-ons or a sequel if I am stuck in this hole.

Simply put, this is not a replacement for a mouse and keyboard. But can it replace a traditional controller? The answer is a resounding yes.
I've used this controller for about a month now and it's the best one I've ever used; gone are the days of sluggish joystick movements and missing your shots due to acceleration. No, sir - with the Steam Controller you can get close to the precision of the mouse.
That said, you can certainly tell this is the first iteration of the controller - it's bulky, the grips are inverted and not like other controllers, and until you get used to them you will honestly find it quite uncomfortable. You get two back paddle buttons alongside the usual face buttons you'll be used to, LB, RB, LT and RT. There's a single analog stick and two touchpads, one on the left, one on the right.
I wanted to refund this during the first week and I very nearly did -- to do that would have been the worst mistake in my gaming history. Once I got used to the bulky feel, came to terms with the configurator software (which is fantastic by the way), and learned how to handle the touchpads, this has become by far the best piece of kit I've ever bought for gaming... Xbox Elite controllers that go for nearly double the price don't even come close to the Steam Controller in anything but ergonomics.
I would advise spending some time with it (at least a month) and then the rewards will soon follow. What works for me, I've found, is to use the right touchpad for fast, long distance movements and then the super-low latency gyro controls for precision shots - it really does work a treat (and it's even quite thrilling to use the gyro controls once you get used to them, it's surprising how effective they are).
As I said above though, this is the first iteration of the device and it does have a few issues which can detract from the product; any games not in your Steam library will need adding as non-steam games so you can utilise the overlay functionality and setup your configs for each game, you will most likely need to spend 30 minutes setting up a config for each game unless there's a suitable community config available (I often find the sensitivity settings on these not to my liking though. Be honest, would you want to use someone's mouse sensitivity settings? I think not).
Some games also don't support using controller + mouse input at the same time, which isn't really the controller's fault but is a problem none-the-less. For these, you can indeed set it up to use either full mouse and keyboard controls or emulate a joystick using traditional joystick or 'mouse joystick' which was added in a recent firmware update and is honestly quite good, not on par with a mouse but certainly better than a joystick. You'd be better off just setting up bindings for a keyboard and mouse, though. You can bring up touch-menus for games that have on-screen inventories and the likes, which makes UIs designed for mouses a wonderful experience and depending on the UI can even be more comfortable to use on the Steam Controller. Sounds too good to be true, I'm sure.
You might be thinking that if you use solely mouse and keyboard input, then you lose the advantages of analog movement, right? No. The configurator is that good. You can even setup an inverse ring setup on the touchpad or analog stick, so you could bind walk to a half tilt of the joystick and then run to full tilt and push in the stick to sprint. So the three movements of a traditional analog setup all bound on the joystick using a traditional WASD setup... WHAT!? The software really is the best part of the controller and to some that'll be a nightmare.
I will never go back to a traditional controller. I have no reason to. For those that don't mind putting a little time and effort into learning, this will be a rewarding experience and your gaming experience on the TV will be much more exciting, knowing that no longer will you be unable to perform flick shots and quick strafes, due to sluggish joystick precision.
EDIT: Something I forgot to mention in my review above: I would suggest setting in-game mouse sensitivity to 0 (or as low as it goes) and use the overlay software to manage the sensitivity. I find it's much more precise that way.

I used the Steam Controller for little over three weeks now.
Whoever says this controller is inconvenient to use or worse than Xbox Pro is just lazy or forgets one simple thing. We are all PC players, right? We tweak things by nature. And the possiblities of tweaking the Steam Controller are close to endless.
Quick resume: There is nothing you can't do with the Steam Controller that other Controllers can. The XBox Pro Controller justifies is ridiculous price with its customization features. The Steam Controllers costs roughly one fourth and you can customize it much more.
So for me, this is probably the most cost-efficient controller out there.
Is this "best controller" perfect? No. It isn't.
The customization takes time. It's not that you >can< tweak it perfectly. It's not an option. You have to do it. Someone that never used a trackpad before may even try the mouse-emulation-feature once, be disgusted by it and never try it again. Thankfully, you can disable it. Or tweak it. Or use it in an entirely different way. As every other of this Controller's feature.
How is the setup? It's plug&play. Mostly. Sometimes it doesn't work. Sometimes it stops working. Sometimes you end up unknowingly controlling the pc in the other room and wonder why the pc you're sitting in front of doesn't do anything. As always, the failure is the person sitting in front of the screen.
The Steam Controller is not a PS4 or XBox or Switch Controller. It's not designed to work perfectly with one single system. It's designed for you to try and make it work with every game from every developer on every system. It's from Valve, not Apple.
How is the look? When I opened the case, I thought "wow, that's ugly".If you'd ask me, I'd say the Switch Pro is the most beautiful controller out there. But you get used to this look. Doesn't bother me anymore. Even started to like it.
How is the feel? You have to remember not to cramp up. The handling is somewhat different than conventional controllers, So it's like the first time you tried holding a controller as an 8 year old kid,
How is the durability? Frankly, I can't say yet. It doesn't seem worse than any other controller. People who make statements like "cheap plastic" are not scientists. For me, the Steam Controller looks relatively well made. It wouldn't survive a 10-story-drop I guess. Or getting smashed against the wall. But neither would a XBox Pro. Difference is, the Steam Controller is 35 bucks on sale like every four weeks or so.
All in all, I have no complaints that don't involve my own shortcomings (finding the right settings, mostly).
Big recommend.
PS: you can use several controllers with one USB dongle. Don't use several dongles at the same time or on several pcs running steam at the same time.

I play a lot of RPGS, and a fair few of them are JRPGS. I can say with confidence that is one of the best ones I have ever played. There are quite a few things that they did correctly in this game, and there are just a few things that I would like to see changed.

Pros:
Combat
- Classic turn based but they keep the abilities and the mechanics interesting enough that it does not get stale.
Characters
- Most of the characters have been fun and interesting to listen to. I find myself waiting for the next playthrough
so i can engage in different bonding events to learn about different characters.
Story
- I am only on Chapter 3 but thus far the story and world are interesting, lots of mystery surrounding every character so far and still lots more to discover in the world.
Turbo
- I never played original but apparently this was not in it. Turbo makes traversing the maps so much faster, great idea
Difficulty
- Rare to see a genuine difficulty setting in many JRPG games from a couple years ago but it exists here. It is very difficult to out level your opponents and combat can always surprise you with a butt kicking. Although I have never recieved a Game Over on normal difficulty I have come close and that is a great feeling.
Play Time
- 80 hours of good story for $30, yes please.I say 80 hours because that what I should average in a playthrough since I am purposely opening all chests and talking to all npcs.
Cons:
Its a small thing but I would like to the costumes unlock after they are used in game rather than on new game+ The entire first playthrough you are stuck in the uniforms which the main character simply does not look that great in.
The repetitive nature of the field studies is starting to show. As I said I am only on chapter 3 but having repeated essentially the same exact process 3 times in a row just in different places is a bit strange. I have a feeling this is not going to be this way for long.
If you want to complete 100% for any of the completionists out there, get ready to look up a guide. I noticed I missed a few books already which apparently are traded for super powerful weapons. Not necesaarily a con for me but some people will think so.
Conclusion
Amazing game that any JRPG fan would be insane not to pick up. All i can think about is when the sequals will be releasing because of how much fun I am having in this game right now.

What a great game! I haven't really written reviews before, but I feel compelled to offer some positive praise for TGWR because it is a thing of beauty.
---
What do I like?
The art is fantastic, the writing is genuine and the attention to historical detail is very admirable.  The gameplay mechanics aren't a wholesale rehash of other games, although there are bits and pieces that will feel familiar.  The combat in particular isn't groundbreaking, but the buff/malus system does add some fun to process.
What I particularly like is that the game forces the player to choose their path carefully and the rewards reaped are not always what is expected.
---
What don't I like?
Thankfully, most of my complaints have already been acknowledged by the developers, so they are transient issues.  The game needs more potential results to the choices faced by your warband.  The economy needs some tweaking.
A lot of other reviews have hit the broad points regard the weaknesses of the combat system, so I won't hang on them.  The combat is not perfect, but TGWR is not a game wholly dedicated to combat.  I think some people are expecting this game to be a pillaging simulator, but TGWR is not marketed in that fashion, and focusing on that aspect would disregard the other, perhaps more interesting, aspects of life in northern Europe in the middle ages.
---
I hope other people will take a chance on this game, I am really enjoying it.

The thing that makes this controller worthwhile is the gyroscope feature, the gyroscope allows you to aim by tilting or moving your controller up or down. I'm playing through Rise of the Tomb Raider again using this controller and it's by far the most fun using the bow and arrow while aiming with the gyroscope. Hunting animals or people in the game is way more fun for me when i have the visceral movement and control rather than just moving the mouse left and right or having to continually adjust the right analogue stick on the Xbox controller.
I got this controller a year or so ago and i don't use it as much as i thought i would. One of the main reasons is it takes 20-30 minutes to map the controls for a new game and get them perfect for you, and i'm talking about after you import someone else's template that has done most of the work for you. The mapping is both the best and worst part of the controller, it allows you unparalleled access and customization for every aspect of the controller, and you can adjust the sensitivity for everything including the gyro (which is the most important part for me). The downside is most games don't have native support for this controller and even if they did the way the touch controls and sensitivity works means you would want to tweak the native setup anyway probably.
If you are looking for the best all rounder controller i still think the Xbox One S or the Elite controller is best, nearly all games have support for that and more importantly have in-game button prompts mapped for it. In Tomb Raider using the Steam controller i have to remember what i mapped spacebar to cos the prompts which are displayed on screen in quick time events are the keyboard prompts, so when it tells you to press E to attack i have to remember to press Y on the controller. This isn't too much of an issue, but if you leave the game for a week or two and come back to it you will have to relearn/remember what everything is mapped to.
I would say the steam controller only really excels at one genre which is the third person action adventure one like Tomb Raider, and i'm talking about single player. I've tried using the steam controller in counter strike and Battlefield and i could never get the sensitivity quite right in those to feel comfortable, in some aspects it's better than a traditional controller, but at times you find yourself flicking the movement too far on the touch pad so it takes you longer to face an enemy than on say an Xbox controller. I think if you really put in the time with it you could make it work. If it had two analogue sticks on it you wouldn't have this issue.
The PS4 Dualshock 4 controller actually has a gyroscope on it as well which i tried out in battlefront on the PC and it actually works ok, but the gyroscope isn't as accurate as the one in the steam controller i find, but that's also another option to think about if you want a controller for first person shooters.
For racing games i still default to the Xbox One S controller, if you only play racing games then get that controller, you won't regret it. I tried Rocket League with the Steam controller and it's perfectly playable with it, but again the Xbox controller is a much better designed and comfortable controller to play with for racing games.
If money is no object and you already have an Xbox controller i would recommend the Steam one in certain games over the Xbox one, but again mainly where aiming is important thanks to the gyro on it (in single player).

An enjoyable tower defense game.
I'm somewhat a TD enthusiast. I know my way around the genre. It can be a really addictive and rewarding kind of game. I've even designed my own TD game on paper (though I could never code it).
Space Run Galaxy has a lot of what makes TD games fun. It also has an interesting and fairly well implemented concept. You are a space runner running jobs for several characters throughout the game. The main story line that you progress through the missions involves fighting off an invasive species. That's about as deep as the story seems to get, though.
The main gripe I have with the game is that after several hours it just isn't fun enough. Here are a few ways in which I think the game could have kept my interest long enough to complete the game.
1: More varied levels.
To some degree, by the time I get to the second quarter of the game it is beginning to throw some unique challenges at me by changing the dimensions and conditions of the transported cargo. However, this is not quite enough. It comes off as a bit of a chore to have to alter my ship slightly in order to solve this problem.
By variance I mean fewer planets/runs and more interesting conditions placed on runs. Since there are 3 types of units (Red/Blue/Green) It would have been nice to have runs or missions that require only a single type be used or that a type not be used.
It would also have been nice if some of the runs involved enemies only coming from a single direction. A mission like this would be a fun diversion from the monotony of dealing with all the directions enemies can come at you from.
A mission with a limited amount of resources in which your primary resource is action points for your turrets would have been interesting as well.
This point simply is to say that the game is lacking in creative ways to make it fun and enjoyable.
2. Tower Scaling isn't as satisfying as it could be
A lot of TD games allow you to level up your towers over time using different mechanics. I personally prefer the experience points mechanic. SRG levels up towers by giving you structures you can build adjacent to the towers. This comes at the expense of tiles, a resource that is very important and needs to be well managed in order to win. This does bring up interesting problems, mostly to do with how you want to build your ship and place your towers. However, most of the time it just feels like an inconvenience considering you have no idea which direction you're going to be attacked from in the future which could cause some upgrades to go wasted. Towers also can only be upgraded twice (and will need to be adjacent to two upgrade structures to do so). Connector tiles seem like a way to make upgrading less wieldy, but in the end take up a crap ton of space themselves.
I would have made it so that other structures can be built on top of connector tiles. That way I could realize the fantasy of connecting an entire ship with various upgrades.
3. Lacks a "Long" level or "infinite mode".
Granted I haven't played to completion (it's a long game to complete) but the game lacks a mode which just lets you see how long you can last as wave after wave crashes against your ship. Modes like this are fun because it lets you attempt to get to that min/max fantasy of having a killer ship that is better than the last one you made, and the one before that. (and before that). Levels are too short to really let you feel the power of your end game build. Which leads me to point 1. There are too many "levels". Less could have been more with less levels but more intricate and perhaps longer levels.
4. Scaling Economy options
The best TD games IMO are those that have levels designed in such a way that using good strategy can allow you to "run away" with the level. That is to say, if you play it really well early, the end game becomes an romp in your favor. This is usually done with a level up mechanic, but it can also be done with a "currency multiplier" effect. This game is a bit too fast paced for this and it's economy a bit too easy in the later stages of a level for this to work. Usually by the end of a level I'm getting so much money I can't spend it all in time! And it's not like it's that hard to do.
To some degree, this is implemented in the game through those first moment supply/science ships with no offensive capabilities. It creates a situation where you ask whether it is worth it to throw resources at those ships even if they are coming from a direction that no offensive ships are coming from. Ditto with some of the asteroid waves that might force strange turret placement/timing. But this isn't enough for me. It gives  a small boost at the beginning of a level... but doesn't create the snowball effect I'd like it to have.
Final Verdict
A fun while it lasted kind of experience but a bit too repetitive even for a TD game. Lacking in imaginative level designs and certain mechanics that I consider to be important to making games of this genre fun in a long lasting way.

This game is terrible.  Not because it's just a jigsaw puzzle game.  I wouldn't have bothered getting or playing this at all if that were the case.  The issue is that pretty much every aspect of its design is flawed.
It plays background music in the form of a single track that loops endlessly, which is a harmless enough little tune, but gets tiring with no variety for any of the 25 puzzles the game has.  Thankfully you can mute it in the options menu, which you'll do if for no other reason than to shut up that stupid fairy.  Whoever programmed that in was a jackass.  The fairy talks way too much and says annoying things, taunting and harassing you constantly.  Even though you can make it go away as you work on the puzzle (which removes the ability to use hints), because at least somebody had a shred of common sense, it still bothers you in the menu screen.  I can go to the puzzle select screen and before five seconds have passed, it'll start bugging me to hurry up and pick one.  I could understand if I was just sitting there for a minute or two without choosing a puzzle or exiting out, but when I have barely had a chance to look at any of them it needs to shut up and leave me alone.
As you work on the puzzles the pieces float around the edge of the board, constantly moving, which is really annoying.  It isn't helpful and it doesn't make the game more interesting, so why make them move around?  If nothing else let me turn that feature off so I can find pieces more easily.
The puzzle pieces snap to the correct spot on the board, if they're rotated the right way, but even if you have two pieces lined up properly, knowing they fit together, they will not connect unless you find their proper place on the board first.  That's really annoying when you find pieces that line up but aren't able to work out where they go on the board, meaning you have to use a hint to find out where one of them goes.
Rotating the puzzle pieces can be annoying because in order to do so you have to hold the left mouse button down, selecting the piece, and then right click it.  If you aren't holding it with the left mouse button and right click on it, it gets flung back in with the other pieces around the edge.  I don't need a button that does that, as I can always easily drag a piece off of the board.  Instead, allow me to easily rotate each piece by simply right clicking while my cursor hovers over it.
The pictures used for the puzzles aren't really interesting.  It just has people standing around in various environments.  There's no action or dynamism to what they're doing.  It could have involved pictures of combat, magic, slapstick, or anything happening, but that isn't what we got.  Many of the color palettes were quite aggravating as well, as they would use similar shades in multiple parts of the same image.  This wouldn't have been such a problem if you were allowed to reference the image of the puzzle whenever you wanted, but to do that you have to use one of your hints.  Why does reviewing the image require the use of a hint?  It doesn't help you place any of the puzzle pieces.  It's no different than just looking at the picture on the box and nobody would call that cheating or using a hint.
This game is a great demonstration for why real-life jigsaw puzzles are better, as the biggest puzzle in this game is 350 pieces.  In real life, that would be a pretty small puzzle, but it's a nightmare to play on the computer.  The pieces are so small that it's very arduous to work on it.  The best puzzles were the smaller ones, making it feel like more of a punishment than a reward as you unlocked the larger ones.  To think that a 60 piece puzzle was even programmed into this game, when that wouldn't even be bothered with by a child over the age of 7, is a real testament to how poorly this game was implemented.
I don't recommend this game at all and am honestly shocked it's reviewed so highly.  It's a puzzle to me.

As a disclaimer for those who do not know, Space run Galaxy is the Sequel to the game Space Run.  WIth that out of the way, here is my review
The original space run offered much in the ways of a fast paced and satisfying experience.  Each mission gave you cargo that you needed to fit on to your ship which has a design of hexes exclusive to the mission you were attempting.  The cargo acted as a handicap preventing you from having all the space available in order to fit weapons and equipment that would make dealing with threats easier.  Your objectives were to increase thrust in order to beat certain times (Which were graded from 1 to 3 stars) and to protect the cargo from being destroyed, (1 star for at least 50% cargo, 2 stars for 100% cargo) successfully completing a mission perfectly will provide 5 stars, indicating that you have fully completed that mission the best possible way.
Space run's original system had an internal challenge into each level, some of which would be impossible to perfect on the first attempt because of a lack of weapons or utilities unlocked.  Some missions might require a stronger engine to get enough thrust, others might need a weapon unlocked in order to dispatch with enemies fast enough.  Some might need a better power generator in order to unlock the best capabilities of the objects on your ship.  Either way, returning to previous missions felt rewarding as you could further accomplish the missions in order to advance through the game.
Now for Space run galaxy, this game changed up the formula of the original in several ways, instead of having a list of missions to choose from, you now obtain missions on a planetary map, the missions will make cargo appear in certain areas, which then have to be delivered to a specific destination.  For delivering this cargo, instead of having a preset ship design to work with, you as a player now have the capability of customizing your ships design so you can have the ship shaped however you feel like.  There are limitations however, your ship usually requires to be fit into a certain ship designs shape, or you need to purchase ship designs that allow more flexibility but require more hexes purchased.  It's complicated to explain in a review, but essentially you can decide the shape of the ship.
This change allows you to have more flexibility on where the cargo can fit on your ship.  Since you can create spots to put the cargo and have less inconveniences that would have normally been caused.  However, this along with a couple other factors I feel start to drain away from the game.
The first factor is, you no longer have to deliver all the cargo to a destination at once.  You could have 8 pieces of cargo that need to reach a specific point, and delivering all 8 at once would be really really difficult, but delivering 1 cargo at a time is the easiest thing ever.  Some missions auto-complete when 50% of the cargo has been delivered, others complete at 100% delivered cargo, for the 100% delivered cargo you can complete the missions in a very very slow way by only delivering the cargo one piece at a time, or you can challenge yourself by delivering them all at once.  For the 50% of cargo being delivered, you can deliver a minimum of 49% of the cargo, before the next trip has to contain the remaining 51%, as the moment 50% of the cargo has been delivered, the mission ends and the remaining cargo doesn't matter anymore.
Delivering more cargo grants you more rewards, which is either in the form of money, or Crafting Materials, which is a new feature to the game.  Instead of spending money for research after unlocking new equipment like the first game, you can now craft modules to attach on to your ship, whether it's a laser, a shield, an engine, an extra hex for your ship, or other such parts.  You can also craft more than 1 of a specific part, and the reason this is important is because the amount of parts you have crafted is the max amount of times you can build that on a ship in any single missions.  If you have 6 lasers, you can build 6 lasers per mission, period.  If 6 of your lasers have been destroyed and you only have 6, you can't build anymore lasers.  This means that you would have to craft a large surplus, such as 20 or 30 lasers, since at that point you shouldn't need anymore than 20 or 30 lasers per mission, since you'll probably only ever have 6 or so lasers per ship and the extras are just to rebuild them.
Crafting is an unlock system, raising your quantity of parts is more expensive each time, but you will have that quantity of parts for every mission going forward.  You'll never be in a situation where you can't start a mission because you have no more lasers.  but instead, being able to build only 6 lasers during the entirety of that mission might not be enough, you might want more lasers on the ship, or the lasers need to be replaced when they are destroyed because they are important for the design.
When you get to more advanced modules, they get more complicated to craft, and require harder to obtain parts, so you end up starting a mission with 1 super laser or 1 super missile launcher, but several smaller lasers and missile launchers.  You'll probably use your shields to protect the important weapons more than the less important ones, at least in the beginning.  Until you have enough parts that the quantity doesn't even get noticed anymore.
Here is the problem with space run galaxy, it feels very grindy.  Your completing story missions, side missions, and player made missions repeatedly in order to maximize your ship overtime.  Eventually you will have every module at such a high quantity that you won't need anymore.  And eventually your ship will be so large that you can fit all the cargo in the middle of the ship, and have all the room in the world to put the best weapons in the best positions and enough thrust to complete the mission the fastest way possible.
The issue is that the challenge of the original space run is gone, instead of having a preset ship design with preset amount of cargo that YOU HAVE to work with, you now have all the design room in the world, and the game allows you to complete these at whatever pace that you want.  Completing runs at the highest possible speed has lost it's initial value.  Since you can get max stars for speed on a route by completing the run with NO cargo at all.  The first time will give experience which allows higher levels of unlocks.  Every other time will provide a static amount of credits, making fast runs with cargo no where near as important as it used to be.
Space Run Galaxy is a good game, it provides a different approach to what the original space run provided.  Going from a game where customization was lacking, but the challenge was thrilling and set in stone, to a game that has alot of customization but the challenge is watered down and controlled by the player.  Space run galaxy allows veterans of the game to create their own challenges, using ship designs and cargo loadouts that would be incredibly impractical, but probably very entertaining to watch someone attempt it.  However for the completionist it will feel like a game that just exhausts you with the repetitive nature of how all the missions end up feeling the same.  The good news is, compared to the original, space run galaxy slightly randomizes the enemy patterns and enemy types each time you retry a mission, which makes you have to adapt on the fly, rather than simply memorizing the enemy positions.
Overall, I WOULD recommend this game, but only to people who have ALREADY played the original space run.  I loved the original so much that I just wanted more space run.  What I got wasn't exactly what I was hoping to get, but I wanted more space run and I got it.  I am only slightly disappointed because an amazing idea on paper didn't work in practice.  Start with the original, then decide if you want this one.

Summary:
Galaxy improves over first game, but in doing so adds a little grind.
Major changes compared to first game:
-A simple set of missions is replaced with few system maps with routes between planets and a set of story and side missions
-Player can purchase and modify ship size and shape to suit their playstyle (rather than being given a different ship for each run)
-Instead of power boosting nearby constructions we now have upgrade buildings that upgrade adjacent buildings of the same type (offensive, defensive, utility)
-New building type transers received bonuses and improvements to nearby constructions, this adds number of different building tactics as with clever planning you can now build one set of upgrades and a good shield then just transport that upgrades across majority of your ship.
-There is a fixed amount of particular constructions, so for example you can build only X simple turrents doesn't matter if they are destroyed or demolished, you can build only X of them per one run
-To increase that number you must collect crafting materials from completing missions and deliver them to planets where you collect enough of them to craft a construction (in addition to quest buildings you can put materials on your ship to transport them)
-That transporting and getting materials is a little grindy stuff
-Multiplayer options - you can buy/sell materials to other players, you can create missions for other players to transport your materials (this is a way to limit needed grindy transport missions)
-New guns and constructions
-New enemies
-Some random elements in missions, so the same mission will not play the same twice in a row
Overall I find the improvements to the gameplay good and I like the game. Overtime or as you go further and further into the game there are less and less players to buy/sell with and to transport materials, so you might be needed to make more trasport runs than you like to.

I'm going to start off by saying that I originally had this as a No recommendation, but I changed my mind. I'd say this is more of a neutral recommendation rather than me screaming "YES THIS GAME IS FANTASTIC BUY IT IMMEDIATELY!" There are some pros as well as many cons, so I think you should take everything into consideration over the type of gameplay you like if you're on the fence over buying this. Overall, I have mixed feelings about the game, but I liked it more than I disliked it. And I did enjoy the endings despite them hurting my heart. I just wanted to make note of that before you continue on reading this.
Alright, so, this is the last Cheritz game I've played. Meaning, I started with MM and then Nameless before playing Dandelion. I LOVE Mystic Messenger, and Nameless was a great game as well! I highly enjoyed both of those. On that note, let me say, this game isn't bad; the story is interesting, but it is my least favorite from Cheritz. This was the first game that they made, so that's probably why, as I feel as though they improved more and more with each game. Having said that, I did enjoy the characters. There was a pretty good range of personality, although I found Jieun and Jihae to be the least interesting to me. Jiwoo was my favorite, being a typical tsundere-type character. His personality grows a bit, which happens to every character, and it's cool to see, even though you really do not get to spend a good amount of time with the characters and getting to know them up close. Your real interactions with the characters are few and far in between the stat grinding, which gets boring.
This game relies HEAVILY on stat grinding. Honestly, I was put off by that in the beginning... and my feelings didn't really change at all about it as I kept playing. I got used to it, yes, but I found the stat grinding aspect to be extremely tedious, and if you took that aspect away, the stories/cutscenes/interactions for each character would be extremely short. If you're put off by that, I wouldn't recommend you to get the game.
The heroine, Heejung, has her own name and voice, which is pretty cool. If you like to immerse yourself as the MC, then this isn't really for you. Heejung is actually pretty relatable, though. She's a college student who is extremely stressed out and has an immense amount of pressure put on her by her mother. She has a lot of past family troubles. I honestly felt bad for her, because dang her mother is a jerk! But these aspects of her life make her likable and relatable, and she's also pretty goofy sometimes too, which I enjoyed.
The overall story is pretty interesting. It's nothing extremely deep, and I wish we could have seen more with the special/real ending. I feel as though they had a great story idea in mind, but they didn't go as in depth with it as they could have. It has potential to be an amazing story, but it feels a bit lackluster.
A lot of people say this is a good "intro" game to otome games, but I would say no. I do like it, it's not awful, but it gets boring and tedious. I highly enjoyed the moments where I actually did have interactions with the characters during cutscenes, though.
So, I'll just say this: for the price, I don't recommend the game. If you don't mind paying the price for the game, then I'd say buy it. Just don't expect some grand, in-depth plot with engaging gameplay and freedom of choice. It's not like that. Really, it's not terrible... I was immensely bored with stat grinding for each day that I played as Heejung, but looking forward to the cutscenes helped me to get through it. Even if you get as annoyed as me, I managed to get through it all and get all of the good ends, and I'm too much of a completionist to end it there and not finish the bad ends, so I'm still working on that! If you want a game that'll just make you feel, "Meh, I'm bored and I got money to spend, so I'll play it," then by all means, go for it! If not, then you'd probably want to move along and try Cheritz's other games (if you haven't played them already!)
