This isn't a
game, it's just pretty "meh," and for the price, that makes it one I can't recommend.
This is a stat management game (think Tokimeki series) where you choose different daily activities that affect the main character's intelligence, stress, etc, to build your appeal for the love interests, with the slightly novel spin that  interactions with the love interests occur based on choosing rooms of your house they currently occupy (because they are literally your pets and live with you) and engaging in particular activities in those rooms. You can also choose to hang out with a particular love interest on the weekends and there are cut scenes that trigger based on date and level of affection with that person.
It's a solid setup of this type of game. But the interactions with the male characters feel pretty shallow and disjointed; and after a while they become really repetitive too. I can understand the male characters' motivations to a certain extent, and won't get into them for the sake of avoiding spoilers, but it feels like you're kind of forcing the protagonist into a relationship that never seems to pick up steam. It's like you're friends, and there's no romance, and then bam, suddenly you're supposed to be downright Shakespearean.
The ending I received was the only part where it finally felt engrossing, but it took hours of mostly boring repetitive gameplay to get there. I know repetition is the stock and trade of these types of stat building games, but you truck through them for the little rewards you get when you interact with a love interest or get a cut scene. The problem here is that those rewards did not feel...
, so the stat building just ends up feeling like a slog.
The storyline I chose also suffered from the same type of borderline absuive relationship that makes Amnesia a dubious choice--as in, anyone can see this guy is actually a major chode and you'd tell your best friend to run screaming from him if she was dating him in real life. And yet you kind of have to force the kind, shy, unassuming heroine down that road to get anywhere in the story.
All in all, it was an okay diversion for a day, and you might consider picking it up if you have the money to spend and are just curious. But it's not something I'm interested in playing again, certainly not through all the routes-- which is a shame because there is an overarching plot that seems like the completionist playthrough could be really interesting. I'm just not willing to slog through several more hours of stat building for flat cut scenes and bad relationships to find out.

Overall, however, the game is cute and charming if a bit weird.

TL;DR - The Great Whale Road, in its current form, is a decent TBS light RPG - There need to be more updates to add depth and additional content, but right it wouldn't be a challenge to hit $1/Hour. With further content updates, I expect to see this be very similar to The Banner Saga but with far more minutia and a longer campaign. It's worth the 15 USD even in early access, and should be kept an eye on as it has the potential to be a strong feature of 2017.
The Great Whale Road is off to a really strong start. It popped up on my radar in early August, and this December (2016) I decided to try it out.
The combat at this stage has been described as hard but is fairly simple if you don't try and get fancy with it - Simple squares with spearmen and an assault works perfectly.
The side quests appear to pop at given intervals, and the content provided at this point in early access is impressive, if a little slow.
Management aspects for the winter are relatively satisfying if somewhat easy to cheese - I'd like to see more compexity there with the different base resources being able to upgrade to higher tiers that sell for more if you've got the craftsmen to do it. I'd like to see a lot more depth and really get into the minutia here, because who doesn't want to manage a tenth century Danish settlement and watch it grow while simultaneously having the opportunity to go a-viking?
Travel time is slow - The events are mostly repetetive, and you do eventually get to the point where you hope that you don't get an unlucky combat roll which means that things need to be made more fun or alternatively worthwhile and exciting there. Random events need to see more variability, but I'm imagining that'll definitely come with more content updates given the breadth of what you can access now.
Longship upgrades could see a little more variability - Different prows would be supremely nice, and more customizability in general on that front (perhaps requiring different materials) would be nice. I'd love to carve a bloody path through my rivals and take their strongests prow.
In the line of customizability, I'd really like to see character skills expanded upon (ala Drakensang) - Gear choices as they stand make sense, but should have more ... variability. Restricting specific classes to specific pieces of kit restricts customizability. The classes ought to be defined by their abilities, not so much by 'Support wears a dress. Assault wears one kind of mail. Heavies wear a differnet kind of mail'.
All said, The Great Whale Road is ambitious and with further attention to detail and expansion I think that it could make a genuinely phenomenal game. I look forward to coming back to it in future updates, and really do hope that it picks up more attention as it goes along.

Ordered on Nov 25.  It didn't arrive until Dec 14.  Yes, I live in the US.
Anyway onto the controller itself... I'm not very impressed to say the least.  It's a very special application piece of hardware.  That is, if you really need a gamepad that emulates KBM at your TV or whatever, this can be useful.  However for games that have gamepad support, just stick with either a PS3, PS4, or XBOX controller.  These work out of the box nearly every time on my Steam Link(even on games that don't advertise controller support), whereas the Steam Controller needs a lot of configuration for literally every game I've tried with it - and end results are usually sub par.  Even after watching tons of tutorial videos for setting it up for TPS or FPS games, I can never get it as smooth as an analog stick.
The biggest flaw in my opinion is that the tracking pad does a VERY poor job of emulating a right analog stick when you need it to.  Camera movement is wonky under mouse-joystick emulation or even joystick-camera mode.  What's worse is that the joystick emulation mode doesn't have a sensitivity setting, it tells you to adjust this in game.  The problem with that is that some games have very limited options in this regard (like Lego Worlds for instance which only has low, medium, or high for sensitivity - high still not being sensitive enough).
So the bottom line is, unless you need the tracking pad for mouse or trackball applications, a wireless gamepad of your choice is a better option for most games.  The tracking pad is certainly more precise for FPS games, but for this limited application it's just not worth the money or the trouble in my opinion.
One final point.  Notice the button layout on the Steam Controller.  Compare that to a PS or Xbox controller.  It will take you some getting used to if you're accustomed to normal gamepads.

Space Run Galaxy is an interesting take on the tower defense genre. It's moderately fun but perhaps too grindy for some players.
Let's start with two disclaimers. (1) I didn't play Space Run and (2) I'm not a huge fan of the tower defense genre. This is one of those games I got on a bundle at some point and decided to give it a whirl.
Space Run Galaxy starts with your ship. It's an empty little thing, consisting of only a command console. You must protect that. If that goes, you're dead and the mission is over. You start in a little spaceport and get a contract, which is to run cargo from one planet or port to another. So you go to the cargo loading screen and put it where it may be protected trying to ensure a good run.
So then the game takes you out into space. You'll start with a bare amount of upgrade points (whatever they're called) to start to add components to your ship. These components come in 3 flavors - red (offensive), blue (defensive) and green (utility). Later on there are a couple of more types you can add but those are the big 3. You're constantly balancing these upgrade points to determine what you need to put next on your ship. As you sail along, you'll be notified of upcoming threats. You'll then - using the points on hand - build modules to meet the forthcoming threat. This threat can come from any direction and can consist of tiny fighters that are easily destroyed to aliens who attach themselves to your ship to boss fights of other big vessels.
There are special abilities with these components but you have to use these in a limited fashion as they take time to recharge and you can only use the ability so many times before you're tapped out and waiting for a recharge of those points.
It's this constant demand of scarcity that makes Space Run Galaxy enjoyable. Do you put on another thruster to get their faster and get more bonuses for beating the time parameters? Do you load up your last weapon to take on a known incoming threat knowing that the rear port side of your ship is unprotected if you end up attacked from that direction? Do you fire off your special ability at that huge asteroid and pray you're not regretting it later? These are the decisions that make up these tense space runs which last around 5-6 minutes each.
If your run is successful, you'll get XP, money and components to upgrade your ship. Only certain upgrades can be done in certain ports and your inventory is by planet. This requires you to either buy cargo (because if you have that component it might be 4 jumps back and you have to haul your own cargo to the appropriate port) or perhaps wait on that upgrade. I understand this approach - which is to bring a bit of scarcity to the meta-game - but it's also highly annoying to have the right stuff but it's in the wrong place and to bring it up takes too much time so you just sell it for 1/6th of the buying price. And finally you may decide to buy a bigger empty husk of a ship so you can add even more components and take on more risky runs.
As I said, it's a fun game. However, it has its annoying points.
(1) It's online. The MP component allows for other players to create runs for you but in reality this is just annoying. Passtech Studios is a one man shop. What happens if he shuts it down? Will the game totally die? I don't like unnecessary online components (aka Diablo 3, SimcCity) and these feels like it doesn't need to be an online game.
(2) It's grindy. I'm 6 hours into the game. I haven't completed it. But even now I can feel the grind settling on me. Since the runs are short you don't have to play this for hours on end but I wonder how easy it will be to pick it back up if I don't play for a month or two. Either way, it feels like there's a big grind here.
(3) There are story missions and twice now missions that I completed that didn't trigger the next part of the story. Considering that I'm only at the start of the story that's disheartening.
Overall, this is a well crafted game which I think generally achieves what the game set out to be. So it gets a thumbs up from me. I wouldn't pay the asking price of this game (heck, I wouldn't pay 1/2 of that) but then again it's not my general genre. So if this type of thing is in your wheelhouse - or if you are like me and you found it in a bundle - then it's worth the time and money.

To paraphrase another reviewer, 'different is not necessarily better'.
I really enjoyed Space Run, and was excited and hopeful when Space Run Galaxy came out.  However, despite my familiarity with Space Run, the new mechanics of this game took some getting used to.
In Space Run, one of the things one did was re-run missions to generate cash to purchase upgrades so that one could progress.  I somewhat didn't like that mechanic, as it felt like re-reading a chapter in a book.  This has been fixed in Space Run Galaxy by having different non-story jobs available for you to run for cash.  This feels more realistic to me.
However, now they have added a crafting mechanic to the game, which is how one gets both slots for each placable item on a ship (weapons, defensive items, thrusters, etc).  The placeable items are limited based on how many you have crafted.  So, for example, if you need more engines during a run, you have to have crafted them first.  It is sorta like you only carry so many spares, even though supposedly you're building them on the ship as you travel.  I wish the developers had made up their minds here.  Are we building them or merely placing them?  If they're pre-built (from crafting), then why do we need to collect the hex nuts?  If they're not, then why do we need to craft the darn things?  This feels like something arbitrary that was changed 'to make it harder' or something.  A significant disadvantage of this crafting is that you are given crafting components as random rewards for doing Runs.  You ALSO have to haul these components to where there is a mechanic of the apropriate level who can craft the modules you need.
All of the above has made the game a big grind.  Not enough of a grind to unrecommend the game to those who loved Space Run, but enough to say don't get this game if you hate grinding.
I give this game 2.5 out of 5 stars.

I should preface this by saying I have NOT completed the game yet. So far, however, I'm hooked on the storyline. It's hard to give a comprehensive review without giving spoilers, so I'll take a Lovecraft approach and say it's impossible to describe.
What you should know is that this game is primarily a walking journey with narrative. There are some unlockable notes that you can find throughout the game, so that gives it a little bit of challenge; the word 'challenge' here is used lightly, however, as more in-depth exploration of each chapter will ultimately lead you to each note.  While exploring you learn about the main character as well as your own role in said character's story.
Positives so far:
1) The plot is intriguing. It has enough depth that makes you want to keep walking around and discover the details of each chapter's story.
2) The narratives are voiced by a gentleman that is pleasant on the ears. This is especially good since some of the monologues are a bit lengthy.
3) The scenery is nicely imagined and you will encounter some things that will make you wonder if you took a hit of acid or ate some shrooms before you started playing.
Critique so far:
1) If you turn on subtitles the lengthier monologues are lumped into one paragraph, taking up about the bottom fourth to third of your screen. The developer should have broken it down into two smaller chunks so as not to detract from the scenery while you continue to walk.
2) It's a little wonky to interact with some of the doors. If you're not standing at just the right spot, it may take some maneuvering to get them to close.
3) I wish the run function was just a wee bit faster.
4) It is possible that you may go through a door or other passage and accidentally finish a chapter before you fully explored it. A bit of a bummer with continuity, but it's the chance you take with a not completely linear game. Fortunately the game offers chapter select and you can go back to explore things you might have missed.
Overall this is still a great game and you will think so too if you enjoy a casually-paced mystery that keeps you guessing.

TLDR: A good game unfortunately burdened with too much grind.  Play the first Space Run and skip this one.
I have one more hour in Space Run Galaxy than I do in Space Run.  The difference is I beat Space Run, but I'm only about a quarter of the way through Space Run Galaxy and it's worn out it's welcome.  I wanted to like it, but ultimately I was turned off by the amount of grinding I had to do.
Let's start with the good: the graphics, the sound and the gameplay are all improved over the first game.  We also have the addition of being able to choose our own ship which is fun.  You can also expand the ship the way you want which allows for even more customization.  Basically, the core of this game is as good as the first game plus more.
Now let's get to the bad: there is just way too much grind.  Instead of completing a mission in one run, you know may need to make multiple runs in order to move all the cargo.  Additionally, there can be multiple legs on each mission forcing you to run each leg multiple times.  By itself, this isn't so bad.  I frequently did missions multiple times in the first due to losing or getting a low rating and wanted to come back and get a better rating.
On top of the multiple legs/multiple runs missions, they added upgrade materials as being real cargo.  You get them at whatever point the in the star map your mission ends on.  To move them, you'll need to load them on your ship just like cargo and do the run to get them to the next point.  And you will need to move them.  You'll end up with upgrade material all over the star map because frequently you can't carry it with you while your carrying the mission cargo.  So you might have enough material to craft what you want, but it will be split between two star systems.  On top of that, some upgrades are only craftable at certain nodes, so you may have to move these items to some third point on the star map just to get craft what you want.
In theory this is mitigated by the fact that you can hire other players to move your material or you can buy and sell it from other players.  In practice nobody wants to wait for some other person to maybe move your materials so you can craft something later.  Buying and selling is a little bit better of an option, but it's not great as each market is specific to the node on the map and of course everyone has too much of one type at that node and not enough of a different type.
Ultimately, it feels like the upgrade materials system was not created because it was fun, but simply to justify the multiplayer features.  That could have been acceptable if the multiplayer part was fun, but it's mostly boring and not worth the time.  And so the upgrade system feels like more grind on top of already grindy missions and frankly ends up ruining what could have been a pretty fun game.
Hopefully Passtech Games will learn from the mistakes of Galaxy and make a better third game.  It would be a shame for this to be the final game in the franchise.

A very atmospheric walking simulator, very beautiful philosophical game with a weird story/plot and a great aesthetic.
Story is pretty weird, I liked it but not everyone will like it, mainly because of the fact you're going to have to read a lot if you want to actually follow and get invested in the plot of the game, and I highly recommend that you invest yourself in the story, so if you don't like reading I'd recommend you stay away unless you'd just like to explore a nice world.
Some people on here complain about the narrator, that he uses "overly complicated words" to sound smart, the he is cringeworthy etc...
I don't find this to be true at all. If you think the words the narrator uses is to complicated and if you think the narrator misuses the words then yea, it's not the games fault, I think it's you specifically that the words are to complicated for, I think it's YOU that don't understand them. Because he doesn't misuse any words, and words are certainly not hard to understand if you understand basic English.
The narrator in the game was very nice to listen to and only helped with the already weird philosophical story, plot and setting of the game.
I will not spoil anything but the atmosphere in the game and the story take many weird, or more correctly dark and gory turns. Find out for yourself but I liked it.
The game itself, the graphics are very beautiful to look at, which is almost always the case with the Unreal Engine. The music is amazing, and the game is
what you're told it is, it's an exploration walking simulator with little to no actually content/gameplay, this game is obviously marketed to already-fans of walking simulators, so don't buy this if you don't know what you're getting into.
If you don't like reading I don't recommend it either, there is a lot of reading as I said if you want to follow the plot, which I recommend that you do. But you don't have to read, if you just want to explore in a very beautiful game while listening to a nice voice actor then there's nothing wrong with that.
The game is a philosophical art piece, so if you enjoy philosophy then get in, and if you enjoy art in the form of games.
I enjoyed it very much due to that, it got me thinking. I very often say that Walking Simulators aren't always bad due to the lack of content, they can be great in the way of how they can make you think about things you never thought about.
I don't care if you refuse to call walking simulators games, I don't care if you'd like to call them a "First Person Art Piece Exhibit" or whatever you want to call it, it's a nice game for what it's quite obviously marketed as.
A must buy for any walking simulator fan, for any person who loves philosophy, and for any person who loves art in the form of games, and I recommend it as a new experience to anyone who haven't played a game like this before.
A must buy in my opinion.

Unpolished and seriously underrated, yet quite fun game on the mainstream theme - "zombie rampage". This time - in the distant town somewhere on Mid-West of USA. What I like about the game - is that it stays on the bright side of things. You know, the Zombie Games are usually Dead Serious. Not a bad feature, but all of them are so similar on the basic level, that it is absolutely no fun. Stubbs the Zombie was different, one-of-a-kind gem... But there are too little count of games trying comical approach on the zombie pattern - and that's a mile behind the cinematography. Which is strange, as generally games are far more creative with things, in comparison with Hollywood...
Now, Pound of Ground is not something worth a long review, really. The "Hero" there doesn't have Ash Williams charisma and chainsaw, but other than that - it's the same type of guy.
The game starts a bit confusing, but quite soon you'll get a bat to crush z-sculls, then a car, a pistol, a shotgun, a long-ranged crossbow, and finally, a dynamite. Zombies will be upgrading as well, there will be monsters with distant attacks, sages-which-raising-hordes, and even bigger things on the dessert. Controls are a bit off, but only a little. In general, it is rather easy-going arcade game with semi-open world, some zombies to kill and some hills to jump with your red cabrio. Full complete in less than 10 hours, and way better aftertaste, than with so many other Zombie games. Especially when we're talking about smaller ones, like Dead Pixels, which so many people seems to like without proper reason...
Sure, Pound of Ground has many flaws, if you care to look for them - like strange name in the first place, followed by wacky start of the game, somewhat clunky controls and gameplay in general... and not-so-good code, as the game tends to crush every now and then, usually on the loading screens.
On the other hand, it is doing well the thing the games are generally made for - it is entertaining. I really like it just the way it is (except for unstable code, of course). It is short and fun, if a bit mindless, comedy action game about zombies. With great fusion soundtrack, which I really enjoyed.
My mark is 8/10. I usually play serious long-winded games, like epic RPGs and strategies... But sometimes you just can't force yourself to take the playtime so seriously. After 16h-work day, for example... And Pound of Ground is perfectly fitting that niche of short and easy action. There should be more games like that!

The writing was really great, the protagonist was so relatable and well written which is ABSURDLY rare, the characters were very multidimensional and surprisingly stereotype defying on more than one occasion. The story has a surprising amount of depth. All of the routes were enjoyable and surprising, even the one I liked the least (Jiyeun).
However, this is a stat raising game. There is serious stat raising and it can get tedious at times, but is honestly worth it for the story. My major grieviance with the game as a whole is the DRM, purely because I personally have dodgy internet so it interfered with my experience. Usually not being able to play in offline mode is enough to make me not buy/play a game but Dandelion was a definite exception.
From skeptic to Cheritz fangirl, I can do nothing but reccomend this game. And to play Jieun's route last for the most emotional impact. Consensus? If you're a dating sim/otome game fan, this Dandelion is a must play. Honestly even if you're a visual novel lover it's worth a play, although I doubt it will convert anyone who doesn't like the medium. It is what it is, a very well made visual novel and stat-raising sim.
8/10. Easy 9 if not for the damned DRM!

I'll start with this - ALWAYS have an internet connection up, or you could lose data.
The game is barely worth $30, if not for all the extra interaction it gives the player. The depth of the story was impeccable, I was totally immersed as the game progressed. The art is beautiful, but not my taste. The male characters are shallow, and the main character has no presence. She may have a different personality from other heroines as she doesn't start with amnesia or the like, but her obsession got old. Their "love" was not exactly present, as they don't really get to know each other. The translation is far from what I could do, but sloppy as there are plenty of mistakes. The game requires an internet connection. I have much larger games on steam that I can play in offline mode, yet this game needs an internet connection for cutscenes. My game is extremely buggy as the sound glitched every 5 minutes and it never completely exits out of the game. The reason why I've clocked so many hours on this game is because it never fully exits until I restart my whole computer, exiting steam is not enough to shut the game down. Some music choices don't exactly match with the game, this isn't a huge deal, but a good soundtrack makes a tremendous difference. The skill levels take a lot of grinding, and I spent a few weeks without needing to level up anything. Although I was happily surprised to interact with the game unique from other visual novels, it takes away from the player getting to know the character, and expressing the player's individual personality. The only real times you as the player get to pick responses is on dates. I really enjoyed my time playing this game, and I look forward to finishing it completely. But I can't recommend the game. The story was completely unique and refreshing as I love the premise of the story, but it fell short of my expectations. It got to the point where after my first playthrough, I got bored as I felt that I, as the player was not involved in a visual novel game. This game was made with love, but there are better games to buy instead.

So what did I do over my winter holidays?
I played Team Fortress 2. Also played Hatoful Boyfriend: Holiday Star.
This is a visual novel game, being more on the "novel" end of the spectrum with all the reading involved. There are still opportunities to make decisions, and said decisions can still have consequences. So make sure you save when you need to.
There are 4 main episodes, with about 6 mini-episodes and about 6 radio episodes. Each are fairly independent from each other, though there are some occasional small references to other episodes. I also find that the game makes some rather obscure references to Japanese culture, birds and the visual novel genre itself, so it helps to have an internet browser open to look up anything weird you come across like "manyoshu" or "moe".
The storyline is as ridiculous as you would expect it to be, especially with the introduction of Miru+Kaku (comedy relief), Tohri
and The King
. Much like the first game, things start off with a simple plot, and then escalates to a bigger scheme and then finishes with a final punchline.
Sometimes the main episodes can feel longer than you'd expected, and I think it took me about 15 to 30 minutes per episode, since I try to read the story and all.
I liked the Picture Book sections in the last two episodes. They can be rather abstract stories, but really set the transition well for the last episode because of the tone used and the stakes in the storyline at those key moments.
The last episode was certainly a real gut buster. Not only because of the inherent shift in storyline tone, but also because of the feels that each character struggles with and how to overcome themselves. I mean, I sort of felt bad for The King at that point of the story, but you know enough of the truth by then.
The mini-episodes are tremendously shorter than the main episodes. They revolve around little non-canonical adventures, like Legumentines with Okosan, and the Kyoto field trip. Nothing too serious but still moderately entertaining, sort of like the filler episodes from your favourite anime show.
The radio episodes are essentially Q&A sessions with Ryouta and other characters to answer fan mail...apparently. Some of the episodes reference the secret BBL ending of the first game, so be aware of that. Otherwise, nothing too serious there and moderately entertaining.
The music is nice, I still can't believe Yuuya gets his own theme played whenever he enters the scene. It's a groovy tune, admittedly. Sound is used occasionally, and is usualy just for simple things like plates being smashed or Okosan running off.
Achievements are fairly easy. Just watch the episodes and their variants, and that's basically that.
In conclusion, I'd say this is a good 9/10.
It would help to have an autosave feature after certain segments of the story so I don't have to skip through everything
. Also, I miss the option to have human versions of the characters (this is only available in the Shrine Visit mini-episode).

Also there are quite a few romance options for the main character as well. Although this blooms into fruitation in the 2nd game (your save data will carry over.)

It's one of those Early Access that you want to quit and uninstall immediately... because you feel the full version will be so awesome that you want to come back later to it when it's polished and has all the content in it. Still, the itch was there and I couldn't stop playing for a few hours, now waiting for the update.
Despite the looks it's not a clone of Banner Saga or King of Dragon Pass. In fact, it's a witty reference as it has enjoyable elements of the games mentioned above, while offering much more plus new and fresh additions to the genre.
As of now (version 0.2) the game is a perfect example of how to do an Early Access game. The price is right. And the game shows a vertical slice of everything: there's a city play part, quests, weapon progression, text quests and battles. I've encountered a few bugs and thus can't advise to play the
game immediately. But I want to encourage everyone to support the making of it as this feels like the most promising strategy game in Early Access I've seen this year.
Worries and concerns:
One of the decisions I don't like is promising more campaigns. With a game like this I think it's good to have one strong story than a few mediocre ones. Banner Saga is with significantly less gameplay will have only 3 stories (trilogy) in like... 7 years I guess? And everyone's crazy about it simply because it's well polished.
Adding the card element is very intriguing, but developer will need to put a lot of hard work to make it work. As of now, there's no deck building of any sort and it feels like better items or character development should add some new cards to keep it fresh.
One of the implications of that gameplay is that with better AI the game will become a long run for leaders around the map. It's fine by me when AI lets me kill him quite easily, but 'give me hell' race of players will definitely want something better.

As the game is of now (16/8-2016) its simply not worth it, due to a lack of balance within the game.
For example, the travel time is close to ridiculous, which make the RNG decisions available during the boat trips furiating!
Spend 1,5 hour trying to get to the second objective, and i keep running into RNG instand game overs.
And there is simply no way to speed up the tedious process of repeating the same boat trip over and over and over and over.
So if you like suffering due to RNG, go right ahead, gamble your time away.
But if you like your game to be balanced, and playable, then wait untill stuff like this gets a fix.

This is a review of an early access game and therefore subject to change. The game is not completed and it shows.
TL:DR:
Let me start by saying that The Great Whale Road has a lot of potential to be a good game. The art is nice, and the references to historically accurate (!!! that's incredibly rare!) naming for characters, depiction of every day life through the winter-events and above all, the relatively accurate art (I mean, it's still a game, so of course it's not realistic in all senses).
What's less accurate is the depiction of Viking shieldmaidens. However for the sake of the game, I feel like it's interesting regardless. Also, who doesn't like female warriors? But the existence of female shieldmaidens historically is debateable and, actually, there is barely any mention of them in historical sagas.
Moving on to _actual game content_ which is obviously what people are looking for:
CONS:
* The content is scarce at the moment. There is more content in creation however I feel like the price is very steep for a game I couldn't play for more than an hour, maybe an hour and a half before finishing it. I replayed it to see if I missed anything, but besides a few rumors that I couldn't do anything with, basically you're gonna play through it once and then be done.
* The story writing is vague and does not explain anything at all. First off, the resolution can't be changed and so the opening screen was only barely readable to me since the text was way too large. So, right off the bat, the story was hard to follow. Also there is no explanation as to why I am doing any of the things I am doing. Why am I going south to travel to the priests.. twice? With no reward? I am helping them without reason? I was supposed to avenge my Jarl, but suddenly I am helping priests for no real explained reason.
Developers should look to invest in help from more writers or otherwise from enthusiastic people because the story is very bland and doesn't make any sense.
* Combat is easy to grasp, but doesn't get harder. Actually, combat is too easy. You just dogpile the enemy leader = automatic easy win. I would expect a system similar to the Banner Saga where you need to kill everyone or a specific hero (in story events). But no, I can kill the enemy leader and the fight is over.
The way you get heroes into the battle is stupid too and completely dependant on luck. I once lost a fight because I couldn't get my heroes on the field before they killed my leader -> I lost, because RNG decided it didn't like me. By the time I got heroes, my leader was trapped and basically dead.
* Combat is unrewarding. The first few times I tried to play like a typical 'fantasy viking' because I felt like that's what the game wanted me to do. So my first time sailing to the local trade city, I got ambushed by pirates. I am not a coward so I stood my ground and fought! Also, I died. There wasn't really any punishment for losing except for losing adventure stats.
When I entered the city someone tripped my character and of course, I fought them because, I am not a coward! I won. Didn't get anything. Not even a story sequence where I regain my honor or where I roll their purses. Absolutely nothing. I felt cheated.
I fought pirates a few more times and realized you get absolutely nothing out of fighting. So I just chose to ignore fights and escape. It seems you have a 100% chance at escape every single time so whatever. I only fought when I had to. And as mentioned before fights are incredibly easy so it wasn't a challenge either way.
* Combat unintuitive and poorly explained. Sometimes I'd click a character, and there's like no indication if I clicked him properly, so I'd click him again or right click somewhere trying to figure out how to move/attack (even after playing it a bit, I still have no idea, lol) I'd sometimes skip a move for no reason. Also, I can't re-do a move so if I make a mistake by misclicking I'm boned.
* Game doesn't feature gods. At all. I am pagan and that's why I was very excited for this game! But actually the only reference of Óðinn I got was like, at the start of the game, your character will 'touch a pendant of Odin' or otherwise one of Frey if you choose the female character. Besides that nobody but the Saxons seem to give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about religion. I think Wotan is more important to the creators of this game than Odin, and if that is the case, then the game should've been set in Frisia or the Saxony area. (Yes, the gods are _more or less_ interchangeable with different rites and rituals but the same concept is at the core of these two gods and their extended family.)
* Bugs. By god, bugs. If I give a character a new armor, his old armor gets destroyed. What, does he throw it in the water and let it rust for 5 years? Please..
* Just stupid mechanics. If I send my characters hunting it seems like they go out -> kill a deer -> skin it and then leave the meat behind.
Are you daft? I need food! My men are starving and you're just taking the pelts! I have 200 pelts on my ship already AND I AM RICH JUST BY SELLING PELTS. PLEASE. I CAN'T EVEN SPEND THIS MONEY ANYWHERE.
* Village management is useless. I can spend all my points on diplomacy, it won't matter one bit. Since I always seem to run out of food, I suggest for now you just place all your points in agriculture and husbandry. I really hope to see more features. Like attacks in the winter, or the ability to build a palisade, a longhall, or anything. From the art it looks like I am living in a homestead, not a village. There's like 1 house and a shed. It makes me wonder why the hell there's a blacksmith there and a trader and other stuff..
PROS:
* The game looks really good. Art is A++, I really like it.
* If combat system is made more interesting, with combat stats that actually matter (really, support doesn't do anything remotely supportive except give you cards..) and with the ability to obtain new cards and switch cards on characters (for example, say I obtain a card that lets me give a heavy character 'taunt' like abilities, I would be able to switch it with a card he already has so that I can use it in battle.)
then the combat system would be great. Basically, try to do what Banner Saga did, but don't rip it off and make it more viking themed. Basically because ripping off is illegal. If you can rip it off legally, please, it'd be awesome.
* For what it's worth, the developers seem to be working on the game rather hard. I appreciate that because most of the time I buy a early access games, it never gets developed. In this case I don't feel ripped off, I feel like I am supporting this game. This is the one exception to my rule of never buying a early access game again after the disaster that was DayZ and the Stomping World.
* I really like the village management but actually it is rather useless at this point. Make it more like King of Dragon Pass, allow me to build stuff, allow me to _see_ the changes in my village through the artworks! That is so important. If I am just reading numbers and letters on a screen, yeah, that's great, but I want to _see_ it!

Now what to say about The Great Whale Road? Promising? Innovative? Yeah, it sure is both in a way. But the dominant factor in this earliest of public alphas is boredom. That is bad for a game and especially so if you as a developer are looking for feedback and many played hours.
In The Great Whale Road the player manages a small danish village by spending 10 focus points every year. Those largely decide with what goods you start your voyage in the spring. Because thats the second part of the game, and sadly the boring one.
You spend hours looking at the 2D animation of a rowing viking boat in different weathers waiting for a) a random event to happen or b) a port coming in sight. This sequence is only interrupted by nightfalls. Now don't get me wrong, I like the basic idea of that. The hard part is the design of it. If there is a random event, you have to wait for some text to pop up in the middle of the screen. It fades in slow. Then it takes what feels like aeons to have your virtual comrades come up with hints on the matter. After that another few boring seconds pass until you finally are able to take action.
To make matters even worse, every action (and nightfall) ends with a slow fade to black and a continue button. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ It took me 4 hours to play through this Alpha and most of the time it was just waiting on fade to blacks or another UI sin the developers built in. Every time you visit a village/port the camera focusses the horizon, holds for 2 or 3 seconds and then swipes down on the actual village. Whatching a sandclock is more interesting.
Now, the pictures and GFX look nice, the game has a good viking vibe to it. The battles happen in a look down perspective hex strategy way with some trading card game features thrown in. Looks nice, feels good but is not very rewarding. Why you ask? Because there is no loot! How can you make people play your stuff if you don't reward them for theire "work"? After I realized that I never fought any battles that I didnt have to take. It was just faster this way.
To sum it up:
+ nice ideas
+ nice mashups of different game concepts
+ cool visuals
+ nice music style
+ promising
- very bad UI/UX concept (holy ♥♥♥♥!)

To me, this is essentially "Space Run: Definitive Edition". This means: Yes, this game is pretty much more of the same, so if you didn't like Space Run at all, you'll probably dislike this one as well. The core gameplay is the same, but there's a few things added around it - they seem to be really minor things, but that might be deceptive. A short description of that core gameplay is in the last paragraph.
If you played Space Run, you'll find some differences...
For example, there's a space map now. But it's not just visual fluff, it adds a layer of simple logistics: Instead of picking one run to play, you're now placed into a network of stations, and the mission / cargo is separated from the run / path. This means that a mission might take multiple runs, either because there is no one-run connection between two stations, or because you want to split the cargo and run twice, or because you want to avoid the only direct connection and instead take a detour. Conversely, you might be doing two or three missions in one run, if you manage to defend yourself with that much space on your ship being blocked by cargo... and don't worry - unless you want to transport goods, you can switch from station to station in an instant and for free.
Together with "multiplayer" (or really, player interaction) this has drawn me in much more than Space Run, even though I liked Space Run.
The whole upgrade system was overhauled. Components don't get upgraded over time anymore - they have their abilities from the get-go. There is also no "power" mechanic anymore with some components requiring power for basic function and others only for their special ability. There is now a resource called "focus" that is gradually generated by the thrusters, and that is used up when activating a components active ability (which seem a tad more powerful than before) and there are upgrader components (that basically replace the old power stations by making components around them more powerful). There also is a build limit per component per run now, which is what you spend your ressources on between runs (instead of enabling new abilities for components).
This really doesn't reinvent the core gameplay, but it does improve the pacing a fair bit. Positioning of components is still of utmost importance, but it's also less pre-determined and more up to tactical choice and preference. Losing components is punishing, which shifts focus towards long-term thinking. Finally, the active abilities are quite powerful (and can be rather frequently used) which adds a direct action layer.
So you're running cargo between stations and you get ressources to improve your ship and your build limits. Which is another point: You now have a ship. Like, a ship that you pick and customize. There's different blueprints with a fixed shape at the centre and optional additional hexes that can be built around it up to a maximum shape. The additional hexes have to be bought just like build limits (they are valid for ALL your ships simultaneously, though) and you can even colour the base of your hexes - you also don't have to use up all potential hexes, you may opt to leave some spaces, it's actual customizing between the base and the max shape. Now, these services are performed by mechanics, who have a level, limiting what they can do, and the resources they need to craft stuff for you is actually cargo that has to be transported to the station where the mechanic is.
This is where player interaction comes in. Not only is there a market where you can buy and sell resources, but you can create missions for other players to transport your resources as cargo. And the game gives heavy incentives for that. For example, while you may spend some cash to pay a prime for the player completing your contract, you don't have to: There is an automatic reward (and a sizeable one - ranging from okay (just a few credits) over good (some of the same resources as you transported) to immense (like a new ship)) for every item of cargo delivered, added by the game, for free. Also, if you transport your own resources, they are lost if destroyed. If another player does it, it's mission cargo, and is basically "returned" to the starting station on failure or destruction. So essentially there is a bit of risk transporting your stuff yourself, no risk in putting it out as a contract, and a good (risk-less) reward for doing other players contracts... it's win-win.
Don't get me wrong: The game does have a fair bit of repetition and can be frustrating at times, and I'm sure I'll encounter some serious grind along the way, but it's a fun game nonetheless. What Space Run should have been from the start, the light-weight logistics, the better pacing and moment-to-moment experience and the player interaction really make this a more well-rounded experience.
Core Gameplay of Space Run: You have a ship, which is a field of hex-tiles. On those hexes, you may build components. You start each run with your command bridge and one thruster built, and have to build other components, such as weapons or defensive measures, as you go. For this, you get a currency called hexnuts, of which you also get starting budget on each run - but they are also generated slowly as time passes, and you get them for destroying foes that will come at you from different sides (usually in a certain pattern, and with ample warning). Your first job is to stay alive and keep your cargo intact. Your second job is to get to the destination as quickly as possible. For all interaction you do, your ship is at the centre. Your "movement" is a calculation of the power of your thrusters against the length of the run and the time goals set for it. The main challenges is managing your space and your components - building them in such a way that they will counter the threat you're building them against, while leaving you enough room to be able to react to new threats, maybe from a different angle - as well as using active abilities to quickly dispatch especially dangerous foes.
The game can be immensely hectic, but in most cases, it pays off to keep your cool and think a bit ahead, as hard as it may be in the moment.

Tl;dr--I had mixed feelings.
In greater depth, let's get this out of the way first--yes, this game is *gorgeous.* Not just in terms of its commendable graphical prowess, but in terms of its visual presentation. Its labyrinthine levels are sumptuously designed and evocative, somewhere between City 17 and Giorgio de Chirico.
The writing isn't as bad as some of the other reviews have made it sound--the game definitely feels pretentious, and it has some pacing issues, but if you can look past that, there's an interesting (if heavy-handed) meditation on futility and truth to be found here--very Kafka-Lite. The best bits are definitely the ancillary notes and text posted around the game's environment, which represent the views of people who've lived in the game's mysterious environment and struggled with the miserable emptiness of it.
Unfortunately, the narrator you're saddled with spends most of the game as the sort of nihilistic, dull teenager who just discovered Nietzsche and wants to sound important. It's not a dealbreaker--like all good fictional characters, he undergoes a change as the story goes along--but it definitely drags down what feels like a thoughtful experience into something that feels pedantic and not half as smart as it thinks it is.
All told, though, if you like walking simulators, thought-provoking narratives and environmental storytelling, it's easy to look past the narration and enjoy The Old City.

Do not read this review if you are easily offended.
*************************************************************
Once in a while I like to play a walking simulator: relaxingly walking around in a fantastic world, exploring and being fed a story. The Old City Leviathan (a.k.a. TOCL) is such a game ... and I have a hard time recommending it, even though it pains me to admit.
First, realize very well that this is truly a walking simulator. You will not shoot things. There are no puzzles. There is basically no interaction with the game world. You walk. You discover the story. That's it. If this is not something you can live with, please do yourself a favor and steer far away from this game.
I repeat: THIS IS  A WALKING SIMULATOR. DO NOT BUY IF YOU DON'T LIKE WALKING SIMULATORS OR IF YOU DON'T KNOW WHAT A WALKING SIMULATOR IS. Pardon me for shouting b.t.w.
There, now that 99% of the readers have left, we can actually start with the review.
TOCL casts you in a bizarre, dream-like environment consisting of sewers, palaces and underwater cities amongst others. Exploring the strange world around you, your aim is to walk to the end and figure out the meaning of everything you saw and heard meanwhile.
This is a major point of difference from other walking simulators, which focus on telling a story. There is no story in TOCL: a story has a beginning, a middle and an end. This game basically has neither of those three. Or to put it in another way: it has no beginning while the middle and end are the same. Does that sound confusing to you? Welcome to TOCL, your journey is only just beginning.
Instead of a story, we are fed with pseudo-psychological rants & contemplations and journal pieces which more often than not refer to Jewish mythology. And that is where the game's ugly head reveals itself.
First of all, the psychological rants come in the form of fully voiced-over and subtitled monologues. These are unfortunately immature and just ... well ... uninteresting. It is the type of pseudo-psychology that a college or university student might find interesting, just because it is so "far out there" or "it makes so much sense (in a sheltered environment)". But in reality it all is laughable, cliche and predictable. And boring, oh God it is so utterly, mindbogglingly boring. For the first time in my life I have actually screamed at my screen: before I knew it, I yelled
when yet another endless soliloquy began in this game.
Second, all through the game world are paper sheets attached to the walls, completely filled with text (and occasionally text in other forms as well). Hidden in every chapter are also "Solomon's Notes", which give even more insight in what happened to the world. It is necessary to read all of that text to get a full understanding. But there is just so much of it ... stopping in nearly every room to read up did get on my nerves at times. A walking simulator is about walking, not about standing still!
To add insult to injury, the writing itself is just not good. If the developer ever makes a part 2, then I strongly suggest to hire a professional writer for such a text-heavy game. The writing now is incoherent and never invites you to continue reading; it never pulls you into the game, which is a real shame because the graphics do allow solid immersion.
All the writing is also overly pompous. Using a variety of words to add colour to your text is good. Using dif-fi-cult and va-ri-ous words just for the sake of using difficult and various words, being overly wordy just for the sake of being overly wordy, is pretentious. Lots of highfalutin language here folks. See, I can do it too! Oops, that should read:
Finally, to understand what is happening, just must have some understanding of Jewish mythology. The story of Jonah forms a major plot-point, the figures of Leviathan and Ziz are frequently referred to and there are several clever references all through the game (see the above screenshot with "Sheol" for example).
Without such background it will be difficult to understand some elements or you will even be mislead. So can the figure of Leviathan be confusing based on your background, as it was originally a sea-creature that tried to kill Jonah's whale while the game seems to imply that
. "Leviathan" in Christian mythology, even though also based on the Old Testimant, refers to Satan for example, which would give an entirely different meaning to the pieces of literature you find. I have no idea how the Islamic interpretation of the story of Jonah goes (it probably ends with the whale being blown up -> this is satire, relax people), but I can imagine that a gamer with an Islamic background will give yet another completely diferent interpretation to TOCL's story.
All in all, the weak and pompous writing, boring and uninteresting attempts at psychological monologues and reliance on elements not in the game drag down the quality of TOCL by a lot.
What remains are the technical aspects, which are great: the world is incredibly beautiful and leads us from one stunning vista to the next. Just look at the screen shots above! That is what you will get in game as well.
One disappointing fact about the graphics are the lack of movement: except for a very few exceptions, almost everything is static. If you brush against leaves of a plant, those leaves will not move for example. There is basically zero interaction between yourself and the environment. But maybe that is the intention and I was just too stupid to catch the metaphor (
- now that is a plot twist!)
The sound and music are nice. Not outstanding but nice. There are not a lot of sound effects but you are mostly treated to ambient background noise and fragments of music, which suit the game well and add to the creepy and disturbing atmosphere.
Finally the game really awards exploration by hiding the above-mentioned Solomon's Notes in far-off places. Unfortunately it is not always clear what is the exit to the next chapter and what is a side-passage, which easily results in you missing out on a Note. Imagine this: you are in a room with 2 identical doors: picking the right one ends the chapter, forcing you to restart the entire game (!) if you wanted to find the Solomon's Note hidden far beyond the left door. For such a game where reading everything is mandatory, that is just not good development.
All in all I do not recommend TOCL unless you have a fetish for Jewish mythology, you crave some "baby's first psychology lesson" or are just a graphics [edited:] "lady of the street" who wants to walk through some gorgeous set-pieces and otherwise ignore the writer's musings completely. I kinda enjoyed this game but only because I am such a graphics [edited:] "lady of the street" and have a good knowledge of middle-eastern mythologies, yet If I had spent more than 3$ I would have feel scammed.

I've already played this game on the PS Vita (and loved it enough to Platinum it), and the PC port of this game fixes all of the technical problems that I had with the game.
ToCS is a great JRPG in a time when I'm finding my patience stretched thin by other JRPGs like World of Final Fantasy or the latest Pokemon generation. The story is quite slow-paced, but my opinion is that this works to the benefit of the game; the worldbuilding and unexpected depth of interaction with the numerous NPCs sets the stage properly for its sequels, but also tells a story of learning to work with others, even if at first glance, you find nothing in common or nothing likable. Despite its slow pacing, I don't think that ToCS wastes my time unnecessarily. You can choose how much you want to play, since the majority of quests are optional, and story-related mandatory quests interesting.
The core gameplay involves moving around a world filled with NPCs that each have their own stories to tell, in the midst of a growing national crisis. Combat is turn-based, but it is my favourite turn-based combat system to date, staying simple to understand at a basic level, but providing a great deal of tactical depth and satisfaction when fighting the wide range of boss fights.
As for the quality of the PC port, XSEED did a wonderful job of improving upon the original in terms of performance (basically no FPS stutters like in the original PS Vita version), and adding additional voiced lines for the protagonist, Rean, who had several scenes without voice-over when others did. The new Fast-Forward feature is also a welcome edition, especially since I was replaying the game, which saved me a lot of time in the story cutscenes and combat animations that I didn't need to see again.
As a final note, there is a method of replacing the voice-over audio with the original Japanese audio, if you have a preference for it.

This is about as bare bones as you can get for a sports game,  Very limited options, no trades during the season, no free agency, no multiple seasons...  it's generally lacking in many areas which sports games have become known for in recent years.
The good -  it has the official MLB license, which means real teams and players.  It's simplistic and very casual, you can just pick up and play, other than getting timing down for hitting it's easy to play.  If you are an older gamer you'll appriciate the throw back to old sports games.
The bad  -  The game just isn't anywhere near the standard sports games have been held too far years.  Lack of options, lack of customization, lack of multiple seasons.  While these things were common place back in the the early 2000's when games were limited, those limitations don't exist anymore.  The graphics are kind of meh, that normally doesn't matter in sports games but the player animations are rough, they glide rather than run.  Also it seems to have quite a few issues with fielding on line drives...
Generally speaking, Super Mega Baseball is a far superior product, which is only held back by it's lack of a MLB license.  I'd only recommend this game if you're a massive hardcore fan of throwback games.  Even then it's a tough recommendation because the game just isn't very fun to play..

I heard about this game a while back, I think a friend posted a link to the kickstarter page. I was super excited about it from the get go, and decided to buy it when it entered early access. As you can expect from an early access game, it's not quite there yet. With that being said, I haven't really encountered any game ending bug's its just mostly a few minor translation errors and the combat system while fun and interesting isn't quite there yet (I'll get into that a little more later.) In it's current state I'd say get it if you want to try something new and have the patience to deal with a game in it's infancy, otherwise wait.
It plays like an old text and graphic strategy game, think King of Dragon Pass crossed with Oregon Trail, but much improved and with vikings. Even in it's current state, there are numerous events and choices with usually humorous outcomes. In my opinion however, the main thing that makes this worth buying is the combat system. Both the player and NPC have a deck of cards from which they to draw heros and special attacks. I think it has a lot of potential, but from what I can tell the NPC draws a lot less randomly than the player right now, getting all their heroes in the first couple turns and you can go the whole combat with out drawing another.
In it's current state? 5.5/10 but I'm optimistic it'll get better and the devs seem really commited to their project.

Speaking as a fan of The Banner Saga and FTL, I'm pretty excited by The Great Whale Road; right now, the game has a *long* way to go, but it's showing tremendous potential. Essentially, half of the game is about trading and resource management - at the start of each year, you decide how much labor goes into farming, hunting, etc.- then, you set sail and can take certain resources, such as pelts, with you for the sake of trading.
The other half of the gameplay is traditional SRPG combat combined with a sort of deckbuilding? The deckbuilding element of the game needs further development before I'll comment on it, but I see where it's heading and I'm eager to see it developed.
All of this is interspersed by adventure-game style timed-decisions. There's a lot to the story already, and I like the way it's both written and told- overall, this game is worth checking out, but bear in mind that it suffers from some glitches and is quite incomplete- if you want to go for it now, go for it- if you'd rather wait, you'd best wishlist it. This will be an ongoing review.  Currently I've  played about 3.5 hrs, but there is still lots going on.
The game reminds me of Banner Saga & Battle Brothers, but with more squad/caravan/tribe managing.  It was 35 minutes before I even had my first battle.
The UI is very good.  There are tool tips for EVERYTHING, which is very helpful.  You can also pull up old tool tips anytime from the help menu in case you forget how to do something.  It is a very text heavy game, & like nearly every game ever made, the text is too small for those of us playing at higher resolutions.  Hopefully they will increase the font size for the many event boxes that pop up.
Fighting is card based, which is different.  You don't begin each fight with your entire squad, you start with your hero and have to draw other squad mates from your deck.  Obviously this can put you at a disadvantage if several turns go by & before you know it you are outnumbered 4-1.
Some cards allow you to play squadmates, others use abilities.  Not every ability can be used on every unit.  Eligible units obtain a faint glow upon clicking on the ability card.  You then click on the unit to apply the effect.  The glow is very subtle & I missed this for quite a while, trying in vain to apply buffs to units that weren't eligible.  Ability cards also have a turn restriction, meaning you can't play some until turn 3, or 5 or 6, etc.
First major thing.  Your turn is on a 90 second timer.  I hate this.  There is quite a lot to do during your 90 seconds.  The only goal I've seen so far is to kill the enemy leader.   Right now my squad is only 4 strong, All 4 can move to various places on the board.   After moving them, you can choose to defend, or attack.  But each weapon also has 2 different types of attacks to choose from.  None of this uses cards.  Before attacking, you can choose to apply buffs to attack if you have the right kind of unit that matches the card you are trying to use.  Likewise, you can apply defensive buff cards to a unit as well.  In my opinion, having only 90 seconds to move & position 4 units (and possibly more later), deciding about defense or multiple attack options + additional buffs with the cards feels too rushed.  Especially during the first few battles when people are just trying to learn what to click and how to fight.  The developers have already stated they will allow us to disable the timer in a future build.
Quick word on performance.  I play a lot of indy games, many of which are poorly optimized, with my computer struggling to got above 30 fps (usually Unity engine games).  I'm getting between 300 to 500 fps, with the average around 400!
I'm still trying to figure out the village management.  Each year you assign 10 points to things like farming, crafting, hunting, diplomacy, warcraft, etc.  Depending on the points your village harvests/gathers some number of produce, meat, pelts, etc.  There is a minimum amount you must produce each year to feed the village.  This really doesn't take all that much time though.  At the beginning of my year two, there was no food for me to take with me on my expedition.  My warriors lose health each day on the boat, since they are starving.  There are lots of random encounters, (think Banner Saga) & you come to lots of villages where you can get quests, rest & recover health, hunt, buy weapons.  Most places I've visited haven't had food to sell, so we are still hurting some.

Score: 3 out of 5

Graphics, sound, music, gameplay, it's all good and fun. The addition of a galactic map with visible trade routes, more story elements, tons of ships to build is all fine. Bosses are very well designed and there's a lot of overall variation. So it can't be bad right? Think again.
"More isn't always better"
A famous quote the developers should have thought about but obviously didn’t. Especially in the last sector, this game is such a monumental grind, I'm getting tears in my eyes just from wishing it to end.
Some missions requiring you to do several runs (from point A to B to C). At the start of the game, this isn’t much of an issue, but it gets more common the further you get. And this doesn’t add anything. It’s just making you to do the same set of runs over and over and over. And it gets worse. Some missions even require you to do the same set of runs multiple times because you cannot transport everything in one go. So after finally doing your multiple run mission, you have to jump back and do it all over yet again.
As a reward for missions you’ll get credits and materials. Both are required to buy gear at mechanics. Mechanics only have up to a certain type and amount of gear, locked behind progression walls. But guess what, you need to transport these materials as well! So you’re again doing the exact same runs over and over. Luckily it’s possible to create multiplayer contracts, allowing others to move your cargo from source to destination. This is actually done very well since it’s always beneficial for both parties. Even if you don’t give them credits for it, other players will still receive a certain randomized amount of credits and materials.
The missions aren't easy either. Sounds good at first, but balance is way off. Most of them will turn out in a complete disaster and you'll know that mostly within the first 30 or so seconds. Misplace one item: restart. Misjudgment in what's coming at you and from what direction: restart. You can't plan ahead either since runs are somewhat randomized. Although, the amount of variations is limited so you can restart several times in a row until you get the one you remember.
Also less fun than expected: the ship design. Sure, you can have tons of ships and select or even build anything you want whenever you want. That is, after buying them with credits AND buying additional space upgrades, which adds yet another layer of grind.
At least in the original Space Run, you knew the ship you got was designed for a mission. Or, better said: the difficulty of that mission was designed around the ship. Now, you not only have to think about placement of objects, you also have to take the layout of the ship into consideration. The annoying or even destructive properties of some cargo types you need to transport doesn't help here either.
It's not easy to rate this game fairly. On paper, everything sounds like it's much better than the original and would deserve a decent 4 out of 5. But in reality, the total experience is far from what I expected. It just keeps dragging on and on and gets more annoying the further you get.
Especially the last sector ruined it completely for me.
Edit: have to be fair here. The first three sectors were fun and somewhere in the fourth sector, things were getting very frustrating very fast. The achievements for this game are well planned out and also helpt keeping me playing. It would be too harsh thumb this one down. Just be prepared.

This has to be one of my more recent obsessions... I really love this game. It is a mixture of tower defense and a hex based placement puzzle. The tower defense is based on the hex tiles so there are 6 different lanes to defend your ship against as you transport cargo from one planet to another. I am almost done with making this a perfect game (completing all of the achievements) and I still find it highly enjoyable. This is a more flushed out game then the first one, it seems to fill all the issues I had with the first one.
From the quirky characters that are back from the first game Space Run to the new characters, the voice acting and atmosphere of the game is quite enjoyable. I really enjoy the simple story here as it adds a bit of flavor and humor to the game, but don't be expecting Star Wars level story here it is a bit lack luster. The controls are fine, do I think they could use some improvements, yes. First off the hotkeys work fine, but "releasing" the selection is a bit of an issue. I really want to just hit esc (which brings up the in game menu... if I had a penny...) or something similar but I haven't found that through my gameplay to be there. I also got to the point where some of the gameplay got too repetitive, the balance wasn't quite there. I did find a bug in the quests however, I don't think I should have been given a quest as I didn't have the planet unlocked yet.
To continue on, I think they added wonderful multiplayer features that really add to the game in my opinion. Some feel as though it was simply an add on, but I think it was a deliberate design decision. It allows asynchronous and hands free multiplayer play which I think is ideal for a puzzle/tower defense type of game through a contract based system in which you contracts are posted publicly to everyone on the server. It also allows for built in longevity in the way it was designed as new players play through they can always find others contracts out. Essentially eliminating the need for someone else to be on at the same exact time to play together.
The progression system is fair but it essentially ends at 75% of the game. This means you aren't unlocking any new components for your ship for the last 25% of the game. I think this is why I felt it started to get grindy and repetitive. I do have to point out one more thing, I did have some performance issues at times. The framerate would drop sometimes and just make the game feel sluggish. Overall, like I said I love this game, but I think I love it because it's core concept is sooo good even though the implementation is not quite there yet. Don't get me wrong it is still better than it's successor, but there is still more work to be done before I say it is flawless. I give it a 4/5 because I do really enjoy the concept and the core gameplay is really entertaining!

If you like generic anime style pictures, you may like this entry in the Pixel Puzzle series. But, like in the other games, don’t expect any replay value over the pre-defined two dozen or so jigsaw pictures.
One of the advantages—and at the same time, the main disadvantage—of the Pixel Puzzles series is that all games are essentially the same: you get a set amount of jigsaw puzzles with pre-set tile shapes and numbers, and that is it.
The result is that each Pixel Puzzle game boils down to whether you like the theme of its pictures, which in our cases is anime style ones. (None of the pictures are from any actual anime, they are just decent-ish drawings.)
The inherent problem with drawn pictures instead of photos in a jigsaw puzzle is that sometimes it is a lot more difficult to determine where a tile goes. In some of the pictures here, this goes to rather extremes; this never reaches frustrating levels, but the game feels like a step back from other entries.
Also, as a final note: while the ambient music is not bad, I really advise to mute the game, because the overly enthusiastic fairy helper can get on one’s nerves rather fast.

There are two types of people who I'll recommend this to:

1) This game is like a Unreal Engine 3 tech demo on steroids. So if you like tech demos, and are willing to move around, then this is your game. It's quite beautiful.

2) Or, if you're interested in a seeing beautiful atmospheric scenery, with interesting dialog, and are willing to read AND walk around slowly, with little action / interaction with the environment, then this is your game. The dialog is quite artsy, and the story is very odd, so not everyone's cup of tea. There are no puzzles, and you don't die... it's just walking, reading, and hearing dialog.
If you're the former, then you'll be happy to know, once you complete the game, you can skip to various sections, which makes it easy to navigate to each 'tech demo' scene. The graphical settings are minimal though, but they look very sharp, even on an older engine.

If you're the later, then you'll probably enjoy this quick romp. The voice acting is good, and the writing style interesting. I wasn't too fond of the story, but I'm not really interested in this type of game.  The game is short - I probably completed it in 30 minutes to an hour, but if you take your time reading everything carefully, it might be a 2 hour game. Make sure to wait for all the character's monologues to finish before moving on to the next scene, or he might get cut off.
Me personally: I give it a 3/10... not my cup of tea... extremely boring, with too odd of a story, and too static of a world to be interesting to explore. If there was much more animation and more interaction - maybe even a puzle element, it woudl be better.

This is a very linear visual novel, but split into four episodes with a bunch of smaller bonus episodes. There's at least one choice in each main episode. They're used as a way to make sure you're paying attention (as you game over for the wrong choice at times), though the last episodes may still trip you
up.
Ah, yes, there are text errors again, but they're not typos this time, just mostly formatting errors. Sooooo close, but at least this version seems to be the second release of the English script, as opposed to the first game being third.
There's a new resolution bug this time around, too! When you press Esc to pause, the screen appears to zoom in if you're stuck with a 1024x768 monitor. Thankfully, since there aren't branching paths this time, you won't need to pause to save too often. And, it's fixed by just exiting to the main menu and reloading a save.
The progression of the story itself is similar to the previous game, in that it starts out cheerful and silly, then slowly becomes more of a heavy experience. Since it's much shorter, there's less time spent sobbing than previously, but it will touch on very serious and delicate topics. Be warned for episode 4.
But, yes, l have played this game's full experience and clocked out at 11 hours. l enjoyed every minute, so l can't complain.
Oh, and there's an alternate universe thing going on when you try out the short episodes and you're left to figure it out on your own. The game won't tell you what's going on, so somewhere such as TVTropes will be a good place to check when you're all done.

"Mindless fun". Literally.
Pound of Ground is a simple, open-world game, focusing on stemming the tide of a zombie horde in what is presumably the Western Wastes of the USA. The operative word here being "simple". You either shoot zombies, beat them about the skull with a bat, or run them down in your very own hot rod. There are little "metagames" strewn about, such as setting distance records for jumps in your car, or how far you can knock away a zombie with your bat, and these help stave off the monotony that sets in with every zombie-killing game.
The graphics are chunky, and the voice acting is evident of a development team whose first language wasn't English, but the music is pretty cool, and the cartoonish nature of the visuals make up for any cutscenes you'll inevitably want to start skipping.
The lack of polish on this game makes it hard for me to recommend to anyone when it's not on sale, but it's definitely worth at least a run through it's demo.

The Legend of Heroes: Trails of Cold Steel I picked this game (and some other ones) up on a whim just to satisfy a JRPG craving I was having and was really surprised by game itself. However, before I go on with giving a decent recommendation let me first preface and say most of the negative things you hear about this game are true. The game really develops at a slow pace, this is undeniable however if you consider this is the first in a four game series it is understandable. The voice acting is generally terrible, and there is no option to my knowledge to switch to Japanese language with English subtitles. Lastly the game doesn’t do anything incredibly unique in terms of mechanics making it rather unsurprising in terms of game play.
That out of the way I was never once bothered by the lack of originality of game play mechanics, what is offered is what I expected and I didn’t feel that it detracted from the overall game. The story is unique, the characters are compelling, and the world feels sufficiently fleshed out to where I never felt like a dissonant element was introduced that broke my experience. In fact I was so absorbed in the world the developers created I played the game three more times just to ensure I got to see everything that is offered. The DLC’s offered are completely optional and are primarily just cosmetics minus some low priced game play boosts such as money, crafting material and some accessories. Most of which can be achieved through normal game play or multiple playthroughs.
Anyway, I highly recommend Trails of Cold Steel to anyone that wants to play a solid JRPG and can handle bad voice acting.
