Dandelion: Wishes Brought To You Review
Since it seems dating sims geared toward female players (otome) all get glowing reviews from the majority of players it's hard guess what kind of game you'll actually be buying. Thankfully Dandelion does have a demo available on Cheritz's website and here on Steam plus plenty of player videos on YouTube. I only recommend watching (part of) a play-through if you don't mind having the story development spoiled a bit.
What sets this apart from so many other otome games for me is the main (really the only) female character. There was a lot of thought put into her character which I really appreciate. Unlike 99.9% of protagonists in other otome she isn't flat, transparent, nor more or less non existent. Any weakness or flaws she has are clearly explained/have a very clear reason for being. She's completely relatable (at least for me) and very likable... most of the time. Even if you find yourself being disgusted by her actions you are still experiencing a well fleshed out character not some cookie cutter archetype who's only actual purpose is to give narrative to a nearly non-existent storyline and when she actually does speak it's nearly always things like “Uuugh!” “Um...” “Yes” “No” and “......” if that last one even counts as speaking. The male characters are well thought out as well. They each have though own unique stories and requirements for a bad or happy ending. While there are a few fixed events none of the routes felt like a copy of the other. Unlike your typical visual novel you have more to do than just pick the answer that gets you (the most) relationship points with the guy you're pursuing. Though I must admit keeping up the MC's maintenance can feel a little pointless toward the end of the game especially if you aren't playing natural aka attacking the save and reload buttons like crazy to ensure you get the best reaction from the characters as possible. I think for people that play though without crushing the save and reload buttons the time between certain events would be adequate in order to ensure everything is on point for a happy ending.
The art was alright but nothing special. Sometimes it's really good and others it looks rushed. The images during game play are a mix between realistic portions and miniaturization which I found kind of cute. Mechanics wise the game worked just fine. I didn't notice any weirdness going on. The only issue that I think many might run into that isn't really addressed or admitted to as one is when you try to start a new route from a previous save. Most don't want to spend time going through the prologue five times over so they make a save file to skip over all that and start earning relationship points with the “animal” who's route they want to get. But, if you do this the game will probably ignore any stamps you collect making all the time you spent trying to get them null. If you want the stamps to count just sacrifice the 3-5mins it'll take to skip through the intro scenes. This is every so slightly annoying but not really a big deal (unless you've just completed a route only to find none of the 60+ stamps you collected registered). Speaking of the skip feature unlike most games in this genre I've tried the skip button actually works/you don't have to hold it down for it to work. One click and everything fast forwards, although it would be better if it just skipped entirely, but I'm happy with how it functions.
While I thoroughly enjoyed the game and recommend it to everyone who likes a good story I couldn't help being slightly annoyed by the number of grammatical errors. Some of them were borderline story breaking; prime example being the characters were consistently confused with each other. The second most common is repeating lines. The second most common is repeating lines. (See what I did there? :)) You're left wondering if the character said something relevant to the story or scenario taking place and mostly just why the heck are the there so many repeated lines? While the number of grammatical errors is moderate they occur far too frequently for a professionally done game. This is especially atrocious since it's been a good number of years since the game's release/more than enough time for the developer(s) to go back in and correct these things with a patch. When they transferred the game to Steam they di ddo some updating but it was mostly slight cosmetic changes/nothing that really improved the game. There are other minor errors in the game; you might see some script code a couple times for example, but that pales by leaps in bounds compared to the spelling and grammatical errors.
Again, while you are not utterly bombarded with errors and can follow the story pretty well for a game that is centered around text, particularly for those that are not fluently in Korean, the rate at which they occur is still very deplorable. Perhaps if this was a beta it'd be okay, but this is the finished product and has been sitting like this for years with not patch to correct any of it.
Oerall I found it to be probably the best compared to the currently available otome games despite obvious flaws. Although the voice acting is Korean only I think the actors did a pretty good job conveying the characters. The bonus material for completing the game is pretty interesting too. I'd be thrilled if this was made into an animation, manwha, and/or novel. If I got wind of it becoming available in English (with the assumption much better job would be done grammar wise etc.) it'd definitely be on my pre-order list.

Although EnsenaSoft's ABC Coloring Town is a fun little educational tool for young gamers to have the alphabet reinforced to them.
As the game winds its way through its little town you will stop at 26 different houses. Each house represents a single letter in the alphabet. The player clicks on the door and it opens up to represent a picture beginning with the representative letter. Consequently, you'll expect to see that E is for elephant, C is for cat and Z is for zebra. You have a choice of sixteen different colors that you can choose from to color and each picture has a number of different panels for you to color. Once you complete the alphabet it cycles through with different words until you've completed the alphabet three times.
There is no right or wrong answer so children are able to be as creative as the color palette enables them to be.
Unless you are fanatical about coloring in most adults will likely find that the game isn't engaging enough for them. This is specifically aimed at those learning the alphabet as well as learning to use the computer. It is extremely basic. The words are very easy. It is on the same level intellectually as Sesame Street. As a result, I warn anybody over the age of about six or seven that you'll likely not find anything of value here.
The presentation is very basic. The biggest negative is the music that may in fact be worse than intentionally making yourself deaf. The graphics are cute but given that it's a coloring game for children that is merely meeting the requirements of the game.
There are two things within the presentation that I did not like. First, even when you skip coloring an image you are congratulated on a job well done. This renders the process pointless when children make this realization. Secondly, when you have completely colored in a picture I expected the game to tell me that I was done with that picture and to give me the opportunity to move onto the next image or to stay on that one. Instead you need to manually get out of each picture to move onto the next.
One way to increase the presentation, gameplay and educational quality of the game may have been to incorporate a color matching feature. This feature would have required children to color in the animals and items in realistic colors (e.g. yellow and black for the bee).
Is any EnsenaSoft game Steamified? No. They all lack achievements and trading cards. Not that achievements would matter here as the game can't tell if you've colored in anything or not. Trading cards would, however, be nice.
If you have a child between the ages of three and five then you may want to reinforce the alphabet through ABC Coloring Town. If this is not you then I can't recommend the game.

ABC Coloring Town is a game for kids, where you're coloring drawings of items or animals beginning by the letter represented at the house you're currently stopped at.
Each drawing has the name of the item or animal on it. You have two coloring modes: one with a paintbrush and one with a color pot. In other words, the color pot allows you to paint an area respecting its outline. For the paintbrush, you can choose its size. On the side, you have a cube rotating, showing also the progress of your coloring.
And that's all. Once exiting, you're moving suddenly to the next house, whether you're finished or not with your drawing. And you can't go back. Nope, you're forced to follow the alphabet. And once you're back at the letter (after Z, you're back at A), the drawing is different. It's impossible for you to save and come back later or to find again the drawing unless being lucky.
The only pertinent audio is the letter being pronounced, because not coloring a picture is still rewarded by an "Excellent" or an "Awesome". The description of the game is confusing with Basic English prononciation. So don't expect the words to be spoken.
Despite the great idea to associate a word to its picture, the rest is just so frustrating that I largerly prefer
, even with its major default of not having any word. At least, you can come back when you want to the game, you have a little animation, three modes and a better presentation.
Even the cute music or the 3D house and village aren't saving this software of a thumb down. Avoid this, even with a discount. And while I'm an adult, I can see the disappointement for kids that have to interrupt their coloring and can't resume it.

I think that's the highest score I've given a game. Maybe Goetia got an 8 too, I'm not sure. Either way, let's clarify that I am in no way afiliated with the developers, creators, game scriptors, audio technicians blah blah blah. I'd like to address that I'm a little bias towards liking this kind of game too. I have a condition that causes severe irritability and lack of concentration. Playing games that I use to love has become a chore so this was a breath of fresh air.
Instead of giving my own pros / cons, which have been addressed in other reviews, I'd like to address some of the common items in them.
1) Controls. I personally have no issue with the controls. I think the mouse is perfectly acceptable to use for turning, stepping forward etc. but others have listed it as a huge criticism. The reason I've mentioned it is to counter those negatives with the fact that you don't want to overlook the smallest detail in this game by rushing around. If given the chance, most people (myself included) would generally head to the furthest point they could and work backwards. The control scheme in place allows you to check your surroundings carefully every step of the way and with that, you'll find useful tools and items that you're going to need. Hell, I managed to overlook something in the very first screen because I wasn't in the right way of thinking when I started.
2) 'That code'! Yeah, there are some tough puzzles. They require some thinking and even with all the materials in the game, it will take you some of your own working out to get the answers. The computer lockdown code gave me a hell of a lot of trouble. I'm happy to admit that. But with a bit more searching, I found a note that explained it clearly. With some of my own hand written notes, I worked it out. Be prepared to make your own notes during this game and make sure you keep them properly labelled. There's another one later on that requires you to click items in sequence. Without making notes, it would have been impossible without backtracking numerous times.
3) Story. Considering you're 'alone', the story is: How the hell do I get out of here!? What you can learn during the game is more about where you are, the people that once called it home and what their reasons for being there was. This is discovered through audio logs (each has a puzzle to finding the correct information to hear it), diaries or notes around the building. I found myself wanting to know everything I could about these people and discover what drove them to their actions. It was truly fascinating. Some discoveries will lead you to more questions and are open to interpretation at the end.
I'm genuinely looking forward to the next project the developer works on. Oh, and the developer has explained why there isn't linux/mac support. He doesn't use the systems so doesn't know how to do it properly. He'd rather keep working on quality than allow a port that would be subpar. A normal, human, response.

Basically SRG but with online features and more options, PLUS the grindfest.
+ Lots of missions to do over 4 galaxies
+ New weapons with secondary abilities. Can be upgraded to 2 levels.
+ Extension of power up via links
+ Online feature to create contracts for players. Buy and sell items with players around the world.
+ Lenghty voice acting. Great gfx.
+ Lots of ships to purchase and upgrade, secret trade routes to unlock.
- Can't transfer online profile to offline or vice versa.
- Regardless of challenge in terms of cargo type and danger, you get the same amount of XP from a given mission.
- Grinding, grinding, grinding.
- Building up your ships with tiles requires expensive parts and appropriate leveled mechanic.
- Can't transfer obtained parts from one galaxy to the next. Gotta sell them for credit only.
If you like grinding to next level, while doing missions that give not enough XP for the danger you face for each mission, then this is it for you. It is a great game no doubt, but the grinding will seep into your mind as you see how slowly the leveling up takes place. Pair that with separate offline and online profile and you get a "start from the beginning" vibe that takes away the joy of doing missions to reach a certain player level. Player level unlocks new weapons and ability-based items, but you have to craft them using appropriate, leveled mechanic. More often than not, you feel like they placed those mechanics in a way that you can't easily level up, even if you have the parts with you.
The MP aspect is perhaps good for unlocking some achievements, but after those are done (assuming you love achievements), there isn't really any incentive to play it on MP. If you don't care about achievements or MP, I highly recommend you go for offline mode profile; you won't be missing much.
Speaking of parts: the ones you have in one galaxy can't be transferred to the next one. So if you want those parts, you have to sell them, go to next galaxy and buy those parts again with money again. You can do MP contracts so that other players can take items for you, but that is tideous and more often than not, many won't even do them. Basically, in more than one way, it feels like a grindfest in every aspect of the game.
If you can get over that issue, the combat will give you a good time, and challenge. Sometimes quite unforgiving, the wave of enemies and the type of cargo you choose would force you to think fast on what to do in a situation, until you get some really powerful weapons unlocked.
Overall it's a very good game, but it's one of those titles, that I wish I could vote more than just "YES" or "NO" for recommendation. Compared to the original, this one feels not so great due to the overall aspect of the MP and grindfest.

And I've even taken advantage of the ability to put out contracts for other players to move your stuff around for you if you don't want to do it yourself. But that does NOT justify the existence of this game's biggest, deal-breaking problem:
Always Online DRM. What happens if your internet hiccups in the middle of a five minute mission? It doesn't inform you there's a problem until you've completed the mission, at which point it boots you to the main menu and erases your progress. That's inexcusable.
After dealing with this a number of times, I returned to the main menu hoping to be rescued by the proposed "Offline Mode". After waiting at the "Initializing Offline Mode..." screen for over an hour, I tabbed out and searched for people who had the same problem, and if they had any solutions. What I found was people having a different problem. People who entered offline mode, but were still randomly disconnected. WHAT? "Offline Mode" removes the multiplayer features, but doesn't remove the Always Online DRM requirement. That's unforgivable.
Trying to play this game is a nightmare. Even when my internet is working fine I'll have difficulties starting the game, and face a lot of unnecessary lag.

Just finished playing this game, and holy♥♥♥♥♥♥I am genuinely confused. But in a good way.
First of all I would like to say that this is one of the most beautiful games I have ever played, not only because of the graphics but more because of the design, if you know what I mean. Once you've seen the palace-esque buildings overgrown with plants and the light coming through cathedral windows you will understand.
Also it has a really nice atmosphere, melancholy at times, frightening at others, and always perfectly accentuated with music. There are elements of gore, bodies lying around etc. and you are constantly at edge but it's very well done.
Then there's the bible quotes and symbolism, and I'm always a fan of that. It's subtle and probably to be overlooked if you rush through but this is really not the game for rushing (though it is quite short, unfortunately. But maybe the concept wouldn't have carried over a longer span of time ... who knows.)
As for the story: although I am fairly sure I've read all the pages hanging around and read through all of Solomon's notes (they are quite lengthy and a bit over to top, in my opinion, though interesting) and yet I wouldn't say that I can see a full picture of what is going on. There are clearly distinguishable characters and obvious relations but no real story to speak of and quite a lot ominous bits of information. And it gets really philosophical at times.
But then again, I really liked that. It makes you go through possible outcomes in your head and has you trying to figure it all out instead of sitting back and just consuming it. Some may say that it is pretentious and actually quite pointless but in my opinion a game (like this) doesn't have to get a point across or educate you. Still enjoyed it.
AND, a big plus is that there are no jumpscares and no enemies to kill or hide from. That would totally have killed it for me. You will hardly encounter any living things in this game (only people you meet are dead or ... turned into stone? Are they statues? Hmm.) and that's good because the atmosphere of decay and hopelessness really profits from it.
'nuff said. The pictures say pretty much all. And you should be an avid reader if you want to have fun with this.

A good walking similar / exploration game will engage and carry the player with careful pacing and an interesting storyline. The game will take hold of them where they are and lift them into a new world, guiding them and teaching them. The Old City fails to do that. Instead it alienates the player with wilfully obtuse language and bores them with a complete disregard for pacing.
Creating a game that is entirely exploration with a single narrator is challenging indeed. Although we have seen how effective it can be when done right, such as in Portal and The Stanley Parable, the difference between those games and this highlights the need to speak TO your audience, not AT them. Flat monologues with sentences such as "An assertion from an assumption is still an assertion, making any deduction from that foundation subject to critique." and "Epistemic humility can regress to the deconstruction of stagnation." distract the player from the immersion of the game, and break the illusion that the person speaking is the character they are controlling. It is hard to get into a first-person character when they are practically speaking a language you do not understand.
Games such as Doom 3, Bioshock, and The Last of Us (particularly the starting acts of each of these games) show us how well a world can be portrayed through notes, events, and other environmental clues around you. In fact the opening segments of each of those games works without any of the main game action. Coming back to The Stanley Parable again we can see how well pacing can be managed with the narrator filling in the gaps of otherwise mindless travel. Imagine, if you will, a long corridor or expanse that stretches before you. You know that you must walk to the far edge of that space. In The Old City this is mostly done in silence which, while it gives you a moment to appreciate the obvious beauty of the landscape, soon falls into dull trudgery. Not helped by the many times when you must travel back to point X to explore the other fork in the pathway as the one you have been following has lead to a dead end.
On a technical note, the lack of advanced video controls make this game hard to tweak to run on lower end systems. You can turn motion blur off, change the resolution, and that is about all. As a result it ran very clippy on my steam-powered crank-started laptop (no one's fault but my own I know).
All in all a dissapointment. There was so much potential here for an incredible experience, however the flaws above coupled with the lack of richness in the environment (particularly a complete lack of anything to interact with in any form) mean that I would not recommend it to anyone.

The Old City: Leviathan is a first person exploration game. You control an unknown, very talkative, character and explore the outskirts of "The Old City", with your intention to find your way into it's walls.
Do not start this game and expect to be told a story about the downfall of a city and the struggle for survival. While the narrative in the game does have some elements of that, the creators are much more interested in exploring the philosophical viewpoints of the people that allowed it to happen and of those that are still around.
Understanding the story of this game is challenging, but ultimately rewarding. I still don't know what exactly happened to the City, but upon finishing the game I know why it happened and and fully satisfyied with the answer the game presented.
If you liked The Witness or the Book of Metro 2033, you should know what to expect here. It's an atmospheric take on the philosophies of people and what happens when their different viewpoints are allowed to bounce off each other. If that doesn't sound like your cup of tea, it probably isn't. But it does sound like mine.

The Great Whale Road is a great new addition to the interactive narrative game genre. It adds some lite-RPG and resource management aspects as well as turn-based tactical combat, all of which is firmly set - thematically speaking - during the Viking Age.
Adventuring is interesting, even if a bit sluggish during this current build although I found the longer sea voyages to be quite theme-specific and it’s not like things don’t happen during them. Combat is exciting thanks to the “defeat their leader, protect yours” approach and the randomizing inherent in the card drawing.
The game excels in terms of atmosphere, the art style has a pretty clear focus and direction and the music is a wonderful complement to it. They do a great deal to immerse you into a Viking Age-like atmosphere.
This is a super-fresh Early Access release so it is bound to have a hefty amount of glitches, bugs and gaps in content but considering the amount of time, effort and money that already went into developing the game, I’m pretty sure the devs are planning on a bunch of rebalancing, changes and content patching to happen in the near future.
Nevertheless what is available at the moment is more than just promising, it’s a pretty solid gaming experience that can only get bigger and better.

Summary of the full preview:
The Great Whale Road is currently too boring, repetitive, and buggy to be enjoyable.
The promising (but currently only half-finished) story of the Danish campaign is padded out by a lot of dull "sailing" segments which completely ruin the pacing. It's perfectly realistic for the setting, but these long, long sailing journeys just feel like a waste of my precious leisure time. I spent at least 80% of my playing time just starting at that ship screen. Offering a time skip feature would greatly increase my enjoyment of these segments; unfortunately, it would also make the game really short.
In fairness, the sailing is meant to be livened up by random events; sadly, there are far too few of those in the game right now, and they'll already start repeating after 10 or 15 minutes of gameplay.
Combat is currently too simple and the AI is too weak to be enjoyable; every battle feels the same.
Basically, the game needs to have much more variety, more content, a more engaging sailing mechanic, and a more complex combat system to become enjoyable. However, this total lack of fun is not unusual for an Early Access game, and if you want to support an indie turn based RPG that
eventually become fun to play, then I fully support your efforts.
I will continue to play newer versions of this game during Early Access and will update my rating to a recommendation if it becomes appropriate.
Full preview:

The Great Whale Road marks the Steam debut for Sunburned Games. This is a development studio based in Valencia, Spain. They are studio of ten people who have poured their heart and souls into creating a story-driven RPG with turn-based tactics and cards.
The game is set in the seventh century. You travel the famous Whale Road, the North Sea. It is up to you, brave leader, to not only save your clan but to make it thrive. As a result this is an epic challenge that is full of danger but also full of reward. It's not going to be easy. These types of games never are. But it will be worth it in the end if you are victorious and become one of the legends of your time.
The locations are all drawn by hand within the game. This is undoubtedly one of the highlights of the game as they are beautiful. They help set the mood and the atmosphere. They remind me of some of the old viking picture books that I used to read as a child. As a result, the graphics were a resounding victory for me and kept me playing.
The soundtrack appropriate for the time and the setting. I'd like to see an increased selection of tracks by the time that development is complete. A little too early to be too critical in this department but a more varied soundtrack would add to the richness of the experience.
Winter
The primary gameplay mechanic utilized here is that of two seasons - winter and summer. Winter is where you do your planning for the upcoming summer. In summer you carry out your actions and perform your quests. I found that this system has been well designed and that it works well with the game. Many players will feel somewhat at home immediately.
Learning how to be successful in the planning stages of the game is of vital importance. Here you get to allocate your points into a number of different areas such as hunting, farming, traditions, etc. In many ways these concepts are borrowed directly from city building or God games games where you control your populous.
During the winter a number of random events occur. I've played through the game several times now and each time I've gotten a different event on the second and subsequent events. The first always appears to be the same. Selecting the right option can give you a helping hand. However, I believe that if you pick the wrong option you can ultimately lose just as much.
Summer
The summer is the most active part of the game but no more or less important than winter. Summer is where everything is active. The gameplay forces you to think on your feet especially when you get into combat. Random events can and do occur throughout the summer seasons.
Summer is also the part of the game is where card and turn-based combat enters the play. This was a system that has been utilized in different games but the developers have honestly tried to implement their own version of it. Some of the changes were relatively tricky to come to grips with and I admit I lost early on, quite devastatingly so. However, I quickly learned that this is where even more strategy came into play. This is an area of the game that needs tweaking and refinement. It's not there yet but there is an opportunity for it to become more
I have a feeling that this will elicit quite a few negative reviews by players who only put in an hour or so worth of time into the gameplay. It's not for that audience. This is a game that will arguably take a couple of playthroughs before people truly appreciate the game and what it has going on. I wont suggest that there is as much going on as a Civilization game. However, that is the type of crowd that I believe the developers have targeted. I certainly had similar feelings starting out with this game as I did in my first hour or so of playing Civ.
There is a lot, arguably too much, to take in at first and you will probably suffer through periods where you feel lost. You may even feel that you're playing multiple different games. So be warned - the tutorial screens are your friends. Read them thoroughly and take your time to absorb the information. Please don't just rush right through them even though they are all able to be brought back. There's not much worse than having to re-read and re-read tutorial screens that you rushed through in the first instance.
I ran into a glitch in one part of the game. I feel that it is worth mentioning, however, it did only occur the one time. On my first quest I discovered a graphical bug when I attempted to click on the journal and subsequently the map. What happened was that whatever was supposed to load clearly didn't like what I was doing and refused to load. I ultimately quit my game and started again. Thankfully, upon reloading and not being over eager to do something I was able to continue successfully. Hopefully
This is really just the tip of the iceberg for The Great Whale Road. Though what has already been released with the Early Access release is one storyline the developers intend to release three more. There will be one each for the Northumbrians, Franks and Picts. The second half of the initial storyline is to be developed and released as well. The developers hope to strengthen what is already a very reasonable AI. They also want to improve the trade system (I wouldn't call it bare bones at the moment but it can use some improvements). There is much more to come.
No. The game has yet to make the additions of Steam trading cards or Steam achievements. As always these are a very simple addition to the game and will likely be added before the game leaves Early Access.
There are questions that you must ask yourself before I can advise you to purchase The Great Whale Road. Those questions basically boil down to whether or not you have the time to invest into a game that, if you find yourself involved, will demand your attention. Are you willing to provide feedback to the developers? If you are happy to provide feedback and have the time to commit to the game then I believe you will be satisfied with your purchase. There is much to learn and a sizable learning curve. It will frustrate some players but the game is worth it.

Text:
First things first: Visually this game is pretty damn great. Everything ties in nicely and fits the theme from A to Z. While I'm not a fan of the music, that mostly boils to it being repetitive and having no volume control.
Which is also my second biggest gripe: There is a absolute lack of any option in the game. No resolution, no windowed mode, not even a damn volume slider. REALLY needs improvement.
BUT, my biggest grips with the game is an absolute lack of content. Currently there is about ~3 hours of content in the game... with zero deviation. I feel it needs serious time in the oven still before being pushed to players, because right now, halfway getting into the grove of the game (even with the Early access moniker) i was met with a "THANKS FOR PLAYING" screen.
So, the while game play is pretty nice overall through with the various well written and funny random events and encounters, as well as various management mechanics (while limited). The combat is still the weakest part, but i feel reworking the balance / card-system would solve most of the problems there. But other then that i feel massive parts of the game are missing, even excluding what the Early Access page already points out, a proper inventory management system or even a way to buy armor is not available making the experience not only limited but also frustrating.
Trading is currently impossible because of hull sizes limiting what you can bring (mostly food... fills it up) and prices for various goods having no way to keep track of anything.... and no other ships being in the same OR free form travel being in the game for actual trading.
Outside of all of this, I need to come back to the lack of content, even the random encounters suffer here with the same encounter often playing within minutes of each other.
Whole a solid start from all aspects, but i feel the game needs more time before it's worth picking up. The lack of content, and basically every system being under developed, if developed at all... even when you consider it's early access.

I will first say that, as a sequel, this is definitely not a game you should play if you haven't played the first one. And by played, I mean finished (yes, THAT ending.) You may get routes from the first game spoiled if you play this one first. Also, this one probably just won't do much for you if you don't already know the characters and scenarios.
A fair amount Holiday Star is fanservice for people who liked the first Hatoful Boyfriend (and how could you not?) When I first started Holiday Star, I was a bit disappointed that it didn't seem as substantive at the first game. It doesn't follow the typical branching-path format of visual novels like the first game; rather, Holiday Star has a main menu with many options, which take you to the four core stories and some shorter bonus stories. None of these stories have a very large amount of choices or endings. Imagine that if the first Hatoful Boyfriend's story structure is a tree, Holiday Star's is a hedge. The advantage of this is that there's less repetition and less trial-and-error than the first game, at the cost of feeling more episodic rather than like one cohesive plot.
With that said, there is some VERY GOOD content in Holiday Star. The first two of the four main stories are pretty silly (but the premise of the games is pretty silly on the surface, so what was I expecting, I guess.) One is about some thieves stealing Christmas trees, and the other involves magical girls and a fashionable supervillain. They're fun, short-ish romps that fans will probably get a kick out of, but no tears. The side stories are also pretty cute, and you can play some of them using art of the birds' human appearances, which are more expressive.
The real meat, though, is in the third and fourth main stories, which center around the cast going to a dream-like world called the Holiday Star, where they meet a very important new character called The King. If you've finished the first game (yes, THAT ending - I can't figure out how to do the spoiler tag thing here, but the letters BBL should ring a bell) I think you'll have an idea of what to expect here in terms of depth and emotional impact, although the feel is quite different. These stories are significantly longer than the first two, and directly follow one another, as well. They have really pretty, storybook-esque art that fits with the weird fairytale atmosphere of the Holiday Star itself. They explain some backstory not revealed in the first game, and may make you view one or two of the characters is a new light. They are also maybe MORE depressing than anything in the first game. No kidding.
The bottom line is, if you finished the first game and the idea of getting more content like that interests you, do yourself a favor and throw a few bucks at this. You can finish everything in under 10 hours. If the first game didn't appeal to you, don't bother with this unless you go back to the first game and realize it's been great all along.

Cold Steel is something a player, a reader, an adventurer of their dreams needs to see and experience.
It can serve as a jRPG, action-packed and very elaborated on its mechanics and terminology, or as a visual novel about life itself: plethora of insignificant and, therefore, precious stories are scattered around the Erebonian Empire and are dwelling in an everymen’s pockets and hats.
Such complexity is possible because everything — multiple chapters, focused attention on certain backgrounds and town aesthetics of all kinds — everything happens one at a time, and authors apply tireless efforts so you would never be overwhelmed. You can always pinpoint your position in the grand story, thanks to the in-game calendar, and with peace of mind place a ribbon amidst pages. Sure, Cold Steel is a charming book, where beneath an avant-propos emotions await their owner.
Emotions that flourish each time an ambient resonates with a book. Theme of Nord Highlands awakes every bit of your freedom, melodies of Legram will make sure its landscapes are your most treasured ones and notes from the Abyss have an arcane taste of magic. The music will help you to remember forever every chapter, especially the final one, from beginning to end and to brace yourself in every battle.
In the latter case, every element of the battle gameplay is one of the bestest jRPG can deliver: encounters lead to various types of satisfying level-ups, Class VII’s teamwork results in intimate chitchat, UI/sound design aims at kindling a brave’s spark.
After all, Trails series is about the bravest, who are meant to make a family hearthside the warmest place in the world — again and despite all the calamities.

Once upon a time, Tribes: Ascend was a fantastic multiplayer shooter. Matches were frantic, the skill ceiling was high, and the parkour-esque skiing mechanic made it unlike anything else in the market.
But Ascend was screwed from the start due to horrible decisions on the business side of things. While calling it "pay to win" wouldn't be quite accurate, it DID take a ridiculously long time to unlock even a single gun with in game currency. The result is that free-to-play progression could best be described as "glacial". The game quickly grew stale to all but the most dedicated players, the userbase plummeted after just a year or so, and before long entered the dreaded death spiral that has marked the end of many multiplayer games-- a community too small to sustain itself, too skilled for new players to join, and getting smaller all the time. Ultimately, Hi-Rez cut their losses and abandoned development to throw more resources at the much more successful SMITE, the final nail in the game's coffin.
There was a brief attempt to revive the game a few years later by smoothing out the progression system, but it was too little too late. The damage was done, the game's time in the spotlight had long since faded, and many had moved on, never to return. The game died again just a few months later, and this time it seems to be for good.
It's a damn shame. Ascend had everything going for it, but in the end, an overly stingy free-to-play model was its death knell. All that remains, aside from a small, devoted fanbase, is yet another cautionary tale for future game developers-- if you dripfeed your game's content, it needs to be steady, or you'll find players won't come back to your well.
Pay to win.

A very niche product but it has its place when paired with the Steam Link.
Pros-
+Sublte rumble feels great
+As someone with large hands who is often disappointed with controller ergonomics, it felt great to hold and use as long as the batteries are inside it for the weightier feel.
+Customizability is through the roof, especially for the trackpads, the standout feature being the ability to bind the left trackpad to a small menu of onscreen buttons for up to 16 inputs.
+Huge amount of raw inputs to be bound, up to 52 different inputs when including onscreen buttons and that's without including modifier buttons or the gyro cntrol.
+Importing user created controller configurations for official steam games and modifying them to your liking is incredibly easy, as is exporting your own
+Dual thumb typing with the trackpads is faster than using a d-pad 9/10 times
+Options for wired and wireless right out of the box
+Analog triggers and grip buttons feel fantastic
+Basically makes every game playable to some extent, even games as complicated as Torchlight, Planet Coaster and System Shock 2 are more than playable on it
Cons:
-Using the left trackpad as an emulated D-pad is a hassle to get used to and isn't even worth bothering with unless you're using the steam controller to emulate an Xbox controller
-Face buttons feel a little too cramped due to the size of the right trackpad
-No option for a concave analog stick without hardware modifications if that's your preference
-Bumper triggers feel unreasonably stiff, as does clicking down the trackpads
-Desktop controls are very hard to modify
This is a good controller for sure, but it feels very lost without a steam link or a home theater PC to back it up. Of all the games and genres I tried, there wasn't a single one i wouldn't have preferred to just use a wired 360 pad or my keyboard for. It really does feel like an all in one package, but it has no place at a desktop when you can swap between keyboard/mouse and controller easily.
Again: Very niche and feels like it needs a steam link or home theater PC, but when it has those things to back it up, it shines.

I've been using this controller as my main peripheral on my HTPC for 2 days now and I love it:
After using all of the Xbox and PS controllers gen's (yes even that bulky OG Fat Xbox controller) throughout my life and this is the first controller I actually enjoy playing shooters etc. with, as I never enjoyed looking around with a joystick.
I also did not feel there was a steep learning curve, although BPM did take (or is still taking) some time to get used to and I don't think I'll ever prefer it to default Steam. The first game I played was Portal 2, and this is a great game to get used to the controller. (Default setup is pretty good IMO, I just changed a few buttons around to my own liking.)
The design of the controller is also perfectly suited for me, it is the first controller that I find comfortable to hold with fingers on the L/R-trigger and the L/R-buttons and in this case, 2 fingers on the grip buttons. Speaking of grip buttons, my only complained about them is that there aren't enough of them! I wouldn't have mind it if they had split both grips in 2 (or more) buttons, I absolutely love them and have been using them for mouse clicks on desktop mode etc. where I like them more than the triggers.
As I've been using this controller for a few days I can't say much about the build quality yet, but it doesn't feel cheap to me. Some say its feels flimsy and light, but it actually weights about a tad more then my wireless XB360 controllers. (I did not weigh all the other controllers.) Also, it doesn't squeak or anything when putting (excessive) force on any of the parts.
My only actual dislike is that it is a NOISY controller, its not one I could use next to my sleeping GF. The haptics are very clearly audible even on low and the buttons have very loud clicks to them. As a comparison: The clicks of gaming mice, the RAT 7 and the G502, seem quiet next to this beauty.

A lot of people seem to gloss over the fact that it has a gyroscope, thus making it absolutely perfect for casual FPS games. By setting the gyroscope to a low setting, you can use it to make slight aim adjustments effortlessly, while still being capable of general aiming using the touchpad. I absolutely recommend this controller for the gyroscope feature alone. The touchpads can be a bit hit-or-miss, but I love the configurability and versatility that this controller offers. I recommend waiting for a sale if you're on the fence. It's definitely worth trying.

This is hands down the best tower defense game I've ever played and I played a lot those games ever since StarCraft Brood War UMS TDs. It's very unique, has a great replayability, decent challenge and most importantly - fun gameplay.
You're playing as space trucker and your day to day duties will be (guess what) delivering cargo from point A to point B, but that's not as simple as seems at first. On your runs you'll be fighting dozens of pirate ships, various space monsters and even unofficial AI competitors and on top of that - cargo could also be a problem or even a threat to your own ship. This is where puzzle-like element kicks in: you gotta build your ship always in a specific way to deliver goods fast and safe, and those "goods" will often have some quirks to them, some will even try to sabotage your runs by damaging your ship, teleporting into inconvenient places or spawning useless junk all over the ship limiting your defense options. And this is why this game has tremendous replayability: you can experiment for hours with ship layouts until you build a perfect one (you can even develop ships specialized on delivering certain types of cargo), there're dozens of various ship configs and a few fully customizable too. The game features 4 solar systems with a bunch of planets in each of them which interconnected by routs. Every delivery route has a different type and amount of enemies which attacks you from random sides (yes, a certain degree or RNG persists, but it wouldn't be fun without it), only boss ships/monsters have a fixated spawn point. On top of all that game looks amazing with colorful graphics and impactful explosions, also features a great atmospheric soundtrack, comical characters from the campaign and an online mode.
Speaking of which. Online in this game is a subtle feature, it's not forced (game has an offline mode as well) and in my opinion it does everything right. It basically let's other players to help you transfer you materials from one planet to another
while benefiting from it since for every material you transport via player contract you get a random prize and it could be money, another material or even a new ship layout in rare cases. You can also sell excessive amount of resources to other players for the custom amount of money. I heard there were sever outrages but as you can see I played quite a lot and I honestly never had a single issue regarding online mode on both servers.
Lastly I want to address two main complaints about this game. First one is "grinding". Honestly? You can get the necessary things just by doing campaign missions and side missions, yes, if you want some extra modules or cells you'll have to grind for them, but no one forces you to droningly do it with just one ship, experiment and you'll have your fun even while doing monotonous tasks. Secondly: Active Pause. Yes, there's none and I hope will never be. Why? Can you imagine an active pause button in, say, StarCraft? You could buy everything in the buildings, order every upgrade, use every unit ability, spend all your resources and give a command to every unit, watch events unfold and pause again. Would it be fun? Well, for a few people I guess it would, but with just a little common sense you can clearly realize that it's basically a god mode. And Space Run doesn't even have that degree of difficulty which SC has, all you have to do is provide defenses for your ship in real time, which is the core gameplay by the way, there's not really that much management involved and the game also supplements you with all necessary hotkeys and shortcuts for every structure. Active pause in this instance will just break the game, there will be zero challenge and no points to play. But people will obviously rather complain than learn, nothing unusual.
As a closing comment I want to thank developers for this brilliant game (which is absolutely bug-free by the way), it was really enjoyable for me and I hope will be for many others.

This Space Run sequel isn't quite as good in my eyes, but it's still a nice game for the most part.  It feels a lot more grindy and less intuitive.  The UI is more confusing in the sequel.  I also do not appreciate the cargo system since I'm given little chance to carry my cargo with me to my next story mission unless I want to fail a run.  That ends up making this game more of a hassle to play because I have to run between planets over and over again just to micro-manage my upgrade components.  That said, the multiplayer features are kinda nice, and I enjoy returning to this franchise.  I wouldn't pay full price for this, but definitely get this game during a sale if you like creative tower defense games.

It is exceptionally pretty, and fairly well paced. It's a "walking simulator," with all the pratfalls of that genre. Games like this live or die on their atmosphere and the strength of the story that is revealed. Leviathan has the atmosphere. It does not have the story. What it does have is a massive boner for relativism and post-modernism. It's pretty sure that this is all SUPER DEEP, and so most of the narration explores these themes, using lots of big words and slightly archaic sentence construction. Because we're so sophisticated, oh yes.
The underlying plot, which exists only in notes pinned on walls, is (as I understand it) a slight variation on those abominable Divergent books. Post-acopolalypse, survivors are split into camps based on philosophy, the camps all fight. "Divergents" are, in this case, called Minotaurs. So there's lots of statues of Minotaurs. Did I lose you? Like I said, it's very deep.
If you can stand the undergrad-philosophizing and painful speed of walking, it's not a bad use of an hour or two, but I just can't recommend it.
Pages and pages of portentous notes on the walls. Bogged-down, unclear narration. Despite the promise of beautiful scenery, we were alienated by the heavy, inept storytelling and abandoned the game.

Giving this game a fair shake: while I found it interesting, it definitely wont fill everyone's cup with great expectations, and ultimately it is so niche that I have to down-rate it.
The graphics in this game are nicely done, but they aren't always perfect. In some areas I found the lighting odd/extreme. Windows did not always match up with incoming light, and the closer I looked at certain areas of detail, the easier it was to see that not everything was quite "perfect." However, it is still an incredible game to walk through, but it also wasn't exactly something my system felt even remotely taxed to run. I personally wasn't "hovering over F12."
Story wise this game is highly philosophical and if you're not familiar with certain biblical stories, and even a few ancient greek mythologies, the concept behind this game is probably going to have a hard time sticking with you. Given that, it wasn't badly interpretted, and there is further/deeper meaning behind the story that I feel most (almost all) don't actually preceive.
Building on that, my personal /critique/ of the game is that it is not delivered in a form that the player can unify their experiences with the narrator--in a fashion that keeps them driven on the same path--through a desire to understand, and grow, within the exploration of the Leviathan in order to walk them coherently along the structured philosophy of the game and its totality. The game lacks an event or trigger to bring them into the world more cohesively in such a way as to encourage their aimless wanderings and  intellectualization; this may inherently be a downside to the nature of a walking-simulator style game and its inept ability to do more than mosey.
Overall I think it is unfortunate that the deeper concepts are missed, and likely will never be realized if the indie group doesn't manage to continue in their second and third games that Leviathan is supposed to be a triology from. The walking-simulator aspect of it could have done with a faster "run" option to help facilitate a more effecient experience for those who desire it (I know I wanted to double the pace often). Combined with good, but not (in my opinion) stunning visuals, there isn't really anything that immediately brings me to recommend this game.

Really wanted to like this game - an unassuming little horror/mystery point-and-clicker (a MystLike point-and-clicker- so static screens, first-person perspective, as opposed to a LucasLike or KingsQuestLike or whatever).
For a while, I was into it. Maybe not the greatest game ever, but it had an atmosphere and a good sense of the unknown about it, so hey. I could forgive having to click five times to get from a doorway to an object visible from the "doorway entrance" slide, but inaccessible unless you moved forward, turned right, moved forward, turned right, moved forward again. I could even forgive occasional forays into outright pixel-hunting (spoiler alert: the vent grate, after you remove it, is reduced to about 15 pixels at the very top of the frame). Whatever.
There was even a fun little math puzzle!
But then the puzzles veered into the illogical, nonsensical, and downright irritating.
At one point a random door suddenly unlocks when you view a certain completely unrelated event across the map - you have no way of knowing or reason to suspect that this particular door is now accessible. There's no in-universe "reason" for it. It just magically unlocked. Magical door-unlocking gremlins - oooOOooOOoOooOoooh, scarrRrrRrrRrrryyyy!
One particular puzzle requires following an insane series of left/right/straight directions along a map - switching between the directions and the map is a multi-click process. Screenshot ahoy.
When looking through security camera footage at one point, you need to search for the "<place> #" camera - not "xx" (the in-universe room reference number when looking at a map of the entire facility) or "<place> 0#" (with a leading zero, as it's labelled on the in-game map). You also have to deduce that "hh:mm" is referring to 24-hour time notation, rather than the 12-hour time we're all used to, despite 12-hour time being used everywhere else in the game text. Because inputting the required fields is a cumbersome process (accompanied by a slight delay after each "guess"), trial-and-error at this point is not encouraged, and it's easy enough to put "Cell 07" instead of "Cell 7", get the standard "nope" result, assume that you were barking up the wrong tree, and wander around aimlessly wondering what clue you're missing.
But worst of all is the in-game Google.
See, there's an in-game computer with a "web search", but pretty much everything you enter returns zero results - the name of a central organization, the names of leading characters within that location's organization, hell, the name of the large city near which the game takes place returns "0 results". But you need to search for a particular place of business (mentioned in passing) into the web search and, huh, all of a sudden there's a result!
Then - as if this wasn't enough! - you need to know to put a person's nickname - not their first name, not their last name, not their first name and last name and nickname, but just the nickname - into the web search so the computer will vomit up some more puzzle-solutions.
Look, I respect that the game doesn't have a giant pink elephant holding a neon "TRY SEARCHING FOR THE NAME OF THE HOTEL!!" sign next to the computer that does web searches, and I understand the developer may not have the time or patience to create an entire exhaustive fake web history for every character, including social media accounts, press release mentions, their old high school site that mentions them by name in a photo caption, and of course the social media accounts / press releases / high schools of their facebook friends, but my capacity for trial-and-error is a finite resource, and seeing central themes within the game return the exact same "0 results" page does nothing to replenish that resource. A bit of backstory and filler text for major characters or concepts within the game-universe would go a long way to ensuring that, eventually, I'll feel compelled to put "Fargo Lane Hotel" into the search and advance the plot. Failing that, at the very least, have me find a memo where someone says "hey, I forgot the address of that hotel" and the other person writes "do your own web search" or something, because I've run numerous complex statistical analyses and it turns out that in the current state of affairs there's precisely a 0% chance of me ever deciding to type that into the search box.
Anyway, my reward for finding a walkthrough and following the walkthrough to solve the above idiotic puzzle was a five-minute monologue delivered by a voice actress who honestly, truly sounds like she's trying extremely, incredibly hard to not sound wooden but unfortunately ends up sounding wooden AND mentally challenged instead, accompanied by buggy subtitles that occasionally glitched out ("<first line of text> <second line of text> <voiceover keeps playing, subtitles remain on the second line of text> <fourth line of text>") and hence kept me from just muting the bad voice actress.
At that point, it's Seinfeld wincing, putting his hands up, and getting out of his seat. The puzzles really are unsolvable without the walkthrough, and the game mechanics - the clicking, the pixel-sweeping, and of course the awful awful voice acting - only serve to detract from the plot. The sum enjoyment of "<game> + <walkthrough>" is less than "<walkthrough>", so I'll just close the game and continue reading the walkthrough.
Not the worst point-and-click MystLike I've played (that award still goes to the stunningly awful "Real Horror Stories Ultimate Edition"), but not worth paying for either, and certainly not worth paying $8 for. Even at its lowest-ever sale price ($1.59 at the time of this review), it's probably a "meh", and if you're not into trading cards then that "meh" would be a "nah". Just read the walkthrough.

Corrosion: Cold Winter Waiting is an immersive mystery horror point and click adventure game that you
to play. You play as a sheriff who is investigating what happened to Cold Winter Farm. You get trapped by a snowstorm in a basement. You quickly discover that you’re in a secret underground lab, and so the adventure begins.
The game basically consists on you trying to find out what the hell happened there. You’ll get information through computer archives, the Internet, personal journals, etc. It mostly consists of lore: about what happened before, à la Dark Souls. The execution of this form of storytelling is absolutely phenomenal. I was asking myself so many questions as I uncovered more and more. “Who were these people?", "What were they trying to do? Why?", "Are they completely insane?", "Is this just another crazy cult, or are they onto something?”. The questions in my head didn't stop bubbling up. The realistic tone works incredibly well, as l felt like this place actually exists, like I was actually there trying to piece it all together. I felt horrified, disgusted and appalled as I got a clearer picture about this organization, but that didn't stop me at all. The more I fed on information, the hungrier I got for
. It pulled me in and I couldn't resist. I felt like I
to know exactly what the hell was going on. I felt a bit disgusted with myself as I realized that I was actually enjoying the horror, dysfunction and suffering that I was witnessing on these people. I personally couldn’t stop playing. I beat it in one single 9-hour-long sitting.
As you’re reading this, you’re probably thinking: “This game resembles a history class: You’re just reading facts about something that happened a while ago. You’re just a historian who is only feeding his curiosity on something that already concluded. You take no part on it, and you’re completely free of danger.” No worries, because that could not be further from the truth. I got a constant feeling of dread, like you’re being watched at all times. Some events will happen that will make you wonder: “What was that?“, “Did that door just close by itself?“, “Is it automated, or is there someone else in this place?“, “This thing was in a different position when I left this room…” The feeling greatly resembles what you feel when you’re reading a Lovecraft novel, or when you hear an odd noise at night: “Was it the wind, or is someone breaking into my house?” Of course, I’ll have to stop writing about this as I feel I’m about to tread onto spoilers…
The ambient music amplifies those feelings of dread greatly. I don’t have much to say about it, other than it fits perfectly with the game, and does an excellent job at pulling you into the game’s depressing world.
All in all, it’s a great Lovecraftian (sort of) horror story that deserves your attention. Seriously, why is this game not popular?
Anyway, this is a game after all, so let’s talk a bit about the game aspects of it:
The way you interact with the world is pretty standard: The mouse pointer icon will indicate that you can click on something to interact with it. You click on the edges of the screen to navigate. You can pick up things that fill your inventory. You’ll sometimes need to combine certain items to progress. You also interact with computers by typing with your keyboard. One con about the game is that there are literally NO keyboard controls, except when you’re using computers.
You’ll have to use the mouse at all times. Navigating the world with WASD would have been a much appreciated option. Inventory hotkeys would have been nice, too. It’s a shame that the game wastes the chance to have the keyboard as an input option.
The gameplay consists of you solving puzzles, basically. It’s a fairly open map, where you need to solve the next puzzle to unlock a door to progress to the next area, or similar stuff like that. Some puzzles were satisfyingly hard for me. I had a notepad to write stuff on at all times, and I also took pictures about relevant stuff for future reference. It was mentally stimulating. I think that the difficulty level was perfect.
Sadly, it has those “Monkey Island” moments, as I call them: Sometimes the solution to a puzzle won’t be intuitive at all. Sometimes you’ll need to do a crazy, unintuitive, oddly specific item combination to progress. Or sometimes you’ll have to input a REALLY specific set of data to a computer that you had no way of figuring out. I recall a time where you needed to input the exact time in which something happened: (Spoilers)
. I had to use a guide for these segments.
The inventory interface isn’t too pretty. It gets really messy when you get a crap load of items, and navigating through them is a slow and sometimes frustrating process. The interface consists of one row of items that can be scrolled, one item at a time, with a timer that limits the scrolling speed (What I mean by that is that after you click the arrow to scroll, you have to wait a certain amount of time to scroll again. If you click again before that amount of time passes, nothing will happen). These might be engine limitations, I’m not sure. One idea would be to have 2 extra arrows that scroll one entire tab of items at a time. Or maybe displaying more than 1 row of items at a time. Of course, keyboard controls would have helped a lot here.
The movement isn’t smooth either, sometimes. At times, you’ll need to do something like 5 units of movement to get somewhere right beside you. But at 90% of the time, the movement feels just right. Again, I wouldn’t have any complaints about it if you could move with the keyboard.
The environments are breathtakingly realistic. They give a creepy, claustrophobic and gritty vibe, reminiscent of the Resident Evil pre-rendered backgrounds (The REAL Resident Evil’s (1 to 3, and especially REmaster). You really feel like you’re there. It’s really hard to believe for me that it was all made by one guy, as I understand it.
For the people who are game developers (like me), or are just interested in the process, the game was made in the Wintermute Engine, and the beautiful and photorealistic environments were modelled and rendered in TrueSpace 6.6.
To Viperante: Thank you so much for creating this amazing game! I Hope you get the recognition you deserve in your future projects (Maybe by investing a bit more in marketing ;)). The fact that this game isn’t popular is baffling to me. You inspire me as a game developer. I can’t wait to see your future projects.

I was taken for a pretty mind-blowing 8-hour ride. The plot is quite extensive, and concludes pretty brilliantly.
It's easy to lose your bearings because of the angles they give you in each room. Sometimes you have to go "up", "left", "down", then "right" (or something like that) just before you can look at objects that are otherwise right in front of you! Because of this, it's easy to lose track of which way you're facing, and subsequently which direction you should go.
As the game progresses, you acquire an extensive inventory. There were at least 3 different instances where I could think of other perfectly reasonable ways to solve the puzzle at hand by combining different inventory objects from what was required (e.g. Item A could be combined with Item B to give the same result, but the game
that only Item B be combined with Item C for the solution, or something like that). And in many cases the solution required was ridiculous - you'd have to
that you had to use those items, otherwise you'd never logically think of it.
I kept seeing "there" being used instead of "they're", and other small but glaring linguistic errors. It got quite irritating to a point, especially when some of these errors were being made in things like in-game newspaper articles and official government docs, which one would expect to be impeccably written. The mistakes undermined the realism.
To be honest, the game was far from impressive when I first started playing it. But then as I found out more (don't worry, this happens quickly) and the story started to unravel, things got pretty intense. Add to that the superbly effective music/sound/ambient noise + sleek graphics, and I was completely immersed.
It's rare to find an adventure game that effectively manages to convey a sense of urgency. Very often you can spend as much time as you like dawdling away at any location. Not with
though. There were a few times I felt a heart-pounding need to get out of one particular location as soon as possible, because it was so unnerving! And at a certain point in the game, there's even a chase scene - that sure got my adrenaline pumping alright!
Money well spent - in terms of conveying the desired mood, atmosphere and story, this game succeeds brilliantly. Puzzles, navigation & other game details may be less than perfect, but the overall gaming experience is still pretty awesome.

Naruto Ultimate Ninja Storm 4 is a fun game. I really enjoyed my time playing it. I have played it on xbox one and pc which is why I haven't played it too much on PC as I played loads on xbox. To exact I have played 54 hours of it on xbox.
This review is not going to be in a massive amount of detail.
To start this off the game looks awesome and the combat style is super fun if you have played a previous storm game you will free right at home here.
The story follows the actual story with loads of awesome battles such as Hashirama v's Madara which is what the game starts off with. Straight away I was amazed with how awesome the combat was the battle felt great just like something out of the anime. It blew my mind when you got to the cut-scenes and how awesome they were. The best part was yet to come... The boss battle segments are simply wonderful it just made story mode so much funnier to play and it also made it more challenging.
Once you have finished the story mode you have Adventure mode to sink your teeth into which picks up after the forth great ninja war. In this mode, you actually get to move around the village. Which, if I might add looks sweet. This mode has you do a load of small missions in which you get to meet and learn more about other characters. There is also a bunch of little challenges you can do which make the mode last a little longer.
After you have either finished or had enough of the story mode is when you realise there isn't a massive amount to do after that.
You have your online mode which is fun providing you can deal with the constant move spammers. I personally didn't enjoy the online in this game. I found it far too frustrating which to be fair partially comes down to my lack of skill, but hey, I can't put all the blame on myself right?....
You then have your versus mode, which is your typical versus mode where you pick your character and you face off against whoever you have picked to face off against. You do have a tournament mode, which is a lot of fun and they also offer a survival mode which is also a lot of fun. The survival mode is where I spent the most time after beating the story. You have an endless survival mode or a bunch of preset scenarios which get super hard later on.
Overall, I really enjoyed the game the main problem being that the moveset's pretty much stayed the same. I would definitely recommend this game to anyone who has played the previous storm games or has seen the anime. That being said, you may still enjoy it if you simply like fighting game and haven't seen the anime.

If you're unsure about getting this for full price, don't get it, wait until it goes on sale.  I bought it on sale and I have had such a blast with this thing.  I've been gaming on PC for the past 7 years almost exclusively only keyboard and mouse, controllers have been lost on me for a while, so I was extremely skeptical.  Spent a solid 10 minutes after plugging this thing in (yes it has a wired feature, which I love) trying to figure everything out and it made me want to rage quit.
A controller made me want to rage quit, what a time to be alive.  Anyways, after finally figuring out some of the controls and terminology, determined to not be beaten by a controller, I started having a blast controlling my computer and games with this thing.  I'm still fine-tuning controls for this just for ONE game, but I found this extremely enjoyable to navigate my computer with from a distance, so I think the majority of my use for this thing will be like a fancy remote control for my PC, and that's okay for me because I got it on sale.  I'm still going to dable into it for gaming because it's really fun and awesome if you can find a layout that works, it makes old games feel like new, but I'm still really leary about diving into a new game with this.
I still recommend it to people because this controller is like no other, it's extremely smart and I really love the design and figuring out cool custom button combinations feels amazing.  I'm not a huge controller person and mainly use keyboard and mouse, so don't get this if you're like me, but do get it if it goes on sale, if you're comfortable with just using this as a fancy remote control with partial gameplay use, and if you're comfortable spending a good half hour learning this thing.  If you like really cool gadgets that can do fun things and are different from the rest of the competition, then you should already be getting this. It obviously has a really steep learning curve, so just be patient with it and I think you'll enjoy it.
If everything I described does not sound appealing, then obviously don't get this regardless if it's on sale.  I'm a sucker for awesome tech stuff, even if it seems like a silly fad, but I hope Valve keeps pouring support into this thing because I will continue using this for years.

I'm going to leave a positive recommendation for The Old City: Leviathan.
First:  I played it on Windows XP, and it ran fine - so if you're still an XP gamer, give it a go.
Secondly: Be aware that there's some pretty heavy (dense) philosophy that at first was off-putting to me, especially the amount of reading that wasn't making sense to me.  It seemed so over the top - but as the game progressed that became less of an issue for me and I started gathering better what was going on with the story.  The world is what is left from a literal war between ideologies/philosophies - and the narrative is one man's story of trying to make sense of it all.
The visuals, world building, and attention to detail are truly "stunning".  There is so much care put into designing the world.  So many little details.  I took alot of photos (f12) while playing.  There's not much you can interact with, but if you like exploring, this feels like a place that was lived in.
Understand that this is very much a world that you travel through - not a world that you interact with in any meaningful way beyond opening doors.  At first I was frustrated by this, but once I understood how the game worked, I was OK with it.  It's not like Gone Home or similar where you pick up items to learn about the story.  In The Old City you are an observer - a passer through.  The story is told by what you see, short snippets of spoken narrative, and by the notes you find on the wall.
Anyhow, in total I feel like this game had a considerable amount of heart and care put into it - and despite any shortcomings is well worth a playthrough if you like walking simulator type games.

I like Walking Simulators. I don't like Walking Simulators that fail to tell a cohesive story.
Let me start with the things I do like about the game:
- The art direction is beautiful, your finger will hover over F12 the entire game
- its very atmospheric
- the voice acting is rather decent
The story however is not. At no stage did I have a decent grasp of what was happening. The narrator is always spouting some vaguely mystic cerebral heady statements about truth and dreams. I had no idea if I was inside the mind of the main character or if I was exploring an actual city that this character inhabited. I additionally was unclear as to whether that distinction even mattered to begin with. I began to ask myself if the confusion was intentional. I decided that even if it was I was not having a decent experience regardless. It is shame that this 'narratively focused experiment' main take away is confusion about reality. At the end the character seemed to find some solace but I had no exposition as to why this was occurring and full disclosure I only read a few of the notes. So before you dismiss my experience for not reading the ABSURD amount of writing in this game; let me explain why reading (this volume) of notes is like I said, absurd.
When the main narrative is told through notes in something construed as an interactive narritively driven experiment to the degree that the only interaction is walking, opening doors and actually reading much more than a few essays worth of writing. MAYBE, just maybe you've chosen the wrong medium to deliver your tale.

I had some mixed feelings about The Old City: Leviathan, but luckily they were more on the positive side.
The good side of The Old City Leviathan is that it's landscapes are beautiful and immersive. It is very non-linear, and hard to explore everything. The graphics are great, and the music is good. However that's where it ended for me.
The story is way too confusing, and mostly just the narrator sprouting fancy words. The game clearly wants to give a clever story, but overused metaphors. The lighting in the game is pretty dark. While it is possible to see, it still feels a little too dark. Most of the light is orange-ish in the inside areas, which causes it to look like it's all candles even when it is other things like light bulbs. A light bulb would normally give a brighter light and make it way easier to see. Heck, I'm in my room right now. It's dark, no light coming from outside and only my ceiling light lit but it still looks brighter than the beginning area of the game which even has light from the outside coming in. And the other thing is, why are all light bulbs giving off orange light? Did they not have fluorescent light at the time? Back to the story, there is on thing the game never explains you. What are the locations you see? Yes, we know it is a dream, but what are we seeing them for? What is that small room we saw three times? Your son's room? What is that recurring room we see with the three tables and window? It's strange how the game doesn't explain these to you, or perhaps I just missed them.
As always, do watch out. As can be seen in the tags this is a walking simulator, which means that it heavily relies on walking without much interaction. Do watch out if you are not into these kinds of games.

On the upside, this game is absolutely beautiful. It switches back and forth between a HL2-inspired industrial setting littered with corpses and a Dark-Souls-inspired fantasy setting scattered with giant sleeping monsters. I honestly suspect that the developers had been halfway through developing both a HL2 clone and a Dark Souls clone when their funding ran out, and they had to cobble this game together from all the assets they'd created for both.
The game is FILLED with text; there are typewritten pages plastered to walls throughout the game, there's graffiti on the walls, there are boxes you find that contain so much text that there's a separate menu to scroll through it, and there's a rambling first-person narrator. The developers boast that there are over 30,000 words of text in the game.
This wouldn't necessarily be a downside, but most of the text is the shallow philosophical ramblings of the narrator, and the rest is overly-long and flowery exposition about the philosophies of three warring post-apocalyptic factions. None of the text is engaging, and none of it has any pertinence to what the player is doing, or contributes anything to the setting.
Ignoring the uninteresting and unrelated narrative, Leviathan is a beautiful but empty experience, like wandering through an action game in a developer mode with all of the monster spawns and puzzles turned off. There are numerous areas throughout the game that are clearly designed to be combat arenas, boss fights, and ammo caches, but are all strangely empty. I would love some day to play the HL2 clone and the Dark Souls clone that the developers clearly started out trying to make, but I can't really recommend this.
