I apologize for spoiling this, so stop reading now;
there is no 'ending'. I assume the player is tasked with finding some meaning through the largely incoherent introspection of Jonah, however, it's incredibly unsatisfying. I kind of knew, once I got near the end, that it would be like that. There just couldn't have been anything to follow that would have really "fit"... unless there was nothing /at all/.
I understand that is a valid type of storytelling, however, it really doesn't work that well in such an engaging and atmospheric world to pull the player away from the beautiful visual stimulus and environment and "leave it to them to work out"... it's just unsatisfying.

I've got 72 hours-ish on this game. I played it when it was popular, tried to keep playing it after it died and now I've come back to it. Originally I was planning on uninstalling it and was taking a final look around before I put down a game that had died, but then I realised something.
most of the players play on the Co-op casual mode. I've consistently gotten games in under 5 seconds on that game mode and I've played a number of games since I worked it out. under 5 seconds. Every time. it's not perfect, but for those that just want to get one last game in or even try to bring popularity back to loadout, it's worth a shot (that might be restricted to the north American servers but idk???)
Now for an actual review: this game is f*****g amazing. There isn't any other way to put it. I read the reviews before I originally downloaded Loadout and I still use a quote from one of them when I tell people about it:
"It's like a looney toons cartoon directed by Quentin Tarantino"
That sums up Loadout perfectly. A few good points:
-it's entirely based on skill. Yes, there are upgrades, but you need to play to get them and the worst gun in your hands
might be the best in someone else's
-It's balanced fairly well and as I've previously stated, it's based on skill. Can't use fire weapons? change to electricity.
Can't use that? try regular bullets. Bullets are failing you? You've got launchers and lasers so pick something else.
-the movement is great. It's fluid, the diving is an actual thing that well help you rather than simply be a gimick, but at
no stage does movement stop you from being able to blow someone's torso out.
-Guns. You can think of it, you can make it. Want a gun that can accurately place a mine on a corner from across the
map? boom, you can do it. Want a gun that you don't need to be accurate with to use effectively? I call mine the Death
Machine of Wild Firing. Literally the gun customisation is ♥♥♥♥ing amazing. I've seen people make sniper rifles that
shoot rockets, I've seen one donkyditch use a rocket launcher that ♥♥♥♥ed anything that was anywhere near the target.
I've seen a rocket launcher that shoots 8 rockets that rain fire filled cluster bombs when they explode. Yes, you need to
earn the parts you use to build the guns you want, but you can make it, level it and upgrade the parts. Weapons that
work to your playstyle and what you need in a weapon can work far better than a weapon that takes advantage of the
balancing issues.
-there are several more good points but I'd spend too long naming them all (the game modes? capture the flag but the
flag is a superweapon????).
A few negatives:
-The devs got bored and gve up on it. There was a single player mode released a few years ago that was pretty
interesting, but after that the devs  seem to have outright given up on it. No new updates since 2015.
-The player base is fairly small. You can still get a game, as I previously said, but you might be waiting for ages and/or be
restricted to a scertain gamemode. Also last I checked, the ranked game mode is dead (which sucks hella bad because
that gamemode was absolutely freaking amazing. Imagine every other gamemode combined and that's it). You can still
get a game though.
-I'm don't know much about hacking, but every now and again you will run into an absolute f*****g beastmode player
that's getting consistent headshots with a sniper rifle. One shot kills every time. Chances are that they're just a
beastmode player and not a hacker, but holy hell do they devastate the opposite team
Would I recommend it?
-F**k yes. It's free, it's a good game to put hours into, it's not all that taxing (I use a 4Gb 32 bit windows with really low
specs and it runs pretty ♥♥♥♥ing well) and the more people that start playing it, the better. You may have a rough time
starting out, but seriously; it's worth it if you're in for the long haul.

I loved Hatoful Boyfriend. I got every achievement, and enjoyed getting them. Some parts dragged, but overall it was incredibly enjoyable, which is why I bought Hatoful Boyfriend: Holiday Star. I'll preface the rest of the review by saying this isn't a bad game. That being said, because there was so much user interaction in the first game, I expected the same here, and was sorely disappointed. I think had I gone into Holiday Star knowing it was mostly just stories to read, I would have appreciated it more, and I'm hoping that reviews like this one can keep other people from making the mistake I did.
My pet peeve in regards to sequels to games are continuity errors, and this one definitely has a few. Nothing game-breaking, just a couple things that, if you've played through all of Hatoful Boyfriend, you'll kind of pause and go "that doesn't seem right."
For me, because this is a primarily story-based game, it doesn't have any replay value. Once you've read the stories, you're not going to get anything else out of it. It's not like there are multiple endings like in Hatoful Boyfriend; unless you forget the stories, you're never going to have a need to reread them.
All of that being said, for what it is, Hatoful Boyfriend: Holiday Star is an enjoyable game, and a fun sequel to Hatoful Boyfriend. It gives you an opportunity to interact with all of your favorite birbs again, and experience some fun and weird stories with them. If you really enjoyed Hatoful Boyfriend and if you really like visual novels, then Holiday Star is the game for you.

The first game of the Dungeons serie. Dungeons is a strategy game that takes place in, as you may have guessed, dungeons! Remember all those countless RPG's where you play the hero and battle countless monsters? Now it's time to play the other side!
In Dungeons you play as a Dark Lord. You need to build up your Dungeon in way that Heroes who enter actually have a good time. By slaying them after they enjoyed themselves you gather Soul Energy which can be used to upgrade your monsters, lord or just to make your dungeon more fancy!
The fact that you can't control any of your monsters but just your Dark Lord, makes this a tad different than your average strategy game where you control whole armies. Sadly this sometimes can also lead to a slow repetitve gameplay where at some point you'll just be busy running your lord up and down to kill heroes or do other objectives that are required.
The storyline of the campaign is not too serious and is filled with some cheesy jokes and references. Personally I adore some humor in a game so I could defintely appreciate it. The graphics are ok, its what you can expect from a game this old.
The major downside of this game is that it still has the occasional crashes, especially during a moment which should be followed by a loading screen. So remember to save your game now and then!
So if you want to try a strategy game that works different than your average game, with a not too serious attitude and some cheesy jokes you might feel like slapping someone for, then this game is defintely worth the try!

Dungeons is the first game in the 'Dungeons' series. The game's setting is strongly influenced by the popular Dungeon Keeper -series and tells the tale of the evil Dungeon Lord who has been betrayed and overthrown by his power-hungry consort. Now he seeks to rebuild his status as the supreme ruler of all Evil and take sweet and well-deserved vengeance on his betrayer.
Although the setting is influenced by Dungeon Keeper, the gameplay is entirely different. It's a sort of combination of role-playing and strategical dungeon building, where you control the Dungeon Lord throughout the underground dungeons while simultaneously having your minions digging and building different types of rooms. But the main difference to a traditional dungeon builder is that you're not necessarily supposed to slaughter the gold and XP-seeking heroes right away, unless you're low on gold. Instead, you're supposed to give the heroes what they want. The heroes come in several types: some want to disable traps, others want to fight monsters or even take a sufficient beating from the monsters, and some want to loot  weapons and armor or to read ancient magical books.  For as the heroes become satisfied, they amass soul energy, which you can then collect for yourself by  incapacitating the heroes and imprisoning them with Dungeon Lord. An interestingly cunning and devious  method to deal with troublesome do-gooders if you ask me.
To ensure that the heroes become satisfied, you must build different rooms with various gimmicks, make your dungeon interesting, and place the monsters strategically as they only spawn in the proximity of the pentagrams. You must also level the monsters in a correct manner, so that they won't be complete pushovers but also because you lose some soul energy if the hero isn't taken out by Dungeon Lord. All the while you must also ensure that the Dungeon Heart isn't destroyed and fulfill the quests given to you by higher ranking lords of Evil (the disadvantage of being overthrown is that you're at the rock-bottom of hierarchy of Evil.... for now at least.)
PROS:
+ A genuinely interesting take to the traditional dungeon building genre.
+ Various rooms with different gimmicks, along with various heroes who desire them.
+ Witty and comedic dialogue provided by the Goblin Advisor. The setting itself contains many humorous descriptions and subjects, and even some quests, such as watering the flowers of an undead.
+ Of course, you get to be the evil Dark Lord who shows the heroes who is true master.
CONS:
- The levels are somewhat repetitive.
- Mastering the micromanaging playstyle of the game may require some time before one can learn it properly. (This, of course, doesn't necessarily include everyone.)
- Requires a Kalypso account to play. (Not that big of a deal if you ask me, though. It asks hardly any information.)
VERDICT: Supposedly many people are mighty upset that the game's playstyle differs from DK so much, but I recommend to ignore the hate they leave behind. The game isn't flawless, but the flaws are relatively minor as far as I'm concerned. Overall, it's a fun alternative take on the popular dungeon-building genre, and if you love being the evil Dark Lord, dungeon-themed/dungeon building games of any type, or traditional fantasy settings in general, you shouldn't ignore it.
Start your path of darkness, fellow champions of Evil!

My decision to ultimately choose "not recommended" was a tough one. I kind of enjoyed the time I spent with this game, and found the story interesting at times. If nothing else, it inspired me with some story ideas for some tabletop horror games I run for my friends.
But in the end, a number of flaws keep me from recommending this:
1. FIrst and totally foremost, this game has
backtracking required to get anything done. There are several moments in the game where the only way to progress is to literally go room by room looking for anything at all that might have changed, without any clues as to what you're looking for or where. And outside of those specific moments, there are many more instances where you learn something new and have to
run all the way back to one of two different separate computers to look things up (all done via very, very specific typing sequences, too). It feels like artificial time-padding, and didn't really maintain the suspense or tension.
2. CONTROLS: The backtracking wouldn't be anywhere near as annoying if the game had functional keyboard controls to make moving around less tedious. But being restricted to arrow-only moving when the majority of movement in the game is "Forward, Back, Left, and Right" makes the entire back-tracking significantly more cumbersome. I've gotten used to mouse-based controls for many other games, but with this one, the lack of key controls really hurts it when so much movement-based back-tracking is required.
3. STORY: As others have complained, the voice acting is pretty weak, and there are too many weird holes in the story. Certain characters are mentioned and then never followed up on, others too heavily contrast with their text, and others make no sense at all. And to top it all off, the game just... Ends. No clarity, no epilogue, no explanation, just... Game Over, Thanks for Playing, Watch Some Credits.
Ultimately I think the game could use a story overhaul, and some enhanced controls to mitigate the tedium of backtracking. WIth those in place, I'd likely change my recommendation.

Corrosion has everything I love in adventure games: a strong atmosphere and a tough challenge (be prepared to be very attentive to details if you want to finish the adventure). Making an horror game is difficult, and hopefully Corrosion succeed it very well. The game never falls into the easy and silly jump scares, but build its atmosphere on deep psychology. If you love horror and conspiracy, the ride definitely worth it.

A sheriff, a stranger, and Cold Winter Farm. Three words from the stranger, the only three words, and three months in the saying. An insufficient answer for why he was wandering the road in the outskirts of Deacon Oaks. Sheriff Truman wants – needs – more. Cold Winter Farm and its stately home beckons.
A snowstorm, a tree fall. Trapped in a basement, a door is revealed. A door to a corridor. He can’t go back, so Sherriff Truman goes forward. What he finds he cannot have imagined.
And so begins Corrosion, a self proclaimed “dark, shocking, and fear-charged mystery horror game”.
A large part of Corrosion’s thrill is discovering what the hell is going on, with tantalising hints dropped in at a satisfying pace, leading you down that dark and terrifying path towards the inevitable truth. You’ll spend a lot of time hunting down keycards and codes to access locked areas of the lab. This does get a little repetitive, but the excitement of exploring a new area keeps you going - you’ll be dying to see what’s in next room, despite - or maybe because of - the potentially nasty things you may find.
The game is packed with journals and recordings, which fill in the story of Cold Winter Farm’s past and flesh out the characters. It’s a well-worn but trusty method of driving the narrative along, and pretty much the only option, as this is one of those games where you’re on your own 99% of the time. Of course, the occasional self-locking door and mysterious noise hints that there’s someone - or something - else inhabiting the labs, but to say any more would spoil the surprises.
Aside from tracking down keycards, you’ll have to solve the occasional brain-buster to progress through Corrosion’s plot. Puzzles are about 50/50 on logic and inventory ones and they tend to lean towards the brutal side in terms of difficulty. These aren’t brainteasers. These are migraine-inducing hard puzzles. There are moments where there isn’t a logical connection between where you are and where you need to go next. You’d expect a hint as to what to do next, perhaps one of those handy keycards for accessing another part of the lab, but three or four times I was left clueless. It was only after scouring the entire building that I discovered a previously locked door had been opened, with no warning at all. It’s a simple case of patiently covering old ground, but I could’ve done without it. With that being said, there’s a cool little maths conundrum, which I thoroughly enjoyed, and you’ll need to work out times and dates of specific events that occurred in the lab, then play back recordings using the handy security archive.
After several hours of creeping through Cold Winter Farm’s eerie corridors, I sat back and considered the key question: is Corrosion actually scary? It’s surprisingly tough to answer. “Fear-charged” is probably an apt description. Psychological horror might be another. Things don’t go "boo", and I have already said it wasn’t frightening, in the scary sense of the word. But there is fear in the game, as an emotion expressed in a variety of ways. People who were here before you were clearly fearful, and some frightening things went on. After unlocking the door to the medical lab or morgue, I hesitated before plunging inside, for fear of what I'd stumble into. Some of the contraptions I saw, including a particularly memorable chair, definitely surprised or shocked. Those with weak stomachs will also balk at some of the diary and computer entries, while the sinister music gets under your skin and creeps you out. This understanding builds, and by the time you get to the chase, all the little parts – the music, the setting, the sounds – may well have come together to produce a tension waiting to be relieved. Or run away from.
Corrosion: Cold Winter Waiting isn’t an easy game, so it ended up being a good length, and it kept me engaged and wanting to play some more. It suited a lot of my preferences, and what didn’t appeal was outweighed by what did. In a way, the theme that revolves around this game reminds me of Exmortis. It's one of the better (if not my favorite) free horror/adventure point & click that available out there.

Corrosion is a rather unusual point&click adventure game. There's a lot to praise and a lot to complain about.
The game has simple but sufficient graphics that suit its atmosphere well. Sound design and music is also fine. Voice acting is a bit problematic; the voice actors actually do not "act", they just read the lines.
Also, the game is locked at 1280x720. This may cause problems on certain displays.
This is interesting. Unlike classic third person adventure games this one plays in first person. And the way you move around reminds me of old-school dungeon crawlers - like Dungeon Master, you know? I'm not saying I want every other point&click game to play like this, but it was refreshing and it's one of the reasons I will remember this game.
But yes, the movement is a bit too clumsy. That's because you can only step forward and turn right or left. Having an option to sidestepping and walk backwards would definitely improve the control scheme.
This difficulty is brutal. Tons of items, some entirely useless, others absolutely necessary but pretty easy to miss. Several times you need to enter a date or a search term into a computer - the dates are not that hard but the search terms? The documents mention hundreds of names, things, people or events. How the hell am I supposed to know what to search for? Or do I have to try everything?
Sometimes you need to build a rather complex contraption without any hints whatsoever. No item descriptions, no goals, no info on active spots, no reactions to correct/incorrect actions, nothing. The developer expects you to think exactly the same way as he does. Or to try everything on everything. Or use a walkthrough.
I admit I'm not the most patient player in the world. But I've rarely spent so much time reading walkthroughs like I did in this game.
This is one of the highlights of the game. It's presented to you through many articles, notes and journals you find along the way. I don't want to spoil anything so I'm just going to say that it's a rich, well-written story that likes to play with your interpretation of the events.
I really enjoyed it... except for the ending. What was that supposed to be? The game just ended suddenly, leaving many thing unexplained. Ok, it's not that bad as in other games, at least you have some understanding of what was going on, but it still feels unfinished.
Overall, I can't say I had a lot of fun solving the puzzles, mostly because of their hardcore difficulty. But the mysterious atmosphere and the story are the reasons why I do not regret spending time with this game.
Some of the puzzles are tough, and the graphics leave a lot to be desired but this has a great plot.

The opening of Corrosion:  Cold Winter Waiting, in some ways, reminds me of The Blair Witch Project.  The story is set up to be a "recreation of true events," and you play as the sheriff of a small town who stumbles upon a secret laboratory far beneath a farm on the outskirts of a small town.  The game has a strong indie feel--and that just adds to its creepiness.
Corrosion is a traditional point-and-click adventure game presented in the first person, in the style as classics like Myst.  The entire game takes place in one environment, a large underground lab.  Over the course of the game, you will explore this solitary environment, solve puzzles, and read journals of the labs former occupants.  As you do, you will slowly discover the lab's true purpose and the events that occurred prior to your arrival.
Graphically, the game falls into the "indie" category.  And in that category, it looks good.  The environments are suitably creepy, and the game oozes atmosphere.
The game's music is fantastic and really sets the tone for the environment.
Where the game really shines, however, is its puzzles.  This is not an easy game.  In a modern industry plagued by simplicity, I found this to be a welcome change of pace.  While the puzzles are a challenge, they also make perfect sense.  The game's sense of progression is entirely logical, in a way I seldom see in adventures.  Every item that you use has a logical purpose.  Every step you must take toward the completion of the game makes sense, and the layout of the maze-like environment complements the steps you must take--you are never too far from where you need to go next.
As for the game's plot...well, I won't spoil anything here.  But I will say that it is incredibly dark, and things may not be quite what they first seem.  The story is well-written and has a nice psychological element that is missing in many horror games.  You won't experience any "jump moments," but I appreciate that, as I find those to be a cheap way of scaring the player.
The game isn't perfect, of course--no game is.  The interface is pretty bare-bones, the voice acting is somewhat amateurish at times, and the game lacks a climactic ending.  Despite these downsides, however, the game is still definitely worth playing.  For me, story is what matters most in games, and in that way, Corrosion succeeds wonderfully.
Overall, I found Corrosion:  Cold Winter Waiting to be a fantastic and suitably creepy adventure.

I've never played a proper walking simulator before playing this one and I think the kind of game it is is actually very interesting and could be a great medium for storytelling and philosophical thought provoking and such. This game however just doesn't quite acheive it. It seems to be loosely based on the biblical story of Jonah and the Whale which is a fantastic story with wonderful imagery; great stuff to base this kind of game on. My problem however, is that there is basically no plot, what the protagonist says is usually pretty poetic babble with a loose basis in actually very interesting philosophy.
The "plot" is more like an idea for a post apocalyptic world order based on three opposing philosophical doctrines: extreme  religion (there is no truth but God), extreme atheism (there is no God but truth) and extreme agnosticism (there is no truth, period). These all have their justifications which you explore by reading the various posters and book pages scattered everywhere.
My biggest problem however, was the actual gameplay; you have no way of knowing whether you will progress to the next level if you open a door. That means that you can't be sure you've explored everywhere before moving on which means its almost inevitable that you do not have the complete story (not that there's much coherant progression anyway). What this means is that I was perpetually in the dark about what was really going on, who I was, where I was gong or why and where everyone else was.
The most impressive scene was the last part where you enter the whale but instead of reaching some new place that might give you some indication of what it was all for, you end up where you started. Perhaps its all an elaborate metaphor for the spiritual journey of Jonah but really, I'd have preferred more guidance for that.
You can collect secret stashes of documents written by another character you never see "Solomon", but when I saw how long they were I did not want to read them. So the only vaguely interesting part of the actual gameplay (I love finding secrets and collectibles) became completely undesirable.
Since the pictures looked so pretty (and the game is pretty; the light is beautifully rendered and some of the landscapes are stunningly surreal) I was quite dissappointed in the lack of variety in the environments (but maybe I'm demanding a bit too much from the developers here).
Generally, I'm sad to say, I was disappointed in the game.

Video Review:
Dungeons is a mixture of a lot of different genres. You have some strategy, some tower defense aspects, and even RPG elements. When it was released it was a highly anticipated un-official followup to the Dungeon Keeper series. That is not what it turned out to be. Though of course since this is not Dungeon Keeper, we should not be expecting it to be that and should speak of its own merits. So, does Dungeons stand out as a game worth your time?
To start, you have two main ways you’ll be playing the game. You’ll either follow through the narrative-driven campaign where you play as a dungeon lord whose evil girlfriend Calypso betrays him and steals the underworld from him; or you’ll play in a sandbox map of your choosing with any game mode preference you want (or just sandbox game mode to create your own dungeon at your leisure). The main goals in gameplay are to earn gold from heroes that invade your dungeon, earn prestige by decorating your dungeon, and earn soul energy by killing heroes that find themselves highly satisfied from the experience of raiding your dungeon. The campaign brings you from mission to mission and gives you a different premise or goal in each one to differentiate it from the random game modes.
The story is decent and the campaign really just ends up being used more to teach you how to play the game and then challenges your knowledge of the mechanics you just learned every few missions. The biggest problem with it lies in that you need to focus on completing challenges in every mission in order to have enough skillpoints for your overlord not to get his♥♥♥♥♥kicked in the following mission. If you don’t complete challenges for that then you’ll have to grind the xp out by staying on the previous mission longer. This makes the campaign uninteresting and boring after you play enough of it.
The gameplay itself is fun in itself. You can open gates to let heroes invade your dungeon and then you need to place monsters, gold, armories, libraries, and etc around to make them happy. Then you need to either have some sort of trap prepared to kill the heroes before they escape or go kill them yourself to harvest their soul energy. Soul energy allows you to make numerous upgrades to your dungeon and increase your own power. It’s a bit of an annoying concept but it helps provide enough to do. Summoning minions relies on a pop cap that’s influenced by how many monster dens are in your area of influence. The types you can summon relies on what dens you own. You place them around by leaving a pentagram of their image somewhere inside your zone of control. This will summon a specific amount and respawn them every few minutes after being killed by heroes. The population caps are unfortunately very restrictive and usually make it so that to properly rule your dungeon you can’t just rely on strategical placement. You’re usually forced to go fight the heroes yourself as well to make up for what your minions can’t do. That’s not exactly what I was hoping for from a dungeon management game.
The graphics certainly haven’t aged well since the game released, but that’s not my main gripe. My main gripe is that the graphics are what they are, but the game still manages to only really give about 22fps that I’ve found regardless of your settings. I tested this on two PCs. An old one running AMD and a new one running Intel and Nvidia. Neither could even hit a high of 30fps. Seeing as the game is played in an overheard strategic perspective you could argue that’s not a big deal. Although since the game is in real time and requires quick response times you could argue that’s a huge problem.
The audio itself is decent though the default sound mixing makes no sense and makes it so that the intro title music is leagues louder than the actual in-game music. So prepare to deafen your eardrums upon first launching the game.
Overall Dungeons is not at all what you’d expect based off of the store page. It’s unfortunately disappointing. It makes a lot of sense why I was able to pick the game up for $1 on sale. Six years old or not, most games should not be $1 at this point unless they’re bad. And Dungeons? It’s bad. It’s not bad because of bugs or bad design choices though. It’s bad because it’s limiting, boring, and repetitive. Moreso if you choose not to grind out the challenges in story mode to level up your overlord properly. Was it worth the $1 i paid? Probably. But this is not sold round the clock at $1.
Dungeons gets a 4/10. It’s just below average. It could have been fun, but it’s not. I plan on checking out the future titles in the series and hopefully they stand better on their own Dungeons does.

No Dungeons isn't Dungeon Keeper and it should be reviewed based on its own merits and not because it is not the game people wanted it to be. You have to create dungeons that amuse visiting heroes and then kill them once they are fat with soul energy which accumalates faster the more "fun" and interesting your dungeon is. Some heroes have different needs. Some like to be hurt by monsters, mages like to find libraries wth knowledge, warrior want to happen upon an armory and thieves want love undoing traps. It is fun expanding your dungeons and adding new gimmics like treasures, monsters and decorations. Speaking of decorations, the more you have, the more prestige you have which unlocks more gimmics to place in your dungeon and increases your overall power. The campaign is fun. Each levels tasks you with creating a new dungeon along with a main objective and other optional objectives along the way. Your dungon lord has attributes and even a skill tree. So you grow in power as the game progresses. The game also offers a fun sandbox mode which allows you to set your own goals and start a dungeon from "scratch". Dungeons is an excellent game when appreciated for what it actually is. It is no Dungeon Keeper and that is ok.

The player will take on the role of Sheriff Alex Truman, who winds up getting trapped in an underground lab. Although the store page says a basement, it really is more of a lab; equipped with a morgue, sleeping quarters and many places for the player to explore. The story itself is solid, although for the first few hours of the game it will be shrouded in mystery. You will slowly unveil it as you progress, and the ending has a surprising turn that will leave you wondering.
While there is really no linear way to play the game, in order to progress you will be required to trigger certain events by finding, crafting or viewing certain objects. I will go ahead and admit fully that I used a guide, and while doing so I still clocked in at almost 5 played hours. Without the use of a guide, this game could take upwards to 10 hours to complete, depending on your competence regarding hardened point and click adventures like Myst and Dark Fall. Make no mistake, this is no casual point and click.
My only gripe with Corrosion: Cold Winter Waiting is that it isn't grittier. There are very few sections that include blood or gore, and there is no horror to speak of. Sure, the story once you reveal it in its entirety is horrific, but quite honestly I would classify this title under suspense rather than horror. This isn't a huge issue though, as the story and gameplay are both compelling enough to hold the interest of the player. Once I started playing this and uncovering the truth of what happened, I couldn't put the game down.
The game is worth its asking price for any point and click fan; especially those who are looking to venture away from the current casual industry standard. If you can get it on sale, that's an even bigger bonus, but don't hold out for one... it's rare that a $10 point and click will last for more than two hours. With this game. you get a minimum of 4 hours if you're using a guide for $8.79 CAD.

Without question, this is a game you should play if you are in to point/click adventures and an immersive storyline.
Well worth the time, Corrosion is extremely well written with a storyline that is so compelling that I actually found it frustrating that I couldn't solve the puzzles fast enough.  That's rare for me -- hell, I played World of Warcraft for seven years and I still couldn't tell you any of the silly backstory that Blizzard concocted.
The plot of the game is GENUINE psychological horror as you are charged with investigating just exactly what the hell happened at this facility.  I won't spoil the game for you by disclosing any of the story line.  Truly, I saw the twists coming but I didn't care, it was compelling and a wonderful distraction from life.
The game is short but the puzzles can be extremely complex.  Many solutions, though not intuitive given many of the mystery games you have played before, take some creative, out-of-the-box thinking.  In retrospect the solutions are pretty obvious if you pay attention and if you think about it.  But you'll have to concentrate and pay attention to details.
Graphics are good, sounds are good -- I enjoyed the computer "interface" as you "connect" to the Net.  If you aren't a fan of point-and-click adventures you ain't gonna like the graphics or sound on this.  It's a product that does its engine, Wintermute, a great service.  Especially considering it's open source.
Replay value is, obviously, low.  If you go back and read fiction novels two or three times, you might find yourself doing that with this game as well.  Who knows, in a couple of years I might want to experience the Cold Water experiment again.
Heartily recommended, worth the time and the money.  One of the few times I've felt so positive about recommending a game.

The Good:
I really, really enjoyed the story of this game. It was engaging, mysterious, and very well put together. A lot of games like this leave lots of holes, or leave you completely hanging at the end so that you have no idea what was happening - but this game has a great pace of releasing information to you. You'll slowly understand more and more until, near the end, you realize the truth. And when you do, it's extremely satisfying. I genuinely enjoyed exploring every aspect of this world and learning about the game - and I think the story is much stronger than the average game. For this reason, I highly recommend playing this game.
The Bad:
The controls are completely wonky, especially at first when you're trying to get used to it. It's kind of hard to navigate and the interface is not exactly user friendly. As an example, there are rooms in which you have to move to the back and then return to the front on the other side in order to get to something by the door - which is a lot of clicks that really just shouldn't be there. It's very easy to become disoriented and confused in attempting to navigate, and some hidden objects are very finicky and require you to be on a certain exact spot in order to interact with them.
The Very Bad:
This game is impossible without a walkthrough. Like, the puzzles are completely absurd. There were at least 3 parts where the things you have to do and find are so ludicrous that I felt like I was building a Rube Goldberg machine. Honestly, the story is so good that getting through these is worth it. But I do recommend a walkthrough, which you'll end up using more often than not. I honestly have no idea how the walkthrough writers managed to figure this stuff out because there's simply no way you would know some of the things that the game expects you to know.
For example: entering precise phrases into a fake google search (including proper capitalization) without being prompted (maybe if I were psychic this wouldn't be a problem), clicking on a random screw hiding on a random table that doesn't even highlight when you hover over it, building contraptions that honestly don't really make sense and are unprompted, returning to random rooms and finding that something very small has changed, and solving very tedious puzzles that take more work than they're worth.
I'm generally pretty good at these kinds of games and usually try very hard not to use a walkthrough, but this was the most ridiculously difficult one I've ever encountered.
--
Anyway, all in all I think the story is so good that the game is absolutely worth it. Just sit down with a walkthrough and don't hesitate to look things up if you get stuck. You probably won't figure it out alone, so no use fretting over it.

So, I put in about over 140 hours into this game, and also did a second playthrough. As a guy who played the original trilogy (this includes the 3rd and final installment which happened to have been a dungeon crawler more than a JRPG), I think I can give a pretty well rounded review of the game mechanics as compared to the previous games, the story, the characters and etc.
1) So, let's talk about the game mechanics. It follows the same basic premise of the battle system found in Trails of the Sky, except it's a bit more robust. They've added linked attacks which weren't present in the original trilogy, as well as more robust magic system (which is nice). So, I definitely enjoyed the upgrade battle system a lot.
What really bored me was the school setting, because you're pretty much boxed into the main town Trista. You're also forced to interact with the same characters, same NPCs and same environments over and over and over - and it can get rather dull and redundant at times. I also didn't like the quizzes sprinkled throughout the game. I don't like to be quizzed about a game's lore. That annoys me.
2) Now, let's talk about the graphics and environments. Well... The graphics are a bit better than the TotS trilogy, but of course, it's a port from a PSP game (I hear it's also on the PS3), so the graphics aren't exactly going to wow you. They did add a nice distance blur effect, which adds dimension to the environments, but that's about it. Many of the characters (or all of them) have very low poly counts, so you'll notice they look very blocky - especially up close.
Unlike the previous games (I really should just say chapter one and chapter two of TotS), there's not a lot of environment to explore. You're first introduced to a town called Trista, but after you've explored everything about that town, you're kinda forced to get familiar with that town all the way up to the very end. Of course you visit other towns, but only small selected areas of those towns, and even then, when going to towns like Heimdallr, there are districts you can go to, but some districts are really very very linear, and you can only travel so far. It's not like the previous games where you could walk from one town to the other. When you go to a town, you're forced to finish off a list of quests before you can go off to the next one. Someone could argue that it was kinda the same way with chapter one and two of TotS, but at least I could walk from one town to the next without having to watch a cut scene each and every single time I traveled to a town.
3) How about the story and character development? Well, many of us (I'm sure) enjoy watching anime, and I'm no exception. This game follows behind the typical school setting of most anime out there. So, in regard to the setting in which the game takes place, it's very cliched. The story, of course, follows behind a kid named Rean Schwarzer who goes to a prestigious military academy. From there, he goes through field studies and gets thrust into various circumstances dealing with terrorists, rebellions and eventually a
. (I'm trying not to spoil anything).
People say the story is great, but I think it's pretty meh - at least up until the very last chapter. Then the game turns on its head and becomes one of the best moments I've played through. I think that may have a lot to do with the pacing. The story goes very very slow. In this game, it really just feels like they're preparing you for the meat and potatoes in ToCS II & III. So, in other words, it feels like a prequel of sorts until you play the _actual_ game and jump into the main crux of the story.
The game does make many references to the previous trilogy. It'll also bring up names and titles of characters from the previous game, and if you haven't played those games, you will be completely lost. I.E. The Enforcers or who Cassius Bright is. I have to admit, after playing through the previous trilogy, seeing "Olivert" playing his role as a prince did seem rather awkward (play the previous games to understand why).
The characters themselves are actually interesting, and each one has their own personality quirks. The dialog between them is quite fluid, but there are times when they discuss things unrelated to the main story that becomes rather boring. Often times I wondered what some of the dialog had to do with even developing their characters, but I digress.
4) So, here is my final verdict. It's a real good game and worth the purchase. Not a perfect game, mind you, but it's a solid JRPG and I can't wait until the sequel is available on Steam.

I wish there was a neutral thumb for steam reviews, because I mostly enjoyed (well in that way you "enjoy" horror anyway) this game, but it's definitely not for everyone.  The game is in a "slideshow" style and you navigate by clicking to move to different views. If you're not used to that type of game it might be a bit irritating that you have to sidle up to some items in just the right way to interact with them, and there's no free looking. You are going to be doing a LOT of clicking in this game. The game is set in a single location but it's surprisingly large, and you'll be doing a lot of backtracking as you acquire items and keys that can be used in previous areas. Additionally there's a puzzle involving a safe combination where you have to click once for every tick that the knob turns, which was kind of ridiculous.
The voice acting is passable. Nothing super memorable but not making you wish the game wasn't voiced at all. I was impressed to see afterward that the game only has two voice actors to cover 6 or so characters. There are only a few instances of voice acting in the game (from listening to recordings) and you will be doing a LOT of reading. The story was pretty well-written and I was interested until the end. (YMMV on the actual ending, which was kind of far-fetched and weird, but I liked it)
There aren't really any jump scares in this game and the story is much more of a "slow burn" horror where a lot of things are left to your imagination, which was very effective. If you don't like blood though this is probably not the game for you.
My chief complaint is really that you are going to be wandering around aimlessly a lot if you don't use a walkthrough, because some things happen at very specific times and there's no real indication that they happened aside from checking every room once you're not sure what to do. Some of the puzzles themselves are quite complex but overall they make sense and are enjoyable, but sometimes things just happen in a way that you as the player can't predict (eg. you read an article in one room and a door is unlocked in another room). Also there are a few sequences where you need to make 'internet searches' on computers in-game and if you don't use the exact phrase the dev intended then nothing will come up (eg. an article about a pharmaceutical company developing a new drug can be found by searching the name of the company but not by searching the name of the drug even though it's in the article)
Overall though well-done, one of the better indie horror games on steam.

Tries to be a space game. Fails. Is actually a tower defence game. Because it's 2017 and idiots pretending to be programmers are trying to stay relevant by putting worthless games from a long dead genre into otherwise decent Humble Bundles.

A bad tower defense game can be characterized by any given level only having one valid solution or arrangement of resources.  Space Run on the other hand, has so many viable strategies for a given run that it's actually rather daunting.  It's a good problem to have.
Many people are complaining about how the multiplayer hauling feels forced or tacked on, but I really rather like it. Opting to assign extra spaces to cargo lets you tailor the difficulty to suit your needs, which is nice.  You don't really even get punished for losing multiplayer cargo either, so it's largely risk free.
I'm never a fan of 'always online' single player games but I've never gotten disconnected for any reason, and there is an 'Offline Mode' with all the multiplayer content cut, so that hardly feels like a reason to leave a negative review.
It's certainly not a perfect game, but it's still really good, and hands down better than the original (which I also enjoyed)

I posted this on my tumblr months ago, and it may be more of a conspiracy theory than a review, but here it is anyway.  ~*~*~*~SPOILER ALERT!~*~*~**~  (I probably wouldn't read this if you haven't played the game yet, but if you haven't, please know that I would definitely recommend it for all the feels.)
SO I’ve been done with Dandelion - Wishes Brought to You - for a number of months.  Once I had finished all routes and unlocked the “true ending”, my mind was BLOWN.  For days and days afterward, my head was absolutely consumed with only thoughts of the Wizard, swimming with all sorts of thoughts, and it wasn’t until now that I think I have found a platform on which to share said thoughts.  So here goes….  (Sorry, it gets long-winded.)
Alright, I’m going to come out and say it.  As mentally unstable the Wizard is, he is my favorite suitor, with dark horse* (note: not an actual horse) Jieun coming in at a close second.  That’s right.  Baby bunny FTW, you know, if the Wizard didn’t exist and all.
In order to understand what a crazy puppetmaster and schemer the Wizard is, let’s first take a look at our suitors and their motivations for being in The Game.
Bossy, opinionated Jiwoo doesn’t give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about romancing your♥♥♥♥♥  In fact, the only reason he’s playing The Game is because he wants to run away from his old life.  I know, technically he wants revenge on his “family”, but eventually, he changes that to wanting a fresh start.  If he happens to lose his memories, painful as they are, so much the better.  As for serious contenders, Jiwoo is pretty down there on the bottom of the list.
Much like Jiwoo, Jiyeon (that ♥♥♥♥ing heartbreaker…. all the tears I cried for him) wants revenge and/or a fresh start since his world no longer holds anything he cares about.  He’d be going home to an empty life.  If you don’t play his route, he seems perfectly happy; if you can take the abuse of chasing him down, then yeah, eventually he’ll be happy and all, but really I think he just wants to be left alone.
Beautiful Jihae also doesn’t give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about romancing your♥♥♥♥♥  He’s too hung up on his past lady and being uber depressed about her to even notice you have boobs.  In fact, the only reason he’s playing The Game is because Jieun is making him!  Does he care if he wins the heart of a new lady love?  No.  He had already surrendered to his depressingly overwhelming need to be needed, dedicating (tenfold) his life to caring for Prince Jieun.  So, not a contender.
The rabbit prince, while my darling, also has no desire to actually win your heart, or the game.  He wants Jihae (”Eddy”) to be happy, and so the two are each wishing the other would win, but never striving to win themselves.
For all four of these characters, it isn’t until you start trying to win them over that they take notice of you.  But pay attention to the phrasing there: You win them over.  YOU.  WIN.  Not them.  They are still pretty much inactive players in The Game.
Which brings us to Jisoo, the only player of The Game who is actually trying to win.  Even in routes outside of his own, Jisoo tries to appeal to Heejung, whether it’s as the big brother “please depend on me” type, a confidant, or an outright rival to the suitor in question, and this is because he is the ONLY ONE with something to lose if he does not win.  If he does not win, his sister will die.  End of story.  So yeah, he tries real hard, whether you notice him doing so or not because you’re making moony eyes over some other dude is irrelephant.  Even the Wizard himself had said that Jisoo had been his choice to win the game, but stick a pin in that and we’ll come back to it.
As gorgeous and mostly dependable as he is, Jisoo is not without his flaws.  He has a violent jealous streak that is frightening under normal circumstances, and CRAZY TERRIFYING when he finally snaps (see the bad ending OMG).
Enter the Wizard.  (My husbando.)  So far we have 4 not-entirely-committed players, and one must-win player with a history of violence, who has been hand-picked as the prize-horse* (note: not actual horse) by the Game organizer.  Naturally, The Wizard must have known about Jisoo’s violent temper and jealousy, and therefore knew he was a ticking time bomb. He must have hoped that he would win so that Jisoo’s relationship with Heejung would eventually become so abusive that Heejung would have a desperate wish, and then, FINALLY, meet The Wizard (possibly again?), and he can step in and save her.
The Wizard is really such a tragic character, constantly being denied his own happiness, it’s no wonder why he’s so twisted.  I really wished that he had his own “after” route that we could play through.  He sacrificed everything he was just to be with Heejung, not even fully knowing if it would work.  Since he wished, he probably lost his memories, but you know what?  I think that’s okay.  He would wake up without the pain and bitterness that twisted his personality like it did, next to the one he loved so much.  Granted, he wouldn’t remember that either, but, this way they could start off and build a real, true, lasting love.  That’s a story I want to play.

Now, this is my first trial of games called "walking simulators". I  will admit, it was a different experience.
PROS
This game is gorgeous, beautiful. I ran it with a slower processor than called for, but most of the game still held up beautifully and I found myself wanting to see more, even when there was no more to see.
The voice over was done well, the tidbits I found around the game were philosophical and did feel as if I was part of the conversation. The triggering of said monologues was odd, and I'm not exactly sure what sets them off. Decent job overall.
CONS
For a game with no mechanic other than walking, I would have hoped that the walking was a bit faster. Of course I stopped to see the scenes, but without sprinting I'm sure my playtime would have been double what it is now. The normal speed is painfully slow.
The hidden journals around the world contain notes that are incredibly dense. While interesting at first, they can degrade into what feels like Solomon's thesis being submitted for review. This became so bad that I didn't go past the second note.
Many of the levels feel very obviously like simple forks. There is a path that leads to the exit and a path that leads to narrations. It became a trial of walking down one path, realizing that was they way I'm supposed to go, and subsequently going back to go down the other. Sort of annoying really.
VERDICT
Wonderful game for one wanting to see the sights and wrangle with some philosophical thought. I'd say go ahead and give it a shot, but wait for a sale.
Why am I now question my entire existance and life after playing this? Green pipes/10 -IGN.

This is one of the better walking simulators on Steam. Engaging dialogue and beautiful environments. Almost no repetition at all. Enjoyable pacing. Contemplative. Peaceful soundtrack.

Stunning. I hadn't realised how much it would affect the feel of an exploration game to not have your exploration constantly interrupted by puzzles or combat. This game dedicates itself fully to the experience of the environment, and feels very very different for it.
If you enjoyed 'Gone Home' you'll have some idea what to expect, but this game is spread over a much larger and less familiar area than a house, so it's significantly different as well.
If you enjoyed the feel of 'Myst' but were frustrated at being blocked by the puzzles, this will probably be much more pleasant.
It deals with very emotionally heavy themes, and there is some gore/horror imagery, but nothing too excessive (especially by the standards of the average video game). I'm fairly squeamish about these things and I wasn't too bothered.
It's a few hours long, which felt just right to me.
Looking forward to more from this team.

Pros:
-Environments are gorgeous and sometimes unnerving.
-Story is interesting.
-A lot of exploratory value.
Cons:
-Moving onto the next chapter before you're ready is likely.
-Notes can be easy to miss.
-Dialogue tries too hard to sound deep and philosphical at times.
Summary:
The Old City is a story to be discovered through the exploration of two contrasting yet beautiful environments. You go chapter to chapter, finding notes pertaining to the Old City. Every note is worth reading, and those that need to be collected in each chapter are easy enough to find - once you realize you have to interact with things that give no indication of being clickable.
Rather existential in its monologue-riddled storyline, sometimes this crosses the border from intriguing speech to psuedo philosophy. For the most part, it's still entertaining.
A little too vague at times, The Old City offers directions at limited points in the game, and you face the possibility of leaving a chapter before you've seen everything. This gets better deeper into the game, almost as if the developers are improving as you go.
With an enchanting atmosphere, a few well-placed unsettling moments, and a foundation built on biblical reference, this game ultimately offers a great 5 hour experience. I can't wait to see what comes next.

The Old City: Leviathan is an example of why video games are my favorite storytelling medium. I can get a great story and have the immersion of being central to the whole experience.
Due to the labrynthian nature of the level design, this game does linearity while avoiding the 'on rails' feeling. The narration and writing were top notch and the philosophy aids the plot well.
If you've not already done so and you're into the genre, take the leap and buy this game.

While I wish the story was more accessible, I don't see it being a reason to avoid playing this game.  If you enjoy exploring in games or narritive driven games free of contrived gameplay mechanics, please give this a try.
For the short amount of time I played this game, I feel as though my outlook is changed. Worth giving a try.

DUNGEONS is a game developed by Realmforge Studios and published by Kalypso Media Digital
First off, DUNGEONS is definitely not Dungeon Keeper. With that out off the way, this game is good in it's own right
The first couple levels are basically tutorials and are slow, but if you get past the first couple it does become more challenging. When I first bought this game I had the idea that it would play similar to the Dungeon Keeper games
Your objective is to give the heroes that enter your dungeon everything they want filling their soul meters, then destroy them before they get a chance to leave your dungeon. Using their souls to buy "gimmicks" that you use to fill your dungeon leading the heroes throughout it, and making you more powerful
There is a balance you need to strike to get the heroes happy without having your creatures accidently slay them to soon, and losing soul energy in the process, as yourself the "Dungeon Lord" gets more soul energy from killing the heroes personally
I find trying to build my dungeon in such a way to completly fill the heroes soul bars and leading them to my dungeon heart, where I await them, to be challenging but rewarding
DUNGEONS is a mixed bag but I thoroughly enjoyed playing it. But at times it has crashed while trying to autosave and there are a couple missions that are still broken and cannot be completed
Just give it a chance it may surprise you, like it did for me, but don't expect the next Dungeon Keeper

This was actually a rather enjoyable little time waster. The game had that classic, cheesey adventure game feel. The story was admittedly quite flimsy and rather silly, and as expected the ending was rapid and lame - some more closure would have been warmly welcomed.
As with most adventure games you have to be prepared for some really wonky, convoluted puzzles. They're not difficult per se, but simply a little confusing. One of the few negative things that I'd give some scarce minus points for would be all those darn locked doors that you can't ever enter or explore. I understand that when we're exploring around in what is essentially a secret secret science facility, not every can be opened and, not every place holds any more secrets than the magic of stale coffee. Still, a few less inaccessible doors would have certainly enhanced the feeling. All in all it was a fun little experience, even if some of the puzzles were rather funny and the story was cheesey. I really did enjoy it! Had that classic corny adventure feel.
Though I wouldn't exactly say that the horror tag fits the game; there is some gore & demonic themes yes, but I would honestly say the game would belong more in the "atmospheric tension" category rather than horror. Nevertheless, I'd actually like to see more! A sequel perhaps, would be fun!

Now, that's some classical adventure game with slideshow-style visuals and spooky deserted environments. Remember 'Dark Fall'? That's how they used to make games in 1990s - and that's how I like it :) No WASD, no real-time - just good old unhurried point-and-click.
'Corrosion' is rather suspense and thriller than 'Horror' - there are (almost) no monsters, besides those you read about in journals and diaries. You spend the whole game inside, in dark underground rooms and corridors - some people could find the graphics outdated, but it does serve its purpose well.
As for the puzzles and gameplay - well, my impressions are rather mixed. The first real puzzle, that of figuring out the code to reset the computer system, was in fact the best math puzzle I have seen in years - great job! Too bad some others are not so good. And not so logical - for example, if you turn a power switch off, it is indeed logical to go several rooms back and to check whether that changed something with the working fans you saw before. But there are many points in game where one action leads to another event with no logical connection between them traceable: take this item here - and the door is unlocked far out there... So you have to go all the way back and to check if something has changed there. I have to confess I would probably not finish this game without a walkthrough - luckily, the one available for the 2012 edition works fine with the enhanced one.
So, despite some flaws, I would definitely recommend 'Corrosion' to all old-school adventure-game lovers!

This is an excellent, spooky point-and-click game.  While it's not "scary" in the shaking-in-your-boots sense, it is atmospheric with all the creepiness that abandoned places are prone to.  People who like the Myst/Dark Fall static-slideshow style will likely really appreciate this game.
Visually, the game does a great job of setting the mood, and the sounds/ambient noise only enhances it.  I didn't love the voice acting, but it wasn't horrendous and I tend to be overly critical of voiceovers (so what I think is sub-par might be fine to others).  My only real complaint was a strange font issue with captions and with areas needing screen input (i.e. the computers), but that could easily have been a setup error on my part and there's so little of it that it didn't impact the game in the slightest.
The story is very engaging, doing a good job of feeding scraps of information a bit at a time and ultimately letting the player lace them all together into a final plot.  It's open-ended enough that two players doing exactly the same playthrough might have different interpretations of what "actually" happened, and a player who didn't choose to look into side-information (i.e. using the computer to search a few things) might have a whole other interpretation as well.
Personally, I like stories that don't spoon-feed every detail, because I like doing some of the detective work and deducing myself.  If you like your stories to be clean cut with orderly chapters and a decisive ending, this might not appeal to you since you are definitely required to connect the dots yourself.
The ending is a little abrupt.  This isn't a bad thing, as you are expected to be left going "hmmmmm I wonder...." afterwards, and any further drawing-out of the story would be detrimental to that.  The game doesn't want to tie everything up for you with a little bow on top.  I think it works well.
So all in all, I was very pleased with this game and would recommend it especially to fans of the Dark Fall series and Myst series.

You won't be shaking in your pants for most of the game, but there are some nice atmospheric moments that made me pretty nervous. Before I write my full review a bit of a disclaimer. I had to use a walkthrough to get through this game. Particularly very early on. With that said, Corrosion: Cold Winter Waiting is very much a game oozing with mystery and the unknown. You're trapped in the basement of an abandoned farm looking for clues. What you find, though, is conspiracy upon conspiracy and what amounts to supernatural forces at work. Or is what you experience just a figment of your imagination? I'm a fan of games that treat the player with more questions than answers by the time the credits roll and this one doesn't disapoint. I'd love to see more from Viperante. It's not a perfect first-person adventure game, but if you're a fan of horror and don't want jump scares, this one might be up your alley.

Right, so I am a huge fan of horror games, and when I saw a new one that had apparently come out of nowehere, I was excited to see what it held in store for me.
The first thing, the fact that it is a point and click horror wasn't quite to my taste. Now I know that some people love point and click horror games, but it just didn't feel right. Eh, mixed point on that. But then we get into the actual gameplay and hoo man.
The puzzles start off mildly complex and require you to flex your brain, and only get more intense from there. I won't outright say what they are, but one puzzle that comes aout.. a quarter of the way in, and serves as your introduction to what ends up being a core component of the gameplay, was rather absurdly difficult and nearly had me give up on the game then and there. I managed to perservere though, with the help of a walkthrough.... a walkthrough that was written back in 2012. Over three years ago. Welp. Seems like this didn't come out of nowehre after all, just out of nowhere to me.
But yes, the puzzles which had been slightly difficult before get more and more so, and end up requiring you to wander back and forth throughout the area of the game you've already explored, to find what has changed after you solve a pzzle. I wouldn't have minded this as much, if there had been clues on where you were supposed to go. There weren't.
Then there's the fact that this walkthrough from three years ago exists. I don't mind that, but the edition available here is supposedly the 'enhanced edition'. Nothing at all had changed from the experience the walkthrough guide had, as all his solutions were the exact same in this game. Maybe the graphics updated or gameplay changed between the two version, but for nearly seven dollars, this game felt like a rip off.
TL;DR: Point and click obtuse puzzler from years ago. Buy the original if you want to play, it's probably cheaper.

I knew I was getting something wrong when all of a sudden my cute boy pictures for transitions disappeared back into pictures of me.  Suddenly I have a creepy set of eyes on me and a whiny plea to let me be their woman.  In some games I've played this is undesirable, but ok.  Here in Dandelion you have plea after plea until "BAD END" appears in stark red text over a black background.  Somehow even the game realizes that your friend is only a friend, and anything else is uncomfortable or even creepy, let alone his promises of you being a kept woman under his family's chicken business.  When the eyes peek beyond the glasses, you know its too late and your cute boys are forever lost to you.  Unless you made a handy save spot past most of the beginning and as desired bonds were forming.
You're a girl struggling to find her identity and escape a life of pure pressure and stress to just study and succeed under the standards set by others.  Suddenly this new responsibility literally dropped on you over night seems to give you new purpose and open your eyes to other options in life and the pursuits of happiness.  You're surrounded by cute animals and depending how you play it, they can all develop feelings and care for you.  Then they turn into a bunch of boys, and all that closeness does seem lost.  You can keep getting points, but you don't seem to get any closer.  They're boys now, which means one of you has to keep the other at bay.  If you don't find the balance in activities and learn the items that will provide you with the needed effects, you'll fall under pressure and have chicken boy not taking no for an answer.
Fun game, despite some days feeling a bit repititious (especially if you are seeking someone that likes doing a lot of the same thing). Minor frustration when you get a gift and that ends the day, but the exchanging of gifts does say a lot of the bond being formed and makes up for the time lost.  I prefer games where you can choose a couple of activities in a day, but oh well.  There's a lot of things that subtly present a lot of options and variety to the interactions had and you have to start learning (like many sim games, but this one seems to take it to a higher level than most) what the guys like, what activities they want to do with you, and what you can bond over.  Otherwise you don't get cat or bunny, the game gives you the bird instead.

MC. For me, MCs in otome HAVE to have strong presence, be full characters with a personality and story to tell. Quick Summary: A mix of tower defense and freight hauling between planets that would be more fun if it didn’t require so much grinding. There are some multiplayer elements, though you never directly interact with other players. You can post “contracts” that other players can take or vice versa (transport this cargo from planet A to planet B). The random elements of the combat keep things spicy but can be overwhelming at times too.
You play a Space Runner, kind of like a trucker (in space) transporting cargo from one planet to another, with a bunch of pirates attacking you on your trips. Your “ship” is made up of hexagonal sections that you can build various turrets on, and you need to make sure you have room for your cargo too. This means the bigger your ship is, the more cargo you can carry, along with the guns you’ll need to protect it. In combat, enemies can destroy not only your guns, but also the hex sections they’re on, so on some levels you will be scrambling to rebuild after asteroid fields or powerful enemy attacks. The main things holding you back from becoming master of the galaxy is the limited number of guns you can buy, and the limited number of hex sections that you can attach to your ship. Both of these things cost not only money, but “materials” that you get as quest rewards or buy from other players.
Note that most of the guns only point in a narrow arc so you can’t just build one badass gun and think you’re safe. You might need to cover all 6 hexagonal directions. This is where the “random elements” come in. There’s really no way to know which of the 6 directions the enemies will pop out from, so your weapon layout will probably be different every time, even when you’re playing the same “level” (for example the trip between Planet B and Plant C). Over time and as you level up, you unlock different weapons as well as support turrets, such as repairers, shields, upgraders, etc.
You should enjoy this game if:
+You liked FTL: Faster Than Light, but wanted more laser fire involved, and less luck.
+You are looking for a “long term” game. Despite how simple it appears, beating Space Run Galaxy will take a very long time due to how slowly you progress (level up and acquire money). It’ll take at least 30 hours to beat the campaign.
You won’t like this game if:
-You’re looking for a story to get immersed in. The game has some story elements linking the missions together, but it’s mostly all about the combat/strategic transport of materials.
-You want an easy/casual game to spend a few hours on and then move on to something else. Space Run Galaxy will eat up your time and you’ll spend a long while thinking that you haven’t actually progressed. The story missions are locked based on character level, and you can’t replay missions over for more exp. For example, if the trip between Planet J and Planet K is too hard, you can’t just replay earlier missions to level up more, because you will already have received the exp rewards from the earlier missions. You can get more money though, and hopefully buy more turret stock. Some of the missions are shockingly hard for beginners.

The game is good, but not for its price. It's a unique take on Tower Defense. I don't know how much replay value it has, I have already uninstalled it since I know I'll never play it. Beyond visually, it's not really a special tower defense game. ALL the qualities that makes this a unique tower defense game are purely visually. As far as gameplay elements go, it's mediocre for the genre. You build a structure, you repair a structure, you place it on a square cell, you protect stuff on this area, it's been done a million times. It's hard telling if I have missed out anything special, but from what I can tell that is not the case. Watching footage of later gameplay hasn't convinced me so, I feel I got the gist of the experience with the first fifteen minutes. What's interesting is its lack of multiplayer, in spite advertising it.
It claims it has multiplayer, but it simply doesn't. It's a single player game that allows players to indirectly interact with each other's saves, but one player at a time. The only example that comes to mind is Animal Crossing on the gamecube. Animal Crossing for the gamecube was NOT multiplayer, you had one player visit another town and did things by yourself. Instead of there ever being any multiples of players, it's always single player. This game has that in common, it has always a single player on screen but attempts to falsely market itself as multiplayer by having it so you can visit other people's saves. Fantastic, I'm sure my friends will love taking turns to play with me, but by playing with me I mean I get to watch them on Steam Broadcast.
If it's on sale, I would say $5 is a great deal. Don't expect anything too amazing, the great qualities of this game is the unique perspective on the genre, not anything amazing as far as actual mechanics go.

I love my Steam controller and just ordered a second. The layout is thoughtfully designed and the addition of the paddles on either handle -- a feature I hadn't had on other controllers -- was both easy to get used to and would now be hard to part with.
The ability to configure button combinations makes it possible to directly access in-game features, items, and abilities that would otherwise require diving into a menu. And because buttons can be bound not just to individual keys but to key combinations, it's possible to get very creative with what buttons will do, automating combos and other actions that aren't otherwise available, even for games with the ability to fully rebind the controls. This has completely smoothed out gameplay in Witcher 3, for instance, allowing for easy quicksaving and eliminating the need for one sub-menu altogether.
That said, there is something of a learning curve. The trackpad in lieu of the second joystick definitely takes some getting used to. And customizing the controls is not very intuitive -- you'll need to be patient the first few times you set up the controls. But ultimately it's worth the investment.

This is basically THE pc controller! But what makes it such a good PC controller?
1. This controller is fully costumizable with multiple Action Sets (Costum button profiles to switch) and ''mode shifts'' which basically takes customizability to the next level.
2. You can use this controller even for the desktop/internet browsing.
3. You can use this with EVERY game. The game can either see it as a 360 gamepad, mouse and keyboard or combo of both!
Cons:
1.The click sound on the touchpads are a bit too loud and a tiny bit to hard to press.
2.The Left and Right Trigger have a secondary press button at the buttom (last half cm of press) which are a tiny bit too light to press.
3. It comes with a dongle extension dock but still you should'nt be further than 5 meters away. from it.
4.Input lag over 1-2 meters is kinda meh, understandable and still more usable than a 360 controller (still more precise aiming).
Most steam reviews and popular youtube reviewers say that the controller isn't that good, why you may ask?...Well, I haven't seen them actually using the software in ''Big Picture'' mode to actually costumize the thing. They thought it's just a plug and play and miracles will happen. wow... These are so low effort reviews by them it's actually kinda sad for the Steam Controller's reputation.
Conclusion:
If you like customizability and want more presice aiming, then you'll love that gorgeous thing.
I don't give number ratings, rather then that go and look at the cons and pros I listed above. For me personally the cons aren't a big issue. The pros EASILY dominates it.

"The Old City: Leviathan" is a existencial, philosophical piece. It's  far from a game, but more of a First Person Experience.
This short, but brilliant work of art tells several stories, which are open to interpretation. All of these stories are filled with direct and indirect symbolism. It speaks about the human condition, about choices and about progress. And it does so in very beautiful, expressive writing and amazing visual acompaniment. Even though the symbols used are quite original in thought, they suffer the same problem all western-born symbolism shares - there is too much religious undertone that holds the entire structure. However, here it's at least done properly. The symbols expand from one to several meanings and ultimately - grant truth in thought.
Very few gripes can be had here otherwise. Overmapped surfaces sometimes cause you to bump into rocks or edges, slowing you down. And it's a bit tiresome to stop and read all the text scattered across the landscape. All pages that can be found are well written and interesting, revealing quite a lot about the miracle world you walk in, but stoping to read causes the player to stop exploring, which is the biggest drive in intriguing place like the Old City. It's sad that they were not voiced, so the player could listen to them while exploring (simillar to Voxophones in BioShock, etc).
Beyond that, "The Old City: Leviathan" is the most thought-provoking and meaningful "gaming" experience I've ever had. It's the closest thing to art I've felt since "Journey" and it's a shame it's so underground. This also speaks a lot about our society, for if this had been a book or a short story, even a movie, it would have gotten huge praise. But that's a talk for another time.
Those who crave something meaningful and beautiful, which will leave them sinking in thought - Leviathan calls for you, so fall and be brave. To everyone else, who thinks that philosophical artpieces are not their thing - you are probably right, but still keep in mind that the game is very beautiful - there is loads to see in this world. And even if you deny the symbolism, the pure story told is very intriguing, as the world built seems surprisingly believable.
"The Old City: Leviathan" is one of the best experiences available in the market. If you think you are going to enjoy this, you mos tcertainly are (for one reason or another). Spread the word, get more people to feel this, as it is a masterpiece worthy of something much more than a GOTY.
