Greetings…What to say about this game?  Well, the game was frustrating at first and boring at the end.  I’m not really sure what to say to introduce it, if you wanted a Dungeon Keeper move on but there is a game here, a boring, redundant game, but it is here…
RPG Classic:  The mechanics in the form of leveling and talents are pretty standard, just think of an old MMO where when you level you get some stat points and some talent points, the interesting thing is that you don’t actually level through experience but achievement like objectives.  Now, most of them are wasted time as you only get scrolls (which I rarely bothered using, if there was a spell I wanted I learned it) but some of them gave stat and talent points.
No Polish:  The game lacks many of the modern shines that are needed, can’t move the Lord via the main map, too hard to find certain things, game crashes, save corruptions.  The game mechanics themselves are solid overall if you remove all of that.  The tutorial is okay, need a bit of work and needs a help menu to verify things.  The game seems more interested in the cute narratives of objects and less on the purpose.  One thing the game needs to focus on is being clear on what it is…
Tycoon not Keeper:  This game is NOT a dungeon keeper (or Evil Genius) it is more in line with a Tycoon game, you have to build a ‘Dungeon’ which has attractions (Gold, Monsters, Books and Equipment) in which adventurers come in, fight monsters, loot gold and other activities, but unlike other tycoon games you want to kill them before they leave.  This isn’t bad on its own but…
Endless Tedium:  I really hate to say this…but the campaign (the thing I love in most games) is what kills this, Tycoon style games just don’t lend themselves to level based campaigns.  Maybe if it was a living environment (similar to Evil Genius) this could have been much more entertainment.  But, it is hard to tell as all the flaws just make it impossible to look at this part objectively.
If you love the Tycoon games and want a darker environment with some silly commentary then maybe you will really enjoy this game.  The game is very easy and I personally enjoyed the free play mode over the campaign even though there… the main annoyance is that this is a Tycoon game that requires you to basically right click on an tourist before they leave, giving you something (boring) to do…

I am fond of walking simulators. I am not fond of this one.

The narrator is busy annoying the player with his pseudo-philosophic soliloquies, juggling with overly complicated words and misusing them in an unheard of frequency. No first-semester philosophy teacher would accept this as an essay.
Then there are volumes of references to bible stories posted on every second wall in the sewerage, making their complexity appear so trivial that the player will likely ignore them altogether to not interrupt the walking flow.
In conclusion, a visually stunning experience utterly destroyed by an absurd narrative which is stubbornly distracting the player from what the title does best.

From the tutorial and the first few levels I think you get pretty much all the experience you're going to get from this game.
The gameplay element teased during the tutorial levels of having to control multiple characters at once definitely shows promise. It can be quite a challenging mechanic when used correctly. However, based on the levels I've played so far, there isn't enough of a puzzle focus.
The game would be better if there was less of a focus on just walking through levels and more immediate focus on puzzle solving. Simple platforming levels can be nice when there's lots to do and explore, but if you've gone down the super-minimalist route like this game has, they can be (and in this case, are) boring.
Minor issues that don't help the game's case:
There is "definitly" a typo in the tutorial.
Sometimes the larger spinning squares dont kill you, sometimes they do.
It would be nice to have more distinction between the dangerous moving elements and the useful moving elements.
Sometimes other animals kill you but sometimes they also disappear anyway, suggesting you did the right thing in jumping on top of them.
There are areas with frame drops which is odd considering the minimal graphics.
Fall fast enough and the camera can't catch up to you
Camera can only be manually moved left/right, even though there is an up-down component to the game
Also, this is less of a problem with the game, more of an observation having played multiple other games: In a platformer - where jumping is usually a key component - I like to have responsive jumping depending on how hard or how long I press the jump button. Here, each jump is the same height, which makes it a bit hard to play sometimes.
Some good points though - The music is nice, and the detail on the pixel graphics of the characters that run about the levels are nice. It would have been great to have that level of detail applied to the environment as well.

I played Tales of Symphonia with a friend back in the day, and thought JRPGs were never gonna be like the old days ever again.  Well, I was wrong. It's fairly linear (don't expect to wander around too much) in terms of map design and direction, so don't expect to get lost (which is a good thing).  Gameplay is deep, and there's so many mechanics in play that you could get stomped in a boss fight if you never take advantage of any of them, while sweeping the floor in as little as 5 turns if you do take full use of them.
Other thoughts—The story is great.  It starts off reaaally slow, then suddenly gets me stoked for every chapter as soon as the pace picks up.  And another fun thing: You end up caring about the NPCs.  Never in a game have I chatted up every NPC to see what's going on after every story event.  They all have names, and even crazier, they have character bios!
Anyway, be prepared to sink tons of hour into this puppy.  It's massive, and the included turbo mode (many thanks for implementing that!) helps so much.

I really want to like this game, but there are too many issues, unfortunately. And the way it is now, I can't honestly recommend this game to anyone. My gameplay can be described like this: several minutes of fun arcade-style baseball at a time, punctuated by confounding, frustrating bugs and glitches. It is fun when it is working properly, but then reality strikes and I wonder why I plunked down $20 on this. I'm a die-hard baseball fan and loved playing PC baseball games back in the day. I used to play a game called Hardball! on my old Mac. And on my old Nintendo, Baseball Stars was the best. I was hoping RBI would be a throwback to those kinds of games, but not yet.
Let's start with the cons:
- Awful keyboard set up with no re-mapping. The controls are unintuitive and irritating to say the least. The right arrow key is assigned to "back" in the menu system. Really? And the mouse is unusable for the entire game, including navigating menus. But for some odd reason, the mouse arrow is still there anyway. Just allow me to map my own keys and use the mouse if I want. Trying to navigate through stats and other menus is really a pain in the @55.
- Pitchers lose stamina very quickly. I'm lucky to get my starters to go 4 or 5 innings before they're tossing 60mph grapefruits (CPU, too). And I rarely use the "fast" or "slow" pitches or the left/right movement.
- Pitchers don't seem to field groundballs. They will be available to catch the occasional pop-up, but a slow ground ball right to them? Nope. Through the legs and into center. EDIT FOR CLARIFICATION: the pitcher does get activated for some ground balls, such as a swinging bunt or weak grounder near him. But it's the grounders that are hit right at the pitcher where no attempt is made to field it, even though it looks like he's in fielding position and should be able to make a play on it.
- Something is off with the overall "timing" of fielders, throwing, and baserunning. What I mean is, if I hit a gapper that rolls to the fence, I'll be lucky to get a double out of it, when it should be an easy stand-up double for even the slowest runner. I get thrown out fairly often trying to get to 2nd on what is typically a sure double. Want to tag up from third on a deep-ish fly ball? Good luck with that. It's nearly impossible. Want to score from 2nd with two outs on a single to the outfield? Good luck with that, too. I don't know if the runners are maybe just too slow or the fielders throw too fast.
- Fielding glitches: I've had an outfielder catch a ball and then get stuck in the fence, unable to throw. Luckily, the computer runner didn't advance and eventually the play ended and went to the next at-bat. On one occasion the CPU had bases loaded with one out. It hit a routine grounder to my third baseman which should have been an easy 5-4-3 DP, but when I threw to 2nd, no one was there! The ball rolled all the way to the right field fence. When the CPU is fielding, it makes odd decisions. If I have runners on 1st and 2nd with less than 2 outs and I hit a grounder to an infielder, it tries to get the out at 3rd rather than go for the traditional DP. Even if I hit it to the second or first baseman! Also, with CPU runners on base, a routine grounder near 2nd base bag will not be picked up by the shortstop, even though he's running right over the ball! The second baseman is activated to field the ball, but he's no where near it. Similar scenarios happen between 1st and 2nd with pitcher, second baseman, and first baseman.
- Baserunning glitch: Sometimes, when I have runners on base and I hit a fly ball, the CPU outfielder will catch it for the out, but not throw it in. It's just frozen there. The game will not continue unless I let one of my runners get out. Frustrating.
- Quick-pitching by the CPU. Especially to start the game. If I'm visitor and have first at-bat, as soon as the pitching screen comes on, the first pitch is already on the way! It would be nice if there was a pause before the CPU starts pitching. Even for the later innings, although it's not as quick. But a slight pause would still be nice to get my batter set up or see who's pitching, etc.
- Manual fielding (outfield) is kinda tough! Just when I think I figured out the fly ball indicator and sound, another ball goes way over my outfielder resulting in an extrabase-hit for the CPU. Is that just me? I'm reluctant to turn on the fielding assist because I want to do 100% of my fielding, but sometimes I wonder if the indicator is outta whack or I am.
- Non-responsive throwing direction. Sometimes my fielder will not throw to the base I'm indicating with the WASD keys. For example, I'm clearly pushing W so my outfielder will throw to second, but the throw goes all the way home or to first. Initially I thought I was doing something incorrect, but I've been experimenting with this and there is definitely something else that is wrong.
The pros:
- Fun gameplay when it works. There is a sense of satisfaction when you time the swing well and get a nice solid hit somewhere. Or turn a tough 6-4-3 double play.
- No annoying replays or cut scenes. I like the minimalist production. Even the homerun scenes are quick and unobtrusive. Most shots of foul balls are cut off so you are right back at the at-bat (although some scenes still follow the foul ball all the way out of the stadium for some reason).
- Can call "time" even when pitcher is starting to throw. This is great because the CPU quick-pitches already, so if he's quick-pitching me to start an inning and I want to pinch hit, I can still call "time" before the pitcher releases so I can put in a pinch hitter.
Anyway, I apologize for the long review. But I feel that discerning consumers want a real, honest review, including details.
I will keep playing RBI in the hopes that more updates will come along to address these issues. But I can't help but be disappointed that they released a game like this with all these bugs and issues. It's so obviously a half-@55ed port from console and they didn't even bother to test it thoroughly. They're using paying consumers as testers. Not cool, guys. Not cool.

I'm very happy to see a baseball game on the PC (aside from management sims).
RBI is, as the other comments make clear, a classic arcade-style game, not a sim like The Show.
So it should be reviewed as an arcade game, not a sim.
---Pros---
-Controller and keyboard support.
-Decent graphics.
-Very good difficulty levels (not too easy, not too hard).
-Full, 25-man, rosters.
-Baseball on PC!
-Season mode (up to 162 games).
-Postseason mode.
-Stat tracking.
-All-star game scheduled in season.
-Real MLB 2015 schedule for 162 game season mode!
-Roster updates.
-Unique ballparks.
-Simply fun game!
---Cons---
-No trading.
-Graphics are only decent (player models look nothing like them).
-Controls take some getting used to.
-No HR derby.
-NO TRADING!!!
-If you press the swing button (A on Xbox controller), and you are hit by that pitch, it will still count as a strike...
-Controls are sometimes unresponsive.
-No AAA.
-NO TRADING!!!!!!!!!!
-No injuries.
-AI is usually good, but can be pretty stupid.
-Can't sim games in season mode.
-No way to change controls (beyond "Classic" and "Modern" options).
-NO TRADING!!!!! THIS IS A BIG DEAL!!!
---Verdict---
Overall, RBI 2015 is a fun game to fill that baseball gap, but it is far from perfect.
If the bugs are ironed-out over the next few weeks, then it would be a no brainer to buy it. However, the bugs make it very frustrating at times. I have lost games due to AI issues or controller bugs.
Even with its issues, RBI Baseball 2015 is a good baseball game and you should pick it up if you're a fan of classic arcade sports or baseball in general.

I'll start with saying that I remember the original RBI baseball.  The gameplay in a singleplayer session of RBI 2015 is largely on par with that experience, which is okay.  There are a lot of additions I want in the singlepalyer experience, but I it wasn't lacking anything it promised on that front.  So if you want a singleplayer experience, it will probably be okay for you.  Not too many bugs.
That all being said, I wanted a game with good multiplayer.  What I got was a game with TERRIBLE multiplayer support.
- The games frequently don't start
- games crash out with regularity, and can't be resumed
- When pitching; the baserunner icons on the HUD disappear with disturbing regularity (multiple times per game)
- when batting: if the opposing teams pitch hits my batter, but I've started a late swing it counts as a strike.  This is bad because the animation only looks like I've lifted my leg, not made any swing motion
- sometimes when fielding the ball, I can't throw it.  Play literally will not progress to the next batter until all base runners are sent home

Curse: The Eye of Isis Review - Raymond KT
Though Capcom's Resident Evil series achieved legendary status by the late 1990s, both it and the survival horror boom that it spawned haven't been quite as popular in the past couple of years. However, Asylum Entertainment is not following the prevailing trends. The small British developer, best known for a handful of kid-friendly PlayStation games like Powerpuff Girls: Chemical Xtraction and Teletubbies: Play With the Teletubbies, Despite the company's lack of experience with this sort of game-making, and a few noteworthy miscues, the designers have traced the footsteps of Resident Evil as carefully as a chiropodist. This leaves the end result without even the tiniest smidgen of originality, though it is a convincing memorial to a classic genre. – Gamespot
One of the most memorable game I ever played. There are all sorts of fun moments in the game. Cool bosses, the undead zombies, hard-to-kill mummies, intriguing puzzles and wonderful locations- the game has it all. It is a marvelous game with a very good Storyline. Something in which the today's games really fall short . I would love to play a reboot. I think I like this game a lot because I was a fan of Resident Evil (early titles) but who knows!

We have a great review coming up. Wonderful review, I assure you, but first we're going to open with a little something. Curse: The Eye of Isis has great controls. Hard to believe with all these reviews that are just "the controls are bad", sure, but they're there. You just have to coax them out.
Boom, fixed. Thank me later. On with the show.
Curse: The Eye of Isis doesn't really do anything wrong.
There's great controls, not quite 1:1 but you can run rings around opponents and even avoid bullets with ease. It has well designed characters who manage to make the conventional look unconventional. There's nice pacing, it never settles. There's even great production values - the shaders aren't great but the texture design and asset variety is there.
Add a hammy plot that's straight out of a Saturday Morning cartoon. It's all there, all the ingredients, and it doesn't grossly mishandle any one bit on what should be a heart-filled and memorable clone of a popular game, that just sadly lacks the budget to compete with the best.
So it's a challenge to really articulate why Curse: The Eye of Isis is so wholly forgettable and generic.
There's no real puzzles. 90% of the "solutions" to the item-based puzzles are located about two meters from the challenge in question. There's no real level exploration, you're led around by the nose and exploration outside of one select instance is either punished or forbidden - by wasting your time, or burning resources for nothing.
There's no depth or variance to the world or story. Everything plays out exactly how you'd expect and does an incredibly tired job of it. There's no real horror: a few "monster closets" right at the end aside enemies just sort of sit in rooms, and then stay dead while spewing more resources then they consume (which is a fair bit to begin with, the average alive enemy will take five headshots before they die).
There's no real character arcs - characters sort of just state what they want to do, or don't, then do it and occasionally scream each other's names from offscreen. The itty bitty arc there is, doesn't so much exist, so much as the Arabian fez-wearing save point flatly tells you it does.
Everything is incredibly underwritten so you don't even have that much ham in this hammy story to enjoy. There are no surprises at all in this brown, grey slop of a game.
Some games bore you to tears. Curse: The Eye of Isis manages to avoid this while also avoiding doing a single thing of interest. It is a perfectly playable, well executed corporate product, that I am going to go to sleep tonight and completely forget about.
If you're interested in a very cheap, very playable game then Curse: The Eye of Iris can contend with the other fifty billion of those on Steam. Otherwise just forget about this game, like everyone else has.
Some games belong in the echelons of history. Some games belong in a garbage can. Curse: The Eye of Isis doesn't really belong anywhere.

I'm happy to confess that I'm criminally underqualified to review games like this one, so let's start with a brief disclaimer.  I'm not usually an impulse buyer - as God is my witness, I'm a cheap 'n' nasty "sales ♥♥♥♥♥" if anything - but since I'm on holidays I found the opportunity to be one of the first reviews for a freshly-released horror game all too tempting, and this one looked intriguing and wasn't too bad a price, even at a mere 15% off.  Sold!  The first lesson here, boys and girls, is to properly read the Steam Store page, as what I foolishly assumed to be a "regular movement" kinda first-person game is in fact a point-and-click game, and if there's one genre I have ambivalent feelings towards, that'd be it.  Oh well.  The good news, however, is that even an adventure gaming dumb-dumb like myself can tell that this is one of the QUALITY specimens of its genre.
For the hour I've played thus far, it has all the hallmarks of a well-made horror point-and-clicker:  Nice visuals, spooky music, atmospheric sound...and, perhaps most importantly of all, a genuine air of MYSTERY.  Granted, Scratches started off similarly well, before steadily devolving into unnecessarily convoluted storytelling and even MORE convoluted "puzzle"-solving...but as far as I can tell, the puzzles in this one are super-logical and genuinely clever, though the downside to this is of course that UN-clever people like me have precisely ♥♥♥♥-all chance of getting anywhere in them without constant reference to a walkthrough.  But at least I could work SOME of it out without resorting to such cheating, and the bits which I couldn't made perfect sense once I'd looked them up.  Which is more than I can say for a LOT of "adventure" games I've attempted over the years...
What I'm trying to say, in my typical long-winded fashion, is that if you're the type of person who can actually get their noggin 'round this kinda game, this is certainly shaping up to be one of the good'uns.  Me, I'm a university student at the moment, so I'm inclined to find my leisurely pleasures elsewhere for now, but if at some point in my future I feel like this kinda high-level cerebral challenge, I'll be sure to recall how this one actually impressed me, not least of all in the fact that I was able to make a teeny, tiny bit of progress before seeking out that much-needed help (hell, most point-and-click games I can't even seem to get past the first ROOM without a walkthrough, I'm that feckin' stoopid).
Verdict: 8/10.

I now have 2 steam controllers.  They are fantastic for any game in steam.  I've had very few problems with the device.  The in game menu is super easy to configure on the fly which means you can map any button from a pad, mouse or keyboard to any input on the steam pad.  Configurations can be saved and you can switch between these saved presets meaning if you're swapping a pad around and someone likes different buttons these can be accomodated.  If you're a tinkerer there are multiple settings and options to tweak.  Having 2 pads means that you can either clone your setup onto both pads or configure each separately if both parties want different control set ups.  Because the menus are so intuative, this doesn't take a lot of time.
The touch pads take a little getting used to and I compare this to when dual stick controllers were first introduced.  I spent the first few months playing games accidentally looking at the in game floor / sky and thinking it would never catch on.  Basically what I'm saying is practice will be needed so don't give up on them straight away.  This also includes the button locations as they are slightly different to other controllers on the market and you may end up pressing B when you wanted to press A at the beginning.
The plastic the controllers is made from will get finger prints and smudges on it.  After a few months use, you'll also probably find surface scratches on the plastic.  These can't be felt and won't detract from their function but the asthetics will be affected.  When the batteries are inserted the pads feel weighty and solid.  The upturned hand grips are surprisingly comfortable.  Overall the pad feels good and after many hours of gaming, my hands haven't become tired of holding it.
The steam pad is basically a halfway house inbetween a keyboard and mouse and a control pad.  You get the comfort of a control pad with the accuracy of a mouse.  I've had it working on flight sims, racing games and platformers (where it feels most like a control pad) and first person shooters and stratagy games where it really shines.
Niggley points about the pad are few but there are a couple.  The pad (obviously) doesn't work with games outside of steam.  You can add external games to steam and then use the steam pad but this doesn't always work.  Windows Store games cannot be added to steam as they aren't saved as a .exe file meaning no steampad / windows store compatability.  The pad is BEGGING for an external app which will emulate a standard pad in other applications.  Still waiting for this.
Certain games (mostly first person shooters) have item selection wheels.  You have probably encountered these; press weapon select and hold up on the right thumb stick to select a certain gun, kinda thing.  If you are using the very helpful mouse emulation using joystick input (which emulates a mouse when you're using a standard control pad input) this wheel selection is quite broken.  Instead you have to scroll constantly in the direction of the weapon you want and often select the wrong weapon as a result.  I don't think there's an easy way around this one.  Either you use standard joystick mode and it works or you use the more accurate and comfortable mouse emulation and scroll like crazy in this menu.
If you have multiplayer games and you want to use 1 steam pad and the rest of the players are using regular pads you'll encounter the next problem.  The steam pad isn't classed by windows as a pad.  Therefore the steam pad will be assigned to pad 1 and so will one of the other pads you're using.  This leads to 2 people controlling the same character on screen.  It can be circumnavigated with 3rd party software used to assign pads numbers to windows so you don't have a pad assigned to pad 1 (and therefore the steam pad will work in this slot) but it's for higher level users to configure.  There isn't an official work around to this so if you're a multiplayer fan and you aren't 100% comfortable configuring windows then it might not be for you.  The easy way around it is to plug in 1 too many other pads and leave one on the floor when playing.  Also it's not a problem if you only own steam pads.
Final problem isn't really a problem, just more of an annoyance.  If you own multiple steam pads, each will need its own dongle plugged into a USB slot.  If you have 4 pads, you'll need 4 USB slots.  It would have been a lot better to have just one wireless dongle serving as many pads as you buy but hey ho.  At the end of the day, it's the same as using wired USB pads.
Overall the pad is better than a standard pad but not quite as good as a keyboard and mouse.  Having said this it lets you play a whole host of games you'd otherwise only be able to play at a desk.  If I had the choice between using a steam pad and a standard pad I'd pick up the steam pad every time (even with the niggles).

It's not a bad controller by any means. It works great with Steam and a number of games not associated with Steam or any other client. However it will not work on games from other clients (if added as a non steam game to your library) or only with very few,  such as Origin and Blizzard's.

I keep trying to like this game, and on the surface it seems like a good improvement over the last (which I quite enjoyed). But there's just too many design flaws in this sequel.
The good:
+ A lot more levels
+ A few new items over the last game (though most are rehashes)
+ Developer tried to add some multiplayer-esque elements
The bad:
- Levels follow a pattern, but have random elements. One fun aspect of tower defense games is that you can develop a strategy for each level, fine tuning until you dominate it. But in this game, enemies can come from several randomized directions.
- Some missions have many stages, but you only get a reward at the very end. It makes you feel kinda ripped off for completing the middle stages. There's just no good sense of progression.
- You can only build X number of tower Y. To build more, you have to grind missions.
- You get crafting material to make more towers... but those materials generally end up on planets that cannot craft what you need. The game then forces you to transport the materials to locations that CAN craft it, giving no direct reward for doing so. This furthers the grindy feeling.
- The interface, while intuitive, requires a lot of clicks to do very basic things. Good UI, bad UX (user experience).
- The controls leave much to be desired. Some towers can switch modes or rotate. But to do that requires several clicks, where it could've been so much simpler: hover over tower, use mouse scroll. No clicks. No radial menus. Again: good UI, bad UX.
- Some levels are just mean. They can be very easy until the very end, where the game throws some CRAZY firepower at you (usually with attack ships named "Avenger"), obliterating your hard-fought ship and ending your 10 minute run, leaving you with zero reward for your time. This is absolutely rage inducing.
It all ends up making the game unpleasant, grindy, and generally infuriating.

This game is a hidden gem in the tower defense genre. Had I not gotten it through the Humble Bundle, I would have likely never picked it up due to the mixed reviews it was getting. Imagine my surprise when I started playing it until late night on work days.
Right off the bat, the game is pretty difficult. There are a lot of things to consider when trying to complete a run. Each ship will have different advantages and disadvantages based off of its shape alone. Placing your cargo safely without obstructing your defenses is another challenge. You have to manage your budget, both in planet menus and during your runs. There are virtually endless combinations of turrets and boosts you can place, each one with unique capabilities, and the way you place them, combined with the adjacency bonuses (similar to districts in Civilization 6), will make or break your run.
Many people complain about internet hick-ups causing runs to fail. I have yet to encounter such an issue.
Others complain that you can't pause the game and build. Although I see where there may be some appeal to that, your aim, timing and quick thinking are things this game aims at challenging you with.
I will admit it can become a little grindy, and the steep difficulty curve will discourage some players. All I can say that once you have one or two connectors, some missions that seemed impossible will become more realistic challenges.
All in all, if you're smart, ergonomically inclined and quick, this game is definitely for you. I wholeheartedly recommend it.

So, I have finally found time to write a review to this wonderful game. Please, don`t look at the playtime displayed in my Steam account. I bought this game almost immediately after its official release on CheritZ, when it wasn`t available on Steam at all and used a special security server to play, and played it for around 6 months (completing all possible character stories, of course).
I actually love Dandelion. One of the reasons for it is the main character - Heejung. Even though I never was in the same situation is hers, I still can feel her sorrow and pain. She is not some lifeless female protagonist that we can see in many otome games. She has personality and we can see her developing during the game. If you have heart, you WILL want to make her happy, though the road to happiness for this poor girl is a really difficult one.
Now, after I have talked about my main reason to love the game, let`s look in details at what it offers.
1)	Characters. There is a lot of different personalities here: timid and dreamy Jieun, tsundere type Jiwoo, dark and "bad-boy type" Jisoo, mysterious and level-headed Jihae, charming Jiyeon (whom I started to hate at some point because....well, you need to play the game to understand what he really is). And of course the Wizard, a crazy person who is obsessed with Heejung in some way (or in all ways). There is also Heejae - Heejung`s friend from the university, but he doesn`t play any major role in the story.
2)	Story. This one is quite interesting. As I understood, there are two words – the normal one, where Heejung lives, and the parallel one, where animal-people live. The main two classes mentioned are rabbits and cats: rabbits are royalty and wealthy all in all, and cats suffer from poverty and rabbits` policy. That`s the reason why Jisoo and Jiyeon – the cat-boys - don`t like three other young man (who are rabbits). Developers of the game did quite a good job showing the society of cats and rabbits. As far as the romantic part of the story is concerned, it is also worth mentioning. All male characters are really different and their attitude towards Heejung is different too. Some of them are pretty shocking, to say the least, for example, Jisoo`s one. He scared me at some point. However, I don`t want to write spoilers here, so I can`t add anything else without opening some part of his route. It is also really appealing to me that male characters develop along with the protagonist and that all of them are not what they seemed at first sight. Don`t trust your first impression, dear friends, because it will fail you. Every character is unique, so the game has great replayability. Despite having already completed the game I still decided to start it again in Steam, because it is better than many other otome games, its story is more consistent and it provides something apart from love story. Yes, Heejung has to fall in love with one of them but it doesn`t mean that everything will be in pink colour. There is great social context that will make you think about different things, including how to raise your children (Heejung`s mother is one of the worst possible examples, to say the least).
3)	Voices. Something I really liked was that Heejung has her own voice. Yes, she speaks, and I like how she does it. She is emotional and sincere. Male voices are very good too, they suit the characters well and if I have ever to imagine them in real life, I would give them the same ones. Though I should also say that at first I found the language funny, no offense here, people from Korea. It is just so different from Russian, and the way some words are pronounced…that`s fascinating. Nevertheless, I got used to it pretty fast, so there is nothing to complain about.
4)	Interface and game mechanics. Both were nice and easy to understand in the non-Steam version of the game, but in Steam it has become even better. I like how the Status of Heejung is shown, I like how simple the stats are that you don`t have to run around the map or house to understand what to do and how to improve the protagonist. Everything is simple and it is good. At the same time I can`t but mention that all this stat raising may become a bit repetitive. By the end of the third route (it was Jisoo`s one, btw) I have already learned by heart what to do and where to go to achieve what I want, so the story is the main feature that makes you want to play, not the process of playing itself.
5) Art and CGs. I love the style all characters are drawn. It`s neither childish nor too realistic. Heejung is not a super model and she never was presented as one, she is just a common young woman who is concerned about her future and current life. It is also worth saying that characters` emotions are well shown with both the art and the voice acting. The CGs are all well-drawn, I can see love of the artists who created them. Some are funny, some are scary, some are mysterious (remember the crazy Wizard?) and some are lovely and romantic. I strongly recommend completing all the routes and opening all CGs, because you will most probably love them.
All in all, Dandelion - Wishes brought to you – is worth its money and your time. I do believe that you will like the characters and the plot and that you will not be disappointed with any of the endings. There is no fairytale here, even though it looks like one. But there are actual problems of the real world that Heejung has to face every day.
I wish you good game and hope my review will help you in any way. ^^
P.S. Don`t forget to complete Bad Endings too, they are more then worth it. As I said before, Jisoo`s one is pretty shocking.

The Nancy Drew Dosier games take a slightly different twist on the usual hidden object genre, there is no list of object you need to find on the screen, simply a counter that tells you how many hidden objects there are. Its up to you to find them and then figure out which ones match to solve the puzzles on the screen. A fan with a broken power cord? Match it with the sticky tape. A piece of paper stuck the the ceiling? Match it with the fixed fan to blow it down. It's a enough of a twist that it gives the dosier games a unique feel. The voice actor who plays Nancy in Her Interactives main Nancy Drew series is back for the dosier games and gives a good performance, in fact all the voice acting is good as is the music and general presentation. The plots are suprisingly good for this kind of game too and I found myself quite caught up as the mystery deepened. Reccomended for fans of Hidden Object games or the main Nancy Drew series who are looking for something a little different.

You get presented the solved puzzle, the puzzle parts get randomized, floating outside the placing area, and the solved-/target-image fades out.

Contrary to a traditional (physical) puzzle, I found myself try-placing puzzle peaces, rather than only placing it on fitting positions. Especially since it snaps from pretty far away (a whole peace away) its a viable strategy.
In the more complex puzzles, my strategy/workflow was:
1. Try to remember key areas of the image (how many people, distinguishing color areas)
2. Pull a lot of border bieces on the placing area as well as strong colors/structures
3. Try-place the border pieces until it randomly snaps in place
4. …
5. Only for the harder/later pieces did I check for the connectors of pieces, which peace fits where (especially when they do not have structure you can locate them by)
So it’s not how I would (have to) play a physical puzzle. But that’s ok.

Lion Quest (not to be confused with the Lion Cubs scouts program), a quaint indie puzzle-platformer developed and published by “Dracula’s Cave”. It was released on the 11th of July this year and is currently on sale for £8.99 or $11.99 on Steam.
A surprisingly enjoyable yet frustrating little platformer, I found that this game quickly burrowed deeply into my mind after such a short meeting with it. The game has no problem with showing its unique minimalist take on the platformer genre of games whilst simultaneously keeping the game light and upbeat in a Zen like manner.
From the very beginning of playing this game, you will be enraptured with its cute setting. Even with the hidden-depth from behind the scenes, I personally couldn’t help but notice that at every turn, the game would capture me with its cute character designs. And by the time that I would forget about the cuteness in this game, I would hear a new score from the Soundtrack; the combination between modern bit music and Zen style music would leave me relaxed and chilled. As I progressed through the game, I soon noticed that the use and contrast of colours within the expansive and vibrant levels was just as scrumptious as the characters designs leaving a satisfied sensation. The puzzles were just as intriguing as you will find yourself controlling multiple characters at once trying to traverse through the well built and designed levels and puzzles.
One of my favourite features within this game was it’s Zen powers in which the player could pause gravity in a “Force” like manner. I found that this caused a unique interaction between the level design and platforming elements as it forced the player to do more than most puzzle-platformers would normally offer.
However, don’t be fooled, as you carry on through the levels, the game takes a sudden curve in difficulty. Jumps onto molecular sized blocks will soon become normal and the environment will take a turn to becoming hazardous. With these intense portions of the game, I found that the puzzles and platforming elements would lack the fine control that I was expecting; “stuttery” controls and unexpected character movements left me trapped on one part of a level for up to half an hour trying to complete a single jump. Even though that I found the game enjoyable, it also felt repetitive and overly simplistic as the innovation behind the game diminished in the later levels. Lots of sections felt “Copied and Pasted” and the lack of new content made the game have a stale feeling about it.
In Summary;
This game is enjoyable,  a simplistic puzzle-platformer that can be played on your own or with friends casually and definitely something to pick up when on sale, if just to experience how nice a game can look without having AAA graphics all of the time and I can definitely see myself coming back to this game again and again when I want to pick up something for a casual half hour or so. However, it is also easy to become bored with the game as it felt overly repetitive and occasionally had poor performing controls.
Pro's:
- Cutesy Styling/Design
- Beautiful Soundtrack (Over an Hour Long)
- Unique Platforming Puzzles
- Very Peaceful & Calm
Con's:
- Repetitive Gameplay
- Stuttery Controls
6.5/10

They definately tried to grab that Dungeon Keeper vibe but the game itself is it's own game that borrows elements of it - right down to the very simular CGI cut scenes.  The simularaties are so uncanny many (myself included) thought they were trying to make a cheap knockoff.
Once you figure out it's not Dungeon Keeper and figure out how it works, you start to get an appreciation for what it really is - a satire of fantasy dungeons and the players who play them.  You then dig into the game further and watch how it lampoons all the popular favorites right down to Diablo and does it with a self awareness that Dungeons itself is NOT to be taken anymore seriously than the game it borrows inspiration from.
Indeed, I think Dungeons probably did a better job nailing the satire of fantasy dungeon crawls than anybody - it indeed did NOT DESERVE the flak it got for appearing to be a knockoff.
While you have a dungeon heart and workers that dig out your dungeon, the simularities end there.  Where Dungeon Keeper looked at the heroes as an invader to be destroyed, Dungeons approaches Heroes as an important resource.  You see, your dungeon is there to entertain them, and make them gain soul energy.  When they have sufficient soul energy or make themselves too much of a nuisance - you knock them down and imprison them to harvest them for soul energy.  In essense, they are your cattle to be cared for till it's time to slaughter and harvest them.
Dungeons also gives the Dungeon Lord an actual avatar - a wandering nightmare mob that you the player have control of.  Anotherwords, YOU ARE THE DUNGEON EPIC BOSS.
Said soul energy is used to build gimmicks - which are essentially the decorations for your dungeon.  Each gimmick raises the prestige of your dungeon, which in turn directly influences your power by unlocking stronger monster and better devices to better care for your little hero piglets.  Pretige also directly influences the strength of your Avatar.
Soul energy also serves as the currency you use to raise the universal level of all your monsters, and is also used for other odd purchases such as creating a guardian for your dungeon heart, or increasing the number of workers you can have.
It's not all screams and sacrifices though - your actions of harvesting said heroes comes at a cost.   The more you destroy, the more it ticks down a timer that spawns a champion.  Said champion can be thought of as the end-game player.  Maxed level and fully geared - his only goal is to destroy epic mobs - like you.  His presense aggrivates the other heroes and unites them in his cause - and thus you have to deal with him.
Oh, there's also the other weakling dungeon lords that invade your realm - but that's another story.
Game deserves a chance - I'll probably pick up it's sequal soon.

While I like the visuals of the game and it is for the most part a technically good game, I found the actual game play to be extremely dull. The only thing you will ever do in this game is walk. You wander around several abandoned areas discovering pieces of narration (which was quite good) and notes which vary in quality. On occasion, you will bump into a little cube which gives you one of "Solomon's Notes". These things take a LONG time to read and are probably the equivalent of 10 pages of reading per note (there are seven total). While I don't mind reading, when I play a video game, I want to actually PLAY the game and not read it. The music and atmospheric sounds are incredibly good and create an eerie atmosphere. I'll be honest in saying, I didn't complete the game because I didn't find the story compelling enough to suffer through any more of the slow plodding through this abandoned complex. My only assumption as to why all these walking simulator "games" have such slow movement speed is because you could blast through them in fifteen minutes if you could move at any decent kind of speed. This game will probably run you about two hours if you skip reading Solomon's notes. I made it to chapter 5/7 in about 100 minutes. Exploration is excruciating because of the slow movement speed and really made me weigh whether the little bits of exposition were valuable enough for me suffer through the journey to look around everywhere. The story itself is quite confusing. There are a great many biblical allusions, symbols, and allegories. The names Jonah and Solomon are both used (Jonah being the man swallowed by a giant fish for three days and Solomon being the son of David, one of the great kings of Israel) and Jerusalem and another town (I can't remember the name but recognized it as being mentioned in the bible) are also referred to. There are two groups, one called The Guild, the other's name I've already forgotten. They appear to be at odds. The identity of the character you play was not revealed to me in my experience. The game probably has some pretty cool stuff in it if you feel like reading the novel that was put in Solomon's notes and finding every piece of dialogue and reading every note pinned to the wall. For me, I couldn't justify wasting the time on it to find out. I got this for 75% off at $2.49. I imagine it would be worth it if you like these sort of games but I just couldn't get into it.
Progression is lost, and I cannot remember not being. I best incinerate myself before the universe is forced to deal with me through age.

This is hardly a game I would recommend for most people, but I liked it. It's a walking simulator with a ton of writing, some of it may come off as pretentious, but I actually really liked the world, characters, and story to the game, so it worked for me. It succeeds at what it sets out to do since, while the gameplay is little more than walking around, the locations are interesting, sometimes breathtaking, and other times creepy. Each area has a hidden event you can uncover (or not) that usually puts a grim dark, sometimes horror-esque, twist on the location, and helps run with the games themes if we're crazy or 'see beyond the void.' The writing is optional, but also not if you really want to get the most out of the game. It is long-winded, and you'll spend a lot of time reading if you get into it, but I found myself engaged by it most of the time and liked the way the story was told, and how the writing would be reflected, sometimes much later, in the game world itself, leading to a feeling of it all being connected.
The characters are well-realized and flawed despite there not being a single cutscene in the game and you never meet another character in person (just read things from them or about them, our character speaks of them, and we see places where they once were or lived in). The music is well-done and fits when it creeps up. The before-mentioned events and effects of those events you can find are well done. And the game has a level of subtlety to many of its themes and small changes.
Basically, for what the game sets out to do, I think it succeeds, and I quite enjoyed it. But what it sets out to do I don't think would be universally appealing, and really I'd only recommend it to those that like walking simulators and exploring, cryptic psychological stories, and don't mind reading a lot. A worth-while walking simulator for the mind that doesn't mind some reading, thinking, and and visual-audio stimuli to keep oneself invested.
A good waste of an hour.

A genuinely great game. I love Turn-based JRPGs so this game was a natural pick-up for me. I hadn't heard of the series before nor had I played any prior installments and yet I had no trouble learning about (and getting immersed in) the world this game is set in. Sure the plot has some cliches here and there (Hero boy has some special unique power, he happens to be in the right place at the right time throughout the story and other such tropes) but they're completely offset, in my opinion, by the way the game pushes into the player into the situations and if that's not enough for you then the plot twists will definitely re-engage your interest in the plot. The world is an enjoyable one and if you're a nerd for lore like I am then you'll find you've spent far too much time in this game reading books about the history of the world or talking to sub-characters to squueze out any information you can.
The Characters for the most part are all very likeable and have their reasons for acting the way they do, some secretive about their past/families, others outright hostile to certain individuals through beliefs they hold which have never really been challenged by those around them, only enforced. The only character I didn't like from the main cast was Emma, she felt very bland backstory-wise through most of the game and even when other characters started to open up or give individuals a chance she only really dropped hints about herself (until the end where she half-reveals her past) and I can only assume that she will give us the full story in the sequel.
The battle system, whilst not revolutionary, was overall enjoyable. Being able to custom tailor your characters via quartz' was certainly a system that allowed you to feel like the characters were yours and not preset into roles (to an extent) like so many other JRPGs. Whether it be switching Master Quartz' to change a characters playstyle somewhat drastically or switching up the regular Quartz' to fine tune your characters and their ablilties/stats made each decision feel like it had an impact upon your characters, a minor one at first but as the quartz' got more powerful the choices of what to equip became harder. The characters unique abilities all felt good to use in battle and all served certain purposes whether it be knocking back enemies so that you could survive another turn, an AoE to quickly clear out weak/low hp enemies or to heal your whole team. This made party composition quite important and made you have to choose carefully about who you brought into battle (when you're given the opportunity to choose who you can have).
Finally, the waifus (or husbandos for those so inclined). As I mentioned prevoiusly the characters all (bar one) have interesting and enjoyable personalities and have multiple layers to them which makes improving your relationships with them all the more rewarding. At the end of the game you get to make a choice of who to spend the festival with. You can pick from pretty much any of the major characters and a few of the sub-characters (assuming you've achieved the pre-requisites) and you get a nice heart-to-heart scene from the characters (no love confessions, just good quality bonding time). Alisa is the obvious choice for this as she is the girl that the plot pushes towards you but there are so many options that you shouldn't need to go for her out of obligation (saving before the festival can allow you to experience a few of the heart-to-heart scenes if you want to try a few out). My personal favourite is Sara Valestine, the alcoholic teacher but I'l llet you decide your waifu (or husbando) for yourself.
I get that with this review I'm pretty much just preaching to the choir as most likely only fans of the game will see it, but, if you're thinking of buying this game and are looking through reviews beforehand then I strongly recommend buying and completing this game.

The Legend of Heroes: Trails of Cold Steel (or 英雄伝説 閃の軌跡 Eiyuu Densetsu Sen no Kiseki in japan) is a role-playing video game developed by Nihon Falcom. As a part of The Legend of Heroes series, it was first released for the PS3 and PS Vita September 2013. English version is later released at the end of 2015. Followed by PC port in late 2017. The game sets in the same universe of that of famous Trails of the Sky series.
The quality of PC port is on the top form. With introduce many of PC exclusive features such as a built-in turbo mode, auto save etc. There's little to no bug or crash at all.
The game is set in the Erebonian Empire. Rean Schwarzer, the 17 years old who enrolls at Thors Military Academy and a main character of this game, find himself in the military-powered Erebonian Empire struggles with its internal conflict, the upper class and commoners attempting to rise to power both militarily and politically, their struggle for power steadily intensifies with each passing day. Rean, himself will soon learn all these experiences throughout the new class program invested by The Thors Military Academy called Class VII, where in this very class, rank means nothing but skill means everything. Rean's adventure along with Class VII's nine hand-picked students from various backgrounds and different class, begin through the political quagmire that threatens them and the very foundation of the Empire itself.
Though not only they have to face the country problem, but as well as their own flaws. These students will find themselves having to come up with own resolve and moving forward together into big elegant yet unknown world, and surviving together out there.
In Trails of Cold Steel, the player controls a cast of characters, embarking on a number of quests to progress the story.  There are two different type of maps when navigating in the overworld of the game: field maps(dungeon) and town maps. In field maps, enemies roam around and a battle ensues if the player comes in contact with one. In town maps, the player can visit various shops to purchase items, replenish health at an inn and, for the major cities, take on and report quests to the client. In addition, the player can interact with numerous non-playable characters (NPCs) in the game. The unique aspect things in the legend of heroes series is that each NPC's dialogue changes as the game advances, allowing the player to follow along sidestories that accompany the NPCs throughout the game, making a world itself feel much more lively.
In addition to typical RPG standard gameplay like exploring town and dungeon. The game also brings in the school life element into Cold Steel. Which mean not only they'll be making a journey throughout the land, the students will also be attending in classroom, and have to study various subject much like school life, and hang out with other friends in campus as to learn more about them and strengthen the bond with them. School will be considered as the main base where characters will find themselves hanging around most of the time.
Combat in Cold Steel takes place on an small open battlefield turn-based, where your characters can move freely within their moving range assuming that it's their turn. During the character's turn, the player can move or make an attack. Each character also have three other methods available for attack/support: Arts, Crafts, and S-Crafts. Arts are kind of action involving magic spells that characters can use to attack opponents or support teammates but must take an additional turn to cast as well as using EP as a cost. Crafts are character individual abilities that are similar to Arts but can be used in the same turn; however, they utilize a special gauge called "Craft Points" (CP) for the cost to perform. S-Crafts are powered-up Crafts that can be performed once a character has over 100CP but completely depletes the CP gauge upon using it. Further extending S-Crafts are S-Breaks which allows characters to immediately perform an S-Craft regardless of when their turn order is.
The "Tactical Link System" also introduced in this game, which allow players to follow up with three different kinds of link attacks, dealing additional damage and providing various other benefits. Tactical Links becomes a more useful asset to the player as the story progress and characters level up their "Link Levels" or "Bond" with other characters. In addition to that, the game also introduces Orbment system, which allow player to customize "Master Quartz" and "Quartz" which has various effect mostly related to battle, such as allow player to use certain Arts or make your regular attack able to cause status debuff on enemy. Master Quartz and Quartz also gives addition status on character, making them generally more powerful.
The game offers your quite an alright challenge and reasonable balance. Player will be forced to use various tactic like buff and debuff in other to gain upper hand in combat. As well as utilizing the Tactical Link System. There's no need for grinding level since the gap on enemy level in each sector is by no mean big. EXP multiplier is depended on player's performance during a combat, you will always get the decent among of exp as long as you fight them with your best.
In addition to main gameplay. The game include some of mini game activities such as fishing, cooking etc. They reward player with an useful items that can be used during on main story journey, make it easier to progress with lesser problem.
The game's scenery is very beautiful and engaged with well composed music in a background. Story itself flows very nicely and addicting with worth of 70+ hours pure story telling excluding battling and grinding. Involving not only sci-fi but also super nature and magic. Balancing with political story and divine-legend alike. You will be seeing several moments of memorable, and make you want to find out about this massive world more. It's truly worth calling this game has taste of JRPG game from golden age. I recommend any RPG gamer to give this ones a try, and you will never regret spending time on playing this gem.

The keyboard controls were so awful I ended up using a controller, but those controls were only slightly less awful. The biggest pain was the ever changing camera angles which seemed to be almost purposely meant to frustrate movement on a level I have never experienced. The combat was absolute trash, especially the boss fights. When a billy club can dish out more damage than a mortar cannon, you know there's some serious issues. There's an endless supply of respawning minions that further make combat more mundane than entertaining. Finding the next objective is near impossible. There are no way points and there is no objective list to aid your quest. You do have a fat dude sidekick that always spawns after whatever obstacle you were trying to overcome, but he can't help you get past the obstacle. The inventory system was a mess to the point of not having slots available to pick up key quest items and no way to actually drop items other than giving them to said fat man or your alternate character.
I honestly can't believe I finished this game because there were so many moments where I just wanted to rage uninstall. If you're like me and enjoy enduring constant pain and misery, then this is a title worthy of playing. I'm going to go walk on some broken glass barefoot now.

first of all: the servers are fine now. in 100 hours i saw the 'waiting for servers' message only twice and for half a second each. i was never dropped during the game or kicked out of a mission.

after having finished and 100%ed the game i still have very opposite feelings about it.
on the one side you have combat, humor, missions and the actual space running itself and it is glorious! some changes were made but mostly for the better i guess and all in all it's still really big fun. it's interesting and challenging, there's lots of stuff to do and to try and you can tinker with your ship like a boss. i love it!
on the other side you have the whole thing about upgrading, crafting and crafting materials, ferrying your own stuff around for hours and deal with huge artificially imposed limitations to make that pseudo multiplayer work (there is no multiplayer!). it's a pure pain in the #ss. i hate it! i've hated it after 20 minutes and i still hate it after 100 hours!
so sadly that's half good, half bad and not recommended because i feel pretty disappointed and more than mildly annoyed.
after the first 20 hours / 25% completed i almost gave up on this game. it would be an overall great game if it wasn't for that cursed pseudo multiplayer stuff that makes big parts of the game a slow, utterly pointless and  unengaging grind without end and purpose. every successful mission is followed up by the totally annoying job of organizing your sh#t and bring your stuff on the right way so you can actually use it some time in the future. MEH!
i have played the first space run quite a lot and i liked it very much. the idea was refreshing and new. it was a challenge but a rewarding one and all they had to do was to keep that gameplay and just tweak it a little.
instead you feel like they wanted to go online and real big like eve or elite and they failed miserably at it. absolutely miserably.
somehow they couldn't do it but instead of dropping the multiplayer stuff entirely they held on to it and _bent the whole game around it_ to make it somehow work. that includes putting a lot of restrictions into the game that serve to other use but to annoy people and give some purpose to that multiplayer stuff that otherwise would be totally superfluous and pointless.
i say that was the worst mistake ever.
there are some other small issues with controls, interface, usability and stuff but that seems minor. so i will just focus on what nearly killed the game for me and it certainly left a bad taste in my mouth.
let me tell you a long but important story about a young space runner new to the business. so sit down and have a big mug of coffee.
you start off with pretty much nothing and what you have is no good at all. nothing new here, that's just how it goes in games in the starting phase right? well, to get out of the 'starting phase' it took about 10 hours!
progress is so agonizingly slow and  the game throws all kinds of sh#t at you to make it even worse and slower. rewards are usually  tiny and you need to play missions over and over again to get a bit of anything together.
but when you do...time to go shopping and buy the good stuff, right?
wrong! now the game throws completely artificial restrictions at you to make progress even slower and more agonizing.
after you have earned a few credits you can't just go to the store, put the cash on the table and grab some new shiny lasers for your ship. that would be too easy and not grindy enough! you need to see the mechanic first. he crafts (!) stuff for you and takes money in return. crafting in space. seriously?! to craft stuff you have to bring crafting materials (!!)  to him. there are 3 different types with 3 different qualities each! but the fun doesn't stop there. the mechanic of a planet needs to have a certain level for the stuff you want to craft. if his level is too low you just can't craft anything. plus on most planets you can't craft in one or two categories for no reason at all. for example on one planet you can't get any weapons while on the next planet there are no shields and no engines. why? because that's needed to make 'multiplayer' work!
that means you have to split your resources and ferry your crafting materials around the whole system to a place where you can actually use it! either you have to do it yourself and that takes really looooong or you make somebody else do it for you. this is when the 'multiplayer' aspect of the game kicks in!
like i said there is NO multiplayer! no pve, no pvp, no co-op. just nothing. you can only create contracts for other players to ferry your stuff around and you can accept contracts to ferry other players' junk around. by doing so you can earn some credits and earn random loot boxes. that is mostly your crafting materials. of course that stuff is then stuck where your trip ended and you have to pay somebody else in return to ferry the stuff to the place where you want it to be so you can actually use it!
of course you can just buy the crafting stuff but it's so insanely expensive that you wont even consider it in the beginning of the game. crafting materials can be bought from and sold to other players (yes, glorious muliplayer again! and that's already all there actually is to it.) as well but it's still a really expensive idea unless you get lucky.
if you are willing to wait a night then chances are good somebody will take and fulfill your contract. if you are in a hurry you gotta do it yourself and that takes patience and nerves.
one way or another it will take hours until you have the stuff you want at the place you need it to be so you can finally use it to craft new equipment.
plus some planets don't even have a trader so you can't buy your crafting stuff on site and you are _forced_ to bring in your tons of cargo by ship.
back to the game progress:
so you need to find a mechanic with the right level who is actally able to craft in the category you need and bring him money and tons of boxes with stuff before he goes to work.
you make your way through the first system at a really slow pace and sooner or later none of the mechanics is able to craft anything useful for you anymore.
now it's  time to move to the next system (the game has four), ferry over all your crates, find a good mechanic and get the glorious new stuff!
yes!
...
NO!
of course you can't carry your cargo to the next system. your ship and your wallet can come along but your cargo stays behind. either leave it to rot there or sell it to other players at a cheap price. hooray! so you are in a new system with a decent amount of money and good mechanics but you still can't craft because you had to leave all cargo behind and sell it off!
so in the new system they want you to spend hours of terribly slow and tedious grinding to get the stuff you already aquired  before by grinding them for hours. because that was so much fun and did not take like forever at all! or you just spend almost all your money and buy the stuff you need at the next trader. you decide.
of course the new system comes with new and fun missions that you can just barely beat with the stuff you already have and you wont get any better stuff for a long time because you lack the resources. plus the restrictions on the mechanics and their crafting capabilities are even more disgusting.
that's when the sh#t really hit the fan and i nearly gave up.
i don't mind a good grind as long as it is fun, not too repetitive  and there is progress being made. but that's simply not the case in this game. it is designed to keep you busy for days for no reason and do the same f#cking missions over and over again.
just to p#ss you off.

Ever wanted to play the original ps1 GTA, but on acid? Then this game is for you, thats the most basic summery I can give this game.
The game feels very much like the original ps1 classic gta with how it plays on the most basic level, but the similarities stop there, I just needed a launching point for discription. Graphically the game is actually a minimalist graphics game done right, still maintaining a gorgeous look without going too crazy on the graphics budget. The simple colors and painting of the world is very much Mirror's edge in design. The only pixel graphics used in the game are the communication graphics with the characters and surprisingly it kind of works, it doesn't end up jarring to the whole look of the game.
Now we get to the gameplay. This has a bit of genre mix mashing going on, the sandbox world and what you accomplish in it is very very gta, while the combat is what would happen if you made Frozen Synapse true realtime and actually fun. Once again you have the option of taking out your targets guns blazing or sneak your way around, stealth is encouraged wherever possible due to the one hit nature of the game. If you are hit even once (on normal and classic) you die and have to start the entire mission over, however this one hit rule also applies to your enemies, making the matches very strategic in nature.
The game also during its sandbox sections has what is called a Nemesis system, while the word has been used in other games, how it operates in this game is a little different. In this game a Nemesis is basically a rival assassin that will attack you assassins creed multiplayer style by blending into the crowd of civilians, you have to get him before he gets you, they basically translate into chances for bonus money and a way to try to break you making high score streaks (if you care about that), they are largely annoying until you unlock the ability to use a power known as the trackcat which helps you locate them easier.
The biggest flaw in my opinion to the game is its camera, its very awkward to keep shifting the camera in combat and often I don't even try to cause it'll get me killed faster trying to seek a better angle than just trying to work with the angle I am currently in. I did try the game with both a controller and keyboard, and I will atleast note the controls "feel" more apt to be done with the a controller because of your rotation on easy access shoulder buttons, so this really comes down to your adaption ability.
Another flaw is possibly its world size, it does feel rather small after all is said and done, but for an indie game its really not bad. Dispite this small world they manage to cram alot of secrets into the game too for your exploring pleasure.
I recommend this game if you are looking for a sandbox game that manages to actually be fun, in an age where AAA has managed to make most sandboxes painfully boring to explore.

My first ever Steam review...semi-tragically.
I'd been intrigued by Tokyo 42 ever since it was first announced, mainly due to its distinctive look. But 20 bucks seemed a little steep for what was clearly a glorified indie title (and being a completionist idiot I'd have to spring for the soundtrack too). But when the new DLC arrived with a minor price cut, I decided my anticipation outweighed any lingering concerns. I'd waited long enough to play this.
Turns out I could have waited forever, probably.
A lot of reviews have made all the obvious comparisons to Blade Runner, Ghost in the Shell, Hotline Miami and whatnot. These are more or less accurate, although T42 has the sense not to take itself too seriously. I mean, if you're accused of a murder you didn't commit, it only makes sense to try and clear your name by becoming a hitman and murdering a ton of other people. Oh, and the game is gorgeous, yeah. Its bizarre and colorful architecture, a shiny, candy-coated version of Blade Runner's Los Angeles, is like eye crack, and the various little details here and there - not to mention the sheer variety in NPCs, like the goofy gangs - will ensure you always have something pretty to look at.
If you can actually look at it, anyway. As a three-quarter view shooter, I guess Tokyo 42 does the best it can with its camera, which allows you to rotate it in 45-degree increments. The problem is that the architecture is sometimes structured in such a way that there really isn't a decent angle from which to view the action. This is a particular pain when you're in a  hurry, since your fingers are too busy making your character run around to try and turn the damn camera at the same time.
In fact, the combination of the camera and controls is what ultimately threatens to break the game. In fact, it works far better when you rely on stealth as opposed to balls-out action. When you're crouch-walking around, silently killing enemies with your trusty katana (or the golf club), the game's mechanics are competent if unremarkable. Avoiding vision cones and figuring out patrol patterns is challenging and actually quite fun, turning each mission into a kind of puzzle with a decent degree of flexibility to how you complete them (an early, Die Hard-esque one, for example, lets you either walk in the front door or make clever use of some external elevators).
When the boomsticks come out, however...oof. While switching weapons by pausing the action and going through a radial menu is smooth enough, the actual targeting of enemies and hitting them with your rather slow-moving bullets is a mess. The aiming reticle does its best, with a decent line-of-sight indicator, but combined with the camera it's way too difficult to figure out if your shot is going to land, and unless your opponent is standing perfectly still it probably won't anyway. On top of that, the cover system is wonky; it makes sense that you have to pop up to return fire, but several times I was hit by a bullet I was positive the wall would block. Or maybe that's just the utterly relentless AI, which unloads on you with guns and grenades like nothing else unless you manage to hide long enough for them to give up. This is one of those games where spraying and praying (or ambushing around corners) is actually more beneficial than taking the time to aim. Once in a while the frantic, bullet-hell nature of the combat is genuinely exciting, like a moment in which you have to help a "mate" fight off wave after wave of attacking gang members, but too often I had better results just sneaking and slashing, restarting from the last checkpoint if I set off the alarm. It's even worse when the Nemesis system comes into play, as you often don't realize that random civilian was after you until you're already dead.
Navigation, too, is bad. Although a circle under your character is helpful for lining up jumps across gaps or to lower levels, the clash between the camera and the architecture makes it way too difficult to leap with any prevcision, which really sucks in levels like the one where you have to hitch a ride on flying cars to infiltrate an enemy stronghold. Becuase your charcter can't scale anything higher than his waist, you'll spend a lot of time spinning the camera, trying to determine how tall a particular object is, and why you can't tuck your knees in a little more when you jump. This is especially frustrating in the parkour missions (where the time limits are punishingly strict and the checkpoints demand perfection) and in the motorbike missions (which are, for lack of better description, broken af).
After four months of waiting and nearly 40 bucks, I simply can't recommend Tokyo 42. For every mission you pull off with a sigh of relief, it's built on top of 20 or 30 attempts where you felt like punching the computer because a sniper capped you from off-screen, you missed a checkpoint in midair, or the bike, the ♥♥♥♥ing BIKE, went completely off the road again. If you must experience this game - and I have to admit, I'm glad I at least tried it - wait until it's significantly on discount. And don't bother with the soundtrack or DLC if you can help it; one is rather unexceptional and the other doubles down on the jumping stuff, when in fact the whole thing needs a bit of an overhaul.

I highly recommend playing this fantastic otome/visual novel game! It's a must have for people who like these sort of games!!
Although it wasn't perfect in a case where I encountered a few visual/interaction game bugs mostly because I was speeding through the game to get all the endings. I'll say my experience with this game has been very good none the less.
With it being my first ever otome game, I can say that this is a very player friendly game to play when it comes down to getting good and bad endings compared to some other otome games. It's actually easier to get the good endings than the bad endings in this game... which is good imo! But I still think they should of made the good endings a little harder to get or at least have an achivement point system where you are actually bothered to get all the endings in the end to get a secret good ending when you have completed all of the good ending-routes.
The characters are also quite interesting and unique (so-so on some such as Jiyoen and Jiuen). You can instantly notice that they have their own unique personality off the bat as animals, and once they turn into humans they get even better and easier to build relationship with them.
Thankfully this game managed to gather and develop all the usual romance personalities a heroine can fall in love with (tsundere, yandere, outgoing, shy, inteligent). Although some of them did stray off a bit or it got too much of it, it usually all ended up being good near the ending of the game where you hear each character's backstory and their ending.
When you know you are torn about chosing a spotted rabbit or a black cat, you know there's something going on here...
To sum it up:
PROS:
* Characters
* Beautiful Artstyle (some angles are a little weirdly drawn though)
* Humor
* Pro voice acting
* Overall good story
CON:
* Gameplay (it gets very repetetive - esp if you go for all routes + endings.)
* Music is somewhat bland/repetetive
* Minor visual bugs when quick speeding
* Translation is sometimes off, but understandable anyway.
* No achivements
Overall score: 7/10 - 8/10
