So many people complained about Dungeons and gave it a bad name simply because "it's not dungeon keeper".
It wasn't intended to be a dungeon Keeper, only inspired by it; which not many people seemed to understand the difference between.
This doesn't stop it from being a good game.I loved Dungeon Keeper as much as everyone else and always wanted to see a return of it however I still had plenty of time spent on this (Outside of steam so more than the amount shown.)
If you can go into it without expecting to be playing Dungeon Keeper it's a really well made and fun game.
The only similarity is that it's in a dungeon, you have workers (goblins) which will dig the walls out, maintain your placed objects and bring you gold. The whole concept and game play/mechanics are a different thing altogether.
In dungeons, you control the dungeon lord who can roam the dungeon instead of being the large god hand. You don't cater for your creatures, you aim to please the humans that come down.
They have different needs and are impressed by a wide verity of interactions.
As the humans travel through your amusement dungeon they interact with the scenery objects (gimmicks) and the rooms you build.
When they do this, they will gain 'soul energy' until they are fully satisfied and will head back out the dungeon... however that soul energy is what you are after and letting them escape will lose this valuable resource used to create a more impressive dungeon, killing them or torturing them is the way to collect it before they leave.
Creatures are summoned by placing a summoning location down, these are unlocked by having getting a nest within your influence area, which you expand by placing the summoning locations.
These creatures will stay in close proximity to the spawn and fight any of the humans that they see. Whilst they can kill the humans it's not the main purpose. Some of the needs are related to combat weather it's to deal damage or be hit, creatures will fulfil this need.
There's no management for the creatures, they don't require sleep or food.
You will need to manage your hero quite a bit, making sure to kill people when it's time and also to protect the dungeons heart, if destroyed you will lose.
This happens if the humans are unhappy with the dungeon and would rather destroy it. They can also decide to attack after sharing their experiences with each other as the humans do like to talk to one another meaning one unhappy person can trigger others to join.
Dungeons is definitely worth playing if you liked Dungeon keeper (who doesn't?) and are willing to accept that it's not the same game but still want a dungeon management game.
Everybody else says it: this is not Dungeon Keeper. Just not fun to me.

is the not-quite-a-sequel, not-quite-a-prequel to
the infamous “pigeon dating simulator” that turned out to be so much more than just a lulz-y joke.  It takes place in an alternate timeline from the previous game (ignoring the events of what
players call “the BBL route”), and assumes that the player already has some basic familiarity with the characters.
Most notably from a gameplay perspective,
abandons the dating-sim structure of
in favor of a straightforward visual-novel approach.  The player is given a few choices to make over the course of the game, but most of these either advance the plot or result in insta-death, rendering the choices essentially false.  In other words, it’s basically what fans of the genre call a “kinetic” (i.e. choice-less) story.  This is a game for people who love the characters of
and just want to tag along with them on some silly holiday-themed adventures, rather than control the story from the driver’s seat.
I use the word “silly” deliberately.  Although there are a few genuinely touching moments (a conversation between Ryouta and Yuuya about love and the possibility of rejection comes to mind), most of the game is taken up with deliberately absurd, even surreal humor.  For example, in one chapter the nefarious villain (a flamboyant scientist with a score to settle) tries to destroy St. PigeoNation’s Academy by blasting it with a cannon powered by female manga nerds. ("I have heard that the fantasies of fangirls surpass those of any fanboy. Observe, and be destroyed!").  There’s also plenty of fourth wall-breaking moments, including radio interludes where the characters respond to questions from real-life fans of the series about their taste in underwear, etc.
this ain’t.
Cynics might say that the developer just wanted to milk
surprising success for more money, but I disagree.
feels like it was made with genuine affection and inspiration.  Certain plot details might be head-scratchingly inconsistent between the two games, but it’s still an endearing and sometimes hilarious experience, and I would recommend it to
fans who don’t mind losing control over the story in order to spend more time with Hiyoko and friends. Nearly all of the characters get a moment in the spotlight, with extra attention paid to Anghel, Nageki, and my dude Yuuya this time around.
It’s certainly possible to play
as a standalone experience, but I wouldn’t recommend it.  It’s meant to be a character study and a cheeky gift to fans;  first-time players will miss out on the subtleties of the character interactions, and feel a definite
as in-jokes fly over their head.
And yes, it’s about a bunch of birds.

For the ones who already played
, enjoyed it through its genuine absurdity and mind-wrecking revelation that takes place during the BBL route,
is the collection of some side stories hailing from an alternative universe where BBL route never took place. The game serves to be both some ridiculous fan service and some fourth wall breaking story interaction. For the ones who are yet to play the original game: drop this supplement and play
immediately to avoid spoilers!
In the Holiday Star continuation, the shocking yet gruesome BBL route never occurred. All students of St. Pigeonations live happily and obliviously, approaching the end of yet another school year. Here around this time, we observe a series of short side stories from our usual heroes' daily encounters that will enrich both character backgrounds and answer some questions unanswered in the original game. Aside a handful of irrelevant comical situations Holiday Star also includes one genuine storyline which would foreshadow the events of BBL route and introduce unnerving new characters: The Day the Night Slept. Even for that story alone, you are in for a treat everybirdie!
Gameplay is not that different from the original. You are Hiyoko Tosaka, the young human girl who attends St. Pigeonations alongside her bird class mates and teachers who will witness casual - and not so casual - random ongoing in and about the school. This time, gameplay is fairly straight forward with little to no choice options at all. As I described before, Holiday Star is more of a supplement to the original rather than a stand-alone game. It consists of 4 storylines, 6 short chapters and a fairly interesting radio program section where Ryouta will answer fan mails.
It's cute and short - aside The Day the Night Sleeps storyline, which is heart and mind-wrecking as expected from any game coming from Hatoful universe. I sincerely recommend the experience to the fans of the series, and the ones who'd still have some questions within their minds after completing BBL route.

To be completely honest: you probably won't like this game.
Not to say that The Old City: Leviathan is a bad game; after all, if it were, I wouldn't be recommending it, now would I? The problem is that the games greatest strength is also it's greatest weakness: the writing.
The Old City: Leviathan is as much a game as it is a book. There's a lot of text here. Solomon's Notes tend to have a rather circular nature, with the occasional horrible tendency to have a lot written to say very little. While true that one could chalk up the writing style as a character quirk, it doesn't make reading the notes any less arduous of a task, at times.
Speaking of horrible character quirks, let's speak of Jonah, the character you play as and the one that narrates the game: while what he has to say tends to be interesting, and far less circular than Solomon, it's not uncommon for Jonah to say things in a cryptic manner. I occasionally felt as though what he said was a code to be deciphered rather than just a straightforward thought. WIth Jonah, I felt I spent as much time trying to understand what was said as I did understanding the implications of what was said.
This game is nigh-on unapproachable for most. It might lure you in with pretty scenery, but underneath it all is a narrative that seems to almost be actively opposing your efforts to understand it. It does not want to make your journey easy. Perhaps that was intentional. Perhaps all of the negative points I've listed above are artistic choices, and not necessarily flaws.
Still reading? Good, you might just be a part of the target audience. There's something to this game. Of course, the visuals are solid and the soundtrack is superb, but the writing really is the star of the show here. For all its flaws, the writing is nevertheless interesting. The island and its inhabitants have a strong sense of identity, of realness, which contrasts fantastically with some of the surreal elements of Jonah's fragmented sanity. I wanted to know what happened. By the end, I wanted to know what was in the old city.
But I don't know what was in the old city. Perhaps that's for the best. I think Jonah would agree with me.

While I say I recommend this game, I do not recommend it for everybody.
This game will not suit the person who abhors the idea of reading large books on their own accord. (An actual novella is within the game). This game will not suit the person who doesn't like to be uncomfortable (Major themes of loneliness, depression, mental illness, anxiety, and death are at play). This game will not suit the person who does not like to take their time and truly savor each area (Without exploration, the game becomes fragmented and confusing). This game will definately not the suit the person who is afraid to dislike a protagonist ( Our protagonist is to be questioned, analyzed, and dissected by the player.)
In summary, if you are the person who enjoys investigation and analysis of major works, then this is probably for you. To fully understand will take many hours, but the catharsis is the same as at the end of reading a large novel. The only critic I truly have is that it took awhile for me to configure the settings correctly but in the end it was worth the hassle for the amazing story, landscape, and wonder the game created.

I don't know what it is about The Old City: Leviathan. The initial pretentiousness should have, as with other games before, put me off. The lack of typical gameplay should have put me off. The slow pace, cryptic story and short length should absolutely put me off.
And yet, none of this mattered. The Old City has grown to be one of my favourite games of all time. It's not the sort of entertainment you'll get from an intense online shooter, or a fast paced game of Hotline Miami, but is instead akin to seeing a beautiful landscape. In essence, The Old City is more of a walk-in painting than it is game, but I couldn't say that any painting left me thinking as much as this game did.
The visuals are stunning. The story isn't so ambiguous it feels unfinished, in fact it had me enaged right up until the end, and afterwards had me searching the community hub for answers. It left me intrigued, and I think that's a good thing. If you're looking for an intense, blood-pumping experience, this isn't it.
However, I personally think it's great for what it is. 8.5/10

These materials also stay at the planet you earned them, so you have to transport them to planets with higher ranked mechanics if you want to use them there. More needless grinding in other words, and this ruined the experience for me.

It's not often I am disappointed so quickly about a game so pretty looking.
The premise sounds great; one hit kills, fast paced bullet-hell-like combat. Core gameplay works well enough, nothing to write home about but I could see myself getting some good fun out of it.
But it doesn't take long for the major issues to pop up, and from that moment the game becomes an excercise in frustration with the occasional fun to be had inbetween.
The camera is a gameplay element in itself, intentionally. You will often (very often) have to rotate your camera around to see where you're going and who's shooting at you. At times the level design goes out of its way to intentionally obscure your view, and especially in the middle of combat, when bullets are flying everywhere and enemies are swarming in every direction, you will be forced to constantly spin the camera around in a futile attempt to keep track of what is happening around you.
It's every bit as fun as it sounds. Which is to say it's not, at all.
The driving sections are borderline broken, with the bike physics being unable to reliably handle a slope without spinning out of control and the constant danger of either falling off the map or getting your bike stuck in the scenery if you don't hit a jump at the right speed, which you're not going to know without plenty of trial and error.
To potential buyers I say: tread carefully. Do not be blinded by the pretty visuals and understand that you will possibly have to try really hard to get some enjoyment out of this, and for that I can't personally recommend it.

Half of this review has been chopped to fit on Steam.
.
I’ve been following this game since its first appearance on Greenlight. It’s published by Mode 7, the devs of my all time favourite game Frozen Synapse. I used to watch Paul’s many Tokyo 42 videos, including his ‘Cop Drop Daily’ where he would try to beat his best level, and I could hardly contain myself, everything about it looked awesome. When the game was finally released and I got my hands on it I was so excited a little bit of wee came out.
[snip]
I recently watched John Wick 2 with Keanu Reeves. This game is exactly like that.
This is like a mini game. If you kill too many civilians a police hover wagon will descend and drop 2 police. This is Level 1... [snip]
You can do Cop Drops whenever you like, just for fun or challenge, but for me they are usually triggered when I’m desperately trying to kill my ‘Nemesis’. You see, at the end of some missions you’re notified that your Nemesis is after you. This can turn out to be any of the civilian population wandering around, and frequently you get murdered immediately by a Nemesis who suddenly appears within 2 millimetres of you and slices you. This tends to make you paranoid and I’ve taken to shooting any civilian who comes near me in case it’s my Nemesis, and hence the triggered Cop Drops. I have managed to bag a few Nemeses(?) though, my ratio is probably around 50/50.
[snip]
In this game there’s more than one way to skin a cat, as they say. The challenge is to work out the best way to do it, and I often have to try several different plans to find the best way.
I’ve never experienced anything like it. It’s as crazy as a box of frogs, seriously. Right from the start of the game you’re confronted by a bewildering array of buttons, options, menus… Every single feature of the controller is used for something, and even those things have sub-things. After many hours of play I still forget how to do stuff and find myself mashing all the buttons trying to accomplish something seemingly simple.
The first time I played I used a Steam controller. DO NOT ATTEMPT THIS UNDER ANY CIRCUMSTANCES! The aim is totally impossible with the right glide-pad, which does not go into strafe mode, instead it thinks it’s the mouse and my cursor was veering wildly all over the place while a gang of punks rushed at me, guns blazing. It’s also useless for sniping because you can’t accurately position the shot. I’m not ashamed to say, after many attempts at this early mission, I rage-quit and refused to play for another 2 weeks.
When I ventured back I tried it with mouse/keyboard. It was a little better, aiming with the mouse is the most accurate but it’s still awkward to strafe in the heat of battle when they’re coming at you. WASD movement isn’t ideal and you’re also having to contend with keystrokes to change the camera view. Way too much to handle.
Another hiatus ensued, then I finally took the plunge and ordered an Xbone controller specifically to play this game with a proper right-stick. This turned out to be the best method. It’s great for twin-stick strafing in tight situations and it’s also not too bad for positioning shots when sniping, although I do still reach for the mouse sometimes for this job.
There is a special place in Hell for whoever came up with the motorbike missions. That thing is impossible to control, and you’re expected to fire shots while doing it. Being an actual biker myself this is especially painful to behold.
There are some easy missions (find the cat for example) but they’re mostly very difficult. On the flip side, this makes them rewarding and satisfying when you beat them.
The difficulty of the missions is exacerbated by the tricky controls (see above). There’s an isometric camera view which turns in increments so you’re either looking straight or diagonally, always from above, from one of eight angles. More often than not, buildings and other obstacles obscure your view and this can be especially frustrating in the heat of battle while you’re already trying to control two sticks with enemies swarming at you, and now you have to think about pressing your shoulder buttons to change the camera angle. I’ll never get used to it, I usually try to set the most useful angle at the start of a battle and then hope for the best.
There are waypoints dotted all over the place in the form of vending machines. You can only use them when you’re not being chased but they are very useful for completing missions one portion at a time.
Just look at these screenshots. Aren’t they just fabulous? The pink/blue pill logo is a brand that a real global company would give their right arm for, don’t you think? The sharp, clean vector graphics, pastel colours and interesting little secret items littered all over the place make this a great world to explore. There’s a distinct cat theme going on. I love cats. You can even collect them and deploy them to track down elusive prey. Another thing that warrants a mention is the comical running style, all knees and elbows, with oversize quiff haircuts wildly bouncing around. It’s hilarious when you get a conga line of them chasing after you sometimes.
The rhythmic electronic music suits the environment perfectly, and it changes as you move around different areas of the map. It’s one of those rare games where the music is actually worth listening to and enhances the experience. Top marks.
They’ve said it’s on the way but meanwhile, for those (very few) of you who might be interested, I’ve tried running it a) via Wine-steam (or standalone Wine-Tokyo42) – graphics had thin stripey lines but were generally good, but you can’t run Big Picture so you can’t set up the controller, and b) via Linux-steam, linking to Wine-Tokyo42 – Big Picture/controller sorted, but graphics are fuzzy and some areas of the world are inexplicably obscured by thick clouds making it unplayable. Weird. So in conclusion, I’ll have to wait for the proper Linux version.
The interface looks pretty slick but unfortunately I haven’t found anyone online in any of the 3 available regions so far. I don’t mind, the single-player campaign is more than enough to keep me occupied.
There is just so much content here. There are secrets, new mechanics, huge varieties of gameplay and replay value up the wazoo. The midrange price, in my opinion, is too low. You get more than your money’s worth here.
There are 19 achievements. The first 4 are quite easy but then global completion takes a nose dive down to single figures and before you even get halfway it’s below 1%. As I said, this is a TOUGH game!
No trading cards yet. Usually I don’t care what a badge looks like, I just go for the numbers for level increase, but in this case I would dearly love to display a Tokyo 42 badge on my profile so please get onto it devs!
Steam Cloud available which I will hopefully get to use later on when I transfer my progress to Linux!

I'm a toe-dip in. This may be useful to new players. It plays as a puzzle-shooter within a directional 3-D environment. Camera rotates on an eight-point star (probably favourable to controller play) and player jumps in a Sonic style (directional while mid-jump). Use this to negotiate building jumps to reach objectives. Luckily there are many save points so far so the death falls off the map aren't so punishing. I like the camera style as it gives the sense of some impassionate surveiller (the narrator or a murderous voyeur). I bought a weapon from a flying sushi-mobile vendor but also got weapons from a random drop-point (similar to an isometric Sonic-the-Hegdehog-style powerup). PC controls are clunky but weapon selection pauses so mid tactical choices are possible.  My first shoot-out was disastrous but that was down to me. On third attempt I enjoyed flanking the b******** and began to feel the skill involved/using cover etc. Enemy using grenades felt a bit end-boss-like in a platformer but you can too.  This is basically a clever 3-D platformer. I like the hat-tips to B-movie 1980's 3-D platformers and games like Syndicate. It's exciting to see where the stealth-play goes and the feeling of getting dumped straight into the story is fun. As I say, I've played less than an hour but this taste is for prospective players due to a little too much stress getting started but I really love the direction and the enthusiasm/mania of the opening segments. I recommend exploring this plush, clinical Tokyo but I'm not sure if I should check my ammunition yet :)

I like this game but it direly needs a Crusader Kings 2 or Stellaris style vassal/sector system so that I can hand off huge chunks of my empire to the AI to manage. Picking individual buildings and tax rates for 6 cities is fun, but doing the same for 60 is a tedious micromanagement nightmare. Which sucks because otherwise there's a lot to like about the game even if the AI is completely incompetent and falls over at the first sight of cavalry. Cavalry can disengage and charging gives you massive bonuses to melee combat so you can easily bait and cycle charge huge enemy blobs to death.
Again, other than that it's pretty good. The logistics system is neat -- supply carts and civilian units more generally need to be capture only, having them killed by ranged attacks adds obnoxious micro -- and the combat model works pretty well. It definitely feels like more of an operational game than a tactical one.I think it'd benefit from moving the scope slightly higher up and removing the insane benefits from flanking and charging.

Hegemony III: Clash of the Ancients is a rather enjoyable game, for me, only when played in small doses. This is due to the game itself, which is just a massive amount of repetitive content. The game is entertaining at first, but eventually dissolves into a dissatisfying case of rinse and repeat. The repetitiveness that occurs later in the game could possibly be resolved with new gameplay mechanics or just new things to do in the game; however, since I only frequent the Unification of Italy scenario, the constant sense of boredom may actually be nonexistent in the Eagle King DLC or the second scenario that comes with vanilla. This issue could also be resolved by downloading mods; however, since I can not successfully enable mods for some reason, this statement is only a guess.
The point I'm trying to make is that I enjoy the game, but since it is largely just rinse and repeat gameplay, I don't enjoy long sessions of the game. Because of this, I can not recommend someone buy the game unless they can bear repetitive gameplay and can get it on sale.

Hegemony 3 is an overall improvement compared to the old titles in the franchise.
It has a 8-9/10 solid micromanagement system for the economy and logistics that outshines even TW franchise, though it needs an automation option for late game as you will have too many cities to manage yourself.
Combat system is acceptable, 7/10. Units have morale and level and you can promote your vets to generals.
Diplomacy is still as basic as the old titles with little improvements 6-7/10. You only buy peace with your neighbors so that you can destroy them later. There are more historical/fictional trigger events than what the old titles had, that will keep you busy though.
Music is okay-ish, 6/10. I prefer the Hegemony Gold's soundtrack more. H3's soundtrack won't leave you any significant impression.
Scenarios and contents are various, 8/10. You have tons of maps and eras in the ancient Italy to choose from. And mods will get you going for even longer.
Overall, the game knows its strength and weakness. It shines when it needs to. It strikes exactly the spot where many franchise avoided. It could've risen to the level of Crusader king franchise even, as there're so many potentials for further development. All in all, if you're fan of grand strategy games with a taste for governing rather than commanding, this game will hit your bullseye. I've spent hours trying to maximize the value out of my messy logistic network to squeeze out an extra piece of gold. I've spent nights calculating the best course of action, befriending whom and attacking whom first. It's that great of a game. I recommend you to give it a try if you're a long time hardcore strategy fan.
FINAL VERDICT: 7/10

Pros:
-	Strong overarching story
-	Characters are interesting and more complex than they seem at first sight
-	Nice artwork (not particularly innovative, but professionally done outside of a few awkward proportions)
-	Expressive VA cast
-	The protagonist has a defined character and her own deep-seated emotional issues (unlike the blank slates found in many other otome games)
-	Evokes a wide range of emotions
Cons:
-	The writing/translation. It’s certainly a localization and not just a computer translation, but there are a lot of typos, mixed names, repetition, and awkward phrases.
-	3/5 guys will do things that are off-putting; how you feel about them individually will depend on your personal tolerance levels and preferences
-	Though the protagonist avoids one otome game cliché, she does fall into another: being really clueless about love

After completing all the routes and the bonus story, the whole of Dandelion feels greater than the sum of its parts. Most people would be able to find at least one character they can connect with, and the story has more complexity and emotional weight than the premise suggests.
I just wish more care had been taken with the prose and translation, which hold back what is otherwise an entertaining, professionally made visual novel. Nonetheless, it is one of the more ambitious and well-made otome games available in English, so I would recommend it if you are interested in the genre.

I was gifted this game by a friend a week or so ago, and cringed when it popped up in my gifts tab. I thought to myself "why would this kid spend ten dollars on a weeb game just to make me cringe a little bit?" Unfortunately for me, "a little bit" was a huge understatement. I load up the game and am met with a extremely cringey transition, and the words "PRESS SPACE TO PLAY" appear on my screen. At this point, I could feel my organs begin to fail, but am kept alive by the fairly catchy beat of the song in the background. I push space, and the cringe hit me all at once.
The catchy song turned into some f**king J-pop sh*t, and the title screen appears showing some anime girls with at least 90 lens flares in the picture. A high pitch voice tells me "Welcome to Pixel Puzzles 2: Anime!", and that's when I knew what had to be done.
I ran downstairs, and quickly grabbed some bleach, and a half empty bottle of Antifreeze. I ran back upstairs into my kitchen, opened the cupboard, and grabbed a large Coca-Cola glass. I began to mix the Antifreeze and bleach together into a nice delicious beverage. The glass was about three-quarters of the way full when I stopped. I then reached down under the kitchen sink and pulled out a couple Cyanide tablets. I dropped them both into the mixture I had just created, and listened to them sizzle as they dissolved. Satisfied with my creation, I quickly ran to the fridge and grabbed a freshly bought Kiwi. I took a knife, cut the Kiwi in half, took the half slice, and cut it again. I put the quarter slice of Kiwi onto the side of the glass to add a nice decoration, and began to down the toxic mixture.
I finished the glass, and I stood there surprised at the fact that I was still alive. In fact, I didn't feel sick at all. I was completely fine.
But that's when things got way worse. I heard the voice again. "Welcome to Pixel Puzzles 2: Anime!" I wish that was all, but it kept repeating itself over and over. I then saw my walls change into the design of the title screen. I fell to the ground, blinded by all the lens flares in the picture, I was defeated.
I am broken now. I sit here writing this review begging you not to play this game, and if you gift this to one of your poor, unsuspecting friends you are a terrible person. The voices won't stop.

Hatoful Boyfriend at first seems like a little bit of senseless fun, and of course at first it is. If you come into it looking for more you will be dissapointed, but if you are not you may find yourself a pleasant* surprise.
Just like in the first game, "Hatoful Boyfriend: Holiday Star" starts off a little slow and is a silly game just for messing around and enjoying yourself. The story however progresses in the fourth chapter, where the tone changes drastically from senseless fun to a more serious story. You tend to forget that the characters here are birds, and if you have played the last game you can make some very interesting connections.
I would reccomend playing the first game first, but keep in mind that until the BBL route in the first game and the fourth chapter in Holiday Star, you may need some patience to get to the good stuff.
I personally found the first part a little boring, and even started to wonder if it had all been worth my time. The lack of options reminded me of the BBL route minus the tension and atmosphere so I was a little unhappy, but I kept going and managed to discover that the way that these games work is consistant. It gets good at the end. Sure, it is also largely up to personal taste if you like the sort of story it presents when it "gets good" but for me it was certainly worth the patience.
If an upgrade to "Dove, Actually" becomes possible from having the normal edition, I'll be putting it on my wishlist.
TIP: During chapter 4 save your game when you remember! Wrong choices end in an instant game over and if you haven't saved you have to start the chapter again. I failed at every option the first time each of them showed up and It was really annoying.
*by pleasant I mean it hurts but it's good.

Rating - 64/100
I have no idea what this game was about. I am a HUGE fan of other walking simulators like Dear Esther, and I have spent dozens upon dozens of hours trying to from a unified theory of what that game was about, but I am completely lost about The Old City, and I have no idea where to start.
The story hits tons of biblical references, such as Jonah and the whale, Solomon, and various others, but I don't have the slightest clue as to what the meaning of it all is. It's strange, and metaphorical to the bone, but where I felt like Dear Esther's meaning was just beyond my grasp, I haven't the slightest clue what The Old City was trying to convey.
It could be that the game was just simply not meant for me, but I found the story to be completely nonsensical, and really meaningless. Essentially, it felt like an 8th grader writing a story that is trying to sound deep, but really is utterly beyond comprehension. Being hard to understand is not a sin as long as there is something meaningful there for those that dig. If, however, there is nothing deeper, and the plot is just incomprehensible, then that is a major failing.
I really wanted there to be something more to The Old City, but either I completely missed it, or it is not there. There was a rich backstory, talking about 3 different factions of humans, but nothing was resolved in any satisfactory way. Were the different factions real? Is the story about humanity after a post-apocalyptic fall? Was everything an allegory? Was the Leviathan a metaphor for the world, or was everything happening on a micro-scale within a human body? I couldn't answer any one of those questions, and where I had a solid idea of what Dear Esther meant, I was left with nothing but questions when The Old City's credits rolled, and no desire to find the answers.
As I mentioned before, being hard to understand is not a sin. Being completely beyond comprehension is.
I have no idea who this game is for, realistically. I was raised with a strong belief in the bible, and while I'm not a staunch believer in it now, I have read both testaments in their entirety at least 5 times. I am extremely familiar with the stories of Jonah and Solomon, but I can't make sense of this game's plot. It's as if someone just used those well-known names as an excuse for "this story is deep".
On the plus side, the game world is FANTASTICALLY designed, and I was awe-struck on a regular basis as I trudged through the world. It is at times beautiful, at times peaceful and calm, and at other times disturbing and unsettling. I was never completely comfortable, and I never knew what was coming around the bend. Perhaps that was the point of it all, but as mentioned before, I have no idea what the main point of the game was, so I couldn't tell you.
What I can say is that if you are looking for a deep, hard-to-understand game with a fantastically-designed world, you should check this one out. Don't expect any sort of satisfying resolution, but if you're a fan of wide-open endings that you can project yourself on to, you may find something here to enjoy. I am a huge fan of story-driven walking simulators, but this one was rather underwhelming to me. Perhaps I missed the entire point, or perhaps I simply played it wrong, but I did still enjoy my time in the world of the Leviathan, even if the resolution wasn't satisfying.

In my opinion, this game was amazing. I purchased this off of a Steam Sale because I was a little skeptical (which I would recommend because this game is not for everyone). It is short game, but should be given time for full immersion and discovery (for me, it took 11 hours). There is no objective but to explore and discover as you please. While it is not totally free roam and directed towards a singular path, there are areas that are easy to miss if you are not careful. Even some subtle but interesting and sometimes amazing details. The environment has moments of beauty and moments of creepiness thanks to the amazing visuals and perfectly timed ambient. The true value I found in this game is the story. There are a lot of philosophical elements and analogies that are very interesting. As you read through a variety of notes and explore new areas, you learn more things about the world around you and follow the intriguing stories of a few specific characters. Sure, you are not given a final big reveal of everything, but the game doesn't leave you empty handed either, provided you journeyed through this game right. It has room for interpretation, which is something that I value.
Like I said, this game is not for everyone. I would recommend this game for those who enjoy exploration games, reading, philosophical elements, and an open ended yet full story.

This review is on behalf of the “The Twin Stick Shooter Aficionado” group. “Broken Arms Games” contacted us via Steam and provided us with two free keys for testing.
It is with genuine regret that at this time we are unable to recommend this game.
Despite it's many issues we have found much to enjoy in ATOMINE, however it's current flaws and bugs are too many and currently leave us no other choice...
We would happily return to this game and reconsider our current view if any significant updates are made to it in the future!
Starting with the good, the visual style is nice as is the story and setting in which the battles take place. It's an original and well executed concept in this regard!
The controls are fluid and responsive, the shooting is suitably joyous, and the levelling up via modules(not perfect, see Gameplay issues below) at special points throughout each map serve both the game and it's theme well.
There is a good variety of weapons, upgrades and ships on offer. The slightly RPG feel introduced via these is something that works well!
A nice variety of enemies and original ideas are present throughout and helped to sustain our interest during our time with ATOMINE.
Now to some of the less positive things we encountered during our roughly four hours of combined play time...
I) Windows timeout during game start up, it recovered from this!
II) Several freeze ups during play, lasting from around one to ten or more seconds each time, again the game always managed to recover.
III) Level exit gates not triggering, caused by the kill counter freezing at “1”, only an exit to the main menu and a restart of the level via “Continue” corrected this bug.
IV) Enemy drops floating around strangely in the air.
V) Ship lost ability to shoot. Despite trying every button on the controller(and mouse), in the hope that it may have switched itself to a different control scheme, nothing worked. The “exit to menu” solution mentioned above was the only fix for this issue too.
I) Unbalanced difficulty throughout.
The
enemy in the game that provided any substantial challenge was the first Boss, a long and tedious battle that can only be described as a major difficulty spike.
The underlying causes of this spike are the boss's lack of visual cues for it's attacks, overly generous health bar, it's black rotating shields being hard to see against the black background, and most annoying of all the player ship speed being far too slow to consistently dodge the spinning lasers(which frequently change both direction and speed...).
This boss accounted for all but two of one of our testers deaths, with him only getting past it twice, the second time he went on to complete the entire game with ease(barring replays and unlocks). The rest of the games Bosses all fell on his first attempt with the final Boss being by far the easiest of the lot, offering up almost no resistance at all and taking only a matter of seconds to destroy...
II) Poor AI and path finding on the regular stage enemies. They often get stuck behind level structures, most notably at the side of doors leading into a room.
On many occasions, if you keep your distance, they will stop moving and attacking altogether. When this happens you can just sit there, in the same position, and shoot them until they expire...
III) Enemies can spawn on top of your ship.
IV) Random module options offered at upgrade points, some really are much better than others and this will possibly dictate your success/failure more than your actual ability at times.
V) Hard to see what is coming if you are travelling towards the bottom of the screen, the lower view is too restrictive.
VI) Level structures can obscure your view, the later stages long(red coloured) corridors being the worst encountered as it makes some of the enemy projectiles impossible to see.
I) The menu's both in game and on the main pages were problematic...
One of us used an Xbox 360 pad and found the menu's have almost no dead zone. Getting the menu to stop rotating through the options at speed was a constant irritation.
The other used an Xbox One controller and found the bindings to be utterly bizarre.
II) A ridiculous camera shake effect, we thought it was a bug at first. Thankfully this
be turned off in the menus!!!
III) We thought the secret rooms were a missed opportunity. Generally small and offering up little if any challenge. We thought it might have been better if they were super hard optional challenges, more like the bonus rooms in Smash TV for example.
IV) It's maybe a little light on content(stages wise), a single complete run will take around one hour(a little over for us due to a bug requiring an exit and restart). Without the barrier provided by the first boss we might well have polished this off in under two hours...
Despite all this there really is something to like about ATOMINE, we have played many games that we have enjoyed far less.
We really do hope that the developers remain active, this game
have real potential and we hope they put in the time to make it reach that potential!
However it would be irresponsible of us to recommend ATOMINE in it's current state as it feels like an Alpha build rather than a finished product...
Unfortunately there is nothing in this update to warrant a change in our view of Atomine at this time. Most of what is said above still applies!
Noticeable Fixes :
i) The controllers now have a decent dead zone(360 pad) and bindings(XBone pad)!
ii) The first boss seems to have less health.
Bugs :
i) The freeze up bug no longer locks up the game for several seconds, instead it now carries on running but at an incredibly low frame rate until it recovers, you are left playing almost blind during this time.
ii) The “Immortal enemy” bug has been added. All affected enemies no longer take damage meaning the stage cannot be completed. A slight variation where the bullets pass through the affected enemies also happened.
An exit to the menu and a restart of the level is the only fix we found(as for many of the previous version's bugs).
iii) The new AI no longer gets caught on door entrances, unfortunately the enemies now file through the doors in an semi orderly fashion to the certain death waiting for them on the other side. The technique of sitting in a room and letting them walk into your fire works very well for the majority of the game.

This mess has a lot of potential, but of course there are massive issues. This review takes a constructive look at this game.
It was only 7 minutes and I finished it, read all possible dialogues.
I understand it was free, but it is completely pointless. There is no message, and I don't count the blatant religious message as a message, because this game handles it very poorly.
I want to support the developer, so I'm leaving a Thumbs Up, but I didn't like it.
Here is why:
A huge problem is the immaturity of it all. You can't take it seriously, and if you aren't supposed to the game still fails on almost all levels except Unity stank. Yes, big, long, eloquent words are used, but that doesn't mean the writing is intelligent. There is no form, all the characters are the same 2D low-res JPEG, there is no substance, the maps and textures are half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and probably not even original. The music is super boring and it's like a 15 second loop. Whoever made the music, if you had a guitar, why didn't you record and mix an actual song instead of a lame melodic string loop? Audacity is free.
The reason I think this could have potential is if there were; Actual choices that affected the story, AND AN ACTUAL STORY. THERE IS NO STORY. THERE IS NOTHING BUT RANDOM DIALOGUE THAT I COULDN'T CARE LESS ABOUT. You have to grab the attention of the reader, get them invested and this falls so flat, It's just pretentious drivel. This is the main problem, there is nothing to hold the experience together.
This game probably took a few weeks to make. If they had spent more time on it. If they made something interesting, with an arc or a point, at least a cohesive plot/point that I care about or at least HELP people care about through the atmosphere, characters, and the writing, the game would be super cool! But it isn't.
And the gameplay is set up like this: Dialogue options with the illusion of choice, and letting specific people into Heaven or Hell. There is no reason you are doing this. Motivation: none. The people you meet might as well be text. It's almost insulting. It is an interesting (while not unique) concept that doesn't even work. God damn it!!!
This is a message to the developer: Don't be discouraged when you see the tsunami of negative reviews. You can learn from your mistakes and build off of them. I just hope you aren't stubborn and toxic. Take the CONSTRUCTIVE criticism, and MAKE A BETTER GAME. I know you can. I can see it through the cracks.
Good luck. And I'm sorry but...

As you can alter your course somewhat while in mid-air, this icon is very helpful to see if you are going to land on a ledge or fall to your death.
But jumping from high point to low point is only a small portion of the challenge.
Your real job is to seek out jobs of assassinating various people for clients.
Some jobs can be very simple, and as long as the subject in question is killed, the client is happy and will reward you.
Other jobs can be very specific as to the type of weapon used and various other objectives that must be met.
Targeting and using the various weapons, which include pistols, rifles, sniper rifles, grenades, rocket launchers, swords and even bananas all have a distinct and pleasant feel to them.
Targeting via shooting weapons is line of site. As long as you have the target lined up and fire, the bullets will follow a straight path to where you aimed.
However, bullets do not travel instantly to the target, so you must time your targets movements so they will be in the same location as the bullets when they arrive.
Melee weapons work as you would expect, be next to the target, and slice and dice before they do.
Grenades and other explosive types have different methods of being deployed and are a pleasure to use.
Once you have taken out a target be prepared to "get lost".
This can be done in several ways.
Your character has the ability to transform their looks instantly, using an energy reserve, which is used each time you change.
Use up your energy reserve and you can not change anymore.
The other caveat is that you must not be seen to change by the enemies pursuing you.
As long as you change out of their sight, and are not in a restricted area, the enemy will not recognize you.
Once you have escaped, you can go to recharging stations and recharge your energy levels or save your game at various save stations.
But you can not save or recharge if you are being pursued, so the challenge can be tough.
There are hundreds of citizens and others all around the city, and if you pull out a weapon in front of them (or an enemy) they will react in different ways.
So it is wise to only deploy your weapons once ready to take down a target.
In addition to the main missions, there is plenty of other things to keep you busy.
You can visit floating weapons ships and purchase new weapons and ammo, you can find hidden Easter eggs that change your appearance (Meow), and you can take side assassin jobs to earn more money and respect.
The more respect you gather, the higher paid jobs you will get.
You can raise your allegiance with on group and lose it with another.
Kill and innocent or mess up an assassin job, and you will lose respect.
There is an underlying story to the entire game, so not everything is what it seems on the surface.
The graphics in this game are just amazingly well done.
Although everything is rather small, the amount of detail to each object is outstanding.
THe world itself may seem rather small at first, but once you complete your first real contract, you will start to see how much there is to the world.
From the clean crisp edges to buildings, to the animated signs, to the numerous people going about their day, Tokyo 42 feels like a living, vibrant city.
Combat effects and explosions fit the aesthetic perfectly and everything feels like a part of this world.
Although the main communication are text messages, you don't really care about the lack of voice overs.
THe readable text is handled like phone text messages and are short enough that the reading does not become cumbersome.
The sounds of the city, the great background music, and the full booms of explosives and gunfire give your ears plenty ot focus on.
I think they made a good choice not using voice overs, as it would be distracting to all the other sounds around you.
I first played with a keyboard and mouse, and while it takes a little getting used to the jumping mechanic, once you learn about rotating the screen to the proper angles for jumps, movement became second nature.
Keyboard and mouse works especially well for timed shots and letting loose grenades etc.
I tried using the Xbox One Controller, and while there are less key commands to worry about, aiming and jumping just didn't feel as controlled or fluid.
I noticed missions that were easy to pass with keyboard and mouse were a lot more difficult to accomplish with the controller.
Overall I was pleasantly surprised by how well this game plays.
I was already liking the look of the game when it was first announced, but I didn't expect the game play to be this fun and addictive.
For the genre it represents (Action, Adventure, Indie, Platformer, Stealth) I give it a:
For game quality in general verses all other types of game genres available, this game gets a very solid
I would recommend this game to anyone who enjoys any of the genres it represents.
Even if you don't like one or two of the genres it uses, it's great enough in the others that you shouldn't care, as it doesn't tie itself to one type of genre too much.
The difficulty can seem rather harsh at first, but once you get used to the mechanics and how the game's AI reacts, you should be able to accomplish most missions easily enough.
Sometimes you will have to really think outside the box to achieve your goals. You can go in guns blazing, and sometimes that really works, but many times you need to watch the guards patrols, and time your movements and attacks accordingly.
It's a treat to see another addictive game being released by Mode 7 and I can't wait to dig into all the aspect of this experience.
There's a lot to see, a lot to do, and plenty of little secrets to find, that the game opens up to you, the more time you put into it.
The extra content coming down the pipe for this game look to be worth the wait as well.

You then kill them to take back this happiness as soul power. The game starts off slowly as you try to become accustomed to this, but then accelerates into you having to manage all of these, as well as ensuring your main objectives are met, to prioritising spending on dungeon improvements or objectives. I blitzed through the campaign and as it is an older game, did not try the multiplayer. Buy this game on sale for a bit of enjoyment, but don't expect to have your mind blown.

Hegemony Gold is my favourite strategy game. I enjoyed playing as Sparta; tearing down the walls of Megalopolis, recapturing Messenia and burning Thebes to the ground. I enjoyed playing as Athens; rescuing the Plateans from certain death, playing cat and mouse with the Persian fleet, protecting Corcyra. This kind of immersion is rare, especially in historical games - Hegemony Gold succeeded like no other.
Hegemony 3 applies this formula to the Italian mainland during the rise of Rome (DLC/mods include Spain & Macedonia ATM). So you can be Rome, capture Veii and be rather nasty to the Sabines, defending your small Republic from northern invasions. Or you can be Phyrrus, the last hope of the Italian Greeks, driven by overarching ambition to confront Rome & create a Greek empire in the West. Just like Hegemony Gold, it is your choice.
PS Some of the "do not reccommend" reviews are by players who were defeated by
A)spikes in difficulty (some factions are tougher than others, with geography protecting them)
B)the repetition (conquering huge maps containing dozens of towns can be monotonous, an interest in history helps greatly with this)

There are so many reasons for this game to succeed, but it fails to meet the heights it promises.
After multiple attempts to work through the problems i have to admit that it was just my hope that with more experience, with more patience i would find it enjoyable... alas, it was nothing but a wasted hope.
It is a city builder, empire, trade and resource manager... and the bones of the game are excellent, conquer territory, take over the resources and use the soldiers of your enemies as slaves to produce your food, wood and income.
Where it fails is the unforgiving pacing.
For example, you might be at war with 2 different nations, each on the other side of your territory, neither of them allied... yet so many times if you go to attack one, the other launches a powerful attack! Radios were not invented yet (another 3000 years to go) but somehow your enemies work together to launch attacks at your weakest points.
OK, you think, what i need is more dakka... so you build up your armies... nope, now winter comes around and SMASHES you with starvation because of the armies appetite.
OK, lets drop the food requirements of the cities... Nope, their morale drops too and they go into rebellion...
So you rush off to put down the rebellion, and at the exact moment you are
too far away from the border you were protecting... guess what... another invasion force comes barrelling in!
Wash, rinse, repeat.
Eventually your supply of reinforcements starts to drop and the invaders make short work of their target cities.
Now this would be fine if it was happening to the AI cities... but their magic-radios (to their non-allied battle partners) also seem to spew out food and reinforcements as well.
There are so many moments when you look at this game and think how cheap the AI is... there is no fun in a constant (and i mean CONSTANT) tidal wave of enemy attacks as you are hamstrung by the seasons in a way the AI is not.
In individual combats you have the upper hand, no doubt about it... but even this is 'fixed' by the AI just spawning more units or launching a flank attack out of the blue.
Diplomacy consists of paying a huge cash blackmail to a faction that will suddenly backstab you anyway "because reasons" (by this stage of the game you are so sick of the sound and message box spam from constant attacks that you no longer care enough to read what BS reason your close friend has made up to justify attacking you)
It COULD be a great game... hell, even putting a half-speed option in there could make it less aggravating.
Funnily enough, the game only has Pause or Full Speed but the Menu system is a tedious bunch of pointless slow screen transitions that make even the Menu frustrating as hell!
But in the end that is what it comes down to... how long you can stand watching the game chip away at your willingness to put time in to it.
FYI i also played with some of the Mods from the Workshop, just to take the edge off... even that didn't help - dont waste your money or time on this rubbish.

I have put hours into this strategy game, have played from a little rome to owning a qaurter of italy, so far this game has yet to let me down on my strategic itches, logistics and tactics all play a MASSIVE part of this game. Exploration is fun because you never know which area of the map will offer a new challenge to overcome, where you place a defensive fortification matters more than having the biggest army around. While you're off fighting your enemies you have to remember to keep your economy on track, winter will cost you food and during summer you need to be building up a stockpile of food or your people will go hungry in the winter (fields grow slower, fish are caught slower, you go from fully positive food stockpiling to fully negative).
I have truly never seen a strategy game this in-depth and this challenging and mind-boggling in a sense of tactics, logistics and combat, strategy in a battlefield is as important as scouting out your enemy for weaknesses or to know what you can do to fight them off. Hegemony III is easily one of my favorite large-scale city and empire builders in the gaming industry, yeah you can't build your city specifics or build anywhere you want, it's very controlled there but that doesn't kill its fun. This isn't meant to be a city builder specifically but more like a war theatre simulator, economics, everything comes into play with this game, from moving units on the larger scale theatre map to commanding them down on the strategic map, which is extremely seamless, this game has a LOT of time to offer.
I truly look forward to more games like this, maybe even bigger! i hope they keep true to what Hegemony III Did, maybe able to scale it up with better animations, but THIS IS A GAME WORTH BUYING if you like a challenging theatre-esk styled strategy game with much needed thought to tactics, logistics and Economy down to individual cities happiness.
CONS: I will honestly say that the micromanaging can be an issue in this game, it will keep you moving back and forth between cities constantly pausing the game to make tweaks here and tweaks here. This isn't a truly bad CON to this game though as it does challenge me to manage my cities especially until i get my research up to assimilate cities into my growing kingdom/empire.
Another CON was how hard it was for research to progress, however I do see it as more of a good thing too as it gives you a scope of technological size and the time-frame of the game, as you are conquering you have to be smart about what buildings to place in which cities where and it does make for a sometimes strenuous activity while you are trying to also defend your borders and move troops.
One last CON is the lack of multiplayer, this game would be interestingly fun to play with a friend, hopefully that's going to be a thing for Hegemony III
All-in-all this is a MUST HAVE for the strategy geeks out there, i know you're out there so stop hiding!

There are a few bugs, but none are game breaking and are easy to ignore. In the end it's a great indie strategy game that is worth every penny.
7/10-- Keep up the good work Longbow

Atomine is an interesting game. You control a little box that magically spits out lasers or rockets or blobs of explosive goo, while dodging in and out of enemies and projectiles like a standard twin-stick shooter, while choosing from small upgrades and finding unlocks along the way.
It has a great aesthetic, it uses mostly monochomatic colors and looks very clean and futuristic.
The gameplay is simple and fast, but the main issue by far is the camera. You will constantly have no clue what you are about to literally just run into because the camera only shows a few angles well, and the others have close to zero visibility at all. I routinely run into enemies and bullets that could have been easily avoided if you could just see where you were going.
It's a decent title. There isn't very much variety in the weapons and powerups so replaybility was fairly low for me, but I was happy with the few hours I did spend with it.

NOTE: This game was given to me by the developer for review purposes. This did not influence my review in any way.
ATOMINE (all caps) is an action-packed twin-stick shooter with rogue-like elements from indie developers, Broken Arms Games Pty Ltd.
In ATOMINE, you take the role of a hacker intent on breaking into a nuclear missile system through the National Army Database. The details of the plot are not completely clear to me -- I'm not sure if you're trying to take over the missile system or prevent others from doing so -- but in any case, you need to gradually work your way each system, defeating the defences and progressing to the next system via a backdoor.
Graphics - The graphics in ATOMINE are stylised, with a somewhat clichéd 3D virtual reality feel to them, but don't let that put you off. Your avatar in the computer systems you're hacking is a cube with various decorations, depending on the particular version of software you're running and the modules you have attached: V1.0 software with a single-shot laser looks like a cube with some coloured edges and a single weapon mount, whereas V2.0 software with a quintuple-mount missile launcher looks decidedly more "bad♥♥♥♥♥quot;.
Enemies come in various shapes and glowing colours, but there isn't that big a range in each system, which is a bit disappointing. The systems themselves have different 'themes', which is pretty cool, but they do get a bit samey-after a while, even with the procedural generation. Some decorative objects and interfaces in the systems would have provided welcome flavour, as well as made the levels look a bit more varied.
Weapon effects are excellent and varied, and the particles in the game look simply fantastic. Destroyed system defences leave little 'bits' lying around, too, which are a nice touch. The interface is stylised and rather elegant, but confusing when you first play. Bear with it, though; it becomes easy to use once you know what you're doing.
The camera is at a fixed angle, which is fine, but also at a fixed rotation, making for some hard-to-see parts on some levels. It's a shame the developers didn't include an option to rotate using the shoulder buttons (controller) and Q/E (keyboard).
There's a reasonable choice of graphics options that includes toggles for the 'screen shake' and 'glitch' effects. My advice: turn screen shake off, but leave glitch on. It's distracting sometimes, but gee it looks nice!
Sound - The music in the game seems to only be one track, unless it's a number that all blend in together exceptionally well. Regardless, it's a really good thumping sound track that sounds nice turned up loud, and reminds me of the opening track from the first Blade movie (a New Order remix, maybe?).
Sound effects and system voices are good, too, but there's a big problem: the volume controls don't work! I was able to change the sliders in the settings, but pressing 'confirm' just restore them back to how they were: everything at 100%. This means the thumping music and loud blasts are way too loud to hear the more subtle effects, or the system voices.
Gameplay - ATOMINE's gameplay basics are the same as every other twin-stick shooter: dodge incoming fire while aiming your weapons at your enemies independent of your movement. The game is played from a 3/4 top-down view, with a fixed camera that follows your avatar around each computer system. And ATOMINE includes rogue-like elements, such as permadeath and procedural level generation as well, which are also becoming very common to twin-stick shooters.
Your hacking attacks on the computer systems take the form of destroying the defences with various weapon modules that you can compile into your avatar's program, along with stat increases to damage, range, shot lifetime, and precision (D, R, L, and P). Destroyed enemies drop little glowing green code chunks. Collect enough of these and your software progresses to a new version. They sometimes also drop energy to replenish your own, which gets very quickly depleted when you are hit.
Each level is procedurally generated, but within each system they do tend to look very much alike: not enough variation in the pieces that make up the levels, I think. Each level includes a little code repository where you can pick up a good chunk of code, and also a darkened room where you can be sure to find a free module to attach to your avatar. This latter room also lets you choose your new version reward (one per version you increase) from a random selection of four options, as well as choose which four weapon, shot type, fire rate, and bonus modules you wish to use, if you have them.
There are plenty of new modules and enhancements to unlock through playing, as well as to buy with BitCoins, which you earn slowly while you play (and can also collect along the way as level-up bonuses).
And that's basically it. When you've fought your way through enough levels in the each system, you encounter a boss. Beat it, and the backdoor opens to the next-higher system on your way to the nukes.
ATOMINE includes great controller support. Unlike many other twin-stick shooters, which require you to press a trigger button to fire, ATOMINE takes the 'pure' twin-stick approach: just push the right stick to aim, and the firing is automatic. Hooray! I usually play twin-stick shooters with keyboard and mouse, though, and ATOMINE's support for those isn't quite so good. Mouse sensitivity is too low, making aiming slower than it should be, and there's no aiming line when using keyboard and mouse, so it's actually much harder to aim than with the controller. There's also no support for remapping controls, for any control method.
There are only a couple of issues I feel need mentioning. The first is fairly minor: a weird design decision, allowing enemies to shoot you when you're inside the module selection screen. It would be much better if this paused the action, like it does in most other games.  The other I've already alluded to: the lack of variation. Even with the Steam Achievements, procedural generation, and plethora of unlockables, the game becomes more repetitive than I'd like, sooner than I'd like. The levels within each system are too similar, there aren't enough enemies, and almost all of them are beaten most easily in the same way: by sniping or kiting.
Pros:
+ Nice graphical effects
+ Great soundtrack
+ Good number of unlockables
+ Steam Achievements and Trading Cards
Cons:
- Not enough variation in enemy types, levels, or required tactics
- Volume control doesn't work
- Minor control issues
I'm always on the lookout for a rogue-like twin-stick shooter that can topple Neon Chrome from its pedestal. I'm sad to say that ATOMINE still isn't it; it just doesn't have the variation of that classic. It is, however, a very good game, with plenty of replayability, some nice graphical effects, and a thumping soundtrack.

I found the anime high school tropes fairly uninteresting, and by the time the plot started picking up steam literally at the final hour of the game it transforms into a mecha anime and then ends on a cliffhanger.
One major thing I missed from the earlier Trails games was the expressive 2D portraits for dialogues, which are now replaced by blank-faced dolls of the CG characters which have no personality when speaking. I also felt the NPC stories and such were much less developed and lacking compared to FC and SC, and overall the repetitive nature of the school trips / anime school structure of the gameplay dragged on too long. I hope the second game shakes that formula up the way the ending seems to hint at.
Combat was still the least interesting bit of the game, honestly, and the fact that the player knows more at this point (if they've played the previous Trails games) about what's going on in Zemuria than the main characters makes it frustrating that so little new info or significant development on that point happens in the plot here until literally the final few minutes.
Overall, I have to say this is my least favorite of the Trails games so far, though I'll give the second Steel game a try before I decide whether the series has really jumped the shark for me or not.
For folks invested in the story since FC/SC/3rd, Steel will not build on much of what those games have laid as a story foundation. I'd almost recommend waiting for all 3 of Steel's games to be released before playing them (as maybe together they will progress the story more significantly than just this one does).

Do not think of the first Dungeons game as one where you raise an army of minions or build a dungeon full of death traps for the sole purpose of murdering invading heroes.  You can, but that's not the purpose of the game.  Wanton killing is not the brand of Evil that the Dungeon Lord pursues.  That's too simplistic for him.
It's about designing and decorating a dungeon full of interesting features that heroes can admire.  It's about treasuries that can make thieves lose their caution, libraries that can make wizards forget about the dangers, and constant battles that can make knights get lost in a haze of battle lust.  It's about creating a complex that heroes can admire for its beauty and can feel good about themselves for "conquering".  It's about those invaders not realizing that the place was designed that way, not until the moment when you crush them under the heel of your boot.
It's all about the sin of pride.  Pride over the aesthethics of your dungeon.  Pride over how you've led those stupid heroes by the nose to where you want them to go with the lure of gold, books, and kills.  Pride over how fast you can "fatten them up" before you personally slaughter or capture them for their soul energy.  It's all about showing off how great the Dungeon Lord (you) is in terms of prestige and prowess.
In summary, the game is not about how great you are at training the might of your minions.  It is about you personally beating the crap out of invaders through melee and magic.  It is not about how good you are at designing dangerous deathtraps.  It is about building beautiful complexes that even heroes admire.  It's not about how well you can build an army for conquering the world.  It is about how good you are at bleeding your enemies dry of energy and gold while you pursue your primary goals.  This game is all about you regaining your reputation as being the top Dungeon Lord by showing off your dungeons and your skills.  It is all about... Presentation!

Save your money buy Dungeons ii.  This game is overly complicated and you feel like you aren't really running a dungeon. Also you have to get something archaic called Soul Energy from the Adventurer's which means you have to let them beat up your creatures, steal you gold, etc so their green bars go up before you kill them because they are worth more soul energy that way and you can lock them up in cages to get some extra soul energy also. You also get archaic Prestige points that allow you to build "gimmicks" to occupy the adventurer's and make their soul energy production go up as well. Just finished my first playthrough of this game today, and I loved it.  It has a well-developed backstory for our protagonist and she's relatable and quite ordinary - in the best way possible.   It plunges you into the storyline quickly, so you don't get bored waiting for the game to "start".  The art is gorgeous.  Both animals and humans are insanely adorable visually, and (especially a certain spotted one that captured my heart immediately) insanely adorable emotionally/behaviorally.  :>  They all have their own personalities and quirks that add to their charm, and if the route I played through is any indication, they likely all have backstories worth learning.  I'm certainly satisfied with my choice of romance and experiencing his story.  Honestly, I rather fell in love with him and the protagonist as a pair - they had similar heartbreaks in their pasts and seemed a natural fit together, both able to empathize with and support the other.  I hope the other routes are as fulfilling (although secretly, in my experience the first romance is always the best, otome game or other, since you gravitate toward the one that speaks to
, not the protagonist per se).  That ending, though... ye olde heartstrings be pulled, aye.
One thing I wasn't aware of when I first started playing was that various scenes have Korean voice acting!  Which was an interesting surprise for me, since I'm extremely familiar with Japanese, but extremely unfamiliar with Korean.  Had to train myself to pause a second before furthering the dialog in a voiced scene, just in case there was just a pause in the sentence and not a full stop.  XD
Word to the wise: save often and don't let the pressure get to you.  >:)  Have fun!  I'm sure you'll love it.  <3

Pixel Puzzles 2: Anime belongs to a series of games focusing on jigsaw mechanics on a thematic. The previous ones are about Zombies, Japan or Birds. Here, you'll get images in an anime style - remember, anime is the term often used to describe cartoons from Japan.
The goal is the same: unlock more complicated puzzles (more numbers, more shapes, etc..) and rebuild the picture. You can use bonus if you collected enough fairy dusts, like the right place of the piece, or the complete image shown for a few seconds. While the pieces are floating in a sort of water, they're not necessarily already in the right direction. I mean by that that you'll need to rotate them to find the exact fitting.
I enjoyed the art as it was well drawn, like I've enjoyed the soundtrack. However, while I understand the pseudo-need of putting a fairy in the game, she was speaking too much with her screams or her reflexions. After a while, you just want to make her shut up because her voice is really really striking your nerves.
True, it's a classic jigsaw game but every game in the series is bringing something different: Japan is probably the basic game, UndeadZ added more actions and Birds got a new menu and a new way to bring bonus. Anime is adding rotation and a character to guide you and to help you. However, I can understand those that can be bored by it, as it's a question also of patience. Some puzzles requires really time to be finished and once it's done, the satisfaction is great.
Yeah, I recommend this one. I suppose that the fairy will annoy many of the players but don't let the game being reduced to that. It's still a good moment to pass.

Great puzzle game. Includes 25 anime themed puzzled. Number of pieces are between 60 and 350. In comparison with a previous game (Pixel Puzzles: Japan) they improved a lot of things. For example the floating pieces around your table don't get stucked anymore and the puzzle is saved on exit, but pieces on the table which are not on the correct spot get resettet.
Another great improvement is the special abilities you can use (either show the original image, correct rotation or show correct spot). But the anime fairy which will grant you magic dust is very annoying after a while.
You can disable her, but then you won't get any dust and can't use those special abilities. The HUD element showing your current dust meter yet remains.
The big puzzle with 350 pieces was very hard, not because there were so many pieces and it took a while to get them all places, but the fact that you cannot zoom onto floating pieces. They were so small, my eyes hurt after a while.
Another "eye-hurting"-feature comes with the background. In some images yellow is a very common color. Too bad when the pieces with yellow color a floating on a yellow background, making it very hard to see textures. Especially hard when pieces contain horizontal or vertical lines where another color starts and you think: "oh yeah, an edge piece", but after picking it up it turns out to be something from the middle
Fairy and dust meter are above the floating area, makes it hard to spot the right piece, when those are floating under it.
Although there are still things I didn't like, I can recommend the game.

I'm pretty sure no one expected Hatoful Boyfriend to be as good as it is (me included), but given what the original Hatoful Boyfriend did; how could one expect the sequel to end up?
Unfortunately, not much. Since the previous game had wrapped up just about everybirdie's character arc, there wasn't much room for expansion in the characters. Holiday Star abandons the "pigeon dating simulator" thing for a more linear story. That's not to say it's bad, in fact it reduces the redundant dialogue from replaying the game. But with the branching story gone, it's hard not to feel something was taken.
Sadly, if you've already played the previous game Holiday Star doesn't give you that morbid curiousity that makes you say "this is a weird dating sim"; since the previous game perfectly elaborated the backstory. And without that sense of curiousity, Holiday Star just isn't as mind-blowing as the first game.
While Holiday Star's writing isn't as good as the previous game's, it does make it up with the story. Since Holiday Star has almost no pretenses of being a "pigeon dating simulator", the story focuses less on the character and instead on your bizarre adventures in St. Pigeonations. What Holiday Star has a hard time doing compared to the previous game is to subvert expectations, since the first game blew it's load on that department; there wasn't much Holiday Star could do in that regard.
Also, Holiday Star has the nasty habit of giving you a choice that actually could give you a bad ending and makes you restart the game. This would be fine if Holiday Star was closer to a dating sim, but given the linearity of the game it's easy to forget to save and end up repeating an entire episode. My best advice here is to save if a choice pops up.
Holiday Star is accessible without playing the previous game, but it's still highly recommended that you play the previous game first; just so you'd already be emotionally invested in the characters.
Holiday Star perfectly supplements the previous game's story, but unfortunately that's as much as I can say about it. Think of Holiday Star as a doujin/fanfic that adds the story of the previous game, but without the joy of it being as new as the original.

Great piece of hardware, the learning curve is a little off putting, the best way to learn about the controllers capabilities is to first try to play a game with it, then reconfigure the controller as needed. Don't worry about not having enough buttons, each one can be set to perform multiple functions depending on how long you press the button for. With a few macro's you can easily play an mmo with this. Takes a little bit of time and effort to adjust the controls for an fps, but in the end it will be much better than using a traditional gaming controller.
Yes, it's weird and will take time to get used to, but it has great flexibility in the controls which is where it shines. Don't like the analog stick? Replace the controles with the d-pad. The analog stick does feel like it's in a bad place due to the size of the d-pad, it's not as bad as the n64 controller, but I did prefer to swap it for the d-pad. Not to say that it's unusable or anything, I still use the analog stick for the actions that a d-pad traditionally perform.  The abyx buttons are also in a bad spot, but again that's due to the size of the mouse pad that's on the controller. Which is why I put the buttons I use the least on abyx's.
It's definitely worth it's price tag for it's cabalities, but it does take some time to get used to and will probably change your normal playstyle. If you want to eliminate the need for mouse + keyboard and play everything on a controller then you should give this a try.
