I'm really feeling the urge to review this game. Not something I usually feel. But this game got me thinking, likely as it's designed to.  It challenged the player as a person, and in the end, judged them as the player judged the sinners.
At first, the black cosmic Tagalongs of moral conflict daunted me, especially after the corporatist. But as I progressed, and made more decisions, developing a basic ruleset for who was worthy of redemption or not, I left my fear behind and began entering those portals without a qualm. "Welcome to Heaven" gives a different perspective to a popularly vague dreamy concept. While the setting felt romanticized, the people felt down to earth, crude, and in the case of the man in front of the temple, bossy. I enjoyed the references to to other games, the world itself, however limited, and the complete, refreshing ignorance of what was going to happen next.
This game is far from perfect, of course. The controls are clunky and the story is far too short, so savor every minute of this game while you can. There aren't enough desicions to make before the end of the story arc, and the ending itself isn't sufficiently explained, and left my guessing what I did wrong. The dialogue is simplistic and while the setting(when you include the NPCs within it) is multi-faceted, the characters as individuals are as flat as their rendering. Finally, there weren't enough text choices for the player. I felt that I was merely one part of the creator's brain talking with another part, that I wasn't an autonomous choice-maker but a tool to complete the narrative, which ends without a resolution.
Overall, though it has many flaws, it managed to enchant me and it drove me to play through the game as I would if it was real life, thinking hard about these choices as if real peoples' fates depended on it. With more time to develop, perhaps the game wouldn't feel so rushed. With more resources to develop it, it would feel deeper. Keep in mind, this seems to have been largely the work of one person, and its nature as a thinking game, an essential indie, more than makes up for what it lacks in graphics and controls.
This makes me interested in the creator's work, and I'd even be willing to lend my support, not because I'm looking to influence the story of any future games of theirs, but because they have convinced me that with help, they can make a true masterpiece.

Having played and enjoyed Cities: Skylines (C:S), I thought I would give Cities in Motion 2 (CiM2) a roll since it is from the same publisher.
When you open a new game, you are presented with a very large city with a few demographics maps.  In order to add your first a bus line to the city, you have to first zoom in and place each and every individual bus shelter, and then you have to go back, navigate a web of confusing menus, and finally link the bus stops together with a bus line.  It can take 20-30 minutes of manual labor just to add line.  Subway lines are even worse.  For comparison, in C:S, you simply draw your loop on the city streets, and the game automatically places the bus shelters and routes the vehicles for you.
I was initially drawn to the idea of customizing timetables, which you can't currently do in C:S.  I was thinking that timetables would allow me to do cool things like make timed transfers: have two infrequent buses that arrive at a particular transfer point together to reduce wait time.  Unfortunately, timetables in CiM2 are little more than a way for you to say, "I want more buses on the line during rush hour and fewer in the middle of the day".  I felt that I had very little control over the logistics of making timed transfers.
Another subtle improvement in C:S that makes a huge difference is that you can assign colors to each bus line, but it appears you can't do that in CiM2.
One problem in both C:S and CiM2 is that the speed of the buses is completely incompatible with the time-of-day tracker.  It takes half a day or more in game time for a passenger to travel across the city.  This completely defeats the purpose "morning rush hour" and "evening rush hour", because people who started in the morning are only first getting to their destinations by the time evening rolls around.  Another problem is that the simulation speed is simply too slow; in CiM2 particularly, I should be able to fast-forward super ultra fast and run an entire day in a matter of seconds, but even on my modern Macbook Pro with graphics card, the simulation speed is dog slow and I have to wait minutes to see if my new experimental transit line worked or not.
In short, this here is really the fundamental flaw: instead of giving me a quick and nimble way to draw and experiment with transit lines, CiM2 puts a huge emphasis on visual details of the city that make the game incredibly cumbersome and not enjoyable to play.

I received this controller as a gift from a person who had no idea how to set it up thus thinking it was the worst controller ever.
Best controller I've ever used.
THE  CONFIGURATOR:
The fact that the buttons are fully configurable in more and more ways as Steam drops updates and patches means that it can only get better. The configuration menu is a bit difficutl to understand but once you get the hang of it it's gets easier and the descriptions of what each control option sometimes leaves you even more confused but making the changes on the fly, in game allows you to set a parameter, test it in game, and switch it if you don't like with the press of a single button.
The first game I wanted to set up to play with it was Arma 3. If you're at all familiar with this game, it has a practical use for almost every button on the keyboard. After struggling to learn ExistentialEgg's setup, I for the most part understood the ins and outs of the configurator and can now think of cool additions to add to my controller and quickly add them.
Speaking of ExistentialEgg, the configurator has option for you to pull the game developers recommended controller setup (if they made one), a generic set up for starting a build, as well as, and this is the best part, community made builds. Each game can have its own configurations that you can save. MAKE SURE YOU SAVE YOURS!! What I generally do is look up a popular community build and tweak it to suit my playstyle and needs.
COMPLAINTS:
I wish there was an optional attachment to the left pad to make it feel like, and ultimately work like, a traditional D-pad. The indentions are too shallow for me to feel where the buttons are and in a game were quick reactions are necessary (most fighting games) its hard to find the right direction on the pad.
An option for rechargeable batteries would have been nice. The way they designed the battery placement has one AA on each side, tucked into the hand grips so I don't see a rechargeable option surfacing any time soon.
I also wish there was an option to turn off the controller outside of Big Picture Mode. I understand that this controller was made to go seamlessly with Big Picture but it makes websurfing possible from my couch so no need for Big Picture anymore. Now that I think of it, no wireless controller made by Microsoft, Sony, or Nintendo has ever had a shut off button on it. You either have to turn the entire consol off, wait for the controller to time out and turn off or pull the batteries.
EDIT: TIL that holding the center button for what seems like 5 or so seconds turns it off.
Also, there is an option in the configurator to set one of the buttons to function as a
power off button as well.
OTHER TIDBITS:
The front four buttons do seem a bit small but it might be because I'm used to xbox controllers. The controller does feel natural in my hands. I have over average length fingers which always made PS controllers feel small, but this slides in my hands like magic done right.
The paddle buttons (that's the buttons beneath the hand grips) feel real spongy. While I can feel and hear a very faint click when pulled, sometimes in game I pull them and get nothing forcing me to pull it once or twice more to be sure. Sometimes I'm sure I'm also pulling WAY too hard by the third time.
NOTE TO STEAM:
An option to add audio output to the next version of the controller would be awesome. Right now unless you want to shell out $100+ on a wireless headset to do in game chat or just play your game at midnight so your family still sleeps. All other options are wired. Most gamers that play in the living rooms have a good bit of space between their tv and the couch. having an option to plug the headset directly into the steam controller would be clutch.
ALL IN ALL:
Like I said, best controller ever, virtually limitless options, If you intend on playing not only steam games, but any pc games from the comfort of your couch then this controller is a must!
I'm loving it, along with Steam Link. Jam on any tv in my house, awesome....

There was a point where I'd recommend this game. It honestly pains me to see what has happened to it.
I'd like to say I actually stopped playing Tribes for a long while. I heard they were updating it again, ignored it. Tried playing it again this January. I have a few words as a tl;dr I'll post here in the beginning and elaborate further down.
tl;dr: "What the ♥♥♥♥ was Hi-Rez thinking? This game is a ♥♥♥♥ing dying corpse of what it was!"
Now let me elaborate. I'll start with some immediate key changes to the game that I personally do not understand why they changed.
God just... what the ♥♥♥♥ were they even doing. This isn't neccessarily a 100% bad change but it's not good either.
Before this game was changed a lot, you had three basic classes, each had three sub-classes of it. You have the light, medium, and heavy. For light you had the Pathfinder, the Sentinel, and the Infiltrator. Medium you had the Soldier, Raider, and Technician. Heavy the Juggernaut, Doombringer, and Brute. Each of these had their own specific set of weapons with a degree of loadout customization. To add to that there was this perk system which while it had it's own issues, is definitely better than what we have now.
After the update, it was stripped down to "Light", "Medium", and "Heavy", all with their own loadout slots. The classes of before are all a legend of the past at this point. You could choose "Light", and give it any weapon & ability combo you want, which is one of the major downfalls of this game now. It removed the barrier between classes, or at the least severely lowered the gap. For reference, a Pathfinder trying to fight any of the heavy classes. It was possible to win this situation as the Pathfinder, but it would require concentration and the ability to out-maneuver the enemy. To any of the players playing post-update, they shall know that pitting a light against a heavy is a lot more "even balanced", in that the light class, if set up right, can easily dispatch a heavy when played correctly.
This is one of the things that really set this game's base floor, was that the classes used to actually be different in ways more than just movement speed & health/energy. You could argue that weapons are still class-restricted in that only the heavies can get heavy variants of the weapon, sure. However that doesn't matter in the grand scheme of things when a light class player could just give themselves a bunch of explosives, or design a class loadout specifically for taking out heavies.
What the ♥♥♥♥ was the decision making in this part? Seriously?
Base upgrading has been outright removed from the game entirely. Turrets, Generators, Sensors. Nothing can be upgraded anymore. In fact the credit system was removed entirely. This pretty much makes playing technician exceptionally stale & boring. I have no inspiration to sit around my generator room for the entire goddamn match with an enhanced repair gun just to repair a generator stuck at level 1 for eternity every 30 seconds it gets taken down by a rush, because our turrets are level 1 and even the worlds fattest heavy class can just ski right past them. I really don't have much more to say about this. It's a bad feature removal and should be brought back.
As mentioned above, the credit system has been removed. From what I've tried, the call-in system just doesn't work anymore, even though you can still equip the call-in markers, which no longer have a display or show how much they used to cost. Of course this doubles in with the removal of base upgrading.
Bullet guns have been turned into pepper spray. The shotguns may as well be literally shooting pepper spray canisters. Other weapons have actually received buffs and assorted miscellaneous changes, with other special variants also being introduced. Most of the new variants I personally think might have an interesting change on the gameplay, if only the gameplay of Tribes: Ascend was still the way it was. So unfortunately, they don't really do too much.
Weapons have had inane changes to their stats that feel out of place, and alienate me from wanting to continue playing this game. Just the same as the developers did eliminate some of the weapons from the game that no longer exist.
I cannot recommend anyone this game in it's current state. It feels like they picked up a game they abandoned at one point, said they'd update it some more, and then just tweaked a whole bunch of stuff to see how the community would react and then never change it back.
Also another huge negative from what I'm seeing in some other reviews and discussions, apparently people can no longer register to play Tribes: Ascend. So if you already have an account on this game, lucky you. You get to play it. Were you reading reviews to consider playing this game? Well sorry but you're out of luck. Even if you install the game, you apparently can't make an account from what I've read. If anyone can prove those dozens of claims wrong, by all means go ahead.
On a final closing note, I genuinely hope Hi-Rez realizes this game is dying, with population numbers declining still. With hope they'll revert the game to the way we all enjoyed playing it.

There's a lot that shows that SMAC really handcrafted this world to look beautiful. The world is larger than I have come to realize in Tokyo 42, and there is a lot to explore and discover. Of course, there's a lot to play along too. And the action, should you choose to accept it, is fun and exilerating.
If there's one thing someone should not do in Tokyo 42, it's to restart in the middle of a mission. If everything goes to♥♥♥♥♥♥ the game gets much more intense. It's what makes the game fun, by the fact that bullets have way slower travel time. Fights become bullet hells, as you bob, weave, jump, and block bullets and fire yours. Stealth is as much of a challenge as fights, as you both have to deal with enemies above, below, and on level with you. Should you die, bam. Respawn is just a second away. Should you want to fast travel, bam. Teleportation is just a second away. No load times.
The game remains fresh as new stuff gets thrown in as you progress through. You face against assassins atempting to kill you, you get items and many different other things to help you go through the game.
The only two things I would critizize are the lack of other stealth weapons. The only way to go with stealth is croutching with a melee weapon. Stealth would definitely be more interesting if SMAC adds more silenced versions of weapons. The other thing: the motorcycle missions.
It's way easier on PC with a keyboard and mouse but it's somewhat infuriating. So far there's only one mission with the motorcycle that works, and it's basically a racing mission. Any other time it's irritating but not to the point of rage.
Other than those things, the game is very entertaining. The visuals will wow your eyes while bullets fly by over a very futuristic rendition of Tokyo in the skies. It has a job, and it did its job well.
Would recommend, if they fix the ♥♥♥♥ing bike missions.

The game is not only beautifully written (bar the odd error, which can be excused) but it has an in depth plot based on all characters, including the wizard (who does not have a route but it gets explained why.)
You play Heejung, an overly emotion, workaholic with low self esteem, who one morning finds a basket full with 5 animals, 3 rabbits and 2 cats. Why are they there and who put them there? With no signs of a break in, you decide to put the animals up for adoption but people from the shelter can't come until the following day.
You decide to talk to Heejae, a fellow art student at university but when you find out that most people don't adopt cats and rabbit and that non adopted animals get euthanized, you decide to keep the animals.
This is where your journey with the animals begins. You have the option of 5 routes with either, Jisoo - the black cat, Jiyeon - the ginger cat, Jiwoo - the brown spotted rabbit, Jihae - the silver rabbit and Jieun - the white rabbit.
The animals are not who they first seem. You have a year to find out who they really are and why they were placed in your room. All while managing the stress and pressure of your final year at university.
I absolutely love this game and would recommend it. I know the price seems steep but I thought it was well worth it, with each route averaging at 10 hours plus the wizards story.

Stat building could get a little tedious at times, but I did use different stat routes for each character, giving me some variability. I've only seen one dark ending, which was a little unexpected and off-putting (first time with bad endings), but then went to the walkthrough for the "good" endings and loved how they interacted and how different facets of the characters were revealed. For the amount of time I've played it, I consider it well worth the money and it did lead me to buy Nameless which I felt was even more refined and with great storylines as well (not to mention even darker/creepier).
There were some mix-ups of names or translation grammer errors, but I knew what they meant and am not that picky. Not to mention some actually gave me a good laugh.
Can't wait to see Cheritz's next game!

I have mixed feelings. These are my impressions after my first - but I expect not last - playthrough.
It's a game that appears somewhat bold, ambitious and imaginative. It does come very close to my experience with "Dear Esther" sharing the "walking simulator" gameplay, a rather strong voice actor providing narration via monologues, eerie and thoughtfully placed music and corners to explore aside the "main road" with certain details visible only to those who look closer.
However I'm not sure what to think of the story. The narrative can be extremely confusing, I think it does outdo Dear Esther a big time there. But it isn't necessarily confusing because there is any big depth to it - it's just bloated and maybe too proud of itself. The whole deeper message of this game as I understood it I can summarize in one plain sentence without all the mind hiccups the (admittedly seemingly insane) protagonist/narrator goes through. There are religious references and a lot of symbolism, but I can't judge them as much. I assume a better understanding of them wouldn't change much about that general life-practical message.
There are nice details all over though that redeem for the somewhat pretentious story/narration. Carefully placed items (albeit at times a bit repetitively used ones - for example the books scattered around could have deserved maybe another cover texture or two, as frequently as you see them) and corpses (put into what looks like a second - alternative reality - level layer) as well as lenghty texts you can find in the levels give you some insight into the background of this decaying, seemingly post-apocalyptic shadow of a city you find yourself in as well as into the factions and characters that apparently once roamed it. Even though the narration may not live up entirely to this interesting background setting I still feel a significant substance to it's design, as if a great deal of thoughts went into it, likely enough to make one who doesn't hate "walking simulators" admire it in some ways and appreciate the experience. I did, and I'm looking forward to another playthrough or two to find the details I missed. I want to see if there is a pool of random possible lines per spot to appear too as there was in Dear Esther.

I never post on threads like this, but I'm breaking that rule to say: this is a great game! Like the original, the game addicts you to obsessively building the perfect ship.  After a few runs and a lot of upgrades, the ships become absolute death machines.  I was so perplexed in the first game that there was no option to build your own ship frame, but eventually appreciated that it was part of the challenge and a chance to throw in some kitsch (like the frame the looks like the Millennium Falcon.)  In this game, you can buy dozens of frame foundations to use in any mission, and build those frames out to make space for whatever world ending cannon you want.  The still animation is kind of like watching an old Spider Man cartoon, but the goofy humour really grows on you.  The main appeal is making the perfect machine to obliterate whatever comes your way, and then jump into hyperspace to finish the run ahead of time.  If you haven't played the first one, start there then jump to the sequel when you're just about bored of killing everything, and have your♥♥♥♥♥handed to you.  Awesome.

Like a sophisticated picross, but definitely the weakest game of this series for me.
There are a couple of issues here
The logical problem of finishing up levels is solved whether you are right or wrong.
E.g. you get up to a point where you are stuck, you analyse all the clues you have and you finally make a decision.
If you are right, well done, carry on.
If you are wrong, well then the square automatically blocks you and flips to protected, carry on...
Its solved either way, the game attempts to mitigate this issue with a star system, but that ends up being more tedious than fun as the few problem levels had me quickly restart and sweep out everything back up to where I was before. (Also, on at least one occaision I lost a star and had no idea why.) Whats more, when you see how easy it is to solve any issue on the grid I could feel my frustration rise knowing I could cheat it at any time rather than go through the possibilities.*
Second, the rules are hazy. Take the final level, which is fresh in my mind, and also shows that even by the time I finished the game I still wasnt clear on this. You can draw the I in FIN one square higher and shunt the bottom square to one side. This fulfills all the given rules, so why does it fail? Well the column you are shunted to has no numbers indicating any blocks should be in them, but there are already blocks present so that cant be it, unless its only the on grid numbers that can override that? I honestly cant say for sure.
This level is easy comparatively speaking because it obviously spells a word so you know where the I should be, but when this kind of confusion over the rules happens in more complicated levels you are left wondering if youve some logic to solve or if you are just missing some nuance in the rules.
This isnt exactly game breaking, it didnt become a huge deal for me until the last row of puzzles, and I can still recommend the game, and preferably the whole pack, but it just doesnt feel as good, nor as satisfying as the other games and would be last on my list to get.
*A quick thought on this. Im not sure why the game doesnt just let you make mistakes and only finish up when you have a completed grid, much like all the nonogram puzzles Ive played do. There maybe some problem Im missing that stops the mixture of mechanics working if it was made like that, but it would remove this problem and the need for stars entirely.

This is an excellent historical RTS game in pretty much every respect, with one exception... No multiplayer.
To clarify, my fiancee and I bought this thinking that it supported co-op multiplayer (similar to Total War), but after playing it for a while, I realized it didn't have that. In researching it, it looks like multiplayer support was a stretch goal for their Kickstarter campaign, but they didn't make it... I just wish I had known about it! I would gladly have donated toward multiplayer in this game.
Aside from that missing feature, this is hands-down my favorite historical strategy game so far. It has a "grand campaign" map that is
-- it just dynamically changes the look of the map as you zoom out. (somewhat similar to Supreme Commander) It also does a great job of integrating mechanics I've often seen in Total War and other turn-based strategy games, but adapting them well to an RTS. It keeps the flow of an RTS (no sitting around waiting for someone else to take a turn!) but doesn't feel like one long, frantic battle either.
I hope they add co-op multiplayer to the next installment of this series; if so, it'll
be at the top of my list. Until then... I may just have to go write that game myself.
The people who complain this game is too hard are really bad, trust me, as long as you figure out the core concepts its an easy, but challenging, game.

Great game satisfying a niche in the historical strategy genre that other games like the total war series or paradox grand strategies don't quite fill. While you can control individual units to do ambushes and simple flanking maneuvers, this game's main focus is on campaign strategy rather than battle tactics. The strategical questions you'll be confronted with range from "Can this enemy city be taken before my army runs out of food?" "How many units can I assemble at this city for an upcoming campaign without draining the city of all its food?" "Will expanding in this direction actually pay off in money and resources, or will it cost me more to adequately feed and defend it?"
The fact that it's all in real-time also makes waging war feel more seemless and realistic compared to turn-based games, as it makes the occurrence of field battles, hit-and-run raiding, and sieges all feel very organic.

This is a brilliant and gorgeous game. The main issue is that it has a pretty steep learning curve, but if you want a strategy game that challenges you in different ways than most 4x games, which seem happy to hit 'end turn' until the heat death of the universe, this is a good place to start. Don't be fooled by Total War comparisons: the tactical battles are pretty good, but what makes the game excellent is the way they tie into logistic and geographic considerations. Chokepoints and limited supplies and mean that doomstacks simply do not work here and battles always require thought.
If you like quirky strategy games like Paradox games, Star Ruler or AI War, I strongly recommend you give this a go. Also, try the beta branch (3.2), which currently adds some extra goodies and QoL changes.

You play as a modern Korean who's buckling under the immense stress of her successful mother's high expectations.  At the beginning of the game, five men who before they come to you were of varying social status in their medieval-fantasy homeland end up as your roommates.  With their help you find your way in life.  Also you have to date one of them because this is that sort of game.
Both the personalities and the backstories in this game go very deep.  I kept getting surprised by each new side of a character I found.  There are even a decent number of unexpected but nicely foreshadowed twists.  Whenever I heard a conversation between the current path's love interest and another character, I found myself anticipating playing the other character's path so that I could find things out from his perspective.  Each new perspective turns out to be very worthwhile to learn (the plot of each path is completely different, and you learn a different facet of the shared backstory).
Also, the $30 pricetag seems kinda big, but it's totally worth it.  This game has a loooot of content.  There are five love interests, and within a given love interest's path, both the good (happy/bittersweet) ending and the bad ending (separate from just failing the relationship) have very different stories, depending on which one you're headed to.  As of writing this I've reached nearly three endings and have played over fifteen hours (and this includes skipping everything in the shared beginning part of the story).

Pretty boys in cat / rabbit ears... What else could you ask for?
This game offers fairly in-depth characters that actually develop as the story progresses. They're not just quickly drawn pretty boys, they have reasons for how they act and why. For men in animal ears, they're pretty realistic in terms of behaviour. (except falling for this clueless MC, ofc) The music is beautiful, art's well made. The GC's are quite breathtaking.
The game takes you along for an emotional ride, and you'll notice yourself getting attached to the characters. Each new playthrough with a new guy felt like a betrayal every time. Until I accepted the fact I just need to touch all of their butts or I won't be happy! The game play gets repetitive quite fast though, with the stat raising and waiting for the days to pass to get to the good parts. For a completionist like me, who needs to get all the bad endings, good endings and extras, after a couple playthroughs it's not that fun anymore. The character dialogue and GC's are deffo worth it though, and skip function for the heavy story parts ftw.
Them speaking Korean caught me off guard first as it was the first time I ever heard the language, but you get used to it! So don't let that be the reason you'll miss out on this game. The voice acting is actually really good once you get used to the new language (although I admit, I still think they'd sound better in japanese) and their voices suit them well! It's worth the money, and I highly recommend it for anyone interested in dating sims.

My initial impression of this game was poor. The narration seemed like arrogant, pretentious rambling and the game immediately places you within a room that features six story notes to read. I swiftly tuned the narration out and after a few rooms stopped reading the notes. Finishing the game at about 2 hours, I was left fairly underwhelmed bar the very impressive graphics and occasional fantasy-like vistas.
However, there must have been *something* there as for whatever reason I replayed the game immediately – this time reading the notes and listening to the narration (albeit with his volume reduced). I enjoyed it considerably more. One of the factors for this is that in the first few chapters of my first play through I had completely disregarded that some of the doors were labelled 'Exit'. This led to me actually missing entire scenes/events, with particular note to the first chapter where it arguably matters most when trying to engage a player. If I don't want to admit to being stupid, I chalk this up to modern gameplay and quite simply not having to care or pay attention to environmental details such as this in most games. Either way, I find it very odd that the developer intentionally gives you the ability to skip game sections in this manner. I don't understand how this makes sense in a linear game.
Additional Notes:
It's probably a technical consideration but the fade to black between certain doors and chapters sometimes hindered immersion. It would be fantastic if the levels could be streamed together, giving a better illusion of a complete world – or even an unexpected, disjointed entry into fantasy.
When ending a level with a fall, the player can often be heard audibly landing.
It's the players own fault but during chapter introductions you can jump, making it sound a little silly.
Performance is pretty much rock solid bar chapter 11, which halved my framerate.
Movement input is digital hence annoying with a gamepad – especially those with sticks that don't always sit neutral!
The run speed is quite pedestrian, bordering on tedious.

An atmospheric puzzle platformer. I'm generally not a fan of platformers--not only do I generally suck at them, but my disability also makes it difficult for me to play them, and both of those factors make me not enjoy them very much. But I enjoyed this one quite a bit. Interesting concept, didn't rely too heavily on timing (which is one area where my disability is an issue), nice design and graphics, great sound. It's quite short; I played it through in one sitting, about 2 hours, but there are a few challenge achievements that give it some replay value.

A minimalist puzzle-platformer focused entirely around the "screen-wrapping" gimmick: the player can lock the screen in place, and walking off screen then transports the character to the opposite side.  All puzzles revolve around proper positioning and timing of these screen locks.  Different levels also put new spins on this mechanic, such as inverting gravity when the character wraps around, or only being able to scroll half the screen at a time.  The ideas in the game are not particularly innovative when looking at the broad spectrum of existing puzzle-platformers, but it executes well on them and is a pleasant little experience.
The game is surprisingly short, and can be completed in about an hour.  The length sadly leaves much to be desired: puzzles are simple and never really feel like they get out of the tutorial stage.  Just when it seems like a stage's particular gimmick is about to reach its potential, the stage ends.  This makes the game great for casual players and streamers, but diehards of the puzzle-platformer genre will find the game quite lacking.  Two achievements do challenge the player to complete the game in a limited number of screen wraps, but this is largely self-imposed difficulty more than anything.  Additionally, the game suffers from occasional bugs, causing the character to clip through floors or not trigger achievements correctly.
What ultimately pushes the game into the positive side is the general atmosphere it gives off.  Different levels progress through the seasons of the year, and the minimalistic art style combined with bold contrasting colors evokes the feeling of Impressionist-era paintings, and the memories of a simpler time.  A peaceful, ambient soundtrack throughout gives just the right amount of music to carry the player along without really even feeling there’s a soundtrack at all.  There may not be much to this game, and less isn’t always more, but sometimes less is just enough.

TL;DR: Gamebreaking bug prevents completion, and that's not the only issue.
This game is cute and I was excited to play it, but it's poorly made. The art style and concept are great, and it even teaches you how to play endemically, which is a rarity. But the level design, animation, and functionality are lacking.
First, the level design. Really, the levels are short and completely separate, but they chose to make it appear "continuous", by connecting the levels with long stretches of walking straight ahead and nothing else (if the stretch wasn't long enough, you might be able to cheat levels by bleeding them into each other), and even using weird unnecessary "tricks" to separate levels further. Had they simply gone for a more direct approach, the game would be much less boring. (A smaller complaint is that the levels themselves never get too complex, as they are short and connected by long stretches. You don't get, say, a maze-like puzzle where you have to freeze the screen in different places to get to the end. Instead they introduce a new mechanic rather frequently, changing the gameplay and proceeding with more simple levels with the new mechanic.)
There's not too much to talk about with animation. The put little effort into animating the player character, as if it were a background element that not many people would notice. That's not the case.
Finally, and most importantly, the bugs. Collisions aren't done very well, allowing me to clip through levels (unless that was the intended solution which would be weird). During a later part of the game, where the screen is split, I would see two player characters at the same time, which at first I thought was a real gameplay element until I saw how it interacted with the actual game mechanics and caused strange teleportations so if it was an intended gameplay element, it's severely bugged, or the whole thing is just a bug. But the last straw was a bug that when my character died, it failed to respawn. I had to return to the menu and start the "chapter" from the beginning, which was quite a ways back because again instead of arranging the game into short, purposed levels they try to make the levels seem long and continuous by making you walk forward for long stretches. And then when I reached the same point, the same thing happened.

I quite like this version of the game.
It keeps the same base with additional upgrades, for instance, you pick the shape of your ship (depending on your blueprint and the number of tiles you have, though you can buy one massinve blueprint and design whatever you want), the number of units you can build in battle is limited to how much you have created, not like the previous game where you could build 100 of 'em, assuming you have the space and money.
You do have to grind more than in the previous one, if that doesn't float ya boat, I doubt you'll have fun with it. The addition of "Focus" meter can seem cheap, since it limits the usage of units abilities but it makes for more strategic run. The use of "connector" tile can save ya♥♥♥♥♥though it take a bit of getting used to. Pirate boss battles are still around, though, you can travel around them if they are too tough for you. Eve's classic comments are awesome, but that's personal taste so yea.
All in all I'm at start in Titan system and it's a blast. Getting a new ship, change of tactic, adding new units and firepower, just awesome.
Multiplayer part is well, kinda there. All you can do with it is buying other people stuff they don't need for range of prices, deliver their cargo for a small gifts and such, and well you can do the same. Sometime you'll run into nice deal which will save you money from Roma or few trips to get 'em at certian location so I guess it's ok.
Few things that are off. Your units aiming is sometime dumb.... Instead of focusing on one or two enemy units to quickly take em out, they will just randomly target anything, even if all they need is one shot to the enemy, some manual or smart targeting would be great. Next thing is, you can have odd number of units before you need to get to higher level mechanic, which is rather wierd, having only one unit of decoy or Aegis shield, but oh well.
I had only 2 crashes, one where I wasn't doing anything and one where I just finished a run, resulting in me have to do it again, but since I played like 80-90 runs so far, it's not that bad.
Aside from couple off things devs did I quite like the game, and believe anybody who played Space Run will enjoy Galaxy, oh there are also some in game achievements for all those uber-core bastads :)
TLDR
The game is step froward from the prevoius one with some upgrades and changes, so if you like what they added you'll love the game, which I do :)
Cheers

This is a great little puzzle game that combines Minesweeper and Picross, with a solid learning curve that starts easy to teach the basics, but steadily (and fairly) climbs to puzzles where figuring out each single square as a yes/no feels like an accomplishment.
Despite what all the negative reviews seem to say, these puzzles are all 100% logic solvable with no guessing needed - I was able to work my way through all of them, and when I did make a mistake, I was able, on taking a second look, to figure out what I missed that would have saved me from that wrong move. But each time I made a mistake, I learned from it, reset the puzzle, and started over - and eventually solved them, no guessing or using guides.
Only downsides are:
1. It would be nice to have a "maybe" flag, similar to Minesweeper, for use in testing "what if it's this square" theories, without having to keep track of it all in your head.
2. There's not a lot of replay value. All the puzzles are pre-made, so once you've beaten them, you know them. But I got 9 hours of distraction out of an $0.89 investment so I'm still feeling I got my money's worth!
Fully recommend.

Tokyo 42 is a game which looks very very nice and could have been something like a "hidden gem" next to all the more big games next to it. Before i go into details here, i can say i sure enjoyed it and actually waited for its release. It looked promissing and the trailers and pictures made hunger for more. This is not a "pur good review" so just keep reading why i "up" voted it.
T42 is a iso-3D-action-adventure game, basicly you have a "fixed" overhead cam view which you can change viva button with 45° every press on it. That actually makes it feel very classic and makes the world sometimes look like "cubes/cubish". Its not bad if you think about old games which works with hexagraphics or, again, iso-3D-graphics.
Sadly, even if you are able to spin the cam with the current system, the world actually feels like sometimes the cam doesnt really "fit in" with the view it has. Sometimes you keep spinning the cam so often but none of the angles really works out "well" so that you actually get lost sometimes coz of the fixed cam. Sometimes the cam can be that bad that you actually need to pause the game best between mid-mission and fix the cam wile you run a parkour - which is actually very annoying sometimes if you still think about the iso-3D style...
Honestly, T42 is one of the best looking games which i played lately. Its really nice to look at and playing in this great iso-3D world. The only sad thing i can say here is that sometimes here, again, the fixed cam views "ruins" the view sometimes.
Without spoiler to much, the plot of this game is actually pretty good and actually keeps the player doing the missions. Its something which could work very well for a movie (if its not already done) with its own plots and smaller twists. Sadly here again, the story also feels somewhat rushed. Characters where you think they "could" be important just get a small "side-role" and nothing more, you maybe only see them 2-3 times before they got unimportant or they are "just there".
This actually is something which is sad since i would like to see the story...well..."better told" somehow. I enjoyed the story pretty much (even if a lot people maybe just skiped the text...). If i can say so, it was something "new" at least.
Wile i played T42 (I finished it with around 93% as i wrote this review, missing only some collectables), i found some stuff which is not told or, so i guess, are somewhat "buggish". One of the first things i wonderd was that im able to collect "coats". I duno if i might skiped this part but its actually never told that you can use a coat as cosmetic viva caps lock key.
Another thing i think is somewhat broken is the "weapon" i actually think is the most helpful and "usefull" weapon in the game,  namely the shield. Here a video for:
The shield is....strange. It works as melee "weapon" but also as wall AND shield, of course but it doesnt only "blocks" the shots, it bounces them off. So you actually can run around in stealth-like missions just with the shield, running into enemys, you will not be seen if you run into them with the shield infront of you and even if they attack you, you can kill them if you let them eat their own shots. Actually, i finished the endboss(es) with the shield only, if im honest (i come back to that part later).
Another thing i found out, youre actually even able to fly with the shield. You can get bananas and a bunch of bananas as weapon. I dont know if they have a actual use or if they are just there for fun but, if you use the shield and throw a bunch of bananas, you are able to fly somewhat viva push. Here a video about:
As i said already, the story feels rushed mostly at the end. I really enjoyed the game and its story actually till the last few missions since then T42 got to a point where i thought the devs didnt know better what to build in. I dont wanna spoiler to much but the last few missions are actually very hard and very unfair fights against "boss like" people. One of them can take 5-7 shots before you are actually able to "kill" this person (and you one), the other fight is over waves of enemys where you just get one hit between those waves and you have restart from the very beginning of wave 1, making it feel very hard and very frustrating (srsly, i tried at least 15-20 times before i beat the last boss and oh boi, im finally glad i did it).
With that in mind, T42 actually "has" the possibilities. The problem is just that they feel "unused". Missionwise as sample, its kinda repetitive. 80% of the missions is "kill this person and escape", which is sad. It gives actually some sidemissions which feel, next to this "kill" missions refreshing or "out of place", like a race on a motorbike, sniper missions or parkour missions where you have to kill people next to run to the end. I liked the idea using the motorbike but this was only for a very short period, sadly.
Other things where i think are "underrated" is actually the cat you get for the "Nemesis" system. Ones a wile, if you did a mission, a NPC assassin got your attention and is on the way to kill you. Sadly for you, the assassin could be "everyone" since it looks like every NPC in the game, hidding him-/herself between the civilians. So the only opinion you have is either you wait till the Nemesis does his/her "first move" or you shot wildly around till "one" of them shoots back. Its a bit like "where is waldo" but more with a "who" insteed of a "where". The cat, which you will get later on, will actually help you tracking the Nemesis by following him/her and telling the real possition between all the civilians, making the "hide and seek" game maybe faster but nothing more.
Here again, i could say that there are a lot of possibilities unused/"underused". As sample, for actually "praising" the cat all out of the weapons in the trailer, it only has very little use only for the Nemesis system which feels also like it could be much more like a PvP "invading" system or like. As sample, the cat could be "played" from a second player, helping you distracting enemys and like, one of the samples i got in mind wile i played the game and saw its possibilities.
the game has a pricetag from 20$ which is a bit to much if you only see the open possibilities which they sadly didnt use. The devs told it has a story from about 6-7 hours of gameplay, which seems about right. I actually played it now about 15 hours~ coz i runned around a lot, tring to get all things and stuff but again i only finished it 93%, giving up since some stuff is out of my range or i dont see a possible way to actually get those stuff if not using the Banana+Shield combo. Here one sample:
I also saw that the OST is 18$ which i think is just for a quick "cashgrap". I sure enjoy the "music" but it feels for the game more its ambiance and not really music you could listen to. I will not say its bad music but 18$ is way to much for it if you compair it next to the 20$ for the original game...
Its sad steam has not a "middle" rating so I say sure it is worth playing. I loved to play the game till the very end and its story
i wish there would be more. I hope that actually Tokyo 42 will get some more content in the future next to the already good content it has. It sure is not perfect but it shows that it has a lot good possibilities. It might is a bit expensive in one point but it sure is worth playing. Recommened.

Trails of Cold Steel starts off confusing, you get thrown into the 'prologue' which is pretty much the main part of chapter 5.By doing this, it shows how powerful your characters will become, and yes. They do become this powerful. However i'll explain that later.
Throwing in at the deep end with no knowledge or the characters is confusing as you are constantly foreshadowing what will happen 1/2 a year down the line (in game). As it leaves you at a pretty big cliffhanger.
When you start attending Thor's Military Academy, you come off the train and head into the city, where you'll meet quite a few main characters, bumping into a fine lady whom you will be spending a lot of time with.
Once this occurs you'll have about an hour at most of dialogue to get through. Which, does seem heavy. However the trails universe does a very good job at introducing those characters and developing them as time moves forwards.
I went into the game with no real expectations. I was looking for a good JRPG game, which I could throw my hours in over the remainder of the summer holidays.. I was and am impressed. The game lasted a hell of a long time, while. Yes, it only took  me a week. I had a lot of hours invested into this game. The main thing which I enjoy is the character development and the world building which was amazing inside of this game.
There are a lot of main characters, so much so that you'll start to lose track of what and who they are. However, you have the handy feature of the classbook or whatever you call. WHich you have to painstakingly hand out to everyone in your class quite early on in the game. This records all the important information which you will find out about characters. This could be through the bonding events, or just general interaction.
The flesh out the world more and more as you immerse yourself deeper and deeper into the game. With places which are mentioned early on, being places which you visit on Field Studies. You also get to learn about family members of the big 11. Along with their homes and way of life.
You will start off hating characters. While the hate never really faded for me with Machinas. However out of the eleven characters he is the only one that I didn't like. Mainly because he's a whiney little ♥♥♥♥♥.
However he does have his moments. Near the end.
The pacing of the game at times does get a little dull and repetitive. As you fall into the rhythm of being the student council's little fairy, doing their tasks. Beating a floor of the old school house, having a practical examination (getting your♥♥♥♥♥kicked by Sara for the most part) then off you pop onto the train to the next city where you will spend two or three days solving a relationship dilemma within your group. Since you are the almighty Rean; the loveable hellspawn decides that it's your responsibility to deal with this as she cannot be arsed.
I digress, the structure is not very flexible as you do get into this rhythm and it's hard to get out of it.
However, Cold Steel makes up for this by having an absolute killer soundtrack. I am honestly impressed with how amazing the music was for this game. I would have the volume on full blast for the majority of this game so I could appreciate the music; as it fits the mood perfectly. However I would've liked for there to be more of a diverse set of music for each area of the game. Yes, the music is amazing. However it plays for half the chapter and doesn't change often. However, thank god it changed each chapter.
The Combat system is very impressive. With Attacks, Magic (Arts), Crafts (Character driven abilities), the standard items and run. I threw away Magic for the most part of the game as waiting for it to activate wasn't effective and just used mainly Attacks and Crafts. Which hit harder and faster. However once I got the Adamantium Shield Art, I started using magic again as it is insanely powerful.
The Combat system is refreshing, while it's nothing amazing, it is at least enjoyable.
The last few chapters, I was expecting the game to end anytime then. I could see many places where they could've ended it and resumed it in the next expansion of the arc. However to my delight, it continued on for quite some time! Once I went to bed after I got into the last floor of the Old school house and decided I'd clear it tomorrow, as it must of been where the game ended. As I had a little time free in the morning... I finished the dungeon after a good number of hours... then the boss battle... then the final chapter sprang up which meant that it still wasn't down for the count.
The game ends with a cliffhanger. To my great displeasure. As I have read many reviews that even told me that there would be a cliffhanger ending. I was not happy in the slightest. I did not want this game to end. I was in the developer's pockets until the very end. While, it isn't satisfying at the least. As you get CRAZY over powered towards the end and everything starts to kick off. You find out C's identify. Which while there were many signs in the game all along, is still a shock. The capital is occupied and they're coming for Thor's. Class VII with their fearless (and clueless) leader Rean, heading out to fend off the attack until the Military can send relief.
You fight off two enemies (Not spoiling it) and then fight C for the last time in Trails of Cold Steel I. After that, you leave. Not out of your own choice either. Flying off to the furthest place from Thor's as possible. Heading home. The game ends there. With the fleeting text from the developers to port the next game to PC. Which was enough to satisfy me.
In conclusion, this game is phenomenal. The characters are thoroughly amazing, they are fleshed out and you really get to know them. The game took me about 40 hours to complete. However, this was with the amazing feature of Turbo mode, allowing you to speed up the game to allow you to get back into the combat as quickly as possible. I had it turned on for the grand majority of the game. As it allows you to waste less time doing the side quests and running about from destination to destination. I am also ashamed to say that I found a way to go undetected by monsters that roam in the wild. Allowing me to breeze through the last dungeon.
I would heavily recommend this game to anyone who is an avid reader of fantasy novels, as it achieves the same thing that reading can do in a short time.
Those who love JRPGs will be in for a treat as this is the best which I have played in a long time, beating Final Fantasy X by a long run.

What an absolutely incredible roller coaster ride this game has been. I haven't felt so strongly about a RPG ever since FFX and even I feel that this game may be on par with it. Before I begin my review, I just want to reiterate that although I have 96.3 hours in this game and counting, that was only through my first playthrough. How I was able to amass that much time in a game will be stated shortly.
Character Development
Though you are introduced to an astonishing and somewhat intimidating amount of characters, each character has been developed with proper care and it isn't long until you begin to care about each of them. The characters are probably the strongest part in this game and they are all very much human. It is an absolute far cry to the last JRPG games that I played that consisted of FFXIII & FFXV along with some american RPG games that I've played such as Skyrim, and Far Cry. They also develop very realistically all having their own faults, as normal High School Kids are. And yet, their struggles are things that you care about as you get to know each of them. On you off days you are able to get to know each of your classmates, but it never seems like it drags on as you are only allowed a certain amount of bonding points per day.
Even the NPCs you interact with seem to have very interesting stories. And It's actually probably what I spent most of my time doing in this game even though it wasn't required. The shop keepers don't just have a "shop option" in them, and you can actually get to know what their backstory is along with many of the other NPCs that you are introduced to throughout the series. All the characters, I feel, in Trails of Cold Steel added so much to the immersion.
Story
The story starts off relatively quickly. You play in the perspective of Rean Schwarzer and you are just confused as he is in the class when he is placed in with the rest of his colorful classmates. Though each chapter is set in a school setting, the strongest part of this series come from these Field Studies that Class VII distinctly goes through. Throughout each chapter you go to these trips called field studies where you embark on other areas of the country along with subtle tidbits about the history of both the continent and your classmates. Along with these Field Studies are tasks that you do in order to A) progress the story forward & B) able to get to know the people in the city/town. And once you get to know all of the characters there, the story really starts moving along along with some mind jarring twists that even the most observant wouldn't see coming along.
Port
The port is Fleshed out really nicely in comparison to the PSVita version and it almost makes me sad that I will probably have to wait a year or 2 before the second game comes out. I am tempted to buy the second one just on the PS3 and deal with the lower frame rathes, but to be honest the graphics wasn't something that I wasn't paying too much attention to anyways. There are some dated moments that have to do with the graphical engine at the time, that you will see as you're playing such as teleporting students or even the way characters walk may be a little jagged, but all in all it is a really clean port that I was able to run very nicely with my Asus 1070 I5 6600K which may even be overkill for a game such as this.
Sound
Almost all the cut scenes have voice lines, though they are mainly in English. Though I'm pretty sure it is possible to find a Mod for a Japanese voice acting, the English voice acting in itself is superb and that is coming from someone who has watched a long list of animes and is rather picky with the amount of Dub there is in an anime. Though be warned that according to the port, there was apparently 5,000 additional lines of text that was able to be voiced which may not be included if you were to mod this game.
The Soundtrack in this game fits absolutely well, from rocking action to some school-appropriate subtle spring music, I felt that the music only added to the immersion as it made me feel like I was a student that was studying at Thors Military Academy, or a citizen in Erebonia. The music felt very simplified and yet absolutely fit the theme to what the developers at Falcom were aiming for.
Overall
This was the JRPG that I've been looking for this whole time and I felt like I found an absolute jewel in this game. I also feel that this game is criminally underrated, especially since Destructoid and Famitsu gave it some subpar ratings of 7/10 and 34/40. There is a ton of replayability in this game and you can bet that I will be replaying this and reliving the days with Class VII and playing the second part of the series on the PS3 and maybe someday play it on Steam as well when it comes out on PC.

This is the second time I've bought this game.  The first time was on Vita and the PC is the best place to play it by far.  The near instantaneous load times and high frame rate make a huge difference in terms of making everything just plain better.
What makes this game as good as it is, however, is the depth and quality of worldbuilding.  That is what this game is all about.  Each chapter introduces you to a new region and delves into one or two of the character's in your party.  Which will seem slow at first but after a few chapters you begin to realize that the game has tricked you into learning about it's world and it's character at a crazy level of depth. Then there are the characters who are universally great. Until you find out he's nowhere near as normal as he seems and is every bit as deep an interesting as the rest of the cast.
So if you love old school JRPGs with a deep story and don't mind a bit of a slow burn storywise.  Get this.  It's fantastic.

Sooo first review, first thing's first:
You do not need to have played the previous Trails (or in Japan "Kiseki") series; the game makes some references to those games, mostly Ao no Kiseki (Trails to Azure?); but for the most part you really won't be spoiled for those games, in fact this game was made with newcomers in mind.
I have played the PS3 version and I can tell you if you get this, you are buying the definitive version, I cannot tell you how great it is to replay this game in 60 FPS with extra voice acting. This game, like most of XSeed's localizations: has no censorship. Unfortunately there’s no dual audio since they couldn't get it (Japanese VAs are very protective of their work, or so I'm told), however you can mod them back in, but the dub VAs are excellent! Better than your average dub, give or take; a lot of people don't like the VA for Alisa though; personally I think Laura sounds too old.
What of the gameplay though?
Well if you got that old Turn Based JRPG itch that needs to be scratched; this is the game for you. It has some of the best elements of other JRPGs old and new.
I think the battle system is a lot like Final Fantasy X's battle system, but unlike FFX your party's positioning is taken to account on the field, so sometimes positioning is important. Crafts are unique moves that each character can use, S-Crafts/S-Breaks are your limit breaks and Arts are your spells, which take a turn to charge and a turn to cast (which makes sense IMO), but arts do not miss.
One of the new things in this game that wasn't in previous entries is the ability to physically attack and unbalance your enemy and follow up with the party member that character who unbalanced is linked to for more damage.
My biggest disappointment though with this game; is that Falcom dumbed down the orbment system compared to Trails in the Sky (also on Steam). Orbments are the game's explanation of the type of technology of how they can run vehicles, appliances, guns, cast Arts (spells), etc. What your characters use are combat orbments (The ARCUS in this game's case) which either increases each of your character's parameters such as increased Attack or HP and Arts such as Fire Bolt (basic fire spell) and Tear (basic healing spell) and later on a chance to inflict status on you opponant.
You can give spells to any character, although not all character's stats are the same, so ot's better to have offensive Arts to characters with a high ATS (Arts Attack) stat! This is done by inserting what is known as Quartz refined from sepith (dropped from enemies, which you could excange for cash, but I don't recommend) into your ARCUS orbments. In Trails in the Sky, Quartz has a value and that is determined by what you can cast. In Cold Steel: what you see is what you get.
This game’s music is exceptional. I put it up there of what Square Enix, Capcom, Konami makes. Yes it can be that amazing. Falcom always has good music in their games. I still listen to them.
,
,
,
and
; but stay away from Cold Steel II's music! The album art is a BIG spoiler; you have been warned.
This game is also Story heavy; were talking long cutscenes and not every scene is voiced, but we’re talking War and Peace in terms of how big this games dialogue is. I will say this, after the opening scene, the game does start off slow, because of world building and character development; this story is a time investment that WILL pay off; I guarantee you. As you advance the story, like Sky; NPCs usually have something new to say and usually have their own stories going on; this is what I mean by War and Peace, a lot of dialogue is optional. That's how detailed this game's world is. Playing this game on New Game Plus is also worth it because you can also pick up subtle foreshadowing and hints, that you will definitely miss the first time playing and you can carry over your items and character’s levels – if you so wish.
If you like this game and plan to get the Cold steel II, which will be coming out on Steam soon (as I write this, it’s not out yet on Steam), make sure you have a complete game save file. You’ll get some nice items by how much AP you get in this game, as well as carry over character relationships.

This otome visual novel and second title of the Story of Eroolia series as a sequel to roseVeRte's earlier visual novel
features a new female protagonist Regina who was magically transported to the island of Eroolia from her homeland of Ozzwa by a mysterious black cat and ends up right in front of a bridge unit(diplomatic agents) consisting of Juli, Mars and Ronan who are en-route to Laarz, a hidden part of Eroolia inhabited by luccretia(cat people featured in
) where they hope to make contact with Lillia/Leea's father Gao who left for Laarz earlier and had not returned with any update on his mission.
Amidst the backdrop of mutual distrust and suspicion between humans and luccretia, Regina's sudden appearance in front of the bridge unit with her cat ear hair accessory and her martial prowess lead Juli to hire Regina as a bodyguard for the bridge unit. Over 7 chapters, Regina will develop feelings for Juli and meet a cast of new characters consisting of Gao, Lio who is Lillia/Leea's younger brother, Princess Myana who is the current ruler of Laarz and her two followers Leona and Simon.
As with
, the game has plenty of save slots to allow different gameplay and dialogue choices to be made during the game, with a small popup icon of Regina/Juli to reach a slightly different storyline branch and open a secret unlockable scene at the end of the prologue and the first 3 chapters. The chapter summary and the option to skip and fast-forward any part of the game are retained in this visual novel. The story and plot is also written as a romantic comedy and has its share of humour and two nice happy endings. Theme songs, background music, voice acting, artwork and overall game presentation are great to match the themes featured in the game. The theme song and Insert Song DLC are recommended if you like a happy and catchy song and a melodic and uplifting song respectively. Also, if you like Ochiba, Haru no Yokan or Zantou in
,
will also have an appropriate set of background music Piano Melancholy, Positive 5 and Suspense 7 to match the similar themes featured in this visual novel.
After spending more than 5 hours to read and listen through both routes in this visual novel, I decided to give a score of 9/10 on the following factors:
Plot and character backgrounds: Each route will require approximately 3 hours of reading (2 routes altogether, both of which are romance options with Juli). The English text are translated with few errors. As a romantic comedy and short indie game, I feel the romance routes feel rather short and rushed with not enough emphasis given on Juli's magical ability to influence others except Regina with his magical gaze. Also, the part when Princess Myana competes with Juli to get Regina to become her spouse for a reason that will be explained further on in the story seems tacked on with the princess giving up barely a few days after kissing Regina once in front of a lot of people. I understand this is a short indie visual novel production, yet at the same time I feel the plot holes in this visual novel would lead me to give it a less than perfect score. The character backgrounds remain consistent with the character backgrounds of the same characters from
and the new characters as supporting characters also have their background and relationship with the protagonist or at least one member of the bridge unit adequately mentioned and established.
Artwork, backgrounds and CGs: The character sprites, backgrounds, opening and insert themes used in the game are attractive and colourful with animated glitters in each CG and the opening theme also does well in introducing the cast of characters and voice actors and actresses featured in this visual novel.

Voice acting and background music: Tone and pace of delivery from all voice actors and actresses match each line of spoken dialogue in the game with appropriate moments to grab the attention of the listener. Background music is also pleasant and appropriate to match the different moments in the game with great theme songs in the opening and insert themes.
Overall, this visual novel is recommended with both DLCs for fans of roseVeRte who might be interested in collecting the titles by roseVeRte and to know more about the characters and background story in Story of Eroolia as a romantic comedy with fantasy featuring humans and luccretia.

At the time of this review, the game has not been released on Steam although it has already been released on the developer's site.  There may be a bit of an inaccuracy (in regards to criticism), as the game has been updated since my review.  Also, I was a beta tester for the game, so thus, I received an early copy of the game.
is the sequel to
.  Although it is not necessary to have played
in order to play this game, it helps a bit, as there are certain parts during the game which make references to events in
.  In
, you take on the role of Regina, who magically ends up on the island of Eroolia, and immediately meets Juli, Mars, and Ronan, characters from
.  Juli, Mars, and Ronan are on a mission from Leezera, the home of humans, to Laarz, a country of people who are half-cat and half-human (otherwise called luccretias).  Regina joins the party in the hopes that she'll be able to find out how to return to her home.  During this journey, Regina learns more about Juli, wondering what secrets he holds.  Along the way, the party will meet new characters and yes, they will end up in Laarz, where certain events will happen...
Ok, I don't want to spoil the story anymore so I'll stop right there.  However, I will say this.  If you've played
, then you may have a good guess as to how
plays out.
is a comedic, romantic visual novel, and the choices you make determine which one of two paths you end up taking-Regina's or Juli's.  Although the endings of both paths are pretty much the same (again, not spoiling lol), you do get different perspectives of the same situation, depending on the path you take.
Now that I've laid out the information here, it's time for the critique.  I really enjoyed
.  First off, the story was fun to read and follow.  I liked Regina as a main character, as she is strong, both physically and emotionally. , which is a positive since I liked the art in the first game.  The music soundtrack was fun and good to listen to.  There's even a special song vocalized during the game! You can check out the unlocked CGs, music tracks, and movies in the Extras section on the main menu.  If there is one thing I would criticize, then it would be this.  Now this is just my personal preference and I can be nitpicky when it comes to writing and such but I felt that some of the sentences were worded a bit awkwardly so they could have been worded better.  However, the writing is quite readable and this doesn't take away at all from how much enjoyment and fun

Overall, I totally enjoyed

(Also, I'd like to emphasize that we really NEED more high quality VNs like this one.  A lot of effort was put into making sure that the game would be as wonderful as possible, and no corners were cut to do so.  It's clear that there was lots of love, care, and passion put into it, as the dev wanted to make this game as wonderful and high quality as can be.  I highly respect such devs who do this and purchasing
would show that you want more high quality VNs like this on Steam.)

I've been using the steam controller for a while, and I like it. It offers near unlimited ways that you can bind it due to action sets.
You can easily change the settings on the track pad to add acceleration, or adjust a setting so that when you swipe the mousepad it keeps going in a direction. It can be adjusted to desired sensitivity through the controller configerations.
I have tried using this controller in Life is feudal: MMO. I was able to set up the X Y A B buttons so that hitting Y a single time was bound to my inventory, hitting Y twice brings up my paperdoll, and holding Y for a long press brings up my map. Each X Y A B button is similarly set up with multiple functions on each button. Quite cool, considering usually i'd have to take my hand off the mouse to hit this buttons. When I added autorun to one of these X Y A B buttons, I was able to do a lot of the grindy stuff on Life is feudal with just my right hand on the controller. This was good for long hours of teraforming, and I was happy about being able to chill on the couch and use the controller in one hand for extended gameplay sessions. Depending on your mousepad position vs your shoulder, using a mouse for extended periods can be stressful. The right trackpad mouse and right trigger left click template binding is very easy to use for non combat situations. I was even able to set up a double click B button binding to my right click (the default is left trigger right click) so one handed gaming is definetely possible. I would recommend this controller to anyone with only one hand, or left handed people, as both sides of the controller are almost identical and depending on how you set it up, you can play most games with only one hand.
Each trackpad can be set up in a bunch of ways including radial menus, directional buttons or X Y A B buttons that can be bound to anything. You can also have a setting where another button ( ie: the left bumper) on your controller will change the configuration for the trackpad. So one could be a directional pad with 1-4, and then you would set up a button to select your alternate buttons, which could be mapped to 5-8. Honestly though with the way you can map multiple activators to each directional or X Y A B buttons, you can have your trackpad (with alternate switching button) set up to perform 24 different actions. That's just with mapping your trackpad as a directional pad or button pad. You can turn it into a radial menu with 12 buttons, set up each of your 12 buttons to have 3 different activators, and that's 36 different actions you can perform before adding your alt button. Add your alt button and that's 72 actions you can perform with just one trackpad. If you sacrifice your right mouse pad and turn it into 2 radial menus. That 144 buttons or multi buttons (like Ctrl C, or Alt F4, or Enter /tptoplayer ((yes each button can be set up to enter entire sentences at the click of a button)) ) that you can map to just your trackpads. Add another 72 buttons if you turn your joystick into two radial menus. Add your X Y A B buttons and that's another 24. Ultimately you can turn the front of your controller into 240 buttons if you use all radial menus, and use another button as an alternator. You only need one alternator. Obviously you won't really want to sacrifice your mouse pad, or joystick on your main action set, but you can have a button (ie the left grip) on your controller change between your WASD/mouse movement action set, and your 240 button action set. You can have multiple action sets that you can cycle through with a single button, or set up two buttons to go backwards and forwards in your action sets. You can set up a HUD at different opacities that layers ontop of your game to let you know which action set your switching to. Eventually I want to set this up to have an action set where each activator of each button represents a short multi button keyboard sentence. The pen is mightier than the sword.
I found for combat in Life is feudal, the mousepad is difficult to use or maybe I haven't tweaked it enough. For a non target physics based game where you have to (for example) aim yourself at your opponent, cue a directional attack by slightly moving your mouse (or mousepad) up, down, left, or right, aim at your target while performing your directional attack, THEN do something called dragging where you continue to move your aim towards your target after you attack to move the metal part of your weapon into the opponent. Dragging is difficult on a controller, and having to aim your blocks and attacks is also difficult using the controller mousepad at my current settings (which i've tried to tweak a lot). The mouse is much better for the intense combat that life is feudal offers. I would likely utilize both the mouse and keyboard and the steam controller in my play session depending on the task.
The really great thing about this controller though, is that when you map the joystick to WASD, or map any of your buttons to keyboard buttons, it recognizes the controller button press as a keyboard press. I guess this only works on games that don't already utilize the controller setup. ANYWAY, this means I can use the entire left side of my controller (joystick, left trigger, left bumper, left trackpad, left grip, Select button) and also use a gaming mouse in my right hand, and in LIFE IS FEUDAL:MMO the two work perfectly together.
Ultimately with the hybrid Controller-Gaming mouse setup I can sit on my couch and not have to use my keyboard unless I have to type to someone.
My only complaint is that the show keyboard function on the controller is a bit clunky, and slower than typing. The controller would be perfect if it had a small area for a dedicated keyboard (either clickable buttons or touch screen keyboard) like some cellphones. Instead it uses the left trackpad as half the keyboard, and the right trackpad as the other half. It's not really a problem to put the controller down breifly and use the keyboard for typing, but if it had a keyboard on the controller (on the front side under the buttons and joystick, between the grips would be perfect) it could potentially replace the keyboard in my set up.
All in all it's the perfect alternative to mouse and keyboard if you have the patience to set it up like a mouse a keyboard.
