I thought the Total War franchise was good, until I tried this.
Pros
-No loading screen between tactical and strategic view, so you can immediately command troops by zooming in.
-AI is difficult on normal. It actually seems like AI is intelligent. It's not cheating or getting non-player bonuses, except that it starts with all native cities, regardless of whether the player does or not.
-Raiders and enemies alike will mercilessly invade and pillage your lands, so there is a point to building defenses IE fortifying rivercrossing, border towns, camps and coastal ports.
-There are limitations to resources, so you have to carefully decide how to spend your resources.
-If you run out of a resource, then the consequences can be harsh. You get punished for overextending yourself or improperly investing what you have.
-The UI is well thoughout and adds to the immersion of the game.
-Very active developers. The dev team is currently doing a map-building tutorial series on the Greek peninsula. Once they are finished, they promise to release it as a mod campaign!
Cons
-Only replayability is in starting as a different faction, but the campaign map is very open-worldish, so you can try different strategies the next time your play. It may get repetitive after you have won the campaign the first time. The game needs more scenarios. I don't care if it's DLC or playermade, but the game needs Scandanavian, Russian, Brittania, Iberian, North African, Middle East, Greece, Macedonian (think Alexander), Asia Minor, Mongols (think Gengis Khan), Far East Asia, and Native American scenarios complete with there own style of units, technology and buildings. I want more, haha!
-Some issues with commanding and pathfinding the troops. Minor, but the game needs tools to adjust the width and length of formations, like in Total War. The player can move the individual units to change the formation, but it gets a little repetitive and tedious.
-No multiplayer.
-The game is merciless, so children are advised to stay away. :-)
Definitely worth the $15 winter sale price.

Preface: Is the game necessarily bad? No. However, because of the Yes/No only on Steam, I cannot fully give it a recommendation for everyone to play. There are still flaws to it as seen below.
The idea of Four Sided Fantasy is somewhat original, at least in the fact that games have not frequently used the wrap-around screen as an actual puzzle itself. The controls of the game are simple: You move. You jump. You lock the screen in place. By locking the screen in place, you can walk to an edge of the screen and wrap around to the opposite side (this applies to both left/right and top/bottom).
Now, the game makes it a little more complex because of things like walls blocking part of your path on a side of the screen, or you having to lock the screen at an abnormal height. You can bypass walls easily by walking off of the left side and wrapping around to the right, for instance. Or, if you jump high enough so that the ground is not visible - then locking the screen will allow you to fall down through and wrap around at the top of the screen.
There's a bunch of other examples, and the game adds in more pieces to the logic such as a split screen later on, or being able to transfer between the foreground and background of levels. But all in all, the premise is the same throughout: angle the camera at the right place, do some jumping, and move quick enough to avoid obstacles (which are basically just blurriness that will cause you to respawn).
Artwork is a strength of the game, as the levels are definitely nice and relaxing. The same goes for the music and sound of the game, all combining for a rather chill-out mood when you play through it. None of the puzzles are that complex, so you shouldn't get angry at yourself figuring them out.
So why do I not recommend the game overall? The length, the longevity (different from length!), as well as some upkeep problems like bugs.
As the puzzles are overall not too difficult, you should complete the game in under 1 hour. It is definitely short! Now, the game gives you a New Game+ which changes the way the camera moves. And it actually did give a little bit of difference to the game so I played it again right afterwards. However, about halfway through the New Game+, I started getting a little bored. And by the time I finished, I had determined that I don't have any plans to come back to this game.
While the idea is interesting overall, the game does not have a long-lasting life. Once you've been through it, you've seen it all. There's no extra paths to go down, no other ways to solve puzzles. They're all very particular and about specific locations and timing. The replayability is pretty much non-existent.
Take note that even if you do really want to replay the game, the saving mechanism is messed up once you complete it. You can only start New Game+ from the beginning, or choose to begin at a specific level. Therefore, you'll have to play through from the beginning to the end in one sitting; and if you quit out, it'll be from the beginning when you come back.
Then there's the bugs I ran into. Most of the game (though it's short, as I said) was running alright and the puzzles executed normally. But I had a few times where the game would mess up the screen, making me stuck. I would then have to exit and restart the level I was at during the normal playthrough. Most of the bugs were during the split-screen section towards the end, where one of the screens would change to something incorrect and I would be unable to move any further. This was definitely a big flaw because I would have to restart the section and hope by chance that it would work properly the next time around.
Overall, my experience with the game was not exactly bad. But I wish that the game was bigger. I wish it had even more creativity in it, allowing for larger, more complex puzzles that allowed multiple paths. And I wish that it was better bug-tested as the few times I had to restart were bothersome.

Four Sided Fantasy is a puzzle platformer that takes an seemingly-illogical early video gaming mechanic - that a character can walk off the screen on one side and appear on the other - and creates an entire game around it.
If I were to describe the game in one word, that word would be "chill." The game could be a mentally stressful and exhausting experience, but the design decisions - including the peaceful score, the lush pastoral environments, and the short breaks of downtime as players move from one puzzle to the next - all contribute to a sense of relaxation.
On the flip side, the game is also relaxing because it's not very challenging. I found most puzzles to be solvable within seconds, minutes at most. The game also has some bugs - none game breaking, but I had a couple of instances where a glitch allowed me to skip a puzzle. It's a shame these issues detract from what is otherwise a game with a great deal of polish.
The lack of challenge is also a problem because the game is pretty short - it took me about an hour and change to complete it. I enjoy shorter games, but even with the new wrinkles introduced to the mechanics as the game progresses, the game feels lacking in content. There isn't a story (at least at the surface level) and both the New Game+ mode (a slight tweak to how the game plays) and the performance-based achievements weren't compelling enough to get me to replay the game again.
I had the good fortune to play Four Sided Fantasy years ago when it existed only as a prototype and the impression it left me was favorable enough to convince me to Kickstart it. The final result is a solid game, but one that failed to take the concept to a level I thought it could. Ultimately, the experience it provided was a bit too forgetable for me to recommend it (especially at the non-sale price).

Four Sided Fantasy is a side-scrolling puzzle game with a unique and awesome gimmick. You run and jump as normal, but at any time you can hold down a button and freeze the screen. Freezing the screen also causes it to "wrap": the top and bottom are connected so that if you jump down a pit, you will reappear at the top of the screen, the same for the sides. So, if you run into a wall, all you need to do is freeze the screen, then run to the opposite side of the screen from the wall, where you will appear on the other side of the screen, on the other side of the wall. Unfreeze the screen and viola! You can go to the next puzzle.
Since this is sidescrolling, there are areas where you can die, shown as static in the world. Should you die, you are instantly returned to solid ground, no muss no fuss. Your character(s?) also have a soft glow about them, which is useful for figuring out where they are when the is frozen. Why can't I go forward, you think, and then you'll see that you are trying to walk into solid rock from the light you're giving off.
You would think that this freezing screen thing is good enough for a free student game, but not for a full game. You'd be wrong. Four Sided Fantasy likes to change things up, like all good puzzle games do. For some sets of puzzles, when you freeze the screen and exit one side, gravity will be reversed on the other side. Others, the screen will split into 2 parts, where freezing will freeze the screen you're in. I found the puzzles to be a little on the easier side. They're not mind-numbingly easy, but they're not Snakebird hard where you have no idea where to start. I usually take half a minute or less to finish one of the puzzles, except for the odd tricky one where I'll have to experiment or think for a few minutes before I get it.
If the puzzles are on the easy side, it doesn't matter because it feels so cool to solve them!
The music is pretty and the graphics are beautiful.
There are 2 downsides with this game. First, puzzles are divided into sets, shown by the landscape/time of day. There is no saving within these sets, so if you're in the middle of Summer - Night, and you want to stop playing for the night, well, there goes your progress. Thankfully, sets aren't too long I found, so that's good.
Second, it took me around 2 hours to beat the game! I wanted more!
Buy it and love it, like I do!

I am not much of a puzzle gamer. I will admit I am used to games that give me a reason to drive, destroy, seek adventure, and deal with dangerous opposition. However, running into a puzzle 2D adventure with a unique art and play style caught my interest. I was a bit intimidated at first, but after a few hours, I was hooked. Let’s take a look into Four Sided Fantasy from Ludo Land.
Four Sided Fantasy gives players the opportunity to puzzle their way through obstacles on a 2D plane. As stated by using the ideas of “Pac-Man” where if he goes through a tunnel and ends up on the other side of the map. You have the same ability at your command, but with a twist of switching up characters when doing so. This is one of those silent games that give you the courtesy to concentrate on the puzzle itself. I have played for few hours just concentrating on what is going on and what will I face at the end.
There are a few cameras planted around the levels which gave me the idea that maybe someone us watching us in this world. Why they are watching is still a mysterious and why within each season our powers seem to evolve or manifest into a new ability?
Visually the game is beautiful, I am captivated by the level designs as simple as they are they are fun to look at. I think my favorite level was the night time scene with the falling stars and the darkness of a thunderstorm you have to navigate through.
You are free to play without fear. That is right this is a game that helps you focus on what you need to do. There is no worry of losing lives or continues. If you fail, you just reset right away to the last spot you were at and that is a nice gesture or rather a relief from playing games where there is too much to worry about instead of just getting to your destination.
There is not much else I can say about it without spoiling the ending, but there is a uniqueness that is missing in many games these days. I am just happy that I gave Four Sided Fantasy a shot, it was a nice change of pace, subtle gameplay that made me excited that I figured out the levels. That whole, “I did It!” feeling was rewarding and each level progression felt seamless. It stayed continuous with little to no loading.
Conclusion:
Four Sided Fantasy gives me some form of nostalgia when I used to play an old school title “A Boy and his Blog” with my cousin. The puzzles are fun to figure out and comfortable controls. It is a game that teaches you while you play on what to do. In that, I give F.S.F a 4.5 out of 5. I would not say it is too long and at $9.99 that is a great deal.
Be sure to check out Four Sided Fantasy which is out on August 30th. I do hope you enjoyed this review and check back for more news and more content. Stay frosty gamers!

In respect to those who give this game where credit is due, I find that this game can be pretty lacking in the field of public transit. In my eyes, a "perfect" public transit system is where all forms of transit follow three requirements: Convienence, Punctuality, and Reliability. Convience: To an extent, it's only the connection in this aspect that matters. If you are a regular transit commuter you will know that sometimes a train, bus, tram, plane, or even a ferry will run late by a few minutes to almost 15min-1hr. in this game this factor is taken accounted for, but it doesn't allow the player to have a convience factor. If a train station also doubles up as a bus station then it's easier to figure out your connection timing. From my time in San Fransico and Oakland the bus, tram, and trains would normally run on time and run inacordance together. That's what I hate about Cities in Motion 2 the most. Punctuality: With any transit system you want to see that your bus or any other form of transit runs on timme according to the schedule. CiM2 does catter to this by having correct departure times, but sometimes the vehicles will fall behind by a substantial nummber. Reliability: For a realiable transit system you must know that the bus driver will wait for you, CiM2 does not take this into account for any reason. In my  opinion for this game after playing 400+ hours of it, CiM2 is not for the modern day simulation world.

This game had a compelling story that kept me wanting to play on and on. It is definitely one of the best contenders in the visual novel/dating sim genre. There are some things to be aware if though, which I will be addressing in the cons section of my review.
Pros
+ Each of the characters are supremely unique and have interesting backstories. I've completed the routes for each of the guys, and each guy turned out to be more than what meets the eye. All the characters have positive & negative sides to them, and they each come with some surprises.
+ The art is gorgeous! I love a game that will take the time to show you some of the pivotal scenes drawn out, and this game does it awesomely! If you look through the screenshot collection on Steam, you will easily see that the story doesn't skimp on engaging cut scenes with wonderful pictures.
+ I *felt* a lot during the game. I really did empathize with what was going on. You can't go wrong with a game that gets your heat invested.
+ The voice acting was a great touch! Even though it was in Korean, I loved being able to hear the emotion behind what the characters were saying.
+ The stat system felt balanced. The stats you needed were different for each character, and I did find myself having to pay attention to make sure I was on track. It added a challenging element to the game without it making it feel bogged down.
+ The game is VERY replay friendly! I've spent over 30 hours playing and I haven't even gotten all the endings yet. Every romance route is different and enchants you in ways.
Cons
- You unexpectedly run into some uncomfortable stuff in this game. Some of the guys get extremely verbally abusive, posessive, physically violent, and stalker-ish. I did fine with it, but just beware - if you are triggered by any of these things, you might want to look up a walkthrough beforehand and avoid certain routes.
- This is kind of spoiler-y, but whatever: Jieun's route was BORING. Like... why include this dude as a romance option if the entire time he's just gonna be like "lol i'm too young though." I felt more like I was being his babysitter and it was weird. I know plenty of people loved his story, but I thought it couldn't hold a candle to the other stories. That can be up for you to decide though.
In short: If you like anime dating sims and can appreciate some upscale art, definitely give this a shot. The majority of the romance routes will tug at your heart, but prepare yourself - the stories WON'T be all rainbows and butterflies.

The statistics you need to raise are Art, Beauty and Femininity. Each love interest has different requirements that you need to meet in order to continue the relationship. I saw a problem in the stats. In the writing as well, in certain routes.
Heejung can only act within the walls of her house. Heejung has the function to save the male interest from his painful past. She is unaware of her feelings, unaware of her needs, incapable of relating personal experience to the same romantic clichés she criticizes when she reads Harlequin novels or goes to the movies. True, Heejung overcomes her fear, but she does not accomplishes it by herself. Her knight on a white horse does the talking to the source of her nightmares. She needs her prince to save her. (Notable exception is
's route, which favorably impressed me!) Typical otoge MC that I can't identify with: despite the universal nature of her conflict, it's approached in such a childish way that it made me feel annoyed instead of empathetic.
Despite all this, I still recommend the game--it's Cheritz. Just beware the stat grind!

Space Run Galaxy is a well polished revision of the original Space Run with what looks to my eye at least an improved aesthetic.  The incorporation of the galaxy itself that you can travel around, plot elements to keep things moving, multiplayer features for creating contracts for other players or accepting them to make some coin yourself are all welcome features that give the game a bit more of a sense of life.  The voice acting is good, the characters well designed if intentionally cliched and the gameplay is smooth as silk.  This is the kind of game, similar to something like Binding of Isaac or Enter the Gungeon where dropping in for a run or two and then not touching it again for a few days feels totally normal.  I like games in this vein where you can spend a lot, or a little time and still feel a sense of accomplishment.  For a $20 game, it is definitely worth recommending.

As many have lamented, I wish steam had a middle ground option.  The thumbs down implies that space run galaxy is a bad game, which it isn't.  However, when I look at the question of "Do you recommend this game" very simply, my answer is no.  The fact of the matter is that Space Run 1 is a better game.  They've added a great deal more grind and called it content.  Yes this game will take longer to beat than its predecessor, but that's not a good thing in this case.
Worth the small price tag, good for approx 2.5 hours of gameplay to finish. I'm satisfied with the purchase and will keep buying from this developer.

What can you say about a game that exceeds your expectations on every level?
If you are a fan of the Trails in the Sky trilogy then you are going to love this game. Take my word for it.
Have you not played any games from the series but you are a generic fan of anime/JRPG?  Then I say you should give it a try. Because Trails of Cold Steel  marks the start of a brand new story which adapts certain aspects from its predecessors but swings to a unique direction. Some background knowledge may increase the taste you take from the story but it is not a necessity.
It has a fascinating story that deepens with every step you take.  You watch the story through the perspective of Rean Schwarzer, a junior student in Thor’s Military Academy.  Yet from the very start of the game you find yourself surrounded by a bunch of different characters, your classmates and instructors. Characters who have travelled from different parts of the Erebonian Empire.
Each of these characters possess a different personality, an uninhibited view of the world they live in. That’s right! Those classmates not “your gang” who keep following you blindly in your self-proclaimed quest.  They have their own thoughts, feelings and remarks. While some of them are rather friendly and modest from the very start of the story; you will find some are quite cynical and rude, rather hotheaded and prickly, quite cold and reckless, irritatingly proud and serious, amusingly childish and immature or rather polite yet completely shrouded by mystery. Every character has their own past and secrets which you discover throughout the flow of the game. These secrets vary from small ones like favorite foods or childhood dreams to rather serious ones like real name or lineage of a character. And these details make you feel like you are surrounded by real people instead of an army of side-kicks.  Only after experiencing some serious bonding events they will start to open up to you and respect you.
While you are trying to get used to your new life in the military academy, a much thicker plot starts to unwind  in the background which contains components of an international crises, an ever-growing civil unrest  between different social classes, a dark organization with a mysterious agenda and an ancient fairy tale that starts to show signs of legitimacy. And each answer you get will only trigger more questions.  And get ready for some unforeseeable twists!
Apart from the fascinating story and fulfilling character development, Trails of Cold Steel also offers a vibrant atmosphere and a great soundtrack. The characters will travel to different points of a giant empire and each step of their journey will take place in a completely different setting  varying from the others with an authentic  NPCs and fitting background music. Unless you are rushing the game, try to talk to as many NPCs around as possible. The things you learn, or the items you acquire may surprise you.
As a fellow RPG-gamer I give this game 10/10 and recommend it to every JRPG lover. And keep in mind that this game is only the first installment of a trilogy. Therefore do not expect to see an “end” yet. ;)

Definitely one of the best JRPG's out there. This game originally released for Playstation 3 and Playstation Vita in 2013, but XSEED did a really got job at improving graphics for PC version. If you are interested in a good story, great characters and good turn-based tactical JRPG - this is the one for you.
Pros:
- High quality PC port, no crashes, a lot of available video options and tweaks.
- A "Turbo System" which will speed up your game, when you press and hold a specific button. Very useful for grinding levels/items or traveling over long distances. Seriously, every game should include a button like that.
- Awesome story and main characters, most of them is not your-generic-anime-cliche-stereotype.
- Your choices actually do something, so you better read the books in-game or search answers @Google.
- Some boss battles may be hard at first, but there's a key to each one of them, either it's some status ailments(that will help you tremendiously) or magical attacks vulnerability and such. Limit Breaks (aka EX skills) do a decent amount of damage. There's a lot of possible characters/squad combination in this game.
- Character customization. There's a lot of passive/active skills that you can equip. You can get those from treasure chests, as monster drops or even craft them.
- There's 50% more voice lines, compared to PS3/Vita versions and i would say english voiceover in this game is really great.
- There's a lot of optional quests and content, however, be aware that THOSE ARE EASILY MISSABLE! If you advance from June, 25 to June, 26 and did not finish all hidden or optional quests(related to June, 25), then you can't complete those until next playthrough. Hidden quests are never marked in your quest book and you must search for them manually.
Cons:
- Some people may not like the graphics, since the game is kinda old already.

This is one of the greatest games ever made in the modern era of gaming. My favourite entry in the Deus Ex series, a step back to the original formula of Deus Ex, instead of continuing on Invisible War's path (not a bad game, but I wouldn't call it a much of a Deus Ex game outside of its story). It has a morality-and-conspiracy-theory-centered storyline with tough decisions, and all the while, is an action-packed first-person shooter with stealth and RPG elements. It's an incredibly long game; it took me 38 hours to complete story mode (actually this game is only story mode, the only downside I see to this game) on my first playthrough. Every time you think the story is over, it's not, until you reach the obvious climax. The gameplay is solid. There are several weapons to choose from, the video game standards (pistols, revolvers, shotguns, assault rifles, sniper rifles, rocket launchers, and miniguns), non-lethal weapons for the pacifists (stun guns, PEPS [a concussion-inducing weapon], and tranquilizer dart rifles), as well as laser rifles/plasma rifles. The highlight of weapons in this game though is the Typhoon Explosive System, which will utterly annihilate anyone within approximately 10 feet of you, allowing you to take out even the most "unkillable" enemies with one attack. There are several types of grenades as well (frag, concussion, gas, and EMP) for several different purposes, the last two being especially useful for knocking out groups of enemies immediately, and for temporarily disabling cyborgs/destroying robots, respectively. The main focus of a Deus Ex game, of course, is the ability to augment your character (Adam Jensen, a SWAT commander turned corporate security officer) in a variety of different ways, allowing for better resistance to damage, the ability to see through walls, to sprint and jump faster, cloak and run silently, etc. By the time you finish the story, no matter how overpowered it seems you are, you will die. And you will die again. Damage received in this game is incredibly brutal and sometimes the autosave system just isn't on your side. But that's why I love this game. It presents an excellent challenge, even on the "medium" difficulty. And at the end, you are faced with a dilemma (actually a quadlemma, because you have four choices, each giving you a distinctive ending). It's a tough choice to make, one of the hardest I've ever made in a game. Luckily you can save whenever you want so you can just go back and see all four endings for yourself. I, on the other hand, am content with my ending, and refuse to know what the "canon" ending is (according to Deus Ex: Mankind Divided, this game's sequel which I have heard is not exactly the best). Overall, this game is amazing and is worth picking up even at full price (I purchased it on sale with the Deus Ex collection almost two years ago).

The Old City: Leviathan is more of an interactive story than a game, one that you have to piece together yourself, and the experience is definitely not for everyone. Those looking for clear-cut objectives, indicators on where to go and in what order to do things and a narrative that's easy to follow, doesn't leave itself open to many interpretations and doesn't assault the player with philosophical ideas expounded in lengthy sentences will feel frustrated and likely unable to enjoy the experience.
However, if you like pondering the deeper meaning behind the protagonist's monologues or journal entries found throughout the environments, or enjoy seeing the world through someone else's eyes and listening to others' perceptions of places, people and facets of dreams and reality, all the while exploring beautiful or moody environments accompanied with a suitably evocative soundtack, The Old City is a tale that's really worth experiencing, in my opinion.
It's not an easy tale to follow (especially if english is not your native language) and some of the connections might not dawn on the player until subsequent playthroughs of the various chapters, but there are no challenges, tasks or jump scares to distract you from collecting all the tidbits of information, so the story can be unfolded at your own pace.
The trailers on the store page might suggest a very gruesome, dark tone to the game's story, and while there certainly are eerie, gloomy parts of it, the overall experience in my opinion is a positive and uplifting one, once you've learned to accept the characters' personalities. If slower paced, thought-provoking games are your stuff, do yourself a favour and get The Old City: Leviathan.

This feels like someone played Dear Esther or Gone Home and thought, "Gee, that's great, but how about I replace narrative with some guy babbling about all the stuff he learned from that semester when he was getting stoned a lot and taking multiple philosophy classes."
Many of the environments are pretty interesting, but at times I felt the length was padded out with repetitive use of the sort of bland industrial corridors that haunt virtually every first person game, and at times it seemed like a deleted scene from Half Life 2. Sometimes post-apocalyptic wastelands are just an excuse not to have to render living creatures.
The setting and the narrative didn't feel engaging or intriguing enough to keep me going for any reason beyond sight seeing. It's mostly just someone babbling at me, repeating the same thing rephrased by abusing a thesaurus, while I try to figure out my way forward.
By the end some of the narrators statements had me rolling my eyes so badly I think I may have hurt my vision.

As this is not really a "game" in the conventional sense, but more of a a "walking simulator" or a story that progresses by you walking through it, it's hard to give a conventional review.
It's an amazing "game". If philosophy interests you, or at least you're somehow considering yourself a thinker, you might really enjoy this ride.
The atmosphere nonetheless is great, it has some very beautiful and creative scenes, a lot to read (which you should not avoid or else you have no clue what this is all about), a very interesting "plot" and a fitting nearly epic soundtrack.
It is not really "fun" to play, yet it is a one of a kind experience you will fail to find a second like it.
So even if you don't give a damn about the story or it's underlying message, you will constantly stop and admire the scene.
It's quite short though, i was done with it in roughly two hours. Yet there are two "Solomons notes" left i could not find.
Even regarding the fact i missed some fragments of the plot, i don't feel like running around a second time yet...it's not that the story would change or you could miss a lot.
Still worth it's price?
Well i enjoyed the short, not very funny, ride. MAYBE i will play it again in the future but right now it was a very fast shot. If you enjoy "experimental" "games" with a very specific intention to make you think, this could be still worth your money and time.
I quote the developer here (freely) as "...this is a title that no major publisher would have risked its money on...". And i'd second this. Brave developer, and it obviously payed off!

First of all, I should be clear that this is NOT a game for everyone. If you like action packed games or clear, strutctured linear stories (because those are fun too, right?), then you might want to think about buying this game.
If you have a pretty open mind, like narrative driven stories that make you really think and you enjoy immersing yourself in an environment, then this is a great game for you! The Old City: Leviathan is a narrative-driven game which some have deemed a 'walking simulator' which I feel is rather unfair. It's a unique game, to be sure.
The Old City Leviathan is, first off, a beautifully crafted game. Very few games, even AAA titles today, can really pull off the amazing sense of atomsphere and environment. As you, the player, walk around this world of the Old City, it carries a strange air of eerie beauty. Even the sewers you find yourself in have a charm to them, having been turned into tempoary abodes by the sparse population. Perhaps its beauty lies in the sense of decay and the lonliness of the character as he explores an empty shell.
Now and then, you alternate from 'reality' to dream although it's difficult to tell sometimes. You may find, as I have, that re-visiting areas yield changes, some marginal, some noticeable.
There are no puzzles, no traps and no enemies in this world and this is very deliberate. Your role is not to fight, but to explore, to immerse yourself in this strange and exotic world.
The in-game story is a little vague at times, partly due to the mode of storytelling which is told through monologues and pages. As you explore and read the notes left for you, things become a little clearer. The monologues and many of the notes are generally philsophical in many ways although you do receive some backstory into the main characters.
The theories esposued are not altogether clear or easy to understand, but as I mentioned above (and as the developer explainned) this isn't a game for everyone. The theories are interesting though and as you learn more, you might form your own theories. The main one, or rather, the one I latched onto, was seeing the game in a biblical sense but there are probably many theories in this game.
This is a game that is very different from many other games. I might go so far as to call it a 'therapy game' because I found exploring the Old City and the dream worlds quite relaxing. It is a beautiful, detailed and thought-provoking story-driven game and I hope big game developers are taking notes on this.
I am certainly looking forward to more from this developer. Keep up the good work.

The simplest way to describe the movement is free form. There are the simple routes most people take, but once you know the ins and outs of your capabilities, its an endless sandbox of potential. The use of grenade and rocket boosts can change a player's trajectory and elevation, but usually is used for the speed to catch opposing enemies or to speed through their base, and by god, once you hit past 250, you will know what true happiness feels like. The exhilaration of gliding through the huge maps the game has to offer is incredible, using your time in the air to guide your character from slope to slope, bringing the flag home or taking down the opposing team's flag carrier.
I would have begged anybody give this truly free to play game (Oh yeah, that's another good point too) if I made this review two years ago, but now, the community is dead. There are usually one and a half to two servers that have activity in them, so people wont get the same satisfaction as before, which is the worst part of this masterpiece. This game shoud've never died, and I hope HiRez finds the time to make another installment.

**This review of Dandelion - Wishes brought to you - may contain minor spoilers.**
Dandelion - Wishes brought to you - is the debute otome game for the Korean video game studio, Cheritz. The game was released in South Korea in August 2012 and was released in the US in August 2012. The game was released on Steam  on September 29, 2014.
The game revolves around Heejung, a Korean college student majoring in business with a penchant for art. One day, she wakes up to discover a basket of animals in her room: two cats and three rabbits. Heejung eventually adopts the animals as her own, only to discover that the would-be animals actually have human forms. Moreover, they're actually from another world entirely.
DISCLAIMER: While I have beaten the good routes for all of the characters, I have not yet played through the bad routes. I'm sure I'll play through them eventually, and will amend my review accordingly if needed.
The protagonist:
Heejung Kim, our leading lady, is an incredibly relatable character. Ever since her parents divorced, she has struggled to meet her mother's expectations. In doing so, Heejung has lost her sense of self. What does she want to do with her life? What kind of person does she want to be? As the game progresses, Heejung finds those answers.
While the game does not explicitly call the relationship between Heejung and her mother abusive, the characters of Dandelion universally acknowledge that Heejung's mother's behavior is unacceptable. No one ever attempts to encourage Heejung to make amends with her mother; no one ever makes excuses for her mother's behavior (e.g., "she just wants the best for you!"), either. That definitely won brownie points with me.
While Heejung's characterization is fairly consistent across all routes, there are some routes where her growth as a character is absolutely outstanding. If you like lots of character development in your protagonists, I highly recommend that you start with the Jieun route.
The love interests:
Before I bought the game, a friend warned me that the bunny routes were all much better than the cat routes. After clearing through all the good endings, I absolutely agree. The interaction between the bunny characters and Heejung were mostly positive; those relationships -- for the most part -- involved mutual support and care and respect.
Unfortunately, the same can not be said for the cat routes.
While the game did a fabulous job of addressing familial abuse, some of the romantic relationships on the game were abusive. While I don't plan on addressing those issues in every route, there is one love interest where the abuse is especially prevelant; that's the fan favorite, Jisoo's route.
During his route, he does the following:
-follows Heejung without her knowledge
-tells Heejung she can't be friends with any other men
-assumes that Heejung secretly has a boyfriend when he discovers Heejung crying about her mother and then retaliates by /pining her down/ and demanding to know why she lied to him about her relationship status
-repeatedly drags Heejung off by the wrist and holds her down against her will/protests
Unlike the relationship between Heejung and her mother, the game fails to acknowledge that this behavior is abusive; disappointingly, it's even romanticizied.
All of the bunny routes managed to make up for extremely unhealthy relationships that Heejae had with Jisoo and, to a lesser degree, Jiyeon. If you value healthy relationships, you'll enjoy any of the bunny routes.  If I had to recommend one, though, it'd definitely be Jihae's route.
Final Thoughts:
Dandelion - Wishes brought to you - is your standard otome game. You play a female protagonist, you fall in love, and Things Happen. While the story itself doesn't bring anything new to the table, it's (most of) the characters, the character development, and the way the game thoughtfully and respectfully address familial abuse that make Dandelion a stand-out title for me. Highly recommended.
Final ranking: 4/5

Welp, I found myself hankering for another puzzle-platformer in the vein of Braid or Fez, and this was first on the recommendations list.
Let's see, is this where I'm supposed to list pros and cons? Well, let's start with some pros: the game is visually gorgeous, the use of the video-camera frame graphic to differentiate between wrapping and not-wrapping is intriguing, the music and sound design are great.
Oh, and the gameplay is marvelous. The puzzles are well-crafted, with a great learning curve to introduce you to the mechanics, and by the end you will have explored all the potential exploits of the format. This game is masterful at an underappreciated aspect of designing a puzzle-platformer, namely, using the layout and environment design to guide the player toward the correct solution without making it so obvious that they don't feel clever for figuring it out. That is a harder balance to strike than you'd think, it's something that most players don't even consciously realize is there and consequently many devs don't consider it, but this game is good at it.
The game introduces new mechanics promptly as it runs out of ideas for the existing ones and it's at risk of getting repetitive, and I didn't have to look up a playthrough video once to get through it, yet the puzzles weren't too easy either.
That said, a couple of the puzzles I solved more or less by mistake, and those made me go "Wait, what did I just do, and why did that work?" Fortunately those moments were few and far between... until I got to the last level with the splitscreen, in which they started coming hard and fast... exacerbated by the fact that I encountered my first few bugs in that level (the bugs continued into the achievements, BTW... I completed the game for the first time, and it gave me the "finished New Game Plus" achievement, rather than the "Finished the game for the first time" achievement).
Which in turn brings me to my main complaint, that the game is too short. I get that there's probably only so many puzzles they could get out of the mechanics plus each level's new gimmick, and there's only so many new mechanics you could devote a level to without it becoming too forced, but I really must recommend that you wait for it to go on sale, because even at $9.99 I feel like it should have been longer.
My other major complaint is that there didn't really turn out to be a story. The blurb on the store page, the usage of the video-camera motif, and the ending level all seemed to hint at there being some point, but nope, nothing really happened in the endgame except for a sinister musical shift, a graphical distortion, and a slow iris-out before the torus thing, that would probably have been really cool and chilling if there had been any discernible narrative meaning to it. Is there some clue in the "Secret Area" that the locked achievement wants to goad me into trying to find? Not sure I'm up for that.
In conclusion, I tentatively recommend this game IFF you're jonesing for a puzzle-platformer with a good mechanic explored in an innovative way and pretty graphics, but as mentioned above, I recommend you wait for it to go on sale.

This is a platform puzzler with a unique twist. The 4 edges of the screen can be 'wrapped' so that your character disappears off one edge and appears on the opposite side, then you let go of the 'lock' for the character to continue along the path you've set.
The main thing I have to say about this game is that it's very disorienting and strange (in a good way). I completed the game and I can honestly say that I never reached the point where I properly understood what I was doing. Even towards the end I was still using trial and error sometimes. Maybe if I do this, that or the other it might work...
You can use keyboard/mouse or controller. Both are efficient but I found controller to be more natural.
You control a boy and girl who are "trying to find each other" in some kind of abstract story. The gameplay makes it feel like they are the same character but switch whenever you edge-flip.
The game progresses through the seasons and each has its individual art theme and game mechanic. You start off normally just flipping the edges. Next comes gravity where the boy walks normally but the girl is upside-down so there's a lot of inertia-freefall-bouncing up and down. Next comes background-foreground where the girl appears nearer and the boy further away, each with their own platform of course. Then in the last phase it's split screen where you have both girl and boy separated by a central screen split. It's so weird I don't even know how to explain that one.
The checkpoints are all placed at the points where you're likely to die, so you're always popping up again exactly where you failed. The game saves are far less precise. There are only 8 level selection points, so if you decide to close the game and take a break you may have to repeat several minutes of gameplay to catch up again.
Rather beautiful minimalistic 2D artwork. The colour themes change with the seasons so you have brown/orange-themed autumn, winter with dark blues and white ice etc.
The music is more of an ambient sound than a tune. Nice and restful but forgettable.
It depends how your brain works. For some people it might just click and seem easy, to others impossible confusion. I found it medium difficulty mostly, but I confess there were one or two levels that stumped me completely and I had to google the solutions. It's easy when you know how!
There are a few levels that require timing to get the jump just right but for the most part it's brainwork rather than coordination.
There have been previous issues but these have all been fixed during the past week and I can report that the game now runs smooth and flawlessly on Windows at 1920x1200 res, windowed or fullscreen. No glitches remaining.
There are no in-game settings at all. You can set the screen resolution via the Unity startup dialog so that's fine. However, the game's sound levels are too loud by default and the only way to turn the volume down is with your system sound. This may not be convenient if for example you're streaming a TV show at the same time which you're then unable to hear properly.
The quality and unique concept are excellent but if you judge games by the quantity of gameplay I have to say the main playthrough is too short considering the price. There's maybe 2-3 hours' worth at a leisurely pace. Perhaps wait for a sale.
Normally, since this is a puzzle game, I would say there's no replay value but in this case I've found that the puzzles are so beyond my normal way of thinking that I can complete a puzzle then go back and try it again 2 minutes later and I've already forgotten how I did it.
Completion of the game unlocks a 'Plus Mode' where instead of the edges wrapping it sort of wraps in the middle so you're often looking at a screen split into 4 quarters. It's the same game but from a different view - as if it wasn't confusing enough already!
There are two particular achievements that encourage replay to complete the game with limited numbers of wraps and locks. There's also a hidden area achievement - if you manage to find it please let me know so I can get my perfect game.
No trading cards yet. 11 achievements and at time of writing some of them drop on completion of the game when they're not supposed to, so if you're an an achievement hunter buy it quick before they fix it ;)

Unique and interesting puzzle platformer that takes such a "game-y concept" as screen-wrapping and bases everything around it. The first time I encountered this strange behavior of connecting virtual screen edges was when I played Balloon Fight on the NES as a kid. I always wondered if it would be possible to make a full game out of this. Four Sided Fantasy beautifully manages to do this. The game will open your mind and forces you to think "with screens". Like Portal before it, you will start to think about spatial relationships in a new way.
Four Sided Fantasy is relatively short and not too difficult. The last stages are especially interesting, although I would have loved to explore some of the their corresponding gameplay mechanics a bit further. Also, some of the puzzles felt more like trial and error than actual mental puzzle-solving; however, this was fine by me, since the very nature of the screen-wrapping mechanic is about trying things out by moving around.
All in all, Four Sided Fantasy is a nice little gem that strive to explore one single game mechanic, namely screen-wrapping and the "invisible space" between virtual edges. Even if you are bit tired of the puzzle platform genre, I think this game provides a fresh and unique take on something that hasn't really been explored in other games before.

Four Sided Fantasy is a game I've been looking forward to for a while. When I first saw it on Kickstarter, I was really excited about it premise (disclaimer: I did back it on Kickstarter) so I played the prototype of the game and could see the promise of what the team could do. Having played through the game I am overall pleased with what I have received from Four Sided Fantasy, but there have been a few negatives. Let's break the positives and negatives down.
Positives:
+ Interesting mechanic. Like VVVVVV and Braid before it, it takes a mechanic (in this case screen wrapping) and explores it to the fullest.
+ Great art style and effects. The game is vibrant and stylish. Kudos to the art team on this one!
+ Challenging puzzles. There were a few times I had to come back to the game because a certain puzzle was a bit too much for me to deal with at the time. However, I was able to figure it out and felt rewarded (the “aha!” moment) every time.
+ Character changing. This might seem a bit silly but I like the fact that the character changed from a man to a woman when screen wrapping. I thought that that was a nice little twist that brings a little bit extra to the game.
Negatives:
- I had occasions where the character would disappear after a screen wrap. While a little frustrating, the game could have used an obvious restart from last puzzle element or a button that kills the player if they become stuck. What could make this problem more frustrating is if I had been going for the achievement to complete the game under a certain amount of screen wraps.
- The game is short. Far shorter than I thought it’d be (my time is 99 minutes). I feel like this is comparable to the prototype in length, but it’s entirely possible that I was able to play through the game quickly because of my prior experience with the prototype. Having said that, this could be off putting to some but the game is priced fairly low and I think that the experience is worth it.
In the end, I enjoyed the game and I think it’s a good addition to the puzzle platformers like Braid, VVVVVV, and Fez. If you like those games, you’ll probably like Four Sided Fantasy as well.

SquareCells is a puzzle game (and the sequel to the Hexcells series, in case you played those).
Deductive logic is at the core of it all: You are presented with a matrix of coloured squares and it's up to you to figure out which ones need to go and which ones can stay. Your only help in this task is a bunch of numbers both on, around and below the matrix. These numbers give you just enough info to figure out the rest on your own. They may inform you how many connected squares there are in a row, or column. Or of how many connected squares an area within the matrix consists. Or how many squares in general still need to go. You will have to pay attention to all of these, and then it will be possible to solve each puzzle entirely with brain power. Guessing is never necessary.
The game starts off easy and gets pretty hard towards the end. In the later levels, sometimes you're expected to think a few steps ahead. In case that got too taxing, I found it helpful to take a screenshot and draw "what if" scenarios on them (this might just help if you can't wrap your head around a solution, hint, hint).
This game may make you feel stupid sometimes but it's rewarding when you finally figure it out. If your strong suits are logic and tenacity, I can give a recommendation.

I rarely write a review so soon after getting a game, but this game is good. First, IF YOU DO NOT LIKE games that require dexterity or real time reaction, this game isn’t for you. Space Run Galaxy demands that you think on your feet. Many games allow you to pause, think, and build. Many people hate Space Run Galaxy because it does not let you do that. For me, the fact that you can’t do that is part of what makes this game exciting and therefore part of its overall appeal.
With that out of the way, let’s get to why this game is awesome. Personally, I like tower defense games but if you’ve played one, you’ve played them all. But this game genuinely brings something new to the genre. It has a story, a meta-game, and a grand strategy layer. You have to decide what components and blueprint you buy to even have a chance in the actual “run” (the tower defense phase). You have to decide where and what to buy. Get something that will help you now, or save your resources for that advanced component? Haul your cargo to another port or just sell it for a quick buck?
Each run has just enough unpredictability that it keeps you on your feet, but the enemies are generally predetermined so you can still learn from mistakes and plan ahead if you fail the first time. There’s no frustrating RNG. It’s just plain exciting in the best way possible. The boss battles especially will keep you on the edge of your seat.
And what really pushes this game over the top, for me, is the polish. The voice acting is colorful and entertaining. The art is well done and immersive. The music is top-notch. And there are no bugs. I always find bugs in games. It used to be my job. I was a software developer. This game has more polish than a lot of AAA games. Finally, the writing is good. The story takes itself just as seriously as it should.
If you have kids, one more thing you might consider is this game is all-ages. It’s difficult after a certain point, but the content is perfectly fine.
I recommend this game to anyone without disclaimer or caveat (well, except for the one in the first paragraph). This is just a really well-made, fun game. I guarantee at least 50 hours of enjoyment!

Note: for the purpose of this review, I didn't play the game with a VR set.
The TL;DR version of this review is: it's a bad game, but it has its own charm.
I cannot say it's not a bad game, because it is. The graphics are terrible, the voice acting is abysmal and there are major flaws in the game - right in the first chapter, you can actually "find" one of the shadows that comes as part of one of the jump scares, as it's not removed from the game after the scare moment is gone. If you walk outside, you can find it just sitting there.
It also doesn't help that the last chapter of the game tries to be a multiplayer mode. You'd think that last chapter would have more story that would fill in the blanks of the first three chapters, but nope - it's just a large level that attempts to pit players against each other, as you can set up scare traps and follow other players' footsteps while looking for clues at the same time. It's not actually a bad idea. The problem is... No one is playing it. There were two servers available, both of which were empty.
It also doesn't help that the game is incredibly short (you can finish it in less than an hour, possibly less than half an hour), has a 3-stars score system that makes no sense (I completed chapter 2 as quickly as possible while completing all events and still got only 2 stars) and has a story that is still left filled with questions once you've played all chapters.
So, why do I recommend the game despite all these flaws?
As bad as the game might be, it has its own charm, in a way. It's actually decently scary, even if mostly all scare events are predictable, and the game leaves no breathing space - unless you stop playing, it's one jump scare right after the other. And I'd be willing to bet that the game is actually a lot scarier if you're playing it with a VR set.
For the ridiculously low price it has, I'd recommend it as a one time experience. if you're a fan of horror games. Don't get me wrong, it IS a bad game. But you might find some redeeming value nonetheless.

This is among my favorite games of all time like the Trails in the Sky series. (Trails in the Sky does not need to be played to enjoy this game. It does, however, give background to the history and goings on of the world Cold Steel takes place in)
Similarly to Trails in the Sky, it builds up a fantastic story with lots of character progression, not only from main characters, but from a bunch of characters that you can optionally talk to throughout the game.  This game tends to be humurous.
One can choose how much they want to know more about certain characters, especially when it comes to what the game calls "bonding events", which serves to help give perks in battle as well as give background to characters.
There's also a great deal of voice acting done in this game, and it is some of the best voice acting for a game I've ever heard.  The Voice Actors do a great job giving personality to the character's voices.
While each character is better suited to certain fighting styles, each can be greatly customized to battle a certain way with the game's orbment system. If you've played FF7, it's kinda like materia placed into weapons, but in this game it's called quartz and it's placed into a kind of "cell phone" device this game calls an Arcus unit.  It allows one to use that device to use orbal arts, a.k.a. magic, and augment their powers.  It can be fun to try to figure out a nice setup, but it also can be tedius at times to try to set up (since party members change a lot, except for the main character, and the quartz can be freely exchanged between party members).
The music is fantastic.  I want to say it's worth it for the music alone, but $40 is a bit much for music.  However, experiencing the music along with the game makes it totally worth it.  All the tracks feel well placed and enhance the experience.
I played this game entirely with a steam controller, so I can't comment on the keyboard & mouse experience, but playing it on a controller is very nice.  I've had lots of long play sessions (if my play time didn't make that obvious) and didn't have any hand fatigue.
The game also runs very nice and smooth.  It looks great, and there are already mods that can make it look even better.
My first time playing through, I tried to experience everything that I could blindly, and I ended up with 116 hours played according to steam, but it was probably closer to 105-110 actual hours since I had some afk time. So there's quite a bit to this game to enjoy. The New Game + mode, nightmare difficulty, and extra bonding event scenes make it worth another playthrough as well.
Given the amount of fun to be had, and how great this game is, it's well worth the $40 price point.
