is a visual novel in which you control a female protagonist, Heejung, and build stats to pursue one of five men, each of whom sport adorable cat or rabbit ears. The premise revolves around two cats and three rabbits mysteriously being brought into the protagonist's home, then taking on a human form. How did they find their way into Heejung's home? What is the "game" they keep talking about, and what is Heejung's role in it? These questions are answered throughout the game's multiple routes, encouraging replays until all are completed and all of the story's pieces come together.

Heejung is a very likeable and relateable protagonist. Unlike the majority of dating sim protagonists, who lack personality and backstory for the sake of "immersion," Heejung has a life and personality all her own. Watching Heejung handle her conflicts, such as an overbearing mother and her uncertainty of what to do with her future, makes her an enjoyable and relateable character.

's dateable candidates offer a variety of personalities and backstories. They all feature a level of complexity that can only be experienced by playing their route. Their diverse plots and reasonings for participating in the "game" results in wanting to know these characters beyond their initial introductions. The stories pull at your heart, with just the right amount of silliness sprinkled in with the sincerity. Each route is a fair length, and the voice acting is stellar, bringing life to each of the characters in conjunction with their bright, animated portraits.

Gameplay is simple point-and-click, doing various activities to raise your stats, and interacting with the men to boost their affinity for you. The Stats menu lets you know if your stats are high enough to keep going down the character's good route, and you are given ample time to raise them, making playthroughs fairly straightforward.

Features such as Auto, Skip, and Quick Save/Load make replaying the game for different routes convenient. Once you have viewed a specific scene, it becomes available for re-viewing in the Memory menu, making revisiting a previously-finished character's route hassle-free.

Ultimately,
is a touching, memorable experience. The characters are all unique, interesting, and multi-facetd, with appealing designs and engrossing stories. Fun, emotional, and heartwarming, I highly recommend this title to any fan of the otome genre.

In the forums, the dev commented that they're thinking of later adding more content that ties things together, adds a payoff.
Quite disappointing, because there was a lot of unique ideas, and there are setting elements of a post-apocalypse background world (hints of "Fragile Dreams: Farewell Ruins of the Moon"), but they never manifest or realize, much less complete, any more than temporary blotches on a confusing campus. Without any grounding, it's all just shifting sands.
Pretty sands, mind: Great graphics and sound. But ultimately disappointing. If the devs get back to grounding some story elements as aluded to in forum comments, then it might be worth a revisit.
Also: Wonky controller support (even setting buttons for Zoom, Run on an XBox controller does nothing); limited key assignment functionality (could not assign run button to Right Shift, only Left; and NONE of the mouse buttons other than Mouse 1 are assignable, what?); and finally walking is Extremely Slow, and running is Slightly Less than Extremely Slow. The game is something I found wonderfully fun more than a year ago when I started playing it. You modify your characters, you make your own weapons, you go into battle and hope you don't get fragged to death or the person you're trying to kill doesn't have a teammate with a healing beam weapon because, you know, that'd suck.
The graphics are cartoony, but match the feel of the game and help take aware seriousness to add fun. Despite that, they're really very well done. Actually, in a way, the graphics remind me fairly well of Borderlands, now that I think about it.
The worlds are nice and large with several vantage points if you're going for the sniper role, or just to lob a grenade at and smite others from on high.
Animation is smooth and glitches so rarely as to say 'pretty much never', while the engine itself is nice and smooth as well, handling all the action, polygons and activity.
Guns are ... hard to explain. You build your gun with various features and then test it to see how it handles. Sometimes, you've got a first-time-use dead man's switch in your hand and you don't even realize it. Others, you PWN the unholy crap out of some cannon fodder.
My only dislike is that it IS a multiplayer/online game, so you can't play around with it as a skirmish against AI or any mission-style goals. I use satellite-based internet and the bandwidth doesn't allow for me to play the game any longer. *Sad face*
I should also mention it's a lot of fun to play with friends, especially when you end up on opposite teams.
So, I'd like ot see the following:
1) New character models for a bit more variety,
2) Missions for single player since I like the game/world/concept of weaponry and could see a lot of fun with it.
3) Added variations to the weapons.
4) BIGGEST wish - More maps, perhaps even a trapped maze.
I guess in short, just make the game a little bigger, really. After a few months of playing, it begins to grow stale unless you're really into first person shooters and prefer the realism of Call of Duty, zombies of 7 Days to Die and what have you.

Never thought I'd need a gamepad/controller for the pc, however decided to buy this and was pleasantly surprised.
You can customise every button for any game, you can have multiple action sets that change the entire button configuration when you’re in a menu using the mouse or when you're in game. It feels great to hold, and the touchpad’s are slick to use, never before have I used a controller that I choose to use over keyboard & mouse.  (at least for most games)
The right touchpad is used primarily as the mouse, and the left is used as a touch or click based menu. Having the left touch pad as a touch menu feels very smooth and comfortable to use. Then you have the paddles on the back underneath of the controller which provide those two extra buttons which help it match the keyboard for number of keys you can use. These paddles do require you to getting used to using your forth and fifth fingers otherwise the placement of all the buttons feel very natural.
Then there is the gyro which I do not use however many do, and it effectively is a very accurate motion control used by tilting the controller and can be used for aiming in shooters or driving in racing games or anything else for that matter.
The rumble feature is very nice with its own multitude of options, and if you are using the right touchpad with trackball mode it simulates the feeling of using a track ball.
A total of 26 controls/buttons that are fully customisable, taking into account the dual stage triggers which are half press and full press. The left touchpad which can have one set of controls for touch and another for full click.
Certain genres like fps games or space sims will require getting used to however for all others it feels very intuitive with the touchpad’s and very and easy to use as configure.
This controller is a dream for pc users being fully customisable and working with any game imaginable old or new.

Four Sided Fantasy is a lean but charming puzzle-platformer in which the player essentially plays out a "movie," if that "movie" were housed on a corrupted old VHS tape. At any point in the game, the player can create a "freeze frame," turning the then continuous world into a self-contained screenshot where the rules of physics no longer apply. For example, in this "freeze frame," if the player were to jump off a ledge at the bottom of the screen, they would then would reappear falling from the top of the screen; much akin to when one leaves the maze in a Pac-Man game and reappears on the other side. As the game progresses, additional rules and limitations come into play, forcing the player to think about the compounding effects of each new element while trying to progress onward. It feels quite like a cross between the space-based puzzles in Portal and the time-based puzzles in Braid.
The puzzles themselves are interesting, but not overly difficult. The player may need to tackle a couple of the more difficult puzzles a few times, but won't be stuck for long. I was able to complete my first playthrough of the game in just under 90 minutes, and while I enjoyed what was offered, I found myself wanting more. The ending comes abruptly and is somewhat unsatisfying, both in terms of puzzle design and in the bare-bones narrative the game offers. However, after the credits roll, a trickier "New Game Plus" mode unlocks, and there are a small number of secrets and challenges available for those wanting to stick around and test their puzzle-solving skills.
All in all, this game is a solid one-off for a rainy afternoon for those looking for a unique puzzle-solving challenge. Just don't expect the appeal to last a great deal longer than that.

If you love puzzle games, this game would be perfect for you. It’s a mix between Braid and Portal but is simple enough to understand the basic controls. It’s all about puzzle solving to get your character to continue forward to the right side of the screen. Overall, Four Sided Fantasy is a fun little puzzle game. People who I have seen play the demo loved it. It can be a challenge, but just remember to always think outside of the box. You never know what’s going to work.

Hegemony III: Clash of the Ancients is a great improvement upon the last two historical real-time strategy games developed by Longbow Games. Although comparisons with the Total War series will undoubtedly be made, Hegemony III takes a somewhat different approach. Whilst military conquest and political domination are most definitely your ultimate goals, their successful execution requires a greater degree of planning and strategic foresight. Simply marching an army into the lands of a rival city-state and attempting to annex their territory will often not suffice and instead supply lines and the availability of recruits must be managed in order to gain victory. The production of foodstuffs and effective supply lines are also dependent on the seasons and these fluctuations can affect both the morale of your soldiers as well as the loyalty of subjugated cities, making stockpiling and forward bases a necessity. Newly conquered cities must therefore be colonised by your own citizens in order to secure their loyalty long term and large armies cannot be maintained in the field indefinitely without a burgeoning economy at home to sustain them. All of this combines to create a greater degree of in-game realism which I really like.
The game features a sandbox campaign and a smaller tutorial campaign based in Etruria. The AI is solid and an improvement over Hegemony II, although diplomacy is still somewhat basic. The main campaign itself centres on Italia, Cisalpine Gaul and most of Magna Graecia during the 3rd-4th century BC and there are over 25 playable factions set across a number of ancient cultures including Etruscan, Gallic, Sabellic, Greek and Illyric. You can of course also play as the Latins (Rome).
Personally, I am enjoying the game immensely so far and am hoping for future expansions to add in more unit variability and introduce the Punic (Carthaginian) culture into the game.
I'm finding this game to be extremely educative about early Italy. I've learnt a lot about where the various tribes were located, which were of which culture.

Introduction:
Cities in Motion 2 is a City Management game, where you are in charge of the public transportation of different cities. The game comes with 6 standard fictional cities: Central, East, West, South, North and Tutorial City, and many more cities avalible to download on the Steam Workshop, where you also can download rulesets, which changes the capicity and more, and Scenarios. The graphics are a lot better then in Cities in Motion 1, and you now can change timetables and you have a 24 hours day-cycle with rush-hour periods. You can have buses, trams, metros, trolleys, waterbuses (boats) and if you have the Marvellous Monorails DLC, Monorails. You can play and build freely in Sandbox mode, and if you want, even with unlimited money. If you have had enough playing alone, try out the Multiplayer mode (I've never tried it out, so i know nothing about it).
My experience:
So, i didn't enjoy the game in the beginning, as i didn't know how it worked, but after about 3 hours i understood the basics and after almost 200 hours, i'm still learning new things. This game has became my second most played game and it is soon going to be the most played game, and i have it for over a year now. I have 6 of the 12 DLC:s and i've probalbly only wasted 20€ in total on the game, as i've bought everything while it was on sale, if you compare it with Train Simulator, where i wasted around 150€, even if it was on sale.
Positive things about CIM2:
- The gameplay is amazing. When you get the hang on how the game works, you might get addicted, like i did.
- The graphics are so great. Comparing to Cities in Motion 1 or Transport Tycoon Deluxe, it has the best graphics of any public transport management game.
- The amount of DLC. If you ever get tired of the normal vehicles, you can always buy DLC:s to expand your fleet.
- 24 hour day-cycle with rush-hour periods, which make the game more realistic.
Negative things about CIM2:
- It takes a while to understand the gameplay. For me it took about 3 hours, but for some people, it took even longer. You have to learn how to choose your line's route, how to make a line, and how to manage it.
- Because the graphics are so good, you will need agood graphics-card to run this game at a high framrate.
- The vehicles you get if you buy it without any DLC are not many. You get 3 buses, 3 trams, 1 trolley and 1 waterbus.
- The DLC price is high. The European Cities DLC and Marvellous Monorails DLC are very expensive comparing with the other, which i would pay for.
Final Statement:
I really recommend this game to anyone who likes construction and manangement games. It takes a while to get the hang over it, but when you have, it is amazing. I would recommend to buy the European Vehicle pack aswell when you buy the game. And i would recommend to buy the game while it's on sale.
Final rating: 8,7/10

This is a fairly deep RTS, focusing on the unification of Italy before the rise of rome.  The game has a wonderful historical feel to it.  The units are varied, there are some great strategical choices to be made along the way, and it is a lot of fun.  There is always something to do, be it chasing down Raiders, expanding your Empire's borders, building up your cities or culture converting enemy cities!  There are a few minor issues - for example, with an older computer, the game sometimes struggles when you've conquered almost half of Italy, mouse movement can sometimes be very choppy, but overall, the latest patch is very stable.

Let's get down to it    ->     Should you buy this game?
Yes.
Why?
Here's where I'm comming from:
I've mostly played strategy games for well over a decade now, mostly playing turn-based games like the Civ series, Total War series (Rome I, Empire, Rome II, Atilla), CKII, EUIV, and more recently the endless series and Galatic Civilizations III. Earlier I was into RTS more, first strategy game was Star Trek: Armada (and damn proud of it). Loved Celtic Kings, Rise of Nations, Age of Empires, and the like. Didn't get into star craft or command&comquor. Also really enjoyed the first Wargame pc game, Airland was okay, havent played china rising.
>> You should buy this game if:
- You are a fan of historical strategy games (duh) - specifically, you love the challenges that come with large scale strategy games.
- You like the option of meticulously planning each move in turn-based games, yet find real-time to be a refreshing and different sort of challenge.
>  For example, your a big fan of Total war, or perhaps even Endless Legend.
>>  What I don't like about this game:
-  There's a few graphical hicups, but it seems that the developers are on top of things with updates etc.
- THE CAMERA:  One of the things that makes this game great is the scale, and how detailed gameplay-wise that scale is. One of the things that big scale entails, usually, is a large map - a big surface area for the tides of history to unfold on.  USUALLY, games with scale allow you to be able to SEE that scale by zooming out.  In Hegemony III, the 'graphical map' can only be viewed from what feels  claustrophobically close to the ground.
Don't get me wrong, the seamless Strategic Map -> Graphical Map feature of this game is very lovable. But I wish.. no, its more than a wish.. it's really a NEED for this game in my opinion to be truely great instead of forgettable as soon as some other major title comes out... This game needs to allow the player to zoom out more - even just ONE or TWO more 'clicks' of the mouse wheel out would be PERFECT.
I don't know anything about software or coding etc, but it seems like this would be a really simple change?
Perhaps Modders can once again be our heroes and saviors. Rome II and Atilla suffered from constrained cameras, and with mods they became foundationally better experiences.

After chugging through The Witness I had a puzzle itch to scratch but I wanted something cleaner, more pure, something where alternate viable solutions don't come back to bite you in the behind. Thinking longingly about an alternate universe where I'd never played HexCells and could play it all again for the first time, I checked if Matthew Brown had published any new games. Lo, he had! I bought it immediately.
SquareCells is slightly less beautiful feeling than HexCells - I feel less like I'm revealing underlying art with each puzzle - but it is also a little more forgiving without sacrificing puzzle difficulty. The mechanics are simpler and require less explanation, but the resultant interactions are just as complex. I didn't really have to stop and think until somewhere around puzzle 20, but the first 20 were satisfying to solve nonetheless.
I'm pleased by the dark theme option, but I wish there were a way to choose slightly less jarring colors for the accents on each "world" of puzzles. Staring at 100% saturated red blocks kinda harshes my puzzle buzz, you know? Either an adjustable slider for saturation or different palette theme options would be a fantastic addition for the inevitable (fingers crossed) sequels.
SquareCells is a great contribution to its genre and an example of thoughtful puzzle construction. I wouldn't suggest it for complete beginners but for a new puzzler looking for a challenge without any gotchas it feels pretty ideal.

So if you are a big history buff, some little things might irritate you, like how Piceno is used as the capital of the Piceni, when in fact the capital was Asculum and there was never a place called Piceno (its Pisaurum).

The downs:
On anything higher than casual, the raiders are a little unbalanced - way stronger than the player and the AI nations.
Its very easy to farm enemies for slaves instead of having to pay your own workers, its almost unfair. Almost.
The battle animations aren't total war good, and the size of the field of battle is way too small to do any serious strategic moves.
The ups:
Everything else. This game is the first strategy game to tackle ancient Italian tribes in a pre-Roman/early-Roman era, and it is everything it should be. You get to upgrade your cities, much like Civ 5, manager resources much like Total War, take regions and worry about manpower and attrition much like Europa Universalis, and you get the close in battles also like Total War.
Incorporates all the elements of games I love and turns it into something new in a time period I love.
Get this game if you like strateg games.

This game had some good parts, but I would recommend passing on this one.

The gameplay centers around understanding the needs of the nearby residents and building attractive businesses, services, etc. for them. The guide talks about checking every single file in these folders but I just took them right out because I didn't have time to play programmer.  The game then ran without crashing, and my save games weren't affected.  Also, if you have the quit to desktop or minimize to desktop issue make sure that your Windows screen resolution is configured in the games config section. After almost a year of having the Steam Controller I feel confident in finally writing a review. I received this as a gift but refused to allow them to purchase it at full price, it is just not worth $50. If you can get it for $40 or less I'd recommend buying it.
What I like the most about it is that everything is customizable. While it can sometimes (in my case just twice) be tricky binding every key to the controller or finding a good community template that works well, when you finally get it right you're all set.
I really like the triggers on the back of the controller. Between using it for downsighting and shooting, sheathing or drawing a sword or cycling through some UI in a game, its just a nice added feature that I've taken advantage of.
You have to use two AA batteries to power the thing, however, I have yet to have to replace them and I use it quite a bit. There's some heft to it too, which I like, and it feels very comfortable in my hands. However, there is definitely a learning curve using the mouse/touch pads and when you first start using it, it will feel bulky.
The biggest drawback IMO is the mouse pad. In almost every new game I have to adjust the sensitivity to some degree. It sucks, but a once you find the right balance its a one time fix. If you're willing to put in a little bit of time fixing all the settings, it'll be no problem. However, if you're looking for convenience this may not be for you.
I've used this controller on games between BeamNG. drive, Witcher 3, Payday, Cities Skylines, MegaMan, 7 Days To Die, Hotline Miami and it works perfectly on them all. I'd recommend at the right price, especially if you are an FPS and/or driving gamer.

I really think this is a great device, just know that it is not a replacement for a PS4/XBone controller: it is a compliment to them. You can play games like the Total War series or Pillars of Eternity or Divinity Original Sin and it works great as a replacement for M&K. I don't use it for anything requiring twin sticks, but I am pretty okay with it for anything else and prefer it for a lot. For most games you can find a community uploaded configuration and they work well, or if you are into spending the time make up your own configuration and be almost infinately complicated.

At anywhere between three to five hours, you could be forgiven for thinking this is a shallow game. But that could not be further from the truth. The story of a man trying to find Truth in his exploration of the remnants of a world long gone, The Old City: Leviathan is a hell of an experience.
If you don't like to read, I would have to suggest this game is not for you. I would recommend turning subtitles on and then just exploring the world. Read the pages scattered around the world, pick up Solomon's journals and follow his progression (digression?) across the course of his words and just feel the story.
The visuals, sound and all around atmosphere are completely absorbing. Though there's no enemies, no other living entities you encounter apart from some mythical beasts that form more set than interactive partner, at moments there was real tension, a terror of the unknown and what you may find next.
This story does not hold your hand. You have to piece it together as you progress, between your character's musings, the journals and scattered books and pages you find. It won't explain what The Fall is, it won't go into the reasons why the world is how it is... It just Is.
But if you are willing to let go, to engage in the story... it will take you all the way down and engulf you in its depths. I don't know if I feel elated that I finished, or heartbroken.

Set in a desolate industrial world where the declining mental state of the protagonist has personified the walls and rendered the environment feverishly amorphous, 'The Old City: Leviathan' is a haunting, epistemological journey that touches upon the universal questions of truth and the human condition with startling acuity.

A beautifully crafted Walking-Simulator/Art Game, offering a Dear Esther style game in a range of environs (remeniscent of Dishonoured, Bioshock, and, in some places, the opening levels of Portal 2), that details the exploration of the narrator (your character?) through the Old City, and its deceptively byzantine past, through which the philosophy of epistemology is explored.
Graphically pretty, with several interweaved layers of plot and subplot, but I would have liked to have seen more (it took me a little over two hours to play through with a reasonable amount of exploration), buy for quality not quantity.

I remember playing this game back in 2012 and thinking that it's one of the best out there.  Playing it in 2017 made me think a bit deeper about it. Although there have been lots and lots of good games coming out since 2009 ( when this game was released) this one has something special to it.
-The map of New York is pretty big (though not with the level of detail from Grand Theft Auto IV) with enough "side-quests" to do and they tend not to be that repetitive.
-You can do almost anything in this game, you can run really fast, you can climb up on building or just go nuts and kill everyone and everything. There isn't much that you can't do.
-The graphics aren't that bad for an almost 10 years old game.
-The gameplay offers a petty good variety of fighting style, there is something for everyone.
-I did not find the story very interesting, to tell you the truth I couldn't have cared less for it.
-The controls aren't always the best, neither the camera angles but I can somehow understand it considering the type of game this is.
-The collectibles aren't the easiest to find and they are pretty hard to see from a relatively close range.
-There are a few minor bugs that you will encounter throughout the game, but nothing that bad.
I would recommend getting this game when it's on sale and only if you're searching for something different than other games.
If you say this game is bad, then I say your face is bad.

Well, first off, I have to say this is an absolutely beautiful game. If you’re looking for a subpar dating sim, you will have to look elsewhere, because Dandelion is very well put-together and a blast to play. The graphics are very nice and the characters are interesting and adorable in different ways. The stories for the different boys are very cool to learn about over time and the mysterious voice from somewhere is, uh, very mysterious. Very
. So yeah, very mysterious to me. One of the only issues that I had with it was the typos that popped up sometimes, but overall the translation was well done. They did a very good job of maintaining the sweet, giving nature of Heejung while also revealing her struggles and discontent. She can almost seem too placid, but it is understandable, given her past, and as the game moves forward, she does show signs of a backbone as she comes in to her own (thanks, furry adorableness?), which I whole-heartedly approve of.
It takes some time to recognize the voices and names (very creative, Heejung…lots of J’s @_@) but once you do, it becomes very easy to know who is speaking during scenes that don’t show faces. The different colors help and the personalities are so unique from one another that it becomes clear pretty quickly. The stat system is very intensive if you want to buff them all out, but the options are cute and for some of the boys, it’s important to max out your stats as quickly as possible. Just think of it as primping and sketching your way to the top. I actually do enjoy the grind, because the little illustrations are cute and it’s nice to become beautiful just by taking a bath. Unfortunately there have been no side effects in real life.
The most important thing that you should keep in mind when playing this game is FOR THE LOVE OF ALL THAT IS FURRY AND CUTE DO
TRY TO GAIN HEARTS FROM ALL OF THEM. You may think, ‘Oh that’d be nice to be friends with all of them! I’ll just hang out with everyone and become a more well-rounded person!’ That is the quickest path to a bad ending, except in a few special cases, which I'm sure you'll figure out after a couple of hours of playing.
Yes.
I was there.
Let me lay out the scene for you:
There I was on a different guy’s route, when I thought I would go out on the weekend and have a nice, friendly lunch with Jiwoo, you know? Just two buds hanging out and becoming even better friends. Maybe he’d even stop calling me stupid one day! During lunch, he says something about me feeding him, and being the desperate-for-points-and-new-interactions player I am, I chose the ‘Open wiiiide” option, thinking it was a little weird, but hey, I don’t judge friendships. Then he goes and says something about not dating any other boys. And if I were really Heejung, I would have stopped in my tracks and wondered, ‘You think we’re dating?!?!’ But of course, I am not her, and the game just continued on, unmindful to the fact that it had just rocked my world. When I started the game, I thought that Heejung was very oblivious when it came to boys, which was cute but almost a little much. Now, I know the horrid truth. I am JUST as
and
about boys as a main protagonist of a DATING simulator. TT_TT
Let’s just say there is one bad ending in particular which is more than a little traumatizing and I couldn’t stop thinking about it last night. On the bright side, they did an excellent job of unobtrusively sliding you into an abusive and very dangerous relationship, with you torn between thinking there is something very wrong, and thinking that it will turn out okay once he calms down.
He didn’t calm down.
I am still a bit emotionally scarred and I have been hesitant to play his good route (I just need some recovery time…). I recommend you get all the good endings before you try to get the bad endings for completeness—that way you’ll still be able to sleep at night without thinking someone’s going to be hovering over your bed. Following you to the bathroom…not letting you talk to people…scarring the actual player for real…or maybe that’s just me. But, what the heck, do whatever you like!
On a completely random side note, I like to pretend that the silver-haired man in the city panoramic scene that pops up once in a while is actually the main protagonist from Persona 4 (just to spice up the scenery for me). Unfortunately, no matter how many times I click on him, he does not become a dateable furball of cuteness. If you can and want to try a visual novel/dating sim, please look into Dandelion.

*This review is based off of the version of Dandelion directly from
. This is why Steam only claims I have played this game for a few hours.*
Basic plot:
A college student, Heejung, is living alone in her apartment. The influence of her overbearing mother forces Heejung to frequently second guess herself. To add onto her worries, Heejung wakes up one day to find a basket of five animals next to her bed. She questions where they came from but accepts them as her own after a week or so. Now she must take care of five animals and manage her college expenses. Things only get more complicated when they turn into humans.
The Gameplay:
This game is classified as a visual novel but is more of a stat raising game with visual novel elements. The player must focus on raising their relationships with each of the available suitors while maintaining high femininity, art, and beauty. However, the stress and pressure levels must remain low. Doing activities such as going to work or taking a shower will change the stat levels. The key is to find a balance as to what activities raise the most stats while raising the stress and pressure levels as little as possible.
Each suitor has stats that they prefer. Some have lower standards, while other have higher standards. If the requirements are met within a certain period, usually 1-2 months, an event will occur. Unlike other visual novels where the player picks different options to make an event occur, the stat raising activates the event. When an event occurs, there are no text options to make. I felt that the stat raising element was a nice change from the other visual novels I have played. Having to watch my stats kept my interest and made it hard to stop playing the game.
There are even collectible stamps. When you get enough of them for each character, it unlocks bonus content.
The Characters:
I feel that the character development is one of the best parts of the game. The stat raising game play allows close interaction with each of the characters. The characters are confined to one house most of the time so the player is forced to interact with each. There are not a lot of events for each character, maybe seven or so. That means that whenever an event occurs, something important is bound to happen. I commend Cheritz for creating characters with faults. For most visual novels, the heroine seems to be either perfect while the options have faults or vice versa. In this game, both the heroine and the characters have problems. This, added together with the stat raising actions, gives the game a sense of relatability.
The Voice Acting:
Each voice matched the characters perfectly. I have no complaints. The voice actors of the cats even meowed; that is dedication at its’ finest.
The Music:
The background music often sounds like elevator music, but surprisingly, that is not a bad thing. The music matches the calmness of a house or a stroll around the park. As a whole, the soundtrack is very happy. There are only a few songs for perilous situations, the rest are very calming. I really liked the OP song as well.
The Art:
The artists for the game are absolutely amazing. I am assuming that the CG artist and the sprite artist are different people since the CG’s look different than the sprites. However, the CG’s still look beautiful. The backgrounds stay consistent from behind the sprite to the background of a CG in the same room. The interface is drawn to look like a notebook and has very cute flowers and drawings throughout.
Positive Aspects:
Here is a list of some of the best qualities of Dandelion.
-All of the characters have distinct personalities; none of the characters are alike.
-The art is consistent.
-The music matches the scene.
-Having to raise stats keeps the player engaged.
-Having the characters live together forces the characters to form relationships. These relationships are explored throughout each route, stay consistent, and add to character development.
-Players of both genders could enjoy the game.
-The main character is not a ‘wall flower’.
-The main character develops alongside the suitors. Heejung changes for the better as the game progresses.
-The game has ‘collectibles’ that the player can hunt for on dates.
-The opening theme song is amazing.
-The primary bad endings made sense for each character given their personalities.
Bad Aspects:
Here is a list of minor complaints.
-To get the best end for one of the characters, another character must like you a decent amount as well. The game fails to make this obvious. I was half way through the route before I realized I was on a bad path that I could not fix.
-There was no true route for Heejae.
-One character is significantly harder to satisfy. Some people, like me, may do his route first and fail a lot. If you are like me, playing his route first makes the other routes extremely easy.
-It was never clearly stated that the game ends in  about a year. It only shows signs of ending a month before the game actually ends. For their first route, players will probably be scrambling at the end, reloading past saves just to raise their stats high enough by the end of the month.
-It is not always clear what option is considered the best on dates.
-Some of the character’s required stat levels did not make sense when you take their personality traits into account. (I cannot explain this further without spoiling anything).
-The translation had minimal errors; Jisoo’s route seemed to have the most errors and the ‘Special’ menu’s ‘back to title’ button was still in Korean. Otherwise, the translation was pretty good.
Aspects that will be good to some but bad to others:
-Since the options are living with the player and are treated as pets in the beginning, it takes a while for any romance to start.
-Events are caused by raising stats instead of dialogue options.
-All routes connect to each other in some way.
-All of the endings except for maybe one ended abruptly. The endings are left to interpretation.
-The ability to quick save at almost any time makes the game really easy to get collectibles and items to sell. This also makes it really easy to pick the proper responses on dates.
-The game focuses on character development as opposed to plot.
-All of the plots are connected, so the player may be confused during their first play through.
Final Thoughts:
I really enjoyed this game and would highly recommend it. All of the characters had distinct personalities and I liked the stat-raising. Sadly, I wound up playing the hardest route first, and then found out how to raise each stat really easily. This caused the rest of the routes to go by really slowly since my stats were already so high; I had nothing to do between events. However, this did allow me to get the collectible stamps with ease. I disagree with the people who feel that this game is difficult. The game takes time to get used to, but with the ability to quick save almost everywhere, learning what raises what and finding items on dates is really easy. Also, people complain that the stat raising gets monotonous; I disagree with that as well. Once you learn what to do, you can raise Heejung’s stats so fast that it does not feel monotonous for too long. After going through one route, raising Heejung’s stats becomes easier.
There is no clear order to play the routes in, but I would recommend one of two orders:
Play Jieun, then Jihae, then Jiwoo or Jiyeon, then Jisoo
Or
Play Jisoo, then Jiwoo or Jiyeon, then Jihae, then Jieun
Either way, make sure that either Jisoo or Jieun is first or last and that you play Jihae near when you play Jieun. As you can guess, their routes go together. I would recommend order two over order one if you want to go by story since Jieun’s route is completely different from every other route. However, if you want an easy play through, go with order one.

They have taken some things away, they have added some things. The play style stays consistent with the original, but there are some definate differences. I for one enjoy both the original space run and sr galaxies. The fact that you can participate in the multiplayer online experience, limited though it may be, is a nice add. I also enjoy the fact that you can map runs out by looking at a map of the galaxy you are in instead of just being told, here is your stuff, deliver it.  Certain routes will be more difficult then others, meaning that after you have completed a run, you know what sort of obsticles will present themselves helping your plan for future trips. I enjoy the fact that you are not allowed to build an infinate number of each componant, you have to use equipment earned during missions to increase the amount of guns and thrusters you can build. This requires a bit more planning on the part of the player as you can not simply sell weapons that are damaged, unless you have something to replace it with. It also makes me more frustrated when I lose a gun, which I think is good, you should feel accomplished when you make it through a run in one piece. Overall, a good game, I am excited to see what happens as it gets further developed. I would recommend the game, but if you do not have interest in following it as it is developed, wait until a later date to purchase it.

Lets talk Multiplayer
This is by far the best implementation of multiplayer into a single player game I think I have ever seen.
You have other space runners who dont interefere with you or your job.  They do what they do and you do what you do.  Speaking to that, lets say they have an excess of materials, they put them up for sale and you can buy what you need.  Maybe you have an excess of materials but you need them moved to another planet where their is a workshop that can build you that shiny new weapon.  Just put up a contract to move your stuff and someone will get around to it.
You get to move other peoples stuff too...but dont worry, they cant steal it or destroy it.  If it gets "destroyed" on their run, it just gets sent back to the planet it was on ready for another player to pick up the contract for the missing pieces.
You also get a bit of a reward for helping to deliver those rewards in the form of a little cash and materials.  So maybe you need a few materials yourself and dont want to buy anything.  Just do a few runs for other players and you might just get what you need.
Thats not to say the game doesnt have its pitfalls.  Difficulty can ramp up pretty quick if you dont know what your doing.  Strategy is a big part of the game and you cant just place whatever you want wherever you want and expect to have a flawless run every time.  Finding a balance between engines, defense and weapons can often be daunting...but the only part of your ship you need to finish the run is your command center and hopefully your cargo.
There was also some people complaining about turrets not being turbable...yea...not an issue.  You do have a couple that can turn...like the plasma and the twin cannon...you also get a laser mini gun that once hooked up to some weapon boosters get a huge ark...then you have the upgraded missile launcher system that can alternate between firing in 2 directions...so there are still plenty of weapons that can be oriented, but there is rarely a need early on.
I have sacraficed large chunks of my ship for an otherwise flawless run, and ive also been otherwise completly obliterated because i was unprepared.  Using abilities is extremly important, but knowing when to use them is what keeps you going.

If you liked the original Space Run, it's a safe bet you will enjoy SRG. It improves on the original  in nearly every aspect. Gameplay is once again solid. The missions are difficult, yet not overly brutal (especially during the first hours of playing - but it gets beautifully hectic before too long). The multiplayer function is a nice addition, and the graphics look crisp.
The ability to run missions in the order you prefer helps make SRG's progression feel a little less linear. The crafting system is well executed, and upgrading your ship is now more tactical. Advancing in Space Run Galaxy feels more rewarding than it did in the orginal game.
The addition of ship designing is another excellent feature. You can buy pre-existing ship blueprints and build on them, and you can also design your own ships from scratch. Want to build the Millennium Falcon? A Star Destroyer? The USS Enterprise? You can, if you want to.
A tactical pause function would be a helpful choice for people who want and / or need it. I prefer not to use one, but this option would be nice for those who enjoy racing through less intense cargo runs, and would like more time to set up a firm tactical strategy.
Space Run Galaxy is a lot of fun to play, and it looks sharp. It certainly has that addictive "just one more run, and then I'll go to bed" aspect going for it. This game takes a compelling approach to the "tower defense" genre, and provides a good amount of replayability. When you get to the point in the game where you have a large ship and lot of different weapons, it's exciting to watch the entire screen light up with massive amounts of firepower eye candy.

This is going to be easy. Do you like logic puzzles? If yes, then Mathew Brown, the developer of SquareCells and HexCells, is your best friend. Tip him the cup of coffee this game costs, you can't go wrong.
This is a simple, short, no nonsense puzzle game in a minimalist package. You can call it a cross between picross and minesweeper if you want, but the important thing here is: it's neither. With just a couple of tiny changes in the mechanics, SquareCells actually forces even veteran puzzle solvers to step out of their comfort zone and start thinking for a couple of hours.
The game is deviously smart in its simplicity and, as always with this dev's puzzles, absolutely logical at all points. If you can't find a solution, think harder, it is staring you right in the face. (Or get a tip by listening to the explanations in Innocentive's
- they will help you figure out that one logical step you're missing. Cause puzzle 35 is mean I tell you!) There are only 36 puzzles to solve, with none of them being throw-away easy, even at the beginning. In fact most of them are just difficult enough to make you scratch your head for a few minutes before you start feeling smug about how smart you are for solving them. I appreciate a puzzle that lets me feel smug. :)
Like Hexcells previously, this is a Unity game, without any frills, with nicely forgettable (and mutable) ambient music, but with some nice little touches that prove attention to detail. Zero complaints all around. Now when is the next one coming so I can throw some more money at you Mr. Brown?

Yesterday is a point-and-click adventure game with good story, but it is too short.

Yesterday is a classic point-and-click adventure with a dark storyline told in a unique comicbook style that came out in 2012.
The puzzles for the most part are inventory based, i.e. you need to find and combine items. Fortunately, there's no pixel hunting required and if you still manage to miss something, there is a hotspot viewer and a good hint system.
The game is pretty linear although there are a few instances in dialogues where you can choose from different answers and get slightly different results. You can replay these scenes from a seperate menu so you can check out the other options if you want, which I thought was a nice touch.
Even with avoiding any hints and exploring all dialogue options, it took me less than 6 hours to complete.
+
: Hotpots open new "window" that looks like a panel in a comicbook; you have large scenes you can walk around in and still look at places of interest in detail
+
: Well integrated in the storyline, medium difficulty, logical; mostly inventory puzzles, though
+
: Man who lost his memory retraces his steps to find out who he is; involves torture, murder
o
: For the most part pretty good but dragging items out of the inventory to use them was a bit fickle
-
: Not one likeable character, not even the main one, which is the reason the story never really gripped me despite it being pretty tense
-
: It took me 5-6 hours to complete w/o using any hints but I probably could have done it in less if I haden't effed around so much; I know the trend goes to ever shorter adventures but that doesn't mean I have to like it
I recommend it for fans of the adventure genre and people planning to play Yesterday Origins, the sequel (prequel?) to Yesterday published by Pendulo Studios last year (2016).
John Yesterday lost his memory and now retraces his steps to find out who he is. He piece by piece recovers his memories when events or items trigger flashbacks that catapult him (and us) back into these situations. We as the player know a bit more than the protagonist, at least in the beginning, which adds a lot of tension. The truth, though, is even worse than you'd expect and involves murder, torture and a long gone cult.
As I've written above the game uses comicbook style pop-up panels to let you look at details which allows them to have large scenes with a lot of different things happening in them.
are generous, so pixel hunting is not an issue. You can either look at or interact with what's in the panels. If you want to use an inventory item you have to do that from the main screen, though, which I found a bit strange.
The
itself can either be fixed at the bottom of the screen or appear when you move the cursor to the bottom. In addition to your inventory you also find there the hint and hotspot buttons as well as a button that lets you replay key scenes. The latter replaces a save system; apart from autosaves when you quit the game you can't save. I found that initially a bit irritating but it turned out to be a pretty useful systen. There are a few situations were you have different choices in conversations or in what you are going to do and the "saves" are optimally placed to let you explore all options.
As mentioned above, you "drag" items out of the inventory by holding the mouse button, which is my only critisim of the gameplay. If you didn't drag the item in a perfectly straight line you could either "lose" the item or inadvertantly try to combine it with another item. Especially, if you are stuck and want to use an item on multiple hotspots that can become a bit annoying.
On the plus side, the game has some unique and funny "fail" comments for certain far-fetched combinations of items and hotspots which added a hint of humour to the game.
The puzzles were mostly very well integrated in the story but unfortunately, the game designers weren't very creative with them. Almost all are some variation of find item and combine it with another item or hotspot. They are not too easy and there is a decent amount of them but all in all the puzzle in this game are not very memorable.
I'm a bit conflicted about Yesterday. In many respects, it is a very good game. Pendulo Studio has published a lot of adventure games, the most memorable probably the Runaway triology. They know what they are doing and the technical side of this game shows that. The story, even if it is not necessarily my cup of tea, is unusual and you actually want to know how it ends.
But at least for me, this game was also forgettable. The story felt a a little rushed. There are maybe two, three puzzles that were a bit unusual. And none of the protagonists is likeable. This is also due to the story, but still, if I end up not caring what happens to the main protagonist you kind of failed. But, as always, YMMV.

first off: i'm not completely through with the game but it already tied me to it... it's fascinating, beautyful and somehow depressing.
like "gone home" and "dear esther" this 'game' is not about certain mechanics or a score but the journey in itself is the goal. take your time, enjoy 'the ride' and let this interactive piece of art touch you. honestly, i love games like these that just let you move along, look around and explore and find things on your own. at your pace (mostly) and the way you go about. even without real threats or goals the atmosphere gribs you and you can't easily stop playing. the art-style is quite fitting going from delightfully colourful to depressingly grey-brown-ish... even tho sometimes the line between: "this was a artsy design-decission" and "this looks not really finished" blurs, because some textures seem just too low-quality while the rest is stunningly awe-inspiring. the game has a half-painted look to it - similar to what "dishonored" looks like - but not to that extent.

This controller is very good for some things, but not everything. Here's what it's not for. It's not as good as KB&M or a dual analog stick controller for FPS's, nor is it good for third person action games. It's not bad for FPS's, but you probably will prefer a KB&M or Xbox controller due to the right touch pad not being as precise as a mouse, nor as comfortable as an analog stick.
It is good for side scrollers and 8 bit/16 bit style games. It's great for turn based strategy games like XCOM or CIV, and slower paced RTS's like Ultimate General. It is not for fast paced RTS games like Company of Heroes or Starcraft.
I've heard complaints about build quality, but I think it is good. The left analog stick feels nice, as do the jewel buttons. The triggers feel good, the bumpers are a bit stiff but fine. You'll read lots of complaints about the size of the handholds, but I have very average sized hands and it doesn't feel too big to me. It's very comfortable to hold. It connects much more reliably than my Xbox controllers, and it makes navigating Big Picture a breeze.
So I do recommend it, but only if you're getting it to play a genre where it works well, as described above.

Similar to Dear Esther, but with more exploration and things to think about. The naration is done by an insane individual whom you cannot wholly trust. The narrative is about deep philosophical themes as the actions of Jonah and the rest of the world are discussed between Jonah and Leviathan. You cannot trust Jonah's sight or mind, but you are carried by his words and reasoning. You are left piecing together the end of mankind through the notes plastered on the walls, the various markings of other people, and the scattered journals/notes of Solomon. You read about the life, philosophy and pessimism of Solomon through these lengthy notes you collect, and while slow at first, they piece together the broken world you now inhabit. Solomon's movements are occasionally noticeable via clues in the environment, as well as the other Minotaurs that were once used to create peaceful discussion between the three factions (Guild, Unknowing and Order).
Jonah does not just dream, but creates engaging discourse and reasoning from his dreams. He uses them to pursue a potentially unknowable truth when he cannot necessarily trust the foundations from which he reasons. With him, you adventure with uncertainty as you witness the demise of those with certainty, and all in all, it makes for an engaging experience, though I'm not sure I could call it fun. I simply wish the beauty could have lasted longer, which could have happened if the dream sequences held bigger areas. They certainly beat the sewers.
There is little to no interactivity in this world besides opening/closing doors and collecting Solomon's notes. It is not always clear where the exit to a level is. Sometimes it is close to the beginning, other times it is the last thing you will find. But through most of my playthrough, I had a pretty good idea of where the final door was, and then went back to explore whatever I had missed, triggering as much of the dialog as possible. Most of the chapters go through a rinse and repeat cycle of exploring half the level, entering a dream sequence, then exploring the rest with the level being altered in some way, encouraging backtracking. But unfortunately, movement is very slow. While it forces you to take in the atmosphere, backtracking or going back to that one room you skipped is a pain, though the levels are small enough that it is still worth the effort. There is a run button, but it is only marginally better than walking. There is jumping, but it is almost never necessary as there is no platforming. It is an engaging walking simulater, and the best one I have played so far. I am left desiring to enter the Old City, and cannot wait for the next game to come out.

In the game Prototype you play the alpha of a new species, your DNA has been altered in a way which makes you indestructible to an extent, you can consume people to gain their mass (which is how health works) and in the process gain the ability to turn into them.
You can also transform your arms into a variety of different forms each with their own benefits and practicalities, you can run really fast and jump over ten story buildings, you are essentially a superhero, but evil … sort off … but not really … okay onto the next point.

I'm happy to see this getting on Steam. (: I've owned and finished the game quite some time ago before they even got on Greenlight, if you wonder why there's little time on my record; however, I'm playing it over and recalling all the reasons I loved it. The price may seem steep for what this genre is usually worth, but is it worth it in the long run? Totally. Is it a simple visual novel with sappy stories? No. It's a lot more than that. It consists of characters with realistic traits and feelings that we can all relate to one way or another. Even if their circumstances are mannered to fit the fantasy world more, the morals are there. There are several features along the gameplay that will require some careful planning and your attentive eyes. I don't want to spoil much, if at all, so I won't go into too much details about them. Play it for yourself and find out, you'll enjoy the ride.
I will, however, mention a few keys you should know. Firstly, the quick save and load feature will be your best friend in this journey. It's crucial to take advantage of this to make progress with your guy and keep track of everything else. Of course, use the real save too when you need to. The game wants you to be devoted to whoever you wish to pursue, so don't be wishy-washy. The moment the prologue ends and you've entered the playable stage, you need to determine a route and stick with it. You'll be spending a few months in the game raising affection levels and stat meters before the real romance starts. It'll feel like you're playing house and raising a few cute animals. Simple, right? Or not. Pay attention to the animals' affection levels by hovering over their head icons under the room diagram and you'll notice that there are hearts and numbers, displaying things like 0/7 or 0/16, etc. This is very important, make sure you interact with the one you want and get that number maxed as soon as you can, then you can sit back and worry about your other meters until the required level goes up. And it will, so check often! If you goof on picking the right interaction or don't manage to encounter him, quick load until you succeed. You can use the same method for finding stickers when you go out (which you will want to do if you wish to collect their extra images), so work a lot and use the money to buy Eye Medicines at the shop. When Fall rolls around, which is September, the event with your guy will automatically trigger if you've done everything right. And you will know, because the loading screen will change and it'll be the image of that person. From there, you can still get bad endings if you slack off or pick the wrong choices, so watch out.The stories of each individual will tug at your heartstrings, and bit by bit, the bigger picture of the whole game will fit together. Be sure to check the extra/special stuff by the end if you wish to know more about the backstory, it'll also reveal things concerning a particular wizard. The whole process may prove to be tedious or frustrating at first if you're not experienced in the stat-raising scene, but it'll be worth it when you finally get to the end to enjoy the fruits of your labor. Don't give up!
Overall, Cheritz has proven to me that they're capable professional creators of this game genre with their wonderful story-telling, clean + pretty graphics/designs, realistic character traits, and great voice acting. I look forward to continuing in supporting them and seeing more of their future releases. (Psst, check out their other game if you like this.)

You play as a 21 year old girl named Hee-Jung, who is an art student at a university. Fairly quickly you find out she has an inferiority complex stemming from issues with her mother and the fact that her mother never considers what Hee-Jung is doing is good enough. I found this game very relatable considering I am a girl in college, who picked her major based off what her parents wanted, and I pretty much hate my major now. In another aspect Hee-Jung reminds me of someone who has depression, so she is not a happy go lucky heroine, and I feel that she is more realistic than some of the other main characters in other otome games that I have played. She doesn’t seem to have many friends, except for this guy (sorry I forgot his name) in her art club who obviously likes her, so Hee-Jung does not have much to do besides school and her art project. Which as a college student in a time consuming major, I find this to be very accurate. It’s also apparent that Hee-Jung feels lonely.
How the story begins is that Hee-Jung come home one day to find a basket with a black cat, an orange cat, a spotted hare, a silver rabbit, and a white rabbit on her doorstep. All of these animals are just peacefully chilling, and not fighting, which is really odd. She can not bring herself to get rid of them, so she decides to keep them. Hee-Jung names the black cat, Jisoo, the prange cat, Jiyeon, the silver rabbit, Jihae, the white rabbit, Jieun, and the spotted hare, Jiwoo. For the first portion of the game you do various things like studying or taking a bath in different rooms to increase your mood or grades. By looking at the map, you can see where all the animals are. If an animal is in a room that you are doing something in then you may get to interact with that animal also. This usually increases your relationship with the animal. Also you can talk to, give gifts to, and touch the animals. Be careful on the touching because if you touch the animal in the wrong place then you may lose relationship points. After a certain point you actually get to the point where Hee-Jung actually figures out that every animal is actually a guy, who can switch between the two forms (surprise if you hadn’t figured that out yet). So no, this game is not like Hatoful Boyfriend, the guys are not actually animals. By the end of the first section, you are more or less on one guy’s route, which is determined by which animal you became closest to. This doesn’t mean you can not interact with the other guys. In fact you can make some characters jealous by hanging out with the others more than him. In the second part of the game, the focus is more on going out with dates with your desired guy, and raising up the stat that goes with him. On dates you can collect stickers of the guy you are out with, which unlock extra content from the extras section on the main menu. By the end of the game Hee-Jung has grown and become a strong character.
Be warned the characters do have good endings and bad endings. To be completely honest, the good endings are bittersweet, and they will stay with you for a long time. The feels you get from the good endings are amazing and indescribable, so I hope you experience them yourself.
SPOILERS, SPOILERS, SPOILERS, YOU HAVE BEEN WARNED!!!!
The magician is the guy who sent the animals to Hee-Jung, and created the whole ‘game’ that keeps getting mentioned. Each guy made a deal with the magician to try to get Hee-Jung to love him, and in return the Magician would grant the guys wish. Pro: guy gets wish granted. Con: Guy falls in love with Hee-Jung, but ends up forgetting her after his wish is granted. He doesn’t completely forget her, but he doesn’t really remember what he is missing, and this is what causes the bittersweet endings. Towards the end after the guy has won the ‘game’, the Magician is allowed to actually meet Hee-Jung (he has a very pretty CG), and this is the only time that the Magician ever gets to interact with her. It is hinted at that the Magician is in love with Hee-Jung, and is constantly creating alternate realities (or rewinding time) back at the beginning of the game, so that he can keep meeting her over and over again. In a way Hee-Jung, ends up with every guy. This is speculation, but I like this interpretation. Also the Magician guy supposedly pops up in Nameless also.

This is a pretty good game.  The single player mode seems to be quite a bit like the previous title, but bigger and grander.  The new multiplayer mode adds some cool new additions.  You can help other players haul goods and be rewarded with cash and materials, create contracts to move your goods, and buy/sell materials on a player marketplace for better prices than the NPC market.  There were some server issues in the opening week of launch that created a flurry of angry internet reviews because apparently clicking 'offline mode' for a day is harder than brigading negative reviews.  The devs have already spun up a new server to deal with the unexpected load of players.  Since the patch and addition of a second server, I have played about 10 hours of online mode with zero issues.  Be wary of negative reviews focusing exclusively on the online mode issues.  Those issues appear to be resolved and those reviews should be ignored.  I've encountered zero bugs in offline mode and haven't crashed one time that wasn't due to the overloaded server this past weekend.  The only negative aspect of the game so far was the server capacity being too small for the player base and let's be honest, we've seen billion dollar companies launching AAA titles with multi-million dollar budgets fail on that aspect too.  Let's not kill an indie dev for an easy mistake that has already been corrected as of this review.

This game is a lot of fun, now that they fixed the server issues. The multiplayer business model is pretty cool, the contracts are beneficial to both parties since the hauler earns random bonuses for each crate they deliver, as well as some credits if the contracter decided to include any.
If you enjoyed the first game, you will enjoy this one as well; there are some similarities, obviously, but also many differences. For example, you cannot buy upgrades to your weapons and other modules, but instead must build upgrader modules during a run which improve nearby modules of the same type, similarly to the power system in the first game. Repairing damaged modules is a bit trickier, you need to use new modules to do so. Also, you have a limited number of each module that you can build on a run, which is what you will need to spend resources on increasing.
There is still no pause button, so keep that in mind, don't buy the game and then complain on the forums like so many other people. It is a design decision, there are plenty of other games which focus on the strategic aspect of tower defense, this one is more action/quick thinking oriented.

The fun of the first game packed in a bigger universe, together with some new equipment and the choice between multiplayer and offline mode.
If you don't know the first game: This is a tower defense game, just that your plattform for towers is a spaceship, flying straight from point A to B without you beeing able to change the course. On the straight flight numerous dangers will apear, from asteroids over pirates to space-monsters.
You start each flight with your cargo (which can be placed to your liking) and one tiny engine. You have to build guns and support according to the arising dangers and you will have to build more and stronger engines to make a timely arriving. The less time you needed and the more cargo arrives intact, the more ressources and XP you will get to enlarge your ship and buy new guns and support.
Pro:
- each stage is repeatable, you will never get stucked with too less resources/xp
- each stage is randomized to a certain point. No flight is like the other, but the randomizing is pretty well balanced - you won't get obverpowered by pure chance.
- choice between pure offline or pure online gaming
- pretty well grafics and sound
- transporting cargo of other players is always bound to a random reward, even if the other players pays nothing for it (payment of other players is always a bonus to you)
- a damn good feeling hauling the cargo of other players :)
Con:
- some server issues since more player bought the game as anticipated (but the new servers went online only one day after the crash and it is working stable now)
- offline play misses a bit the random reward for hauling other players cargo, since you get reward for each piece of cargo and the NPCs from the first galaxy only offer three or four pieces (while player can offer more, like the NPCs from the next galaxies also offer more)
Neutral:
- offline play is a seperate profil (so no cheating online, which is good, but you would have to start from anew)
All in all, a game I will invest much more hours into it. :)

Very good improvement over the original, tactical maps, better strategic resources (used to build the weapons / upgrades you use on your ship) and with an innovative MP aspect.
Why the bad reviews? Two reasons:
#1 No pause button. This isn't a static tower defense game: it is intended to be dynamic and time pressured & hectic. It was never intended to be a feature and would break the game if included.
#2 Server issues. Being fixed as we speak. When people complain of "crashes" they actually mean "lost server connection". The dev team have been very open about this issue and have kept the forums up-to-date on their solutions.
If you read through the "reviews" ignoring those three complaints, you'll notice a pattern.
Onto the game itself:
Very well balanced & an improvement over the original (with some changes - specifically power has been removed for class type enhancers and 'focus' that is used to power special abilities).
If you liked the first Space Run, you'll love this. If you're put off by the reports of server issues, the single player is functional (if a little tricky to get running on some systems).

It really pains my heart to have to review Tribes: Ascend like this.
The core mechanics are quite solid and the skiing is undoubtedly the thing that drew me to this game the most. The maps are varied and distinct and make for some very fun team gameplay.

The players that do play regularly are typically at max level, so it's extremely difficult to compete unless you're willing to be at the bottom for most of the journey. It's a shame because the skiing is definitely where Ascend becomes something of its own and not just another shooter, and it's sad to think that it will likely not appear outside of Ascend for some time.

This is one of my favorite games.  I already own CSI and CSII both on PS3 and Vita.  I was also happy to pay full price on the day of release.  I did not buy the dlc constumes as I already paid for them once on PSN.
This game is probably not for everyone.  Graphics overall and character animations in particular can be rough.  This game will probably not appeal to those who like to get into fast paced action quickly.  Instead, this game is best enjoyed with a laid-back approach of talking to every npc, finding every hidden sidequest, exploring and customizing everything, end enjoying the game's excellent music.
The plot in CSI is interesting.  The pacing is intentionally uneven in the careful unfolding of a detailed plot.  Without spoiling anything I can say it will ramp up sharply at the end of the game.  This will make you want to play CSII immediately..  which is somewhat of a problem until the PC release of CSII.  (I just grabbed my vita version.. oh how I miss turbo mode!)
One of the strongest parts of this series is the likable characters.  Many times I find the main character of a jrpg to be shallow and annoying.  Rean, in contrast, is a dynamic character who sees a good amount of character development.  His voice actor in particular makes the character very likable and  accessible without being obnoxious or overly simplistic.  There are a lot of other solid characters as well.  I genuinely feel conflicted in every playthrough over which girl to choose, as there are a number of likable options.  Even the npc's are given unique personalities and are detailed if you go out of your way to speak to them throughout the game.
The dialogue between characters is not as excellent as Trails in the Sky but still pretty solid.   There are a few cringeworthy scenes between characters being contentious in a way that just feels derived and forced.
The improvements to the PC version are also excellent.  Turbo mode, in particular, is extremely helpful.  I am playing on a 4k display with maxed settings using a Dualshock 4.  I am enjoying the fluid performance and instant load times.  Sadly one strange bug that occurred throughout the game is a black spiderweb-like pattern of lines popping out in the sky during rendered scenes.  Also a number of character models have a black shadow on their legs which should not be there.  Hopefully these get addressed in oncoming patches.
I strongly recommend this game if you like rpgs, jrpgs, lengthy detailed stories, interesting characters, and/or excellent music,  It is worth full price.  It is my hope that by supporting this game, we will see a localized version of the Crossbell series that I would love to play.  Please make this happen XSeed!

Remember Dungean Keeper? This is a lot like that, but with a better premise (IMHO). So you're an evil overlord. But rather than wanting to keep adventurers out of you dungeon, you WANT them to come in, get their jollies, have the time of their life, then capture them and suck all the joy out of their souls.
That's a gross simplification, but that's the basic idea. This is sort of like a TD game, in that you have invaders coming into your place and you need to direct them to where you want them to go. But instead of trying to kill them quickly, you essentially want to kill them slowly. You need to give them a good fight, let them find some treasure, maybe even get them laid (not really, but that would be totally expected in this game). THEN you want to imprison them and suck all that contented adventurous soul out of their well-satisfied bodies.
Very fun, very much in keeping with the tradition established by Dungeon Keeper and Overlord.
I give it a B+

What in the world happened here? The original Cities in Motion was a chill little sim that let you fill city streets with buses and trams with just a few clicks. CiM 2 certainly looked like that on the surface, but after just two hours with it I can hardly believe it's from the same developers. I really can't imagine a game that missed the point of its predecessor worse than this one.
Cities in Motion 2 places you in charge of a transit company, challenging you to provide public transportation to a bustling city. Starting from scratch, you place stops for buses and trolleys, lay rails for trams and metros, map out routes for your vehicles, and even select the models of vehicle to use. These basic elements allow you to provide service to the many different people of the city, just as the first game did. CiM 2 goes a bit further, though, giving you control of timetables, charging you with building depots for your fleets, and even granting you the power to lay new roads within the growing city.
Now, when I say "growing" city, that isn't just flowery language. One of the much-touted improvements of this title over the previous is that the cities grow with you. Supposedly your services can influence the growth of the city, and laying your own roads can change the flow of traffic. It's an element of SimCity that feels oddly out of place here, especially after learning to cope with the set traffic patterns of the first game. Similarly the growth mechanic sounds good on paper but has very little obvious effect even after several hours of play.
This leads to the core problem with CiM 2, in fact, because it turns out that none of the new additions to the gameplay are actual improvements. The new control options over your company like timetables and service zones make the game more complex without providing any real benefit. It's just another lever you have to get in the right position, and it's not at all obvious how to best set it. Placing depots is another unnecessary distraction, forcing you to put detours in your lines and cram large buildings into the landscape for no actual benefit. And building your own roads can lead to endless frustration because of how touchy the building tool is.
I need to spend some extra time on the interface now that I've mentioned it because it is a dumpster fire of issues, especially compared to the clean and simple UI of the first game. Building ANYTHING in this new 3D engine is guaranteed to drive you up the wall as it snaps to the wrong spots or jumps over where you want it or simply fails to connect. For one example, trolley and tram lines can be laid in any lane of any road, and also in medians if available. They have to follow the direction of traffic and must be laid by individual road section, so you have to zoom all the way in and make sure your lines are following the right lanes every step of the way. And if you misclick and need to delete a section of track, half the time you'll misclick again and delete the entire road.
Metro tracks became the bane of my existence because of how impossible they are to use. They can't be placed on roads or near buildings, and you have to manually raise and lower them to get them underground or over rivers. Curves that are too tight will break the rails, and rail sections that don't line up perfectly won't connect. The main problem is that the game will happily let you build track that's too steep or too curved for your purposes and then not fully explain why it won't work. Just getting a depot connected to a metro line requires you to manually lay out an entire train yard, usually in far too limited a space.
I could go on, so I will. The menus and windows are cramped and difficult to parse. Your charts provide less useful information than the excellent data views of the previous game. Advertising options have been removed for some inexplicable reason. Missions don't properly explain your goals, and this is a big one because the first scenario of the game challenges you to provide 15% coverage of the city, but no matter how much I built and how many people I moved, my progress never rose above 0%. And somehow on top of all this, the game is just harder. After two hours with the very first scenario I couldn't make a single dollar of profit. None of the dozen lines I built, of all shapes and sizes and makeups, would carry more than single-digits of passengers.
Everything I loved about Cities in Motion is absent from its sequel. The charm, the accessibility, the convenience, the polish... none of that is to be found here. Somehow it's been replaced with tiresome micro-management, an impossibly bad building interface, vague or non-existent feedback, and the worst part of any sim, trying to cram things into places they won't fit. I seriously can't think of anything positive to say about this one, so I suppose I'll just let my overwhelming disappointment speak for itself.
