This is one of the times that makes me want to say " Steam should really put a rating system for reviews instead of a yes or no button", because even though Yesterday is not a bad game, its not so great either. It has its flaws, big ones too, but the game is still enjoyable and fun.
Let's first acknowledge the fact that the whole genre of Point-and-Click Adventures Game is dying. There are some game companies that are trying to make this genre stay alive such as Revolution Games, Double Fine Productions and Pendulo Studios being one of them. So its good to see an example of old school Point and click adventure. The game also has good graphics and an intriguing story. Even though the soundtrack of the game is not too long its pretty catchy.  I also really liked most of the characters, especially Boris and Olhak.
Now let's talk about the problems that this game suffers:
First of all its way too short. At my first time, i finished the game in 3-4 hours. Since the game is short, there aren't many locations in the game. For the money you give, you expect something more than an "extensive demo".  So you may want to wait for a Steam sale or a discount to buy the game. I played most of the games that Pendulo made from its foundation, and gotta say: even though Runaway was an older series it was way better than Yesterday. Especially Runaway 3: A Twist of Fate was  the peak point of Pendulo Studios. So i expected more from this game. I thought it was gonna be a cut above from the rest. Yet the game instead had really really simple puzzles. Most of the clues or items were already out there and you didn't really had to look for them, and sometimes even the same solutions used twice in the game (like the Cross and Alchemy puzzle). BUT, this is not the game developers fault. Nowadays almost all of the game developers are creating games like these filled with really dumbed down point and click elements and simple puzzles. There is always this "Oh let's hold the player's hand" kinda vibe in almost every game genre.
Anyway, other than that the game has really nice references to the previous games, and I really enjoyed the "secret" ending, it was really self-aware. It was good to see some familiar faces.
So to conclude the review i can say; Buy this game if you like point-and-click adventure games and if this game is on discount.

I am not so sure about this game. I am still giving a thumbs up, because there are many good things about it, but I am not as enthusiastic as the other Pendulo's adventures.
On the + side:
- A smooth game, you are going to have a decent time, you won't get frustrated because you get stuck, although it's a bit hort (you can probably finish it in one afternoon)
- You can see that there was a fair thinking and an accurate job behind it
- The comic-like graphics for dialogues and action scenes. It was maybe a way to pass on the most difficult scenes to animate, but still, it works and I found it quite original and fun.
The cons:
- The story is way too complicated and I am still not sure I got all the details. I think they wanted to put a bit too much inside it: the love story, the samurai training, the satanic sects, the travels around the world...
- Each chapter is too short, this makes the game easy as you start from zero each time in a different environment, so there aren't many areas nor many objects or interactions you can do. So, when you're stuck, you just need to try everything and eventually something will work. It doesn't even take a long time. It took me 4 hours to finish the whole game.
- Too dark. But that's just a personal opinion: if you like dark detective stories then you are probably going to love it. I definetely prefer fun and absurd stories, that's one of the main reasons I liked the other Pendulo's titles better.
- The zooming in system for objects and actions: I don't see the reason for it, and at the beginning it is extremely bothering. Then, at one point, you get used to it, but this doesn't mean you actually start to like it.
So, all in all, unless you love dark satanic stories, I wouldn't advise you to buy this game as a stand alone and full price. If you buy it in a pack with the other Pendulo Studios games (I had it with the Runaway series and The next big thing), then you won't regret playing it. But if you have to choose, then you should definitely pick the Runaway series, especially the first two episodes.

I really liked this adventure, though I also found it quite disappointing that there is no german version of Yesterday on Steam.
But even if I liked the story and the characters, Yesterday has still a few flaws, which prevents it to be a top class Point&Click Adventure game.
- It's quite short. It took me only around 4,5 hours to beat the game.
- Why on earth thought the developers it was a good idea to interrupt the game, when the story became quite thrilling? I get it that some people like the slowdown in the storytelling at these points, but for me it was just annoying.
- The humor in the prologue was absolutly cringeworthy. I was totally relieved that later in the game, there was nothing like that ever again.
- The game is easy as ****.
- Most characters are a little bit twodimensional, but honestly, it didn't bother me that much.
But - when there are so many points I didn't like - why still recommend Yesterday? Because I really loved the story surrounding John Yesterday. It was quite thrilling and I always wanted to know what's going on - so i finished the game directly in one sitting. And well - I still can't get the whistle out of my head.

Having used the Steam Controller for a year now, I can honestly say that I have only been able to stomach using it for the initial couple months I used it, and later with a handful of games that supported the SC. Buying (for the same price or far less on sale) an xbox game pad or DualShock 4 controller (that is natively supported by steam) is an infinitely better investment, and has less of a learning curve, on top of better trigger/bumper buttons, better spacing on face buttons, and actual dpad and joystick as opposed to emulated inputs.

This is a controller that will change your life. I got it on launch and have not had a single second of regret. The sheer amount of customizability is mind blowing. I would HIGHLY HIGHLY RECOMEND THIS.
That said, There is a learning curve with this controller (~ 4 hours), both for the hardware itself and learning how to use the customization. Once you get it, especially for games you normally can't play with a legacy controller, it will be one of the most rewarding feelings you'll get. If you don't want to fiddle with the settings, you can always use highly voted templates that others created for the game of your choice.
Games I played using this controller include but not limited to:
- Path of Exile (mouse heavy)
- American truck simulator (I use the gyro to drive as a wheel)
- Dirt 3 (more gyro driving)
- the crew (same as above)
- Faster Than Light (lots of hotkeys)
- Civ 5 (even more hotkeys)
- Witcher 3 and lots of already controller compatible games
- Divinity Original Sin 2

So I got back into games after years of being out (since the days of Starcraft 1).  I've never played any Hegemony games but I love grand strategy (used to love the old civ games and Ceasar 2)    I've never played Total War or other games people sometimes compare it to so I don't have that reference either.  I like games that have empire/city management, and don't completely focus on war at the exlcusion of other strategic domains.  Given this, and my love for history, when I saw this game was coming out soon, it got my immediate attention.  At first I was concerned about buying it as it was brand new and it seems in the forums there were several important issues that needed to be resolved with a patch.  When I saw Longbow the developer being responsive in the forum and releasing their first patch quickly after release, it - along with an early available 10% off discount - gave me the confidence to go ahead and take a chance, so I purchased it.
I have found this game to be quite enjoyable.  I don't care as much about graphics as much as I do about the game mechanics, the sense of challenge, and the strategic thinking involved.  It has been engrossing which is a great sign for me and worth the price I paid, though note I purchased it just before the early 10% off discount expired (people nowadays pay $15 to see a movie at the theater, so if i get like 20 hours or more of good enjoyment out of it, it was worth it.  Does it have some bugs still?  Yes even after the patch, but I'm confident they're working on them.  If the developers are reading this - I also think this game has a lot of potential and would love it if they crowfunded a multiplayer version.
Being a lover of history, including ancient history may bias me a bit.  Also given that some of my ancestors  lived in the middle of Italy for likely centuries, I can only wonder if this was one of my few chances to every play my ancestors (Etruscans or Umbrians) in a game lol
Anyway this is a fun game for a grand strategy lover and my ancestors would be proud. I recommend it.

This is my first Hegemony experience, and I have to say this game is a pleasent surprize.   To be fair there are still a few things that need to be worked out, but the developers take everything into account, from supply lines, and logistics, to upkeep and maintenance of buildings, and of course feeding your growing army.
+ A well thought out economic structure forces you to pay attention to the details of maintaing your army and the supply lines that feed your empire.
+ Raiders and pirates frequently attack making it challenging to protect your resources, and the civilian population.
- The Diplomacy is a bit enemic, but sufficient.
+ The AI is smart enough to flank you, and the raiders have powerful units, forcing you to use tactics to defeat them.
+ The 6 factions, Latin, Sebilic, Greek, Gaul, Etruscan and Illiryan have some similar units, and some unique units, offering diverse game play.
( I have seen complaints about the units, but it's Italy, not Greece.  Just about everyone had some kind of spear units, and Hopplites were used by everyone, until Rome changed the way wars were fought.   There is a diversity of unit types and play styles.  Gaul has more calvary options, and archers.  Illiryans have srtong Infantry and Mounted Javelins, Greeks start being able to train Hopplites, while other factions need to have a Baracks upgrade first, Etruscan has axe men and so forth.  So enough about there not being a good mix of units)
- The city building of the AI needs work, and the AI in general could use a bit of a tweek. But lets be honest, it's AI....if you want a real Challenge play another Person...which reminds me
- No multiplayer...yet
- Just out of Beta, but there are still numerous minor bugs and crashes.  I am sure there are patches to follow.
Over all this is definitly worth the experience.  It still has some teathing problems, but it doesn't take away from the fine work and thought that went into this game.  Hegemony has to be one of the most under rated games I have ever seen.  If they could do this on a scale that covers the entire European theater in the time of Rome, that would be epic!

The base game is excellent. As others have said, there definitely are issues mostly server related. My biggest gripe is online/offline profiles being completely separate (see below for details) especially when coupled with the server often not being available. I still like this game a lot and feel it still deserves a thumbs up with the assumption that the devs will fix these problems.
Pros:
-Galaxy map allows you to traverse between systems, easily see where your contracts are, does not bind you to AI missions, allows you to move about freely. I have not unlocked it yet but there seem to be multiple galaxies as well. Mechanics (to purchase upgrades) and vendors (buy new ships, resources etc.), and the shipyard (customize your ship layout) vary from system to system. You may need to for instance get resources you have in one system to another in order to spend them there at the mechanic. To do this you essentially create a mission for yourself. You haul your own cargo there and play through a battle sequence.
-Pseudo Multiplayer. You can buy/sell items to the market, friend other runners, do runs for other players, post runs you need done (maybe you don't feel like dragging all your loot back to the good mechanic). This part is a very welcome addition.
-Fast Travel. Want to get somewhere but don't feel like playing a mission? You can fast travel instantly you just can't take any cargo with you.
-Several ships to purchase, upgrades available to add more hexes to your base ship.
-While not graphically impressive, the backgrounds and some of the effects are quite nice.
Cons:
-Game server has been unavailable for several hours of the few days I've been playing. I also get some prompts from my firewall which wants to block traffic from this game, never had these prompts with other games.
-Online vs. Offline mode. Wherever you start a profile it stays there. You cannot, for instance, start an online profile and then continue to play it in offline mode when the server is unavailable. If you want to play when the server is down you need to start an entirely new game and that profile can never jump online for the cool online features. This is my biggest gripe. You should be able to switch seamlessly between the two especially if your server keeps crashing (see Dark Souls).
-Offline mode is finicky. First of all switching to offline mode inexplicably takes a long time. I've also hilariously gotten server errors which force the game to crash in offline mode. There have been a few times where I try to switch to offline mode (server is down) and the game crashes with a server error.
-Unskippable tutorial missions. Starting my offline profile was a chore as I had to run through the tutorial again. Please add an option to skip the beginning missions when you create a new profile.
-Strange long loading times at merchants. Sometimes when I buy items it takes quite awhile for it to process. It really feels like this is also server related.
-Very minor but the mission success audio clip says something along the lines of "The client will be happy" etc. even when you are running your own loot.
-Turrets do not focus on low health modules. If a ship is going by it may have several hexes if you kill the bridge hex the entire thing blows up. I have in some cases manually targeted the bridge with a laser turret to have it go down to a sliver of health (ability is then on cooldown). The auto-firing turret will then start to ping a different hex as it slowly slips away. It'd be cool if you could set a mode for all of your turrents maybe something like - aggressive mode (attack low health hex first), defensive mode (attack weapons first). I guess that may unbalance the game, it is just frustrating to see it switch focus to a max health module when you can finish it off by a couple pings to the critical module.
-Game crashes when left idle. I like to leave my games running so I can play a mission here or there without having to load up the game. It crashes 100% of the time if leave it idle like this I believe with a server error, again even if I'm in offline mode.
Yes that is a big list of cons that are mostly frustrating and in the worst case actually prevents you from playing the game at all. I'm very hopeful the devs get to work on some patches as there is a really good game underneath all of that nonsense.
Despite the server issues, the game has been great fun so far. A solid example of a good tower defense game, even if it is slightly overly simplified and too easy.
Loved the first game, and this one follows on nicely.  Despite the initial launch problems with servers etc, I am more than happy to persist with the game whilst the devs work on these issues.

Original review:
I've played the original Space Run and loved it, so I was super hyped when I realised this sequel is coming out.
You are a space runner, and your job is to transport many different types of cargo from one spot to another. Along the way you'll need to protect your cargo from pirates and aliens, while making sure that you reach the destination as fast as you can. When it comes to deliveries, who cares about safety? Speed is all you need.
You have 3 classes (colours) of (weapon / support)modules you can build on each run, at least 6 different things to build in each class, and every single module has 3 different levels. This gives players a HUGE amount of space for creativity, experimentation and fun. Positioning of your modules is of utmost importance, because upgrading of modules is done by building a specific booster module next to it.  (This explains why connectors are so important. They spread all adjacency effects to all adjacent spots, including to other connectors)
Enemies are very varied, from laser-shooting pirate ships to aliens that attach itself to your ship and deal damage over time to huge boss ships with loads of firepower to giant aliens that have unique attacks. The levels are varied too, so it demands that players think on-the-fly.
While warding off enemies that may come at any angle, you still need to keep an eye out for the cargo that you're contracted to ferry. Some of these cargo deal damage to adjacent things on your ship when they get damaged, some of them jump around your ship, screwing up your ship design, some of them even deal massive amounts of damage to random things on your ship periodically. It will definitely be a hectic mess, especially as you reach the later parts of the game.
Definitely highly recommended. Just be patient and wait as the devs solve the server issues and this will be one of the best indie games of the year.

Dandelion ~ Wishes Brought to You ~ is a visual novel otome game that is (obviously) targeted for the female audience. It looks like your typical shoujo reverse harem otome game, which it is to some extent. The plot, however, is outstanding with a slice of life genre.
Let's start with the heroine. Heejung is your typical college student who is struggling to keep up with society and her family's pressure to be constantly perfect (good grades, looks, and social life), even though she is still not aware what she really wants to do with her life. It also doesn't help that her family is quite dysfunctional and somewhat a bit emotionally abusive to her.
Her bleak and stressful life takes a turn, however, when one day, she wakes up to find these animals in a basket beside her bed.
First part of the game is spent raising your affection to the animal you will potentially romance later on. Yes, I said animal. Don't worry, they will turn into humans (or part-humans?) later on in the game. You get to pick one guy out of five: Jihae (the prettiest one), Jisoo (the bad boy type), Jiwoo (tsundere), Jiyeon (cutesy type), and Jieun (the quiet type). You are able to raise your affection on multiple guys but if you’ve played otome games before, surely you’re aware what happens when you do that. For the remainder of the game, you focus on raising your stats and affection for the guy you choose in order to get the good(?) ending.
The game itself remains sweet, cute, and innocent but deals with a lot of real life (and relatable) issues. You grow attached to the characters and the character development is splendidly done well. It does, however, take for a somewhat darker tone later on in the game that will GUARANTEE to make you cry and maybe break your heart into tiny pieces (I know mine did).
The stat-raising game does get repetitive and tiring (like Tokimeki Memorial Girl's Side) and may discourage some people from playing it for that reason. There are also a few spelling and grammar mistakes but easily forgiven for the well-written storytelling and voice acting (and yes, FULLY voiced). The voice acting delivers the characters' personality and emotions well. The music is beautiful and so is the art.
It's definitely a must play for otome gamers. If you want to go for a ride on the emotional roller coaster, this is your game. Also, Jiwoo’s paws are cute and YOU MUST PLAY HIS ROUTE.
Dandelion ~ Wishes Brought to You ~ gets a 9.5/10 from me and I'd like to applaud Cheritz for a wonderfully presented game.

I've always been a fan of Visual Novels/Otome games, but finding ones in English that I really liked was difficult, so when I heard about Cheritz's Dandelion, I didn't wait too long before buying it.

The art is also gorgeous and the music is enjoyable as well. The stories for each of the guys are also nice and I enjoyed the events that happened around the apartment as time passed and Heejung interacted with the guys.
This is a stat raising game so you have to make the right choices for the guy you're going after in order to raise affection points, which can become tedious for some people. The interactions between Heejung and each boy are very amusing and heartwarming though, so try different things out, some actions might be more worthwhile than others though.
The themes of abandonment and then about coping with it afterwards are very nicely addressed in this games story. While we may not all have magical animals suddenly turning up in our real lives, it is still soothing to be able too follow and help Heejung through her struggles.
I also really like that there is bonus unlockable content, the extras are really nice~

If pigeons weren't enough, now you can choose between BUNNIES and KITTENS. Well, kind of. Unlike the pigeons in Hatoful Boyfriend, these animals fortunately (?) don't stay animals forever. (I took a bunny with me to the beach; he was not impressed when I put on my $100 dollar bikini, the fruits of MANY nights of labor at the local art gallery. I would've been pretty weirded out if he was.)
Animal jokes aside, Dandelion is a lovely, very professionally done Korean visual novel aimed at a female audience. I think this may be the first Korean visual novel on Steam, and it's gorgeous, with fully voiced Korean dialogue and English text. I believe you can set the text to Korean as well. There are five different possible love interests you can pursue at the start, though at the beginning I swear it plays more like a pet raising simulator than anything else. Steambuns instead of Nintendogs, right?
But no, there's a mystery that slowly begins to unfold--and eventually romance. With people. Human people, I swear. Just ignore the occasional animal ears. Yes, the $30 price tag may seem very steep to a lot of Steam users accustomed to cheaper alternatives, but before brushing it off, try the demo (available on Steam right here:
. It doesn't take long to see how much work went into it, and how many visual novels on Steam have extensive voice acting? Not enough! I've only noticed a few small translation errors here and there, but they aren't nearly as common, noticeable, or cringe-worthy as a lot of the freemium VNs' rushed translations on iOS and Android. Overall, the translation is very well done.
Hopefully, if Dandelion does well enough on Steam, Cheritz might feel inclined to add Nameless, their latest visual novel set in the same general universe--but with dolls instead of cats and rabbits. Yes, dolls. How can any girl resist?
UPDATE after completing all routes, including Jisoo's absolutely TERRIFYING "bad route" (totally worth it for the extra CGs!):
Yes, I sank 35 hours into Dandelion. Yes, every one of them was worth it. I can't think of another visual novel/dating sim that left me thinking so much after completing it. After completing all 5 routes, make sure to check the bonus content! I was really interested in the mystery behind the story--who left me with these animals and why? The bonus content was the cherry on top of an already delicious sundae--and isn't the cherry sometimes the best part?
First, I have to praise the characterization of Heejung. I know most visual novels/dating sims use "blank slate" protagonists (sometimes without eyes--creepy!), but Heejung is the most relatable, realistic heroine I've encountered in a while. (I may be biased because I, too, wonder where my mysterious new bruises came from and how expensive it would be to install a TV in my bathroom when I take a bubble bath to raise my beauty and femininity stats in real life.) Who doesn't understand the pressures of "making it" and continuously doing things you dread solely to please your parents and loved ones, no matter your culture? Who doesn't fear being left behind?
The love interests are fantastic too, and are much more than their archetypes may make them appear at first glance (pretty bunny, baby bunny, snobby bunny, sweet kitty, glutton/pervert kitty), though of course I had favorites. I started with Jihae, whose route seemed like a good one for beginners (just remember to raise some affection with Jieun too!), and ended with Jieun because I was super stubborn about not pursuing a baby bunny. He's a baby! Heejung is a college senior! ...But his route was one of the sweetest and actually had the best ending. Jiwoo's was great too, especially if you've seen as many Korean dramas as I have and can appreciate how the game pokes fun at kdrama clichés. (Those envelopes of money! Candy Cinderella and chaebol romances!)
There is a LOT of stat-raising, but if you focus first on raising your Stress/Pressure Relief abilities, that helps a lot, and soon you won't even notice your Stress and Pressure stats raising at all. Make frequent use of Quick Save/Quick Reload if you accidentally poke/show love/feed them fruit in the wrong place (sometimes deliberately...!) and get a bad reaction, or if you can't find the bunny/kitten of your dreams anywhere in the entire apartment.
If you're on the fence about getting Dandelion, definitely try the demo first--and then just get it. Unless you really, really hate bunnies and kittens (are you more of a dog and ferret person?), you won't be disappointed.

A highly enjoyable dating sim. Despite the occasional translation errors and the sometimes tedious stat raising, Dandelion offers a relatable heroine, interesting and unique characters with excellent voice acting (albeit in Korean), and an absorbing plot illustrated with plenty of gorgeous CGs. Recommended to fans of the genre!

The Old City: Leviathan Review
Premise: A man with an unstable mind finds himself seemingly alone in a collapsed society. The player sees the world through his manic eyes, unfolding a narrative concerning themes of uncertainty, love, and, most importantly, the nature of dreams.
Gameplay: Nonexistent, but this is a mercy. Any puzzles would disrupt the game's pace; the only challenge exists in finding the notes composing a 30,000 word novella (which I'll get to later), and trust me, you'll want to find every last scrap. The game has a heavy emphasis on exploration, and little inhibits this. My only complaint here is that it is sometimes unclear when a door leads out of an area permanently rather than just to a smaller side room, which occasionally caused places to go unexplored, as I couldn't return.
Visuals: The graphics and art style strike a beautiful middle ground between DIshonored and The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, making good use of the Unreal Engine. While textures themselves are slightly muddy, their stylized nature makes the environments easy on the eyes, and the art direction throughout the game, especially in the dream sequences, absolutely breathtaking. From the dank, oppressive atmosphere of the sewers to the melancholy desolation of the surface, there's never a dull sight.
Story: This is the real meat of the game. While the actual story behind the game is murky (a non-issue which will surely be cleared up in the already-announced sequels), the writing is simply on another level. I'm used to toning down my standards for small indie games when it comes to the quality of narrative delivery, but the novella bits in particular are--no joke-- life-changing. The writer/s have a remarkable grasp of incomprehensibly deep philosophical thought to the point where it will almost always feel like they're ahead of you. That is perfectly fine, as the point of the game is to define a new philosophy for yourself, determining the nature of your own reality. The novella pieces are absolutely vital to the narrative, and a couple playthroughs will likely be necessary to track down any missed sections. It's good to go into the game knowing that you need to scour every area as thoroughly as possible before moving on, because you don't want to miss some of the best writing ever put into a game.
Sound: This deserves a special little section. The ambient sound is consistently chilling, and I honestly felt scared at points upon hearing the rattle of a can in the wind even though I knew nothing would jump out at me. The music, especially during dreams, is spot-on, adding to the experience without overshadowing it at all. It's also very well-synced to your actions, which is impressive given the number of branching paths in the game world. Finally, there is only one voice-acted character--you, a.k.a. Jonah-- and the talent is very, very good. Far better, in fact, than any indie game has a right to. This guy should be doing voicework for higher-paying games, because honestly, this was one of the most surprising parts of the game. Good narration is hard to do, and this guy nails it. Props.
Length: About a five-hour experience if you really take your time. And please, please /really take your time/.
Final thoughts:
This game is a shockingly in-depth exploration of what it means to be isolated in a world where certainty is fleeting. It's a scathing critique of Dostoevsky's Underground Man (I'm gonna stress this: fans of Dostoevsky are going to love the novellas, because Solomon is essentially Raskolnikov), becoming a quest to find a replacement for certainty. I won't reveal what this replacement is, but suffice to say that the experience is absolutely brilliant and worth every minute you pour into it.

In all honesty, "Dungeons" tries too hard to be a spoof of the old "Dungeon Keeper" games to really stand on its own merits. If you liked Kalypso's previous game "Ceville", then you'll probably enjoy "Dungeons" on your first playthrough or two, but the game gets pretty repetitive even during the campaign. If you played the "Dungeon Keeper" games, you'll probably find yourself wishing you were playing those games instead.
This is not to say that "Dungeons" isn't fun, but it doesn't have nearly the same level of detail and control that older games had. You can't, for example, pick up creatures, or create complex dungeons with many different rooms. The concession "Dungeons" makes to customability is to add in lots and lots of "gimmicks", which are decorative items that have the added benefit of making your Dark Lord stronger. "Dungeons" is the smaller, pudgier, comic-relief sidekick of  "Dungeon Keeper 2". If you like humor as a substitute for play, then go ahead and get "Dungeons".

Deus Ex: Human Revolution is one of the classics of gaming’s “second golden age” (roughly 2007 – 2013). Story, music, characters, gameplay are all of the highest order. Belongs in the library of every gamer who appreciates story-telling mixed with stealth-action gameplay. Worth the purchase price of $20, but frequently discounts to $5 or less, where it is an incredible bargain.
Total size on my hard-drive: 18.2 GB
The Director’s Cut Edition adds some visual tweaks and re-designed boss-battle environments. The Missing Link DLC is included, folded into the main story campaign.
+ Story with serious themes. Starts with a literal bang and is paced well.
+ Relevant side-quests that can contain important backstory.
+ Choices matter.
+ Voice-acting is excellent.
+ Superb soundtrack by Michael McCann. Synth-orchestral sound with a techno feel at times.
+ Multiple ways to play (with the right upgrades). Stealth? Shooter? Fall safely from any height? Punch walls (discovering new passages)? Up to you. High replayability.
+ Multiple level paths. You’ll end up at the same objective, but there are at least two paths to get there (and there are frequently more).
+ The Director’s Cut features completely revamped boss-battle environments. Stealth builds are now completely legit.
+ Addictive hacking mini-game. It’s over in seconds, too, so it doesn’t slow the gameplay down much.
+ Individual weapons. Decent selection, and they all look and feel unique.
+ Well-optimized, and not resource-intensive. Locked 60fps @1440 on an RX 470 with everything maxed except Depth of Field (which is an effect I dislike, so it was turned off). Back in the day, it played fine on the desktop APU I used to have (using the integrated graphics). If you have a low-spec computer and are looking for a good game to play, Human Revolution should be near the top of your list.
+/- Not an “open world.” Rather, a few small hub areas that have some side-missions. Allows for more focused level design, but can feel claustrophobic at times.
+/- The Missing Link DLC is included in the main campaign (right after leaving China for the second time). You lose all of your upgrades once this section of the game begins (though you get them back once this section is complete, PLUS any upgrades you accumulated). Generally, the insertion of the Missing Link DLC slows down the later part of the game, but narratively it makes complete sense. And Commander Burke is a great adversary.
+/- Graphics are fair. Light-shafts and shadows look great, but skyboxes look low-res and facial expressions are wooden. Edges are jaggy even with anti-aliasing cranked up (down-sampling is the best solution).
- Mouths frequently don’t sync properly during conversations.
- UI doesn’t scale properly. The HUD is tiny at 1440p; I can’t imagine it at 4k.
- Some odd controls with kb + m. Right click and hold to enter cover. Iron sights is a toggle of the middle mouse button.
- Predictable, stupid enemy AI. Get even a few upgrades, and ghosting levels becomes incredibly easy.
Even with those few drawbacks, Deus Ex: Human Revolution is one of the very best stealth / role-playing / action hybrids. It belongs to none of those genres, but takes the best elements of each and adds in an emotional story whose morals exist in planes of grey. A game to play through, reflect upon, and play again. 9/10

CiM2 is a very different feeling game than the original despite an identical premise. It definitely took me a lot longer to get into.
Cons:
- Steep learning curve. You'll probably fail a few games before you get the hang of identifying profitable routes.
- The default game mechanics make it ultimately almost impossible to fully serve a densely populated city. If you expand too quickly you'll start losing reputation *very* quickly as your vehicles get stuck in traffic jams and your stops fill up with unhappy passengers. Buses and trolleys are difficult to use for mass transit; you'll find yourself forced to use trams a lot, or else build your own bus-only roads.
- More demanding on hardware even on the lowest settings. I had a fairly decent older computer before this one and the game would overheat the cpu on a regular basis.
- Less user friendly in some respects. There's no confirmation before construction or most demolition. Constructed depots and roads take up more space than you would expect and it's easy to cut into the space mapped for city buildings without realizing it, which will cause them to pop out of existence immediately. Save before any renovation projects.
- Some of the randomized tasks are either worded very unclearly or programmed in a buggy way. A lot of the connections need to go both ways; unfortunately, Some won't be recognized even if you do that and I can't figure out what's going on.
Pros:
- CiM 1 was locked to a two-dimensional grid with some canned elevation differences. This game is 100% freeform 3D, with actual hills and valleys and streets curving all over the place. It feels natural, realistic, and alive.
- Higher level of transport simulation. With all your vehicles coming from and returning to depots it feels a lot more realistic.
- Individual and monthly ticket pricing, transit zones, etc. lets you control rider customer experience to an unparallelled degree. Vehicles can return to the same stop multiple times in a route or even loop back around the same route if you so choose. The freedom is yours to design exactly the transit system you want.
- The financial system is easier to track. Loans are simple to understand and repay; the game quickly informs you if your tickets are far too expensive or cheap in real time; there are graphs for every possible purpose you might want to look at. You can tailor your strategy to the situation seamlessly.
- The ability to build your own roads and tramways is *not* to be underestimated. You're not limited by the routes the scenario designer thought you might need. You can bypass high-traffic areas entirely by building a detour.
- Campaigns with a more free-form structure than the original. You can very much choose your own path to success.
- Game mechanics can be adjusted freely, tailoring the experience to what you want.  But it only works for sandbox and custom games, not the built-in campaigns.
- That same feeling of almost zen-like relaxation you can get from the first game is definitely present here.
Conclusion: More to wrap your head around than the first game. This one definitely demands more from your mind and your hardware, but it does start to pay dividends eventually. What you'll find here is a very enticing game which offers the freedom to design the transit system you want to run. It's probably not for everyone, but it can definitely be a very enjoyable experience.

I do recommend this game because I thoroughly enjoy the games put out by Pendulo Studios (especially and most notably the Runaway series).  Though it is an extremely short game, the unique plot and twisted characters make the experience enjoyable.  I’ve seen people compare this game to Broken Sword because of its storytelling style of mysticism and unraveling a mystery with intriguing turns around each corner.
The game is about a man named John Yesterday who has amnesia after a suicide attempt.  He doesn’t remember why he tried to kill himself and the meaning behind certain clews he left behind.  That’s all I can really say without spoiling the rest of the plot.
The pacing of the story is fantastic.  You do not start the game immediately as John Yesterday.  There is a tutorial-like prologue to get the player used to the controls and interface of the game where the player is a different character.  Who is this person? What is his relationship to John Yesterday? The game doesn't just give you the answer right off the bat.
The voice acting is cheesy, but that's what Pendulo Studios always does.  The villain is so lovably campy, and John Yesterday is quite bland, but it leads to rather funny moments.  There is a secret cameo from Brian Basco, but I was unable to achieve it on my first playthrough.  This does lend the game some replayability, but I also can just go to YouTube to watch it making this game only replyable if you want to go through the whole story exactly the same way again.
Revisiting previous parts of the game is actually really well implemented.  From the beginning, the game makes it clear it is trying an edgy comic-book style structure, and on the "Chapter" menu, there are comic book-like panels you can click and replay any part of the game.
The visual aspect of the game is gorgeous.  The backgrounds are stunningly drawn and distort perspective in ways that make the atmosphere perfect.  This game feels like a classic point-and-click game, something from the 90s, especially with the use of caricature stylised character models.
The game is very short and can be beaten in a single session easily.  However, a short game does not equal a bad game.  The artistic effort that went into this game surpasses the Runaway series.  Despite this game being darker in nature, it never strays from mixing in some well-placed comedy in typical Pendulo Studios style.  If you like the other games the company has made, you probably will enjoy this.

If you want to use it with a Mac, don't. Just don't. Seriously.
But... if you're a good person and you decided to get a PC instead of that overpriced Mac Mini, then listen up.
I'll start with how and when I got the controller. If you want, skip this junk and get to the review. Anyway, I am very, very terrible at a gamepad. I will literally get crushed at any game that's not a fighter like Smash or Brawlhalla. Or Splatton, but without gyro I'm a fish out of water (don't judge). I naturally wanted to fix this, so I thought this looked like a good idea: it seemed to have a heckuva lot of features, including gyro. I thought it'd be a nice way to ease into that kind of thing. The negative reviews about the layout didn't faze me: once the Wiimote has dominated your life, not much bothers you. The summer sale saved me about 50 bucks on the Link/Controller bundle (counting that 12 bucks for shipping... basically a horror story for an Amazon Prime user). I liked the concept of the Link because, heck, who wouldn't want to play PS2 on a 4k screen with epic surround sound? Of course, the terrible Mac I have can't really handle 4k, and the Link can't either, but whatever. Anyway, after waiting a week and a half or so for it to arrive (again, Prime user here), it came early Friday morning. After drooling over the very nice box, I plugged it in to the Mac and...
I will not describe the ordeal that followed. Let me just say that it took three days and I had very little luck. And I was seriously conisdering ending my gaming life after that but anyway, I was regretting it.
After very long weeks of LOTRO, trying to get an old laptop to at least run Minecraft, and wishing I had just saved my money, I got a PC for my birthday. I almost instantly plugged the Steam controller in and right out of the gate it worked. Everything worked. I was playing flipping Origin games with it. I was, to say the least, relieved. And that's where the review starts:
REVIEW: Wow, where to start. The controller fits amazingly well in my large, thin hands, but I've met several people with much smaller hands that have loved it. The plastic has a nice, sturdy feel to it, and unlike the Xbox controllers my hands don't flood sweat when I've held it for too long. The layout, while unfamiliar at first, is surprisingly well thought out. And you can customize it, but more on that later. The two touchpads have a very un-fragile feel to them, and are very responsive. The left one's indentations provide a nice "guide" for max precision, but it's subtle enough to ignore it when using it as a joystick. The triggers are nice; besides the dual state, there's not too much about them except for the fact that you can measure how much you're pressing them with an on-screen reader, something I feel might come in handy in the future. The back triggers are... wow, I don't know how to describe how helpful I've found them. And, like the reviews say, the size of the D-pads/touch joysticks can be changed using the "outer deadzone" setting.
The layout is slightly confusing at first, but this sentence might help: IT HAS 3 ANALOG STICKS. And 4 sets of buttons. It's that customizable. Seriously, it's got everything. It might be worth the money just to get to change that stuff. I've found mode shifting alone to be a crazy awesome feature.
I don't know how to summarize it all in so little time, so let me give you some pros and cons:
PROS:
Good plastic (huh?)
Practically infinite customizability
21 buttons not counting dual state triggers
Plays non-Steam games (like Minecraft or Origin games)
Lots and lots of tutorials
Plug and play with very little non-personal setup
Gyro (I absowutewy wuv it)
Easy, instant access in-game
CONS:
Again, if you have a Mac, don't
"HD Rumble" ain't so HD
The "clicks" aren't that great either
Without a mouse, it's pretty slow to get exactly what you want in a short amount of time
Pretty dependent on Big Picture mode, but this can be overlooked. It's actually nice, once you get used to it.
Anyway, aside from all that, you might be considering the reviews. To that, I say, "Heck, most of 'em probably don't know how to use Google, anyway." Use Google, or Bing, or whatever the heck you want. Look up how to use it to the max, or, if you're stupid like me, do it yourself and waste hours on end. (I'm kidding, if you do this, it's actually great practice for if and when they add new features). If you're good at controllers already and you prefer mouse+keyboard, then don't get it. It's not worth your money. Also, if you have a controller you absolutely prefer above anything else on the planet, then don't get it. I just recommend it.
See ya.
(But seriously, it's so flipping awesome that you should get it just to fawn over it. Or something. xD)

Prototype came out during the time I like to call the "Brown Era" where games became more realistic. and lost a ton of colour, COD did it, GTA IV did it, and so did this, Prototype is lacking so much colour, it's boring and lifeless.
Also the peds do nothing except drive or walk, there are no bums, business men chatting on phones, people eating, nothing at all and the city feels so life less.
Also the city is just squares and cubes without any memorable landmarks, everything looks the same, christ this city is so BORING!
For humans you only have your average soldier, who can also use tanks and choppers.
As for infected you only have normal Zombies, Hunters, Leader Hunters, and once in a while (Mostly in missions) Hydras.

The lastest release in the Hegemony Series. I have been a long time fan of this Strategy series and Longbow games for the mechanics they use to abstract logistics and supplies for ancient warfare. As anyone could tell you, an army marches on its stomach and nearly every other strategy game on the market completely ignores this very important concept.
This is their most polished and full-featured Hegemony game and allows for you to customize each unit and city to your liking: want to build a stone wall on that key border city? Set up market places for your economy in your inner cities, and barracks and stables on your front line forts? You make all the key decisions as your little fiefdom sprawls out from your starting city.
The AI puts up a very competitive fight--especially in the beginning when you have few units and are struggling against bankruptcy. The AI factions often raid cities that you just sieged so you will need to maintain Quick Reactionary Forces at intervals, even well  within your front lines.
Units themselves gain XP and allow you to pick from an RPG-like ability tree, so you can customize each type of unit in your army. When a unit is destroyed it doesnt disappear from the game, it is crushed to 0/XX recruits and retreats back to its 'Home' city to be conscripted with new recruits. However, you get to keep all the upgrades you have made to the unit.
I have not had any bugs or crashes -- I started playing after the first patch was released and fortunately it seems to have solved most/all of the issues that other reviewers have mentioned on their Day 1 reviews
Fantastic Game, Fantastic Series, Can't wait for more content and development!

This game is for sure better than H2, need to say that right off the bat.
I have noticed some reviewers saying this is better than H1: Gold though, that is definitely not true.
TL;DR - This is a buggy mess, I constantly get debug screens asking me to save info and send it to the devs. Wait a few months and then check the forums to see if the bugs have been fixed.
Wars are terrible and if the game gets multiplayer it would be a lot more fun but the AI has not been developed enough for this game to be anywhere near as interesting as H1 was.
-More unit variety but they require buildings, everyone gets the same basic spearmen and archers to start with. For the player this means you will eventually have an interesting variety of units. For the AI this means someday they may get hoplites if they form a large enough (Huge) empire.
-Rebels are the strongest faction you will face in the whole game which is really dumb. The AI does not seem to know when or what cities they should be building the upgrades that let you produce better units, whereas rebels seem to scale with time or with your civilization so they will put up a much better fight than the other factions will
-The AI has no idea how to manage lots of cities. They almost only build warehouses in cities and they rarely colonize the cities, so that city with stone walls will probably only last for a few minutes vs 3 spearmen and 2 javelins. The AI will stupidly walk out of every city to engage you, instead of picking you off from inside.
-This is all a major problem because the larger you get the easier everything gets, by a huge margin.
-The missions are far from "dynamic." Random would be a better word. I get missions to hand cities or pay tribute to factions that no longer exist, I currently have 2 missions that have the exact same objective (to burn farms) for a faction that no longer exists. H1 had interesting missions that brought good rewards, I mostly ignore these missions because the reward is either literally nothing (great reward there) or like 100 gold. 100 gold is a pitiful amount by the time you have all of your faction under control, which is when you would get these missions. You also have a persistent mission to get a higher population for the fantastic bonus of nothing. What is the point of the population objective? Can someone please tell me in the comments. Obviously I am going to increase my population it is the most important aspect of city management I don't need a pointless objective telling me to do so.
(To compare) In H1 you were surrounded by weaker factions and as you expanded the factions got harder and each faction also had different builds of armies. In H1 in the far north you have the nomads with huge horse armies that will decimate your javelins/archers if you are not careful, in the far south you have the Greeks and the terrifying Spartans that require huge amounts of archers to deal with and careful logistical planning, in the far east you have the Persians and there assortment of amazing units of all types to test your army with after you beat the game.
In H3 you have some slow moving easy to destroy hoplites if you are lucky and a faction conquered a territory with a lot of gold mines. Hoplites are a particularly garbage unit because unlike in Greece, Italy does not have mountains everywhere. It becomes particularly easy to circle around the hoplites and get 20+ slaves by flanking them. The battle AI has not improved since H1 or H2 because it is very easy to lure hoplites out of formation and take them out one at a time.
I can recommend this game after the bugs are fixed despite all the flaws with battle mechanics and the AI. I really hope that a Gold release comes out for this game that fixes many of these issues.
Addendum - Really sad that this review is sandwiched between 3 positive reviews only one of which has more playtime in the game than I do.
Wow, drastic improvements as far as the game goes. Patches and updates have made this game very playable and easily the best Hegemony game in sandbox form.
New Additions that have since changed my review
- Lots of changes to colonization, now it takest ime instead of just population from an old city. You can still rush it by using populations from older cities once you are big but in the early game you have to wait for the city to be assimilated/colonized.
- New Unit reminiscent of the Hypapists, that grows over time with your expansion and your capital level (improves the unit after so many cities Increases the brigade size by 5 every level your capital is)
-No more bugs, or at least I have not run into any of them. Very nice considering it used ot bug out in the intro screen on launch.
-Tech is still a bit goofy but has been a bit more streamlined
-Tutorial stuff now actually works and helps you understand what to do.
-A totally new interface with cites where you can now regulate how much food to give, how much tax they pay and how many citizens you draft.
-Reworks the supply lines aspect, now if your territorial control extends to the other city or resource you can get it without a supply line, this is nice but makes the later game a bit easier because you will waste so little money on supply routes.

I don't do many reviews, but don't like how the community is reacting to the recent server issues.  As far as $15-20 games go, the Space Run series is well worth the $$$.  If you are a fan of SR (ep1), then SRG adds a multiplayer option and deeper depth of managment (both business and shipbuilding) that is just awesome.  Feel like running the story-line without ever saying hi to another player?  Go ahead  -- you have that option.  Feel like maximizing every square inch of your ship with the perfect cargo run for accelerated risk/reward?  Jump into the multiplayer world and feel awesome for completeing 3x missions at the same time ... or like a chump when 5 minutes of run is wasted by that last #$%@ asteroid.
Like any new title though, the complexity comes with risk.  For those who are reading the reviews, you'll see *a lot* of negative press about the game not being playable  at the moment due to server issues.  What those reviewers didn't do was the 5 minutes of Steam research to see that the Devs posted that a) they had an issue they didn't expect with the server, and b) it'd be down for 24 hours to fix the problem.
So my millenial critics -- if you want to be one of the first guys on the block to play a new game in the first week of release, you need to expect that some shakedown of the code might be required when its popularity taxes the system higher than when tested.
For my 2-cents (or $17 bucks), I respect a developer that owns a problem and lets the community know where they are headed.  If you have the ability to wait a day or two before firing up your inner keyboard warrior and going Rambo/Rebate, my bet is that you'll find an awesome game with some hidden depth (and slightly dated graphics lol).
ps.  I'd recommend making both a multiplayer character and a solo character next time you are able to log in, since you won't be able to make a solo character to scratch your space trucking itch if its not set up ahead of time!
pps.  Thanks to all you awesome people who made a little extra hauling my freight around the cosmos....

The Old City: Leviathan is a project I've been following for a while now. It captured my attention from the moment I read that it focused entirely on story and exploration without the obsessive combat or jumpscares that plagues the common formula for big-budget-quick-profit games today. My intrigue was instantly sated from the moment I ran the game. I'm obsessed. It's an addicting breath of fresh air that is so desperately needed amongst today's games.
This game instead slows you down, sets you free to explore, and unfolds its story through its beautifully crafted environment. It places its trust in human curiosity, and quickly ensnares you in its abstract, fragmented story told through the eyes and ramblings of a madman. Everything done and narrated in this game is terrifyingly meaningful and deep. The intellectual depth and immersion of this game is just absolutely stunning, and combines for one remarkable experience.
This is the kind of game that makes you want to write down everything you see, every question you have, and every reoccuring object in hopes of piecing everything together. It's just confusing enough to addict you into finding the truth, yet clear enough to keep you on the hunt for more. This is the kind of game that you can easily spend hours on without realizing. It just might leave you laying awake at night mulling over what you've experienced. It combines gritty, realistic, post-modern elements with whimsical pieces of myth and mystery, and amongst it all you'll find insight that truly transcends anything in the gaming universe today.
Unlike a lot of current story-based games, you don't feel like a tourist, you actually feel like an adventurer. You feel like you're the one making the discoveries, not being read to on a forced, one-track story. Leviathan is tangible, it's interactive, it feels
The music and ambiance is on an entire different level as well. It really immerses you into the game. The environment you explore actually feels like a living, breathing beast, and it will send shivers down your spine.
It's an experience unlike anything I've ever known in gaming. Do yourself a favour and buy it.

Deus Ex: Human Revolution - Director's Cut (DXHR) is a first-person cyberpunk stealth action RPG, which takes place in the mid-2020s. You fill the role of Adam Jensen, the recently-hired head of security at Sarif Industries in Detroit. One of the company's scientists, Dr. Megan Reed, is soon to present some research regarding human augmentation and enhancement to politicians in Washington, DC. Shortly before leaving, however, a highly-trained and highly-augmented black ops team infiltrates Sarif Industries and kills the scientists on Dr. Reed's team, including Megan herself. Adam Jensen, in a futile effort to intervene, is mortally wounded. The only way to save him is to augment him. Six months after the attack, Jensen is called back in to action to deal with another attack, this time on a Sarif plant. There's a missing piece in this attack, and this leads Adam Jensen to hunt down it down and find the truth behind the attack on Dr. Megan Reed's team.
DXHR was a really enjoyable experience for me, I've got to say. First of all, I'm a pretty big fan of futuristic games, and this game's take on the next step in the evolution of man is really interesting. It shows both the good and the bad parts of the idea of human enhancement technology. While our world has yet to advance beyond simpler prosthetic technology, DXHR is a sort of eye-opener for our future.
Anyway, I'm going to actually talk about what I liked about the game. DXHR is really open-ended, first of all. As I said above, it's a stealth game, but it's also an action game. You can literally play the entire game without killing a single person, with the exception of bosses. I personally used a mixed playstyle, attempting to sneak around when I saw the opportunity, and resorted to using my projectile weapons when I was either discovered or had no other way through. Another thing I liked was the hub-style level structure. Between major missions, you stroll around city hubs, sometimes picking up side quests and finding little secret rooms or stashes. Doing these side quests helps a lot with leveling up your character, which is also pretty interesting. Adam's augmentations need to be unlocked over time, and they're all really interesting. My personal favorite augmentations are the three-meter-high jump and the punch-through-wall one. They're a lot of fun.
I did love playing this game, but it's not perfect. The dialogue is really kind of boring, giving you a maximum of four dialogue options, where other games will offer more. Sometimes, having so many options to get around is kind of unnecessary, because you may be offered to hack the lock on a door, but there's a vent you can open to get past it in one-tenth the time. Oh, yeah, and hacking. I know, I know, it's technically a mini-game, but still, it could be better.
Steam Integration:
DXHR features Steam achievements and Steam trading cards, so you can craft badges and show off to your buddies when you get those secret achievements. Achievements which I can tell you absolutely nothing about because I'm pretty sure I have none of them.
Playtime and New Game+:
When I wasn't playing Counter-Strike with my friends, I was able to play this game and get what I feel is the full experience, all in about 28 hours. That's fairly short, I suppose, for a game, but when you consider that 95 percent of that playtime did NOT consist of trying to find hundreds of random collectibles, I'd say it's a pretty good amount of time. And then, after you're done, you can start a "New Game+" where you carry over your character's abilities, which can unlock a lot more possibilities in the early game.
Pros
You can play the game however you want: guns blazing, sneaky-beaky, or both.
The character leveling is very balanced and you actually have a hard time choosing upgrades because they're all pretty awesome.
The story is pretty good, and there are a lot of side quests to keep the in-game downtime feeling like uptime.
Trading Cards are dropped occasionally.
Cons
The dialogue system isn't great. It feels very limited and linear at times.
Adam Jensen isn't a very dynamic character. Kind of unlikable, in fact, which is bad since you HAVE to be him.
Gah! The ending is nerve-wracking. Reminds me of Mass Effect 3, if you know what I'm talking about.
Final Thoughts:
Despite some of its shortcomings, Deus Ex: Human Revolution shines and isn't afraid to challenge you as a player. After playing this, I'm super excited to see what Deus Ex: Mankind Divided has in store for us next month. Let's hope that Eidos and Square Enix will deliver again! In the meantime, try to pick up DXHR on sale (I got it for about five dollars) and play it; you won't regret it!

Deus Ex: Human Revolution tried to bridge a gap between the original Deus Ex, a true masterpiece in its own right for decades to come and modern gaming. There was only one way this possible could have gone and that was to fail to deliver something as absolutely stunningly perfect as Deus Ex was to gamers 17 years ago.
That being said, Deus Ex: Human Revolution does a lot of things right by integrating most things which made Deus Ex great into a new title which is on par mechanically and graphically with today's gaming industry standards. The main reason why it cannot live up to the legacy of the original Deus Ex is a lack of replayability and a very limited if not completely lacking impact of player made choices on the entire game.
A game does not need to be on par with the original Deus Ex to be a great game though, and Human Revolution is a very great dystopian high-tech-stealth-FPS-RPG, a genre which there exist close to no other games within apart from Deus Ex and System Shock games.
As a stealth title, Deus Ex:HR is fun. As a shooter, Deus Ex:HR ist fun. As an RPG, it is lacking on the narrative side and regarding player agency, but features a lot of character progression, lots of different ways to get to places, different viable playstyles and sometimes actually quite great dialogues. The Director's Cut also manages to seemlessly and perfectly integrate The Missing Link, a 5-6 hour-ish DLC campaign into the main story without ever causing the feeling that it was piecemealed together.
So, is Deus Ex: Human Revolution a deserving successor to the original Deus Ex? No, but it's a very great game nonetheless which anyone who has even the slightest interest in Transhumanism, Cyberpunk, FPS, RPGs and stealthy gameplay should most definitely look into.

This is a variation of the famous Nonogram/Picross puzzle. It includes a couple of new hints, which changes the way you solve it:
* The numbers at the borders describe how many consecutive cells are marked in that row/column.
* A number within brackets at the border describe how many cells in total are marked in that row/column.
* A number inside a cell indicates that cell is part of a 2D group of connected cells with that size. Cells are connected only in vertical or horizontal directions.
* The number at the bottom shows how many uncovered cells are yet to be removed from the puzzle.
This is a very enjoyable game, together with the Hexcells family of games (all of these from the same developer). All of the puzzles can be solved using pure logic.
As a bonus, you can also toggle the graphics between light or dark style.

This is a rather tentative thumbs up. If you have not played all the Hexcells games, get those and play them. They are decidedly better. If you have exhaused those and all the user-designed levels on Reddit (as I have), get this.
Why is it is weaker than Hexcells? Well, you know, sophomore slump, regression toward the mean, whatever. Hexcells is brilliant. It feels like the perfect puzzle game. With this one, Mr. Brown found a good mechanic, but just not that good. I have not worked out all the theory, but basically there is just not as much he could do with it. There are only so many ways to create a logical constraint here, fewer than Hexcells and not as clever feeling. And many of them involve a lot of counting, which gets really tedious. I cannot put my finger on exactly why, but it is just not as fun.
I finished it in two sittings. Only a few of the levels really felt as satisfying as a decent Hexcells level feels (let alone the brilliant ones). Maybe Mr. Brown has some other mechanics up his sleeve, along with some new levels, as with the Hexcells series. As is, however, this is merely a solidly good puzzle game. It is clearly worth the modest price if you like such games (clearly better than the plethora of "draw the line" games), but it is simply no Hexcells.
Just as amazing as Hexcells, but with enough of a spin on the mechanics to make it an entirely different experience.

Though my playtime is quite short at the time of writing, I've previously played and completed this game on Vita. While this game doesn't quite reach the heights of the Sky games, it's nonetheless another great entry in the Trails series. If you're interested in playing the Trails games I'd recommend you play the Sky games first, as Cold Steel takes place after them. Though it's largely disconnected, Cold Steel rather unavoidably ends up spoiling some things from the Sky trilogy - though they're mostly minor plot details, and there's really only one big one. That said, if that doesn't bother you too much, feel free to jump into this one - everything's explained, so newcomers won't be lost! The game's also incredibly long, so if the price looks high to you I wouldn't worry - it's still good value for money.
On the technical side of things, this port is absolutely spectacular. Runs like a dream, even on the most potato-like of systems, and features a number of quality-of-life improvements that raise it far above the original console version. Loading is near-instant! You can fast-forward through battle animations and slow panning shots with Turbo mode! Even the launcher is controller-compatible! Top work.
As always, the future of this series is determined by its sales, and it'd be a real shame to miss out on the games that aren't already localised. So, if you're interested in Trails, do go ahead and give Cold Steel (or Sky FC) a go.

Even if people think turn based combat is something old-school... particularly the turned based combat from the Legend of Heroes introduces a dynamical factor, that even if this is not "active time battle", certainly it can be a big challenge to fight many battles in the matter of how you administer your resources and the battle's bonuses.
Another thing is that, characters have 2 different skill sets: one that can be customizable and another one that is fixed, having the best out of customization along with the uniqueness of each character.
Now adding the link system into the battles, it produces a more dynamic feeling compared to the predecesor Trails in the Sky. However do not confuse "more dynamic" with "better". They are just different systems, made in different dates.
One thing I did not like at all but ended accepting, is the voice of Alisa. Althought at first I was a little annoyed by it, a little later I got used to it (just the tone of the voice, because I liked how the voice actress performed in the end).
Another thing to mention, is that I loved the way the story develops the bonds between the people that came in contact with Class VII (talking more focussed on the main story side, althought there are some exceptions), as well as the bonds within the members of Class VII.

The game can be very “Japanese” at times where in my opinion conversations are stilted or “slowed down” by people over congratulating, apologizing, or being modest which is very typical in games/anime from Japan.

I guess that's all I really have. I look forward to the next installment in this series!

This is my first foray into the hegemony series, however a lot of the game mechanics in Clash of the ancients are similar to ones ive played in the total war series, and civ series respectively.  The game has a great amount of depth and i love the immersion of spreading your fledgling colony throughout the ancient world. Proper planning and preparation are key when you expand beyond your city area, you need to keep troops supplied with food, logistics really matter and add a level of tactical gameplay missing form the Total war/civ series. If you push too far into unexplored regions without decent supplies (making sure to protect your supply routes too!), it will usually end rather badly for your expedition forces.
Really love the city building aspect of this game to, well maybe building is the wrong word...perhaps upgrading lol. All building types have numerous upgrades as do all unit types which add further layers of strategy and versatility to building your empire. Raiding is serious business maybe a little to serious as the raids from barbarians and other factions can become a full time job to deal with. Granted i made some major mistakes on my first playthrough by not setting up proper defenses on the exterior areas of my growing territory due to not building proper forts, more specifically proper upgrades to deal with constant raiding parties. If the raiders get through they do serious damage to your farms, mines, and other buildings which you need to maintain income and resources to fuel your further expansion and empire.
There's also a tactical well fleshed out combat system, quests, and many other things which i just have not played enough of the game yet to really grasp, I might make another review after ive played more of the game.
So my initial impressions of the Hegemony, if you like strategy games with a decent amount of depth and complexity, dont mind a pretty steep learning curve/proper tutorial, enjoy micromanaging... and a love for all things Classical antiquity, then i think i can safely recommend this game to you!!!
P.S.  I also want to mention i think this game has alot of potential to be even better then what ive already seen like adding sicily, carthage and other areas to the map. The modding tools available will give modders alot of options to make even more improvements and new content as well!!!.

Such as limits to amount of structures you can own. This is hidden behind mechanic level, and it only means that the game gets hardrer and more anoying than it was before.
Dont get me wrong. I like the game wery much, but the missions (especialy those with some ramdomness in the enemies apearing in the mission) can be pretty hard at times. I strongly believe that it is design decision, as I was not able to find a way how to finish some missions (with 3 stars and without loosing cargo) without almost completely rebuilding the ship in mid mission and in great hurry. And to tell the truth, I hate that. Usually it is possible to play it in less frenetic way, but that in general meand finishing second or third, or to loose some cargo. Which I do not like, but I do not like that constatnt stress from the frenetic gameplay even more.
I did not have had such bad feel from the game while it was in beta stage and certailny I did not have had such feeling from the first space run either. And for some reason, I enjoyed the original game much MUCH more, even though that there were less equipment and less levels and who know what more.
When I think of it, the amount of things one can build is not really helping at all. to nema one thing I do not like there - for some reason, in every one group (from the three basics) there is some kind od offensive device, and somehow I do not feel like the "red" are actually the best offensive devices at all :(.
But to be fair - the variability of the items is great but yet again, liked the equipment (and especially its leveling up) much more in the first game. Here it feels like in every mission I am starting from beginning without actually learning anything. Well appart from that I can buy few more items. But then again - if I have to buy each device, why is it it not already placed on the ship? Or should it be a "blueprint"? Then why cant one be used several times? And yes, I _know_ it is a game mechanic, but it is one I do not like at all and well, I see no real reason for it. Apart from making the game harder and players more anoyed.
So no, I clearly can not recommend the game and I am really sad about.
Oh, and another issue I have noticed during the last game servers problem (server inavalability): when I tried to run offline game, then I did not have had access to the game progress I have already made while playing online. Of course, when starting a new game there is a warning that offline saves can not be converted to online ones, but why is it not possible to play offline with online saves? Or at least convert/copy the saves as offline saves so the game progress is not lost? What the hell are the devs thinking? This really is a horrible decission and another reason for me NOT recomending this game.

Oh goodness, I can't say enough about thi game. I have lamented the death of Dungeon Keeper 3 for years, and finally it has been reborn in a modern form with new gameplay mechanics. The idea of harvesting soul energy from heroes you have pampered and 'built up', only to tear them down and lock them away is deliciously evil. Managing a dungeon in this manner can be difficult, (it's YOUR gold in those piles....so you end up running out fairly quickly if heroes take alot of it.) there's a good deal of micro management involved, as well as planning, room building, etc. All to tease those heroes with lovely jewels, books, equipment, and more, so you can suck all of that out of them when they fall. The soul energy collected goes to prestiege items which make your dungeon more impressive, and boost your power. So it's a bit of a roundabout buildup until you can build more prisons and have enough prestiege to easily deal with the invading heroes, and even champions. Lots of good stuff here!

As a casual puzzler, I welcome anything that makes me use a little bit of brain power. From the developer of the Hexcells series (easily my favorite puzzle series - think of Minesweeper but better) comes SquareCells. It is very similar to Hexcells with the exception that your units are composed of squares. You will have similar column, row, group/broken group and adjacent group hints that propel you through the 36 puzzles. The game will last about 5-8 hours depending how strong of a puzzle solver you are.
Compared to Hexcells Infinite, you no longer have the ability to infinitely generate puzzles, so 36 is all you will get. The complexity is not quite on the same level either, but the last world of SC was fairly difficult for me, taking about 30-40 min per puzzle. Although the hints are similar, the strategies for solving some of the sections are rather new. One consistent aspect is that you will never have to guess on a unit, nor will you be left with any 50/50 choices like in Fine Sweeper or other Minesweeper clones.
For fans of the Hexcells series that want a little bit of style change, I definitely recommend getting this game. For anyone else, I heavily suggest playing Hexcells Infinite first.

Squarecells, like its predecessor, Hexcells, is a minimal but deep logic puzzle that draws inspiration from Minesweeper.
It’s a short romp of a head-scratcher, giving you 36 puzzles to solve which should take a handful of hours to get through. As with the Hexcells series, the difficulty ramp-up of the puzzles is perfectly balanced, with each puzzle being ever so slightly tougher to solve than the previous one.
While Squarecells is a little on the short side, that works in its favor, it never overstays its welcome, and is priced appropriately for a short game. Highly recommended.

So, this game is pretty fun at first, but after progressing through the first few levels of this game and gaining two allies to join your team, the core aspect of this game is reached and it's rather dull and disappointing.
If you've played any of the 1st person shooter versions of the Serious Sam games, you'll remember how you dodged and weaved between enemy projectiles as you fired back at them.The problem with this game is that damage goes from being avoidable to being UN-avoidable. The enemy will attack you with an onslaught of projectile attacks and you will not be able to avoid (most of) them. This makes the game infuriating because the mechanics don't work very well, when so many enemies come at you.
Maybe I'm just not a pro at the game yet. This isn't like Strikers (old-school top-down airplane game) where you can weave through enemy attacks when you're a pro. You just can't dodge everything. Ugh.
If this is super discounted, buy it if you're a fan of SS like I am.
