This game could be described as Slitherine's Legion on steroids.
Having said that, the game system is much better by far than Legion ever was.
Not surprisingly, it uses essentially the same mechanics as Hegemony I and II.
Hegemony III is a semi-historical sandbox of Italy before the Roman conquest.  It has a lot of historical flavor elements that come into play, but you can pick your favorite obscure Italic tribe and try to see if you can do better than the Romans.
The game is semi-historical because it telescopes several hundred years of development into a few game years.  This is a good thing: if you've read Livy, you wouldn't want to fight the same war for one village year after year over and over again until you finally win.  And if you've read Livy you also know that armies weren't mobilized and kept in the field according to Hegemony mechanics.  You raised everything at the start of the year after you had finished planting your troops, and you didn't raise anything else unless there was a real emergency.  Emergency troops would usually stand down after the crisis was over, and in any case everybody would go home before the fall harvest season.  Nothing ever happened in late fall, winter, or before late spring.
Just to be clear, Hegemony III takes place long before the First Punic War, so you won't be invading Sicily or encountering Carthaginians.  But if you've read Livy, the game is the perfect vehicle for refighting your own version of the Samnite Wars.
The only other game out there that makes a serious attempt (a very serious attempt) at presenting the Samnite Wars is Ageod's Birth of Rome expansion for Alea Jacta Est.
I like the ceramic art-inspired graphics, but people who aren't familiar with the conventions of ancient vase painting may find it takes a little getting used to at first.
I've been playing the game during the first week of release, so entirely without benefit of post-launch patches.  While I'm sure that there's a thing or two that will get tinkered with down the road, I haven't encountered any game-stopping major bugs.  I say that in the context of playing a couple of games (which will remain nameless) a year or two after release that are still riddled with bugs.  The core system was hammered out in the first two games, so all that is probably going to be needed here is some fine tuning.

I decided to edit my review with some positive points, to give you more an idea of why you should buy this game. Just to get it out of the way; Yes, you should buy it if you're into strategy. It has a couple of flaws, but overall it's a great game.
+ The map is huge.
+ The starting situation variety is great. There are, off the top of my head, 27 factions. Each having their own benefits, like +15% mining output and/or +25% combat experience. Then there's the starting general to add to that, which you can fully customize with 3 points. You can make it a frontline general, with for example, 2 points in Defence and 1 point in Morale, which gives it extra % for the unit it is attached too. Or you can make an economic leader to govern your city and get more % tax, etc etc.
+Resource management. There are a variety of resources to be exploited. Like gold, wheat, wood, etc. Food you obviously need to feed your army and workers. Wood to upgrade buildings, resources, siege weaponry and ships. Gold to maintain your army, city/camp upgrades and bridges. Make sure you have a stockpile for the winter!!
+Zooming from the strategical map to the tactical map.
+Strategic map looks great. Seeing your realm rise slowly from 1 city with a couple of resources to an entire empire completely interconnected is awesome.
+Lots of fronts with lots of wars. You can't have your troops everywhere, so you'll have to make some decisions where to place them strategically. Don't forget about the invaders from sea!
+ Upgrading cities/camps/resources. Putting up stone walls is expensive, but luckily can be countered by having level 2 markets in your cities. Mixing and matching upgrades to certain cities is fun.
+ Tech tree. Good decision's can be made there.
+ Indie made and it's only the beginning!
Besides the good points, I don't really have anything to complain besides bad sound effects.

I was not a fan of the original Deus Ex. Blasphemy, I know, but in my defense, about when it came out, I preferred simpler games, in which you went around killing people. "Open World" and "multiple solutions" just confused me, and I couldn't understand why I couldn't just run and gun my way through it, and kept dying all the time.
I did keep up with what was happening with the subsequent Deus Ex games, once I grew up a bit. And they all seemed to be disappointments. I rightfully ignored them. Then came Deus Ex: Human Revolution.
The game starts out well. When you boot it up, it lets you skip all of the various logos of companies that made it, which elevates it in my eyes. Little things such as that show how much thought went into the game.
You play Adam Jensen, an ex-cop turned security chief. You're working for a company that augments humans, allows them to run faster, be stronger, interface with people, even use pheremones to manipulate them. Along the way, you are also augmented, and can buy upgrades, not only for weapons, but also for yourself. It's all very System Shock-y, though I suppose Deus Ex did it first.
Human Revolution is one of those weird games where I enjoyed the sneaking around more than I did the combat. You get more XP for sneaking around without being seen, knocking out guards in melee, and generally just being a ghost. You can get through the entire game without killing anyone... with a few exceptions.
You see, fights against bosses are straight up fights (with guns, and grenades), and they're awful. You'll be going along, not killing anyone, your inventory bursting with unused ammo, and then suddenly, you have to fight someone who can wipe you out in a couple of hits, and it's very jarring. And terrible.
That aside, the game is a lot of fun. There are multiple ways of approaching missions, including the side missions. The achievements are clever. While sneaking around, you do need to figure out what your enemies are doing and then plan out your attacks. And once you've beaten the game (and yes, there are multiple endings), you can do it again in a New Game+ with all of your upgrades intact. Good fun, I think.
Yes, I'd recommend Deus Ex: Human Revolution. There's plenty of world-building, plenty of story, and plenty of sneaky-fun. The only downside to the entire thing are the aforementioned boss fights, and Adam Jensen's voice, which is really annoying (though is, in hindsight, probably a tribute to JC Denton from the original Deus Ex, who was also terrible to listen to).

Yesterday is an original adventure point ‘n’ click game by Pendulo Studios, renown for one of the most eminent adventure game series, The Runaway. Unlike their previous titles, Yesterday is the darkest and most serious game in their catalogue to date as it combines elements of mystery and supernatural; a departure from the quirky comedic styling of their other games.
In Yesterday, you begin with Henry White, a young and rich heir dedicated to a charitable organisation, who is investigating the case of the homeless people disappearing in New York whose bodies are found lifeless later on with Y-shaped scars. Years later, Henry crosses paths with the enigmatic John Yesterday, the main protagonist of the game, whose memory seems to have been wiped clean. From there on, the story of these two turns into a dark and terrifying one involving occult practices and Satanism with a big twist later on in the game in regards to John’s amnesia.
Once again Pendulo Studios have done a fairly good job in drawing captivating backdrops, even though the number of explorable locations is smaller than Runaway 3. They are also a lot darker and less cheerful than in past Runaway games for instance. This is partially due to the dark tone of the game and the fact that most events happen either in dark rooms or at night-time. By now, Pendulo Studios have already developed their own unique cartoony art style which differentiates themselves from other similar games. However, despite the nicely drawn environments, the walking animations for the characters in this game do fall flat. They are sluggish, more so than in previous titles by Pendulo Studios. For a game that came out in 2012, one would expect the quality of the animations to be on par with the standards of the genre at the time. Luckily, double-clicking allows the player to “teleport’ the character to the hotspot they desire, consequently skipping the lacklustre walking animations. This happens almost all the time in this game, perhaps due to a reflex of double-clicking on everything, so you will barely see the character physically walking from A to B. The animations during cutscenes are a lot better though.
The voice acting in Yesterday is very laudable and one of the best I have heard in a Pendulo game so far, aside from when characters try to put on accents. For example, a character you meet in Paris simply sounds way too fake with his French accent. Actually, there is not a lot of voice acting in this game, as seen in a lack of voice acting in scene descriptions. For me, that is not a major problem. Furthermore, conversations are done in a cinematic / comic book style where you see two big portraits of the characters talk with each other. The soundtrack of the game has a certain vibe to it which fits with the themes of the game, sure, but as a whole it is mostly unmemorable. Aside from the track with the whistling (pretty catchy!), no other track stuck with me throughout most of the game.
Compared to other point ‘n’ click games, the difficulty of the puzzles in Yesterday is fairly easy for the most part, even if, mechanically speaking, it does not reinvent the wheel. In actual fact, it is very minimalistic. Perhaps a bit too much. You have got your standard inventory management, combining items (oddly enough, you will have objects in the inventory that you will never use, like the cellphone) and so on and so forth. However, I would like to highlight that there are occasions when the writers tried to be a tad too creative for their own good with their puzzles, making them implausible in real-life, bearing in mind the tone of the story, but I can attest it is not anywhere near rage-inducing. After all, Pendulo is notorious for making similar puzzles in their games. Besides, you could also argue it is a computer game, right? Well, perhaps not always depending on certain circumstances. Anyhow, on the plus side, for people who are impatient, there is a simple hint system available whenever you get stuck which gladly does not spoon-feed the player with the exact solutions. Additionally, there is also a button which reveals all the hotspots in the scene, eliminating any pixel-hunting. Throughout my playtime, I had to use the hint system only in three instances which was more down to me either thinking way too much outside of the box or omitting an object.
Indisputably, Yesterday’s biggest strength lies in the story and narrative – which are not perfect though. The story starts off unimpressively, but to my surprise, as the player progresses, it gets much more interesting to a point of self-indulgence; in a good way. It is hard not to notice some inspiration taken from games such as Broken Sword in some aspects, especially Shadows of The Templars. That being said, the writing is not always stellar, which is sometimes a staple of Pendulo’s writing, and as with past titles, female characters (ie. Pauline Petit) tend to be the ones who are the least fleshed out in terms of character development. Another example is the big twist of the story. While the twist behind John’s amnesia is commendable for its originality, I personally felt the twist did not have a huge impact, the way the writers might have intended, because many allusions were made to it quite early on in the game which made it predictable. I kind of saw it coming, but the question was – how would the twist play out? Now come to think of it, many of the few twists in this game are not as jaw-dropping as you would expect and turn out predictable (ie. you know who the antagonist is very quickly), but the game does a decent job keeping you invested in the journey. The story is fairly absurd, but not on par with the second half of Runaway 2, so do expect to scratch your head a few times along the way. It may seem pretentious at times, but I did enjoy it, oddly enough.
Any issues present in Yesterday are due to its most obvious flaw which is the pacing, which in turn is due to the short length of the game. Yesterday is short and very streamlined as an adventure game and can be completed in 4 hours at most, without using the hint system. As a result, the writers had to cram in as much as they could into the game to make it at least comprehendible, to some degree, from a story perspective. So the player is left with events happening too fast, expositions being served like fast-food (I suppose it is better than longwinded ones), very limited cast of characters and there being not enough time for much better character developments for support characters. It is clear from all these that this game must have been developed with a very small budget which is a pity.
In conclusion, Yesterday is a point ‘n’ click game which does not fulfil its full potential as intended. Whilst it does not reach the same level of brilliance as Broken Sword: Shadow of The Templars, it is definitely an adventure game worth giving a shot for the story, at any rate. It does feel more like this is only an introduction to a bigger story, which may also explain why the ending is left open, intentionally, for a sequel. Yes, there are alternative endings, which are a nice touch, but their outcomes are similar. Now the game would have been phenomenal if it were longer, had more places to explore, more support characters, better character development and a slower pace than its current one. Heck, maybe some cool new gameplay mechanics too. I am surprised there were no mechanics involving using superpowers with all the supernatural elements of the story. Ultimately, I would say to anyone that is fascinated by adventure games with intriguing stories that Yesterday is a game which you will you either like it for what it has to offer with its story or be disappointed by how stripped-down it is as a game. Whilst slightly above average as an overall package, I will recommend this game solely for the story because it kept me invested. I really want to know what happens next.

Grat art style, with some excellent design decisions made that at times allow for movement to flow (so we can see the animation) but at others fade from one position to another to mean less time waiting for repositioning of characters.
Puzzles are simple but effective and the in-game hint feature is always there (and pitched at the right level, clues not answer).
The biggest plus point though is the storylone, which is fairly original and not always black and white.  There is a major twist early on (which is in itself fairly unusual comparedto late game twists).  Most of all pretty much everything made sense (though a trip to the mountains for sensai training is very cliche) to enough of an extent that it never felt like a chore to listen to the dilogue, something not many adventure games manage, certainly not ones that don't fall back on humour anyway.
The only major negative I can find really is the very ending where the final scene can deviate one of several waysdepending on your choice, which is usually a good thing but in this case it seems tacked on almost as an afterthought and two of the choices in the end show conflicting behaviour from the third charachter.  It is also a little short but given the budget pricing that isn't a major issue.
Overall a very good purchase that shows a lot of promise.  Any of the three endings could actually be used as the launch point for further titles in what could be a very good series of games if handled correctly.  Unfortunately looking atthe Pendulo site/forums that doesn't seem likely, which is a shame.

Another excellent puzzle game by Matthew Brown, and for 3 bucks it's a steal. It took me perhaps 7 hours to complete every puzzle perfectly (mostly playing offline, so Steam time is meaningless). Yes, it's a bit like Picross at first, but then a Hexcells-like concept is introduced: numbers within the grid tell you how many squares are in a connected group. This makes for some neat logic puzzles, particularly if you're aiming for a perfect solution (each error loses you a star). It can be a bit frustrating on the longer puzzles to make a silly mistake near the end and have to start over (assuming you want a perfect score, as if we wouldn't). I think Hexcells is probably the better game, but this is still absolutely worth your time if you like contemplative logic puzzles with a relaxing soundtrack. Pity there's no infinite mode.

This is an interesting game in some ways and has good atmosphere and nice graphics. There are two big things about it that i don't like much though. The first is the lack of a separate battle level/ tactical level, separate from the strategic map. This is really just about the kind of game it is, so is the more minor complaint.
My bigger problem with the game is the amount of micromanagement. You need to send troops to capture logging camps, farms and mines - then you need to recruit units of peasants and send them to man those buildings. On top of that the troops themselves need to carry food with them, or else set up a camp and a supply line, or else starve. Putting in logistics and food supply is a reasonable enough idea - it was important in ancient warfare. But it could be done far more simply and automatically - e.g by having an automatic supply line between an army and the nearest friendly city, cut if enemy troops or fortifications cross it.
I was hoping to like this game because Rome II Total War is such a half-cut disappointment, but the level of micromanagement is just too much for me. Other people may enjoy it, but i'd prefer to have at the least an Options setting for the computer to deal with most of the food supply - and to be just capturing cities, not individual farms or logging camps.
Once i learn how to play it, im sure ill love it.

From what I have played (Close to 3 hours at the time of writing this) I can say that I like Hegemony 3, it's much more of a sandbox then 2, perhaps even more then 1? The campagin I am playing is the Italian Hegemony, you have a wonderful amount of choice between what faction you want to play from Celts in the north, Etruscans and the Romans in the centre, Illyrians to the east to the Greek colonies in the south.
This campagin starts with your faction split, as 1's Philip campagin did. In this one you control your capital and the rest of your cities are independant of your rule and your first obective is to bring them back into the fold.
The non-combat improvements in 2 are here, you can build buildings in cities to give you acess better/different troops, ships, siege equipment, for the city to produce more food, research points etc. However, an improvement over 2 is that each city grows over time if you keep the city supplied with food. Whereas in 2, certain cities would have arbitrary X amount of building slots  and there was no way to increase this, now your cities increase in size as they grow and you unlock more building slots and money generation as you do so, every city starts at level 1 and has no building slots (excluding the slot exlusive for walls).
I have only played as Kroton as of this writing, Kroton is a Greek faction and is very familar to those who played Hedemony 1.
Other then some graphical and minor glitches I have no complaints, and these glitches are so minor I can't be bothered to report them. One major complaint: No Syracuse wtf?
tl:dr I wholeheartedly recomend this game, anyone who liked the first game but was dissapointed by certain aspects of the second game (myself inlcuded) this is the game we wanted when we heard "Hegemony Ceaser"

My review for Trails of Cold Steel is more aimed at people who have played the Sky Trilogy. If you haven't played the Sky Trilogy (You should be right now) and are curious to see some comparisons, don't worry. This review is spoiler free.


+ The already great combat from the sky trilogy has been significantly improved.  Arts have been knocked down a few notches, with Melee/Crafts taking the front seat in Cold Steel.
+ Music is Falcom. Enough said.
+ Story and world building are as great as ever. Tons of twists and turns and an all-around great way to kick off the CS trilogy.
+ World is vibrant, colorful, and full of different settings. Graphics are goood.
+ Turbo Mode is an absolute god send.
- A lot of Items (Mainly Quartz) you obtain are pretty underwhelming and never really serve a purpose.
- A lot of side quests felt rather pointless compared to the ones in the Sky Trilogy. I found myself skipping the dialogue in certain ones entirely, just to get to my reward faster.
- Main cast of characters in Cold Steel, which mainly consist of typical anime tropes (Not the case at all in the sky trilogy), aren't all that interesting in the beginning and never fully live up to the cast from the Sky Trilogy. Which to be fair, is incredibly hard to live up to, and I guess an unfair comparison after me just playing one game. They do end up eventually evolving way past the point of being just "typical anime tropes" though.
As a huge fan of the Trails series, it probably goes without saying that I recommend this game. It's a great starting point for newcomers (I do HIGHLY recommend playing the Sky Trilogy first though) and an absolute must play for fans of the series. Despite my little rant on the characters, I still think the cast is great. I really grew attached to them as the game went on. Some of them are definitely bland at times, but I'm rather hopeful they will continue to grow as I play through the Cold Steel trilogy.
Final Score - ★★★★☆

After a year of using Steam Controller as main gamepad, I think I can write down a review here.
I have some mixed feelings about this beloved hardware of mine. There might be a steep learning curve but after that SC becomes the best controller option for many games.
+Great ergonomics. Like Ouya controller, the batteries are inside the grips and this is a good solution. Fits well in my hands.
+It works with every game and you'll play most of them out of the box with SC. If a game supports X360 gamepad, you'll probably play it with SC without problem.
+Highly customisable. You'll find dozens of layouts for games or create your own and share via Steam. Every little setting is at your service (But this is also something confusing. You might have to mess around with the settings a bit).
+The ability to use the SC as a KB/M from your sofa to control your PC is a pretty feature. You can type pretty fast without difficulty, but you need to have Steam Big Picture minimized in order to emulate keyboard.
+Better handling of FPS games than traditional gamepads. It's easier to aim with the right trackpad. Gyroscope based aim is a real fun. But it's still impossible to beat an average KB/M player. Might be good for single player games.
+Driving/racing games can utilise gyroscope as a steering wheel. After a good setting, it's really easy to control the car precisely.
+Fantastic for strategy/tycoon games while sitting on the couch and drinking beer.
+Build quality feels fine. After a year I've no problem with its physical condition, still good as new.
+Good price, especially during discounts like Black Friday.
+Never experienced a connection problem.
-The ABXY buttons are smaller and more shifted to the center than other controllers. Quirky at first.
-Lack of real d-pad. Left trackpad is also a d-pad but it's too big and not useful for 2D platformers like Sonic.
-Lack of right analogue stick. Actually this is not a big problem, but I've been constantly failing with FIFA. Skill moves with right trackpad is the real PITA. Stick with the old controllers you have and don't be a pace w***e. Play fair.
-Bumper buttons are somewhat big. It could've been better if the buttons have a little bit curve, I sometimes find them hard to press.
-A visible, accurate battery level indicator for the Big Picture mode or main Steam window next to the notification icon.
It has its own flaws but every gamer should try for a while because SC is still a game changer, quite useful and enjoyable product.
I'll give a 8/10. Would buy again.

BUT THE ORIGINAL SPACE RUN. It's a great game, and you can play it OFFLINE. This game is also pretty good WHEN YOU CAN LOG IN. I could log in during the beta no issues, no most of the time the servers are at capacity and I can't log in. Doesn't matter how good a game is if I can't play it. If these guys had an offline mode, so I could play it without having to rely on their terrible servers, then I'd probably give it a thumbs up. But for now THUMBS DOWN! Waste of money if you can't play it.
So about the game... it's a fun game when it works. Tower defense on a moving spaceship doing cargo runs between planets. Your radar gives you about a 20 second warning of what type of threat is coming, so you have time to put up the proper offense/defense, but you gotta hurry! There's offense, defense, special attacks, utility slots, tons of customization and ship designs, a wide variety of enemies. Challenging but fair gameplay, just make sure you have a good enough ship prior to doing certain runs, as this is open gameplay and some missions you can take that are just too tough until you upgrade more. So, the gameplay itself is fantastic. You get much of this in the original Space Run, which I give 9/10. Go play that, it's awesome.
The UI here is not as good as the gameplay. You can't hit the 'Esc' or other key to back up on menus. You have to find the little 'x' and click on it with your mouse, and depending on the screen, the 'x' can be in different places (though usually near the top right). This wouldn't be a big deal, but when you're at a base you'll be doing a lot of navigating and switching back and forth through menus. A simple 'Esc' to back out would literally double the speed of navigating these screens. So, UI isn't terrible here, but it's a bit annoying that such a simple feature isn't included, that would speed things up quite a bit. Also, there is a tutorial here, but it doesn't explain all the basics. There are tooltips, but not on all icons, so it takes a little trial and error to figure out how some features work.
The multiplayer aspect, selling/buying from other players, assigning or creating cargo runs so you or other players can take them, the open world (galaxy?) environment, all good ideas. Not as smooth a progressing as the original title, but good and interesting ideas nonetheless.
So to recap: gameplay itself is fantastic and challenging. Requires quick analysis and thinking. Lots of fun. UI is so-so. New gameplay features are interesting but a little rough. Still a plus. There's definitely a learning curve to this game, which will be mitigated partially by playing the first Space Run game, which had a much smoother progression and tutorial. Servers are TERRIBLE, and there's no offline mode. So, most of the time I can't play. This of course is a dealbreaker. Not sure if I can get a refund at this pont, but I'm certainly going to try. Wait a few months and then maybe give this a try, but get a refund ASAP if there are server problems.

Let's look at this game in an objective manner.
The animations look godawful.
The music feels like royalty-free shovelware 30 second loops.
The voice acting is just like 12 year olds trying to sound badass.
The UI doesn't work half of the time, if you want to drag an item from your inventory.
Half of the time, the hints are just "Heat up water" or something else, that's completely useless as a hint.
But, let's talk about the actual thing that people praise: The Story.
So, the first main twist was so damn predictable, that I'd even say that the game accidentally spoiled it and just didn't understand that they did it.
One of the arguments I've heard is "Oh, there's a lot of random killing in this game, which is awesome". That statement simply isn't true. The killing in the game, the only few times that it has a death, is just random and unnecessary. It's killing for killing's sake.
In the beginning of the game, you have a situation, where going in calmly and trying to defuse the situation would be the easiest. Instead, the character just starts shooting. It doesn't look cool, the music sounds awful, a gunshot to the head produces no blood and it just looks really terrible.
I truly cannot understand why people even like this game. It is a 8-year old's wet dream, sure. The maturity that the game has in terms of story and even the basic cohesion, is just as minimal as possible.
It's a "Ooh, pretty girl doesn't like us, now she does, since you did her a favour, that wouldn't in reality make them change their mind at all! Now, we'll touch butts and be happy!
Ooh, bad man comes! What a twist, he's a person that we knew! I guess you should've suspected him, since there was already so much evidence that it was impossible to think otherwise, but we'll still pretend that we're clever!
Now there's a confrontation! What a surprising turn of events!
You have three choices! None of them make any sense!
The end!"
This mess gets an overall 3/10. Strongly below average. Do not buy this game. If you're a point and click fan, then maybe buy it from a bundle, or when it's on a steep sale.

Like all niche games, CiM2 is hard to review because your enjoyment of the game will largely depend on if you like the premise. If the idea of laying down metro lines, bus lines and optimising a public transport system is fun to you - you'll probably like this game. If you complain that there's no option for single-track or quadruple-track metros in Cities: Skylines this game is also for you. On the whole, the game acheives this goal fine - if you want to build a public transport system, you'll enjoy CiM2.
There are some problems, however. The worst (and most baffiling) is the poor way that fares are managed. You have to set each fare for each transit type manually (i.e. bus, single-trip, multi-zone). There's at least twenty options to manually set, and no option for AI control - when the game decides that your city is going through a recession, you can esaily spend 5 (dull) minutes pressing sliders to set fares. You generally aim to keep the fares at the (game-determined) optimum, I don't see any reason why the AI can't do this. Likewise, there's no option to 'upgrade' or 'replace' a road, like in Cities: Skylines. Upgrading a corridor to include bus lanes is unrealistically expensive. The game's tutorial is also poor, much of it is intuitive if you've played a city builder previously. For everything else, you'll need online tutorials.
Without the DLC, the cities are all imaginary, although there's plenty of real cities avalable in the workshop now. The lack of an airport building is also a notable omission. Likewise, the addition of bus rapid transit systems and light rail (as opposed to trams) would have been nice - although it's possible to fudge a system in-game.
This is overall an enjoyable game if you want a city building game that's only about public transport. If this doesn't sound appealing to you, CiM2 is probably not for you.

There was a longer review here, but the steam servers ate it.
So cutting it down to this:
This game's tutorial is woefully deficient.
The game's AI is daft and does not use the game's systems to win. Instead it uses hard-coded resource bonuses to win.
So you can't even review their strategies and implement them yourself, because you don't have the resources to do so.
In all, after 30 hours, I still have no idea what I'm doing.
Don't buy this game unless you want to research game mechanics yourself, or have some uninitiated friends to play against.
It is also depressingly non-interactive with the actual map.
There's no 'Blow up their sun' or 'Create a new path around their warp point choke point'.
Which would be fine if the space combat was good, but the AI doesn't use tactics, there is a rock-paper-scissors guessing game tied to the combat, and you have no way of learning the intricacies of this system in game.
In all, I cannot recommend this game.
You should not need to research a game before you start having fun with it.

This game is inspired by Transport Tycoon, but
. It's more of a puzzle game than an economy simulation. There are predesigned levels with increasing size and complexity and a specific profit target. You have to create a road network consisting of different road types to connect the industry. Then you redistribute the limited workforce to optimize production. Houses need to be supplied with various goods, so they can get bigger and have place for more workers. This part works similar to the Anno series. The products not needed by houses have to be brought to export stations to make money. You don't have to buy anything, all that matters is the difference between income per second and upkeep per second.
The music is surprisingly good for that price range. Apropos price, it seems a bit too high compared to similar games on Steam, but the devs need to eat. If this game won't pay off they can't make any more games, so I see the money more as backing of a startup dev team.

The in-depth customization is a tad too extreme for most people I would say, but maybe over time I will start to learn to customize it on my own. Every button is broken down to customize from sensitivity, to use, input, etc.
For competitive games, ie: shooters nothing (yet) beats keyboard and mouse. I wouldn't rely on controllers for those types of games. But anything casual, platform, most 3rd-person, or most controller recommended will be played with this controller.
A few games have had minor issues with some menus working with the controller, usually older and well known problems due to new controller conversion. So sometimes you do have to get up and use the mouse a little(wow I sound fat).

Trails of Cold Steel is part of the Trails/Kiseki series, of which there is also Trails in the Sky on Steam. Cold Steel is set on the same continent and 1½ years after the events of Trails in the Sky, but in a different country and with a new main cast. Having played Trails in the Sky is not necessary (but highly recommended, they are awesome games after all!), it's fine starting with this one.
Port: Ported by Durante (you might know him as the one responsible for DSFix if you played Dark Souls) the game runs on a toaster and offers a wealth of graphical options. There is also a Turbo Mode, which allows you to speed up the game with the press of a button.
So, what about the game itself?
- GREAT story and writing. It starts slow and steady as you get to know the world and its inhabitants and events slowly and slowly escalate and escalate until it culminates into an explosion of awesomeness that blasts your jaw to the ground while you scream internally (and externally) like a little child and then it's over and GIVE ME THAT SECOND GAME NOW.
- Characters are pretty good. Not as good as the Trails in the Sky cast, but still pretty good. Some of them make a terrible first impression (looking at you Machias) but all of them get a ton of growth and character development over the course of the game.
- NPCs: If you take the time and talk with them (all of them offer new unique dialog after every little story progression), you learn a lot about the world, their lives, relationships, problems,... Many of them even have  their own little story arcs going on over the course of the game and at the end I knew the students of Thors Military Academy as good as the main cast.
- Combat is turn-based with a maximum of 4 active party members. It has elements of positioning and turn-order manipluation and the challenge level is pretty good.
- Music: It's a Falcom game, of course it has an awesome soundtrack :P
- Length: around 60-80 hours depending on how deliberate you are
- Voice Acting: No Japanese voices included, but there is a mod for that if you want. The english dub however is very good and has around 5000 more voiced lines than the japanese one.

Background: I loved Trails in the Sky I and II. III was more of a Dissidia Final Fantasy type game for my tastes.
TL;DR thoughts: Trails of Cold Steel I is very similar to Trails in the Sky, with more streamlined combat, and a number of 'school' and dungeon aspects that seem reminiscent of the Persona series. Overall, I really enjoyed it, though much like Trails in the Sky I and II...there was enough in Trails of Cold Steel I to suggest II is where the real meat and potatoes will come into play story-wise, so to speak.
More Detailed Thoughts
Combat: Very similar to Trails in the Sky, but increased CP generation allows it to be a bit more "fun". Also, you form links with party members, that allow for additional attacks, minor heals, etc.
Characters: Like Trails in the Sky, your party is made up of likeable characters. You can tell, right off the bat, that even the cold ones would soften up over time. The main character is a dude this time, but much like Estelle from Trails in the Sky, is the type of good-hearted individual you wouldn't be ashamed of introducing to your parents. There were moments in both Trails in the Sky and Trails of Cold Steel made me kind of wish for less...heartful characters, I guess, but there's something endearingly charming in that, in a world where I tend to want more Game of Thrones instead. The antagonists are largely underdeveloped, but I suspect it's much like the Trails in the Sky series in that it will get much more fleshed out in Trails of Cold Steel II.
Story: One could say it's a little too similar to Trails in the Sky in its design (it was pretty obvious where things were going, especially the "reveal" at the end if you had played Trails in the Sky), but I still enjoyed it. I think you can enjoy things that are familiar. Others may disagree. I will say that much like Trails in the Sky I's relationship to II, Trails of Cold Steel I really feels like it's going to end up being more of a prologue to the "real story" in Trails of Cold Steel II (and III). That's not to say it isn't good. But, I remember really enjoying Trails in the Sky I, and then when Trails in the Sky II finally became playable...realizing how much larger the story was intended to be. Now that I've seen that formula from this franchise, I think that was always in the back of my mind as I played through Trails of Cold Steel I.
Playability: It is one solid JRPG. As you can see, I played 58 hours for one playthrough. That might have a couple of hours of pad time for when I took a break for dinner, etc, without turning it off, but that's still old school length of play. And, I definitely missed things, as I hadn't realized there were quests that don't have quest markers; you have to either talk to everyone at least 2-3 times to find them (which I didn't), or use a guide off the internet. I never look at guides on a first playthrough, hence me missing them.
There's also a new game+ that allows you to carry various things over. If you're a completionist, you'll have to do a number of new game+s to complete everything. I'm not really a completionist. I did carry over the ability to see all character member bonding moments (by default, you are limited on that front, so you'll miss a good chunk of them in one playthrough), and will likely play this again in new game+ when (hopefully) Trails of Cold Steel II is close to release as a refresher.
Text/voice: There's a TON of text in this game. Which, if you've played the Trails in the Sky series, shouldn't come as a surprise. There's some voice acting. It's interesting to watch as it starts off with mostly voice acting, and how it get's more sparse as the game proceeds. It's pretty normal voice acting for a JRPG that isn't Final Fantasy 12. :D
Conclusion: I already gave it in the TL;DR section at the top. :)

Surprisingly great point and click with super presentation style and well developed story, spiced up with mystery and twists.
The game is presented in a fairly rare mix of comic-styled visuals and animations, that work flawlessly. They even used the music of the game to further strenghten the connection between them, as at a point the comics-like panels disappear to the rhythm of the music. The placement of panels, the way of animation is really well done, easy to see that the game's final form was preceded with serious planning  Furthermore, in some cutscenes it's using effects typical from movies: everything going black but the main characters, special cuts, closeups, changing camera positions.
The story itself is to simply put, crazy. In the first area you hear about a murderer, and during the gameplay you control two characters. In the second scene you control a new character, and the previously used characters are NPCs, main characters in the plot, and you dwelve more into the investigation. The investigation is filled with the secret, the occult, memory loss, mindgames, hidden items and genuine confusion and surpising new informations.
The way of presentation really improves on the otherwise solid gameplay good characters, making it into an even more appealing point and click story that's not lacking humour, mystery, and quite some violence as well. I definitely recommend this title, as this is the wildest point and click I've played - while there is a solid chain of events from the start to the end, it's insane what a wild twist a game tooks every now and then.

Naruto Shippuden Ultimate Ninja Storm 4
Developer: Cyberconnect 2
Publisher; Bandai Namco
Tl:DR This game is an overall treat to play and very easy to get in to. Play this game with a controller and make sure your PC can atleast run this game at 30fps, Overall 8/10
Full Review:
Introduction:
This game is the 4th Installment in the Long Running Ultimate Ninja Storm Series of Naruto Games.This time around every character, and each of their respective iterations, are playable. Play through where Ultimate Ninja Storm 3 left off and fight against, Madara, Obito, and Kaguya, While going through the events of the Anime and Manga. So what does this game have to offer? A surprising Amount.
Story: Well the story does take place right after Storm 3 ended, and honestly, this is a Nice retelling of the material. Some minor changes in the story but nothing extremely large. Overall 9/10
Gameplay: The fighting in this game feels great, the gameplay is nice and fluid and simplistic. Though i feel like this game is too simplistic. There really is only one combo and thats Y B, YY B or BB Y with a lot of Mashing the B Button. This issue isn't really that big especially since the roster on this game is large. Overall 7/10
Content/Replay Ability: Like I said before, there are Tons of characters in this game by itself. It is fun to play each character which is good for the number of characters in there. Almost every chracter has alternate looks and abilities. This game Spans every generation of Naruto. Part 1 Naruto all the way to Boruto which is DLC. There even is online, but I never really played it. Overall 9/10
PC optimization/ PC port: Storm 4 was definitely ported from the consoles. First I STRONGLY RECOMMEND that you use a Controller. Second make sure your PC can handle this game, This game is Not too difficult to run but do not try this game if you do not have a PC that can keep this game running atleast at 30fps. The Reason for this is because the Framerate is Tied to the Time in game. So if you run the game with a lower powered PC be prepared to adjust setting. also please to not use a Keyboard and make sure you have a controller. I had an old Logitech controller that did not work with this game so please make sure it is newer. Overall 3/10
Enjoyment Factor/ Final Score: Storm 4 can be a pain to run correctly. But once it works, it works great. The Story will take you about roughly 18-20 if you do not skip the Cutscenes. Storm 4 was easy to get into and lots of fun watching the battle unfold. I find myself coming back just to create games with characters I want to see fight and play to see who is stronger. Optimization aside, Storm 4 is a great game. If you are planning on Buying this game wait for a sale. Overall: 8/10,
If you like NARUTO and 3D fighting games, then you really should buy this. It's really fun and has local multiplayer, it's easy to get into/good at and it can be relaxing.

Deus Ex: Human Revolution is not only a worthy successor to the first Deus Ex, but does it better in my opinion. This addition to Deus Ex focuses on conspiracies between corporations, enacting violent seizures of patents and top secret technologies by staging a terror attack on Sarif Industries, a top provider for the US Defense Department. Adam Jensen is initially responding to the terror threat on his company's labs and is determined to save lives and neutralize the threat. Jensen's past in a New Mexican Police Department which forced him to see the violence and danger that augmented people are capable of performing draws an interesting dichotomy when Jensen himself is very nearly killed in the attack, his life saving procedure being the removal of all appendages and being constructed into an Augmented being.
Jensen is driven into the conspiracy between a Chinese medical corporation and an American defense contractor when he investigates his girlfriend's death in the terror act and realizes she and several other employees were not killed, but kidnapped.
The DLC for Deus Ex is by far the best DLC I have played and was well worth the money. It dives into the depths of Private Military Contractors, their crimes against humanity, and what horrors they are capable of carrying out in the interest of profitability and frightening scientific progress. I recommend this game to everyone and anyone.
I have precisely 121 hours on the original, non director's cut edition, and I recommend getting the new one for it's improved boss fights and the automatic inclusion of the DLC. The only negative about this game is the attempt at dehumanizing augmented human being and trying to make a social commentary about race relations. It didn't work, I don't care about it, and frankly it felt like background noise.

A worthy successor to the original Deus Ex!
It keeps all of the elements that made the original great, while modernizing it as a whole. The game focuses heavily on allowing the player to choose how they want to approach any given situation. Will you sneak around killing the guards one by one? Or maybe use non lethal means? Or perhaps you just want to go loud and blast your way through with grenades and a machine gun? All that stuff is there, along with all the smaller choices the original game had. You might upgrade your hacking skills and use that to get through a door and into a room, or perhaps you upgrade your strength, allowing you to move a heavy vending machine in order to reach a vent that lets you get into that same room. You can always find an alternate way to approach a situation.
A must play for anyone. The Director's Cut integrates the DLC into the core game, and it's a pretty fun few hours, so that's great too.

"Deus Ex: Human Revolution - Director's Cut" is an excellent game.  It might not be quite as philosophically deep as the original "Deus Ex," but it's close enough.  The story, voice acting, and gameplay are all really good and, in good Deus Ex fashion, almost everything can be done via multiple paths, methods, or styles.  It took me 82.4 hours to complete the game with 100% Achievements, so the price/hour ratio is tremendous.
Even though the "Director's Cut" edition supposedly "fixed" the Boss fights, they (and the fight to save Malik) are still my biggest complaint (as they were in the original version).  Yes, you can now sneak around and find alternate ways to beat the bosses.  But, they're still furious, frenzied fights where the boss HAS to die.  That's very jarring when all the game play in between is slow, calm, and deliberate stealth/pacifist stuff.
My next biggest complaint regards the game-wide Achievements:  you can fail those at any point and not find out about it until you've completed the whole game (see the 82.4 hours number, above) and the Achievement fails to pop.  There's no recourse but to replay the whole thing and hope you don't make the same mistake twice.  Probably the worst offender of those Achievements is the "Pacifist" one (don't kill anyone).  This is still a problem from the original "Human Revolution."  Basically, you can use non-lethal take-downs throughout the game, confirm that those people are merely unconscious and not dead, and still fail the Achievement because somewhere, somehow, one of your victims died long after you left the scene.  It happened to me in the original "Human Revolution," and almost happened again here.  But, this time, I happened to walk past their supposedly slumbering bodies and noticed that they were dead instead of unconscious.  Luckily, it only took me a short time to redo that area and stash their bodies in a better spot.
Still, a darn fun, engrossing, well-done game.  Recommended.

Having bought the HexCells series, I was interested in this game to see if this idea would work in a classic 4-directional format (like Minesweeper).
I'm not sure whether it was the puzzles created, or the concept as a square set-up, but I didn't enjoy this game as much as I did HexCells. There is an adjustment for people who have the diagonal HexCells mindset, but after acclimating to squares, it just didn't have the same spark. The complexity in what you have to account for is traded in for sometimes harder logic, making SquareCells seem less rewarding when solving a puzzle, compared to HexCells.
One thing that threw me through a loop initially was that the representations of numbers changes between HexCells and SquareCells: Numbers in brackets such as [3] now represent scattered numbers, where in HexCells, that representation would be number of square in a row. The focus also changes from ignoring the "mines" to marking them in the style of Minesweeper. Additionally, several of the mechanics that made HexCells fairly unique (such as revealed tiles giving clues to surrounding tiles), were not included here, presumably due to the inability to logically introduce them.
It's not a bad game in itself, but it doesn't meet par with what puzzle games like this should meet. I would argue HexCells is not only a more unique concept, but works much better in the style that the developer created, compared to having to throw away a lot of the charm to fit the Minesweeper mould.

Another pure logic (no guesses necessary) puzzler, by the same developer as the superb Hexcells series.
A slightly different puzzle mechanic, but just as satisfying to solve.  Two thumbs up!  I want more!
As with the first Hexcells release, the User Interface isn't as helpful as I'd like, but it's always possible to work the math backwards for the missing critical hint.  (The game tells you how many tiles *remain* to be removed, but not how many total need to be removed except before your first move, and it never tells directly how many tiles need to be marked, either the total or remaining count.  Do yourself a favor, and write down the total number to be removed when you start the later puzzles, so you can work out the corresponding number of total tiles to be marked.  If you're like me, and can only grab brief times to play, solving the later puzzles can stretch over days, and the original numbers are quickly forgotten if not written down.)

Don't let the Mixed  / Negative Reviews fool you.
If you liked the first Space Run, you will love this iteration of the gameplay.
If you want a "tactical pause" in what is essentially a time management tower defense game, then this may not be the game for you.  The devs designed this game around the management of your resources in the moment. While levels are generally static from what I've seen, it rewards players that can think quickly on their feet, or players that act on the experience of playing the level previously. There are some people that want a tactical pause option most likelye because they believe it will save them time so they don't have to play the level again. But what these players don't realize is that a tactical pause option will actually make the game easier and lessen the challenge that keeps the game interesting.
On Server Stability: The game seems to be a bit more popular that the devs originalliy expected. Why? Well, the servers are having load issues which means the server they purchased for the multiplayer contracts could not handle the amount of requests it was getting. The Devs have been hard at work if you go in the forums and have provided support over the weekend over the server issues. Give it a week and I'm sure the game will be a lot more stable when it comes to internet related connectivity.
On actual gamplay: This game, like I said earlier, is essentially a time management tower defense game. You have a modular ship which you can alter at space ports and purchase designs. Each module can have weapons, support modules, engines, or shields built on them. In comparison to the previous game, this game is more varied in what each weapon does. Each module also has a s pecial ability that can be triggered using tactical points such as a concentrated shot, a missile barrage, instant shielding, instant repair, changing arc of fire, to name a few.
Each match consists of your ship flying l inearly in a straight line which will be assailed by enemy ships, astroids, alien fauna, and sometimes bosses. Your ship starts with nothing but its engine and some in game currency which is used to build each module. However, to maximize your match, you have to reach the end at faster speeds for full XP bonus. But moving faster also causes enemies to spawn faster...
I am still in the early game, a single system out of 4 that are eventually available. Each system has maybe 8-10 planets but a lot more matches due to the travel lanes you fly in between them.
I have/had fun playing this game and I will play more. I have suffered no crashes myself thus far or bugs really. But my computer is a legit gaming desktop so I don't know what to tell those that are having issues. The devs are responsive and appear to want to continue supporting the game. I say give this game a chance.

A solid strategy offering by Longbow Games, greatly improving on their already solid titles, Hegemony Greece and Rome. I've played around 10 hours of the early access version, and I really enjoyed it. For those of you unfamiliar with the Hegemony series, supply plays a huge role in these games. Units and cities all need to be properly supplied in order to function, so raiding an enemy or being raided yourself can be a huge factor in the success or failure of your empire. You start small, and gradually complete objectives and start to expand. There is a bit of diplomacy, but nothing earth shattering in that department. Units have formations, can be flanked, upgraded with new skills and led by generals, further increasing their traits. Cities also can be upgraded, as well as resource producing landmarks, increasing their output or defense from raids.
The map is huge and can be zoomed out to get a "tabletop view of the battlefield". The graphics have been greatly improved upon, with markets having chickens running around, fish swimming the seas, birds flying overhead, people in the cities and birds of prey circling battlefields for fresh corpses. Really enjoyed just checking out the scenery. Also, when you upgrade a cities walls, you see the city grow on the map, which is pretty cool.
The #1 factor in a good strategy game is a competitive AI, and I found the AI in this game to be pretty good. Enemy units would try to flank me, and some of the scripted raids were really challenging to overcome. A big improvement from previous games.
Finally, the potential of this game is huge. With Workshop enabled at launch who knows what some talented modder could come up with. Maybe a DLC of the Punic Wars, with Hannibal and his elephants crossing the alps. Really hoping this game does well and we see some good mods. Anyway, give it a try, you won't be dissapointed.

This game is an (indirect) sequel to the already published Trails in the Sky trilogy. While the Trails of Cold Steel trilogy is intended as part of a series (the middle elements of the series, known as Ao No Kiseki and Zero No Kiseki are, unfortunately,  not yet translated to English), it functions quite well as a standalone tale - the wider series references are so sporadic you can just look them up on various trivia websites if you want to stay up to date.
As to the mechanics - this is a tactical, turn based RPG with a very strong emphasis on story driven gameplay. Basically, the game is split into dungeon crawling segments and story segments. The story might strike you as the typical JRPG "school-driven character development cliche", but it's far from that. The game generally tends to subvert and play with many of the traditional JRPG cliches, which is one of its strongest points.
The story and characters are one of the strongest points not only of the this game, but of the entire Trails series. The main story is complex, yet consistent, with enough subplots to get you hooked, but not enough to make you feel that it's all random. The plot twists are clever and not really that predictable, which makes the storyline all the more appealing.
As for the combat part of the game, the game does quite well to avoid unnecessary grind - killing just the quest-related monsters on the way is mostly enough to level up your characters to get proper EXP and gear. I would say that for JRPG games, this game definitely ranks in the lower part of the spectrum in terms of grinding. The tactical battles are quite interesting, not being your typical, static JRPG combat with just the selection of different actions - positioning also plays a role, making it more varied and more similar to western RPGs in that respect. Characters choose from a range of standard attacks, magic (arts) and special attacks, with the magic fully customizable due to the Quartz system (carried over with minor changes from previous Trails games). Boss battles are usually quite challenging, although the normal difficulty is probably a bit too easy for the RPG veterans out there - if you want a real challenge, it is recommended that you play at least on Hard.
As with the Trails in the Sky series, I strongly recommend this game to any RPG fans, not just the JRPG fans out there. In fact, the Trails series are the games that actually got me into JRPGs in the first place. This game does not have the marketing of the huge Namco titles, but I enjoyed it far more than I did many of the AAA productions.

This is the single hardware purchase I regret the most.  I have wasted hours upon hours trying to get it to work with things, often to no avail; I've installed countless third-party pieces of software just to try and get it to serve what ought to be its most basic functions.
The Steam Controller is designed from the ground up for users who intend to use it from the couch, playing nothing but Steam games, with no keyboard or mouse.  You should
consider buying it if this is your primary use case - it is heavily designed around this, at the cost of core functionality that even the most basic XInput gamepad (many costing a fifth of its price) handle far better.
Most significantly, the Steam controller will not operate as a gamepad if Steam is not running - instead, it bafflingly defaults to providing keyboard input, with no way to override this.  This core flaw is at the root of many of the gamepad's most infuriating failures.  Even with Steam running, you will often have to struggle to get it to function with non-Steam programs, especially ones designed with XInput in mind.  It usually handles AAA software, but more obscure freeware and things along those lines will make it choke.
On top of this, Steam now offers customization (its core selling point) for all other controllers anyway.
Additionally, much of its functionality is tied to Big Picture mode (again, Valve was frantically trying to push "couch Steam" when they made it, and did so at the expense of basic functionality.)  Valve has slowly improved on this, but even today you will often be forced to use Big Picture mode to configure it or to get it working with some games.  If you don't like Big Picture mode, the Steam controller is not for you.
Basically, this is a controller aimed at one specific demographic and one specific use-case - couch gamers running Steam in Big Picture mode and using Steam as a console.  Even then, other controllers will now do that just as well or better; but you could at least consider the Steam Controller if that's what you want.
Anyone else should stay far, far away.  This is a terrible product that was designed more with an eye towards marketing Big Picture and Steam-as-a-console couch gaming than
, and it shows.  It focused too much on pointless gimmicks (like serving as a keyboard-substitute) without considering its core functionality as a controller.
I really didn't want to write this review (I had high hopes for the Steam controller when it was first announced, and kept hoping Valve would fix these issues with updates), but after years of updates that have failed to resolve its core problem of
, I feel I have to warn off other people who might be considering buying it.  Valve is not going to fix it.
It is not a good controller.  It is not a good purchase.  Stay away.

NEGATIVES -

With WASD unavailable for movement, you're forced to use the arrow keys to navigate and the mouse to turn which wouldn't be a major problem if you didn't also have to use E and Q. Do me a favour, pop one hand on your arrow keys then one on your mouse. Now try and reach either E or Q. What's even worse is that Q is sprint, rendering it effectively useless unless you can jog on the spot. Which you can't.
The plot is a mess, the characters are irritating and the multiplayer is one of the most baffling looking things you will lay eyes upon in some time. Maybe the only decent thing I can say about it is that for £0.79, you can experience the unintentional hilarity of the Hat Mannequin Death House, where limbless wooden horrors bob for apples, kick trash bags around and throw hammers at you with their mouths.

Alltynex Second is the first chapter in "The Tale of Alltynex", the game is also a remake of the original FM TOWN: ALLTYNEX, just bought from the 2017 Steam Summer Sales and fell in love with it. Here some pros and cons for the game:
The pros:
+ Simple story-lines.
+ The graphic is good.
+ Very well-level designs as well as using camera angle to make the game more dynamic. Nice visual effects.
+ Amazing soundtracks that fit the atmosphere through out entire game.
+ Responsive control scheme. Still recommend to play with a controller.
+ Very smooth transformation between 2 forms: Fighter and Armor mode, each form has a main and a sub weapon, make that 4 weapons in your arsenal. The core gameplay as well as the scoring system will lie within these 4 weapons.
+ The 3 difficulties are very balance, from Easy to Hard. Adding the last secret difficulty will make the game a true test of skills.
+ The Replay Section will let you watch your journey in a dynamic way. Trust me, if you can play the hardest difficulty with zero death, your replay will be epic.
+ The game is very optimized, runs smoothly with constant 60 FPS.
The cons:
- The camera angle of some points of the stages will sometimes put you in dangerous situations.
Overall, this is a fun and challenging game with a few tweak to the gameplay. The game and the rest of the triology are also known for rich story-telling, but this is just first chapter of that story. Recommend those who want to seek for challenges and even for beginners of this genre. Want to hear a robotic voice says "CHAIN BONUS" everytime you make combos. :)). Wait the series for sales, worth it.
_Final score: 9/10.

After about a year of using this controller, I have several impressions.  It is an amazing piece of hardware, and many new features have been added over time to make it a lot more useful.
Here are the most important things to me:
1: It works as a fully-functional keyboard and mouse.  I use a steam link primarily for desktop mirroring on my tv, and it is nice being able to watch hulu/netflix/downloaded content without having to use a keyboard.
2: I can set different profiles for different activities, e.g. web surfing, spotify, WASD shooters, photoshop; I can also program button combos to switch presets.
3: I love the trackpad, which some people hate.  It gives me way better accuracy for shooters, and I like how it feels as a mouse, especially the way the traction works.
I used to use joystick mapper programs to do the same thing, but the whole experience is way more fluid through the steam client.  It's crazy how much it can do, the fact it saves your presets inside the controller, and how much control I have over every parameter.
Highly recommended!

However, I bought the game to find I could run the game at high settings on constant 60fps. It's smooth gameplay and easy to learn combat system enables you to really enjoy the game rather than tr harding just to be able to get over its learning curve.

The campaign is enjoyable filled with pretty much none-stop action and when you aren't ripping demons in half you can be searching for secrets to upgrade your Praetor suit or find cool little items like toys of your character. One of my issues was that it felt like there wasn't enough boss battles and there is only really one fairly difficult one, which is the final boss.
The perk system is easy to use and th weapon upgrade system is great, including the fact that you can hold a key to change your mod in seconds just for a situation it may require.
The multiplayer is one of the best I've played in a FPS. Its chaotic style and a range of fun game modes make it fairly addicting. You can play as a grenadier blowing everything in sight up with a rocket launcher just to switch the a grenade launcher when your done. There is a huge amount of weapon, rune and demon combinations to choose from, each changing the way you play. There is nothing more satisfying in the multiplayer than going on a huge killstreak with the epic announcer voice saying what killstreak your own whilst rampaging as one of the 6-7 demons.
It is definately worth every penny. Highly recommended.

It is unfortunate, and personally, I enjoy the Serious Sam series a lot. A LOT.
but alas, this is NOT a true serious sam game. this is a VERY SHORT knock-off.
this, my friends, is a joke. even compared to Serious Sam "the first encounter", or worse yet, "serious sam 2", Serious sam the random encounter is a flop. definitely NOT worth over a dollar. I beat the game in roughly an hour. but, in keeping with my professionalism-review-code, I will now proceed to dole out pros and cons.
WARNING: my review has some spoilers. fair warning has been given.
Pros:
- It has very low req. specs to run. Your computer could very well be several years outdated, and still run it just fine.
- amusing dialogue, with references and fun character.
- an okay number of iconic guns.
- amusing gameplay style makes fun of the old random encounters of the old JRPGs.
- Colorful graphics. Granted, there are people out there who hate any graphical level that is any less detailed then, say, DOOM 4. but personally, I enjoyed the old retro-gaming look.
Cons:
- Very short, you can beat it in an hour, even if you DO loot every possible crate on the way.
- some of the weapons are unbalanced. the cannon is too powerful, the rocket launcher is too weak, etc....
- very linear. they give you the illusion of there being multipule paths to choose from, but such is not the case.
- uninteresting bosses. for example, using two grenade launchers and one serious damage powerup, I killed the final boss in a single shot. and the final boss didn't have some sort of "ultimate mode" or something? And that wasn't even mental, either, which brings me to my next point.
- too much emphasis on a character that never appears. Mental. All throughout the game, Serious Sam and his pals keep talking about killing Mental.....but Mental wasn't even the final boss!!! Mental makes NO appearences WHATSOEVER. this is actually quite annoying, and is one of the main downsides of the Serious Sam series as a whole.
- random weird characters. I mean, who ARE these two guys that follow Sam? Some random afro dude and some random cowboy. they don't get their own background stories? memorable NAMES?? Original weapons? (eg. Excalibur for king arthur, Mining lazer for Glitch, A knife for Jeff the killer, etc.) These two feel less like allies on the field, and more like two extra guns.
- Fails to capture the feel of Serious Sam. Serious Sam may be a bit hardcore about destruction, but he's not an idiot. this game portrays him as being a fool who only cares about shooting mental, and hates puzzles. It makes him look like a musclebound pretty-boy with no head on his shoulders. this is NOT how Serious Sam should be. Serious Sam is sarcastic, makes puns, is fearless, and will often stop in mid battle to give a witty one-liner, like "Alien bulls? that's a lot of bull. *kills it* There. 100% alien beef." He's also quite the ladies-man, as well. and somewhat....shall we say....'rougueish', from time to time.
- Where's the C-4 charges? and the quadgun? and the buzzsaw-gun? or even the plasma pistol! WHERE ARE THEY??? It's sad how they didn't put those awesome guns in the game...
- The animations are 'passable'. but not very good at all. Personally, I enjoy retro-appearences, but just because it's retro doesn't mean the animations have to be so TERRIBLE. I mean, look at 'Gone Home', or 'Lone Survivor'. those retro-style games were both made by a SINGLE GUY EACH, and yet their animations were surprisingly good.
- Lack of depth. even the 3rd serious sam game had sufficient puzzles to prevent yer brain from going numb from all the raw combat, but this game's terrible excuse for puzzles wouldn't even float in a Pokemon game. Seriously.
So yes, on with the final Verdict. I give this game a 4/10. Slightly below average. I say this because with all it's flaws, it was still an okay way to kill time. it was okay, going through endless mode for a little while. I've actually seen worse games that had higher expectations. still, that's no excuse to make a shoddy game. this game is currently being sold at a price of exactly $4.99, but it's only WORTH about....eh, I'd say $1.99, to be fair.

Serious Sam: The Random Encounter is a short combination of jRPG with a shooter. It's one of the Indie line games based on Serious Sam franchise, being made by somebody else aside from Croteam. In this case it was developed by Vlambeer and came out in 2011.
And oh boy, is it a mess from technical standpoint. So much bugs.
Windows 8 users will want to check Steam guides, there is one that has a link to a patch. Otherwise it will start crashing every few minutes.
Mind it, even after patch it still can randomly crash or glitch up. And it will not save your progress, only when you quit to main menu, so I recommend you to do it at the start of every level.
And then there is a bug on final level where if you get game over to final boss at 3-3 world then you will be stuck in infinite loop of game over. And quitting during this loop will not save your progress. So make sure to quit to main menu before the fight.
And then the infinite mode you unlock fails to reset all values properly when started so if you choose to play it right after beating the campaign then it will glitch up after the first battle.
Yep, as you see, this game is already quite dangerous to mess around. It's just not serious enough.
And if we talk about game then there is a single word that can descripe it: novelty.
It really has a nice idea of having shooter combined with jRPG system only to not develop it any deeper or have any good replayability. I mean, it's very short and maps feel somehow too linear and small as well. There isn't much left to be seen after you beat it. And it could be better.
I mean, art is real nice, music is fine, presenation is cheapy and plot is too much of a joke. And gameplay is weird. Most people compare battles to bullethell where it's impossible to avoid everything. To be honest, taking hits is totally okay in jRPG, the point is to survive. There is a reason why you always start with 100% health in each battle no matter how damaged you was in previous battle and it's totally okay as long as at least somebody survives.
And yea, each battle goes like this: a horde of enemies spawn in and camera lets you see what this wave looks like. Then every five seconds you set aim, or order to swap weapon, or to use items. And then after giving orders you get to control vertical position of a party, to minimize damage. It's pretty good, you will learn what combination work the best. But near the end of a game it starts to throw battles that might be even impossible. To be honest, the final level is where you pretty much have to use all the items you hoarded up from before, so it's still possible to beat game easily on second walkthrough by knowing this. Still, could be better.
Oh, and there is overworld. Which is small and not much. And not much randomization. There is no leveling. Well, you do have a meter that fills up after each battle, but it just gives you random item or weapon. And in later levels the grinding is not worth it. Just do it in early level.
And infinite mode that you unlock after beating the game is really cheap. Not worth talking about. Move forward in corridor overworld and get battle.
But yea, it's just some short game and don't forget how buggy this is! But I still think that it works, as part of Serious Sam Indie series and as a novelty, which still holds up as I didn't get to play any other game like this one. But yes, weak weak weak thumbs up. It's very cool idea, but too buggy and short.
EDIT: Changed from positive to negative. You know what, as much as I try to get positive fun out of games, this one is too broken to tolerate glitches and must be shamed on until patched.
