Starting off I will say that I love this game. A team based, strategic, first person shooter. That would be the best way of classifying this game. The customization of mech's is very fun and the gameplay takes A little more thinking than the "run and gun" games we see flooding the market these days. I also would encourage anyone who likes warthunder or world of tanks to give this game A try as the mechanics are very similar. Some Downsides to this game are that while it is free to play and nearly all mechs can be bought with in game currency the customization will take some time to get down. Thankfully they include trial mechs that change weekly to help you find your perfect killing machine. Second is that meta builds (mechs designs built to abuse imbalances in the game) are rampant in the community. There is A huge learning curve from controls and tactics to mech building. Thankfully, unless you're in competitive gameplay there plenty of casual players to lessen the skill difference. All in all I think the pros heavily outweigh the cons and would recommend this game to everyone who will brave the battlefields of MWO.

MWO used to be a mediocre game at the release, with poor optimisation and meh balance. The devs proved to learn and improve and in today's state MWO is a pretty polished product with much better balance (not an easy feat for something with such a customizability). Almost every mech can be built with 2-3 different very good builds plus 2-3 that are also viable. So you're not as limited as in WoT, where having a 2 viable builds per tank as rare sight. Quirk balancing works nicely and some of the worse mechs were literally saved this way (Dragon for instance) Gameplay is solid, maps vary a lot and newer ones add some verticality, which fun and fresh. Mechs look great (mostly) and do feel just right.
There is one definite drawback which is the game engine. which is the cause that the game may (or may not) run slower and look less nice than rival session shooters.
Game is akin to WoT in many aspects, with a bit of extra complexity and customizability. Unlike now numerous WoT clones there is no linear progression. You can just buy any mech you like, equip it with any stuff you like and start fighting. New players get a massive C-bill bonuses for the first 25 matches which is an equivalent to 2 most expensive mechs or 2 of average price ones fully upgraded.
There are two major factions: Inner Sphere and Clans (plus Mercenaries/Freelancers). Joining one doesn't actually limit you to use only the faction-appropriate tech, but all the equipment is interchangable beetween all the mechs of the same faction.
The only things you need to pay real money for are newest, just released mechs. These are usually act as sidegrades to currently available ones and some people even complain that the new stuff is worse and is in need of some buffs (Thanatos, Osiris). Cosmetics and slots for your mechs (mech bays) can be earned from the events or bought for MCs which also could be earned by playing the events. So, unless you want too look awesome and NOW, there's no real need to pay. Which is a good true F2P model. The grind is pretty non-existent compared to other F2P games, as you can get almost anything in a couple of evenings (compared to the months you need to get to lvl X in WoT or weeks needed to get some prime stuff in Warframe).

A must have for nonogram/picross lovers! And definitely recommended for puzzle lovers in general.
This game adds some very interesting new elements to the traditional nonogram formula, but retains the same simpleness in the way the rules work. Several levels in I was starting to feel that familiar sense where the tricks to making the most out of each clue start to click!
I was a little afraid that 36 puzzles wouldn't be enough, but the more challenging ones can sometimes take a while to figure out. I'm about 2/3 through with the game and definitely feel like I got my money's worth!
It's very beautifully presented and the sound effects are very charming, although I wish the music and sound effects options were separate.
My only real gripe about the game is that I wish the puzzle solutions made pictures instead of just random jumbles of pixels. There were a small handful that made nice geometric patterns, but the majority of them were just pixelated noise.
It's also a minor inconvenience that one misclear of a tile that shouldn't be cleared will cost you a 3-star rating. Personally, I prefer not being told I messed up immediately and just letting me know when I get the correct solution.
Pros:
- Adds to the nonogram style puzzle in a creative, but in a easy to understand way
- Looks and sounds great
- Challenging puzzles
Cons:
- Have to exit all the way to the main menu to toggle sound or left vs right click controls
- Veteran nonogram solvers may be disappointed by the lack of solutions that make pictures.
- Easy to accidentally click the wrong button and lose a 3-star rating
Edit now that I've finished the game:
I'm not sure if I'm just not good enough or if it's really true, but I'm pretty sure that the later levels require a little bit of guesswork (not a lot, I only had to guess on maybe 3 or 4 of them). I like nonograms/picross because you can make educated guesses based on what the picture might turn out to be but since the patterns here are mostly random it's kind of just a shot in the dark.
This wouldn't be so much of a problem if we could mark cells as possible fills/empties, or if the game didn't immediately disqualify you for a 3-star rating for making one mistake.

Though it may be short, this dark fantasy point-and-click is a must-buy!  The quasi-cel shaded characters, in true Pendulo tradition, are expertly crafted.  The backgrounds look great, running the gamut from super-detailed (the antique book shop) to impressionistic (the mystical Himalayan temple), depending on the mood.  The in-game animations are brief and subtle, full of rapid cuts, dramatic freeze frames, and often taking place within comic book panels.  Just reading this, you may think that this animation style sounds cheap -- in actuality it makes the game feel like an electric combo of thriller film and fast-paced graphic novel.  The narrative involves dark magic, torture, serial killers and a centuries-old Satanic cult.  While all of these elements have been used countless times before,
handles them with real style, assembling them into a highly engaging story with some very unique twists (this coming from a guy who has read a lot of fiction about this type of thing).  The puzzles may be simpler than in some of the past Pendulo games, but they aren't exactly easy unless you turn lousy cheater and invoke the hint feature.  DON'T INVOKE THE HINT FEATURE!  The game will last longer and be far more satisfying if you don't!
For my money, this game is definitely worth the full price.  If you are still on the fence about it, it's constantly on sale for 4 bucks or less, and that is a true steal for what you are getting.

Like many of those who have recently purchased this game, I bought it as part of the recent sale.  It is one of the more difficult games for me to reach a decision about.
First of all, the tutorial for the game is terrible.  If it were not for the user created guides available on Steam, the game would not have held my interest very long in spite of its positive features.
Endless Space is very like one of the mods for Civilization IV.  Endless Space takes things much further that the mod, as you would expect.
The game itself is a plethora of options.  Rather than the simplistic ship building found in so many civ builders, this one lets you design your ships with fairly complete flexibilty.  The down side is, of course, the inadequate tutorial.  If it were not for the gamer created guides, you will find it difficult to know if you are actually doing anything useful.  One you have things figured out, you can have as much fun with ship design as you want.  My current ships look rather like the Hydrans from Star Fleet Battles, once I advance to the tech that lets me arm corvettes with bombers.
When you engage in space battles, again you have a variety of options ranging from abstract to a low level tactical combat view (I haven't used it - so no opinion).  In between the two, you can set basic target and formation.
The game comes with a variety of races, but again it shines in the added touch of allowing you to create your own customized race.
In addition to the normal difficulty level, Endless Space also allows you to select from a menu of the common types of galaxies.  I have only tried some of the options, but so far they seem to add additional grades of difficulty.
When playing the game, the various star systems and planets change as you terraform and build, which I found one of those things that help the game from becoming completely tedious as your turn counter goes up.
There are a two things about Endless Space that I don't like, and they are the reasons that it is difficult for me to recommend the game.   I have already mentioned the inadequate tutorial.  Other problems are more difficult to quantify.  The basic complaint that I have is that Endless Space gets tedious late in the game.  I find that sometime after turn 200 I invariably get to the point where I am pretty sure that I will win the game (or not) and there is nothing to keep me pressing "enter" at the end of every turn.

MAC USERS - Do not purchase.
The game is no longer running on MAC OSX.  The Developer forums have been posted upon, plenty of people reporting the same issue as a crash to desktop without any error message moments after loading the game.
They have not given any response and it is not looking like they will.  Avoid purchasing.
This game does not work in Windows 10... Do not buy this game it will not work.

A proper FPS. The "actual" GOTY 2016 for those that could look past the hype train.
Amazing dynamic soundtrack that is well paced, Mick Gordon nailed it. It is a great blend of modern and retro gameplay elements.
Gunplay is very satisfying, almost all weapons fill a niche AI is remarkably good and aggressive. Scenery is pretty damn nice with secrets spread through the levels, in the style of classic DooM.
Arcade mode and MP extends the potential fun time.
DEFINITELY RECOMMENDED, GET IT IF YOU HAVEN'T ALREADY. Gameplay vids don't do it justice, step up and get shooting yourself!
Now, on to the criticism part.
Here are the "issues" that don't really matter much:
Snapmap is both good and bad. It is good because most modern shooters don't give you even that much opportunity to make your maps. It is bad because the maps will be limited in complexity, compared to DooM II wads, both in monster count and architecture. It's nice and fun, but don't expect mind shattering map packs like Hell Revealed, Scythe, Speed of Doom, Alien Vendetta or Sunder.
Weapon challenges being tied to kills and not separate minigames like runes were encourage farming an easy stage of the game and dying to repeat the process, otherwise you are gimping yourself for future fights on UV and above. Really disrupts the flow of gameplay. They should have been implemented like runes were, or your progress towards the weapon challenge should have been wiped out upon death. Thankfully, arcade mode solves the issue (But I'd rather have points not clutter my screen.)
Glory kills are a bit too forced gameplay mechanics-wise and "in your face". I do enjoy it every now and then, but I prefer playing with the indication glow off. Ammo can become an issue if you don't uitilize the melee/chainsaw. But, overall it is fine.
Also, I am looking forward to even more mobility options in the next title.

I had just gotten back into Serious Sam after much avoidance. This almost made me decide to change my mind. It's not good. It's almost like someone with no experience with the games other than a trailer decided to write a game to capitalize on the recent resurgence of both Sam and sprite RPGs.
Hrm... Almost like that indeed.
It's a turn based game with an overhead sprite view and a party of 3 guys. The gimmick is apparently that it's only partially turn based in that you have control to move your party to dodge bullets and enemies. Much like the game proper. Problem is. There's no freedom of movement and at least one member of your party will be hit even in the best of circumstances. I saw someone else say that this is a bullet hell with no way to dodge the bullets and that's pretty much spot on.
It's difficult, but not in the way Serious Sam itself is. The game proper is difficult but fair and there's always a way to win. Here it's basically luck and hoping you only get hit by most bullets rather than all of them. Plus the weapons aren't in any way like you'd think.
For example, the minigun. In Sam proper do you use it to shoot in a straight line or do you spray back and forth for crowd control? This game seems to think it's the former. The shotgun is probably the most useful hilariously enough because you can use it to shoot down some of the bullets.
Nothing else to say really. Croteam should be slightly more paranoid of who they allow to use the franchise name and aesthetic though.

Mechwarrior online, while graphically and, in most things, technically advanced is
a good game. This game encompases very strange balancing systems and the good ol' PGI microtransactions in what seems to be a game that is the♥♥♥♥♥♥stain on the toilet seat that no one can seem to clean off.
Anyway, I digress. I gave this game it's fair run by with another day or two of playing it. The automatic thing I noticed is that the microtransactions STILL have not changed. You either play with 'trial' mechs or shell out real money to get the good♥♥♥♥♥♥ As typical as ever with this kind of thing, the online matchmaking is as ♥♥♥♥ed up as you would expect it to be.
Want a game quickly? Choose x class of mech or you're going to wait 5 minutes to get into a match in your weight class.
Furthurmore, the mechlab is overcomplicated yet stupidly simplistic at the same time. PGI has managed to imploment a system that was MEANT to originally remove the oppertunity to boat a certain type of weapon, which it does, but the problem is that it FEELS like a stoppage. IF you put more than (for example, 2 gauss rifles.) on a mech and fire them at once, your mech will overheat and shut down. No matter how many heat sinks, local temperatures, etc. This would be fine if it didn't FEEL LIKE A DELIBERATE WALL.
Onto the next topic; BUYING MECHS (oh joyus day)
As I mentioned above, you either pay up to PGI for the higher-tier customizable mechs or you get stuck with, what is litterally, green horn trial mechs to put it bluntly. Furthurmore, you can't even change the paint job so you look less ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ without; Yep, you guessed it, paying up with REAL money!
Up next: Gameplay!
I must praise this game, it runs very smoothly on most computers I have tried it on, depending on how you adjust the settings. What I can't say as well for it is that it has a tendency for me at least to have some 'interesting' ping problems. You'll be standing in one place, seemingly safe. Another second, there's a daishi shoving gauss up your jumpjet ports.
My two cents:
This game, in my honest opinion, does not live up to being called a "MechWarrior" game. It BARELY hangs onto the battletech concepts or other stories in the other games. The whole clan gameplay thing is just a glorified teamplay function. (Oh yeah, and guess what? Gotta buy more mechs if you want to play clan play!) The community for this game is also, while not as toxic as most describe it, strange. I've made a few posts on the forum before of what are CLEARLY bugs with the game and not user error (I.E getting matched against full units of assaults with lights and mediums on the other team.) and those issues are almost ALWAYS dropped back on my head as if they're my fault. The community seems to believe their game is so 'superior' to other games that they're willing to defend what is the rotting carcas of a game. Ontop of that, I've noticed a lot of elitest types. If you go about asking a simple question, let's say "How do I use x function" you will either get no reply or a rather rude reply from someone lecturing you on how you should clearly know what you're doing if you're playing this game.
Comparison to other 'MechWarrrior' games.
I will admit, I am slightly biased. I played this game then played "Mechwarrior: Living legends." and noticed the stark difference in marketing tactics. Living legends has NO microtransactions. You get currency for killing other players, simple as that. The currency starts fresh every game you play, and you also get the older version of cryengine, which doesn't look as nice, but runs a lot nicer on lesser specced computers. The team of developers working on living legends also seems to be much more open to sugguestions than PGI. I've personally talked to them on ocassion on their Discord about bugs and issues that ocasionally happen, and 9 times out of 10 they'll be right on it and it'll be fixed within the hour or so if it's minor.
To end off, don't play this. Go pick up living legends or any of the older MechWarrior games to enjoy. Just not this.

My very first Dues Ex game is Human Revolution, and I could not have had a better time. The game definitely has it's flaws, but I was engaged thoroughly through the whole thing.
I was really interested by the dystopian cyber-punk future setting, it's a setting I've seen a dozen times now, but HR creates an unforgetable environment, gloomy, with uncertainty around every corner.
The hacking system was really cool, and provides you with all sorts of insight into peoples personal lives, open up side-quests, and get you into safes and otherwise locked areas. Leveling your various hacking abilities up is a must.
I would not label this game as open-world per se, it is kind of linear, but you certainly do have a lot of freedom to roam around and check out hidden areas or eavesdrop on cool private conversations.
Characters were relatively standard, I didn't really like David Sarif, his voice-acting just didn't seem to fit for some reason, but I ended up loving the main character (Adam Jensen). The tough guy deep voice character has been overdone alot over the years but there was an interesting quality about Jensens character that made him seem even cooler for being another generic cool guy hero type.
Combat was decent enough, large assortment of weapons and different styles are available for people who don't like just the typical run and gun. The stealth aspects of this game were great for me, as a huge fan of the Thief series, Dishonored, and Styx, I was worried the stealth would be lacking, but it really is a spot on system and provides a great sense of pride and accomplishment after succesfully navigating through a huge group of guards.
I really liked the cutscenes, although there weren't many, they were definitely well done.
Inventory management is my biggest complaint in this game, it was so ♥♥♥♥ing annoying, so please do yourself a favor early-game and spend Praxis points on maxing your storage capability ASAP
The game ran really well, even on an older rig like mine, which I was really surprised by, the game looked beautiful for me even though I've seen others saying graphics were there biggest complaint. I have an R7 Radeon 4 core 7700, this game IS optimized for AMD hardware, the only complaints I've seen were from NVIDIA and PHENOM users, but I would be the first to tell you these problems are very FEW and FAR BETWEEN.
I played this game for 3 hours over a year ago, and then last week for some reason felt like coming back, and it was such a good idea. I hit 44.5 hours which to be honest, is a higher time than it should be for most playthroughs, but I took my time and had a lot of fun. I ran into a select few bugged missions but nothing a simple google search couldn't resolve.
I really do recommend this game and would have to give it a 9/10 you would be doing yourself a huge disservice by not picking this up on sale. Go play!

Bought this game in the Pendulo Studios bundle during a Steam sale, and I only bought the bundle for the Runaway series. With that being my only experience with Pendulo games, I loaded this one up expecting another light-hearted point-and-click, and was confronted with torture, murder, and Satanic cults. What a twist!
The story is unique and I enjoyed the visual style. The voice acting left a little to be desired. However, I thought the game's biggest flaw was its length. I felt like the story could have been so much MORE. This game just skimmed the surface of the universe of the game, and because of this, I never really felt any immersion or connection to the characters. Maybe this was a stylistic choice on the part of the development team to reflect John Yesterday's amnesia, but it mostly feels like they ran out of resources and had to cut parts out.
An example of this is near the end of the game, when two of the antagonists discuss how they murdered a colleague together years previously. This colleague's name was mentioned once in a throwaway line earlier in the game when you examine an object. This left me going, "What? What did you do?? Why did you do it? Who was this guy??", and with no answers present in the game's story, I'm wondering why the developers even chose to include such a detail.
I think I would have been less forgiving of this game's flaws had I paid the $11CAD that is the game's usual full price, but if you are a point-and-click adventure fan, see it on sale, and have 3 or 4 hours to kill, you might want to pick it up. Just expect to be overcome with a feeling of "That's it?" when you finish.

Love Trails games, so I bought this one to support future localizations of other entries in the series, even after already owning a PS3 version of CSI. (I am one of these guys that talk with every npc and in this game, the npcs say new stuff and tell their own stories all the time, so I already invested a few hundred hours in this game in 3 playthroughs on PS3, initial playthrough with talking to everyone I could find, was a fair amount above 100 hours, btw).
For new players: You can jump right into this JRPG without prior knowledge of the series. Mostly you'll miss some innuendos, but nothing major or anything that would shorten your enjoyment or understanding of the game. The cast, location, story etc. are all completely different. This takes places a few years after "trails in the sky" and sky featured another region of this world, so you won't really revisit old places (I still recommend playing the other trails games later on, as it still adds to the overall lore, every trails game is great fun and you will know more about the whole world).
If you like old-school RPG's and found yourself unsatisfied with all the stuff we got offered in the last few years, chances are you will really like this game, as I was in the same situation. While I normally prefer Japanese Dubs, the English Dub for this one is pretty solid. Especially seeing how many additional lines were voiced. Be warned though: There are millions of lines for this game, but for the most part only the main story relevant scenes are voiced.
School setting, some standard character troupes and standard japanese jokes and cliché happenings can be found in this game, yes. But that's only a small part of the whole game. Character development is definitely noticable and will go on as you move forward. This is only the first game of the triology (and I already played the first two games), so there is massive room for even more.
While I like slower-paced stories with good worldbuilding, it's not for everyone, so let me get this out of the way:
The pace isn't fast. The game starts with a situation you will only reach much later on (in the later half of the game). Consider most of this game as introduction to and familiarisation with characters, factions, the empire in which this story takes place, some organisations, circumstances in the empire, slow-pace-build-up for more intense events later on (and part 2) and the lore etc. A slow story, yes but enjoyable nevertheless. Besides some cliche character interactions, there are a lot of great and funny ones, too. The main character might seem pretty standard, but he undergoes character development, too and as most of the time he isn't the only character you play, this shouldn't be a reason to not buy this game. Characters in your party which may seem annoying and stereotypical at first will developed as you move onward and gain a deeper and interesting personality (grew to love the cast after some time, when I first played).
If you are like me and talk to every npc, you will need a 3-digit amount of time for a playthrough, without it's hard to say as I always take much longer than the average guy for my playthroughs and can only speak for myself. A new playthrough offers NG+ options and some neet options. Slower sections you can accelerate via turbo function.
While this game is pretty linear, the story slowly begins to unfold as you move on. The worldbuilding is were this games strength is located. Pretty much every minor npc has his own lines, which will change every time the time of the day changes...  The whole world feels alive. Characters you first didn't know and felt were stereotypical will grow on you sooner than you may think. The amount of characters with more screentime is huge and even this first part of a triology as a whole will only scratch on the surface.
Music is great in this one, once again. The pc port has a great support and you can play it on low-end or high-end-pcs all the same (thanks to customizable settings). If you just want to have a lot of action and grinding, you should look for another game. If you love if there is a lot of text and slow but good world-building: Just try it! At the end of this game, things will be more "lively" and the battle system is still pretty great and will be used often enough :)
Though be warned: The second game was already confirmed for steam, but the first game ends on a huge cliffhanger.
The battle system is pretty cool and a big plus for this game. The battles are turnbased and you will be introduced to new aspects of them, step by step throughout the game. Arts, Crafts, Link Attacks, Special Attacks, later on another kind of battle (though that would be a spoiler if I said more) etc.. In this game I consider crafts as the most useful abilities, arts play a smaller role. In the second game CSII (Cold Steel II) this was rebelanced so that I started to use magic more often. Still didn't influence my enjoyment of the game and you still can focus on magic, all the same, but your chars have to wait for their turns, longer.
Customization of characters via orbment system is another great point. Besides basic stats you can decide how to skill your character. A master quarz will decide some boni, arts and status effects while you possess a a few slots you can unlock and fill with prefered spells, stat boosts, probability to inflict status ailments, more drops etc. via quartz. Hell, Rean hasn't the best stats for it, but you could even completely neglect his physical stats and build him into a mage-type if you want to.
Difficulty is sometimes pretty challenging, but all in all it's not too difficult.
Much grinding isn't needed, either. As you progress through the game you earn quite a lot of EXP. While you can (and should if you play at a higher difficulty)grind for some items, sepith,  money etc. it's not necessary in any kind of great extent.
Another thing: In each chapter there will be field studies which take you to different places in the empire, introduce the world (and slowly some problems/conflicts that grow more interesting at the end and in the following game). Inbetween your missions, you receive some bonding points to absolve mini-events with your party members. They can be quite nice from time too time and net you Link XP. These will help you in battle, too, if you are linked to a specific character. more Link XP---> more advantages when linked with said character. These events are like a small relationship system, although they don't influence the main story per se. Especially the ending event is influenced by the level of your bonds. So while there are possible romantic implications, nothing major here. The second game though has the possibility to take over your save from CSI and you will encounter a few different talks, if you max'd different chars.
SO IN SHORT, once again:
I'm not good in reviews and much is still left to be said, but that would be too much for now. More people than not, like trails in the sky more than trails of cold steel, but for me it's just the other way around. Great worldbuilding, great character development, a world that feels alive, as even minor npcs have new stuff to tell (all the time!), solid english voice acting, great music, a lot of text & content (if you like it), not much grinding required, but a nice turn-based combat system with a few customization options as far as skills/arts are concerned and some (sometimes more, sometimes less) enjoyable bonding events with characters. The story is still slow-paced and there are cliche's from time to time, but nothing to major. I still like the story and the time the game invests in building it up. Trails was always known for it's worldbuilding and the story moves quicker the further you are in this triology. Nice for lovers of classic JRPGs that were unsatisfied in the last few years (no guarantee, though- everyone's tastes are different) and one of the JRPGs of my favorite JRPG series.

As someone who enjoys strategy and building games such as Roller Coaster Tycoon, Locomotion, SimCity and so on I think that Cities in Motion 2 is a great game offering a wide versatility of construction options, vehicles that look great in any setting and comprehensive timetables to accommodate the schedules of the various categories of the cities population.
However there are a couple things missing that i feel are vital to any cities successful public transportation like the ability to put a platform on either side of the track or that there are no roads going to the edge of the map like if they were going to other cities. There for there are no trains or grand central stations or an airport where a large number of bus, tram and subway lines could meet like they do in real cities.
But overall yes, I do recommend this game.

It's a bit on the repetitive side, plus there are some in-game issues such as stupid traffic and customers that become unhappy far too quickly, but if you can ignore that, then what you have is a very nice combination of city simulator and transport simulator. The route building tools are very good and easy to use, there's a wide choice of vehicles, the way the city responds to what you build is also a nice addition, and for good measure, there's a great map editor built into it.

Having absolutely LOVED Doom3 and its expansion, I must say I'm very disappointed in the reboot.
It's purely a mindless shooter with boring environments and minor handholding (interactable objects are all glowy/sparkly). The story of the campaign is nothing more than a lazy afterthought.
Doom 3 had a better story and the environmental design was amazing. The darkness, creaking metal sounds, Demonic breathing (yet no enemies to be seen) all contributed to creating a scary and interesting atmosphere. Going to outer Mars used to create a completely different atmosphere, heavy breathing sounds from the marine, muffled sounds through the helmet, limited oxygen...
What's the difference between indoor level and outdoor level in the remake? You can see the sky... That's about it. There's no difference other than that.
All levels are basically arenas. Kill all enemies to unlock the doors and go to the next arena. Yes, I understand that they were trying to recreate the simplistic gameplay of Doom 1, however back then there were technical limitations that lead to this design. There are no such limitations now so what gives? Wolfenstein 3D was also just as basic and simple, yet the new Wolfenstein games manage to combine great shooting experience, level design AND STORY into one package. That’s what the original Half-Life brought to FPS all those years ago. It changed shooters from basic arena shooters to first person adventures. Yet the new Doom pretends like Half-Life never happened. What’s up with that? Heck both Wolfenstein and Doom are published by the same publisher too!
I’m very disappointed in id, especially since Doom 3 was so good. I think the IP should be handed over to MachineGames.

This game gets a recommended from me.
It's a very good example of how old school and new school can live side by side. I think this DOOM is a worthy successor to the orriginals. Personally, I got no problems with stability; the game never crashed once, neither did the fps drop, even in the most monster packed situations where you will be living through a literal bullet hell. This game has got a very good polish, bar a few minor exceptions, and a very high technical and graphical optimization. It feels butter smooth for me all the time.
DOOM is not the quickest action fps out there. It is very hectic, though. When fighting multiples of enemies this game is very fun. You will need a decent approach to fight them efficiently, too. That becomes especially true on higher difficulties, but you can do casually alright on the lower ones, if you just want to blast stuff. You will be able to see every action of the well animated enemies, respond accordingly and, naturally, aim for the head. If you want to be efficient you will need to choose weapons according to the enemy type you're facing, how far they are from you, how clumped up together they are, ect.,ect. The way this game comes together is a pleasure to play. It is highly enjoyable.
Progression is decent, you have got level secrets--some harder to get, some almost obvious; nothing worthy to write home about. Through those you can get some weapons early plus additional upgrates, which turns your arsenal into a powerhouse of fun. You can do a purist run, if you like, but weapon mods and upgrades really make it just more FUN.
DOOM fullfills all of my expectations and always gives me a good mood. It's a good game choise.

It is, in essence, a highly customizable shooter.  Gameplay is (generally) slower, leaning more towards the preparation/planning/coordination side of things, and less towards the flippy-boom-headshot-blazeit420 side of things.

Nice point'n'click adventure with an interesting plot developing a dark story.  The puzzles are logical and you won't bang your head against the wall trying to solve them (in case there are even some hints). Graphics, music, voice acting and animations are of very good quality.
The biggest downside is the length of the game: 5 hours and you're done. And there is not much replayability once you know the plot: you can try a few different options, but that's it.

Is this a game worth your time? It has lots of casual murder, so yes. YES!
But…
…the game is very, very short and very, very easy. I’m neither a clever man nor an avid adventure gamer and I always need to look up what to do in walkthroughs sooner or later. That being said, Yesterday took me roughly 3.5 hours to finish and I breezed through it. Some of the riddles are just stupid too, like right at the beginning you must reconstruct a payphone to call someone and even though you have a mobile and the person you’re trying to call has one too the game never even allows you to try to use your mobile.
…all the cut-scenes are… minimalistic, is a word that could describe them, I guess. They’re mostly just a series of snapshots and fade-to-blacks instead of a short movie or there’re just animations in front of a black background.
…the game has very few locations, very few riddles, very few dialogs, very few items, very few of everything basically. For example, the cast size is tiny and there are basically no secondary or background characters.
…the story is rather incoherent at times, which is a result of budgetary limitations, I think. Too many holes in the narrative, too. Throughout the entire game I had the impression that half of it was missing. Scenes just start and you don’t know why, scenes just end and you don’t really know how, facts are stated and information are given and there is a general lack of context present at all times.
…there are story twists planted in the narrative but they’re NOT played out so that at some point you just think to yourself “oh, that person was this?” and then you shrug your shoulders because the timing is messed up. And that’s very unfortunate because early on they actually prove that they know how to properly time a twist.
…everything feels really underdeveloped, especially the characters. By now we can see the theme I’m going for, I reckon. Because of the tight budged nothing really has room to breathe and time to unfold. You meet a villain and in the same scene you dispose of him, you meet a character and five minutes later you’re already big chums with them. It’s stripped down to the bare essentials.
So I think what I’m trying to say is this: There is a jarring chasm between the very big and lavishly played out prologue and the rest of the game, which really hammers home the point that they planned a big old adventure game in the tradition of their very own Runaway series but were forced to make a very, very small game in the end.
And still, the atmosphere is fantastic, dark and creepy and weird and aloof and just spot on; the music is sometimes great (and sometimes just cringeworthy), the voice acting is rather good all around, the writing is never bad and quite good at times; the game is not funny nor does it try to be funny and the story is dark and evil and heavily inspired by the occult. They also have played a lot of PlaneScape: Torment, I’d say and that is never a bad thing. And they start the game with a proper mind♥♥♥♥!
So yes, it is absolutely worth the 3-4 hours you’ll spend with it. If 3-4 hours are worth 10 Euros to you, that is for you to decide though.
The only problem is the lenght of the game (too short for me). The story, as its puzzles, it is twisted. Amazing plot. It is nice to see such kind of games nowadays.

I rarely had to use the clues but I noticed that I had to use them a lot for the blind master temple parts(which, by the way, really didn't add much to anything) because they didn't make much sense for the most part.
But I really did enjoy the experience and would love to see a sequel that wraps up the story and its characters

Squarecells is sort of like picross, with a few twists. It is nice and calming, but it has problems: the puzzles don't make shapes (sad!) and they are very, very easy. oh and also there's only 36 of them.
Although a hexagon contains 6 sides and a square 4, the latter won't make it more easy to solve !

Do you like Picross? You know this game is for you already.
Do you like Hexcells? You know this game is for you already.
Do you enjoy reasonably tough logic puzzle games with a supremely calming aesthetic? This game is for you.
SqaureCells comes from the developer of Hexcells, a series of amazingly well designed logic puzzle games that are reminiscent of Minesweeper with shades of Picross, Nintendo's series of logic puzzle games. I'd highly suggest you check those games out before this one, if only because they're fantastic and can be had cheaply during sales.
SquareCells is much more of a direct take on Picross. For those that don't know, Picross is a puzzle game where you're given a square or rectangle and tasked to remove blocks, guided by numbers indicating how many blocks are in each row or column. You'll generally be rewarded with an image of some kind. SquareCells is very much that, though the images are more abstract.
There's a unique mechanic that Brown has added to the mix, a number on a square that indicates how many squares it is directly connected to. It's one of those concepts that really changes the way you think about Picross puzzles, and allows him to get away with presenting less information while still creating fair puzzles. The logical possibilities that arise from this provide the unique spin on the Picross formula that this game needs to stand out.
I've finished the game with three stars on every puzzle, and while it starts out fairly simple to introduce people new to Picross it eventually gets quite tricky, especially in the last tier of puzzles. I never had to make logical leaps or even educated guesses, which is always a plus. Took me 5 hours to 100% the game, which I find to be a decent price/content ratio, even without it being on sale.
It's $3 currently, absolutely worth it for a well-made relaxing puzzle game. I look forward to SquareCells Plus and SquareCells Infinite!

Completely unlike what feedback I've garnered from Cities: Skylines so far, this "urban transport planning simulator" is a TOTAL JOKE. No mod support. No logical vehicle progression. Extremely processor-intensive and inconsistent traffic simulation. WAY too many DLCs. No left-hand drive support (it's more important than you think). Hilariously game-breaking dynamic urbanisation mechanic. Extremely little map content. Pointless, inflexible "campaign" mode. Metric tons of micromanagement. More eye-pleasing cities? NEIN. And most importantly, an extremely user-hostile network construction method. No thanks to my OCD, I usually spend over 12 hours just to plan ONE perfect metro line. The lack of assistance to deal with the gridless game engine is really taxing on my rigid SC4-style urban planning skills. To be honest, I wish Colossal Order had instead tried to emulate the gameplay of the original CIM as much as possible, as well as implementing actual multiplayer support that supports third-world internet connections and properly-synchronised gameplay for once.

When it was published I already have played the classic CIM for a long time and thought that it probably would be as good as the old one (or better) and so I didn't wait and bought the game. However it wasn't that what I expected: It's nice that there are vehicles carrying more passengers and a better track building. But the game design isn't the best one, since it isn't as "realistic" as the design of the classic CIM. Moreover you have to build your transport networks in "futuristic american" cities which aren't  really cities (but Tutorial City :D). I hoped that you could build in NYC or Wahington, but those cities aren't in the game. It would also have been nice to be able to play scenarios in europe cities, but for it you have to buy a ectension pack which costs some money :(.

I enjoyed the first Cities in Motion and completed 100% of the achievements and campaigns.   CIM2 retains some of the themes but rearchitects the engine and simulation.  I eagerly picked it up, played through a little bit, enjoyed what I saw but found some of the controls difficult and frustrating, so it languished for awhile.
Then I started reading all of the excitement about Cities: Skylines in its prerelease phase, saw the simularities in the look and feel of C:S, and thought I'd take another look.  Applying myself a little more, I found I was able to overcome some (but not all) of the frustration with the user interface of CIM2 and in belated retrospect, it is a very enjoyable simulation.
I'm planning to finish the campaign (and in a sale, maybe pick up some DLC) before moving on to Cities:Skylines, which I fully expect to build and expand on the CIM2 experience.

Just be warned, the learning curve is very much there; learning to either lead a shot on a Spinfuzor or a Sniper Rifle, or learning how to Jetpack and Ski to effectively capture a flag will take a while to work out if you don't feel confident in you're own abilities. But Bottom line, this is a shooter that feels like it has the grit, backbone, and level of respect belonging to older shooters, while mixed with the technical wizardry, accessibility, and just straight-up fun of more modern shooters. Recommended!

The Writing.

You see in this game what passes for intrigue is the writer going "Well, that certainly looks like something which could become interesting and exciting at some point in the futu-" at this point the writer walks off leaving his five year old son in his place to fill in the gaps. In crayon.
The Graphics.
Alot of adventure games stick with 2D. Noone holds this against them but when an adventure game goes "♥♥♥♥ that, we're doing abit of 3D." you tend to prepare for something special. Anyway. If this is on sale and you don't particularly value your money? Go nuts for donuts. Otherwise, look elsewhere.

Yesterday is a fun adventure game that I would recommend to fans of adventure and fun, non-linear stories. The story is easily the strongest part of the game, and it genuinely kept me on the edge of my seat and scratching my head in the beginning (in a good way). By the end of the game, it gets a little cliche, but the beginning starts off strong enough to definitely get you to the end. Without spoiling anything, the characters are definitely an enjoyable and memorable cast. You dislike the bad guys, like the good guys, et cetera.
But that's enough about the story, how's the gameplay? Well, it is a point-and-click adventure at heart, and it works as well as you'd hope. Sometimes you'll find puzzles that require a group of items to be combined together, and only using one of the items on the enviornment is enough to solve the puzzle. Combining items also works well, and as someone who will default to "try everything on everything" I never once accidentally solved a puzzle before I figured out what was asked of me. There's also a hint system that works pretty well. At any given time, you can activate a hint that displays a blip over all interactable points in the environment, which proves to help, when in clustered, zoomed out areas, you're not so sure what is part of the setting and what is actually usable, which happens a lot so it's good that there is a built-in system to overcome it. The other kind of hint, which you can only use after interacting with objects a few times, is... a hint! The hints tend to vary from "Use blank on blank." to "What can you use to blank?" It would be nice if there was a way to filter out hints that straight-up solve puzzles for you, and hints that gently point you in the right direction, but there is not.
Okay, so, as much as I would like to pretend that graphics and animation don't matter, I can't pretend that some people might be turned off by the game's lack luster animations. When characters talk, their mouth animations tend to repeat in a somewhat comedic manner, looking like they're just flapping their lips faster than humanly possible. It's a little distracting when you're having a dramatic moment, and the bad guys can't be arsed to have their mouth movements match their words. The cutscenes are also a little comedically bad, but they at least the characters are lip-synced. However, it seems that the cutscenes lacked a choreographer, since there isn't much in the ways of fist-fights. There is a scene where two characters are fighting with swords, and the cutscene turns itself into a cut-powerpoint. It's bad, it's funny, it's a little lazy.
All-in-all, I'd say that this game is great if you aren't expecting a top-class triple-A game. It's humble and fun, and it doesn't forget that for a second. The story is presented well and the puzzles are logical and fun, and the game isn't afraid to lend a helping hand.

Yesterday is a very well-crafted dark thriller and mystery story, revolving around satanic cults and one of the best-written amnesia cases in video games. The quality acting and the well-written story will easily suck you into this world, but sadly not for long: the game is shorter than most budget indie adventure titles.
Yesterday is probably the strangest game Péndulo Studios made since they hit big in 2001. It moves away from the previous titles’ colourful and light atmosphere and introduces us a bloody thriller involving satanic cults, torture, a serial killer, and a big load of mystery in the form of the protagonist, who suffers from a very strange case of amnesia.
Since this is a dark story, the visuals reflect this all the way: the scenes are realistic and use mainly darker tones, but they are not moody. The storytelling is done by using European style comic panels with probably the best voice acting we heard so far in a Péndulo game.
The puzzles are quite straightforward. You will probably spend more time with cross-inventory trial and error than trying to figure out what the developers intended for a certain scene.
The greatest problem with the game is the length. It barely reaches four hours if you are even decent at adventure games. I forgot to make a save by quitting (another shortcoming: you cannot save) and I had to race through the story again to watch the other endings; this is how I realised you can speed through the whole game in less than 20 minutes. The story itself may compensate for it, but since it’s a thriller-mystery, the replay/rewatch value is quite low. Still, for the few hours it lasts, it's good, really good.

A very satisfying game that needs practice for perfection. It's basically a memorisation game that focuses on firearms; which is pretty easy to pick up after you learn the mechanics of the different firearm categories, such as for pistols and rifles. It's a fun and easy game once you are able to segregate the individual parts into modules.
The most interesting game mode is hardcore mode where you are allowed to perform actions simultaneously, but at no fault. Hardcore mode unlocks after you have gone through the game modes for a specific model and allows the player to go through a model faster than the other game modes due to simultaneous actions.
Understanding how each weapon operates also helps with disassembly and assembly as the animations of the weapon's operation have the best detail within their movements; allowing for the easy recognition of a part's purpose. Cutaways and X-ray modes benefits this dissection.
It is possible to enjoy this game as a free player where the in game currency can be earned through achievements. The main form of currency comes from the weapon quizzes and the premium currency comes from first place on the leaderboards for the models. Premium currency takes a long time to earn from the popular models, but you can get it from obscure models that have highscores that can be beaten.

Its fine. The learning curve is a bit high which leaves some layman gamers in the cold. But if you're the type of person who likes to control and customize, you're right at home.
Upsides:
- Some people call it "cheap" but it feels like any standard Xbox controller.
- The analog stick is one of THE best I've ever used. Its not weighty and stiff like the X360 controllers.
- The haptic pads are fairly sensitive.
- It has plenty of buttons to use, including digital click triggers, the backplate finger flaps and the haptic pads themselves bottom out for a click. But the A-Stick will not click like on an Xbox Controller. (with this many buttons, you don't need it.)
- HIGHLY. CUSTOMIZABLE. Every button and input can be reassigned. ALL OF THEM.
- The Gyroscope and Accelerometer is VERY usable which is a surprise.
- Includes a USB cable for wired play and a wireless dongle for wireless play.
- Regular Firmware Updates. (Yes! Something this programmable, its a good thing.)
Downsides:
- Triggers have a short throw. Even though they can be used as analog, it takes some getting used to.
- No Rumble. However there's an experimental mode to have the haptic motors replicate the sensation. (STILL BETA)
- The Ergonomics will actually have you tilt the controller forward a bit to make it less awkward which kind of works against palming the handles.
- Not every game will have a default Steam Controller scheme like an Xbox controller.
- No substitute for a good D-PAD.
- The USB cable is short. (about 2-1/2 feet.)
- A,B,X,Y, is sort of small and pill-like in the center.
The left haptic pad has a cutout for D-Pad like behavior, but the H-Pads are a stiff click and using them in a touch manner for a D-Pad will throw your accuracy(they're A-Stick/Mouse substitutes first). D-Pads maybe old hat but, a good one is always hard to come by. Even the 360 controllers had a bad "D-Pad"(if you can call it that). Not even sure about the uber expensive Xbox One Elite magnets and such. AND I vehemently disagree with Playstation's hundred iterations of d-pads over the years being any good (They never were in my experience).
The "Bluetooth" dongle is not multipurpose (Yeah, low expectations but I wanted it to be...). Also the short cable will force you to find a better one or use rechargable batteries. Both have an extra added cost as the included Duracell batteries are not rechargable, Though they do seem to last forever.
Want a new controller and not afraid to try something new, its fine. But if you have zero patience to learn and just want to plug and play, stick with the traditional Xbox brand controllers.

I'm a big fan of Trails in the sky series, and Falcom always make games that are enjoyable. Trails of Cold Steel is nonetheless extent of Falcom's successful story-rich series; in terms of world-building, there really is nothing like this series. World goes around without you; it does progress with you, but every npc has little stories and problems that they're dealing with, and it's up to you to talk to them. NPCs always have something to say about the things that happened in their town, and if you like walking around the town talking to people about some weird stuffs that you don't even have to really know, then you will spend more time reading texts than playing and progressing main storyline.
Characters will look as cliched as it can be, but as story progresses, you will start to see more of them, so it adds kind of weird depth to their personality. Combat system is tight; if you don't let your guard down and stun enemies before you engage, game won't be a challenge even on hard mode, but it will still keep you at the edge of your seat, and focused because link system is all about that quick button pushing. Soundtrack is still good, just like all the previous series. All in all, I must say I'm satisfied with my purchase, I simply couldn't resist the urges of playing more trails games because I fell in love with this world that Falcom built.

Don't be fooled by my play time as I played this game and its sequel on ps3 and bought it again here to support this series on pc.
The port is very good in terms of performance and graphical settings and launcher thanks to Durante. I have a GTX 760 and I am playing the game at maximum settings @1080p. I am getting between 50 and 60 fps unlike the 30 fps on consoles. It has a turbo mode to boot to save plenty of your valuable time in battles, saving your game and traversing the fields.
The following is my review of the game proper:
This game is one of the best jrpg'sI played in recent memory; it's very long though and has huge replayability factor due to its game plus mode and the need to play it more than once to get all achievements for their hunters out there.
Despite the above praise, this game presents no real innovations in the jrpg genre, but it excels at what it does. It spends so much time in world building and making you so much attached to and invested in getting to know the characters. The characters are, for the most part, unique, complex and have interesting back stories. Even the countless NPC's are unique and have their own personalities and problems. I was reminded of persona sometimes when I played it, which is a good thing, due to its social-link like mechanic with your fellow classmates and exams.
The graphics are a slight letdown but this is more than compensated by its great gameplay, beautiful music, nice English dub, which isn't full but much more is English dubbed than many other Japanese games.
The battle system is turn based in the tradition of classic Japanese rpgs like persona and the earlier final fantasies and utilising enemies weaknesses, delaying enemies' (particularly bosses' turns) and performing links with your party members play a crucial role in securing your victory in battles. Also, despite spending a long time grinding for levels and items in this game, I never really got bored or annoyed by the battle system, which is a huge plus in a long game in my book.
Despite being long and very detailed that it makes you feel part in its universe, the game ends on a cliffhanger, which prepares you for its sequel as it is part of a trilogy.
This is the definitive edition of this game due to the excellent port and its various enhancements, which made me want to replay it despite my huge backlog.

Visually they look nice, the animation is good to amazing, but sound effects of the weapons drag everything to mundanity. I urge you to look up Doom's (2016) weapon videos and if the weapons sound least a bit engaging, this game probably won't dissapoint you. Otherwise, you might end up feeling like I did, where this one thing brings your enjoyment of the game to levels low enough not wanting to bother with the game, even if it's rather short. It's action paced well enough not to feel overcrowded, the enemies are fun to fight after awhile, but once the guns start feeling meh, it makes you think, whether you want to finish the game at all.

Endless Space is a game with interesting ideas, cinematic combat, visually intriguing designs, an easy to follow and learn HUD and lots of other great elements, yet fails to properly combine them into a solid experience.
Admittedly, I don't have the hugest amount of experience with 4X games as much as I love playing them. The grandness of building empires always appealed to me, to pass laws, to build structures, to interact with other empires and fight wars of attrition or rain down on their cities in a firey holocaust. And this game lets you do this, certainly. You colonize systems, discover technology and wonders, build up your fleets and discuss, fight or trade your way out of usually inevitably violent interactions with other races. It's a shame that all of that fighting, talking and trading feels half baked half the time.
I'll start with combat and call it what it is. Glorified paper, scissors, rock...oh, and there's some metagame about ships and technology and resource management. You choose a targeting type, spread fire, 1/3 targets first 3 enemy ships or focus fire on the first ship in the enemy formation. You can choose a fleet arrangement but I only used 2, which was the default of whatever ships have the most HP going first and whatever ships had the most invasion strength going last. You choose a series of card-like 'abilities' which can counter or conversly be countered by other cards and offer slight boosts to things like certain weapon damage. It is possible to also assign a 'Hero' to a fleet and have them provide bonuses, other stat boosts and new abilities, usually costing 'Dust' the game's form of money. Probably the best thing about the combat is its 'camera' which kind of makes you feel like you are watching a sci fi movie but I often just found myself frustrated by not really being able to see what was going on.
The diplomacy screen is well designed and easy to use even though it can be buggy at times and may need to be closed and re-opened to use it again. You start at a cold war with each new race you meet and your behaviour will influence other races' opinion of you. If you are on good terms with them, you can trade technology, systems and resources. If you are in a cold war war they can declare war on you and you can declare war on any race at any time unless you have an agreement. And these agreements suck all joy out of the game. Want to remain in an alliance to crush an enemy? Too bad, your ally delcared a cease fire and now you cannot do anything for 30+ turns. Want to pretend to be at peace just to build up your fleets for a few turns and then break your truce and rush in with all your ships and flatten your enemies? Too bad. The diplomacy and trading is essentially the same. I guess the agreements serve as a great analogy for the rest of the game, what should create 'Endless' possibilities only feels restrictive and frustrating due to how simple the game often is.
I should also say that most diplomatic options have to be researched which makes replaying a pain.
Finally, balancing. I hated it. Early game, I custom made a scientific race and I dedicated all my resources to expansion and science. Once my borders met with my enemies' close to mid game, I spent all my attention on science, every single system meant to churn out as much research as possible. Someone else finds this accursed planet called 'Augira' which gives them huge benifits but I can never find it in my 20+ hours of playing this game. So one race grows way too powerful and large. I start to focus on fleets more and build up a lot of forces. Then I have some scuffles with the nearby races until the big one takes notice and starts attacking me. I try my absolute hardest to push them back, then someone else declares war on me. I try to pull back my forces to my key planets but I'm losing a lot along the way and it's infuriating. No matter what I do, each game more or less ends this way. Now, most of my games last 3-4 hours and I quit before I can win because late game is such an unbalanced, headache inducing mess.
I should also mention, even if you get a ceasefire, the enemy ships will blockade your systems and keep blockading them anyway so you can't move your ships around.
I don't hate the game but it feels more luck than strategy based, pick the card and hope you are right as 9 times out of 10 it is the only way to securely win combat, find this planet 'Augira' by chance and dominate everyone later and that planet can't be turned off so it shows up in every game. The galaxy is too small to try and just develop quietly until later and it just feels messy. I guess I can reccomend that you get some friends together and play LAN, this game should run on mid-range laptops after all and has laptop friendly control options. That way the AI can't be infuriatingly unbalanced like it normally is in this game.
It's not bad and really shows promise in places. The soundtrack is alright but the artbook is really nice. The art in the game itself is good too, the tech tree is well organized, the HUD is great, the world seems genuinely interesting. But...
I just can't reccomend this game if you're a fan of 4X's already, there are better sci fi  games out there which actually offer more complex approaches like Stellaris.
But if you want a game that can run on older machines or mid range laptops, you are hoping to get into 4X games by starting off with simpler titles or just want something to burn some time on, then great, here is the game for you.
EDIT: As stated in the comments, Auriga does not guarantee a win. It obviously helps with one though. My statements about the game being poorly balanced remain true but do I apologize for the error on my part for unintentionally misinforming people about this.

Endless Space is a deceptive piece of work. Aesthetically, it's a beautiful, and the soundtrack is...not too shabby. The screenshots plus the theory of what Endless Space could have been, generally close the sale.
Emphasis on "could have been."
To start things off...tutorial. Or rather, the lack of one. The closest thing to a real tutorial is going onto Youtube, and watching some stranger's "Let's Play Endless Space" videos. The only help the developers included was very light touching on the UI. And how to point and click. Truly innovative stuff.
"But I can just dive in and learn on the go. Trial and error."
Sure, if this was CoD or Civ, I'm sure you could. However, Endless Space is a labyrinth of confusion and frustration.
-  You have multiple planets within a system, and you must micromanage each one to maximize the resource gains for your empire. How should you micromanage different terrain types? Or which tech should you persue to maximize early scouted planets? Refer to Youtube Let's Plays.
-  You have four different fields in the tech tree, massive in scale with a paragraph of uneccessary psuedo-science gibberish on each node. There is no reference on how to even decide which tech is relevant at the moment and which can wait till later turns to be researched. Unless you refer to Youtube Let's Plays.
- Don't understand the heros? Refer to Youtube Let's Plays.
Battle mechanics are hilariously bad. Literally, rock - paper- scissors in real time. Your weapon choices are cards. Pick a card, cross your fingers, rinse and repeat.
The background is pretty though.

It takes a lot of getting used to. Like, a lot a lot, because it's so different from anything you've ever used. I feel like I'd give it a solid positive rating overall. I haven't had a proper FPS to diligently play and test the controller with, so I can't say how accurate it is in that setting. For Dark Souls, Civ V,  XCOM, Fallout, etc. it feels good/great. I love the way the buttons feel and click and their placements. Having all these extra buttons and being able to change them on the fly is something that beats my old well loved xbox 360 controller. It's a bit clunky and taking some use to, but playing an MMORPG with it works and is uniquely fun (my setup is using the gyro to control the mouse and left trigger for right clicking, which frees up your right hand to press more buttons).
I was able to get it for 30 bucks and it feels very much worth it. I've been excited for the past couple months I've had it to simply PLAY on it! It works on ANY game, simply add it to steam if it's not from steam, make sure it's named properly, and you'll have access to community saved profiles (which can save you time on hopping in). The vibrations and clicks feel satisfying, I always have my haptics on everything set to high.
The downsides are as follows.
1) Big Picture Mode is bad. In every way possible, and if you're going to use the controller, it's gotta be set as your default overly or else you won't be able to change buttons on the fly. The only positive aspect about BPM is that it works well with the controller and it looks nice. It does not function with a mouse or keyboard, so good luck.
2) Some parts of the controller are...too close. The X button is less than an inch away from the joystick, which means thumbs will be fighting for space at times. The Y and B buttons are like milimeters away from the right touch pad, which doesn't cause issues 99% of the time (because you're only going to be using your right hand on that side, so no fighting over real estate), but fat or lazy thumb presses on those two buttons might touch the pad and throw you off.
3) The "D-Pad" isn't so much that it's stiff, but it's hard to work correctly. Some have said it's hard to press, that's somewhat true. However, my problem has been that it's hard for the pressing to be accurate. Many times I press right, but my thumb wasn't perfectly close enough to the right side, so it went up instead. I haven't spent a lot of time doing a fighting game, but it felt wrong.
Some people complain that it feels cheap and super plasticy, I disagree. Shipping was surprisingly pleasant. It took them like 3 days to process the order, and one day to ship/arrive at my apartment.
Overall, I feel that it's a very solid controller for "chill" and couch gaming. Just get over the insanely massive learning curve and you'll find a new, happy home in the Steam Controller.
The track pad makes it very difficult to play games that expect you to have an analog stick. I would not recommend this.

The newest adventure of Pendulo Studion, in which they say farewell to the constant humor of earlier titles (the Runaway series) and instead say hello to psychopaths, old cults and things not being as they seem at first.
This game is a blast to play - and while it is not grim enough to be called a horror game (some funny bits remain), it has enough bleakness, death and madness to allow for some very creepy entertainment. Especially when played at night.
The greatly executed nonlinear structure that shines through at crucial times is also a big plus in my eyes.
PS: don't fear the puzzles to be overwhelmingly difficult or illogical - they are interesting and just hard enough. #
You will not die of frustration while solving them ;)
PPS: Don't watch the trailer (propably too late if you are reading this) - this game is best enjoyed without any spoilers!

Yesterday is my favorite of Pendulo's adventure games. It still has a touch of the madcap zaniness that was hit or miss with the Runaway series as well as The Next Big Thing but distilled into a supernatural thriller with enough good twists and turns to keep you entertained until the end.
Most of the gameplay has you playing as John Yesterday, professional investigator for multi-billionaire Henry White. Unfortunately, John has amnesia, but Pendulo went all in making this amnesia story one for the books. As a story, it constantly subverts your expectations, right from the opening dedication where you think it'll be an adventure game about helping the homeless. Gradually, as the layers of the story get peeled away and start to form a cohesive whole, it turns into something special. The characters are memorable aside from John's stock love interest. She has all the personality of Gina from Runaway: A Road Adventure, which is to say she none. Liz Allaire she is not. At least all the dialogue is delivered with much aplomb, or at least up to Pendulo's usual standards.
As for the puzzles, some reviews have touched upon them being easy but I found myself having to use the built in help system a few times after having exhausted all possible solutions, but at least this time most of the solutions make sense in the game world. No 'peanut butter' puzzles to be found. That said, it's possible to acquire 'red herring' items which can add some unneeded difficulty to puzzles. For the most part, areas are limited to two or three screens at a time which keeps frustration at a minimum.
The save system is kind of weird. It doesn't break the mold as badly as The Next Big Thing tried to do but is more like what you find in Machinarium or Botanicula, whereby your progress is saved automatically but you can select scenes to replay as if you were watching a movie on DVD.
Great story, great characters, great presentation. Pendulo's really come into their own after their wacky adventures in Runaway. I'd be down for Yesterday 2 if they've got one in the works.

Prototype is a game developed by Radical Entertainment and published by Activision
Traversing in the open world city of Protoype is amazing, probably one of the best in any open world game. You can easily run up buildings, jump off to great heights and then glide very seamlessly. The side activities are very fun ranging from running obstacle courses hitting checkpoints, killing a certain number of enemies using certain powers and using helicopters/tanks to kill enemies. Every activity has a bronze, silver and gold medal depending on how well you complete it
The gameplay mechanics work well, you are given several different powers/abilities to kill enemies and completing main mission, side activities reward you with experience to upgrade your character.
However, Prototype does suffer with bland graphics even for an open world game. Granted, the number of pedestrians, vehicles, enemies, explosions etc. on screen is very impressive so have bland graphics is easier to accept
The game does have a decent story that is told both through cutscenes and consuming enemies/people. After consuming a person, you are treated to a short video of their memory. A cool way to tell the story and mix it with the gameplay. The game is all about getting you in the action as fast as possible so the story takes a back seat to everything else
The main missions are fun and are somewhat varied but most of them feel like you are either killing tons of enemies or running around chasing somebody.
Sadly, Prototype is a technical mess to put it mildly with a very limited resolution and given the vast number of objects on screen at any given time the targeting system seems to target everything except for the one thing you want it to target and the boss battles can create a frustrating difficulty spike
However, Prototype is a very fun if not flawed game. If you feel like running around and killing things with crazy powers and watching a lot of things explode, then this may just scratch that itch

I used to play this game a lot.
It even was, in fact, my favourite multiplayer.
Which has sadly changed since the last update on the 8th of December 2015.
It is undeniably a very unique game & most likely the fastest paced FPS in the world.
What makes this game so gorgeous is not only its creativity with the gameplay, mechanics and weapons, but also a certain simplicity: There is a concept, but no campaign, no special missions. Just the good old gameplay you find in every server.
FPS are naturally repeatitive, that's not a secret, but what is crucial is its capability to keep combats versatile and allow players to shape the battle for it to never become boring and this game managed to do this oh so well.
What I truly love about this game is:
1) The quick progress.
You are paid very well for your success and the awards you receive for certain actions are limitless.
Just by playing for, let's say... 7-9 hours, throughout 3 days, for instance, you have already made some big progress.
Some weapons might be very expensive, but everything is affordable. This is nowhere near being a Pay2Win game.
And the levelling was also quite quick.
You get to max out your armour, your weapons and gadgets after a few days of playing.
But it always depends, it depends on how well you actually do... Good weapons don't automatically put you head-on with the pros & here's my second point:
2) The importance of one's skills.
No matter how many guns you have & how badass youn look in your fancy skins, you don't get to kill someone who's passing by at 350km/h with a spinfusor if you don't even know what you're doing.
It really takes training to be good at this game & every weapon is unique and most of them, if not all, are really good in their own ways. But, of course, it also depends on the user whether it is any good.
Maybe you like it firey, maybe precise, maybe heavy with a lot of lasers and light effects.
And this has also something to do with:
3) The weapons simply being unique.
If you have played Warframe before, or any MMO RPG, you will obviously encounter weapons that are clearly & simply in every aspect objectively stronger than other "low tier" weapons. For instance, starting of with an apprentice staff in WOW, you won't ever be able to kill the Lich King with that thing. Or starting off with the Skana in Warframe, you will, at some point, receive the broken war & notice that every stat is just green and much higher when you compare it with the Skana.
Not in mother♥♥♥♥ing Tribes, because these weapons have their own strengths. It's not like in Warframe, where you just have a stronger weapon to kill stronger enemies the exact same ♥♥♥♥ing way as ever; "Click-click-Dead" (And their powers are just fancier ways to get done with the enemies, let's be honest) In this game, you are everything that matters!
Hell, you can even kill an experienced gamer with a n00b gun, if you know how to do it.
Sure, some weapons deal more damage than others, but that doesn't make them objectively stronger!
Some are explosives, other are rifles, some are disc shooters, some have splash damage, higher fire rates, and overall completely different projectiles and/or ways to deal damage!
This is not about the guns, the armour, the vehicles, this is about you, the player, and how well you do with what you have to choose from!
It took a lot to ruin this game for me and here's what it was:
The update introduced some really interesting new mechanics to the game. The greatest being the completely free customisation, others being rebalanced weapons, new weapons and also, a bunch of new maps were introduced.
The customisation is really exciting, actually.
One gets to choose from the three armour classes and the rest is completely up to them, with some restrictions, obviously, and specification on the armour types.
Look, I don't think it's good or bad. It is some progress, yes, but personally, I preferred the old system.
It just felt right to me, it gave some feeling, meaning and life tothe classes, I'd say, and a role to the player using them.
Those roles were renderred completely redundant after the update, though, because everyone was unique, which is obviously not bad, of course. It is something I love about the game Angels Fall First, for instance, where the customisation is just like that, but to me, it just doesn't fit in the game.
Like I said, this is completely subjective.
What is definitelly not subjective, but just straight up bad, useless, yeah even gamebreaking, is the removal of the Perks, some weapons and the levelling/upgrading system.
Lordy, do I even need to comment on that?
Starting off with the guns:
I understand why some guns were balanced, some clearly needed to be.
The Nova Colt, especially, I guess we all can agree.
I hope, however, that none were nerfed that did not deserved to be nerfed.
I haven't come across one, so far.
I really love that they added new ones, but maybe the blinkfusors being available for all classes makes the game a bit unbalanced. Not too sure though.
But actually removing some?
I really don't see why they should.
The ones that were removed seemed totally fine, at least to me.

But the ones that♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off the most being removed were the MKII versions of the start weapons.
As you may know, every class receives a certain preset of weapons to use, until one earns enough to buy better equipment and every onne of those start weapons has a stronger version of them.
Basically the exact same (mostly), but just stronger in several ways, mostly damage.
Well, those were removed and that's complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t to me.
Because not only is that one thing bad enough, but also the fact that the levelling/upgrading system was removed!
Renderring every weapon weak and sometimes useless.
You know, you were able to upgrade your weapons by simply using them in combat and gaining experience with them, which made them stronger, but you were also able to pay to max it out.
Welp, that is gone now and you might think... the most logical thing to do would be to leave them in the state they would be when they're maxed, right? Well, NOPE, cuz mother♥♥♥♥ing High-Rez nerfed'em all.

But do you know how ridiculous it is to run around with just one ♥♥♥♥ing mine and having to constantly resupply because of the lack of upgrades and perks?
That, people, is the most ridiculous part of it all, if you ask me.
