Soo I've been using this controller for a few months, before it I used an Xbox One controller.
The Good:
- It is made for steam --> easy to use, fast and simple setup
- grip buttons // the extra you need
- steam button
The bad:
- the two ridiculous touchpads --> these are just terrible: slow, sluggish, uncomfortable to use
- too big // personal preference, maybe my hands are just too small for it
- no right stick, only the touchpad
- touchpad instead of a D-Pad // the "clicking" of the touch pad is much slower than the D-Pad
As you can see my main issue is with the innovative touchpads.
Altogether the steam controller is a solid product in my opinion, BUT the touchpad can't replace a D-Pad - slow and sluggish, way faster using an Xbox One / 360 controller.
There are some games the steam controller is very good (although keyboard + mouse is way better in every aspect), but I will stay with the Xbox One controller for games that are made for or need controllers. The right stick is better for camera handling and the D-Pad is really good if you need to be really fast.
My opinion:
For games which are made for / need a controller Xbox One controller. And for everything else keyboard + mouse (e.g.: razer turret if you prefer couch gaming).

A quick summary of sorts:
The Legend of Heroes: Trails of Cold Steel 1 is a good place for newcomers to get into the Trails series. Cold Steel 1 is a school based JRPG, similar to the Persona games, where you go through school life while the story unfolds. Note that combat is TURN BASED STRATEGY. You control Rean Schwarzer, a freshman attending the prestigious Thors Military academy. You are placed in Class 7, a class comprising of various people coming differing backgrounds. Some are nobles, some are commoners, some have secrets to hide and together they form the quirky bunch that is Class 7. Like the Persona games, social links with the many various characters are available. As these bonds develop, you slowly get to learn about them. Get these bonds developed enough and you can make your favourite girl your waifu. What seems like an uneventful school year, turns into a sinister conspiracy as Rean fights to protect his country and loved ones.
Quick Trails primer for newcomers:
The Trails games are set in the continent of Zemuria and the story is split into Arcs, with each Arc taking place in one of the nations. Set in the Liberl Kingdom, Trails in the Sky the First, the Second and Third Chapter (all available on Steam), form the Liberl Arc; the first arc in the Trails Series. The Second Arc takes place in Crossbell State (Zero no Kiseki and Ao no Kiseki- currently only available in Japanese and Chinese; a fan made English patch is also in the works). When fans cry for the Crossbell Arc to be localised, they refer to this duology. The third arc set in the Erebonian Empire hence the name, Erebonia Arc is where the Cold Steel trilogy comes in. Cold Steel 1 is the first game in this trilogy and like I said, is a good place for newcomers as the game slowly introduces you to the places, people, characters and history of Zemuria. As a result, the game can feel tedious because of its slow start. It’s a slow burn but♥♥♥♥♥♥hits the fan by the end of the game and the story will continue with Cold Steel 2 (coming to steam, eventually). The Erebonia Arc will finally close with the release of Cold Steel 3 which hits Japan on 28 September 2017. No word yet on a western release so we can only hope. While each arc follows and concludes the main character’s story, the different arcs overlap to form a giant web, telling an interconnected, overarching tale. If you want to fully understand the world, characters, organisations and lore of Trails, I would highly recommend that you play the other Trails games.

Let me see if I can do a proper review of this movie. See You Next Tuesday is an indie dramedy (drama/comedy) film which tells the story of Mona, a single twenty-something mother-to-be.  Mona is different, and by different I mean that I suspect the goal was to portray a person on the autistic spectrum, or maybe with some unspecific psychiatric disorder. Mona is estranged from her mother and sister, is tormented by (most) of her co-workers, and lives in a hovel of an... apartment? Bed-sitting room? At one point Mona says she does not have a kitchen, and she appears to share a bathroom, but now I'm losing the point.
Mona is just sort of adrift in life. Aside from living in squalor, near social isolation, and having a job that she hates, Mona does not seem to have any idea of what she is going to do once her child is imminently born, nor is it clear that she knows how to care for a child. Despite having a job, Mona does not appear to be financially stable,
The film focuses on Mona, her relationship with her mother and sister (and to a lesser extent, their own struggles), and the various people who are antagonistic to Mona as she makes a series of very unfortunate decisions. Characterizing the plot of See You Next Tuesday is difficult, because there isn't a plot in the traditional sense. What we are shown are a series of loosely connected experiences, almost like a collection of short stories with an overarching theme.
The acting is believable, in a way that is sometimes uncomfortable to watch. Music is used sparsely, nothing in particular stands out to me. Cinematography is done competently. There is a lot of swearing, bigotry, ugly crying, and raw, nasty emotion. There are occasional dabs of violence, but nothing graphic. There are also a couple of brief shots of women's nether regions, for reasons that are not entirely clear.
The subject matter did not particularly appeal to me, and at times it feels like the movie is just floundering, not unlike Mona herself. There are a number of scenes in this movie I found to be distasteful bordering on offensive. The movie ends on a somewhat positive note, at least. It would be difficult for me to recommend this movie to most people. Probably best enjoyed if you are interested in experimental or off-beat films. It wasn't my cup of tea, personally.

This game is a brutal roguelike with a style that reminds me a bit of Mad Max.  It can be incredibly controller-throwingly frustrating (as good roguelikes tend to be), but it hits the sweet spot so many similar games miss where you can lose and actually _want_ to try again and get further next time.  The entire journey is humorous and badass and just raunchy enough to keep it's audience coming back for more.
Gameplay:
top down view of your vehicle and enemies.  You can move pretty freely on the screen, but want to avoid going off of it on top or bottom, or slamming into the rails on the side of the highway.  As a car, you have options at your disposal including ramming and pushing enemies into the rails or off the bottom (or if you're beefy, the top) of the screen, or shooting if you have the money for ranged weapons.  Ammo is unlimited though, so once you get that shotgun or ak47, you can keep firing it forever.  Your goal, no matter how you achive it, is to destroy their vehicle (or passengers) before they destroy yours.  Is this easy?  HELL NO!  Some enemy cars have mounted sawblades, or built in rocket launchers or gatling guns  Add ot that a crew of passengers armed with who knows what, and a driver hell-bent on scrapping you first.
That's the game in a nutshell.  You go through "stages" of Highway, battling the tropes of Post Apocalyptic societies, such as Anarchists, while also sometimes encountering Nerds (who have super-weapons), Corrupt Police, and a few other oddball groups.  You get paid based on how you score your kills via "jobs" so you can choose whether you get your money from murdering passengers with melee weapons, or blowing up the car, or pushing it offscreen or whatever.  At first, this seems like you should pick based on your playstyle, but after playing a while, I found it much better to pick jobs based on what your car and crew can do.  A car with sawblades is just going to be better at melee than a car with a machine gun mount.
Then there are bosses.  They're gonna waste you.
Pros:
The interface isn't too difficult, and despite staying on theme, it's clear what nearly everything does from just descriptions.
Most games are short unless you choose Endurance Mode.
The Soundtrack is badass
The graphics are sweet
The violence is epic
The cars are ♥♥♥♥♥in

You can run out of hitchhikers to pick up and instead of randomizing them, you just get the same one repeated infinitely after that.
There are a number of one-seat vehicles that make it impossible to finish with other hitchhikers for their achivements and unlockable cars.

You may read customer reviews saying that this game relies too much on RNG, that it's unfair, stupidly hard, unbalanced... etc. I disagree with those statements.
It's hard for sure, and unforgiving. But after more than 35 hours of gameplay, I'm now able to finish every single run I start (except for some really special vehicules). It has nothing to do with luck, it just requires a lot of learning.
I'm going to expand on two points : bosses and essential items.
*I saw a lot of people complaining about the bosses. And I have to admit that they were really painful the first time I met them. But they all have a specific pattern, and a weakness (except for the clowns, they're just a bunch of HP wandering on the screen, but they're quite weak so it's not a big deal). Once you know these things, you'll never die because of bosses anymore. You'll just have to be careful, and everything will be fine.
*However, you can't finish the game without some essential items, and that's the second point I'm going to develop here.
IMO, a wrench (allowing you to repair your car while driving) and a good ranged weapon are crucial.
A medikit (allowing you to heal your characters while driving) is really useful too, but on some cars you just have two seats (one character is the driver, so there's only one character able to use an item) so you have to make choices.
Given the fact that the game is a rogue-like, it's supposed to give you items randomly. So you may think that it's unfair : there are items you have to get to finish the game, but you're not even sure the game will ever give them to you.
Actually, RNG is quite insignificant in Death Skid Marks. They are a lot of shops, and not many different items. When you start the game, it's just a matter of minutes before finding a wrench. Will you be able to buy it? I think that's where a lot of beginners have problems. It's tempting to buy drugs, car upgrades, weapons and stuff. But Death Skid Marks has rogue-like elements, and it wants you to manage your resources.
I hope this review makes things a bit clearer : this game has flaws but RNG isn't one.
Don't be afraid to give a try, it deserves it.

Welcome to the world's most bada** road trip through Route 666, populated by crazy rednecks, the Westboro Baptist Church's crazy inbred cousin, a raving pack of Aryan Brotherhood knockoffs, and mental patient furries, on your way to a kicka** concert at the end of the road.
Gameplay:
This ain't your grandpa's roguelike! Strap yourself into one of many vehicles, strap up with whatever you can get your grubby little hands on, and pick up as many hitchhikers as you can fit in whatever hunk of junk you decided to take to the show. All the way down there though, you're going to have to deal with various factions that all want you dead, and they are more than happy to do far more than just run into your car a few times.
On the way there, you'll find a few road stops along the way with more than just greasy truck-stop food (though don't fret. They do have greasy truck-stop food.). You're going to need more than just you, Mark Skid, driving the car if you're going to make it down to the rock concert in one piece. Hitchhikers can be found at the snack bar, you're going to need vehicle upgrades and repairs at the garage, arms dealers can get you outfitted with weapons, jobs can be found there, drug dealers can get your characters to deal more damage and take more punishment, and the Lernie (TM) Mart gan get you special items and your concert tickets. No. I have no idea how the game's equivalent to a gas station gets an RPG.
Other times, you'll find stops where some fool's playing Russian Roulette. You win, get two stats added to all your character's stats, saving you a helluva lot of cash in the long run. Lose, and you can guess what happens...
This game is all about the long haul. If all you're doing is fixing what the last guy did to you, you're going to get outmatched by later vehicles. That Redneck husk of a truck is pretty easy to kill, but dealing with the Aryan Roadkiller's rocket turret WWII artillery vehicle is going to be a bit more difficult if you haven't done anything to your vehicle. Stock paneling might stop pistol bullets pretty well, but minigun bullets, rockets, jackhammers, geek super weapons, etc. will rip through that easier than wrapping paper on Christmas.
Pros:
+Gameplay is very well executed.
+Music gets the job done, even for a guy like me who generally hates harder rock.
+Difficult, but not impossible.
+Pretty darn funny, especially as the logic of the game gets more convoluted. Seems like it can easily come right out of some young metalhead's book, if he wrote one.
+Good variety in how one builds their road to success. No two rides are the same, save for the dying, which will happen a lot. Trust me.
+Rewards you with repeated playthroughs by allowing you to pay total death count for bumper stickers.
+Don't like standard gameplay? There's a boss rush, arcade mode with no stops, and turbo mode.
Cons:
-BEWARE: RNG is present and higher than your standard roguelike, but I found this did not hamper the experience too much, and is controllable if you do the smart thing and get a wrench, medkit, and a balanced attack strategy. You will be annihilated if you don't heed this sage advice. There are bosses built to punish overly focused battle strategies.
-LURNIE'S SPESHUL ADEVENSHUR WIT MURK SHKID!!!
+Hidden pro. Killing Lurnie and stealing his tutorial car. Stupid Lurnie...
-Unlocking more cars can be a bit difficult in the beginning, however once you knock off enough of the major bosses, you can get really decent cars, not that the ones you start out with really suck or anything. The Standardo XL is like the stock weapons in TF2. Statistically the best, but other cars have more specific playstyles. The Standardo XL is not going to have as strong a melee game as the combine harvester with its rotating bars of death.
Final Judgement:
At about $10 when I bought it, I got my money's worth, but it might be a touch too much for others. However, if it's on sale at all, get it and get your rock on today!

I like everything about this game...except the gameplay. It's got a Mad Max-ish aesthetic coupled with filthy humor, which I like, great graphics and an awesome punk and rock soundtrack. Cars exploding, blood and guts flying and music pumping, what's not to like?
Like I said, the gameplay! There is no flow to it at all. It starts, stops, starts, stops, starts and then stops. This game is a simplistic car combat game where the goal is to destroy one car, most of the time, and then pick your next destination by picking a highway sign. Go straight ahead to attack a neo-nazi convoy or turn right to chase down a car full of Westboro Baptist nutjobs. With each choice, there's also a bonus destination you visit before you go to the next stretch of road. It can be an event that gives you a random car, a place where you can mutate your characters or a place to upgrade your weapons. Those are rare, though, and 99% of the time, the bonus destination is a shop.
The shop is just a menu where you click on things to buy them. You can sell, but you don't really have an inventory (only what your characters can carry, which is one active and one passive item). You can upgrade your car and the characters in them, replace the characters if you find a better one, buy more weapons and find special items. These things are all great. The problem is that you also have to visit the shop, you have no choice in the matter, because you must find and buy "tickets" that allow you to actually win if you survive the game. These tickets are completely random. In the session I just had, there had only been a single ticket for sale when I died about 70% to the goal. I needed four. Because apparently surviving wasn't difficult enough, which it is, winning has to be totally up to random chance over whether or not you find these tickets. Because that's fun.
Not only do you have to keep visiting the shop in search of tickets, you also have to find "jobs" for your characters. That's how you make money. There are a bunch of useless ones like "here's $50 (a miniscule amount) for managing to destroy a car without killing any of its passengers (which is hard)", and then there are the good ones like $100 for destroying a car (which is what you do on every single level, so it's $100 guaranteed unless you die) or $75 for beating a level. I think you can guess which ones are in every single shop and which ones are rare, forcing you to visit every shop you can to find them and maximize your income which in turn maximizes your killing potential through buying upgrades.
And there's the problem. You drive for 30 seconds, destroy a car, then you spend a minute looking through the menu. Drive for 20 seconds, menu for 15 seconds, drive for 10, menu for 40, drive for 20, menu for 120... See where I'm going? There's no flow! You can't just choose to have fun and destroy cars, you have to sit around and stare at a menu half the time. The only way to have uninterrupted fun with this game is if you have the enormous luck to score four good jobs and four tickets in your first four shop visits. Then, maybe, you could actually focus on driving and shooting and smashing and having fun.
As it stands, this is half an awesome and hilarious game and half a boring menu-clicking simulator. I've only played about an hour and a half, but I can't see myself going back to it.

I have not found a single negative review that was really justified. The only big con to be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off about is, that they do not really warn anywhere that your progress can get lost if you didn't play much and were inactive for a long time. Happened to me too.
To all those negative reviewers and those distracted by them:
It is free to play. There is nothing in this game that would force you to buy their DLCs, especially not when your main intrest are the guns. There are no P2W mechanisms in this game. Good players get rewarded and can unlock stuff without paying. If you do not want to play the game, but fiddle with the guns you care about you can pay for them. They offer a variety of things to buy, depending on what you want to unlock in the game, without having to spend a lot of time on it. Trust me: New models are not the rewarding thing. To master a model to a degree where you are proud of yourself is the fun. Beside learning how a gun operates of course.
Very quckly you can unlock iconic weapons like the AK-47, Thompson, PPSh-41, B.A.R., the 1911 Colt and many more. Sure it takes effort and patience, but you do not need to pay anything to enjoy this game, unless you are generally unintrested in the mechanics/gameplay of it. You have to learn. This game really is demanding, if you want to become good at it. It is fun to come back to well known models and further improve your records by fine tuning your process, learning to master the camera and just clicking the parts in the perfect order, to save as much time as possible.
To beat a good daily record somebody put up is really fun and gets you 1 credit per gun once you did it the first time.
It is a competitive gun disassembly simulator. That is your main income source to get Credits and XP. Via these you unlock new weapons. If you subscribe to their mailing list, join the Steam Group and find 5 people who played the game to join your friendslist you get 20 Credits for free. The number of guns is constantly growing so it is only fair they demand money to unlock all of them, because they put permanent effort into this game.
There are puzzles and quizes that demand all from your memory. Can you tell to what gun a piece belongs? Do you recognize any of the nearly 200 guns? You get rewards from answering these correctly. It is really fun to see yourself improve at these.
BUT!!! What are the cons?
- The graphics are... functional. To disassemble a gun on an actual table in a room would make the game a bit more immersive.
- The choice of backrounds is way to small and needs costumization.
- Graphic settings are basically non-existant.
- The music is very annoying and should be turned off right after the start.
- The keyboard controls are not costumizable. They might be ok by default, but I use a different keyboard layout. I always have to set it back to a standard QWERTY when I play this.
- Many functions of the guns do not have a key binding, like putting on the safety, pulling the hammer, retracting a shootgun etc. Also the slow mo must be activated via clicking on menu points.
- Putting a gun on safety or emptying the magazine sometimes forbids you to alter settings of the gun, that would in reality still remain functional. Reloading a gun after having reloaded will not add an extra bullet (oddly it does at shooting ranges). You can not add bullets to guns that would allow that after you fired a few rounds, like shootguns.
- Animations are sometimes strange. Recoil animations make the bullet clip through the barrel etc.
- Some guns have way too low rates of fire. (PPSh-41 is off by almost 100%)
- Some guns do not clearly say what model they show. You can not modify weapons to different barrel sizes or use different types of ammunation.
-Many inner parts of the guns are completely untexturized. Ugly, unrealistic and sadly makes them hard to see against a similar coloured background. Worst about that are all the unrifled barrels... really. More details!!!
- Some grouping of parts seems illogical. Sometimes you seem to have to click every single part, sometimes huge groups come off with one click.
And the biggest con of all:
The sounds are generic and are basically the same for every model. Stupid electric screwing sounds all the time. The same sounds for magazines for every gun. The shot sounds are bad, weirdly timed and show all their ugliness in slo-mo.
That is the main reason why I'd say: Do not pay money for weapons in this game unless they put the effort into the models to actually do some real recording on the sounds they make when fired, reloaded etc. It really makes all the guns seem like toys.

Fun factor: 9/10

You start out as Henry White and his friend cooper who works for a charitable company that helps the homeless. Now you take over our main protagonist John Yesterday who has amnesia and is trying to figure out who he really is and about his past. You work for Henry White doing research for him when you start remembering things and realize all is not what it seems. This all leads up to a choice of four different endings and will give you some replay value to see them all.
The art style is fantastic and really fits with the game. Gameplay is what you would get from point and click adventures with some tough challenging puzzles but nothing too hard to accomplish.  There’s also a hint button you can use to help you out if you’re stuck which recharges over time after every use. This way you do actually have to try. It features a variety of transportation options like busses, trolleys, light rail (they call them trams), metro lines, and ferries.  I've tried both campaigns and sandbox, and find the sandbox to be more enjoyable.  In the campaign, I'd get upset that it would move on just as I was starting to get the city the way I liked it.
There are some klunky parts.  For example, if you want to change a street to add a lane or designate a lane as a bus lane, you have to demolish it and re-create.  Any transportation stops along that street are also demolished and removed from your routes.  You then have to re-create those as well after you're done the construction.
When setting up routes initially, you determine the order of the stops.  However, if you add a stop later, the AI determines where it will go.  This is usually placed logically, but there are times that it would be nice to adjust it.
Building metros can be a challenge with the underground view.  It's not possible to turn off the surface streets, and this hides parts of the metro you're trying to build.
Also, as soon as you start the game for the first time, go into settings and turn on the option to scroll the map by moving the cursor to the edge.  By default, you have to use keyboard commands to move the map.  I almost gave up on the game when first playing, because this was so difficult to do.  It's a whole different game with the scroll turned on.  I'm not sure why the default is off.
All in all, though, I highly recommend this game.

I've had mine since near launch (purched from a gamestop...), and love it!
Biggest pro's:
-I'd rank its ergonomics above xbone and ps4 controllers, though it takes some getting used to
-I'd also rank it above any other controller in terms of being an input device overall once you get a feel for the trackpads. Gyro, dual stage triggers, all the tricks the pads can do... so good.
-some people complain about the abxy buttons being too small/hard to reach... well either get used to them like you would with any other new input device (thanks, Nintendo) or rebind them somewhere else then! because...
-insane customizability means you can get it to work with just about any game pretty much how you want
biggest cons:
-insane customizability means you can get it to work with just about any game pretty much how you want... Its incredibly daunting, especially for someone who may just want to get straight to playing. This is mitigated by community profiles and at the very least workable generic profiles, but...
-there is the big hurdle of having to get used to the controller in the first place due to how different it comes across when compared to the xbone or ps4 controllers. Some of my biggest pro's are only after tons of use and getting used to the dual trackpads... and I still only use the left one if absolutely necessary.
Its kind of a double wammy of 2 substantial hurdles, which hurts the controller (a bit unfairly imo). The barrier to entry is high for this one, the consumer needs both an open mind/willingness to try a different controller as well as a curiosity or desire to delve into its workings. The process of really "getting" the controller takes more than a day of game play imo, fps games didnt click with it for me for several months! That makes the controller a really tough sell.
But once you get over those two hurdles, oh man. This controller works wonders. The only con at that point would be just how loud/clicky and stiff some of the buttons are, namely the bumpers. paddles, and trackpad clicks. Its easy to ignore those cons though imo, considering just how much "power" is at your finger tips with this controller, but if Valve ever works on/releases a revision model I do hope they change that.
Do I recommend it? YES! ... With the caveat that you have to approach it with the mindset of "I'm going to learn it first, then teach it what I want it to do" instead of expecting it to immediately work perfectly how you want.

This is an interesting game to me in that I really like the story it was trying to tell and I like the ways in which the game tried to tell the story. There are a few thematic narrative elements to the game that really work well, particularly in terms of parallelism (i.e., paralleling one set of events with another).
The problem for me was that the good story was wrapped up some clunky mechanics based on how current adventure games are implemented. As one example, your character sort of "teleports" around to make the game a little less tedious, so you don't have to see the toon walking from place to place. However, while nice from a game play perspective, it sort of disconnects you from the environment you are playing in. There is also the standard adventure game problem of being a character that ends up carrying around odd items just in case they become useful and then figuring out strange ways to combine these items to achieve an effect.
Again, though, the story is very intriguing. The pacing of the story is held up a bit by those mechanics I just mentioned as well as the fact that much of the story is filled to you in expository segments that don't flow as part of the story, but rather that take place via "disconnected" close ups of characters faces. Yet, even with that, I go back to what I keep saying: the story is intriguing, albeit very dark. I think this game was quite ambitious in the story it wanted to tell and did some clever tricks in terms of how it was presenting, including a few twists along the way. There are multiple endings and, at least for the one I chose, I found it a very satisfying conclusion.

What is done well:
+Voice acting
+Puzzles (Most of them)
+Overarching & Mature Storyline
+Lead Character(ization)
+No technical glitches (at least none that i encountered)
What could have been better:
-Atmosphere & Visuals (Being partly a hidden item game, some scenes will make it impossible to detect ineractive items unless you use hints)
-Short playthrough (will last 3-5 hours but has tight gameplay for those hours)
-Inventory (Some items you acquire are never used or stay after their use)
-Other than lead characters (nothing special and completely wasted love-interest)
-Storyline leaves a lot to be desired when you finish
-Almost neglible background score/music
Overall - I would give it a 7/10 (vs. expectation and cost at $5). Fans of point-and-click, other Pendulo games and satanic storylines would have a decent time.

This is not simply one of my favorite JPRGs.  It's one of my fave games ever.   And I've  been gaming since....well, let's just say that my original console was Atari 2600, the year it came out.
I've played 100+ hours of ToCS on my PS3s and PSTV.   It's kinda hokey, sappy, and not the best-looking game by far but it just clicks.   The turn-based combat manages to stay fun throughout.   It never seems grindy.  But it's the story that pulls you in and keeps you invested in the game.     For the most part, it's not dark.  It's not edgy.  It doesn't try to be hip.  Fan service isn't obtrusive.  It's sincere and not saccharine in its relatively good-natured approach.   The characters and story mature and develop in unison.   I will say that the game ends on a cliffhanger.   So if you haven't played ToCS2 on PS3/PSTV, you'd better hope that the second part makes it to PC.  [Edit: Apparently it is! :)]
Again, coming from both the PS3 and PSTV versions, the PC version is simply breathtaking.   If you are totally new to ToCS, you won't obvious share and appreciate this evaluation.   It's a joy to have it run buttery smooth at 60 fps.   The models don't look upgraded, but the textures certainly have.    It looks absolutely glorious at 4k on my LG 55".  Even the colors have a vibrance and pop that literally makes the PS3 version pale in comparison.  No hiccups or bugs noticed thus far.   I'm gaming with my X1 controller.   No problems there.   (It does seem strange not seeing my PS prompts though.)

First things first: The game is hard. I ended up aborting 4 or 5 times when my neighbors showed up with eons better ships and slughtered my entire civilization. I took some time to read some guides and watch some noobtube videos to get the process down.
I'm glad I did! The main game is played in turn based stragtegic view, where you can colonize worlds, improve ones you already have, or build ships for your fleets. It can be a little bit luck of the draw, as you can be hamstrung by systems with tons of wormhole entrances and bad or inhabitable planets, or hit the jackpot with easily defended garden world systems.
There are many races and they arent just new skins on the same thing with vague bonus differences like CIV. There are SIGNIFICANT differences in the races that will dramatically alter the way you play. Most likely you will find one that works for you and play it nearly exclusively. (Vaulters FTW!)
Battles are beutiful to look at and it's a real pleasure to watch your fleet blow away all comers.
Which brings me to a negative: The combat, while pretty, was a little bit of a let down. I was expecting something akin to Sins of a Solar Empire or Homeworld, but this is much closer to Civilization. The combat plays out in front of you, with only slight input from you in a sort of Rock, Paper, Scissors sequence where you go utilize Long Range, Medium Range, and "Hand to Hand"
If you enjoy Civilization, will take the time to overcome the 90 degree abgle learning curve, you'll find a great game here.

Deus Ex: Human Revolution is a story-driven, stealth-based cyberpunk shooter in which the player has to navigate a future world where human biotechnology (augmentations) have become commonplace and highly advanced. Placed in the city of Detroit in 2027, you encounter a tense world caught up in a fierce ethical debate over the use of human augmentations. This theme provides an excellent philosophical dilemma to many character interactions and remains a major focal point of the story all throughout.
Heavy on atmosphere, the game takes somewhat after Blade Runner in terms of aesthetics and sticks to its own color scheme very consistently. This produces a fascinating game world that only becomes more interesting as the details of your surroundings are revealed to you. The game has a couple large cities and various other hubs in which you can travel freely, progressing in the main questline and completing side objectives at your own pace.
The layout of these areas encourages exploration, and you need to be pretty crafty to get to certain areas. The level design in general is quite well-done, although the cities can feel somewhat jumbled at first. Many areas are non-linear, allowing you to take multiple approaches to infiltrating enemy bases or whatever else. Want to take a stealthy route, crawling through air vents and dropping down to stealthily knock out your opponents? That's just fine, and often leads to the discovery of some interesting hidden areas. Want to do a full-frontal assault every time? That's equally possible, but you have to know when to harness the cover mechanic and when to conserve ammunition.
You have access to a number of guns and grenades, as well as hand-to-hand combat. Each of these can be enhanced in some way with various upgrade kits scattered throughout the map: increased ammo capacity, faster reload speeds, cooling systems for automatic weapons, and more. When sneaking up on opponents, you also have the choice of knocking them unconscious or killing them with your fists via a quiet takedown cutscene. As for stealth, the cover mechanic is much less frustrating to use than, say, the one in Metal Gear Solid V, and the level design supports its use very well in most areas. Enemies enter an "Alert" mode if they are suspicious of your presence and a "Hostile" mode when engaged in direct combat, and will resuscitate any unconscious enemies whose bodies are not hidden well enough. Unfortunately, hiding from enemies yourself is a little too easy, because they cannot climb ladders or enter air vents, and will give up searching for you after only a minute or two.
Every action you make, including fighting enemies, hacking into computers, and finding hidden areas through exploration grants you XP, which is translated into a "Praxis point" when enough is acquired. These points allow you to upgrade some of your abilities, including getting more defensive armor, stealth enhancements, hacking abilities, and more. They can be saved over time for use later, which is a nice allowance. You can also trade goods with merchants stationed in city hubs in exchange for credits, which can be used to purchase weapons, grenades, hacking tools, Praxis kits, and other useful items. However, there are only a couple of merchants in each city, which can be somewhat annoying if you need to drop off some loot but aren't near a place to sell it. The inventory uses an upgradable grid system, with heavier items taking up more boxes than lighter ones. This design works fine, but some items are oddly unstackable, such as grenades, which can be frustrating.
The game's two greatest strengths are probably its dialogue and its story. You can interact with every NPC in the city regions, and many of them have a couple unique lines to say about your location or current events. Their dialogue changes somewhat as the story continues, making note of newsworthy happenings. Some lines are reused, and there is no visual indication that you have already spoken to a character, but it is still interesting to speak to everyone you meet: they do not necessarily idolize you, and some will even react with disgust at your presence. When conversing with quest-important NPCs, you generally have a wheel of multiple dialogue options, similar to the one in Fallout 4, but with less ambiguity as to the meaning of each message. Your character will occasionally ramble on about things that are not necessarily reflected in the description of your dialogue choice, which is irritating, but you are still given a decent amount of freedom with what you say. One augmentation upgrade even gives you a chance to catch the personality traits of each character based on their dialogue, which can make persuasions more feasible.
I found that the plot became increasingly compelling as it advanced, perhaps because it became somewhat darker in tone near the end. As it became more complex, I felt truly immersed in the game world. The game has multiple endings, and the concluding quests required some major decisions which left me thinking for some time afterwards. I felt that the pacing was appropriate and consistent, and I never felt rushed: with some timed exceptions, you really are capable of completing most quests at exactly your own speed.
The art direction is great, and the graphics are nice enough, if somewhat plain. The only technical issue I had with the game were the cutscenes. While they are fortunately not overused and are skippable, they all seem to be recorded in something like 720p, so they come out very grainy on a higher-resolution display; the transition from gameplay to cutscene is a little jarring. Furthermore, some of the dialogue cutscenes have a bit of echo in the background, but this may have been an intentional choice to increase the realism of certain rooms. The voice acting is pretty good, although the dialogue animations of NPCs are amusingly fidgety.
In conclusion, Deus Ex: Human Revolution is a whole lot of fun. If you're looking for an action-stealth game with a good plot, this is the game for you: the gameplay is polished, the story is fantastic, and the characters are well-developed. The default price is $20, which is pretty reasonable: I got just over 40 hours in one playthrough. For that amount of gameplay, the sale price is even better. Barring the few issues I mentioned above, I really enjoyed this game, and am happy to recommend it to anyone reading this review.

This is an old school RPG based around the Serious Sam franchise. You'll have a top down map with enemy encounters and be taken to a RPG style battle system. The map worlds are literally one screen sections, if your party is wiped out three times, you need to restart that one map. It would feel right at home on the original Gameboy or a mobile phone. Random battles can happen when you walk one space on the map, so if that angers you, avoid this game.
The real game is the combat, each battle pits you and your allies against several if not dozens or hundreds of enemies chasing after you. You select fight, swap weapon or item. Any of your characters can use any weapon. Here's where it gets interesting, the weapons and enemies have uses like in an action game. The revolver will shoot at the closest enemy, the shotgun is a defensive weapon if any enemies or big projectiles get within a proximity of the user, the rocket launcher sends a spread of 3 rockets one per turn, the grenade launcher does big damage.... if you can hit your target in it, since enemies move, they might be gone before the grenade lands, and there's a mini gun where you aim the line and fire until the end of the turn.
Enemies have different properties too. Some will stay far and shoot, others will chase after you and damage you, killing themselves. Enemies are quicker and slower than you, so you can either outrun them or they'll catch you. All of the combat is a really fresh take on RPG turn based combat. Oh and as your turn is happening, you can move your party up and down on the screen to dodge projectiles or stall for time as you wait for the next shotgun blast.
After every battle, you get full health. The items mostly consist of armor power ups, health, attack buffs. All of which seem to be needed for bosses at the end of each one screen map.
So if I enjoy the game how could I give it a negative rating?
The game is a steep climb in difficulty before you know it. Walls of bullets, things become unavoidable, deaths are inevitable even if party members are revived with full health after a battle. Everything needs to be done in battle and that is the real downfall. You cannot use any items such as armor outside of battle. So if you're facing a wall of bullets against dozens or hundreds of enemies, you'll just get slaughtered again and again. Luck of who you fight plays a big part of your survival. You can grind all you want before a boss battle. The catch is once you've used your 3 lives, you'll need to start that map over again without all of the grinding you just did. Another problem with lack of grinding is that you can't go back to a previous map to grind and no amount of grinding will save you from bullet walls that comes with every enemy encounter past a few maps. Another downfall is there is no native controller or steam support. Not even key binding, but everything else is a much bigger glaring issue.
In all, its just a fresh take on old school RPGs and I like it, but its as if the developers didn't play the game past a certain point. If you're looking for a very difficult new RPG that is unforgiving and makes grinding meaningless, this is the game for you.

I own both CiM1 and CiM2 and so far I have to say I enjoyed CiM1 a lot better.
First of all let me begin by saying that CiM2 does have certain improvements over the first version, which includes:
- Now you can build your own roads and expand the city;
- Day/Night shift and timetable settings;
- Ticket prices are now based on distance (or zones) rather than flat fare in CiM1;
- More realistic graphics and city landscapes (for example now roads can be actually curly rather than in 8 directions only in CiM1).
However there are many things which I do not enjoy about this game.
- The game is pretty much DLC/community based. If you buy the base game you will find only 5 maps (including a tiny tutorial map) and very few vehicles. The metro, which is supposed to be the backbone of any serious city transportation system, only has 2 trains available and are pretty much the worst ones. All decent maps/vehicles come from either the community or paid DLCs. You don't get much from the base game.
- Stupid depot system. Yes the vehicle depot is added in CiM2, which some people might consider it an improvement. However I find it too often that my depot becomes too full and too many scheduled departures missed.
- Lack of tutorial. With so many new features added why not add a serious tutorial to explain the complicated features? CiM1 has, in my opinion, a very decent tutorial mission.
- The construction of the metro is very troublesome. Maybe I'm wrong, but it's very difficult to construct an underground metro line within the city. The elevation just don't match. (In CiM2 you can adjust the elevation freely with your pageup/pagedown keys, while in CiM1 you only have 5 levels: 3 underground, ground level and elevated.) This problem is made worse by the underground depot, which I have never successfully connected to any underground line. So far 70% of my metro lines are either overhead or on the ground, and all depots are on the ground.
In conclusion, while some people may cheer the new added features, I must say that I enjoyed CiM1 better than CiM2 even when I try hard to switch from 1 to 2. Would rather recommend version 1 to anyone who does not want to smash their computer and/or keyboard while playing a simulation game.

I'm a gun collector and amateur gunsmith, and have experience field and detail stripping a variety of firearms for cleaning and minor gunsmithing work. It always surprises me how well skills learned in the real world transfer to computer simulations and vice versa.
I wish I had known about this software much earlier! It is an extremely helpful tool, and would be an excellent supplement to gun disassembly guides and videos.
It might be interesting to note that something this software does not capture is how physically difficult some parts of gun assembly and disassembly can be. (This is no fault of the software).
Frequently, parts in the real world are stubborn, and assembling/disassembling them can test the limits of your fine motor skills, hand strength, and cleverness. With real guns, you will bleed, sweat, and occasionally bugger gun finishes; there are also many different (often expensive) tools that you need, particularly for detail stripping.

I enjoy playing this game. It takes some time getting used to controls and then figuring out the mech/mechs that work for your playstyle. Sure there are "meta" builds but as in any game these don't always for for everyone. Many of the mechs and builds I use are from from meta but they work for me and how I play. Hit hard fast and in the face. Do I sometimes get wasted by a sky full of missles? Yep. But do I vaporize an Atlas's front CT armour in seconds with the constant rattle blazing from my Urbanmechs four Heavy machine guns as I dance around his Autocannon as laser blasts. Yep. You want to spend some extra bucks and buy some stuff great. Will it make you a great pilot that wins every match? Nope.
The learning curve is a bit of a climb but there are a number of good YouTubers you can gain insight and information from. Like any online game there will be your trolls and annoying basement dwelling fools but at least you can serve them up a face full of lasers.
The game is in constant motion and the need for new maps is there at the moment but they are coming and the latest maps added are really fun and offer some great strategic play. The seperation of Faction, Group, and Free play mean you can choose how hardcore your experience is. You are not required to play the more hardcoreplayer base in faction play if you don't want to.
Overall it's a good experience for both Battletech fans and those who are tired of a combat knife being the most powerful weapon known to man in a first person shooter. This game not only requires a well thought out mech build with a skilled piliot but it also require that pilot to make sound tactical choices and to cooperate with his team.

The most important thing in my opinion for a mech game is for them to feel big, and clumsy, and dangerous. MWO nails this 100% with big stompy sounds, a decent sense of scale, cool-looking vision modes, and the enforcement of the idea that you are not a giant war machine, you're a little dude inside of one pushing buttons. The default cockpit voice kinda sucks but there are ways around that, and everything else feel-wise is there.
The game itself however has become really, really disappointing. The weapon balance has been moved from one side to another (in early release autocannons were king, then it was LRMs, then lasers, PPCs, etc etc etc) and this is a sign of a bad development team: there should be a happy medium where all weapons can be equally valuable in the right hands. At its state two months ago when I stopped playing, it was all about alpha spam: cram as many high-damage weapons on your mech that you possibly can, and fire them all at the same time. The days of picking your target, aiming for soft spots and carving up your target are mostly over in favor of "stick with the blob and alpha strike everything". Clan Warfare, the big multiplayer "campaign" is a disaster - there are a few high-profile groups/clans that cruise around sealclubbing, and you're either going to be the seal or the club. It almost never feels fair one way or the other.
The company's business model is actually not that bad for an F2P title, especially now that they've homogenized mechs with the skill tree system and omnimechs (previously you'd be limited in what weapons you could mount to which mech variant you had, so a Jagermech JM6-D variant could mount more Autocannons than a JM6-C for example). Now many of the best mechs are omnimechs and can be customized with whatever modules and weapons that you choose. I actually don't like this, but then again I'm a Battletech lore lover from a pathetically long time ago. That's another thing that PGI has dropped the ball on: they can't really seem to decide where and how this game fits into the lore so they're just kinda throwing things together. This isn't a dealbreaker for me, but they're really obnoxious about it and that turned me off of them as a group.
The game itself has just ended up feeling half-done. There is a serious lack of matchmaking, so it's not uncommon to end up in a game where better than half of your team is all running LRM boats or something. With the forementioned homogenization of mechs I can understand why and how this happens but it's still unbelievably annoying to realize you're the only non-sniper on the team, or are the only one prepared (or willing) to play the objective.
Overall this is a tough call. The game itself is fun enough even if I don't like the people who made it, and in a perfect world, without meta-gaming being a thing, mouse timing macros being widely used by everyone to maximize their "efficiency" (and being explicitly encouraged by PGI that that's not against any rules, go ahead), aggressive sales techniques (the age-old "the newest mech is generally the best" maxim holds true here) and the lack of strategy or technique becoming more the norm means that I won't drop another cent on it and encourage you to do the same.

Its story may not win any awards, especially with this pacing, but the sheer variety of the hidden object scenes and puzzles of Endless Fables 2 will provide ample entertainment to everyone.
Although Frozen Path is part of the Endless Fables series, its story actually reuses the same elements as one of Sunward Games’ earlier games, The Legacy of Vulcan: we must uncover the truth about an ancient crime among the gods themselves.
Said crime is the death of the Norse deity Baldur, and to find out what really happened to him, we must pass some standard hidden object tropes, such as a mandatory kidnapped friend, plus meeting and helping a few supernatural entities who aid us in the investigation.
While the story is nice and has no real weak points, it is obviously in a secondary role compared to gameplay. Frozen Path is especially strong in hidden object scene design, where we get everything from list-based searches to single-screen puzzles and fragmented object scenes. Combined with the usual puzzle types, they form a little bit directionless, but incredibly entertaining, colourful (and a bit expensive) HOG.

I don't really like jumpscares or horror games made with the Unity tool, but I do like anime style art and visual novels, so I thought I'd give this one a go seeing as it costs oh so very little.
Some of the jumpscares were a little off. For example:
Even though the story is very short, the jumpscares were fairly repetitive. For example:
...I do have to admit I played this game during the day and without headphones, because I scare very easily. (But that doesn't mean none of the jumpscares got me! It's just, as soon as I was able to predict them, they didn't scare me anymore.)
The voice acting would've been a nice touch, if the acting wasn't so bad. "Ah. It's a ghost." --> that didn't sound like the character was scared at all. It sounds like someone's just speaking the words from the page, without visualising an actual scary scene. (Were the voice actors chosen simply because they could speak Japanese? I'm not sure if this game was originally Japanese or not, but I'm guessing it wasn't.) Anyway, voice acting is nice and all, but without professional actors it just deducts from the whole experience.
In this case I'd say: maybe give the player the option to turn the voices off. Cause every time they started talking (out loud, I mean) the creepy atmosphere disappeared.
After having started the third chapter I wondered why the first two chapters weren't added together to make one chapter. That's because there is suddenly a different main character for the last chapter. I mean, I understand that there's three chapters because of the three locations, but I still think it would've been better to have two chapters with two different protagonists. What do you think?
I really didn't expect the twist at the end of the second chapter, because I was thinking we'd be following DiS for the duration of the three chapters and it's the kind of twist you'd expect at the end of all things.
The twist at the end of the third chapter, on the other hand, was not unexpected AT ALL. The story kept hinting at
in a not-so-subtle way - like
- kind of like the mannequins I was talking about earlier (in the second spoiler).
The anime art style was quite nice, I really liked it!
I just didn't understand Sui's alternate costume: it's not in the game proper, only in the options menu, but just its being there tells the player a lot about Sui.
I'm not sure about the virtual environment, uh, like, I mean the backgrounds and mannequins and stuff: it didn't look very special to me, just another Unity horror game, I guess.
I didn't make use of the VR support, because I don't have an Oculus Rift. (VR horror games just creep me out way too much!)
I'm giving the review a thumbs up because I intend to play it again sometime. It's short enough for that. Maybe I'll try to beat the high score.

In theory, I should like this game... I like adventure games, I like puzzles, and I like supernatural stories.  However, this game seemed to fall flat on every front, and is exceptionally short as well.  Once the story plot gets revealed more, it felt like that should be just the prologue - they could have done so much more with it.  The hermit/monk sequence and overarching plot left me yearning to play through some more flashback scenarios around when the character[s] developed originally to unlock other game mechanics that change things up as you learned about them... but they left that mostly unexplored.
On the puzzle front, there were a couple parts in which it felt like I was accomplishing something, but by and large the puzzles weren't that puzzling or satisfying.  The worst kind of puzzles are the obvious ones or the ones that just leave you trying different things ... and Yesterday primarily had those two kinds.  Consequentially, there either wasn't too much of an 'aha' moment, or that special moment when you eventually figure things out may be marred with a 'no way' moment that makes you question whether that is really practical and saps the fun out of it.
If the game goes on sale for a few bucks, I think it might still be worth it for adventure game fans... but in general I can't recommend it unless you are really looking for something quick and different to change things up for a few hours (it took me about 4-ish hours).  On the plus side, the art is quite well done and charming, but something a little grittier and less cartoony might have been more well-suited to its darker theme.  It's very similar to the Runaway games and The Next Big Thing on the art direction front... but one size doesn't always fit all.

GAMEPLAY: As a classic Sierra/LucasArts-style adventure game, Yesterday tries very hard to smooth over the inherent tedium of the genre. There is very limited walking animation, as the player most often warps directly to the focal point of a click. There is a built-in hint system that nudges rather than spoilers with a timer that attempts to keep the player from exploiting it (the timer is very short however, so if you're stuck, you'll get your answer soon enough). On the plus side, this keeps the game moving; there is some question, however, whether or not this diminishes the investment one might put into solving the puzzles and the sense of accomplishment that acts as the only game-y reward in this style of game. The puzzles are reasonable. The few leaps of logic are easy to work with given the hint system and the simple fact that madly clicking all over the screen will often yield progress. It is also worth noting that it is entirely impossible to fail at this game. There are no scenarios that actually present a failure state despite the narrative suggesting the imminence of danger to the player character.
STORY/PLOT: Classic adventure games are all about story and puzzles. The overwhelming sense is that Pendulo wanted to make a 20 hour game but only had the time/budget/skill for 4 hours. As a result, there are poorly developed characters with inexplicable motivation, rushed exposition, an abrupt ending, and (perhaps most jarringly) an over-reliance on hackneyed hero tropes (looking at you Buddhist Vodoo sensei). The game's narrative approach is best executed in the very beginning. Without giving too much away, if you find yourself strongly disliking the initial player character, rest assured that it is one of the few well-executed narrative devices the game offers.
STYLE: The graphical style appears to be suggestive of a comic book style with text pop-ups and concurrent frames of action. The character models are generally horrible. The presentation of the characters is also not done any favors from the Fallout 1/2 style dialogue windows where characters look directly at the camera while speaking with very little facial animation or proper lip synching. Given the limitations of the game's production, I am inclined to forgive this forray into the Uncanny Valley, but it does have the effect of rendering what limited characterization and drama that does exist flat and often laughable. It would have been much more effective to merely voice the dialogue in the regular gameplay field. As to the voice acting itself, I am pleased that it is far from the game's greatest failing. It is certainly a far stretch from exemplary, but it convey's its meaning ably enough to not be the biggest distraction in the unfolding of the game's ambitious plot.
BOTTOM LINE: I cannot recommend this game unless you are dying for a semi-3D adventure and have played literally everything else. The plot is disjointed. The characters are shallow. The puzzles are uninspired and require little to no cleverness or ingenuity. Perhaps the 70's grindhouse Satanic cult theme will entice you, but much like the afore mentioned efforts, that too does little to honor the glory of the dark master. Avoid Yesterday like yesterday's sushi.

The characters are easy to love and they're all unique with stories to tell. Speaking of stories to tell, all of the NPCs feel like real peaple with real lives. Their dialouge is always changing, so I recommend speaking to them as often as possible.
Besides that, there isn't much else to say, except this is personally my favorite game because of the fond memories I have with it.  It's worth checking out. I also recommend playing Trails in the Sky first, but this is also an entry point into the Trails series, so there's no harm either way. There are just a few things you won't understand immediately without playing the Sky arc.

This is a very enjoyable game on it's own right, and you DO NOT at all need to pay anything to play or win. Also, there is quite a bit more strategy involved than meets the eye. Simply clicking on random units won't win the most challenging levels, though you can still win by doing so. Instead, you need to watch the flow of battle and cummon the units to 1) take advantage of your opponent's weaknesses, and 2) avoid defeat yourself. Also, there is roa lot of roleplaying and progression, allowing you to upgrade your units as you play. Again, this will require grinding to get gold to purchase upgrades, but it is not bad, and it is still enjoyable.
Unlike many Free To Play games, there is NO limit on play time or resources. You grind for gold by replaying previous levels.
Am I a fan of F2P games? NO. But for this game, I'll make an exception.

I originally played Trails of Cold Steel on the PS Vita, but when I heard about the graphical enhancements, new features and added voice work that Durante and XSeed had poured into this port, I knew that I would have to double-dip and pick up what can pretty safely be called the now-definitive English version of the game.  It runs beautifully on a modern gaming PC, and of course, has never looked or sounded better, but options exist that will allow the game to run well on even the most basic device that can manage DX11.
In much the way that Trails in the Sky begins with the familiar archetypes and tropes of JRPGs and anime of the 90s, Cold Steel takes more contemporary cliches to begin with, and then expertly expands upon them, exploring or subverting them in ways that you don't expect, and crafting a world with heart and depth that makes Zemuria feel like a second home for as long as you're willing to pour hours into exploring it.
The turn-based combat can offer as much or as little strategy as you please depending on how you set your difficulty.  Breeze through and focus on the story, or grind it out, maximizing your ARCUS builds until not even bosses can touch you.
There's a social element this time to the game, and building link levels with your classmates will lead to new scenes and stonger link bonuses.  The link attacks and other systems add back a bit of complexity that has been lost in Cold Steel's more streamlined quartz crystals.
While longer-time Trails fans will find plenty of references and through-lines to get excited about, Cold Steel represents a good point of entry for newcomers to the series, particularly as Trails in the Sky continues to show its age, if only visually.  The Erebonian arc starts here, and there are new friends to join you as you begin to explore the history and politics of not only the empire itself, but of the Zemurian continent and its various factions and faces.

What can SSTRE offer you, my dear reader? Timewise, there’s not much: 2 hours if you’re trying to clown the final boss without using any items - i.e. if you like to die a lot. Yes, three sentences into this review and we’re already at the boss - it’s that short. But there’s a lotta game in those 2 hours, you betcha! This little guy is ripped with gameplay. Consider this: JRPG, shmup, and puzzle all within a glorious 8-bit aesthetic. {The 8-bit/retro motif has come back, and actually been back for so long now that the phrase seems to describe little.} First off, the game is incredibly generous, throwing us into the action with minimal story elements to further bog down an already belief-weary mind.
So...There’s a lotta game here. And for those of you who find endless joy in point grinding, this is a great deal for $5. SSTRE puts you on a small map with a few items to collect and lot’s of monsters to dispatch. The “random encounters” work more like minesweeper than FF: moving into certain spaces triggers an encounter. Yet unlike minesweeper, the encounters can’t be avoided - oh and there’s no run option either, mmkay? Vambreem rags on Croteam’s horde shooter by having characters automatically run backwards during combat - now come on, that’s hilarious! Hordes of enemies are, during each 5-second turn, getting closer and closer, some faster than others. A 3-option battle menu appears between each 5-second turn. The choices are limited, but as the writer says “vigor is a byproduct of brevity”. Selecting shoot has your “Sam” fire off his equipped weapon; swapping let’s you change weapons but at the cost of 2 seconds of your 5-second turn - 2 seconds you won’t have when you’re about to be obliterated by dozens of headless suicide bombers; using items is actually pretty ♥♥♥♥ing useful in this game, believe it or not: armor and attack buffs, shmuppy full-screen bombs, and instant full-party revives all seem more essential to combat than the dagone weapons!
Being a short game, weapons are introduced very early. I like that. The variety between the six weapons and their appropriate use pump up the games strategic chops. Earlier I mentioned that the weapons and items were unbalanced and choosing not to rely on the items as much really gives the difficulty a shot in the arm. Behind the weapons and enemies is your basic paper-rock-scissor mechanic. When those suicide bombers come a runnin, get out that minigun and pump em full! Use the grenade launcher on the big boys; and though it’ll cost you a full turn to charge, the cannon is great for taking out hordes of really powerful enemies - just don’t leave anything behind to take you out while recharging the cannon or swapping to a different weapon.
All in all, the game packs three levels. Not too much by any standard, to be sure, but there is some replay value here. Each of your steps is counted toward your score. So, one could play it all again, going for completion with minimal steps. Also, getting to know the different weapons, how they’re used, and who to use them with adds variety to the battles, ensuring you never have the same one twice.
Rough around the edges, but there are more than enough explosions to make up for it.

A game where competing civilizations battle it out for supremacy.  We've never seen that.  Wait there's Civilization.
Ok but this is in space!! oooh..   Wait we have Alpha Centuri and Beyond Earth
No no no this is galactical, multiple planets and totally different races.   So like Masters of Orion?  Honestly I never played Masters of Orion, so ...  maybe?
But there's many games like Civilization, so now we know what it is, how is it?  Well let's use Civilization as a baseline.
Well in Civilization everything is intuitive.  Need a unit, you an just build it.   Need a improvement, you can find it.  There's a very simple (ish) tech tree in every game.  And with the exception of Civilization 3 where you can have chariot units murder millions of soldiers with guns you have a very easy to understand military system for the most part.
And the key to Civilization is you can always look at your advisors and they'll help you build.
Endless Space seems to take the opposite view.  The biggest issue is there appears to be no advisors.  So quite often you're just blindly guessing what will work.  Do you want to build a military power, well... honestly good luck, because I can't advise you.
The other side of this problem is if you want to do "X" do you know how to do it? The game doesn't give you that hint.  If you want to look at a city in Civilization you click on it, if you want to Build it a specific way you usually get options to tell the governor what to focus on.   People complain that Civ kind of plays itself, and it does, but there's also a lot of macro strategy to do.
On the other hand in Endless space, the player often is confused about what to do.  While there IS a tutorial, the tutorial only tells you what screens can do, and often a very fast overview.  I had to go only to learn how to hire a hero, or even colonize a new system.  I'm sure it's in a tutorial somewhere, but the tutorials are usually 9+ piece of information that just show you in general where the screen works.
If you boot up the game and didn't realize there was a hero system, I wouldn't fault you, the game really doesn't do much to bring a new player into it, or teach him to play.  I realize a full tutorial system is hard to do on these types of games, but there's intuitive ways to build an interface, and then there's the way games like Endless Space do it.  It's not a BAD UI, but it's impossible to learn it with out a lot of help or searching on the internet.  Once you understand it, the UI feels like it makes sense.  But a UI should be able to teach people how to use it, without requiring the player to go to Youtube and learn through that way.
The tech tree has a similar problem.  There's a very interesting four branch system where you can learn military might, diplomacy/trade, colonization, and "applied science"  really what you're learning is "weapons, I don't know, how to take over new types of planets, and resources"  there's more to it, but the point is there's a VERY big tech tree, and this is another point where I really want some Advice.  "I'm getting attacked" what's the next military thing I need to focus on.  "I can't take over this world."  Suggest a technology rather than making me have to guess.   "I see this path on the map but have no idea how to go through it".  I have to do an internet search to figure out what tech is required.    So really there's a lack here of really solid feedback.
But both of those areas are just the beginning.  The meat of this game and the biggest issue is the battles.
Let's look at Civlization one more time.  You have units, and they grow.  Have a settler and a scout, then you get a warrior, a pikeman, a cavalry then you get a chariot, and so on up the chain.   Each unit tends to be more powerful the farther to the right it is on the tech tree (except Civ 3, sorry hated that one).  This makes sense, a warrior is going to have trouble with a cavalry and so on up the chain.
Endless space has a more interesting system in mind, and if it was fully implemented I'd applaud it, but it almost feels like it was half way done and the programmer was called onto another task.
In Endless Space you don't unlock units, you instead unlock the base ships.  Ok kind of cool.  And then you unlock weapon systems (also defense and engine systems).  Then you develop ships based on all that.  This is a pretty interesting idea, you design your own units.   But there's a problem.  You don't get stronger units until you create or upgrade a class.  So there's a lot of guess work on that.  If you know what you want, great.  I'm sure this can work.  But as a newbie, you won't know how to build ships, and either guess (probably a mistake) or use the auto upgrade system.
Now If the game created versions of ships that progressively make it better, or just tiers of ships, this could be a really cool system.  Even having to go through and click "auto upgrade" would be good.  But the game does something kind of stupid.  When you click "auto upgrade" on a ship design it gives you what feels like the best ship it can come up with.  Good idea, but it will create a ship that it thinks is the best, not one that you can build.  If you haven't discovered certain technology that allows you to unlock certain materials, your ship might not be able to be built.  If your civilization for some reason doesn't have X resource, it still might use that resource.   It's a good idea for a system, a bad implementation.
But ok let's say you figure all that out and are building a great ship.  You're going to win aren't you?
Ok let's talk about the real problem here.  We talked about how unintuitive the system is and it really is, but you can learn that.  Terraria, minecraft, and so many other games have unintuitive systems that you have to learn through trial and error, or just spending days on a wiki.  That's how some games work.  But once you understand minecraft, or Terraria you can face reasonable challenges and accomplish them.  You might be able to go to the big boss  at the beginning of the game, but you can make progress.
So I decide to play Endless Space and since I was having trouble I turned the difficulty to newbie.   In civilization this gives you rather large bonuses, and often makes the enemies do remarkably dumb things.  The game jokes "As long as you don't just hit end turn every turnyou won't have trouble here."   That's what I wanted, low challenge to learn the game.
I play the game and it seems fun, far better than normal mode.  Then combat happens, I find a civilization who attacks my scout ships.  Send a few units after them, and get in trouble.  Then I realize that I have to upgrade my ships, I build out my military and can trounce a few of them.  Go Kinglink...
Then their military comes back, far more ships, far more powerful ships and they win every battle.
Now I'm not saying the game should be "baby" easy.  But the fact is newbie mode should be helping the player wins.  There's a few people online who says the AI cheats.  I'm not able to say if it does or doesn't cheat, but what I can tell you is that even on newbie mode, I had very little clue what I was doing wrong, or if I was doing anything wrong.
Now I could go online and learn all what I did wrong, but I chose a different tactic, I stopped playing the game.  I don't think that's a horrible move, but it's probably not the one the developer wanted.
So how is Endless space?  Well if you want to play an obtuse game that will punish you and make you work for everything you want, that has an obscene difficulty and hard learning curve,  But honestly there's a lot of these games, I'm going to find one that I like a bit more.  Endless Space doesn't seem to be it for me.

This game kind of gets boring after a while. It at first was really fun, I enjoyed getting better gear, messing around with my pocket universe, and exploring the map. It slowly gets... kind of dull after a while though.
The enemies in this game are all the exact same, except they look different and have different stats. They will try to run at you, and hit you after 5 seconds. Needless to say, they are very easy to kill. PVP is pretty engaging at first, but gets old really quickly. You have 4 types of weapons that each work differently, and considering there is only one developer, this isn't that bad. The issue is the weapons themselves. There are three swords, exactly the same except in damage. There is a gun, that shoots little friendliness pellets at people, and it controls alright. The laser is pretty weird, you charge it for a few seconds, and it shoots a straight line. People actually have made good use of this in pvp, but it seems extermely easy to dodge. Lastly is the hammer, doing a massive area damage, but taking a while to charge. Each of these weapons can be specialized to do well in pvp, and people have become really good at pvp in this game. Regardless, it does get dull quickly, however it is worth trying out.
The community is actually pretty helpful, when I played this game, I actually learned a lot from other people. The only issue is that for an MMO, there is pretty much nobody. 5-10 people are usually online at a time, which is pretty small considering a huge part of the game is Towns. It would be a much, much better game if it were more active. Because of recent events I have heard of (and not participated in, and as such will not talk about), and the game not really being updated, I doubt this will happen easily. The community that is there is fine, though.
Ironically, this is probably the worst aspect of the game. Well, second worst. The mechanics are not that bad, it just takes getting used to. The issue is often, unless you are an expert and know what your doing, it won't turn look very good. This wouldn't be that bad if more materials were available, but microtransactions make it worse.
I get it, I honestly get it. There has to be a way for servers to keep running, so microtransactions are used. Honestly though, when I get a game, I want all the features available (minus DLC, that's different). It's a bit like PVE, and PVE2. Plants vs Zombies costs some money, but it gives all the features immediately. Plants vs Zombies 2, on the other hand, is free. However, there are many micotransactions. I would rather just pay the $5. Not only do items cost money, though this is forgivable considering items aren't necessarilly needed, and they are obtainable through mystery boxes, but towns and pocket universes need money. Towns need money to make, and money to expand. Pocket Universes need money to expand. Even dungeons, a large gimmick of this game, need money to make. The good news is it's easy to get some items via players, and there are shops that sell them. The bad news is they are really expensive.
The style of this game is actually not that bad. It doesn't look really good, but it's alright. The music is really on your taste, however. I personally don't mind it, but I can easily see people turn off the game after 5 minutes from it. It's essentially 8-bit dubstep. Ironically, it is one of the only aspects of the game that doesn't get old after a while.
8-bit mmo, dispite it's flaws, is a fun game. It is a nice little game to pop in every now and then, mess around with, and leave. It isn't by any means horrible, but it isn't a masterpiece either. This is a rogue-lite game: it has random enemies, shops, items, companions, bosses and obviously permadeath. It has a bit progression, so that when you meet certain condition, it will unlock more cars.
After almost ten hours I can say that I wish I could like this game more, but I don't.
My problem with it and the reason why I don't reccomend it, is that you lose really fast. Depending on the enemy or your car, you can go from 100% to 0% in a matter of seconds.
Getting back from the start is not a big penalty, luckly, but the punishment is too harsh, and quite often too fast to understand what you're doing wrong. Even following the users' guides doesn't help you much, and you're left with the frustration of not getting why you failed.
Many people compare this game to FTL, but it's not right. In that game, with care, you may come back from the ground, plan around problems, min max your games. Here the gameplay is more flat, immediate, and with little room for mistakes.
A missed opportunity for a really good game.

Your measly winnings from each leve--nay, survival, barely pay for repairs and flapjacks to feed your carmates. And at some point, you're going to have to upgrade that shitheap you call a ride, so you're expected to deficate coin here and alot that appropriately. It's delicate.. juggling finances in such a chaotic environment. I mean, the entire point of the game is to reach some effing concert (I'm not even sure whose playing, let alone whether or not thay're any good). The music is fun and almost earthy at times. I wish that imaginary quote could include an ending, or some mention of the aforementioned concert. But alas, as I mentioned previously, I have yet to finish this ♥♥♥♥-all hard game.
