This is a fine turn-based cosmic strategy. The game is not without problems, but it is quite challenging and have an addictive gameplay. I had a nice time completing three different galaxies on custom settings (I'm offline player, check achievements as proof). This game is staying on my disk as I'm planning to return to it from time to time. So let's summarize.
-tons of starting settings, galaxy types, density, resources, galaxy age, and more
-nice bunch of factions with large varieties plus custom race ! with long list of possible advantages and disadvantages
-different hero classes with nice skill trees
-complexity, 4 basic resources with strategy goods, luxury goods, artifacts, wonders, monopoly, happiness impacting whole production
-discovery rewards, random events
-diplomacy(although a bit flawed-see below)
-ship designing
-nice bunch of alternative endings (however not equal-see below)
-one more turn syndrome (could last through whole night)
-generally nice graphic
-the game can cost even 1$ on sales
-GUI and drag and drop system (the ship list, buildings list, research list and other lists are way to short, and a drag and drop system is not efficient as it works only on visible objects, fortunately there are at least keyboard shortcuts)
-a simplified combat with low influence from player (those great space battles that you are seeing on screenshot or video are for the most part repetitive animations with few effects changing with the cards you have chosen, yes the combat is mostly card-based (cards represent different tactics), and to make it even better AI is really random at it, so choosing right cards is real gamble, fortunately this is not a whole equation, the equipment, ship class, and commanders counts as well, so with strong enough fleet even really wrongly played "cards" will not harm the fleet. Still Master of Orion combat is so much better, at the end you'll probably end like me and will use quick combat screen instead, effect is the same and it saves a ton of time
-turn resolve in real time, well it encouraging ahead thinking and some quick action moves, but I prefer to make my turn in peace. It is not fun when I'm planning my move in one part of galaxy and I'm suddenly receiving pop-up that my colony ship has been approached and is being attacked during my turn, or after I have issued most orders that other faction is now declaring war and shortly after that few of my systems are starting to be attacked.
-diplomatic AI is poor, the computer may just start a war at the same turn as alliance pact expire, or then you are at really good standings with them, also some other diplomatic moves are completely illogical, for example if you are at war, but are having access to the enemies space (through influence or star lines), the enemy can handle you even all the planets if you just agree to case fire :P, other example is dust trading, if agreement is beneficent to AI he will agree to give you all dust earnings per turn, and then at some point agreement is broken since AI is not having dust, he will immediately happily enjoy agreement again allowing you to milk it from technologies, resources, or planets
-victory conditions are far from being equal compared to other game titles, the economic or research victory is way easier then the advantage one, or diplomatic one, fortunately one can choose which one are allowed
-there is no way to "repair" Harmony cleansed or Cravers overuse planets
-no mixed systems, only one faction can rule it, game relays mostly on systems then on singular planets, I like to build my planets, on the other hand this one is rare approach.
-some mechanics looks that is lying idle, I don't know how that looks on really hard settings, but I have never seen computer using bombers for bombarding planet, or troops to swap the system, and I don't blame it, the building cost is high enough to avoid this, also usually if a faction loses it's fleet and allows one or two invasions to launch it often means start of the end for this faction.
-partly heroes - they are really rare, so at the end the choice is mostly an illusion, for most one will end hiring everyone as he/she will come, also why limiting hero level? I understand it protects game balance, but that could be much better resolved.
-the music is not terrible, but I heard better ones
-basic price tag

However looking past the rogue-like quality DSM posesses there is also a surprising necessity for twitch controls as your enemies spray bullet after bullet on you and your passengers while you're engaged in vehicular combat. To some degree there at times when it actually feels more like a bullet-hell shooter than arcade-esque roguelike.
The topping to this superb sundae of a game is a soundtrack that really gets blood pumping, and art style/humor that borders on funny yet possibly inappropriate.  In reality I literally said to myself while playing this game, "The only way this game could get any more awesome is if I could drive a damn tank."
And then I magically started driving a tank by a method I won't even explain.  Greatly recommended.

It took me a while to finally like this game but I'm glad I kept trying!
Death Skid Marks is more-or-less what would happen if you combined Spy Hunter with FTL and put it in some sort of Mad Max style universe with roguelike elements. The visuals are gritty, vulgar, and generally hilariously exaggerated either through blood and viscera or goofy stereotypes gone horribly wrong. The music and sound effects are pretty fitting for a highway drive full of wanton destruction and I never felt like they were getting on my nerves at any point.
Like I mentioned earlier, gameplay is akin to Spy Hunter in that you race down a highway full of other drivers either trying to kill you or getting in your way. Along the way, you can pick up additional characters (hikers) that can be armed with a variety of ranged or melee weapons, shot up with drugs to improve stats, or used as guinea pigs in science experiments or Russian roulette (also to improve stats, but with a chance of failure/death).
By the way, this game is really, really hard. Chances are, you will probably get ♥♥♥♥ed over by RNG dozens of times during your first few hours of playing the game as every possible thing is randomized: store inventories, hitchhikers present, enemies spawned, and bosses encountered, you name it. This can, unfortunately, result in runs that are impossible to win (like getting sawblade groupie without a good ranged weapon or brain tank without good enough melee). In that way, DSM really reminds me of FTL’s habit of randomly giving you the shaft and forcing you to restart, which can be kind of a bummer if you’ve been having a really good session and believe me, it can be absolutely ♥♥♥♥ing frustrating to get 75% of the way through the game and get obliterated by some enemy who just happened to be the perfect counter to your build.
All in all, the overall atmosphere and fun-factor behind Death Skid Marks kept me coming back again and again, even though playing it was like getting randomly kicked in the♥♥♥♥♥♥ so there’s something to be said about that. This game is a must-have for anyone who enjoyed playing FTL but wanted a lot more action, violence, and ridiculous humor.

SS:TRE is a turn-based action game that lives up to its name: there are a lot of random encounters. On the overworld screen, you play room by room, top-down view, moving a space at a time and opening crates for items, solving minor puzzles and beating random encounters, while making your way to the exit/boss.
Battle is turn-based and takes place on a separate screen, where a horde of classic enemies from the series rush you. You have three options: fight, swap (guns), and use item. Choosing fight lets you aim your current weapon at the horde and, when you confirm, the action takes place. You then run backwards while shooting at the horde of enemies, and they run forward trying to reach and kill you. This goes on for five seconds before the next turn.
You'll recruit additional party members and find plenty of weapons to choose from but, contrary to the description, there's no RPG here. Resolution is ridiculously small, the difficulty is too brutal and random and, overall, it's the worst Sam game I've played, which is saying something.

It's like a puzzle game, but uses firearms, vehicles, and skeletons.  200 or so odd firearms and a handful of other objects are modeled to break out each individual part.  The Devs use real examples to ensure accuracy, in that regard, they do a fabulous job.  If you lke guns or desire a different kind of puzzle game, I highly recommend this game.  It also has a very interesting engineering side where you get to have that "so that's how they did it..." moment with certain firearms.
Pros:
-The builds are realistic (I have experience with several irl)
-Good tutorials for practical application
-Competitve atmosphere yet doesn't require placement to succeed
-Hundreds of models
-Fun in a passive, more relaxing way
-Nice alternative to other puzzle games
-Surprsingly large variety of game modes from assembly/disassebly, shooting ranges, guessing games, speed builds, etc
-Free to Play
Cons:
-Pressure to buy DLC to access the entire game
-Buying the full game relatively necessary to have all models unlocked
-Many iconic firearms are missing still
-DLC way overpriced
Final recommendation:  Play it free initially.  If you like it through the first ten or so models you unlock, you will continue to like the game.  In that case, I recommend waiting for the "Full Game Access" DLC to go on sale for the 50% off or more it does about 3-4 times a year.  That's the best bang for the buck, pun very much intended.

Social relationships are important in the life of a teenager. They open up the way to new experiences, great memories, and unlock powerful combat techniques that can be used to take down monsters from the Dark Ages. At one of Erebonia's top military academies, young people from all walks of life come together to team up and show off their combat skills they've mastered in their brief time on the planet.
The Legend of Heroes: Trails of Cold Steel is the first entry in a trilogy that is part of an even larger video game world. Play as a student who must grow his relationship with his fellow classmen in order to overcome challenges both mystical and political. Customize your skills with the Orbment and ARCUS systems, utilized advantageous positioning, and swap characters in and out in the middle of battle to adapt to changing scenarios.
The writing of the game is something of a mixed bag. While the plot handles some deep and complex subject matters like political uprising, social class systems, and school dances, it's all bogged down by the subpar dialogue. Regardless of how many characters are in a scene, the game feels that every single one needs to voice their thoughts on the matter, no matter how innane or if it's already been said. After awhile, scenes feel bloated with unnecessary thoughts thrown out into the mix.
Characters start off two-dimensional and tropey, but through the course of the game they unfold into more layered people. They go from chariactures to characters. That's part of the overall theme of the game, too. That while things are presented in a rather black and white manner, clear lines of delineation made, the truth is more muddled than that. Your friends might be nobles, but there's usually some element that makes them outcasts within their own social circle. The same can be said of the commoners in your party.
The turn-based system in this game is immensely satisfying. Rather than all your characters standing in a row, you are free to move them across the battlefield, to reach enemies or allies or to avoid oncoming attacks. Movement can only be done on their turn, and moving uses up that turn, however. Think of it likes a "Tales" game, but far more limited. Attacks come in a few varieties (Attack, Craft Skill, and Arts) and you'll need all of them to overcome even basic monsters on the field.
The battle can turn sour quickly, as enemies aren't afraid of hitting hard. Making use of link attacks and damage types will be necessary to avoid having your entire party faint before you even leave chapter 1. Links are formed by building up your relationship with characters outside of battle. Each day you have a limited amount of interactions you can make with friends, and there is always more friends than you can meet in one day, so manage your interactions wisely.
PROS
+ Very enjoyable combat that is never too hard or too easy.
+ Familiar upgrade system (to anyone who's play FF7, at least).
+ Beautifully upgraded graphics that run at 60 fps.
+ Substantial plot and interesting developments therein.
CONS
- Tedious and redundant dialogue slows everything down to a crawl (even in turbo mode).
- Even though characters develop into more interesting people, the main character remains the dullest somehow.
- No Japanese voice cast.

Not the 4x experience I was looking for.
A little over two decades ago, I bought a copy of the most sprawling 4x I've ever seen or heard of: Empire of the Fading Suns. It was like Civilization, but on a hex grid (about two decades before Civ started using one--not that I'm a fan of hexes over squares) and spanned a galaxy. It was a bit like playing multiple games of Civilization at once, except that they were all interconnected, all part of the same universe.
You could also play multiplayer via email... Keep in mind we're talking about the pre GPU era remember. The pre-internet era of the BBS. It made sense then, but I digress for the sake of nostalgia.
The reason I mention EotFS in such detail, is because when I saw Endless Space, I was foolish enough to think that was the sort of experience I was getting. The game falls far short of it. It's a pretty small universe, and if it were tiled out like most other 4x games, the map would be smaller than most 4x games. They create the illusion of expansiveness by labelling what would be a city in other 4x games, star systems. Each star system can have multiple planets, which would be analogous to the resource areas around cities in a Civilization game.
At a glance, this gives the illusion of being very large. It is dwarfed by what a spiritual successor to EotFS would be.
I'm sure it's not a bad game. I find the mythos they are creating intriguing. I've enjoyed other Endless titles. But the gap between expectation and reality is too big on this one for me to enjoy.
This review is meant as a caveat to anyone who thought the game was going to be as big as I mistakenly inferred. This 4x title could readily be returned to the boardgame roots of the genre. The game I expected could not.
Still, if you go in understanding the expansive scope is more about flavor than actual expanse, and you're a fan of 4x titles, you'll probably like it as much as I do not.

DOOM..
For me it's a franchise that started a love affair with games that would last a life time.
I used to stay up late, sitting next to my dad watching him fighting his way through hordes or demons, giving me hints and tips here and there whether he noticed or not. I remember watching him walk across a beam that was easy to fall from by placing the crosshairs on the beam, to this day I still navigate the tight, tall spaces in the same way. The way he was diligent for secrets, not chasing the high scores of rushing a level, but finding all that could be found. It all rubbed off.
The originals were superb, for their day, and even now. Everything about those oldies were golden. The music. The Graphics. The Characters. The level design. All of it. It, in my opinion, did not deserve a remastering in modern day technology simply because it was already nigh on perfect. It was not broken and therefore did not require fixing.
The reincarnation of DOOM that hit PC and Consoles some years ago was titled DOOM 3. This iteration was in fact terrible. Sorry 'id' software, you know, I know it, we all know it.. However..
You have more than redeemed yourselves with this reboot. As a life long DOOM fan I felt so much nostalgia, so much fun and feeling. There's hundreds of nods to the original, and hundreds of ways you did actually improve it, which I wasn't sure was possible. This game has got to be one of the most underrated games of 2016, but maybe that's just the nostalgia talking...
Another thought I conjured up about this game, while playing the saddeningly short but epic campaign, is that it proves that Unreal Tournament 2004 can also be remade with the same flair, fantastic Multiplayer and sense of power and accomplishment that the original had without worrying about that horrible foray that was Unreal Tournament 3.
Thank you id software, I really needed this to remember why I fell in love with games and why I looked up to my dad so much.

The game starts you off simply having to destroy an easy defenseless car by ramming it to the side. You then head to the shop where you can pick up new allies (hitchhikers), buy weapons, buy car upgrades, heal your crew, upgrade your crew, get contracts for $$$, buy special items, and get tickets to the concert. You upgrade your car and your allies along with their weaponry to become better and kill everyone in your way. Along the road you will find special areas and shops such as Russian roulette, a special weapons shop, a mad science lab, a gun workshop, slot machines, and Zugtar who will either help you or screw you over. Definitive buyer's remorse. Every single run drags on for way too long for this style of game, and the vast majority of them will end with you being screwed over by some asinine overpowered combination of weapons on some regular enemy, or the one boss you didn't get good enough ranged/melee for.  Most of the game's problems stem from the extremely unenjoyable "rng" shop system with not only its arbitrary spawning system (the fact that you get a shop almost every single wave early on in the game when you literally do not need them and can't make enough money to even use them, then can't get a single one for half a dozen waves when you're far enough to actually be taking damage), but the similarly arbitrary selection of things that are actually available to buy in any given shop.
This system in tandem with the distasteful pricing balancing of weapons/items/upgrades just drains any enjoyment from a run you play well, and makes ones in which you don't even more frustrating. To add on to the frustration, the only persistent mechanic in place is spending your kills, usually in amounts that take an hour or longer to accrue, on a trivial one-run stat boost. The reason so many games these days implement some kind of over-arching progression mechanic is so that you don't automatically feel like you just completely wasted your time when you get blindsided after half an hour by exactly the kind of cheap trick deaths this game is filled to the brim with.
Ultimately, the game is not terrible, but I can't recommend it to anyone that I would know. Yeah, I know, there's been a new Deus Ex game out for quite some time now. I didn't get that game, though, because I heard it sucked. So... does this game suck too? Well, lets find out in my review of Deus Ex: Human Revolution.
THE PRESENTATION: So there are technically 2 versions of this game: Human Revolution, and Directors Cut. I suppose since I'm reviewing the directors cut version, I'll talk about that instead. But I bring this up because in the original, the entire game had a yellow filter over it. This may have bugged some people, but I feel it really did the game justice. It gave the game some visual uniqueness, and I was sad to see it go. But even without the filter, I feel as though this is a damn good looking game. Although there's a striking difference in quality when comparing pre-rendered cutscenes to in-game ones, I still feel that this game has solid graphics that get the job done. None of the animations look stiff, and things look and sound the way you'd think they would. The GUI is also nicely done, and won't get in the way visually. The tone of this game, dark and gritty, has been used to death, but that's just because it's cool, and this game is no exception. The atmosphere is a different story, however, as a future like this may one day come to be. It opts for the "realistic" route, and tackles real world problems like discrimination and corporate greed, which I believe really makes this game stand out. The only weak part of the presentation is the music, as I don't really remember any songs standing out at all. But in the end, Deus Ex, HR is a good looking, good sounding game. 2.5/3
THE GAMEPLAY: So, you want to know what it feels like to be a swole, cybernetic detective in the middle of Neo-Detroit? This game really makes you feel just that. The game operates as an FPS most of the time, and a TPS when behind cover (and yes, the cover system works well). The gameplay is diverse, as the game revolves around you getting perk points and deciding how you want to deal with tough situations. There are stealth options, non lethal options, and VERY lethal options. The stealth is the main attraction, but I found that the best way to beat the game is to shoot everyone in the head, though that may just be me. You can either find or purchase weapons, which range from pistols to heavy machine guns. Be warned, however, that running out of ammo is a very real possibility. While playing the game, you need to be wise on what equipment you use when, or you're sure to have a real bad day. There's also enemies, did I mention that? I almost forgot, since the enemies are literally the most generic edgy gunmen guards that you could think of. They all look the same, which kinda ruins the whole immersion factor, but oh well. They work well, though, so there's that I suppose. Oh, and the hacking system is good, too. 2.25/3
THE PROGRESSION: You play as Adam Jensen, an edgy cyborg that wears black and is desperately trying to find his girlfriend Megan. I'll be honest, the story is pretty good. Well, at least the characters are likeable enough that you don't want to gouge your eyes out every time they talk. They don't stand out, but they work. Only problem was the ending, which had more to be desired. A cool feature this game has is the Praxis system, which I mentioned earlier as perks. When you collect money, you can purchase some Praxis from the LIMB clinic, and give yourself some sweet augmentations. These include speech enhancers, arm swords, steroids, and even missiles! The options are really fun, and will make you want to get all of the available upgrades. Sadly, I'm not sure if this is possible, but it definitely makes you want to keep playing the game because of how gratifying they are. The coolest thing about the story is that it takes place over multiple destinations around the world, and each area feels different somehow. The streets of China and the US are both interesting to explore, and makes talking to the civilians interesting. There is a lot to do in this game with all of the sidequests, so you won't be bored. The last thing I'd like to mention is that there are multiple outcomes to certain storylines, which enhance replays. Great progression overall. 2.75/3
THE TECHNICAL ANALYSIS: I don't know about other people, but I experienced no glitches whatsoever. The game runs very well, and as long as you've got a good computer, you won't see anything wrong with the game. 1/1
Deus Ex: Human Revolution is a game that will grab you by the balls and throw you into an eerily feasible future dystopia where you'll need to evolve yourself to live. But don't worry, Adam is a undeniable BAMF, so you can live your dream of taking on cyberpunk criminals without leaving the comfort of your basement, or whereever you're playing this game. Certainly a recommend.
VERDICT: 8.5/10

I’ll rip off the band-aid by saying that the Director’s Cut edition is a graphical downgrade from the original edition, with the theory being that its development was based off of a port from the WiiU. While purists may opt to get an original copy and go from there, the two main reason why Director’s Cut is better than the original is because it integrates DLC into the story and gives the player more options in how to handle the gruelling boss fights. Mods like SweetFX have greatly assisted players in improving any graphical slights.
Though you may have to put in a little extra work to tweak the visuals, it won’t go unnoticed. The game’s environments are as beautiful as they are plentiful in terms of many locations and expansive levels. Because of how large and detailed the levels are, I have played through the game a total of four times (three on X360) and still found new paths/loot spots on the fourth go.  Loading times are minimal and far between. There is lots to see and scavenge, with a vast array of weaponry and mods. The biomodification system is perfected not just in terms of the sheer amount of mods you can have, but how you can get them through an experience point system, hoarding credits, and finding the odd praxis kit. No matter which mods you select, it will always feel as if there will be a tailored path for you to take in a main mission or in handling sidequests. This adds an enormous amount of replay value to the game. The achievements are also unique, and could sway you into playing the game a few times over.
The story itself is by far the strongest and most comprehensible in the series without being as pretentious or as tinfoil hat-y as the first. It’s able to do this by having a protagonist (Adam Jensen) that is more personable than in previous games, and you learn the nuances of the game’s conflicts because of how well constructed Jensen’s inner conflict is
. The politics within the game are clearly defined, and missions in the game do an accurate job of portraying the
. The lore is there if you need it through additional reading materials throughout the game, but the world does a great job presenting itself on its own. I thoroughly enjoyed how much of an emphasis the reboot places on well-developed characters through revealing cutscenes and side-quests. I also appreciate how the choices you make don’t necessary carry over through all aspects of the game, so you’re not haunted by mistakes that you can make.
Deus Ex: Human Revolution more than makes up for Infinite War and promises a fresh spin on an old classic. The prequel-sequel does a great job in creating an immersive universe to follow for years to come (which is owed equally to level design and rich story), along with an appealing level-up system. It’s a must-have title for stealth junkies, and will prove itself to be a extraordinary experience for FPS players and sci fi fans.

Okayish idea for a game with acceptable graphics and sound, killed by utterly frustrating gameplay. Too much pixel-jumping with too few checkpoints, and pretty much nothing else. If it was supposed to be a casual game - it's far too hard and frustrating. If it was supposed to be one of the "intentionally hard" games - it misses some sense of reward, any incentive to play another level.
This game could be pretty good (for a low budget indie platformer) after improving quite a few things. For example adding three "hearts" instead of instant death; adding collectibles (energy, weapons); adding some fighting elements, like ability to bash enemies with the lute, some throwable items could be useful as well; adding some hidden collectibles for extra challenge (for achievement hunters). I can actually see myself playing such game. Until then - the Bard goes back on the shelf.

Bard to the Future is a game of contrasts. Its character portraits, writing, music, and voice acting are great; its in-game graphics and actual gameplay are seriously lacking.
Graphically, the game would be much better if it picked a pixel size and stuck with it. As for the gameplay, it's buggy, it's frustrating, and it commits the ultimate platforming sin: the hitboxes are unpredictable, which makes it impossible to tell whether you'll stomp on one of Bard to the Future's swift, erratically-moving enemies or be killed by it.
As much charm as the game has, it's not quite charming enough to overcome its flaws.

Among the many Space 4X games out there, Endless Space is probably the simplest of them that I have played. It's UI and Empire managing system could be considered fairly simple to grasp, when compared to a game like Stellaris.
Again, Endless Space is simple enough because it isn't deep in managment systems like Stellaris, but it isn't as (what I consider) basic as Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion. You basically start the game with a faction of your choosing, each of them having different and various racial traits and bonuses that affect their gameplay. Of course, the game also features a faction creator, which allows you to pick the various traits i mentioned ealier and the appearance of that of any of the other factions, in order for you to make your customized faction.
In terms of the actual gameplay, you have four ways to go about things and win essentially; Destroy, Research, Cultivate and Money management. Destroy means what it says; destroy your rival empires across the stars and secure galatic domination. Research various branches of technology needed to wage war, make alliances, and manage you Empire. Make Alliances with other Empires and rule them through culture (I'll explain it more later). Or simply build up your funds and grow your economy to build up your Empire.
Now, one thing to note however, three of those four are impossible to do without putting in time to research them. Destroy being the only one possible without research, but practically, it's still impossible, because research is a very core aspect of this game.
Through Research, you learn how explore the galaxy more efficiently, make bigger ships, build better weapons and improvements to your Empire and again, manage your Empire. Seeing as I've stressed this so much, let me personally say that this game is more of a test of patience in waiting for your scientists to research new tech. You literally have to learn how to offer peace by researching it! That is what can make Endless Space so frustrating, because its more of a test of patience than anything else.
In short, I've made the argument that this game is a research simulator that tests how long you can wait for that research to finish, safegaurd your empire from other Empires and Pirates and manage your Empire so that it always produces enough research points.
On the topic of factions, if you're playing the original classic version, then you have access to eight factions, (four humans, four aliens), but if you play on the DLC Disharmony version, you get another human faction and a new alien faction. Now, there are almost no real differences between each faction, aside from starting traits and you may have a much harder time playing as the Hissho and the Sowers, because they have a racial trait that makes them less efficeint scientists, but remember that all factions have a different playstyle to them.
Some are better at science, while other warfare and so on. Of course, no faction from what I've seen is good at reserach and combat, so if you're hoping for a faction like that, then you'll have to turn to the faction creator for that. Personally, I think it's a good thing that each faction doesn't have an overbearing edge over the others, but it cuts down on creative play, in exchange for a linear play style.
Another thing to note is that this game is turn-based, so you'll have a lot of time to analyze and adapt to things around you. A pleasant surpirse I found out about this game though, was how fast-paced it can be at times, but the difficulties are very skewed in my perception.
There are seven difficulties, ranging from newbie to impossible, with varying degrees of easy and hard in between them, and also normal. As I went through a few test runs to try what faction appealed to me the most, I found that the AI had a lot of advatages over me. There was how they can build ships much faster than you, the player can, how they can gain access to new tech even faster and some of them have massive economies by at least the 60th turn (believe me, that is really how long it takes early game or so).
But in retrospect, my review for this game became a lot more negative than I had originally thought, becuase the difficulty settings are broken in my opinion, the actual gameplay is boiled down to web browser levels in a way, with space combat being a combination of cutscenes and lucky guess card picker to counter your opponent's cards.
But on a positive note, I can say that Endless Space at least has a simple and effective UI and managment system that can be learned (in my opinion) much easier without the tutorial on.
In conclusion, I don't recommend Endless Space, because it honestly feels like a repetitive chore to play at times with no room for flexibility, but it is good if you want a strategy game where you can grind in relative peace to calm music.
P.S. Multiplayer, I have no comments on because I like to avoid that in a strategy game.

When I first got the controller, getting used to the touchpads was a real hurdle. However, now that I have gotten used to them, I find them to be a real blessing in games that allow both controller and mouse input at the same time. When the right pad is trying to completely simulate a controller stick, it is a bit wonky, though still usable. But if it allows for full mousepad-y controls, it can be a real blessing. Biggest example for me is Dark Souls 3, a game that is so much better with a controller. With the touchpad, looking around is a lot quicker, easier and more precise than with a regular controller.
Most games have pretty decent community-made controller layouts that you can find pretty easily, so it will work well with most games. The two extra buttons on the back of the controller can be a real blessing for some games. I also find that the steam controller doesn't make my hands cramp as much as my PS4 controller does over longer play sessions. So overall, I'd recommend it.

I am sorry. I do not think I will be able to write an unbiased review of this device. The problem is, this controller seems like alien-grade technology only utterly suited for human ergonomics. Although I was used to many types of gamepad and controllers before using the Steam Controller for the first time, it was an "out of this world" experience - so much that after 20 minutes I became nauseated and almost puked (I was playing the training ground of Counter-Strike: GO). But it was just that time. After that, everything went smoothly and frankly I cannot imagine myself using either the keyboard + mouse or regular gamepad anymore. Yes: the controller IS THAT GOOD. It exceeded all my expectations, even though I didn't even like touchpads before using it. It is very well designed hardware coupled with state-of-the-art software to drive and configure it.
Buy it. Buy it NOW. This device needs public and technical recognition  and it is suited for everything that involves human interaction. It is amazing. It is worth every penny, 10 times the price.
I won't get into the details of how it works, or how you map it to specific games. Plenty of reviews and tutorials on the internet will already tell you that. But if you are reading this you might be prepared for some reading - this device is somewhat complex (not too much, don't let it get into the way) and in practice instead of using the general configuration or other configurations for your games, you might prefer to make your own, and that takes some learning.
I am looking forward to using it for 3D modelling too, which is part of my job. Its independent analog axes (2 touchpads + gyroscope + joystick) seem be perfect to be mapped to 3 rotation axes + 3 translation axes needed for free manipulation of three-dimensional shapes.
BTW, I use it in Linux, because I refuse to ever use Windows at home or work. Or Mac OS X, for that matter. Nevertheless, although I do not have the experience in Windows to compare, it seems Linux support is as good, maybe even better, than in Windows.

Avoid at all costs. The Steam Controller is an excellent idea on paper - its goal is noble, indeed - but it fails on nearly every aspect. Physical design, internal hardware, and, most crucially, the software - all of these components range from sorely lacking to fundamentally deficient. And due to Valve's apparent college dorm room development philosophy, there's absolutely nothing stopping those in charge of this side project from simply saying "meh," getting bored with it, and leaving it sit in its half-finished broken state. Which is exactly what has happened.
Its drivers are simply straight-up broken and have been since the beginning, with basic functionality slowly being fixed at such a glacial pace that it'd make Chris Roberts nervous. Now those updates have essentially stopped, leaving this hunk of plastic in a sorry state.
Maybe it's because the Steam Machine died on arrival and no one wanted it. Maybe it's because fixing software bugs requires effort. I don't know, but it's clear the guys at Valve have no interest in bringing the software up to speed. The HUD frequently decides to stop working, seemingly at random. Saving profiles is still - RIDICULOUSLY - a crap shoot. Sometimes they'll save without a problem, others they'll put you in an endless loop that will never end until you kill the program, after which you discover it actually did save...only it saved 30 copies, all of which you'll have to manually delete. Ghost bindings stubbornly remain from time to time, no matter how many times you delete them. The whole package is a broken, frustrating, buggy mess that deep-sixes anything good the Steam Controller tries to do, and it just will not be fixed. I literally do not have space here to list all the problems I have had with it. Basic functions fail constantly. It's neverending.
The big selling point is the gyro. It's a laughable piece of trash. It falls into terminal drift within 30 minutes of play, often much sooner. It's imprecise and lacks a simple means of recalibration. You can't recalibrate while a game is running. Your only hope is to set it on a table for a few seconds and hope that it sorts itself. It doesn't always.
The trackpads are also difficult to deal with. The simple act of smooth left-to-right movement is near-impossible to achieve without intensive, heavy tweaking. It's maddening. The face buttons are knobby and poorly placed. It's an ergonomic disaster that will murder your wrists. I cringe at all the possible hardware failure points on this thing. Clicking the thumbstick makes me feel like it's going to snap off. It's unpleasant as heck. As bad as that is, I can only imagine the triggers are going to be the first to go. The whole thing just feels badly put together, and not particularly well reinforced. Given its price, that's a bad thing.
This thing is essentially an experiment being sold like a product. I just can't support this. The idea is good, but at this point, it's just an idea. The point is to allow users freedom to use a controller in just about any setting, binding controls practically any way they can imagine. It's a golden notion, but the end product just does not work the way it's supposed to. The potential is totally unrealized.

To put DOOM in a phrase, it's a "no nonsense" shooter.
The story is fairly simple and the gameplay is, ultimately, fairly repetitive - you kill things. A lot. However, its the gun mechanics and variety of combat actions that make the game fantasitically good fun to play.
It's a satisfying shooter. It really is. The variety of weapons is just about right - not too many to overwhelm you, not too few to be boring. The guns also feel 'heavy' and powerful - they're not little pea shooters or anything. Additionally, the upgrades that you can apply to weapons adds that little extra to combat in terms of providing a distinct experience. But most importantly, it's the flow of combat - no matter how I choose to fight, whether with a shotgun, assault rifle or rocket launcher, the game flow is smooth and satisfying.
Graphics wise, the game looks very good. It's atmosphere is dark, yet not overly horrifying to put you off playing. Most importantly, the game isn't full of jump scares like it's last incarnation! The game runs perfectly - I've had no crashes or frame rate issues whatsoever.
There is a multiplayer component to the game, but I've not played that. I've not really felt the need to as of yet.
I'm not sure what the replayability will be like with this game. I have to admit, I doubt I'd play it again on a harder difficulty (Hurt Me Plenty is my advised chosen difficulty for optimal 'fun' and challenge). Despite this, my first run through has been very fun.
I'd rate this a 9/10. If any DLC is created for this game, I'll be coming back to it.

This is a must-buy for anyone who is into action roguelike games and doesn't mind or likes trashy humor.
The game is crazy action-packed fun. You're Mark Skid and your goal is to get to a concert. On your way you'll pick up hitchhikers, gear them up with weapons, upgrade your car and kill absolutely everything and everyone that gets in your way.
You can unlock a lot of different cars, each being different than the other. Some give passive bonuses/penalties, some are equipped with saws or even with a freaking rocket launcher.
You can equip your hitchhikers with melee or ranged weapons which you can buy in shops. In those shops you can also buy food to heal your characters, upgrades to your car, drugs to boost stats of your characters, repair your vehicle, all kinds of special items and of course tickets to the concert!
There are also all kind of mini-games that you can enter during your trip. There's a russian roulette mini-game where if your selected character loses he dies but if he wins his stats get boosted greatly. There's also a slot machine if you feel like gambling, workshop where you can upgrade your weapons and other stuff.
There's a decent number of bosses that you can encounter and they get randomly selected for each run. In each run you will face a total of 5 bosses, including the final one but they'll always be different (even final bosses change each time). They all of course have their own attacks and patterns that you'll have to learn if you want to beat them.
The game is pretty challenging but fun and addictive. The RNG can help or screw you over at times like in any game from this genre and I have to admit that when I started playing I thought it's unfair and impossible to win. But as I continued to play I realized that's not the case. Once you get skilled enough at the game and know how everything works you can win almost every run.

Looked into the lore, seen some playthroughs of the older games in the series, still plan to look back at more of them.
Most people knock the Mechwarrior series off like it's some random series that's akin to any other mech game, but as gamers, we owe more than we think to the Mechwarrior team. Mechwarrior was one of the first true 3d computer games to exist, and really set the standard for how a military simulation game should work, and feel. If not for this series, and the tech that it took to make the original game work, gaming today wouldn't likely be nearly as advanced, complex, or fun as it has come to be.
Anyways, yeah, it's a pretty fun, although slow paced game. If you're some kind of CoD fanboy, or some other fast and mindless game junkie who can't be patient or think tactics and strategy to save your life, you probably won't like this game. If you have functioning, healthy brain cells, and more patience than a grumpy chihuaua, i firmly believe you'll find some great enjoyment out of this game.
Side note i forgot to mention when writing this initially: Anyone who loves Xbox Live? You owe this series for it too. MechAssault was the game that most of the original Xbox Live software was created around.

This game is best summed up as "a thinking man's shooter."  For people familiar with the mechwarrior series or battletech, you will know what I mean.  For the un-initiated let me elaborate.
You have mechs - which are like walking tanks,  The torso and legs can face different directions.  But unlike tanks, you can have a multitude of different weapons - lasers, missiles, and ballistics - each with their own advantages and disadvantages.  Inside of those three weapon types there are several different su-types.  For example.  You can have small/medium/large lasers.  You can also have ER lasers (extra range) - longer range but more heat per damage.
So you "design" a mech with weapons and engine sizes and different armor amouns and several other choices ( ex. lighter engine but risk of exploding).  You then launch into a 12v12 match with different maps and different objectives.
Well, I think I've touched the tip of the iceburg here.  So much mroe minutae. . . but the point has been made I think.
One negative I have of this game is that mechs that have been recenttly designed or "heros" require real world money purchases sometimes.  However, you get opportunities to get these credits through in-game events and can even get mechs as rewards sometimes.
P.S. teamwork is OP.

Platformers are a tough game to get right, because the controls and level design both have to be perfect or else the whole thing falls apart. Unfortunately, Bard to the Future's controls are far from perfect. I played my entire time using a wired 360 for Windows controller and it was a half hour or so spent in utter frustration.
The main character is called a "BattleBard", and yet he has no ability to battle. You can jump on enemies or powerslide into them (but only if they are facing away from you.) Any momentum you are able to build up going through the level is lost when you have to stop and watch the movement pattern for the enemy as it begins and changes suddenly. If you miss the head by a matter of pixels, you're dead. If you powerslide as they turn around, you're dead. If you try to speed around them, the controls will not react quickly enough which will also kill you. One would think as a BattleBard you would get to actually... battle stuff without dying in a single touch.
That being said, I do not mind dying in games. It is something that can be used to make the experience more fun at times, but the points in the level that are respawn points after death are too far away from each other. After so much trial and error to get past a tiny portion, you immediately have to do that again when the controls don't let you jump at the exact moment you press the A button causing you to hit spikes. The respawn checkpoints also are not announced in anyway by the game. You've no clue where they are until you die. The game annoyingly pops up a death counter for 10+ deaths in a level and keeps counting with every death. There are also incredibly repetitive voice announcements of your death from the character every handful of deaths. Both of these only increase the frustration factor, especially after a death that is control-related.
I've never before wanted a refund for a game I've bought from Steam, but I can no longer say that after my time with the BattleBard.
TLDR:
+ Fun storyline concept.
+ Music is engaging.
+ I appreciate the art style.
+ It's five dollars.
- Controls need to be fine-tuned. I'd settle for just being tuned at all though.
- Respawn checkpoints spaced too far apart and are not announced by the game at all once crossed.
- Comments from your character about his death get very old, very fast.
- BattleBard is very easily killed by enemies.
- I appreciate the voiceover for the cutscenes, but they are too long. I'd like to skip to the next line of dialogue when I'm done reading the caption versus using the entire-scene skip option provided.
I'll keep an eye out for updates to see if any of these issues are addressed in the future, but I cannot recommend this game in its current form.

Major Thumbs down from me.
Lots and lots of buttons/micromanagement but ZERO information on what anything means/does.
Science tree -  no explanation what it actually does for you. It describes the science itself, but not how it influences game play.   Did you ever wonder what XenoBiology is - this is your game...eesh.  Tell me it improves growth rate or tell me something useful for goodness sake.

Ship movement - There are buttons for almost everything...except the one thing that is actually useful - a button to move your ship where you want.  For that you need to google for the info and find out it is CRTL-L+ Right click.
The route your ship takes to its destination - completely random.  You could be routed via other Systems, or go directly.  I assume it's based on distance - problem is there's nowhere it tells you the distance.   I get attacked, so I send some ships to go defend - problem, it decides it'll route my ships via the Enemy's home base - ships destroyed.  Dumb.
I try to send my ships to invade.   It won't let me despite me being at war.  Is it distance ?   Nope because when I send the ships to my own colony, it ships me via their colony.  Does it explain why I can't go where I've clicked.   Nope.
I wanted to give it a chance - I like 4X space games; Galactic Civ series etc) played those to the tune of thousands of hours.  This one however, can't even finish one game, just too painful
Glad I got it in a bundle because if I had paid full price for this mess of a game I'd have totally lost it.
***- Edit ***
I received some comments back about how certain things can be done.  I will let those speak for themselves.  What I will conclude however is something very simple - "useful" information is NOT explained and useless info is front & center and the amount of useless info is overwhelming.  I spent 30+ hours or so trying out the game - the entire thing felt like Trial & error and I'm pretty sure it'll take another hundred to get even a semblance of how the game is supposed to be played. Several months ago, I wrote a review for this game and said that I have not abandoned my willingness to change this game for future players.
Now I have.
In the past, I talked about the various changes this game could use because I cared enough to believe this game can be improved. I truly thought there was hope for improvement. This game left me with nothing more than disappointment for my own inadequacy to change it, and the frustration that it has been left unchanged. With no omission of detail, I will describe all the injustices of this game I have endured and eventually, what led to my eventual retirement.
I am a well known player, and I have received numerous achievements including the community's recognition for my candidacy as a moderator. As of this review, it has been about a year since the developer displayed any intentions of enlisting new moderators.
Over the course of two weeks, I built this game's only non linear open-world quest. To compensate for the lack of NPC's in the game, I created makeshift ones with pumpkins and hid signs on every NPC, amounting to over 3000 words of dialogue. This construction received no recognition and the only part of the quest that received any major attention was a large boat that represented the last part of the quest.
I built a tutorial for this game to remake the current one. The current tutorial cannot be considered, in any shape or form, a tutorial. It teaches basic controls, but it omitted the most important and preliminary components of any mandatory tutorial. There were no instructions on how to build, how to obtain gold, or even how to use the shop.  Most players are turned away in utter confusion for the game's mechanics. Despite spending well over 40 dollars of premium currency on construction of a new tutorial, the developer declined before I even showed him what I made.
I reconstructed the spawning area for players. The current one is vestigial other than a mild utility of teleport links to two mandatory dungeons; the rest lead to dead cities and abandoned PVP arenas. This too, was declined without a second thought.

I reported two major exploits regarding 9bitmmo (the experimental 3D game viewer).One allows unlimited gold farming and the other allows no-clipping through walls at will. The first was fixed within the day I reported it, and the second has yet to be fixed. The developer has no intention of fixing the second exploit stating simply, "people can already no-clip through more nefarious means". To this day, no-clipping through walls in 9bitmmo leaves all areas open to theft and quest exploitation.
I created this game's first and only Megabuild, a castle that spanned the size of a 6X expanded town. The premium currency spent in its construction approaches well over 500 dollars. The most publicity it received was a visit by the developer and publicity on Facebook, twitter, and the sidebar for about two weeks. No monetary compensation was rewarded for its construction, and a teleport pad was never added to the spawn area for players to visit this place.
I contributed 400 dollars in donations towards the Novemberbit fundraiser event, amounting to 1000 dollars under my name. The only prize for donating this exorbiant amount is a custom item created and implemented under the name of the donator. Ever since the creations of items for the zealous donators of the game, no other items have been added.
What made me quit this game eventually is the ignorance of the developer to sympathize with the players of this game that truly want to make it better for others. If there is criticism to be heard, it falls on deaf ears. It has been over a year since a new building block as added to the game and almost mockingly, the developer still hovers over the forums and regulates posts that criticize the declining state of the game.
Chris_Ramos is correct in his review when stating the incident where two game moderators were banned. It is also true he wrote the Spanish translation for the entire game and for compensation, the developer gave him ONE DOLLAR. Even the head moderator of the game was not granted a response when he sent an email asking for an explanation behind the lack of updates.
The reason he does not improve the game is not because of a lack of time or budget, it is due to his obstinate and outright refusal to do so. What the developer has committed, and is continuing to commit, is no longer within the moral realm of right or wrong. There are players who have donated thousands of dollars to this game and are taken completely for granted, their doubts met with only trivial responses as they ponder the future of the game. It is no longer a morally questionable demeanor, it an ethical crime. Because nothing categorically imperative in his actions can be considered correct; his actions indicate only a betrayal of the players' loyalty and zeal in favor of a personal agenda. In the past I would ask players to play the game before forming a judgment, and to approach it with an open mind. But with the way the game currently is now, it has no future. Not for as long as the players' loyalties are met with an utter betrayal of expectations.

As someone who always enjoyed playing FPSes and other games with guns, but never really paid much thought to how they actually work, this is an eye-opening educational tool. Every time you can learn something new if you take the time. But it's also an addicting puzzle game, memorising how to disassemble and then put back together a huge number of real guns of various design and complexity in the shortest amount of time.
As for the F2P aspect, with a little patience and skill, you can unlock almost everything without paying a dime. There is a handy quiz that allows you to gather lots of exp quickly. You can win prized credits by posting a daily top score in a game mode for a model. The only models you probably absolutely have to cough the coin up are the car models, military vehicles and some artillery pieces. The devs also give out free promo codes whenever a new model gets released.
On the downside, the release rate of two or even three new models per month doesn't feel enough for me, although given their complexity it is understandable. There is also a noticable difference in quality with older 3D models, like the H&K MP5, compared to the newly released ones. Hello Everyone!
I just picked up a Steam Controller this past Saturday. Let me begin by stating that I've held off on buying one for 2 years. I heard a lot of mixed reviews on it, but it was a friend of mine who had one that really convinced me to pick one up. Also, my PS4 decided to die so I needed something to play while I saved up cash to get a new console. So, enter the Steam Link and Steam Controller. Please see my review of the Steam Link on the page for it.
After the usual unboxing ritual and getting everything configured, I was pretty excited to see what this thing could do. The controller for me, feels pretty comfortable but I also have medium sized hands. That being said, it does take some getting used to as I’m used to a PS4 controller with the second joystick. My mindset on this was to get used to the controller and like it; I wasn’t looking for excuses to trade it in or return it. Over the past few days I’ve gotten used to the track pads and actually like using the trackpad as a mouse/joystick. I know others have reported that its a pain in the butt to use and not ideal… but it all comes down to personal preference. If you like having the 2nd stick there, then you might want to look elsewhere unless you approach this thing with an open mind.
So far I’ve played a variety of different genre’s with the controller:
Deus Ex – Human Revolution
Wasteland 2: Directors Cut
Mafia II
Star Trek Online
The Secret World Legends
Ultimate General: Gettysburg
Warhammer Total War
XCOM: Enemy Unknown
The games that have native support for a controller work like a charm. Games that are expecting a mouse and keyboard I have to map out. I found a great guide from PC Gamer about configuring and the features of the controller so that was a big help. But I’ve found that if you take the time to download a profile and make tweaks when necessary, the controller works well. In my opinion its an extremely versatile controller; I think it was a big risk for them to put a trackpad on the right instead of a second stick. Again, it comes down to preference, but it works. It is one of those things you have to have an open mind to, but if you’re not hellbent on hating the controller you’ll be fine.
There are a few things I don’t like about the controller; the haptic feedback can get annoying so I turn it off when I can. Also the rumble feature is in beta mode so it really sucks; turn it off until they get it right. The trackpad and directional button can be a little stiff but its not too bad. Finally, the controller can be a little overwhelming so I wish Steam had a better guide on configuring it, and explaining the finer points of the advanced options. The configuration screen is really good at explaining itself though.
TL;DR
Pro’s
Works well with Steam games. I don’t use any non-steam games in my steam list so its not an issue for me.
Very configurable and flexible
Trackpad works nicely as a second stick or whatever you want
I can sit on my couch and play an RTS or whatever I want out of my Steam list
Con’s
Trackpad and Directional pad buttons are a little stiff but it shouldn’t be a  big issue for most
Haptic feedback can get a little annoying. Makes the controller sound creaky
I hope they get the rumble support figured out. Whats in there right now sucks
At first you may spend more time tweaking your controller scheme and that can consume you. Once you get it right though, it works well.
Overall
I highly recommend this controller. If you’re on the fence about it, you won’t regret buying one unless you just want to hate the controller. I’m not big on buying things I want to hate, so I had an open mind to it. This controller attempts to replace a mouse and keyboard so you have to cut it some slack. It does accomplish that task most of the time. I have yet to run into a game that doesn’t play well with the controller. As long as you’re sticking to Steam games that you’ve purchased through Steam, the controller will work very nicely for you. Finally, theres a lot of talk of the controller feeling cheap or the build quality being off. The only controller that I’ve held that has superb build quality is the Xbox One Elite controller. But that thing costs 150$ and for good reason. I wasn’t expecting that with this controller, personally I think the build quality is fine.
Take what I say for a grain of salt, but I hope this helps in your decision.

I purchased my Steam Controller during the summer sale 2017, which is over 2 years after this controller was first brought to market. As such, many of the commonly referenced negatives about the controller have been resolved through software updates since then.
The Steam Controller is extremely unique, which is why I think it gets a slightly mixed/negative reputation (69% positive over the last 30 days, 75% positive overall). I believe that when people purchase the Steam Controller, they let their expectations ruin their potential enjoyment of the device. The Steam Controller is something that takes a lot of time to learn to enjoy. Even for me personally, who has wanted a Steam Controller since they released, I wasn't sure if I was going to like my controller after using it for the first hour. I had a kind of nervous, "did I just waste $35?" moment there for a bit. However, after using it for only a little under a month, it is my preferred controller (compared to Xbox One/PS4 controllers).
The Steam Controller is not going to be your favorite out of the box, but with time it will win your heart over. It's probably not going to beat out keyboard and mouse in competitive play, but you shouldn't expect it to. When paired with the Steam Link, it is a great experience from the couch. The versatility and customization of this controller cannot even be expressed in words, you can tweak settings that you've probably never even heard of. This is an amazing thing if you are willing to learn the ins and outs of the controller. Even if you don't want to spend time customizing it to your specific liking, the community templates are awesome for grab and go playing.
I would recommend this controller for almost every game genre EXCEPT real time strategy (RTS) games -- stick to a keyboard and mouse for those, unless of course you're just playing super casually.

First and foremost, Death Skid Marks is a fundamentally good game. It's easy to start up and get into, it has a ton of different modes and unique cars, and combining roguelike elements with car combat is definitely inspired.
However, I consistently run into the same problem that ultimately chased me away from FTL. With a little luck, some careful maneuvering, and decent resource allocation I can get about 75% through a run before hitting a brick wall. Sometimes I'll get worn down in a way that feels organic, like my death was the result of mistakes I was making. But more often then not, I run into a ridiculous combination of enemies and environmental challenges that no amount of skill or preparation could defeat.
For example, I was just driving a tank and laying waste to everything. The very first boss I encountered (The Buzzsaw Alien) destroyed my tank in literally less than 5 seconds. In almost 40 hours of playing, I've managed to beat this boss twice (maybe). Usually, whenever it shows up, I just kind of resign myself to death. I still have no idea what its patterns are, or when the "shield is down." Also, the boss is surrounded by a giant saw that is always rotating. Sometimes the saw actually damages your car, which is usually enough to kill you almost instantly. Sometimes it doesn't damage you at all. I have no idea when it does or doesn't cause damage.
When it comes to roguelikes, it's always difficult to determine whether constant death is the player's fault, or the developer trying to escalate the difficulty and going a little too hard in the paint. The general response to complaints about the game's difficulty have been of the "Git Gud" variety, so I'm not holding my breath about any future patches balancing the late-game a little more in the player's favor. However, for the sake of this game (which IS good and worth the effort), I hope I'm wrong.

One of the best games I've played in quite a while.
You are Mark Skid, a trailer trash guy on a post-apocalyptic road trip to the metal concert of his life. Problem is, everyone else on the road is trying to kill you! Rednecks, cops, neo-nazis, furries, religious fanatics and other nutjobs - everyone wants you dead, so obviously you will put an end to that by killing them first.
Upgrade your car and your arsenal, take lots of drugs, pick up friendly hitchhikers and leave a trail of destruction behind until you make it to that epic concert, or die trying - and you WILL die a lot, but will still come back for more, because at that point you'll be addicted already (and/or are a sucker for punishment).
The game has a kind of humor that manages to be immature while still being funny instead of obnoxious. The art style is a great blend of cartoony and gritty, which totally suits the mood of the game (as a fellow artist, I couldn't help but admire it and feel inspired).
In short, Death Skid Marks is addictive, kickass, fast-paced action, all to the sound of a badass metal soundtrack that will make you want to headbang. And I absolutely recommend it.

I've played MWO since late closed Beta stage, played solo for a year before joining a unit and played in that unit until 2015. By that time it became very clear, that game has no future. Its a money-grabbing scheme using an old-school franchise and operating on exploitation of excellent artist and design crew working under an utterly pathetic, incompetent and dispassionate management. Everything that was and is good about this game is what you can see with your eyes and hear with your ears, produced by talented creative people.
Meanwhile, everything that depends on logically-formulated decision, such as balance, game mechanics, game modes, etc is simply AWFUL and gets worse over time. Nothing developers do in these facets makes any sense. Nobody there cares about quality or variety of experience as long as profits from pre-purchase packs are within the margin. Those packs are produced by aforementioned artists on a regular basis, and the quality of the content given is fairly high by modern standards, and is the primary source of revenue for PGI.
However, that is just a shiny cover of the book - a bait placed to lure new people in and keep veterans playing due to monetary investments. Under that visage of quality and fidelity, there only convoluted and unintuitive mechanics (increasingly so at that), lame and awkward game modes and balance being driven into the ground by ineptitude and mediocrity of the leadership branch. These people have no passion for their product or towards their player-base, they only project an illusion of concern about their players' complaints, ideas or suggestions, but always do things and solve problems in their own, peculiar way, which in 9 cases out of 10 only produce even more issues without achieving the original intent. Whatever new comes around, its always more, but not better.
All the while I've been playing MWO I've spent hours upon hours advocating the game on the forums like a naive idiot, but after so much time have passed and little to nothing have changed for the better, the time came when even a fully functional, active team of 100+ players couldn't keep me interested in the game, that has no future to look forward to. Therefore, I give MWO a rating of 4/10 at this point and will not recommend it to anyone, as the potential temporal, psychological and monetary investments will far outlive the title itself.

In 2000 I was floored by Deus Ex, I played it that whole summer.  Human Revolution took everything I loved about the original and blew it way out of Battery Park.  The polished gameplay mechanics executed here by Eidos Montreal (Thief, Tomb Raider) combined with solid CG cinematics by Square Enix (Final Fantasy) has produced a new classic in my opinion that I've been able to enjoy 17 years later.

As a prequel, Deus Ex: Human Revolution Director’s cut is set in the year 2027, more than 30 years before the incidents of the original Deus Ex, mechanical augmentations, conspiracies and technological advancements are the ingredients that will help develop a story full of secrets and lies.
We play as Adam Jensen, an ex-SWAT member, who now works as Head of Security for Sarif Industries, one of the leading companies in technological augmentations, and whose life changes in an instant after terrorists target the company, by facing this threat, he is critically injured, therefore to save his life he is augmented to save his life, forced to be augmented his life will change once again by discovering the many secrets, lies and conspiracies surrounding the attacks.
DE:HR is mostly an FPS with RPG elements and stealth mechanics that offers a system where we can spend praxis points and improve our already augmented organism, making Adam Jensen fully transhuman, eyes, and extremities and mostly our body is improved with several mechanical and technological advancements that make the main character a total killing machine if needed, a silent and stealthy assassin that moves in the shadows and if we want it we can act unseen alerting no one in the area.
At our disposal we have different kind of weapons for different playstyles, which go from lethal to non-lethal, making it a variable depending on situations, mission aspects or the user’s personal choice, we can mix all of the above and expecting different reactions from the AI, the different paths the game offers will always lead you to the same outcome, which is finishing the mission.
The game offers a top notch sound and voice acting, every character is believable regarding the different political, philosophical and social issues the game brings up, something that is slowly happening in real life, the augmentation of our bodies, what makes us human, humanity playing God, as well as ethics, transhumanism and evolution. All main characters and NPCs have intelligent and charismatic dialogues, at the same time, dialogues will change if we get to use some implants that will guide us through the person’s body language, voice and reaction to our arguments. Nothing negative at all here, great work.
Regarding the soundtrack, it is extremely well done, it fits every location and area perfectly, the ambient and electronic themes that embellish the cities and places we visit give the game a deep and cohesive atmospheric sensation, listening to the OST when doing other things will always be a reminder of places we visited, the stealth action and tension when moving in the shadows to avoid detection, excellent.
DE:HR is a modern title, however, it is starting to show its age already, graphically it is okay, as someone who prefers gameplay and mechanics over graphical beauty, I must say that most of the game looks very plastic and lifeless, textures and details are decent at best, many of the NPCs we see around look like mannequins and choppy, main characters are the ones that show true life, of course this makes sense as they are the main protagonists, but overall, it is the atmosphere that gives the graphics a breath of fresh air from time to time. It is not terrible, however most of the time I feel everything is a fake decoration, even trees and plants look like if they were fake, again, not terrible, not great either.
Now, in terms of gameplay, the game is solid, however, it clearly favors stealth over action, regardless of boss fights, most missions are built to be finished in stealth mode, but we are given rocket and grenade launchers, SMGs and heavy duty weapons, which makes no sense for the most part, despite given the option in the beginning to go lethal or non-lethal, most of the missions are design to go unnoticed and noiseless, hence the absurdity of carrying noisy weaponry. I feel this aspect of the game should have been polished a bit more, alerting anyone on open field will give away our position making us an easy target to take down, also, fighting mechanics are not the best either, it feels clunky and slow, which gives the stealth side of the game a more fitting option in the end.
My recommendation is to ditch any big weapon that uses many slots, saving space for grenades, typhoon ammo for boss fights and other more practical items like the stun and tranquilizer weapons and their respective ammo.
Having played the original version of this game plus Missing Link DLC, the director’s cut version is a solid title, it gives the DLC justice by giving it a right place, something that on the previous original HR felt weird and pace killing. Achievements are also a great addition, some are challenging and require patient and practice, so expect many save files being loaded again and again to get that precious achievement. DE:HR is a great game, rough around the edges, but with the right gameplay and implant in use it delivers a great stealth and tense feeling.

Deus Ex is a cyberpunk stealth game with some minor RPG elements. Although the game suffers from a few minor shortcomings, it is all in all a great futuristic game with countless hours of content. Skip to the end for a summary.
Although they aren't the best, the graphics in this game have aged very well, and would've been passable in the current year. All the textures weren't blured and character models are realistic. The only flaw with the graphical aspect is the fact that everything seems to have a yellow tint to it. Sure, it's what the developers were going for, but at the same time at least some color variety would help out here and there. However, I can understand the yellow tint since they were going for a cyberpunk game, and it nails that atmosphere. Everything feels realistic enough to be possible in the near future, which suits the game nicely, since it makes you able to relate with the story (more on that later).
SCORE 8/10
Note: This section won't effect the final score, I just thought it would be interesting to include this. Tested on: 1060 3GB, AMD FX-8320 and 8GB RAM. Average frames: 85, 100 in other sections (maxed settings, 1080p). For any mid to high spec PC's, this game will run flawlessly. I've also heard of this game running fairly well on low-spec systems (on lower settings of course). There are a few hiccups when entering a new area, but usually only for a second or two, and the game goes back to its regular framerate. I wouldn't worry about not being able to run this. On the side of bugs, there is really only one that I was able to find, which would be when performing a dual takedown, the enemies would be in a wall at the start of the animation, but nothing game-breaking.
SCORE 9.5/10
As stated before, Deus Ex is a stealth/rpg game. The biggest thing this game encourages is playing it the way that you want to play it. You can play this game as a stealth game or you can play it as a shooter game, and even in these two ways to play, each one of them have different paths through the level, and have still even more different approaches to situations. Personally, non-lethal stealth was the best way to go, but as I said, you can play however you want. The game revolves around exploring a semi-open world and sneaking (or shooting) your way past confrontations. Apart from main quests, there are plenty of side-quests that are equally interesting. Doing all of the side quests and exploring a lot of the world will get you about 22-24 hours of content, which is definitely plenty in my book. The levels are well-crafted, but for about half of the game, you only have access to 2 areas, Detroit and China. However, when you get closer to the end, a bunch of new levels are thrown at you, which manage to be refreshing and different from the starting two areas. One of my only flaws in the gameplay would be the gunplay, which doesn't feel too great, which is one of the reasons I went for a stealthy approach to encounters.
SCORE 9/10
Deus Ex has a pretty good storyline. It's not the best, but it manages to hold your attention throughout the whole game. One of the greatest things that the story does is it shows the consequences of technology, and how not all change is great. Most of the characters are pretty good, but voice acting feels a bit shallow. It's hard to say anything about the story without spoiling it, so I recommended playing through it.
SCORE 8/10
To sum up the audio in this game, it's ok. The soundtrack is a bit generic, but it manages to nail the atmosphere of the game, which is really all I can ask for. Guns sound pretty bad, mostly like pea shooters. The voice acting isn't bad, but again, it's generic. The audio is definitely the worst part of the game, yet it's still not bad.
SCORE 7/10
As much as I can't see myself replaying this game, and that's not saying it's bad, I just feel it'll be boring if I already know the ins and outs of levels and have no challenge, but nevetheless, the game features a ng+, which is there if you want to play through the game and get all of the augmentations. I don't feel it would be fair to include this in the final rating, for it would drop the score significantly when it doesn't really deserve it.
SCORE 6/10
