Just like a lot of others, I initially tried it after purchase and was a little disappointed - I wasn't sure I would ever like it.  Seeing as I had just bought it however, and given some of the other reviews I had read, I persevered with it.
I have to say, after having this controller for about a year, that I don't regret it one bit;  in fact, I actually prefer it to my PS4 controller now.  When I have to use Origin (for example), I find myself really disappointed that I simply cannot use the Steam controller.
The Gyro-movement is a hugely under-rated feature as well - this works amazingly well for aiming, especially when you tweak the settings.  This is part of the reason I miss using the controller so much when I have to move back to my PS4 one; playing through Prey recently on PS4 was terrible for that as I kept trying to tilt the damn thing when aiming.
And it keeps improving;  since I had it, they have introduced several new features, including an experimental rumble.
For the majority of games, there are an absolute tone of other players configurations;  just pick the one you want, re-map any bits of it to taste and save it as your own.  You can of course set one up from scratch, but I personally never bother - other people have done a much better job than I have, to the point where I prefer them to the developer recommended presets.
The only negatives I have after over a year of using the hardware is the "build quality", the battery life and some of the face button positions.
Hopefully we will see a Steam Controller 2.0 in the future with these issues addressed.
The plastic does feel rather cheap (and very smudge-prone) - this makes the overall build of the controller feel cheap, but in reality it's anything but.  Some of the buttons (and haptic-feedback) are also quite noisy, but you get used to that.  In fact, I usually play rhythmic sounds with the feedback while waiting for games to load, but that's just me!!
The controller uses regular batteries, and they don't seem to last very long either.  I have personally given up now and just have it plugged in via USB all the time (with the batteries left in to keep the weight ratio correct).
The thumbstick does seem to be slightly too close to the facebuttons, and when positioned to the right it is almost touching your right hand thumb.  It just feels a bit unnatural.  On this note, the buttons themselves do seem to be a bit further down - when your muscle memory is attuned to the buttons being higher up, you contentiously press the wrong ones when not looking.  Again, this is something you get used too in time.
All in all, I cannot recommend this enough;  it just needs time.  You HAVE to get used to it;  I saw someone else liken it to when games consoles first invented dual thumbsticks...that was indeed a weird time, but we integrated to it and it would now seem weird NOT to have two thumbsticks.  This is the crux of the matter for me;  this replaces tradition with a new idea; this might not be for everyone, but I heatedly believe anyone can get used to this if they give it enough time.

Because of this it can be difficult to reach them before either getting used to the placement and/or the need for bigger hands. When you do get used to the placement of the abxy buttons or can still be easy to accidently press the wrong button due to how close the buttons are together.
Positive:
The controller's buttons and touchpad are all very responsive. The customization is best phrased as what some well describe as "second to none." With exception to the standard Option, Start and Home buttons they're isn't anything you can't customize to your needs. They can be set to just what they do, to how sensitive each control is. Plus they're are extra features such as the trigger button having a double feature. Say for a FPS you lightly hold the button, you can still, press further till you feel a click and it will fire. Or perhaps racing games, you can set the trigger to gradually to accelerate or suddenly. The rest of the features are similar as such, or if you prefer, you can disable them as you like.
Mixed comments:
The controller comes equipped with two buttons on the back cover where you're fingers will lay on. They can be handy for additional options, or if you're like me it can be a pain and better to just disable them. Any time I tense up, I tend to grip the controller and end up pressing those buttons by accident.
Over all, a great controller if you can't get used to it, just don't expect it to be like any other controller you've ever used before.

Re-reviewed as previous review was too 'thin'.
Overview:
Cities in Motion 2 is a transport simulation game where you get to control and manage a fleet of vehicles, build stops, set up lines, decide fares, and manage employees. It offers a few cities packed into the base game to select with the option to download more from the steam workshop, as well as short campaign.
Pros:
- The game's core mechanics just feel right. The timetable is relatively easy to grasp, the line planner is intuitive, and the vehicle selector is simple.
- The cities packed into the base game are incredibly well thought out, in the sense that they look and feel real. The traffic bunches up just right on that midtown exit, the highway to get from that industrial area to the suburbs is always busy at rush hour, the cinemas, museums and attractions are in the culture district, nestled near a park. The cities have character, but lack a transport system, and that's where you come into play.
- The game is bundled with a map editor. The map editor is so in-depth it practically doubles as a city builder stand alone (granted, your options for buildings are limited to either hand placing everything, or randomly filling in the whole map, then if you want you can edit it and hand place things). For a game already so in depth, I've had endless fun trying to make my own city in the map editor.
Cons:
- What the public think of your ticket prices fluctuates violently. One day everyone is super pleased about your ticket prices, and when you add a new bus line the next day, ridership plummets. I have no idea why it happens at all, but it does.
- Once you've made functioning transport systems for all base game cities, you have no choice but to download more cities otherwise the game gets boring.
- Trolleybusses are USELESS. Nobody rides them. The only way to make money off of them it seems, is to make a single parallel line up and down a large avenue.
- Graphics aren't top notch. Granted, it doesn't affect gameplay, but those who can't play a game without super optimized HD graphics may want to stray away.
- Minor visual glitches. Nothing major, just things like bendy busses ripping apart when making certain turns, or subway trains seperating carriges on some bends. I've seen a waterbus once became a submarine.
- Very limited vehicle choice. There's only 3 different busses, 2 subway trains, 3 trams, 2 waterbusses, and 2 trolleys. It feels like the vehicles that are there are missing a few types. Granted, you CAN buy what seems to be the 'missing' vehicles in DLC, but that's a really cheeky business strategy if you ask me. I personally think there should've been more vehicles bundled into the base game. 5 busses would be nice, 3 or 4 subways, 4 or more trams, and a minimum of 3 trolleys.
Overall:
If you're a fan of simulation games, city builders, and management games, pick this one up. It'll have you saying "why is my tram line getting such low ridership!?" while tearing out your hair.
Also it's made by the same folks who made Cities:Skylines. What's not to like?

Playing through Deus Ex: Human Revolution was great fun! Even though I played it like any average joe would (so no ghosting, some stealth, mostly lethal gunplay), I still felt like I was doing things MY way and not the way the devs intended. I'd say the best parts of the game are (1) the way character progression is handled (2) the amazing soundtrack (specifically the battle themes) and (3) the atmosphere that the environments and characters convey.
The only negative I'd mention is that the story is both very simple and very complicated. The title pretty much tells you what the game is mainly about, and the story here is the typical sci-fi story that goes through all the motions you'd expect. However, you'll come across some crazy stuff that I could only describe as... Anime. Not necessarily a bad thing I suppose, but it's not really a vision of how our future looks and more a attempt to mimic something like Ghost in the Shell or Akira. I think anyone who reaches the end of the game will kind of see what I mean.
Anyway, totally recommended for any fan of the more 'cerebral' first person shooter/RPG hybrids, or just science fiction fans. You'll get something out of this one for sure, just give it about two hours to really show you what it's all about (the first two hours can feel a bit wonky as you are still underpowered and without lots of options). Be cautious of what you spend your skill points on, but don't overthink it that much either to the point where you miss out on lots of potential fun.

TL;DR: For its price, it's a great game, and it can provide many hours of fun, and I would definitely recommend it. However, there are a few other things to consider.
Blockland... one of the games I've owned for the longest. This is a great game, and I don't regret buying it for one second. But I have nostalgia for it now, and I thought a list of pros and cons would be nice for people looking to buy the game today.
PROS:
-   You can build stuff with LEGO, basically.
It's not quite as freeform as, say, Roblox's do-all building system, but it's quite a robust system that works great, and includes a Trust system that allows you to set who can edit or add to your builds.
-   The add-ons are spectacular.
Years of community support have lead to the creation of many, many great vehicles, bricks, tools, weapons, builds, you name it. The community still supports the game to this day. To this extent, I'd say the game is a lot like Garry's Mod: the community addons make the game.
-   You can play on the builds you put together.
A lot of great Blockland servers are based upon a solid build, with a good set of vehicles/weapons/whatever, to put together a nice gamemode. From deathmatches to capture-the-flag, racing, treasure hunting, fighting against an amorphous mass ("the creep"), destroying Christmas, farming... The community has come up with a lot of great gamemodes over the years.
CONS:
-   The community is probably the greatest setback of this game.
It's a mixed bag, between people who contribute positively through great addons and builds, or artwork, or even cool servers, and people who only contribute negatively, with a toxicity that rivals that of more famous examples like League. Thankfully, most of the latter group can be avoided by never stepping foot in the game's forums, which I wholly recommend. Sure, some of it all inevitably seeps into the game itself, but it's not an omnipresent threat or anything.
-   The community is also not quite as big as a game like this needs.
Servers are player-hosted, and aren't dedicated, like Roblox's. Therefore, a lot of great servers might see the light of day for only a while, before the server owners decide to pull the plug, often not sharing their work with others. This is probably familiar to you if you like to play on community servers on, for example, CS:GO or TF2. However, there, the servers are usually hosted by bigger communities rather than individuals, and have an easier time staying up for much longer. The reason this hasn't been the case with Blockland is just... popularity, I suppose. Blockland just needs more people, who stick for longer.
-   The game's lead developer hasn't really done much in the way of official updates in quite a while now. He's still actively moderating the forums, but as far as updates go, the last truly major update has been years ago. I don't think this is a huge issue, since again, like Garry's Mod, this game is supported mostly by the community.
Overall, I think the game definitely has potential for you, no matter if you're just in for some casual lego fun, or want to stay and put together something truly great. It's up to you, and there's fun for everyone. For the low price, I'd give it a go.

I was one of the few people who didn't mind the narrative horror experience that was Doom 3. But Doom, as the name implies, goes back to the source of what made this series so compelling in the 90s, and somehow manages to tell a compelling story with well-written lore (for those who want it) while subverting the idea that these kinds of games need narratives at all (for those who don't). It's smart, funny, gory, and graphically astounding.
My big gripe with the game is its over-dependence on glory kills. The mechanic feels good, and makes sense from a design perspective, but I miss the feeling of a big blast of weaponry splitting demons into mush, or at least atomized viscera. You still get that occasionally, but usually a well-timed blast sends demons into a glowing yellow or blue "prone" state, which means they're susceptible to a brutal melee attack. It disrupts my need for demon gore. It disrupts the flow of Doom.
But really, this is more or a less a small gripe. I see why they designed the game that way. If I want to play something simpler, I can still play the original.

Early concept arts from 2012 showed areas such as a museum, a library and the streets; all indicated this would be the remake of Hell On Earth. It all made sense considering Doom 3 was the remake of the very first episode. Then there was silence till 2015 when - during the summertime - Bethesda showcased the gameplay of the 4th episode. It was great: gory, fast-paced, had great graphics as well as numerous executions.
Story-wise we are back where Doom 3 began. On Mars all hell breaks loose after an experiment conducted by UAC employees goes horribly wrong. But did it really go wrong or the aim was to unleash these foul beasts on mankind? It is our job to put a stop to all this and find all the answers. Interestingly, there is no "zero" level now which showed the base in its peaceful state back in Doom 3. We are thrown right in the middle of it; in fact, our protagonist wakes up from a long sleep only to find himself in shackles. He breaks free, kills a couple of zombies, picks up a pistol then his dark green marine armour soon after and proceeds to the nearest exit.
I liked the story. Instead of Bertruger we hunt down a lady called Olivia. The director of UAC, Samuel Hayden, helps us along the way with the highly-advanced A.I. of the base called VEGA. As we make progress our menu provides us with codex entries, entries that provide more information on the background of these characters including every monster we encounter. This is what we have instead of PDAs (e-mails and audio logs) and it is great fun reading how it is possible, physiologically, that the Mancubus can shoot toxic materials from his arms, why the Revenant has a bony structure and why the Lost Souls are despised by other monsters. All these details tell us a lot about the game's lore. We see the story through via 13 exciting chapters and the ending leaves us with a cliffhanger.
The game is an interesting mix of modern and old-school shooters. It is modern as it has RPG elements - by collecting tokens of fallen guards, energy cells and visiting floating field robots we can apply upgrades to our weapons. Most have two secondary firing modes and these can be strengthened. For the last update a certain criterion has to be met, for instance, we need to kill 2 demons with just one shot of our sawed-off shotgun. You do that for 30 times and you get another upgrade to this already deadly weapon.
The cells are needed to increase the maximum amount of health, armour and ammunition we have and by finding rune trials we can earn runes that provide us with passive abilities. A trial gives us one weapon and the task is usually to eliminate a certain number of enemies in the given time. A maximum of 3 runes can be active at a time. Some are really powerful - one allows us to fire our weapons without losing any ammo till our armour is greater than 100. Points to make upgrades we can also get by completing 3 challenges per level (e.g. kill a Revenant while it is in mid-air).
The creators went even further and hid a lever on each level. These open a secret door somewhere that unlocks a classic Doom 1 or 2 level. Only a small portion is available during the campaign - the level unlocked can be accessed from the main menu. Additionally, we have Doom Marine dolls scattered across each level - they allow us to check the 3D models of our enemies as well as our weapons (again, accessed from the main menu).
But Doom is, primarily, an old-school shooter.  We run around and jump when needed. When we are close to edges our marine automatically pulls himself up. When we acquire the boot thrusters halfway in the story a double-jump will be possible. Forget the narrow, dark corridors you saw in Doom 3 and welcome the large, arena-like areas that are so similar to a multiplayer deathmatch session we used to play back in 2000 in Quake 3.
Usually, the area we visit is in lock-down so you know you have to clear it before you can make the story advance. Disgusting, dark red demonic objects - so-called gore nests - lie in the middle of these areas and by destroying them the enemies teleport in to take revenge. You can always prepare and survey the area - you'll welcome the powerups such as invulnerability, berserk, haste and - my favourite - quad damage. Gameplay is very satisfying - dynamic and as fast-paced as it can get.
As an extra touch when our enemies have low health they become stunned. A short period of time allows us to approach them and perform an execution. These so-called Glory Kills not only look really good but can make them drop extra life, armour or even ammo. Several animations can be played depending on how we approach our victim - an imp's jaw can be broken or he can be tripped only to have its head crushed.
Our pistol and chainsaw deserve a special mention. Remember how some of these weapons became useless? You obtained stronger ones so you completely abandoned the early ones and they were deemed useless. Now, the pistol in Doom has its special secondary fire (a charged shot is pretty strong when applied to the head), plus, it has infinite ammunition. A chainsaw, on the other hand, means an instant kill and if you kill a bad guy a huge amount of ammo is dropped immediately. Not only can it save you from dangerous situations but you can get the missing ammo for your rocket launcher. Naturally, the chainsaw has its own animations.
Every completed level can be replayed so that you can find the missing secrets and complete the challenges you failed to do so. Nightmare and Ultra Nightmare difficulty settings unlock only later as you complete the game on previous settings - Ultra Nightmare is really for hardcore fans as in case you die it means permadeath. Ultra Violence was my choice for a 2nd walkthrough - it was hard but very satisfactory.
An arcade mode allows us to replay the entire campaign where the emphasis is on gathering more and more scores. As we eliminate our foes in a more diverse way we increase our multiplier - we have to keep moving and killing so this is even faster than the regular campaign. We can compare our results with those of our friends and other players on leaderboards.
A Snapmap mode allows us to create and publish our own maps. A detailed tutorial mode explains how to do that - we can play the published levels of other players.
Too bad only Team Deathmatch is available in multiplayer. Several other modes can be played but I was not able to find anybody to join, unfortunately. The levels for TD look great and are many; powerups and stronger guns regularly appear to make the battle more interesting. A demon rune is something that allows us to transform into a demon we met so many times in the campaign. These are heroic versions of mentioned monsters - killing other players will be very easy but we can only do so for a limited period of time.
New weapons, usable items, demons and pieces of armour (to customise our character) are all that can be unlocked as we level up in multiplayer. After the 50th level we get an echelon rank - there are 11 of these so you have overall 550 levels to attain. By reaching the first rank you unlock most of the weapons, monsters and items so after that it's all about cosmetics - there are dozens of colours and even patterns to apply to every piece of armour and even to our weapons. Taunts also wait for us to be used when on the podium at the end of each session.
I forgot to mention that the game looks tremendously beautiful. My i5-3570 coupled with a GTX 1060 allowed me to play it with a constant 60 FPS (with pretty much all options set to ultra). Monsters are very detailed and the effects (lava, lightning, fire) all look quite amazing on the levels that take place in hell. This is the prime example of how you do optimization. I can only recommend Doom 4 - a great sequel / remake for fans and newcomers alike.

You see that thumbs up at the top of this review? The one that says I recommend this game? That thumbs-up is nothing but a massive, smoldering, gunk-encrusted half-truth.
I do recommend that you give it a try, even if all you're doing is dipping your toes in. The graphics are great. At the best of times, the gameplay can be more intense and satisfying than anything else on the market. The way you can customise your Mech and your playstyle is something that can only be matched by another MechWarrior game, all of which were made over 10 years ago.
However, no matter how hard I try to look past it, or how much I try to work against it, it always makes me put this game down after a few weeks of coming back to it: The grind in this game is mother♥♥♥♥ing atrocious.
In MWO, you pay for new Mechs (the giant robots), weapons, and components for your Mechs with a currency called C-Bills. You get these by playing in matches, and you generally get more if you play better in a match. Over the course of your first 25 matches, you'll also get a bonus which roughly amounts to 8,000,000 C-Bills. However, after you've drained that 8,000,000, you only get anywhere from 50,000 to 200,000 C-Bills from a single Quick Match on average.
These sound like very large numbers, but weapons will run you anywhere from several thousand to hundreds of thousands of C-Bills, a new engine to make you move faster might cost a few million more, and a whole new mech can be anywhere from 1,000,000-16,000,000. Specifically, the Kodiak--one of the most large and powerful Mechs in the game--is 16,000,000, the Locust--a mech so small, fast, and lightly armed that you need to be an experienced player to use it right--is 1,000,000, and the popular, middle-of-the-road Heavy and Medium Mechs run anywhere from 3,000,000 to 15,000,000, depending on whether you want a cheaper Inner Sphere Mech, or more powerful Clan Mech.
The combination of steep prices and low income means that buying a single Mech can take dozens, if not hundreds of matches to earn the C-Bills you need, much less an entire roster full of BattleMechs that allows you to choose a new Mech and a new playstyle for each different match.
And this is all on top of the game's customisation and leveling systems for each Mech. Since you might want to spend more C-Bills on a different build for your Mech, and leveling up your Mech to its maximum efficiency also takes C-Bills, taking the time to make your current Mech the most efficient for your playstyle can divert precious millions of C-Bills away from your next Mech.
And even if you get all the C-Bills necessary to buy a Mech that you want, and hot-rod it into a (supposed) killing machine, it's entirely possible that you might choose a completely underpowered Mech, if you don't do the right research. For instance, the Orion has such massive hitboxes that the sides of its torso constantly get blown out, taking out all weapons and systems inside them. The Gargoyle is just too fast and lightly armed for a Mech of its weight, making it almost useless in comparison to anything else. There are even different variants of some mechs which are great, while other variants of the same mech simply don't have the right kinds of weapon mounts to be effective.
This all boils down to a game that forces you to make important financial choices. However, these aren't fun and invigorating financial decisions, like you'd find in a reasonably designed video game. Instead, these are the depressing kind of money questions that you're probably trying to get away from, in the first place. The kind that make you realise that your life (or, in this case, the game) isn't that great anyway, and the kind and amount of cars (or Mechs) you get probably doesn't even matter.
"Do I wait 5 years to buy the gleaming, awesome Porsche that I want, or do I blow my wallet on my uncle's ♥♥♥♥♥♥, worn-down 1972 Ford Pinto so I can have something to drive now?"
"Do I get one really great car that works, but I'll probably get bored of in a while, or do I get several other vehicles that give me a nice variety, but are absolute♥♥♥♥♥♥on their own?"
"Is it even worth fixing up this current car of mine, which really doesn't work right no matter what I do, or should I flush all the money I poured into it down the toilet, and see if I can get a car which isn't a pile of garbage right out of the box?"
"As it turns out, my uncle's ♥♥♥♥♥♥ 1972 Ford Pinto is even worse than I thought it would be, but I don't have the money to get anything else, and it's so bad that putting more money into it won't make it any better. How will I hold out until I can get something better? Should I even try to hold out?"
"There's this one car I really want, but everyone says it's absolutely awful, and I'm not even sure if what they're saying about it is true. Should I buy it, and run the risk of getting a really bad car, or not buy it, and disappoint myself?"
Of course, it is possible to sidestep all of this by purchasing MC with real money, and using that to buy mechs, but the Kodiak is worth roughly $30 of MC, with many Medium or Heavy Mechs proving to be $7-$15.
Even without MC, there is the Faction Play mode, which allows you to earn about twice as many C-Bills as with Quick Play, but even this requires you to have 2-4 different Mechs, which should all be fully optimized, if you want to stand a chance against the enemy. Therefore, it'll likely take you weeks--possibly months--of playing before you can be competitive in Faction Play.
As I said in the opening, MWO is worth a shot. I deliberately focused on the bad parts of the game for this, since they weigh this game down so much, but there is honestly fun to be had in the individual matches, even if you run one of the free, uncustomisable Trial Mechs, instead of your own. However, I simply cannot justify the time or money you'd need to experience this game to the fullest (i.e, trying out the majority of the mechs, and having enough money lying around to screw with different loadouts for all of them). Play this game for a little while, leave it, then figure out how to run MechWarrior 2, 3, and 4 on your computer, play those, and hope Piranha Games does well with MechWarrior 5. That's what I recommend you do with this game.

I have put in over 4000 hours in to MWO (i also used the stand alone client) over the last 3 years and have seen large changes in basic gameplay mechanics, balance etc.
What I will try to do here is summerise the the pros and cons of the game, the way it is laid out etc.
MWO is big giant robots carrying a variety of weapons attempt to either kill the enemy robots or completing objectives e.g. capturing a flag, destroying a base, defending a VIP etc.
Some of these mechs are "light" and run around at up to 160kph, some of these mechs are "assaults" and move at less than 50kph. You can choose to alter the engines in these mechs (except for some of the clan mechs, more on that later) to change the speed but it takes weight and the more weight that you have the more weapons, armour etc. you can carry so there is always a trade off. Lasers hit a single point but take time to apply their damage, missiles spreads their damage out but general hit in one big punch, ballistics behave in their own way so there are more trade offs in play style.
All weapons generate heat as well, some more than others, lasers are hot, ballistics are cooler. If you get too hot you will either overheat and shut down or take damage and possibly explode.
There is also a very complex skill tree system which lets to further adjust the performance of your mech, you will need to look at the forums or some tutorials on it before making too many decisions about what skills you are going to use or not.
This gives the game a lot of depth and ability to change mechs for particular play styles.
The game itself is broken down in to 2 major different game types, quickplay and faction play.
Quick Play is 2 teams of 12 people, 1 mech each, a particular game type and 1 team coming out on top. In the solo queue the game *tries* to group you with people of your skill level although obviously when there are fewer people around you sometimes end up playing in the different pilot "tiers". In quick play individual skill can make a difference in the game but team play does help so using VOIP can improve your chance of winning.
In the grouped up team quick play your team has less tonnage the more group members you have, as team play generally means that your team will be more effective than just the weight of the your mechs combined.
The second game type is Faction Play, this is 2 teams of 12 men with 4 mechs each. This means there are generally multiple waves with different tonnages etc. In faction play it is ESSENTIAL that voice comms is used, it is always helpful to find teamspeak hubs, coordinate your drop decks, bring mutually supporting builds etc. Faction Play is for the people that want to work hard for a win, want to work as a team and want to try new tactics, strategies etc. It also takes a while to earn enough mony to  get enough mechs together to be able to fight effectively in FP.
So that's the over lay of the game. Hiding behind all this is the elephant in the room which the experienced players will think is the biggest point which needs addressing - game balance.
The game is split between the Inner Sphere and the Clans. The clans left known space, hid away at the edges of the galaxy and developed a warrior society based on the technology that was available at the time. Meanwhile the Inner Sphere decended in to civil war and a lot of technology was lost or forgotten. Why is this important? Clan mechs use more advanced weapons, have more advanced engines and smaller equipment which is lighter. This means that they can fit more weapons in the same tonnage, don't need as much tonnage for the same speed etc.
On the flip side IS generally have more armour and generate slightly less heat.
The long and short of it is that clan mechs ARE better, especially when built properly, this makes the Faction Play element of the game much more challenging for un organised teams in the IS. Because of this the population on the game servers is generally on the clan side which means that the clan teams tend to win more.
If you are only interested in Quick Play this isn't an issue as you can use whichever mechs you want but it does make a big difference in the faction play elements. In attempts to balance this PGI have tried to alter wepon heat, cooldown times, drop deck tonnages etc. some people like the changes, some people dont. You will find both sides of the arguments all over the forums and I don't expect it to meet everyone's expectations any time soon.
Finally the payment options. As per other free games there are a couple of areas where you can spend your real world money. You can pay for premium time, this gives you increased in game currency rewards and xp which you use to buy your skill points.
You can also buy mechs. Most of the mechs can be bought with in game currency as well, there are a few which can only be bought with real world money, these are called "hero" mechs. No hero mech is substantially better than equivalent currency mechs, in fact they are mostly just another option and gain no real benefit in game. Spending money on the game will only increase the speed in which you get things, it won't actually give you an advantage over other players.
I would definitely recommend the game for people to try, but try to find other people to regularly drop with, this isnt really a solo friendly game. Search the forums for the teamspeak hubs, check out youtube videos on the game for ideas and how to do things, use in game VOIP etc.

This review will be mixed, simply because the game itself is a mixed bag. It requires skill, and tactics and I can understand some of the Negative reviews even though I think most of the issue is player perception. Don't get me wrong the game has some issues, but I find it well worth playing despite that.
I'll have to break this review up into 2 parts, as Both the Clans, And Inner Spher are very different and have very different playstyles.
1. Inner Sphere.
Pros-
* Mechs are vastly supperior then clan mechs in the area of Brawling and in your face battles.
* Mechs start with more useful quirks, even without skills.
* More weapon types and varyations.
* More Armor options, and available types.
* Higher Drop deck weight Limit, of 265 Tons.
Cons-
* Slower
* Shorter Range then Clan mechs
* Weapons do less damage
* Weapons require more face time
Clan:
Pros-
* Variable Components and Pods make mech far more customizable.
* Longer range weapons
* Higher Damage Weapons
* Faster Mechs
* Lighter weapons
Cons-
* Less armor and Armor types
* Less weapon choices
* Weapons Produce more heat
* Less Mech Fitting Space
* Smaller Drop Deck Weight Limit of 240 Tons
* Squishy and Most can not Brawl at all
Now, reading that, you might go, Huh Inner sphere seems superior, Thats totally against lore. Well thats true, 1v1 an Inner Sphere mech will always win against a clan mech of the same weight class if both players have the same skill level.
And you might say, if thats true why are clans winning? Well its simply really, well... not simple but the answer is, New players Join IS, Veterans and Military Join Clan. The reason Clans Dominate is because the vast majority of their players work as a team, Whereas the vast majoity of IS even some premades are a giant cluster ♥♥♥♥.
The other reason is that clan mechs force you to learn fast, or die quick. They are not forgiving at all. You either learn to play at a competitive level very quickly or you rage quit. This mentality hits you from the very first battle. You will learn adapt, work as a team and dominate, or you'll die horribly.
Inner sphere mechs on the other hand can take massive amounts of damage without dieing, and are VERY forgiving. IS adopts the mentality of learn as you go if you make mistakes your ok. PGI encourages this. If you put a Clan Pilot in an IS mech they are damn near unkillable and will dominate the battle field. Put an IS pilot in a clan mech they are likely to die within the first 90 seconds of the match.
This unfortunatley has thrown the game completely out of balance. PGI bases nurfs on stats player reviews, and information of wins, rather then looking at the underlying causes. Its not that clan is overpowered, because honestly Clan mechs these days are about damn useless in the hands of anyone other then a veteran,  But because of the skill levels and mentalities and tactics, which is not something you can nerf.
So the clans continue to be nerfed into uslessness. Pointlessly, and many Life long Clan players are either quiting or moving to Inner sphere due to the massive pointless nerfbats swung at clan mechs repeatedly over and over again.
Conclusion:
The game is worth playing, its a lot of fun. Just realize the IS has a severe advantage over the clans, and if you choose to become a Clanner, realize that you'll either soon be an elitest, or you'll be crawling back to IS.
That being said, a Clan mech int he hands of a Skilled Clanneris a force to be recond with. But only if the pilot is a High Skilled Veteran player.
So what you choose, is up to you. Become one of the Elite, or Play casual as IS.

Wonderful experience of a culture that is both fantastical and very human in its depiction.
The story does an excellent job of demonstrating the complexity of morality and choice. The story veers from some of the 'standard' point and click genre, where the outcomes and options are not ever fully perfect. There is no 'make all the right choices', it's 'make the best choices you can under the circumstances'. Some may find that a bit too lifelike, and they might prefer something that is a bit more happy-go-lucky. It can get a discouraging, as some characters are a bit limited with having any positives for 'how' you play them. However, I enjoyed the realness of it. Also, I loved how heavily choices impacted outcomes. You can get a completely different story depending on the choices you make, and it's not just 'you died' or 'you survived'. The choices matter for *how* you *and* others survive. And I felt that sort of story did a great job of showing how the circumstances of others impacted their situations. Overall, the game did a great job of making a chaotic, discouraging situation into a worthwhile, challenging, and engaging story.
Pros:
-Choices *really* matter
-Many options/high replay value
-Good depiction of dilemmas of morality
-Fun puzzles with varied solutions
-Definitely a unique game
Cons:
-Some of the outcomes can be really discouraging (some character lines do a good job of balancing reality with reward, some are less so)
-While I enjoyed the demonstration of the power of circumstance, it can also take away from the role of 'player making the choices', and I sort of felt trapped/along for the ride at times
A narrative-based RPG that strongly defies tropes of the genre, providing sensible outcomes to decisions rather than simply empowering the player.

Some sort of disclaimer:
I've played this game before and this is a replay review. Your perspective changes as you go on and restart the whole game just so you could go see what happens if you pick the other choices. You will realise that some quests and most items don't do anything in the grand scheme of things (let's just say, not in the story sequence you're given), and the others do. But all in all, everyone has their hidden agenda, and whatever happens is bound to happen, nothing you do really matters much in the end.
So why not be calculating.
It is said that gameplay itself is heavily flawed, but is it? Surely a priest who has never been violent his whole life couldn't possibly win a fight with a eager ganger with a knife in the slum, a starving lost child wouldn't go ahead and finish a side quest first when she sees a familiar face in the angry crowd.
But that's also where the only flaw lies. The perspective switching works well with the storyline itself and it gives the player just enough information to make their own choices, but at the same time it's difficult to make completely unbiased choices based solely on the characters' own knowledge. A priest from the temple simply wouldn't have known anything about the illness of a random peasant's son, and a mercenary captain who only cared about his men being properly paid certainly wouldn't have sabotaged his own plan. The game puts too much trust in its players for no reason- whether it is a sacrifice on the gameplay to ensure smooth transition between segements or simply an attempt to force the elements from one scene to another reamains unclear.
But it doesn't negate the fact that the game itself is brilliantlly done. The writing in game does its job, serves an educational purpose (of course it doesn't give you free words of the wise, it's just different perspectives, different causes of actions, different worldviews- and they all make sense in their own situation), and is nothing but delightful. Every dialogue has it's usual sharp tone and is brilliantly written- Not that when the writing in a game does its job it deserves a pat on the back, but it's not easy to make everything reasonably brief but at the same time vastly detailed like this, since when a game goes all the way philosophical it's way easier to get itself into the grand hollowness of vagueness (I'm looking at you,
.)

| What it's all about |
8bitmmo is game is an 8bit styled mmo, the game is in third person mode and follows your character around, which is pretty much a square with legs, arms, and a square head. To accompany the retro look it heavily features chiptune while you're playing the game (for all you nostalgia nerds out there!).
In 8bitmmo, it is a very social game as the game revolves around a chat. With this chat, players wouldn't be able to communicate with each other. As the title says, you can literally build anything you want, from dragons to space ships, to pixel art and pirate ships, you can really do it all in 8bitmmo. You can even build quests for players, these quests are always built in towns in which give you your own personal area to build in.
| Pros |
- There is a postive and a thriving community who are all very welcoming.
- The game has recently been released as an alpha and may be updated frequently.
- You can build anything you want, as long as it's not innapropriate.
- It's relatively easy to obatin gold, there is a farming cycle which lasts for 45 minutes and within that time, players can gain 2000 gold.
- There is a market for premium items in which some players are willing to commit to keep the economy alive in the game.
- You can have alot of fun in this mmo.
| Cons |
- The developer is not active.
- Only a handful of players really stick around for a while, many players come and go.
- The vast majority of new players are mainly 3 year olds who spam the chat all day long, it's extremely irritating.
- This game calls itself an "mmo" yet there are only around 10 - 20 players online everyday, if you're lucky, this might be extended to 30 players.
| Over all view |
Personally, this is my favourite game and I do enjoy it. However, the game needs to be frequently updated and as a consiquence, many players aren't satisfied about the games slow development. Although the developer calls the game an alpha, in my eyes it's still a beta. It is still very basic and needs much more time and effort into the game. However, the community are very enthusiastic about new players and they are genuinly awesome people.
| Rating |
Overall, I'd rate 8bitmmo 8.5/10

This is an incredibly primitive 4X game.  It lacks features present in, and includes shortcomings lacking in, the Master of Orion II 4X game from TWENTY-ONE years ago.  It's less playable than FreeOrion, which isn't even a commercial game and has a skeleton crew of developers.  Micromanagement is rampant, necessary absractions to make the game playable are absent.  I gather that this game is now being used as a promotion for the Endless Space 2 game, but that game appears to be more a do-over than a sequel.  Was four years enough time for them to finally get it right, and should anyone pay them twice to get a playable game?
The development team was exceptionally inexperienced.  A sign of experience would be having played the most popular 4X games that preceded it, thus avoiding the pitfalls of those games while incorporating their best features; the net result SHOULD be a game that moves the genre forward.  This game moves the genre backward in terms of both features and playability.  Even the UI is primitive, lacking flexibility that even exists in FreeOrion.  That failure is not a new phemomenon, in fact it's becoming increasingly common as development teams become dominated by twentysomethings who were born long after the 4X genre began and have never even played the games that defined it.  This development team almost certainly fits that profile.  I am still waiting for a new 4X game that unambiguously surpasses all the old classic games like Master of Orion II and Pax Imperia.  Better graphics DO NOT define a better 4X game.
Perhaps later when I am less disgusted I will amend this with more details of the game's faults.  At the moment I need to put some distance between this game and my sanity.

A lighter 4X of sorts, isn't actually that hard or statistical like Civilisation titles or the recent Stellaris, but if you're interested in a new light 4X of sorts, why not give this one a try?
My Overall Feel for the game

Essentially, you choose your 'maneuvers' for three stages of battle - long range, medium range and melee. These can be things you've researched, or just what your individual ships can do. Then your ships carry out the combat without your input as you watch.

Ill start with the cons:
- Less intuitive then other controllers
When you first start using it, it might feel weird and unnatural.
- Customization can feel overwhelming
This con can be negated if you use the standard settings for the controler which are good most of the time. You can also use user made profiles.
- It will take time to use this controller effectively
This controller has a steep learning curve and it will take you time to master it. That said, this doesnt mean that you cant be effective with this controler sooner. Consider this con if you plan playing local co-op, it wont take long for your friends to be effective, however it will take longer for them to master it. I would put 20-40 minutes for effectively playing simple platformers/top down shooters and about 20 hours of gameplay to use all controls intuitively.
Now with the pros:
- Higher skill cap (more room for skill to reward control)
When you master this controller, you will be able to play most games better then with other controllers (Playstation/XBOX types). If standard controllers give you 5/10 control and mouse+keyboard 10/10, then the Steam Controller wil give you 7/10 control.

- Well built, comfortable
It will suit most hand sizes. My hands are rather on the large side and this controler feels good. I can reach buttons with fingers that were not intended to reach them, so this cotroller is small for me without being uncomfortable. This leads me to believe that it will be comfortable for small hands as well.
- Indepth customization
You can customize pretty much any button as well as the touchpad. If you dont like customizing then you can choose either the standard profile for the game, or you can find a profile made by other users for the game. This can all be done in Big Picture Mode with the controller itself.
- Computer remote on steroids
This controller can be used outside of steam and will be effective in browsing the web, texting, and most of the tasks performed by your mouse/keyboard. My writing speed with the controller as of now is about 60-70% of my keyboard speed, however this will vary with users.
Overall i am happy with this controller and will be buying another one.
PS: You should watch some reviews on Youtube. This is a short review and only skims through basics, and might not mention a con/pro which might influence your decision.

I bought one on impulse even though I don't own a Steam machine, a Steam link, a TV, or even a couch. I always liked the idea of the Steam controller and figured I might finally try it, so I got it as an alternative to the PS4 controller that I normally use.
In a vacuum it's really astoundingly good. Build quality is solid. The customization options are amazing. The ergonomics are good (for my thoroughly average-sized hands, at least). However, what a game controller should be is pretty well established these days, and the Steam controller goes against a lot of these norms. This is probably why a lot of people don't like it. Compared to other controllers, the Steam controller has a lot of good things going for it, a bunch of weird things that could go either way (mostly the, you know, the trackpad thing), and some aspects where it really could stand to improve.
Starting off with the really good things, how the controller sits in your hand is awesome. This is the first controller that I've used that seems to be actually designed so that you hold your index fingers on the bumpers and your middle fingers on the triggers, instead of alternating your index fingers between them. That in addition to the flip-flap buttons on the back for your ring and pinky fingers lets you use your hands very efficiently. With other controllers like DualShock and Xbox, I usually only use my thumbs and index fingers, leaving three fingers on each hand kind of just doing nothing. I always felt that was a bit silly, and finally there's a controller that addresses that.
The buttons in general are very nice and clicky. I find the response this gives them nice, but people used to the softer button presses on other pads might find it "cheap" or unpleasant. I particularly like the two-step triggers, which have an analog pull followed by a digital click. The only complaint I have is that the pull is a little short compared to Playstation and Xbox pads, which could be an issue for games that make full use of the analog triggers (eg. racing games).
The face buttons are a bit worse, mostly because of their positioning. I find it a little difficult to press the ABXY buttons and accidentally press the wrong button relatively often. The start and select buttons are also a little hard to find. This is probably something that will get substantially easier after I build some more muscle memory with the controller, but it's still clear that they had to make a small compromise with the button positioning because of the large track pads. On this controller the ABXY buttons do not feel like they're intended to be quite as quick to access as the corresponding buttons on PS/Xbox pads, so for games that have critical actions on these buttons I've found it helpful to bind some of them to the flip-flap buttons on the back of the controller.
Then there's the trackpads. I surely don't have to tell you what they do, but I was quite pleasantly surprised by them. When used for analog stick emulation for games designed to be played with sticks, they're definitely just a substitute. They also take quite a while to get used to for these games. After a while, though, I found myself liking the camera control offered by the trackpad more than joystick camera control, but the games still aren't really designed with this kind of a pad in mind so it's not enough to make it strictly superior to a regular pad. A big issue for this kind of games is that you can't claw grip this controller.
Where the trackpads really shine is FPS games and other games requiring (some) precision, and moving cursors around. Being the shooter enthusiast I am I still feel using them for FPS is beneath me, but it's definitely doable and after some practice I bet it would even be comfortable. For desktop use and strategy games they're a natural fit, and various role-playing games designed to be played on a mouse and keyboard are also particularly suited to this method of control. No big surprises here, to be honest.
The ergonomics are really good, even compared to other controllers. Like I already mentioned, this controller is designed so that all your fingers are doing some actual controlling when you're holding it. With a PS4 pad, for instance, I can't get a solid grip on the controller with my middle fingers on the triggers and index fingers on the bumpers, forcing me to use it with essentially two fingers per hand, with 3 out of 5 fingers doing nothing.
The Steam controller has a sort of a concave-shaped face, which is basically the inverse of what other controllers do. This will feel a bit weird at first, as you'll be maintaining grip on the controller with different parts of your hand than you do with other controllers. Other controllers like PS/Xbox tend to make you hold them between the bases of your thumbs on the face side and your middle/ring/pinky fingers on the back side. The Steam controller balances the grip out across your hand, with the bulk of the controller held between the center of your palms and the base of your little fingers, with some extra support from your index/middle fingers on the bumpers and triggers. This leaves your thumbs entirely free to work the trackpads, which is very important for accuracy.
I really, really love the ergonomics of this controller, but I expect this to be a divisive issue. I would imagine that people with smaller hands might find the controller unwieldy, given the controllers Xboxhuge size.
A major feature is the ~haptics~, which is basically a fancy word for vibration. The trackpads have a small amount of rumble when you use them that's been cleverly designed so that it sort of imitates the motion of a trackball or a joystick or whatever the pad is emulating. For trackballs (the default mouse mode) the rumble emulates the rolling of the trackball, so when you flick on the pad it'll start intense and then gradually decrease as the imaginary trackball slows down. For joysticks it'll rumble more the closer you are to the edge, emulating the resistance of the joystick's spring. This works better than I expected it to, of course for joysticks it's not really anything like the real thing, but for trackballs I love it. Nonetheless it gives you some much needed sensory feedback, and even though it obviously doesn't make it feel like a real joystick it starts making sense after you get used to it.
Finally I have to mention that this controller is quite noisy. The buttons are very clicky, and the haptics make this whirring/rumbling sound that's quite audible. They're not really annoying sounds per se, as they're just sounds of normal mechanical operation. I haven't noticed any truly undesirable sounds such as coil or servo whine with my controller, but I can see how sensitive users might dislike the loud clicky buttons and the haptics buzz.
There also doesn't seem to be traditional rumble on the controller (ie. one of those rapidly spinning unbalanced weights that other controllers use), instead the "experimental" rumble feature seems to use the same haptics stuff the trackpads do except with more intensity. This means the rumble isn't quite as good or heavy as with PS/Xbox controllers, and also that it has the same noise as the rest of the haptics on this controller do.
In conclusion, the Steam controller is a very solid but unconventional controller. It feels and performs like a high-quality piece of hardware, but because of its unusual design one should have an open mind and be willing to spend a while getting to grips with it. The customization options are truly commendable and make adapting to the controller substantially easier. I do not expect that the controller will be replacing my existing DualShock 4 for everything I use it for, nor do I expect to use it as a mouse/keyboard replacement, but there is certainly a niche subset of games where the Steam controller is the best choice.

For first-person shooters, Steam Controller is definitely superior to conventional gamepads.  The trackpad, when used in mouse mode, gives me much better aim than a thumbstick.  I find that a mouse and keyboard are still better for me, but perhaps this is a question of practice.  And with Steam Controller you can play the kind of games that you would never expect to see on an Playstation, such as Civilization VI or Command & Conquer.
But configuring the Steam Controller is fiddly.  You will have to carefully tweak the Controller's settings for every game you install.  This is because hardly any games have been designed around this unconventional gamepad.  The Steam client offers powerful configuration tools to get your Steam Controller working just right, but this process is fiddly and certainly confusing to the less tech-literate.
There is no good reason to buy this gamepad if you're not playing your games on your TV via Steam Link or with a Steam Machine.  But for those who do want to play their PC games from the living room sofa, the Steam Controller makes it doable if not perfect.  Steam Machine could work.  Nintendo, Sony, and Microsoft should consider trackpad-oriented gamepads for their next generation of consoles.

I have been playing this game for 10 years now, and this is my attempt at an actual, objective based view of Blockland.
When it comes to gameplay, Blockland is what I consider to be the best lego-based sandbox building game to ever be released. theres no strings attached. you click "start a game" and you are almost immediately thrown into a blank slate and are free to build whatever you want, however you want, when you want. Whatever brick, item, or vehicle is not provided by default, the community's faithful addon creators have provided for you. Blockland also comes with a intuitve and dynamic eventing system which allows you to assign functions to bricks. This game also supports gamemode functionality. You can host freebuilds, deathmatches, treasure hunts, and even community created gamemodes such as  falling tiles, jailbreaks, drawing games, parties, development servers, RPGs, and more.
you can build something as small as a 150 block house, to a near 1,000,000 block recreation of Seattle. You can event something as simple as a light switch, to the complexity of fully funtioning claculators, computers, and even RPGs. You can host gamemodes that are simple tweaks of the default, to gamemodes that could turn Blockland into a completely different and unrecognizable game. I would argue to say that with Blockland's open-source functionality and addon creating community, you can, quite literally do, build, or event anything.
I'm also fairly certain Blockland is the reason the whole genre that is "GMod animation" even exists.
The only problem Blockland has is that it is online. I can't tell you why becuase I still don't know why, but Blockland has attracted a very toxic community. Don't get it twisted. I have met amazing people in this game. people who have made me who I am. People who have broadened my horizons both intellectually and skillfully, people I very much intend to meet in person one day. If wasn't for this game AND its community, I wouldn't be the happy and successful person that I am. I owe A LOT to this game. Unfortunately; however, just as there are plenty of people who can share a story like mine, there are equal amount of people who have been beaten, torn apart, and broken down by this community.
I don't know this for fact, but I can almost garuantee you the 4-Pack tier for Blockland specifically exists for people who have been banned over, and over, and over, and over again. It's regularly been said since the day I joined in 2007, that once you join you're here forever, and jesus christ that seems to actually be true for some people. even the toxic ones. even me.
It's not a place for everyone. I believe you have to be a special kind of person to endure what happens here, and because of that, this has been the most "community" feeling communities i've ever been a part of. in my eyes, Blocklands community is what you get when you mix LEGO.coms community, Facepunches community, and ♥♥♥♥♥s community all into one. Yes the idiot rampant children, the borderline "submit a tip to the FBI" addons, the doxxing, DDoSing, and raiding. the whole 9 yards....... I adore this game.
I have poured over 5000 hours (including pre-Steam stats) into it and will probably spend thousands more.
The building system is simple, yet works beautifully; the add-on support is fantastic and as easy as dropping a .zip file into your Add-Ons folder; the modding community is small, but its members are very dedicated.
Blockland is a pure sandbox game.  There are some default add-ons and gamemodes, but other than that you're basically left to do whatever you want.  There's an optional tutorial, but the actual game doesn't hold your hand.  There are no annoying pop-ups giving you "gameplay tips" or ideas on what to build; it just drops you into a world, gives you the tools you need, and says "here, make something".  I love that.  The "Garry's Mod with Legos" description is very apt; it's very much in the same vein as Garry's Mod in that you are free to do whatever you want, whether it's building, fighting, roleplaying, or just screwing around with friends.  In fact, the latter is the main reason I keep coming back to this game—it's such a great hangout game.  Building is fun, playing deathmatch servers is fun, but the most enjoyment I've gotten out of this game is just doing dumb things with friends.  In my opinion, multiplayer is where this game really shines.  When you're by yourself it can get lonely, but with friends the time just melts away.
I said it earlier, but the add-on system is great.  All you have to do is put a .zip file into your Blockland/Add-Ons folder, and the game does the work for you.  Client add-ons are loaded on startup, and server add-ons can be enabled in a menu before you start hosting.  Making add-ons in this game is pretty easy too,
when compared to other games.  In fact, many people in the community first learned how to program by making add-ons for Blockland (including myself).  Thanks to the community, the game also unofficially has DLL support, though it's severely underdocumented.
Now, I'm going to be honest: the engine is not the best.  Blockland uses the Torque Game Engine, and the version it uses is from 2005.  While it's been heavily modified during the game's lifespan, it definitely shows its age at times.  There are odd quirks and bad design choices that you have to get around, which can be a bummer, especially when you have a cool idea.  (Though if you're like me, finding workarounds to engine limitations can be a fun challenge, albeit a hacky one at times).  While the engine limitations can be frustrating, and the scripting language (TorqueScript) is awful, the game is still pretty flexible in what you can do with it.
The other reviews are correct when they say that the community sucks.  The only caveat I'd like to add is that the
community sucks.  There are some people that like to mess with you in-game, but it's just like any other online multiplayer game, honestly.  It's not nearly as toxic as the forum, which in a way has become its own community.  I mean, there's a lot of crossover with people who still play the game (obviously), but there are many people on there who don't even play the game anymore and just like to post on the forum.  In general, if you avoid forum drama and bad servers, you should be fine.
Unlike many multiplayer building games, there is a system in place that prevents people from modifying your creations without your permission—this is called the "trust" system.  The trust system basically means people can't build on your bricks, destroy your bricks, or otherwise modify them unless you give them "trust".  There are two different types of trust: build trust and full trust.  With build trust, they can build on your bricks and modify them slightly, but they cannot destroy them or modify them in any significant way.  With full trust, they can build on, paint, destroy, modify, etc. your bricks, but trust can be revoked or downgraded at any time.  This is such a simple thing that many games just don't do, yet it improves the multiplayer experience so much because you don't have to worry about people ruining what you make.
Overall, the game is a wonderful experience that I would recommend to anyone who likes sandbox/building games (and Legos too, of course).  There is so much to do, so much you can make, and it's even better with friends.  I've had this game for almost 9 years, but I still find things to do on it.  Even when I get burned out and don't play it for months, I always find myself coming back; it's just one of those games.

I'll have to break this review up into 2 parts, as Both the Clans, And Inner Spher are very different and have very different playstyles.
1. Inner Sphere.

Cons-

Clan:
Pros-

* Longer range weapons
* Higher Damage Weapons
* Faster Mechs
* Lighter weapons
Cons-
* Less armor and Armor types
* Less weapon choices
* Weapons Produce more heat
* Less Mech Fitting Space
* Smaller Drop Deck Weight Limit of 240 Tons
* Squishy and Most can not Brawl at all
Now, reading that, you might go, Huh Inner sphere seems superior, Thats totally against lore. Well thats true, 1v1 an Inner Sphere mech will always win against a clan mech of the same weight class if both players have the same skill level.
And you might say, if thats true why are clans winning? Well its simply really, well... not simple but the answer is, New players Join IS, Veterans and Military Join Clan. The reason Clans Dominate is because the vast majority of their players work as a team, Whereas the vast majoity of IS even some premades are a giant cluster ♥♥♥♥.
The other reason is that clan mechs force you to learn fast, or die quick. They are not forgiving at all. You either learn to play at a competitive level very quickly or you rage quit. This mentality hits you from the very first battle. You will learn adapt, work as a team and dominate, or you'll die horribly.
Inner sphere mechs on the other hand can take massive amounts of damage without dieing, and are VERY forgiving. IS adopts the mentality of learn as you go if you make mistakes your ok. PGI encourages this. If you put a Clan Pilot in an IS mech they are damn near unkillable and will dominate the battle field. Put an IS pilot in a clan mech they are likely to die within the first 90 seconds of the match.
This unfortunatley has thrown the game completely out of balance. PGI bases nurfs on stats player reviews, and information of wins, rather then looking at the underlying causes. Its not that clan is overpowered, because honestly Clan mechs these days are about damn useless in the hands of anyone other then a veteran,  But because of the skill levels and mentalities and tactics, which is not something you can nerf.
So the clans continue to be nerfed into uslessness. Pointlessly, and many Life long Clan players are either quiting or moving to Inner sphere due to the massive pointless nerfbats swung at clan mechs repeatedly over and over again.
Conclusion:
The game is worth playing, its a lot of fun. Just realize the IS has a severe advantage over the clans, and if you choose to become a Clanner, realize that you'll either soon be an elitest, or you'll be crawling back to IS.
That being said, a Clan mech int he hands of a Skilled Clanneris a force to be recond with. But only if the pilot is a High Skilled Veteran player.
So what you choose, is up to you. Become one of the Elite, or Play casual as IS.

Unrest is an interesting story packaged in a pseudo-RPG package. It is closer to a visual novel than an adventure game, but uses isometric movement to proceed through the game. You play several characters in a variety of situations (some of which partially depend on what you choose with previous characters) and are faced with ethical dilemmas. Chiefly, it's about ordinary people in bleak situations and managing to make the best out of it. You get the perspectives of the rich and poor, the intelligent and the brash, the strong and the weak, and act accordingly. The world is detailed and characters feel like a part of it rather than simply archetypes. Things don't really resolve (there is a climax to the overall story, however) and you're left pondering what choices you made were good and how impactful they even were. The music can get jarring at times, and the art isn't incredible, but it gets the job done. The writing is overall well done, with a few typos and odd sentences here and there. The strongest element is definitely the amount of player responses to NPCs, and the dialogue trees can get exhausting (in a good way).
All in all, if you're into VNs and text-heavy adventures, give it a go. It might surprise you.

NOTICE: this is the third revision of my review, as my opinion has changed about it- seeing how people want this game to come back to its former glory. I regret being so negative about it in all previous iterations of my reviews, especially given my personal connection to this game. I may be going with the current crowd, but I feel this game will be brought back from the dead and we will get proper updates again.
Storytime: The history of loadout, from my perspective
just when this game was in its pre-alpha stages, I watched the promos for this game during a time when, well, "everything happened", and not in a nice way. the promos for this game were my salvation when I spent quite a few days in a hotel with no idea how long it would be until I would leave.
Loadout was the best thing since sliced bread for me, I was on a hype train with blutonium rockets. Hell, I attempted to make a minecraft recreation of the shipping dock. eventually I managed to win a beta key in early september 2012, loadout was insanely fun, I was riding that hype train for all it was worth, I never minded the account wipes, because that meant something new to do for me. However I went through some disillusionment when change after change to the combat formula brought it away from the fast paced arcade shooter and closer to the TF2 Clone it was shamed to be.
I'm not obsessive enough to have been playing this game constantly since I started, but I can claim that I've been there since almost the VERY beginning.
Beta : The golden year
beta was the testing day, the game was fast, you died fast, you kill fast, it was fun as hell. what I find most fascinating about game development is how games evolve over time, how things change. Beta's gunplay was slick, just about everything had viability, some weapons didn't kill as fast as others, but they had their own uses. Guns were fun, and you really weren't compelled to find the best and use it, you used what you liked and it was fine.
when cosmetics first appeared, they were randomized, when you die, you would respawn with a new outfit, this was more or less a filler feature before real customization was added.
First Variation : F2P basics
with changes in accounts and progress, comes the introduction of the F2P system: spacebux were your resource for everything, guns parts, clothing, taunts, you name it. There were also contracts, mini-objectives for you to get ingame to upgrade your weapon parts, these would never last, but the removal of contracts is hardly a nail compared to the boards of what would eventually be the coffin for loadout's arena gaming premise. Midway into the f2p introduction however, things took a drastic change: weapon damage was globally reduced, the pace of the game slowed down, and the menace of Bolt-action sniper rifles was inadvertantly introduced through this. Healing went from a useful buffer to a godly force of nature, juice became mostly useful, Fire and tesla switched places in usefulness, rockets became commonplace, and many weapons that were fairly viable in the old version, had been inadvertantly nerfed into oblivion.
Second variation : PC's last update.
eventually a second change in the system was immenent, but we were still teased with the prospect of new parts, particularly the cryo payload which instead of slowdown, would create obstacles, climbable obstacles, that shiz would change the game up so much, things would be insane!... Sadly, cryo never happened, and this was one of the red flags that had signaled problems within loadout's development team, and it was a shame because it was hyped up since beta!
so what about this second redesign in the system? well now you got a free resource called "blutes" which are used to purchase gun parts, yay! no pay for gun parts woo!... except that this system requires a lot of time invested to get up to par. loadouts were now unlimited instead of five, however you only get one freebie. What happened to game balance? mostly it boiled down to "change it to please the scrubs complaining about that gun that killed them fast" instead of fixing everything else that didn't kill worth shiz, that is one thing I'm still bitter about, I will admit.
what about weapon parts? what about payloads? what about all the costmetic cool shiz we were promised? two years, and despite weaponcrafting being a main focus of the system, all we got were two scopes, one new gun barrel, and one new rocket barrel.
Goodbye PC, Hello PS4 : 5.0 - aiming for the non-competitive
we were shown that PvE was to be added to its next update. or so it was the case.
six months went by, and us on the PC were wondering, "what was going on?" "what are you doing?" and the news we got? no more PC focus, we're doing this straght up PS4 now.
TF2 clone comparisons were being more apt instead of being "Looney Tunes if it was directed by Quentin Tarintino" as was the comparison in pre-beta days. which was quite accurate too. Arena shooter players were being left more and more in the cold as loadout gets pushed closer and closer into being a team game.
I left when they threw they decided to go full PS4, I could see smoke, but it was only until I actually got around to playing the PS4 version to see what had changed.
PvE was pretty interesting, but it's more of a horde/survival mode, it was cool, but I would rather have had it for the PC.
Now? : A crater, but there's a few flowers there.
as of this review there's only one person maintaining loadout.
player funding is keeping this game's servers active.
Apparently the engine was liscensed from an unfinished Square enix game. (I'm not sure.)
I was angry that they left the PC crowd for the PS4, but yet I look at the state of the game now, it hurts, because this is a fun game that deserves a second chance!
TL;DR
Game company formed by the head coder of Turok made an awesome game on thier own instead of making yet another liscenced movie game, but lack of direction almost killed it.
Parts that are consistent in questionable effectiveness:
-scattering rocket exploder
-fire beams
-manually guided rockets
-juice in blitz
what have I learned from loadout's rollercoaster of awesomeness and sad mistakes?
I've seen bad management kill a game company and ruin the customer trust of two others.
but if there's anything that's equally as bad, is a lack of direction, which loadout seemed to suffer rather unfortunately from, first they wanted it to be a fast-paced arena shooter, then they wanted it to be a team game, then they got scared at how much money they were losing so they tried to imitate warframe.
the best thing about loadout, is customizable weapons, and fast arena-shooter-like gameplay!
but hey, not everybody's got multi-million dollar kickstarters where they've can putz around all day in thier fancy offices for half a year doing almost nothing.
as much as I love the game, what happened is what happened, Bad descisions were made, and prices were paid.
Please, give this game a chance.

The main city of Bimbhra is in a state of turmoil and the foreigners, Naga, are encroaching upon their land. What decisions will you make? Can you change the future of this once great city?

This game is really just a story, but it's extremely engaging. It's cut short and sometimes hard to determine how good your choices are, but Ruskarn's writing is totally ♥♥♥♥♥in and Mikk's art is absolutely breathtaking. I feel like the strengths of Unrest totally outweigh the negatives, and that this game is worth your time and money.

First of all, let me say that the game is rather fun. It's fun, addictive, and kills time rather nicely.
However, let's start off with the first and most glaring flaw of the game: Lack of a proper tutorial. There is a tutorial, but it's very basic and fails to explain anything beyond your first basic bus route on roads that already exist, leaving the rest of the game's mechanics a complete mystery.
Second is the gameplay itself. It just feels clunky and unintuitive. When you design a system, you need to get it right the first time, or you'll be ****ed and have to scrap it and do it all over again. There is also zero capability to change said system once it's already in place.
Third is the UI. It's clunky, unintuitive, all over the place, and you have no idea what any of the buttons actually DO. That is, until you accidentally replace that one apartment building with a train station.
And finally, there isn't really much to DO, other than "don't go bankrupt". In similar games like OpenTTD (Transport Tycoon), even if you don't have an AI, you still feel like you're accomplishing something. You start off with a few cities and industries which are in desperate need of connections between each other. But in this game, you essentially start off in a city without any problems whatsoever. Everyone seems to be getting around rather happily, without any congestion of any sorts. Sure, the town is missing public transit, but it seems to be of little concern to its citizens.
You can expand your cities by building roads, but in the majority of the cases, there isn't any room for any more roads. Every spot is already taken up by other roads, or water.
Instead of fixing the numerous bugs and issues this clearly unfinished and unpolished game has, the developers instead opt to release more DLC. The game could've been so much better if the developers had spent a few weeks polishing the game.
If you're a fan of games like this, consider buying it during a sale. 20 euros is way too much to justify buying this.

World of Guns is a "game" where you field strip, disassemble, and reassemble real guns. There's a mode where you can take certain guns and fire them at a range. That's it. You start with a tiny ensemble of guns and earn points by playing the game - field stripping, disassembling, and reassembling the guns. It takes forever to accumulate the needed points to unlock guns but it isn't impossible. Every few weeks a new gun selected by the players gets tossed in to play with.
The best comparison I can make for this game is solitaire. It's a lot of pointing and clicking and you can devote as much or as little thought to what you're doing as you like. I mean this in the best possible way. If you've ever found yourself on an old laptop without internet access and the only game you could play was Windows Solitaire, and 20 rounds later you wonder where the time went - that's what this game is.
For an eyebrow raising price you can buy access to all the guns in the game and all future guns being made. If you can catch the Guns Full Access DLC on sale for 50% off give or take it's a great buy. At full price it is not. I would not recommend the game for full price but I know inevitably it will go on sale again and when it does it's completely worth it as a complete game for a decent price.
