At the time of writing this, I have 29 hours in the game according to Steam. I played this when it just released in beta and then only recently returned to it when it appeared on Steam.
It's a very specific type of game for a very niche group of players.
First off, it's free to play so let me address the main question: "Is it pay-to-win?"
No, it's not. It's pretty much a "pay-to-skip" type of freemium game. Along the same lines as games like World of Tanks, it's got a premium earnings booster and premium mechs that can only be bought with paid currency.
Is it a grind?
Not really. It depends on how you play. As an example, I might get around 50k c-bills (in-game currency) on a losing match and as much as 250k c-bills on a winning match. Bear in mind, I'm pretty terrible at the game. But, sticking close to my team and prioritising targets well helped me out a lot.
There's even a tutorial now that gives you around 2 million c-bills as a reward for completing objectives. Since mechs can cost anywhere between 3 million and 10 million+ credits to buy, you might be wondering how you'll even play the game. Well, there's plenty of trial mechs available. Those are free mechs to try out and they change every once in a while. Think of it like the free hero rotation in games like League of Legends or Heroes of the Storm. They're just as good as the ones you can buy but you can't change their loadouts. Still, it's a good chance to learn the game without the pressure of committing to a mech.
Overall, there's plenty to help you get started but it's a game that requires patience to learn and play. It's not as grindy as some may make it out to be and the meat of the game is truly in the mech building, not the game modes (although it could use a bit more of those)

Literally the only things I disliked was the soundtrack (music looped in a monotonous way) and actual gametime was short, but these are minor issues.
Here's the issue with what I had. I see other people commenting here, "the ending cuts short". When I played, I didn't even know it was an ending.
The story just cuts off out of nowhere and you see the credits rolling and you sit there in confusion like, "... Wait, what? Huh? Is there a second chapter? Did my game glitch?" Because there are so many loose ends and uncompleted story arcs it didn't even feel like a completed game. I actually kind of wonder if they had more planned to be done but simply wasn't. Truth be told, I literally redid the last scene just to see that, yes, that was the ending, and no, my game was not glitching or missing content.
My suggestion? Buy it if it's on sale (like 5 dollars). You'll enjoy it but won't feel like your price tag was too overwhemling when your actual game time is short and cut suddenly. I would say it's not worth 15 dollars.

I started playing this game, and was immediately immersed in the story.  It's all dialogue, and not action-based, reminded me a little bit of old-school RPG's, the pen and paper type.
Anyways, you play through several characters and are presented with response choices that really make you think.  There are a  lot different elements that you're presented with, but I'm not sure if it affects the outcome because...
It has the most abrupt and unexpected ending, that I've ever seen in a modern game.  I took my time through each of the character story lines, and during the last part I'm talking to someone and it cuts to the end credits!
I have no idea what ultimately happened to the city, and it was just a really poor experience... after so much potential.
It looks like the creators/developers ran out of money.
But yeah, this is not worth $15.00.  In reality it's nothing more than a demo that will entertain you for a few hours.  I want a refund, and the devs of this game should be ashamed with charging so much for a product that clearly doesn't deliver enough content.
Grades:
Graphics - 5/10.  This game is not about graphics.  They're stylistic and simple.
Sound/FX - 7.5/10.  Easily the strong point of the game, although the tracks do loop.
Controls - 6/10.  They work without any bugs, but this is a simple point and click game only.
Story - 6/10.  Early on it's interesting, until the terribly abrupt and unexplained ending.
Replayability - 0/10.  There's no reason to play a game again when it only lasts (at most) a little more than 4 hours.
Overall - 3.5/10.  Save your money unless wasting $15 for a 4-hour game is your thing.
This wonderfully absorbing game needs a proper ending!  Perhaps something not so abrupt.  Loved it anyhow.

The tumultuous city of Bhimra comes to life through the eyes of five of its citizens, all of whom fight amidst collective madness to make sense of the role they've been cast. They are avatars providing framework for the politics of Bhimra, which is the central subject of the game.
The game functions like a tabletop RPG where a writer prepares a scenario in which the player acts out a character. Circulating the paradox of Bhimra, the player views it from different vantage points. The dialogue lacks a true unique voice, but with a terse diction the game delves into a full palette of social complexities: class, racism, famine and so on.
The developers show us, to an extent, how to have your cake and eat it too. Achieving the thematic goal has come with a cost of elegance in art and audio; tailored animations and looping music would have elevated the game. Nonetheless, I laud the developers for realizing their vision in a package that delivers just what it needs to, and nothing more.

Flawed, but excellent. The biggest disappointment is the ending; we're not talking Mass Effect 3 here, but it sort of tapers off into nothing, and quite suddenly, too. If you're prepared for that, the game is an amazing ride, where you make difficult moral choices from the perspective of several different characters.

If you're a fan of worldbuilding, dialogue-driven gameplay, non-western fantasy settings, realistic moral choices outside of the facile "paragon/renegade" binary...I can't recommend Unrest enough. As a big old fantasy nerd, I haven't been this enamored with an original setting since Morrowind.
Yes, there are issues that most likely stem from the game being a labor of love made on a shoestring budget. I can't deny that a number of story arcs end abruptly, and that there are occasional bugs (my copy refuses to register Steam achievements). But I'm a sucker for writing, and this is one of the best-written games I've played in a long while. I desperately want more stories set in this universe. Please, Pyrodactyl, make it happen.

To me Cities in motion 2 presented itself to be  competitor to the Sim City series, yet upon playing I realised the core, and only aspect of the game, revolves around public transit management, presented in confusing, bland, repetitive and shortlived gameplay.

If this is the type of game you'd enjoy, CIM 2 is truly mesmerizing.  At the same time, there are many things that stop this game from being as great as it could have been.  As you can see I've put many hours into it, so I thought it deserved a review.  This review is designed for people who are already sold on the concept of running a virtual transit agency and are more interested in an opinion how it's been executed in this game.
In my opinion, here are the pro's and con's of CIM 2 compared to CIM 1.
PROS:
1)Way bigger cities than CIM 1.  One map can provide many hours of gameplay.
2)Easy to make maps that are true to real life cities with the "maps4cim" fan tool.  Recreating a real city is a huge endeavor but some really brilliant maps have been created with it.
3)Although the timetables are more fiddly than I'd like them to be, they're still an improvement over CIM 1.  Instead of messing with the timetables I just set the same service frequency 24/7.  For example, once an hour.  In CIM 1, it was much more painful to make sure your vehicles stay spaced out, and I would avoid modifying my lines as long as possible to avoid the pain of dispatching my vehicles evenly.
4)No lag even on large cities.  In CIM1, performance bogs down with a medium to large network, which is much smaller than the largest networks you can build with no problems in CIM2.
5)You can expand the city yourself if you find you're flush with cash and need a new project.
CONS:
1)Can't color code metro lines!  In CIM 1, the Line statistics Plus mod allows you to individually color lines which is awesome for metros.  Anyone with an unusual attraction to metro systems knows that one of the most interesting things about a metro system is analyzing how all the colored lines meet up for transfers on the map.
2)Ticket pricing is annoying and adds no value to the gameplay experience.  There are 5 transit types, 6 with monorails, and each transit type has 7 types of tickets.  So you have to fiddle with up to 42 different ticket prices on a regular basis.  What cims consider a reasonable fare for each ticket changes frequently.
3)The art direction in CIM2 is much lower quality than in CIM1.  The CIM2 home and loading screens are ugly and use garish colors while the screens in CIM1 are very pleasing and interesting.  Buildings and colors are nicer looking in CIM 1.  The music in CIM 2 is not as good; I turned the music off and instead downloaded the SimCity 2013 soundtrack to listen to while playing.  The UI for CIM1 is much easier to use, and CIM2 text is often difficult to read.  Only the vehicles in CIM2 get proper artistic love.
4)The more complex your network gets, the weirder your cims choose their paths.  I get around this by avoiding double
service in areas beyond connecting points and using the ruleset editor to make sure all vehicles have 100% passenger attractiveness.
5)Random crashes and no autosave.  I've had a few instances where I played for 5 hours straight and forget to ever save, then the game crashes.  Then I ragequit and don't play for several weeks.
NEUTRAL:
1)Metro lines are easier to place than CIM 1 once you get the hang of it.  You can make bendy tracks and underground stations don't take up any space above ground.  In CIM 1 an above ground building may need to be destroyed to build a station entrance.  The tradeoff here is that train stations are less visually pleasing than they were in CIM 1.  Instead of watching passengers take the stairs down to the platforms, they get in a magical teleporter from the steet to the platform.
2)expanding on the above, the ease of placement is almost too easy in CIM2.  There's no challenge at all in building metro lines since you have variable height placement and the street grid above has no impact on placement.  In CIM1, you're limited to only 3 levels of track at intersections as well as the restrictions of the buildings and streets above ground.  CIM2 placement is very easy and CIM1 is challenging, though frustrating at times.  I think the best way to solve this would be to add geology/geography as a bigger placement factor.  For example, make it more expensive to tunnel through bedrock than softer soil, and more expensive to tunnel under buildings than under roads or empty space.  Also, make above ground tracks cheaper than underground so there's an incentive to choose wisely between the two.  This is certainly out of scope for CIM 2 but one can dream for CIM 3 :)
IN SUMMARY:
If you're more interested in an arcade-style game that's visually pleasing, go with CIM 1.  If you're looking for a game with greater simulation depth, more network flexibility, and you're not terribly turned off by bad art, choose CIM 2.  Both games are great in their own right.  I wouldn't recommend either game to anyone, and which game is better depends on the individual's preferences more than one game being any "better" than the other.  If you think you'll probably like both games, play CIM1 till you get bored, then play CIM2.

Also, why isn´t the music enabled when you play for the 1st time, forcing the player to enable it? Despite that, both the menu music and the in-game music are trash compared to the 1st game.
When we look at both of this games, we see again the dialectics in motion, according to Marxist theory, which Stalin himself wrote about ("Dialectical and Historical Materialism"). Stalin Subway is the thesis and Stalin Subway: The Red Veil is the anthesis - but will we have a synthesis? Only time will tell, but me liking the 1st game, I think we need a "Stalin Subway 3" (or a remake) to restore greatness to the series and fix the problems from the 2 games.
In conclusion: do not buy it, even on special sale period. Just get the 1st one.

Pros:
Fun gameplay, graphics, music.
Cons:
You have to be lucky in order to win. You cannot get past a certain point if you don't have certain upgrades and weapons and getting these upgrades is based on luck. Your crew will die very fast if their stats are too low. Your vehicle will be destroyed if its stats are too low. Getting higher stats  (usually) requires money (and there's never enough to get everything you need)  and having the upgrades spawn in the item shop. Of course, the item shop may never spawn the upgrades you need even if you get the money.  Also, you ALWAYS need the wrench and med kit, which can heal your vehicle and crew during the level. Of course healing uses cash and you have to buy both items, which may not spawn in the item shop for a while or at all.  You can upgrade your crew by playing russian roulette or giving them over to a mad scientist but whether or not that works is entirely based on luck.  This game is a lot like FTL in that respect, but more simple gameplay.

Basically, FTL by way of Hotline Miami. Great artwork, appropriately trashy soundtrack, controls feel great. Falls victim to the usual Rogue-ish problems of the player being somewhat at the whim of a random number generator. I even laughed at a couple of the jokes in there. (Though I

Wow, this game is something else. Its a mash up of some of our favorites. It has the top down driving combat of old-school Spy Hunter but taken to the hardcore bloody extreme where death seems to be part of the social norm. It also has the random rouge-like elements that feel similar to FTL, maybe toned down just a hair to favor a more arcadish experience. Toss in a small amount of stat building, nothing too annoying. This in a nutshell is a very TLDR of what DSM is similar to.
The game itself is a blast to play. Its bloody, over the top and offensive as hell. The splash art and character portraits scream of sweet awesome stylized characters influenced by death metal. It all fits the general theme well and is extremely well done. The game play can be a bit simple at first, but as the game progresses, so does the difficulty. You will die, a lot. Thats ok, its all part of the plan.
This game will chew you up at first. Once you get a few rounds in and get a chance to experience some of the bosses, its not as bad. Like FTL though, lady luck can ruin your day.  So for a measly 10 bucks, you to can experience the challenging, bloody and brutal, mad max inspired, arcade car beatem/shootem up that is Death Skid Marks. It is so worth your time and money.

I was never really into MechWarrior, or BattleTech, and I still just take it non-seriously as some geeky kind of Warhammer lore to sell plastic toys. And of course I have to mention, I am not that much into Warhammer either. So for me MWO was purely of interest because of it's game-play.
This being said, other reviews with much more fanboism help you more, if you are already a die hard battletech fan.
It feels a bit like a tank game, so if you are a ground pounder in War Thunder, or come from WoT, you might feel at home fast.
The legs basicly move independent of your upper body, so you have legs instead of tracks and an arsenal of deadly weapons the size of building instead of a turret.
Similarly, the lighter the mechs are, the more they can run faster, but have less room to equip the biggest guns, however they can also make better use of jump jets to fly a bit. From there the sizes go up to medium and heavy, to the true beasts, the assault mechs, which gracefully walk into enemy fire or carry a lot of weapons.
You can fit your mechs with weapons, but you have to think about weight, size, and type of hardpoint (ballistic, energy or missile), store ammo, and make sure the mech stays cool enough. There is no repair in the battle; you carry armor, which can be customized in thickness with direct points, weapons do those points directly in damage, the numbers are flat, and often the name of the weapon basicly does how much damage one shot does. Under the armor you still have structure, but if you get hit in structure, you might also lose fitted components, or worse, die.
You
your mech, but with the differential movement you can get the same effect. it takes a bit with some until you stop or start moving, too. You can improve such parameters with a node based skill system, which is per mech. You earn a special resource per mech (XP), which you use to unlock skillpoints for this - and you also earn a global "GXP" which you can use to substitute XP.
Speaking of resources, the free to play model is excellent, as you have basicly one ingame currency, called c-bills, and one premium currency, called MC. You can earn premium currency ingame by joining faction warfare, or doing one of the quite frequent quests the game offers. Most mechs have some special variants, you can only buy for MC. Otherwise you use MC to unlock colors (permanently for all), decals (permanently for all), or camos (basicly texture sets, permanently, but per mech class). Additionally, you can put 2 decorations into your cockpit, and as third item add a warhorn, which will play some tune both for you in the cockpit, and for the mechs around you per loudspeaker, if you get a kill. And to be honest, positional audio doppler effect warhorning is something that works best in this setting. All of these items are cosmetic, except the hero or champion mech variants, most of which come mainly with an income boost.
The engine itself, based on crytec, runs quite smooth. The mechs look awesome, and battle damage is shown, parts fly off, etc. You have some maps where you can run over trees, shoot cars around or blow them up, or knock over lamps. Missions also sometimes feature environmental changes, like dusk or dawn, where one can also witness the props turning on lights. Each mech has nightvision and thermal vision included, which may or may not be useful in situations, but also is balanced by only having limited sight range.
is dependant on the mech you choose, and I would rather suggest to look up guides, and watch content to choose your first mech. The game gives you the ability to play with trial mechs that are prefitted, but ultimately, you want to assemble your own set of mechs, with your own personal fits. There is small, fast and nimble options, sneaky options, camp-in-the-back-and-fire-missiles options (dont be that guy), go and shoot into the enemies face, etc. etc.
Important to know is, there is no respawn; except in faction play, where you can take in 4 mechs into longer games; there is no repair, no rearm, ammo for missiles and ballistics are limited by your fit, losing the engine located in center torso, both legs, or the head is instant death; and if you overheat, your mechs shut down for a while and might take heat damage internally.
:
- good and fair f2p model. mechs that are upcoming, are sold in packs, and later released for MCs, and finally for the ingame currency cbills, with the dates announced for each mech. You always know what you get, if you pay - you can always be patient and not be left behind. things keep their worth.
- simple but effective weapons, with many playstyles - building your favourite mech for a task is basicly the greatest joy in the game. there are many fits, for many mechs, and you can even buy multiple of the same chassis if you so whish. weapon mechanics and numbers are easy to understand. you can have multiple weapons on the same mech, and define up to 6 firegroups bound to keys. tip: use left-right mouse buttons to group left right weapons for perfect corner peaking.

I just finished playing Deus Ex: Human Revolution for the first time. I played  it on "Give me challenge" difficulty using stealth and non-lethal approach to get the Pacifist achievement. It was very challenging, Especially when I wanted to do some optional quests and show my great heroism... (I don't want to include any spoilers, so no details here ;))
I was a bit frustrated at the beginning of the game. Everything seemed to be so difficult, but after a few hours of playing I felt like I got used to the game mechanics and I got addicted to the game! I couldn't break away for a bit even when I got very hungry ;)
Eidos Montréal created many huge, well-designed levels. It was nice to see that after almost no exploration possibilities and very small levels in Invisible War, Human Revolution offers plenty of different ways to approach objectives, plenty of places to explore and plenty of things to find. Just like the first Deus Ex! For a person like me who loves exploring, this was one of the reasons why I fell in love with the game!
Another reason was the voice acting and music! The character you play, Adam Jensen, has so dark and sexy voice that it makes me shiver ;) Definitely a great choice! But voice acting in general has much higher quality than in the previous Deus Ex games. It's trying to be more serious, but of course for the price of taking away some of that humor which the older Deus Ex games had ("I lost my virginity here", Deus Ex 2000).
The game music was very impressive. Many lovely tracks increasing the intensity of your fights or just reminding you of some melodies from the original Deus Ex.
Deus Ex: Human Revolution is a cyberpunk game. The best one I've ever seen! Look at the attention to detail for example on mechanical parts on bosses. It's amazing! They used mechanical parts with skin color tones. Not some crazy tubes coming from the chest to the head! I think it makes the characters look very cool and absolutely badass!
I shouldn't forget to mention the story. I don't want to spoil anything so I will just say that the developers had a lot of freedom because Human Revolution is a prequel to the original game. It happens 20 years before that, before nanotechnology is being used. They still matched things very well. You can find some hints about what's going to happen in the future.
Deus Ex: Human Revolution belongs to "MUST PLAY" category! That's my honest opinion. The opinion of a person who is not a big fan of stealth games. You don't really need to play the previous two Deus Ex games to enjoy this one, but I would still recommend to do so. This game has high replay value because of all the gameplay styles you can choose from. So it's worth of its price! 100% recommended!!!

Prototype plays a little bit like GTA, if GTA focused more on mass carnage and less on story missions.  While there is something to be said for killing everything you come into contact with, the characters have little true interaction with the world outside of missions and events.  That said, the missions and events are compelling, and gathering memories is addicting and is a clever use of the collectible side quest mechanic.
The varying powers and abilities are where this game shines.  By the end of the game, you'll be doing so many different things its great.  Each ability has different uses and vastly different combos, and swapping abilities leads to very different feels.  It takes a while to master each one, but the game certainly gives you plenty of targets to practice on.  In fact, the repetitive gameplay is fixed a bit by all the different abilities you unlock - killing things is fun again when you can do it in fun new ways.
All in all, it's certainly worth the price.  It's an action game.  The plot is there to give reason to the carnage, but the carnage is the main draw.  And on that front, the game definitely delivers.
Worth it at full price, but goes on sale frequently enough to merit waiting for one.

For me, a good sandbox game needs:
1) A variety of interesting side missions or challenges.
2) Story missions that vary greatly from the side missions (lookin' at you, Ubisoft).
3) A fun way to get around the city (web-slinging, parkour, good variety of vehicles).
4) Plenty of upgrades for destroying enemies and travelling.
My favourite sandbox games have all this. The Batman: Arkham games, Infamous, Shadow of Mordor, Saints Row (especially IV).
Prototype satisfies my criteria well enough. The story is largely forgettable, but the action is solid and the various powers are fun as hell. I've actually re-played this multiple times: once on a friend's Xbox over a week, several times on PS3, and now on PC.
I've heard some people have had technical difficulties and that it's not the best port. Having played it on two different consoles, I haven't encountered any noticeably major issues. Not yet, anyway.
Is it the best game out there? No.
Is it the best sandbox game out there? No.
But it's a lot of fun and worth getting on a discount.

Truth be told, Unrest is not an RPG. Better still, it is not an RPG in the general meaning of the word: there are no character levels, the inventory is just for show and there is one (optional) battle in the entire game. However, what Unrest does is pushing our understading of Role Play to a whole new level. As part of a single, epic narrative, we take control of several diferent characters throughout the game and play their role in the fate of a city on the verge of colapse. We decide the way in which to solve problems, what kind of responses to give to NPCs (harsh, polite, etc.), who to help or not... Simply building a personality for each different character and playing according to that can be a lot of fun.
Graphically, Unrest boasts simple but beautifull hand-drawn environments that evoke an Indian setting. Combined with an eastern inspired (although sometimes repeitive) soundtrack, Unrest really sucks you into its surprisingly deep universe full of luxury, famine and complex moral choices. You will have plenty of time to enjoy these aspects, as the slow walking pace of the characters can make traversing the sometimes expansive maps a chore.
One last note: the game is heavily text-oriented, although it is surprisingly well written and interesting. So get into the world of Unrest expecting more of a dignified visual novel, and less of a traditional point-and-click RPG.
I love this game-- the art is wonderful, the narration is wonderful, the world building is realistic and interesting. The only criticism I have is that it's too short. I would love to play a sequel.

finally got around to playing doom. After 25 years of waiting, I'm blown away by what people could do in the 90s with graphics technology at the time.
Oh of course this isn't the original doom, and of course I've played Doom MANY times on many different systems. But I also did grow up in the 80s and 90s and gave Doom to me as an impressionable child of only 12. And ignoring what Jack Thompson would spout for years later I grew up to be a game developer and not a murderer. Doom was one of those revolutionary games.
24 years later, Doom came out again, the original team is no longer at ID but... if we grabbed that team and transported magically through time, Doom would probably look, play, and perhaps feel the same as this game. And it's really DAMN brilliant.
If I tried to sell a company on "DOOM" as it is, and called it anything else, I think I would be laughed out of an office. A FPS where the story isn't the focus. Where it's just room after room of fighting the same enemies, simple weapons that were made 20 years ago, and just the most ultra violence I could make.
The thing is, DOOM is a game you can't make any more for all those reasons, it's probably TOO violent, it's mostly simplistic, and it's repetitive. But this isn't any game, this is a vitalization of a franchise that started the genre and honestly anything but what this game is, would be a crime.
There's really too many brilliant things to mention. There is a story, but it's clear through action (not words) the main character isn't having any of it. There's repetation but my god the action is INTENSE that even going through the same enemies thirty or forty times is intense. Even the gameplay is run and gun, not "War run and gun" But this is DOOM classic run and gun. An attack is coming at you? Move out of the way. Do that again and again and return fire and that's honestly a bit of brilliance in the modern era. Raycasted bullets are the standard, but dear god, this breaks that mold.
Then there's the violence, and it's QUITE over the top, but you know what? You're fighting demons from hell, using all sorts of weapons on them, and while the violence is visceral and in your face, it fits with the game's themes.
There's the fact you fight enemies over and over, but this is a masterclass in level design. The enemies have a good variety, but change slowly, the locations though are always epic, and you feel awesome ducking behind different areas, and seeing different elements of level design come into play, like the verticality and circular levels. It's really exceptionally well done, something Romero would only have been able to dream of all those years ago.
There's just a solo problem with the entire game, and that's the music. E1M1 (At Doom's gate) is a masterpiece of audio that may not have been topped in video games, it gets you ready, puts you in the fight and gets your blood pumping, just listening to is just so awesome.
New Doom however. The music isn't "bad" but there's definitely a lacking edge to this music and it's the single area that the game hasn't topped the original, but being unable to top a masterpiece isn't a horrible problem. And while the music might not live up to it, the entire rest of the game gives with both barrels.
There's Snapmap, and multiplayer and while snap map is interesting as an experiment, and multiplayer is decent, I didn't really feel a reason to return to either of them even with the improvements. What you want to do here is play Doom, the most excellent of retro shooters, perhaps the only game that should be this retro and does so with the perfect style.
But to be honest, this is a game that's going to be retro, and I really wish everyone could and would enjoy it. The fact is much of this game is a return to form of a 25 year old game, however gaming has moved on in those 25 years, yet every "return to form" is exactly that. It's returning to the great old days, not the rose tinted nostalgia days that were "better back then" but it returns us to what was great about those days and makes us glory in it.
So while not every single person will like it (Some people will never be able to accept the super fast pace action), I can't do anything BUT recommend this game as to me I'd call it the perfect sequel to Doom. And god I can't wait for the next one.
Just please don't call the next one Doom 2, it's confusing enough calling this one DOOM.

8BitMMO is a tribute to the old gaming days where VGA (not SVGA or XGA) graphics cards was the gold standard and CGA the entry level. If you are familar with the blocky character dungeon quest games of the late 1980s and early 1990s as I was, this will bring back fond memories as it did for me. The twist is it's a sandbox MMO too.
In this sandbox you build a place you call your own either in a pocket part of this 8 bit universe, as part of another player's town, or in the wilds where PvP is activated. The building blocks to create your spot are in fact...blocks...block grass, block wood, blook concrete, block glass, and so on. This stuff does not come free though..you pay for it in gold through quests given out initially by a personification of the developer. and later on a dragon architect and a zombie. You can also get gold just by entering dungeons created by players (you can create your own dungeon BTW for players to try) and kill lots of things and scoop up rewards.
The intentional retro look does not take away any artistic creativity on what you can build in this sandbox. I've seen very impressive multifloor buildings resembling a typical downtown area, and patterns of popular comic, video and cartoon characters. Getting the hang of building things is a little challenging but there is a community on online chat and IRC to guide you. Some have been nice enough to give me a few things to get myself going. There's a lot of items that give you the freedom to create nearly everything -- traps, teleporters, roads and sand to change a player's walking speed and so on. You can also buy some weapons to make the quests easier to complete and some articles of clothing to make your blocky figure at least somewhat distinct.
8bitMMO is free-to-play with an option to buy platinum to purchase special things that do not give an edge in PvP.
Would I recommend it? I am not sure how the SkyRim generation of gamers would take to this, but the older players like myself -- as well as those who find the early days of 8-bit graphic games a golden era to be cherished -- will find plenty of things to do. I'd recommend it and give it 4/5 Stars.

This is not the world's best shooter. I love the idea, and even though I could see 0% of the cutscenes, I still liked it.
I liked it for two reasons, really, and I don't care about poor English translation or anything like that.
First? I was startled by sudden movement and opened fire. Blowing a pigeon out of the sky. That is a detail a lot of games wouldn't have and I laughed quite a bit at that. And the "dead pigeon" model, as well.
Second? This had soldiers doing exactly what really would happen in a rooftop chase: running out, going a little too far, windmilling in doomed panic, and falling off the roof. This is the sort of detail I want more of in my games: human error.
So all in all, I liked it. Graphics aren't great, some of it is hard as all get out - but it put its attention to detail in strange places, and I can't help but love it for doing so.

After a lot of hours poured into trying to understand and enjoy this game, I just can't.  As much as I love sims and management games, there are too many half-baked ideas and over-simplified systems.
- Zoning is a nice idea, but the brush to set zones is massive and impossible to use with any real precision.  The handful of pixels that make up stations, is easily smothered by the massive zoning tool.  And precision can be the difference between a perfectly priced line and a total failure.
- Ticket pricing is extremely finicky.  Doing absolutely nothing but letting the simulation run can see costs fluctuate from $1 a ticket, up to $30, and back down to $1.  All over the course of the week, and with no discernable pattern(rush-hours, night time, mid-day, weekend, doesn't matter).  There is no real control, or even logic, to the numbers that are your life-blood.
-Side missions should be a good source of additional income to speed up gameplay, but instead lead the player astray and are not helpful at all.  The paths/objectives requested are not lucrative at all and the small rewards do not make up for the costs of the projects requested.  Holding onto "population increase" and "vehicle purchase" missions can be helpful, but are passive in nature and can be very time consuming.  The point of the game is to build and manage, and to do so well.  Why do side missions work to hinder the core mechanic of the game?
- While the game environment will make way for, and adjust to, whatever roads/rail systems you put in place, the control of routing lines, vehicles, and population can be incredibly difficult.  Often it is easier to rebuild the existing road system instead of using what exists.  But even then, the resulting design or plan the player has can be difficult to implement with the cumbersome and demanding pathing/planning system.
The game has a lot of good ideas and systems that just aren't fully fleshed out, realized, or functional.  And what you do get is not very well explained, defined, or even remotely consistent.  I did better taking out a massive loan, building two huge subway lines, then letting the game run for hours on end in the background.  Trying to build interconnected systems similar to real world cities only lead to spectacular failures and wasted time.

So, I picked this game up with the hope that it would be a bit like those metro scenarios from Railroad Tycoon II (which, I incidently consider the greatest game of all time). And, ultimately while I think it's good, it's not quite ever going to be a classic of the genra that Railroad Tycoon II is.
In many ways the compairison is a fair one. Both games focus on transportation logistics. In the scenarios I describe, both games focus on moving passengers through an urban envrioment. That's where they start to differ. Cities in Motion 2 is zoomed in quite a bit. You have to plan your trackwork, or overhead wires block by block. You have a dozen different modes of transportation to work with, not just a station and a station radius. You plan individual trips for your vehicles on the route and you have to worry about rush hour and adding extra capacity for peak times in Cities in Motion. Where the defining unit of time is a year in Railroad Tycoon, it is a day in Cities in Motion.
The sad thing is this detail is incomplete in many ways. You can't get your subways or trams to revers direction in place, for example. You can't forbid left or right turns when modifying the road work. And, unless you spring for the DLC, you only get 3 choices for each type of vehicle.
The day-night cycle and rush-hour are interesting logistically, but it causes the financial model to feel weird. You might spend hours of wall time waiting for your operation to turn enough of a profit so you can expand. And the random objectives often seem to ask you to do something non-sensical, or don't even work right at all. l
I'm somewhat willing to forgive these gameplay issues because I love the genra and the core gameplay does something that's very ambicious very well. It simualtes (or does a good job pretending to simulate) the movements of thousands citizens's daily lives. While traffic routing (particularly without the road building tools I described) can do some dumb thing from time to time, it mostly works very well and your public transit system fits right in with it. I like this game, and if this review sounds at all negative, it's beause it's tough being compared to what I reguard as the greatest game of all time.

From what I could tell, this game had some serious potential to be great F2P title.
I say had because, if you haven't noticed, the developers seem to have left the PC version to its own devices and, apparently, began to focus on the cosole version of the game. PC servers for PvE are still up and are fairly active, but the real money lies in the PvP, which is nearly non-existant. This would be fine for myself and others if the AI didn't have aimbot-levels of accuracy and the senses of a GOD, not to mention the absolutely ridiculous level of movement normally showcased by most CoD and BF players.
I will say this, though: It's an VERY interesting concept, and one that I do love. Players can create their own weaponry, modify it to their wants and needs, and make even the most simple weapons functional for just about any situation. Want a rocket launcher that fire bouncing cluster bombs around a corner? Make it! Want a beam rifle that sets your enemies on fire? Do it! Want an assault rifel that riddles your allies with healing rounds? Go right on ahead! It's a great system, and one that I wish many games had. P2W is nowhere near being alive here. The only thing you have to spend loads of money on are the cosmetics, which are...meh, to be honest.
But those modifications cost Blutes, the game's primary currency. You could easilly buy what you need to make a great weapon (that may not work sometimes but does some wacky and crazy stuff), or you could have gone and played the game for a fair amount of blutes every match (Best of all: Your K/D doesn't even matter in blute-earning. It affects EXP more than anything). I say you COULD have because, as I said, PvP is damn-near gone. You could pull some buddies into a PvP match if you wanted to, but for players just looking for random players, you really don't have much choice.
And that leads me into the biggest gripe I have, not to mention the very thing that turned me away from this game. Blutes are NECESSARY to develop your weapons, unless you feel like grinding for the part experience (parts can level up and unlock other parts, just really slowly). Because of the lack of PvP, which is where the most Blutes are normally given, players are reduced to grinding away in PvE matches, earning small amounts of the stuff every round. And while you CAN get 2000 to 4000 blutes simply for leveling up, it becomes a chore trying to unlock those bits and pieces you want.
In the game's current state, I simply cannot reccomend it. But if you're willing to give it a try and make your own call, go ahead, especially if you have some buddies to bring in. The game looks stupidly fun, and the weapon-designing is crazy, but, until the developers are able to return to working on the PC version, the game will remain stagnant.

Unrest is an ambitious title. The game is set in a fantasy Indian kingdom and that is something not seen very often in entertainment (at least not what enters the western world). The choices you make are very heavy handed and change how the game plays out. Users who play adventure games regularly will likely know what to expect from your typical adventure game.
This is not that adventure game. From the beginning you get given tough choices. Not everything ends well and sometimes there are no winners. It is worth going in knowing this, that sometimes problems don't have easy solutions and there is no hero that will rise to save the day. The game is fairly text heavy, in that the story is told through character dialog, and background information provided by the in game index, but if you enjoy fantasy games you will likely tolerate the text. The art is colourful and charming in a low-budget way.  While the narrative is broadly contiguous it is told in chunks, through individual characters and is best played through in a timely manner so no details are forgotten between "chapters".
Pros:
+ A unique fantasy setting.
+ Excellent art direction.
+ Thought provoking narrative.
Cons:
- Text heavy.
- Short, expect 4-7 hours.

A good little game, Unrest is a point and click adventure sort of game, there's not really any combat to speak of. There's lot of roleplay (multiple characters and viewpoints), lots of dialogue and some fantastic music.
There remains the odd graphical glitches when the main characters are walking, but these are minor.
Unrest is essentially a story, of rebellion, survival and greed. There's no real white and black morality here, even the bad guys have sympathetic reasons or personalities that are completely disarming compared to what the game sneakily builds upon. Choices are impactful, some have consequences that are visable, others do not and are left for the player to think about. There's a wide variety of colourful characters, and the world here is bleak and despondant.
That said, it is a short game (2 hours) and very dialog heavy. Those who hate roleplaying and dialog/story, should probably avoid picking this up at all. For RPG fans, or those interested in a story that refuses to swan-song you to a happy ending, this is well worth picking up on sale (£10 is a bit much).

Unrest is a very thought provoking "game". It's been mis-characterized as a RPG. It's more of a point n click visual novel with choices. The story is very engrossing and touches on a lot of socio-economic and political issues with modern day parallels. It's game that goes out of the way to de-glamorize various roles you end up playing during the game, be it a ruler, mercenary, priest or bride-to-be. It throws a range of gloomy choices at you and there's little escapism in sight.
It's a low budget title and that hampers it from achieving true greatness. While some choices do have irreversible consequences, it could have been done a bit better. The art style is folksy in a way that fits the story, as is the music which does get a little repetitive. However, the graphics, path finding, character models and animations are merely okay.
Overall, this is a neat little game with a big heart which tackles serious issues.

An interesting game, right on that blurry border between point-and-click and graphic novel.  Play through a rebellion in a vaguely Indian medieval kingdom, having to deal with famine, racial tensions with the neighboring Naga empire, and plenty of corruption and backstabbing.  It's all neatly broken up into short segments, so you won't spend a lot of time backtracking, and most segments have different viewpoint characters, so you see the chaos from all sides and it's pretty easy to put down and pick back up again.
As far as cons go, though...  I wish the interface was programmed a little more smoothly, and that the walk speed was a bit higher and didn't slow down on stairs or at strange angles.   I also wish you didn't have to be standing on top of an NPC to talk to them -- having a larger radius for that, or a "auto-walk to within range and immediately start up the conversation"  option would be a blessing.
Overall, the implementation is a little bit rough, but I'll be playing it through a few times to see what other endings are like.  I also find it to be a pleasant surprise when a fantasy game reasonably portrays/imitates a culture other than medieval Europe or Japan.

If it wasn't for the ending this would be one of the best FPS I have ever played. It is one of the best arena shooters I have played so far, that's for sure.
Guns: Good weapon variation because you can modify 7 of the 9 guns you get in the game with 2 different secondary functions. The gunplay is really nice even though I have to say that I would've liked the energy weapons to have a bit more heft behind them.
Enemies: Also good variation here, enough to not get bored with the same enemies over and over, but also not too much so the player can still distinguish them in a fast fight...most of the time.
Movement: You're always running, the real way to go around in the older generation of FPS and in my opinion the better solution, instead of the stupid low stamina our game protagonists usually get today. You get double jump a 3rd in the game campaign and it works as intended and is pretty fun to play around with. The only issue I have with the doulbe jump, when you jump too late while running at a ledge and are already in the air before pressing jump the first time, you will only get one jump and that normally means you don't get to your target. The grabbing to climb onto ledges also works pretty well even if you can occasionally bump into ledges where the Doomguy just doesn't want to grab if you don't look at it in the perfect angle.
Arenas: Most arenas are well designed, mostly with some bigger open spaces and some corners where you can get yourself in trouble if you don't stay in motion. And some classic elements are also there like portals and powerups. I had one bug where I defeated all enemies in the arena, but the game didn't realise it and I couldn't progress until I loaded from the last checkpoint and played the arena again.
Checkpoints: As far as I have seen all checkpoints are well placed and you don't loose much progress if you die.
Story: I don't really care for the story but except for the ending the story ist still pretty decent. What I really like are the little story fragments you can find in the
-level, where the interactions of the demons with the Doomguy are described from the perspective of the demons.
Ending:
This ending feels rushed and it's clear, it's only there so they can setup another game. It really dissapointed me with the bad end.
So overall, a really good FPS that can restore part of the classic Doom feel. I had many fun hours with it and will most probably play it through a 2nd time to get all or at least most of the secrets. But with a pretty dissapointing ending that is only there to setup another game and not to end this very good game appropriately.

Unrest is an interesting interactive piece of fiction, and it has some really solid ideas regarding the issues it addresses (even if in a fantasy setting) and the way the narrative is told.
The most interesting to me, and a point that should be stressed in video-game storytelling, in my opinion, is not to always give the game a defined plot. Plots aren't very interesting to me. What is interesting, however, is giving you a setting, with questions and different approaches. Then, you can make choices and see how the world reacts.
I can't be bothered to remember a plot. Knowing the world I was "living" in, however, is something that sticks with me.
This game makes you stick with your decisions (although there's also a saving system, if you so wish to use), but it's not perfect in that regard. There were many occasions when the game blocked me some paths that seemed available... it's not very consistent with the doors it closes. One mis-interpretation of the dialogue and you'll have to play the rest of the game with a choice you didn't intend to make. Oh well.
But I'm giving it a thumbs down. Why is that?
Well, above all else, because you play many different characters, several of them in opposing sides of the conflict. It's really hard to "role-play" in this manner.
Also, with the amount of character switching that goes on in the game, it's really hard to keep track who's who.
Regardless, the characters you play aren't all that well defined before you start, and will often be in conflict with your previous character.
It's... awkward, honestly. I'd rather play one character and commit to a certain persona, and then have a friend play another character, with a different persona, and see how the world developed.
I don't know, role-playing this many characters in quick succession just feels wrong, especially with the lack of previous characterization. I couldn't really "defend a point", since the next character might defend the complete opposite.
The game itself isn't bad. The "game" part is a bit amateur, with animations not really matching the background's perspectives and some clunky systems... but I think it's worth a shot. It's trying something different, and definitely something I'd like to see more of. However, after playing this, I've got to admit that it was completely immersion breaking to be constantly switching characters, often with conflicting views of the world. I just couldn't play all of those roles at once.
Would be really cool to see a multiplayer version -- Each person chooses a character and makes their own choices. It would probably have me much more invested!
Still, looking forward to their other games!

Again there exists an
for this game though I have not personally tried it.
If the first game didn't win you over this won't either. Even if you
find some enjoyment in it (I did) this is an inferior sequel in a great many ways. While the first game made up for its low production values with heart and attention to detail in certain areas (level design, weapons etc) this is just low effort all around. Even treated as more of a standalone expansion or something akin to modern DLC than a sequel it's still poor.
Most notably the game is
short. Two hours at most and that includes many, many deaths due to poorly designed difficulty spikes. You will likely not even get all three steam cards in a single playthrough. If you do feel the need to play this game put it on easy as it is unfairly difficult otherwise. Even on easy most of the game is significantly more difficult than hard mode in the first game and this is difficulty of the frustrating/unfair type rather than a test of skill. One rail-shooting segment in a car is essentially uncompletable on normal or hard and a level towards the end, while not overly difficult, involves escorting a massively slow NPC and bored me ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. In addition to the typical problems of forced escort missions the game will spawn enemy soldiers right next to the NPC if you try to move ahead even slightly too quickly.
Another large annoyance is the sudden introduction of a weapon limit. Inexplicably the AK47 and PPSh-41 now share an ammo pool despite being different calibres and not doing so in the first game. I can only assume this is a result of cutting a bunch of guns from the first game though three new weapons are added: Molotov cocktails, a new handgun (almost immediately discarded for a better gun due to the aforementioned weapon limit) and a sniper rifle. The last of these is easily the best addition. A single-shot firemode was also added to the AK47 which is nice but still doesn't make up for the loss of the other guns. The game's soundtrack is somewhat of an improvement but that's about it on the positives.
The level design is also a step down from the first game. A larger number of dead ends, confusing levels (the starting apartments and one flooded bunker part particularly are poor) and a lack of the destructible objects I enjoyed in the first combined with the limited environments  overall bring the experience down considerably. Enemy placement is worse too though thankfully the invincible path-blocking NPCs of the first game are absent.
Finally the voice acting is ♥♥♥♥ing terrible. Again compared to the first game this isn't 'so bad it's good' it's just indescribably bad. No effort was put into it and there is no excuse for such a drop in quality. The story in the first game was hardly stellar but at least it consisted of more than just 'lets run away from the antagonist of the last game'. In contrast a poorly explained internal power struggle in the USSR seems inspired.
If you still feel the need to buy this game get it
cheap in a sale. Do try the first game out though as it isn't anywhere near as bad.

I've loved Cities in Motion since the first version and this second edition builds upon that with great improvements in both graphics and game-play. It features fairly in-depth management techniques dealing with running and maintaining a public transport monopoly using various types of vehicles. Thanks to the Workshop integration and dozens of third-party websites you can easily find modifications for this game to help expand it.
Pros:
In-depth vehicle, route and monetary controls
Improved graphics
More flexible vehicle designs (with reference to the metro expansion)
Less grid-like cities with a larger amount of freedom
Mod support and regular DLC releases
Includes multi-player and co-op
Maps are bigger
Custom rulesets
Cons:
Doesn't have as big of a mod base compared to the first Cities in Motion (limited to maps almost entirely)
Compared to games that inspired the genre like Transport Tycoon - it doesn't feature nearly as much detail or size
There are potentially more pros and cons, but these are the big ones that make or break the game. Would I recommend it? Yes - while it is missing a large portion of mod support and while it isn't that in-depth, it's still a great game that you can easily spend days playing if you're into this sort of genre.

During gameplay the controller randomly switches configurations on you in the middle of the game which makes learning to use this thing even more frustrating.  On top of that once you find a configuration you like to use for a particular game it doesn't stick because once you start the game back up, the controller refuses to load your configuration for the game and you spend a lot of time fighting with the steam software to do what it is supposed to. By the time you get the controller to work more often than not, you don't really want to play the game anymore.
Apparantly testing this controller before release was not a priority.  We just want things to work and unfortunately this is how the steam controller works.
If you are dead set on using a controller for some of your games, stick to the XBOX or PS4 controllers because this controller will undoubtedly cause too much frustration.
Update 10/3/17
I am beginning to warm up to this controller. Deus Ex: Human Revolution is a well respected prequel to the original Deus Ex, the original that is considered as one of the best games of all time.
Human Revolution does many questionable decisions when compared with the first. One of the major ones being its centralized theme of Augmentation, which isn't a bad thing and its actually handled pretty well. But still its kind of hard to overlook the logic behind mechanical augmentation. According to the game, to get augmented, you need get the desired body part removed/biochip installed in the brain and then take drugs (Neuropozyne) to avoid the rejection syndrome plus the augmentions and neuropozyne aren't cheap. The practicality of mechanical augmenations isn't fully realized in the game, since by taking points from current stance of utilization of technology in industries, robots would seem more productive than cyborgs doing the legwork. However, in the game, the use of mechanical augmentations is justified as possessing aesthetic values. All of this can be overlooked by simply accepting the game as self-contained. But since since its "Deus Ex", one would expect a bit realisticly predicted points of the future. But since they wanted to explore the mechanical augmentation era which is directly related to the first game, its understandable and didn't made me think about any of the points that I've mentioned; the game is exceptionally enjoyable. I love it.
In the writing department, its mostly great. Some dialogues, mostly from NPCs, feel adverse to the player's actions. The original Deus Ex had incredible dialogues that were expansive and witty.
The game is also very hesitant in expressing things in many areas considering the fact that its a cyberpunk game. At least the first Deus Ex showed people blasting into tiny flesh bits when you shot GEP gun into them.
Adam Jensen is a great protagonist, clearly has elements of JC Denton and is incredibly voice acted by Elias Toufexis.
Art Desgin and graphics are absolutely stunning. One of the most visually striking game worlds ever created that's worth staring at. However, some people might dislike the forced golden tint in the game (Mankind Divided fixed this). Though it does help in bringing out the contrast of gold and dark related with theme of the game.
Gameplay captures the spirit of the original. A true immersive sim, allowing multiple ways to solve problems. The trasition between First-Perosn and Third-Person perspective is expertly handled in the game. Detailed cyberpunk world included with information found commonly in E-Books and E-Mails scattered throughout the game.
One thing that really stands out in the main storyline structure of the game is the addition of "The Missing Link" DLC. Hands down, best integration of DLC I've ever seen. Also commentary included in director's cut is great. It really shows how the developers were trying their best to make the best possible experience for the players.
And of course I have to mention the beyond amazing soundtrack by composer Michael McCann. It perfectly consolidates with the visual style of the game to create a unique cyberpunk vibe.

This is a bit tough. FIrst, I'm only an hour or so in to the game. However, I really like the setting, and the conversation-based structure. And I love playing an RPG that doesn't have any combat. All in all, I'd be ready to recommend it wholeheartedly, despite it's slightly home-made production qualities. However, it crashes constantly. Every game session I've played of it so far has ended with the game crashing, sometimes after not a lot of gameplay.

I went in without much of an expectation and ended up absolutely loving every minute of it. Great story, beautiful writing, a LOT of freedom to shape the characters personalities and their fate. Best of all: the ambiguity and inherent realism of this fantasy. Do not expect a conventional good vs evil epic. Or even better: expect it ;)
If you're infuriated by the rather unsatisfying end, do a little research about what the developers had in mind artistically and judge then. It is a matter for debate still and seems much less thought through than the rest of the game, but I get their idea. Unfortunately it reduces the motivation to replay a little. Also on the downside: Ingame movement could be a lot faster, I came to loathe staircases, because they slow you down like you're wading through a swamp. Clear recommendation to buy. I can't wait for their next title.

This game has a charming, story-intensive style, but it's very hard for me to consider it an RPG. Really, it's little more than a choose your own adventure game with an overworld in each of the individual sections. There's nothing inherently wrong with that, but it is definitely NOT an rpg by most modern standards.
Beyond that personal peeve of mine, the dialogue and the story itself, at least at the start, are fairly interesting and captivating, painting a unique picture about the current state of the world and the troubles it's going through. However, avoiding spoiling anything, the ending feels incredibly lackluster; it doesn't feel like a satisfying conclusion to the interesting story it finishes. The manner in which it happens, too, just seems boring.
Overall, the style and background to this choose-your-own adventure game is praise-worthy, but the gameplay itself is very limited and the actual conclusion to the game leaves me wanting. It's a bit disappointing, as someone who followed the game for a while before it came out.
That said, I think it's worth the current sale price (about 4 bucks), but my lack of recommendation is for the normal price.

Prototype plays a little bit like GTA, if GTA focused more on mass carnage and less on story missions.  While there is something to be said for killing everything you come into contact with, the characters have little true interaction with the world outside of missions and events.  That said, the missions and events are compelling, and gathering memories is addicting and is a clever use of the collectible side quest mechanic.
The varying powers and abilities are where this game shines.  By the end of the game, you'll be doing so many different things its great.  Each ability has different uses and vastly different combos, and swapping abilities leads to very different feels.  It takes a while to master each one, but the game certainly gives you plenty of targets to practice on.  In fact, the repetitive gameplay is fixed a bit by all the different abilities you unlock - killing things is fun again when you can do it in fun new ways.
All in all, it's certainly worth the price.  It's an action game.  The plot is there to give reason to the carnage, but the carnage is the main draw.  And on that front, the game definitely delivers.
Worth it at full price, but goes on sale frequently enough to merit waiting for one.

4) Plenty of upgrades for destroying enemies and travelling.
My favourite sandbox games have all this. The Batman: Arkham games, Infamous, Shadow of Mordor, Saints Row (especially IV).
Prototype satisfies my criteria well enough. The story is largely forgettable, but the action is solid and the various powers are fun as hell. I've actually re-played this multiple times: once on a friend's Xbox over a week, several times on PS3, and now on PC.

Is it the best game out there? No.

But it's a lot of fun and worth getting on a discount.

The gameplay is quite bare bones as it is, but the addition of a sniper rifle and also a flamethrower are nice when compared to the first game - though other weapons have been left out this time. Even so, all you need to know is that the only good weapon is the PPSh. The second best weapon is crouching. All you need to do is close in on enemies, then crouch and spray. Bullet richochets are in the game, but unfortunately fairly useless... it just serves to get you killed if you decide to spray across a metal surface. But to be fair, that is why there are enemies with metallic body armour in the game (just like in the first game if I remember correctly), as historically used by some Soviet assault engineers. Other than that, it can be tedious to find the right door or objective to activate... just like in the first game.
The voice acting is quite bad. Even now I am unsure if these are actually NA/UK actors hired to do the English voices while trying really hard to use a Russian accent, but failing...
that these are actually Russian actors hired to do English voices while trying really hard, but failing. Either way, I don't hate their attempts, but it should be pointed out that the quality of it is just... quite bad. The music, however, is quite good and fits the game well.
Next, the elephant in the room. Elephant-sized
. To be fair the game itself runs great, it's just... getting it to run at all is the problem for most people. In my case, I can only run it windowed and it refuses to go above 640x480. That definitely made the game more challenging for me, sitting behind a 1920x1200 monitor. Likewise, some people can't play this at all because of their hardware, just getting a white screen at most. It's rather disappointing. There is a fix available on the official Russian site. It's not that hard to find, even if you do not speak Russian, but the problem is that the fix may not actually fix this problem for everyone. It did nothing for me. It's a bit like playing Russian Roulette... either this game will work for you in some way, or it does not.
Regardless, none of this matters if the content of the game offers excitement. Unfortunately, even I had a hard time to get excited, mostly because of annoying moments like the infuriating "car chase". You are supposed to destroy an enemy car or two, but soon two trucks spawn with a lot of enemies that dismount. It seems impossible to kill them before they shred your health. They can shoot you from long range, you cannot crouch; you take hits from enemies in cars, can only turn 90-135 degrees which means enemies can shoot you in the back and you can only shoot the truck soldiers if they are dismounted, which is right before your car turns your back to them. The only way I passed this segment was because I quick-saved and -loaded, which despawned the soldier trucks completely... except for the wheels. Nice.
The escort missions near the end are also a pain in the rear. You must escort Glab, the heroine's lover, but if you stray too far from him enemies will spawn to attack him - a quick spree is enough for him to die. Your best bet is to stay nearby, but that means waiting for him to move and since he is wounded, he slowly limps forward. This slowed down a short mission by a lot of time. Glab is also with you in the next level and he now shoots back. The only problem is that if you move towards the end of the final station... you randomly die. This is because that area is final area, you die if you go there early because we can't have invisible walls. Instead, you must go around the train, but a guard covers it from sandbags. Try to shoot him and you will discover he is invincible. I assumed it was intentional, to force the player to wait for the guard to reload until you move up behind cover. As you do so and get behind him, two more guards spawn - allowing you to kill all three. Clever, maybe, but silly. As you make it past them and go inside you find: a window suitable for sniping. Yes, the last segment of the game is covering Glab with a sniper rifle. However, there is one problem... Glab can randomly die from one shot. My best guess is that the AI can randomly make a headshot which grants the same damage multiplier as your shots against enemy AI. Meaning his health bar is pointless. Meaning the end is one big save and load fest.
The game is terrible, there is no way around it. But somehow, I still recommend it. Games like this are badly developed, but it does one thing right. It captures the charm of old games, though not at the same level of quality. It doesn't pretend it's the world's most serious work of art. It's also not a shameless cash grab. The game is what it is: a poorly developed FPS that challenges you to beat it once. Unfortunately, this game can be completed under 3 hours or less, comes with a ton of bugs from the moment you try to start it up and is generally not all that great. In fact, when you take into account that you will do quite a bit of savegame loading for cheap deaths or looking for objectives, I'd say the game can be completed in an hour... perhaps less for speedrunners. Despite being older (2006), it is quite a bad apple... but one that can be enjoyed for what it is and be used to fill your lone hours. This supplied me with more joy than stupid copy-paste FPS games we have to deal with these days, despite it being terrible.
That doesn't make this game good, this is still a pretty bad game... but it's the type of bad that can be loved. Taking the low price in consideration as well... I do not regret my purchase.

The Steam Controller is much different from a traditional controller. Using it for the first time may feel a bit underwhelming and some might get turned off by how difficult it was to play
.
And that's okay, the steam controller has a huge learning curve.
While the software that Steam Controller uses are not great, Valve has been updating the controller, making the whole user experience much better when it actually works.
If you're looking for a controller that works right of the bat, this controller might not be for you. You'd spend a couple of hours browsing through other people configuration's (through Big Picture and through the Steam Beta Client) or even creating your own customisation where it works best for you.
Despite the unfamiliarity of the product at first + the software limitations, once you're used to it, the Steam Controller is an absolute
when it actually works, being able to play games with the controller + having the precision of a mouse, this controller is like a jack-of-all-trade controller, it does everything well, not as fantastic as compared to a traditional M+KB or controller but by utilising the touchpads and gyro features, it's pretty darn good.
I've been playing a couple of games with the controller and my absolute favourite has been Borderlands 2 so far.
Here's hoping Valve continues their amazing support with this device, I feel like it's not being used to it's fullest potential.
TL;DR - Not your traditional controller, high learning curve and can be daunting but it's absolutely amazing when it works.

Even if you're new to the Mechwarrior franchise I'd still give this game a try. No other game out there offers similar gameplay. Your mechs feel heavy, like you're not the vehicle yourself but are piloting a machine, if that makes sense. (as long as you're not playing super fast light mechs) Positioning and teamwork are probably the most important aspects of gameplay. The learning curve can be high but if you put in a little time to learn, the game is really rewarding. (Watch videos on youtube, it helped me a lot. Look up The b33f and Molten Metal. Both are good players and fun to watch.)
You can customize your mechs to almost any playstyle you like but some chassis heavily favor certain builds. Finding a mech you like and coming up with the perfect build that works for you is awesome. You don't need to use the meta builds to be effective outside of competitive.
The community is also generally far less toxic and is more supportive than in other games. I've almost never seen any of the "gg ez" I'm an insecure edge l0rd garbage you see often in games like Overwatch in this one, which is nice. If you're new and ask questions people will try to help you out.
The game definitely isn't perfect though. Some mechs are just flat out better than others for the same intended role. I think they're slated to fix this soon by assigning values, other than tonnage, to mechs to balance teams more effectively.
Balance in general is sometimes questionable but the meta changes often, so what is good for a while will probably get replaced by something else. The developers also rarely seem to listen to their playerbase and have made several really ♥♥♥♥♥♥ decisions that alienated a lot of people in the past.
Additionally, the grind becomes real after you complete the first several levels and achievements. You'll have a good stack of money to buy and build a mech or two but after that, cash is harder to come by. Getting a new mech is by no means impossible but depending on which one you want, it may take some time to save up since chassis prices vary wildly.
Ultimately the game is free and if you try it for a bit and hate it it's no monetary loss to you. I slapped down $20 bucks for a mech pack and I feel that the game and the investment were both worth it.
Still the best multiplayer mech game arround, in spite of its flaws.

Played World of Tanks, Armored Warfare, War Thunder, World of Warships. Many other games of the sort. Watching random videos on youtube. Stumbled accross B33f's youtube videos, very entertaining. Decided to try mechwarrior.
0~20 hours:
No idea what i'm doing. Gonna play assault mechs because they have the most gunz n armor. Died, lots. Blamed team for dying first. Run out of C-bills again and didn't want to play the same mechs over and over. Bad experience for a bad player. Put game down to play something that didn't require a team to win.
6 months later, found out B33f started streaming. very simple gameplay looks easy, feeling encouraged to play again.
20~100 hours:
Fresh from playing same mechs over and over. Managed to get a new mech. Started to understand why other wieght classes are important. changed builds a bit. Now mechs are somewhat fun again.
100~200 hours:
Focused heavily on improving self, ignoring team results. Learned to avoid using lock on weapons like the plague. Lock on weapons just bad, for war criminals only. Managed to get to pilot tier 3. Feeling pretty good and slowly climbing higher. Managed to break 1k damage and 5+ kills in a few matches quite well. Decided to apply to unit to see if actually a decent player, despite never having played a game compedatively. (Definately a coop player, always a pve player in every other game :D)
200~300 hours:
Not anywhere near a decent player. Turns out unit is compedative only. 1v1's with unit members and many deaths later: straight to pilot tier 2 in just 2 weeks. Actually start breaking 1k damage and 5+ kill regularly. Still not accepted to the unit yet, only an applicant. Attend weekly practices and starts to understand how comp works a little. Learning about many new terms and skills had never really put much thought into before.
300~400 hours:
Actually accepted to unit as recruit. Got a first taste of comp play in comp queue with other recruits/vets in secondary team. Learned that pilot skill rating sytem is basically just an xp bar, not actually a good rating system. Practice accuracy and defensive piloting alot. Got many more mechs now, didn't realise just how many until actually looking the the number in inventory. 30+.
400~500 hours:
Improving every day, Learning different mechs and builds every day. Much better map awareness, understanding map positions much better. Understanding different combat roles and mechs for said roles. Learning all the things about all the weapons. Managing to kill others in 1v1's rarely, but able to fight back substancially.  Starting to build own reliable builds and implementing ideas with science and practice.
500~600 hours:
Promoted to private. Achieved pilot tier 1. Playing all roles and wieght classes. Love 1v1's for no apparent reason. Love doing 1v1's with new people that cant even shoot straight, helping them to understand how bad they actually are, hoping they try to improve themselves. Love losing close matches, easy wins are boring. Still dies alot to other unit members in 1v1's but is fun to win occasionally or die trying. Team played minimum matches in comp queue to qualify for rewards. Still wants to play more comp queue. Still learning builds, science and map positioning. Starting to become recognised in the Mechwarrior community by some and promoted to moderator on a few twitch channels for being a "good boy".
600+ hours:
Still bad at game. Still learning things should have already known. Still losing to unit members in 1v1's. Every match practice. Every day science. Every dream about mech builds. Must git gud. Must always win. Must not lose. Must git gud.

Ahh, Battletech.... well Mechwarrior anyway. Long lost love of mine.
The Heat system is still as atrocious as ever, which is quite funny given that they now allow you to buy the cool shots for Cbills, no more need to waste MC on it. So you'd think they change the system to the proper Heatsystem, and not having a silly system where double heatsinks are just 1,4 times as effective.
Oh well, nobody is perfect, but this game certainly has improved over the years. Heavy Quirk passes have made Innersphere Mechs competitive with Clan Mechs. Gone is the vast superiority of Clan Tech, or at least, they put a serious dampener on it.
Recently they removed the Modules system, and replaced it with Skill trees. No more do you need to invest 6million Cbills (earning about 150-250k per match without premium on average) for a miniscule % decrease to the laser burn time. Now you have a skill tree to do that for you. It still will cost some money to unlock nodes, but on average you should make more money per match than you need to unlock the skills.
The game is further helped along greatly now that they post the time of the game to 3060...  so you get all the nifty little tools. We don't have reflective armor yet, but we have stealth armor, rotary AC5's and 10s. Mechs made famous by the last Mechwarrior game such as the Uziel, the cougar... and other iconic mechs like the Marauder IIC, the Kodiak or the MadCat MKII.. but also Unseens like Archers, Warhammers, Riflemen, Marauders and the like, have joined the fray.
Many of the ingame maps have been overhauled and improved. Old slog fests like Tera Therma, have received quite nice updates, and old fan favorites like River City, are now pretty much the worst of the selection.
The next big planned expansion, before their work on Mechwarrior 5 is supposed to start, will be Solaris. Finally people will be able to compete on Solaris maps, in permanent tournament rosters with sponsors and all sorts of things. Or so they promised.
So if you haven't played the game in a while, or like big Robots.... give this game a whirl. You might be finding something to fall in love with.
