I got this game in a bundle, and was really excited to play it because I love story-driven games with multi-faceted consequence/decision trees.
If you like immersive, narrative-heavy games with a good level of consequence/decision trees, then you will enjoy this game.
The aesthetics are good, the backgrounds and artstyle can be fairly charming. The storyline seems to be pretty fluid, changing in the most subtle nuances depending on your choices - definitely warranting at least a few playthroughs. After playing the extreme let-down known as Postmortem, Unrest really, really satisfied my consequence-based gameplay hunger. The music and sounds are very good, and I left the audio on for the entirety of my playthrough.
The controls are very simple, you mostly walk around and converse with different people. There are maybe one or two combat instances, which are also easy to play through. There isn't really a tutorial, however, learning the mechanics of the game is not challenging; the learning curve is minimal to moderate. Understanding and realizing the consequences of your actions, however, may take some time (and even one or two playthroughs).
Something that really interested me was the pacing of the game - as you develop a connection with your character (I am a very immersion-oriented gamer), you will find yourself put into the perspective of a new person as the story progresses to critical moments. As a psychology research assistant, one theme my lab likes to look at is bias - and something very, very interesting is experiencing the biases as you jump from character to character. I try to play RPGs as true to how I believe I would act (meaning I usually go for evil playthroughs first), but as I jumped to different perspectives, making decisions became very difficult, knowing that the consequences would most likely affect the very first character I played as. When I realized playing this way would be difficult if I did it for each playable character, I decided to take a different approach - I made a backstory for each character and played them using those stories as references. This made the experience much more enjoyable. Eventually, I also had to pick which characters were my "main" or favorite characters. This game made me better appreciate how George R. R. Martin, the author of A Song of Ice and Fire series (Game of Thrones), must feel when deciding which characters to kill/make miserable.
The different character POVs allows you to really get a more complete scope of the overarching story, and the presentation of everything is refreshing and well-done. Overall, a satisfying experience if you are the least bit interested in this type of gameplay.
If you enjoy consequence/decision trees and story-driven games, you must give this game a try.
Highly recommend!
Cheers,

Good idea, poor execution.
I am a huge fan of adventure games. Although I wasn't aware of the game during its Kickstarter phase, I was excited when I stumbled across it in the store. Although the art style isn't my taste, it was refreshing to see a lineup of female characters who were not sexualized in any way. I especially appreciated that the Naga were not given the Michael Bay treatment (ie. giving females of a species breasts when they shouldn't have them because sexism). The plot was as interesting as promised, and I enjoyed the opportunity to play as different characters in the world. The worldbuilding was excellent and because of that I felt very immersed in the world and invested in the struggles of Bhimra.
So why am I not recommending it? Simply put: the game mechanics were VERY poorly done. The lack of distinct endings (both in the way that they play out as a normal chapter and how there is not a lot of difference between the "bad", "good", and "best" endings) not only took away my desire to replay the game, but also made me feel like none of my choices really mattered. In a game where dialogue choices are the prime game mechanic, there needs to be clarity regarding the impact that certain choices have. While talking with people could change their individual feelings for you (as represented by three bars: friendliness, respect/fear, and approachability), since you rarely interacted with the same person twice I felt that my relationships with people were not properly connected to the world around me. I understand that the devs didn't want obvious game mechanics to break immersion, but there is such a thing as TOO much ambiguity in a game. I much rather would have seen them cut back on the scale of the game (eg. cut down on the number of characters and make the relationships between characters both more clear and matter more) than had the overambitious content that didn't live up to my expectations.
I definitely am going to keep an eye out for future games by Pyrodactyl (especially if they keep featuring women as main protagonists), but until I see an improvement in the game mechanics I am going to stick to buying their products when they're on sale.

DOOM is a great game. If you like first person shooters, this is a game you need to have. The graphics are crisp and it plays very well in 1080p or 4K, the sound is amazing.
The single player campaign is a campaign you want to play, and the glory kills mix things up so it’s not repetitive (no regenerating health here). Each mission has outcomes that are achievable (they unlock upgrades for your guns and armor) - and who doesn’t want to run around as the ultimate badass.
Snap Map is an interesting system that lets you create missions for others to play, and offers a great insight to what’s involved in making maps and campaigns.
Multiplayer is where DOOM shines. I'm not sure how active the servers are now, but when the 6.66 update came out and for a few months after it I didn’t have any issues finding lobbies that filled up quick in either US or UK (the OZ lobby was dead).
now that all the DLC is included in the game, you only need to grind out the levels in multiplayer to unlock that sweet cyber-daemon armor- and that’s not the hardest thing to do. It was also great fun turning into the daemons (which are now unlocked easily), and tearing the opposition a new one.
If you aim for 100% Achievements it’s possible to do but will depends on how active multiplayer is.

In Prototype you play as a man named Alex fighting against a shadowy government entity that he’s very mad at for giving him godlike superpowers. I would try to explain the plot further, but I honestly can’t. The volume drops inexplicity to whispers in all of the game’s cutscenes - it’s as if the voice actors themselves are embarrassed at taking part in this travesty.
You’ll battle the government and the plague monsters infecting an island that looks as if someone attempted to draw Manhattan without ever having been there - or even Googled it to see what it looks like. Fortunately, you’ll have a lot of cool powers at your disposal to help you. Unfortunately, thanks to Prototype’s overly complicated control system, you won’t figure how out how to use half of them. It doesn’t help that, despite Alex’s ability to hijack a helicopter in midair and bodyslam a tank, he can’t properly block. This becomes a problem as the creators of this game think that the way to make Prototype’s later missions be more challenging is for them to simply throw thousands of enemies at your face. The longer the game goes the more frustrating it becomes.
Ultimately, Prototype can be a fun way to spend a few hours, but you’ll quickly question why you keep playing it.

Cities in Motion was a decent game that had a lot of potential to be a great game, so does Cities In Motion 2 improve on the original and is it a better game? In short the game is a step above the original and a good game overall but it's not perfect.
Graphically the game looks really nice for the type of game it is and even when you zoom in it still looks good if not groundbreaking. Sounds are ok but not the best when you sit and listen to them but TBH when immersed in the game you tend not notice them as much so doesn't really bother me.
The UI being a major part of this game is an area that is both good and bad at the same time. First off to me it looks rather plain and nopt very stylish but on the other hand all the options you could need are there and laid out in nice manner so it's easy to navigate to what you want once you've played a few games and know where things are. Also i like the fact that when you click on a specific sectiion it opens it up in a window that can be moved about and this is useful if you want to manage/look at several things at once which can easily be done. One issue i have that could be game/UI relates is when selecting create a new route it doesn't auto select the tool to start adding stops which i feel it should do plus if you delete a stop i.e. you added the wrong one, it de-selects the add stops and many times i have clicked on a stop thinking it's adding it only to find i have just viewed it rather than adding to my lines stops.
Now gameplay is another major part of this game and i must say in the short time i've played the game i can't praise it enough. Placing depot's, adding stops, creating routes, building roads and generally building up your transport empire works exactly how you would want. Also managing various aspects like your finances, current routes, planning future routes and future expansions is also fun despit these seeming mundane.
Overall Cities in Motion 2 is a great game for those looking for transport business style sim or those looking for something a bit different to Sim City. Of course the game is not without it's flaw but none the less it's still fun and here's hoping Colossal Order Ltd. and Paradox bring us a 3rd installment that builds upon and improves upon this

This game is really fun. It is like a top down arcade style game, except with more explosions. The comic style cinematics and the vehicular destruction make this game unique and truly fun to play.
Pros:
1. The cinematics and dialogue are somewhat cheesy but very entertaining and well put together.
2. The destruction in this game is like none other - you can blow basically anything up.
3. The variety of characters and abilities. Each one has their perks and it's a different experience with a different character. Also there is a lot of different weapons in the game; lots of different ways to blow stuff up.
4. The missions and objectives actually have a purpose and the story of the game in general makes you feel like you are really on a mission.
5. EXPLOSIONS?!?!
Cons:
1. The game is too short. Even with the Coldstrike campaign, this game should have been longer. There is replay value, but there are 10 only missions and there should have been 30+.
2. The controls and interations with the UI and physics are a little confusing. The driving is difficult to get used to when played with a keyboard.
3. Reseting your vehicle can sometimes be frustrating and not work like you want it to; there should have been a manual reset button.
4. (Coldstrike Campaign) - The villain identity was too obvious. Right after I completed the main story I knew who Coldstrike was.
Overall, I give this game an 8.5/10. The idea of the game is great, and it is executed very well, there just were a couple things that could have been done better. Even though it was somewhat short, it is definitely worth the money, and it is really fun to play.

Is it grindy? I don't know, is it still grind if every minute of it is fun, challenging gameplay that rewards your skill and knowledge?
You have to approach this game with the right attitude. The right pace. A warm cup of coffee next to the keyboard. Sit back. Free yourself from the hero-based twitch shooters so common today. Ready?
There's an incredible variety of mechs, weapons, and equipment to mix and match with. Is there a pretty rigid tier list, and are all the good builds piling on as much lasers or gauss as possible? Yes. Don't worry about it. Build whatever you want. Get good at it. Try something new, fall in love with a setup you never thought possible. Get killed because your build is♥♥♥♥♥♥
*long coffee sluuuurrrrrp* Relax.
Use this time to spectate the game through other player's cockpits. Oh, that's an interesting loadout. Wow, what a nimble little gunboat. That looks fun. Let's look into that.
If I haven't gotten the point across, this is a game you enjoy by playing the game. Don't worry about climbing competitive tiers, or esports shenanigans, or a large, active playerbase, which all those other shooters and their players care about. Just find something you like doing in a mech, and do that.
Play 25 games. You'll get around 30 million c-bills, the free currency. You can buy 2-3 of any mech you want, and have plenty left over to build them however you want. Don't find anything you like playing after that? Don't like any of the mechs?
That's fine. The game's free, you lose nothing for trying it. Thanks for giving it a shot, and best of luck wherever your gaming takes you.
But I hope you find a reason to stay. Once you adapt to how this game works, it's quite a treat.

The most enjoyable part of this game was the story. It was really interesting and inventive.
The most regrettable part of this game was that one's choices didn't really change the story much. Only very small details can be changed, but the overall story will remain the same no matter what choices are made.
Despite its flaws, the game's choices are still good to have, because they cause the player to question their morals a bit. There are people who want to help others and there are those who don't. The former have the more taxing decisions to make, because sometimes it isn't clear how to help people  most efficiently.
Because the story changes perceptions from one character to the next, the player gets to see various different sides to the story, not just one character's point of view. The player could hate the sound of a character they've heard about, then later end up liking them because new information has come to light. A character could sound villainous at first, but then end up being a decent person when the player witnesses their part of the story. I really liked this concept of the game: seeing things from different perspectives of different characters.

Review will contain mild spoilers: Please be wary.
This game is an RPG based entirely on dialogue choices. You can also move around the map outside of dialogue. This is how the game plays and some people may not find that fun. I, personally, did enjoy this system. I didn't want fancy mechanics, I wanted a story and this system was a brilliant way of doing that.
Through the duration of the game you will play a handful of different characters at different sections in the story. The story is broken up into several scenes and you will play one character until it is finished at which point both the scene and the character you play will change. And, unless the character is Asha (the princess of the human kingdom), you will never play as them again.
The way you end the scene, and the things you do during it, will effect future scenes in what characters appear (I have only noticed one instance of this but there are probably more) and characters will reffer to what your character did. For example you can run away from your marriage as a peasant girl in a farm village and the owner of the farm will mention that she has had trouble with a peasant running away in a later scene.
There are alot of examples of this that I could give which is wonderful. I love feeling that my choices mattered.
However I didn't get that feeling. I once tried to refuse to do something as one of the characters and the game pretty much said, "It is plot essential that you don't refuse so you did it anyway." In a game like this having control taken away from your character is pretty much the worse thing you could do.
The core selling point of this game is that the choices you do matter and if the moment you try to do something that will significantly alter the narrative of the story the game takes away your choices and forces you down a path then something has gone wrong.
The amount that your actions affected the world would be sufficient for a more combat-oriented game (in fact I would love it there) as the subtle strokes are so nice sometimes. But for this game it doesn't cut it.
But perhaps the worst feature of this game, the one that made me hate this game, was the lack of a suitable ending. In fact I thought I was still playing the game (the ending is done through dialogue between your character and another) and then it cut to credits. In this ending I learnt almost nothing about anything but the fact there is still tension between the humans and the naga; in every 'ending' that I got. (Even in my most naga-friendly playthrough it said, "The naga army may march on the humans." or something similar)
To summarize:
It was a neat idea about civil unrest and allowing you to play as characters who influence the story but I felt as though I had little impact on the narrative.
There was no closure on the stories of any of the characters (except for maybe Asha; but even then it is still weak) and I felt punished for being invested in them.
And the 'ending' was poorly executed and uninformative.

Brilliant game. Essentially, it plays like a choose-your-own-adventure, but the situations you're placed in, and the decisions you have to make, really make you think. It cleverly has you playing a variety of characters on different sides of the unrest, making what appear at first to be black and white issues to be complicated dilemmas.
Games are usually about feeling powerful. The characters you play in Unrest are often powerless, or struggling to make a difference. It's taken me just over 3 hours to complete, and in that time I've felt helpless, I've made decisions I've regretted, and I've done things against my will for the sake of others.
It did end suddenly, but in a way it fits with the game that there's no definitive conclusion. I'm left with both the sense that things could have gone very differently, but also that perhaps what happened was inevitable.

By the end of the game, I wondered about the gravity of my decisions and my tone as I made them. When suddenly in the role of the face of the violent revolution, I wonder if my gentle kindness in this role actually caused worse bloodshed? Would harsher words have made any difference? Like other narrative games with impossibly-hard decisions, choice is an illusion. I suppose this is fitting for a game titled “Unrest.” Poverty can not be solved by multiple choice questions or violent subversions.
In Unrest, perhaps it’s enough just to see what it’s like when we swap our slippers for another’s sandals?

Hell . . . I like it.  Talking about all the features this controller has would take forever.  It's configurable, down to the sentivity of the buttons.  It's very versatile - you can use it for just about any type of game, and you can even use it to navigate your desktop, browse the internet.  I use it with Kodi, and so it funtions basically like a remote control . . .
That said, not everybody likes the Steam Controller and I feel I undestand a few of the reasons.  They're good to know, going in:
- It doesn't have the officially licensed xBox controller drivers.  This controller gets recognized by Windows as a mouse and keyboard.  Lots of things - especially older things - are gonna be looking for those xBox drivers, and so setting up the Steam Controller to work with those can be a pain in many cases, and impossible in some cases.  I can tell you Hyperspin sure as hell will not work with it - or at least I spent like a year of my life trying to make it do so, and it would not.  There's some mention about playhing non-Steam games via Steam, and no, the Steam Controller is not the way to go if you want that. Other games that did not do well with Steam Controller included - Forced, Insanely Twisted Shadow Planet, Divinty Original Sin, Infinite Minigolf, Hammerwatch . . .  For some of those, okay, the Steam Controller WILL work for one player.
The problems occur with couch co-op  (most games are not looking for 2 keyboard + mouse combinations.)  Also, twin-stick shooter games can be hard as hell to aim using the thumb pad instead of a stick.
- The Steam Controller is big.  It can be tough for people with small hands to reach button combos.
So . . . that's it.  There are the cons.  Basically, I have some xBox wirless 360's I use - and I know those are gonna work on most things, including Hyperspin with all the MAME games.  I just can't take it away from xBox controllers.  Have some.
But, I also have some Steam controllers, and I check first to see if those will work, because with all that said, it's a pleasure to use these controllers.  I certainly find I can switch seamlessly between game, desktop, home entertainment with the Steam Contollers - and for the games they DO work with, they work great.
I really wish the industry would get the controllers standardized better.  I also wish Steam would buy the licensing for the X-Input controllers, or the drivers for the xBox controllers - whatever it is that's holding up the Steam Controllers from functioning just like an xBox controller.  It would be a retroactive sort of move - I think most developers are now considering that the Steam Controller exists - but I think it would be worth it, because there are just tons of older games that people keep on playing.
So there you have it.  The Steam Controller is my luxury controller, and it's not for whiners or people who lack patience, however you want to say it.  If you want a controller you can program to walk your dog and wash your car, this is probably the one - but there will be a learning curve, and it will take some time.
That's all just my limited opinion, of course.  I could be wrong about some of that - just personal experience, and impressions from a couple of years digging into the comparison of Steam Controllers with xBox, and just for anyone out there who is also trying to make the comparison.
I still give the Steam Controller a hearty recommendation - but have some xBox controllers for backup.  Buy the xBox controllers first, by all means.

At first I blamed each individual game developers but at this point with so many games mislabeled it's really the steam client's false advertising that is most upsetting.
If a game doesn't at least work with the steam controller on all operating systems that the game supports, then it doesn't have "full" controller support and shouldn't be labeled to say that it does. Just because some kind of controller can theoretically work on some systems with some specific setups doesn't mean that controllers are fully supported. If one or two games labeled that way didn't work I'd call it a fluke but it's a widespread problem. Go buy a console if you want to play games requiring a controller because steam isn't delivering what it promises.

Positive:
- This controller feels like a high quality product. Right up there with the PS4 and XBox 360 Controller.
- The rumble action is very intuitive. More so than in other controllers I've tried. (Negative Edit: It also feels a bit cheap and is very loud.)
- The customisability is near limitless. Add a game to Steam, launch the game through Steam, and you can go wild on what any of the controls are supposed to translate to ingame. Haven't encountered any problems yet - and 2 of 3 games I've tried it out in I hadn't bought through Steam in the first place, just added as Non-Steam-Game (For reference, GTA V and Star Citizen).
- Very ergonomical. You can get to any and all of the buttons quite naturally without your fingers having to go out of their way. (Negative Edit: The pressure points of the touchpads as well as the underside bumpers seem too hard. It's not easy to use the touch pad effectively while pressing down on it as hard as you have to.)
- There isn't much of an installation process. You plug it in, it does the rest for you.
Negative:
- Shipping takes a few days. I say 'a few' because I don't actually know how much is normal. It was 'shipping soon' for me for three days. And then suddenly it got here in the morning two days after.
- The surface of the controller could have more grip. Perhaps a little more profile rubber instead of blank plastic.
- It is neat that I can load pre-made or recommended (where applicable) templates for certain games, but it is neat only in theory. In practice I'll be more satisfied with my own layout because if I load a template I have to try out what does what anyway.
- The gyro control seems a bit awkward. I'm not sure if it's a problem of finetuning or a problem of the controller, or of the technology itself, but controling anything with the gyro actually makes it harder to control than just using the stick.
All in all, I love this thing. I was never much of a console gamer so having this much freedom in choosing what the controller is supposed to do is amazing. I'm glad I got it at a discount, but even so it is definitely worth its regular retail price.

------

When I first got Unrest I was expecting it to be just another point and click adventure game based around storytelling, I was wrong. Unrest is not just "another one", I'll even go as far as to compare this to the Walking Dead game from Telltale. If you're looking for a real RPG that focus on narrative instead of combat you should just get this one right away.
Unlike most RPGs Unrest doesn't let you create a character to your liking, instead it lets you play as multiple ones such as a peasant girl, a priest, a slum inhabitant, an ambassador from a mighty empire and a mercenary captain. You play all these characters in Bimhra, which to my understanding is a city located in a fictional ancient India.
Like I've mentioned previously, Unrest focuses on a narrative driven experience based around dialogue with NPCs. The dialogue is what makes the game in this case, the writing is fairly good however I felt like the English translation was abit off and I noticed some letters missing every here and there but nothing that really stops you from understanding what the game is trying to tell you. The dialogue basicly works like most RPGs such as Mass Effect and likewise, each NPC you encounter in the game will react different from another depending on which dialogue options you choose. The choices are presented in a single sentece and each one of them has like a "title" or an indicator, if you prefer, that helps you better understand if you're being "hard" or "naive" or "sarcastic", things like that.
You can pretty much be who you want with any of the characters, when playing as peasant girl you can be harsh on people or caring and nice, it's up to you, the game lets you play as you wish. However, playing in a certain way will have it's consequences. I'm pretty sure I can't explain to you how it works by giving you an exact example because that will spoil the story. Just think like this "If I do X with one character it will have X effect later on." and this creates room for some replayability if you wish to go back after beating the game and take other choices other than the ones you took on your first playthrough. It's also worth noting that some of these playable characters know each other and sometimes saying something with another character will affect another one. Usually, between the transition from one character to another some time passes by, if I recall correctly it's usually a few months so very often things in the world will be abit different from the time you played with the last character.
In other words the game lets you roleplay by choosing what your character says to someone and different choices will lead to different outcomes that can completely change the plot.
Upon talking with different people you'll unlock lore in your Journal which contains various types of information ranging from the story behind a certain location or information about someone vital to your quest.
Visually the environments look absolutely gorgeous but I really don't like the way the character models look and how the walking animations look. It's also worth noting that the music in the game does a really great job, right when the music kicked in I could feel myself lost somewhere in India.
If you're not really sure about this one just download the demo and give it a try. There's no way I can't possibly not recommend Unrest, if you're into narrative driven games or RPGs that focus on storytelling rather than combat or customization, Unrest is a game you should get your hands on!

This game is very unusual. The protagonist of the game, if there is one, is the city of Bhimra. As a player you follow the lives of several humans and one naga, making decisions that impact their own lives and also the future of the city and all who live in it. The frequent changes in POV serve to refocus the player's perspective. The personal matters of individual characters, as important as they may be to them, are only the backdrop for the city's history.
To put it another way: there are quite a few games that use histories of war, famine, and civil unrest as the backdrop for the personal dramas of the protagonist. Unrest does the opposite.
So far I've only played through the whole game once. I'm sure I'll have a lot more to say once I've explored more of the options and their consequences. The trait system, in particular, is very interesting. I don't think I've unlocked nearly half of the possible traits for the five different POV characters. The use of three different "approval" meters for character interactions (friendship, respect and fear) is also something I'd like to explore more.
There's a bit of a bait-and-switch embedded in the game's assumptions. If you go in expecting one thing and get something totally different, you're apt to be disappointed. But if you keep an open mind and adjust your expectations to the game's story feedback, I'm convinced you'll find it just as interesting as I did.

As someone who has been around since the beta started I can say this game started out as fun and used to be a staple in my collection. I've spend 200 plus dollars on this game and have a huge collection of mechs and actually probably have close to 300 hours in the game. I've met interesting people and had some really good time with the community.
Over time, I have slowly lost faith in the developers to deliver what I think is a game that has huge potential. I stuck around because I thought things would get better and not worse. I was wrong.
The first thing that annoyed me was when the developers said they were going to add Oceania servers which got me excited but were actually put in Asia. I live in New Zealand so get around 200-250 ping on the American server and on the 'Oceania' server, I get around 300 ping. You'd think being an Oceania server, the server would be in the centre of Oceania which is Sydney or thereabouts.  A huge part of the Mechwarrior community I played with were from Australia and New Zealand so I think PGI has done a crap job by shafting those players out of the best possible Mechwarrior experience they could be having, but aren't.
Secondly, the hoops you have to jump through to play private games with your friends are huge. It sounds simple on paper - two people with active premium time on each team, but in practise it's a nightmare to organise and you have to restart the lobby about 20 times to get it working properly. Why they didn't just let people who paid enough money to fund this game play private games is beyond me. Private games are a great way to introduce people to the game and teach them how to play without the pressure of going up against people who are experienced and relying your team to carry you to victory.
Thirdly, the game is horrible for new players. I've tried to introduce my friends to this game countless times only to wait in the matchmaker for 20 minutes and then get melted in 10 seconds by an organised premade.
Finally, new maps hardly ever get released. If PGI let the community make maps and then trial those maps with the community to find out what maps are balanced and fun to play then this problem could be sorted. Other games let the community design maps so why not this one?
If PGI intends on growing its community and playerbase then it seriously needs to consider addressing the points I've made above. This game can be steered in the right direction and made into a great experience for its playerbase. PGI and the Mechwarrior community can propser if PGI plays its cards right. Sort it out.

It is THE mech game if your looking for more mech and less jetpack dude (if you want the latter, may I suggest Titanfall?)
This game takes out the run&gun COD-style shootouts seen in the Titanfalls and puts you solely in the mechs. That said, there are WAY more mechs to choose from, and the amount of customizations available is staggering, making Titanfall's mech customization look like trash.
You buy (with in-game money) a mech, and then you have the ability to choose what type of, where on the mech, and how many, of several dozen weapons of different types and styles. Add cusomizable systems such as coolant (I almost typed Coolaid), radios, targeting systems, armor, paint, and cockpit props... MWO allows the player to create their ideal personalized mech, catered either for looks or for playstyle.
My favorite mech is a "Crab" that I heavily customized. I call it "WarWeasel-6" (since you can also name you're mechs!).
Oh, I named it "WarWeasel" because it looks like a weasel (not a crab) to me. The number 6 is the version: I modified it six times before it ended up "just right"!
The gameplay itself is quite fun as well, and gameplay has it's own quirks and tricks depending on what mech your using, as well as how you have modified your mech. Individual parts of the mech can be destroyed, lowering your survivability and losing the missiles that was mounted on that arm you just lost. This, however, makes for interesting builds, such as intentionally putting a lot of armor and no vital systems on one arm with the intent to use that arm as a shield, taking damage on the said arm to protect the rest of the mech from damage. As stated, you can create whatever kind of mech you want!
MechWarrior also supports clan (or faction) warfare and there are several game modes, so the game remains fun for many hours. Voice systems are also supported in-game, which is nice.
A good, free to play game for mech fans, especially if you fell in love with your Titan in Titanfall, but wanted more customizations. Unfortunately, the mechs in MWO do not have the same kind of "relateability" as Titanfall (they all have the same OS voice and no unique personalities), but the sheer number of options available to the player is almost limitless, and you often find yourself creating your own story of how your personal Battlemech/Titan/Jaeger came to be.

In Prototype you play as a man named Alex fighting against a shadowy government entity that he’s very mad at for giving him godlike superpowers. I would try to explain the plot further, but I honestly can’t. The volume drops inexplicity to whispers in all of the game’s cutscenes - it’s as if the voice actors themselves are embarrassed at taking part in this travesty.
You’ll battle the government and the plague monsters infecting an island that looks as if someone attempted to draw Manhattan without ever having been there - or even Googled it to see what it looks like. Fortunately, you’ll have a lot of cool powers at your disposal to help you. Unfortunately, thanks to Prototype’s overly complicated control system, you won’t figure how out how to use half of them. It doesn’t help that, despite Alex’s ability to hijack a helicopter in midair and bodyslam a tank, he can’t properly block. This becomes a problem as the creators of this game think that the way to make Prototype’s later missions be more challenging is for them to simply throw thousands of enemies at your face. The longer the game goes the more frustrating it becomes.
Ultimately, Prototype can be a fun way to spend a few hours, but you’ll quickly question why you keep playing it.

Its not often that I write the reviews to games and I was finding many of the negative ones to be misunderstood. This game is definitely not for everyone since it is a 4x turn based game that takes elements of 4x and faction/map creation from fallen enchantress, Elements of research from civ, and the feel of Sins but turn based while boasting its own ship design and combat system.
If your still reading it means you probably have an interest in 4x turn based games and here is where I will review the game:
This game with the disharmony DLC comes with a full set of 12 fleshed out races which is ridiculous since the max game size is 8.  And on top of this you can create your own faction using a point system to pick traits for your faction that can be either negative or positive similar to that of fallen enchantress.  Every race has the same Ship Class setup but they all have different appearances, names and benefits based on each different faction.  To add to diversity races even have unique techs to research and some pretty game changing traits (go play a game of harmony). Ill wrap up the game setup portion with the map settings.  They are very similar to fallen enchantress as well in that you can set up all the parameters to shape the galaxy you are working in which can span from a dozen or stars to hundreds all with 1-6 planets in them making for some pretty large games.
The game is turn based and can build up pretty slow for the first 40 turns{normal} depending on the game speed you choose where you will spend a lot of time colonizing and teching up to make your first fighting force.  You need this fighting force because the first time you encounter any enemies you will be in a cold war and you need to show that they cant just steam roll you (this is how I lost my first game first contact with cravers meant my doom).  this may take you well between 2-6 hours depending on if you like to read all the turtorials and tooltips or just spam end turn.
The battles are not real time strategy like I see some of the negative reviews complain about (its a fricken 4x game!) instead they are fought like chess (civ style moving fleets around).  You load up your fleet with ships up to a cap that you design yourself with researched weapon systems, defense modules, armor plating and ground invasion forces.  You then either attack an enemy fleet by flying to their star and hitting engage, or you get engaged upon.  When engaged a screen pops up with a pretty sweet layout of everyones ships, weapons, stats the whole shebang.  You get to choose battle cards which are basically a generals tactics he chooses for his fleet and what formations and targeting your going to do.  The targeting works in a way that you can focus fire their front line, spray their frontline or spread fire amongst their whole fleet while choosing how your formation will be (high damage up front, or high health).  Next you need battle cards for the three main battle phases: Long, Medium and Melee.  Then you choose your battle card for example: Weapon Overclock, is an offensive card that tells all your troops to wreck havoc with kinetic weapons, there are counters to this such as defensive cards that will get a boost if used against you during the phase you choose offensive.  This allows for further strategic gameplay and a few good counters with correct card placement to allow you to overcome some slick odds (Had a match where my 4 ships obliterated 10 enemy ships in the long range phase because I countered them with a good card that made my damage output ridiculous.
The battles themselves can be auto resolved if the player so chooses but manual is so much more satisfying to watch your ships engage the enemy.  The graphics of these battles are pretty decent, this game is 5 years old at the time I write this and I run it at max settings and I am always satisfied to watch battles.  The music in this game is nothing to write home about its very spacey.  I would recommend this game to anyone open to 4x games, I personally got the game for a dollar during steam sale and I play it more than most games ive payed full price for.

A game that plays like a classic arcade game with a nasty bug and control issues. I truly want to set this game to Recommended but cannot in it's current state.
Graphics: 9/10 - They're great, at least, I think they are. Not much else to say here. Game runs extremely well and had no crashes during my playthrough.
Sounds: 9/10 - Another great area. The sound effects all sound great.
Music: N/A - Nothing really stands out here unfortunately, so I'm leaving it off the scale.

There is a learning curve for them, as for most games, but I believe the controls could've been made "less clunky" and still achieve what this game inspires to be, with the learning curve still attached.
Secondly, bugs. Or bug, rather. I encountered one major one. Was playing on a certain inferno mission chasing a boat and at the bottom you have to ultimately go "inside the boat" to continue the mission. Well there were two boats inside each other when there was only supposed to be one. Thirdly, having to start all over due to losing all your lives is...well... I would call it unfortunate, but others really like that aspect as it revolves around classic Xmen arcade games and an old Dreamcast game called Cannon Spike (it just came to mind, so I'm mentioning it). However..combine this with the bug above and it becomes a nightmare.
Story: N/A - If I gave the story a rating, it would be a 2/10, only due to some actual writing (sooo... effort) and some low-to-decent quality voice acting.
Overall: 6/10 - Would easily be an 8 if the control issues were adjusted, and a 9 if the major bug(s) were fixed. This game will never be a 10 for me unless the story becomes drop dead amazing.

The tutorial in this game is useless, since there's a ton of little annoying things that are not intuitive. But once you know, it works:
You have to delete and rebuild roads to get bus lanes. Trams can have tracks on medians and pedestrian paths, and you have to build the tram station appropriately (in the median or on the side of the road). Metros can be built elevated or underground with the page up/page down key (minimum clearance is 8m, which is two page ups/page downs). Building metro track at elevation zero (0 m) will enable your cursor to snap to metro track stubs. Building a metro track/road curve is like using the pen tool in photoshop: you drop a vertex with left click and you undo the last vertex with right click. Waterbuses cannot navigate through/around terrain, so you have to manually waypoint around those. The metro passenger entry point is that tiny "teleportation box" that appears on the nearest roadway when you build the station. Tram tracks/Trolley Wires need to be connected through intersections by clicking on the tracks/wires on one side, then clicking on the side you want to connect to. If there's no routable path to the next station, zoom in and inspect the roads for one-way streets and missing intersections. When you delete intersecting roads/metro tracks, the remaining road can still have remnants of an "intersection" that makes it count as two roads. That "intersection" can be deleted again to turn the road back into a single piece of road/track.
If you do play multiplayer, PAUSE THE GAME OR SLOW IT DOWN BEFORE DEMOLISHING ANYTHING, and try not to demolish a lot of things in rapid succession. Don't play it on the fastest speed. If you do desync, have one person share their save file with everyone else and overwrite their local saves, then try to rehost the game.
You can adjust the rulesets to do things like make the game speed slower (helpful for big, lagtacular maps) and increase depot size (recommended).
Hopefully reading this makes the game playable, since it's pretty fun once you know all the little things. But then again, I was determined to make it work.

This controller is great. Being able to play (almost) any game with a wireless controller makes gaming a much more relaxing experience. Controls can be bound to standard controller buttons, keyboard, or occasionally to actions directly. The rear paddle buttons add so much space to controller layouts; giving you a good place for quick save, sprint, or just a handy redundancy. The larger D-pad makes it so much more accessible and useful than standard D-pads.
Customizability is where this controller shines. Long gone are the days of "This is the worst sprint controls" and "Why isn't this button assigned to anything?". Being able to means you can t̶h̶r̶o̶w̶ ̶o̶u̶t improve controller layouts making menus more accessible or movement more comfortable. If something feels wrong just pause and change it. The trackpads have several types of joystick like input, but I usually use a mouse equivalent. The controls can be fine tuned with trigger half pulls, inner and outer rings on the trackpads and joystick, input type changes, and more. And if setting all that up isn't your style the community usually has several options to choose from even on more obscure games.
Steam has come up with -what in my opinion is- the greatest controller typing interface. Sadly, there's no way to open on your desktop at the moment limiting it's use for regular computer usage. If you want to use the steam controller on games you have to open big picture mode which isn't my favorite but navigation is simple enough. It can be a bit of a battery hog so I recommend rechargeable batteries. The battery release also seems to stick with certain brands so they're hard to remove.
Overall it's a fantastic controller. Any gripes I have begin with features that are far better than standard controllers.

I've played through this game about three or four times, and, for the price, this is a steal. You will be hard-pressed to find a better value outside of a steam sale.
The plot is somewhat arcane and difficult to follow, but overall it's well-written. The dystopian, cyberpunk aesthetic is engaging and the characters, though never truly fleshed out in my opinion, are well-designed and written. The amount of thought put into this world, especially if you take the time to read in-game books and news, is more than you might expect and very well-done. The gameplay is good. Not truly groundbreaking or noteworthy, but it is enjoyable. The ability to customize your character to fit your playstyle is really cool, and it contains enough decisions and side-qusts to make you feel as though you have a discernable, even if not overwhelming, effect on the shape the story is taking.
The only negative thing I can really say about this game is that Adam Jensen's voice actor is fairly poor. I didn't find it distracting, but it was absolutely a missed opportunity to contrast the main character's persistant humanity with his superhuman augmentations. He sounded comically robotic on more than a few occasions. Not Robocop level of robotic, but fairly close.
Heavily-engaging, fun to play, and well worth the $20. 8/10 would buy again.

I will breifly go through the applications for which I see the Steam Controller as a novel alternative to existing technologies for navigation, control, and configurability.
Configurability is what stands out with this device beyond the realm of gaming; but be warned, it takes quite some time to fine-tune a configuration for "off-label" utilization such as desktop navigation (
), and other custom set-ups - there is no work-around when you are calibrating a device to personal preference, so this is not a fault - starting with a template can help greatly. It is worth the time in the end, especially if a physical disability limits your navigation of a computer, and you want an alternative to existing voice dictation, and body movement/gesture technologies.
This is a subjective area, and so I will simply mention my experience very breifly. As many have mentioned, 3D games and FPS games in particular don't offer the ease and precision that a mouse and keyboard offer. I'm sure habituation has a lot to do with this; but that takes time. I have a preference to use the Steam Controller for more casual games and platformers, and other obvious style games such as turn-based strategy and puzzle games.
I feel the Steam Controller with time, tweaking, and adaptation, will be my primary choice for gaming. It is too early to say.
The configurability of the Steam Controller is incredibly advanced; even overwhelming. and button can be bound to a single function, a macro funtion, or a pressure/axial function - with sensitivity and angular adjustment (for personal preference and off-set) that can change the out-of-box akward controls to the fine-tuned controller that fits like a glove (just rememeber that everyone will hold the controller and handle it differently, so no single config is going to suit everyone).
One of the best resources Steam offers to support the device is the ability to share templates for quick tweaks, and game developer presets that can be slightly tweaked without having to reinvent the wheel, valve, and joystick.
Advanced users may want a task or job specific setup that is made from scratch - and this is possible; although it takes time. You will also have to learn your own config, which is not as easy as some may believe. In time, the fluidity of the control will definately become natural and a great new way to control other, non-recreational applications.
As mentioned above, the controller can be used as the sole USB controller for your computer, taking place of both mouse and keyboard. When you finally adapt, it feels great, however each application will need a new (secondary) config - which can be switched to easily, but often limits you to one or two applications/software programs.
Although I'm not disabled, I can appreciate the potential of the Steam Controller for those that are. Having suffered an accute immobilizing injury, I did find this device to be a god-send, when I had to get work done and I couldn't handle the "fixed" and limiting motion of the mouse and keyboard combo. It came down to either A) Using and configuring the Steam Controller so I could sit comfortably and work or B) Take opioid painkillers and get tired, distracted, and cognitively impaired so I could sit in a position to use the mosue and keyboard, all the while inhibiting the recovery process due to the strain my body was signalling via the opioid receptors as pain/discomfort.
The opportunities are vast with this incredible device, and the compelexity leaves much of this under-appreciated unfortunately. I'll be the first to admit that I am intimidated by the undertaking of setting up a new configuration. And although I could be spending my time on that now, I figure that some more self-disciplined people could benefit from the extensive applications that the Steam Controller offers.

Throughout the game you play different persons, which are all in some way involved in the troubles of the kingdom, your way will lead from the poorest to the highest and you can lead them to different ways how their life and the future of the realm will play out.

Set in India in a fictional universe you follow the struggle of a selection of characters all trying to make their way in a world that is crumbling around them.
As soon as the game begins you feel a sense of importance that other games can only dream of recreating. Full of the sensation that every decision, no matter how trivial it may first appear, could bring dire consequences. Whilst playing the game you take control of a diverse cast of characters from the highest of royals down to the lowest of peasants. From the off you have decisions to make, each of which can affect how the person you are speaking to, or even the entire city will view you. You are very conscious of this and it quickly becomes something that weighs down on your mind whilst conversing with the ensemble of NPCs in the universe.
I approached this game with the thought that I wouldn't get sucked in, I would be rational and logical and beat the game easily, uncovering all of the "best" outcomes for my characters. I soon learned how foolish I was. I ended up with quite a few VERY bad outcomes from what appeared to be good decisions at the time due to my lack of consideration of effects it may have even though at the time I had thought I considered all of my options. Just as an example of how these decisions can really affect you, here are some of the things that happened to me from some trivial decisions, don't worry I'll refrain from spoilers. I got mugged, I nearly got killed for going on a walk (I mean come on, it's a walk!), I nearly got murdered by my own family (how lovely of them) and I murdered someone out of the blue! Yeah exactly, crazy right?
When conversing with people, unlike other games you aren't just skipping through text to try and get to the end as quickly as possible so you can continue to run around, you are analysing everything about the situation, is this person a threat to you? Do they have a weapon? Are they as loyal as they say they are? Would it be worth standing up to them now or biding your time? One thing that makes this more difficult is how every person seems to have an individual personality and will react differently to situations, so you can't just walk through the game by being "nice". Some people are political and will walk rings around you unless you choose your words carefully and consider hidden subtext behind what is being said, others are more upfront and prefer you to be honest and direct, a difficult line to walk when you don't know which people fall into which category! As I found out they don't have to be noble to be silver tongued.
Graphically this game has a simple but beautiful art style, it's a very pleasant place to explore with continuity throughout. Generally the game flows nicely and environments represent the areas that they are designed to depict.
The music on this game is actually one of my favourite things, although it follows the same style throughout the game, it never gets tedious and is actually really nice to listen to whilst you are playing. It's light and happy when it needs to be but it is equally tense and suspenseful when required, providing the perfect backdrop for the emotional rollercoaster that you are riding. My only small negative however is there seems to be a large lack of sound effects and I couldn't help but feel that a lot of scenarios and situations would have benefited much more with a little bit more audio work.
In summary Unrest is a truly outstanding game, holding a huge appeal with its depth and emotional attachment it doesn't suck you in with cheap gimmicks it has true substance. You feel as though you are truly part of your characters lives by forcing you to sit back and consider your options at every turn. If you want to run around spraying at 12 year olds online then this game isn't for you, however if you want play a real game that can only be described as an artful then I would download this immediately. You will be amazed at how quickly you will be absorbed into this diverse world, full of substance and insecurities. Just remember this, decide wisely!

As of now, I have yet to decide whether Unrest is overly-ambitious and underfunded or just a poorly executed concept. The game suffers from superficiality in every aspest of not only the story, but also the game mechanics and setting. To better explain this, I will go through the Key Features listed on the store page.
Diverse Characters - Right off the bat, the game begins throwing you from character to character, offering a short few paragraphs to tell the character's backstory up until that point. At your leisure you might also be interested in reading the single sentence traits which the game labels each playable character with. This, however, is where character development grinds to a halt. Traits have no actual impact on how the story progresses, are more descriptors than anything else, and are only given out to remind you what superficial choices you have made in the development of the character (four at most, as far as I have seen). Again, the game does very little to actually flesh out the characters, and it is really up to your imagination to determine who these people are.
Furthermore, the way the game switches the playable character around so flippantly makes me wish for less diverse characters, not more. There is only one character in the game who the player is able to control more than once, and each session with a character is little more than a 15 minute walk around the village, or pretend intrigue session with nobles and merchants. The biggest insult which comes of this is the lack of any actual ending to the plot or any closure as to how any characters end up. It really is a shame to see the ideas these characters represent so quickly squandered by limited screentime and a failure to empathise with the characters and their ideals (or, rather, lack there-of).
Reactive Storyline - If there is one thing I can say to this, it is "You are technically correct. The best kind of correct." While yes, there are some aspects of the story which change due to your actions, they are almost entirely relegated to the superficial story represented in the paragraphs at the beginning of each mission. Even when characters who are supposably the main characters die, they merely get a short dialogue mention and are then never heard about again. The game is really in the dead zone where it is both on rails and doesn't actually develop the plot in any way. I can see that the developers were trying to go for something deep and in-depth, but really a Mass Effect-esque on rails storyline would have been better than this. At least then we would get to see how the developers wanted the characters to be fleshed out.
No Right Answers - This is the most true claim the game makes. There is no good or bad, at least according to the game. There are just dialogue option after dialogue option presenting supposed moral dilemas which don't actually affect anything at all. In reality, there are no answers at all, as the game fails to come together at the end to provide an actual moral or even a theme. The only thing the game has in common throughout is that people will be people, and even then it fails to acknowledge the importance of the people themselves.
Complex Conversations - This claim I believe to be a misnomer. What they are really going for here is "Long Conversations" or "Conversations with many Options". Complex would be in reference to the superficial attitude bars which are included for every character you interact with in the game. While these sometimes change the reactions of characters, they never actually change how the story progresses, and don't really provide character development for the playable character or the non player characters. Again, you can certainly play the character and the conversation however you like, you just have to realize that whatever you say or whatever supposed enlightenment you bring the character to will have no effect on the bland and jagged outcomes to any situation.
Violence is Rarely the Answer - Violence serves about as much a point as any other dialogue options in the game. It only progresses the story line as far as it is meant to, isn't particularly deep or meaningful, and fails to get the player to empathize with the character on a personal level.
Lush art and Music - The art and music are interesting for a short Greenlight video before you realize how repetitive the music is and how roughly the art fits with the controls of the game. Very little of the environment is interactive and the only thing which moves in the game is the player character. NPCs will suddenly disappear during dialogue as you find out they leave a few dialogue options down the tree. While the art is certainly smooth, especially on the character, there are many times where pieces will not blend correctly, or the indoor art will be covered slightly by outdoor art, or the character will move through a wall or doorframe, et cetera, et cetera. If you are looking for a game with beautiful art and more tense, empathetic, and meaningful decision making, look to other games like Gods will be Watching and the like.

Overall, I enjoyed my experience with this game, but it did end up disappointing me by the end.  It basically plays as a Bioware game (Mass Effect, Dragon Age, etc.) without the combat and item management elements.  You walk around an enviroment talking to people, picking up quests, and making decisions.  You switch to playing various characters thoughout the story, which allows you to see the complicated state of affairs from different sides as the story unfolds.
The story is pretty good, and I liked how it constantly pits you up against morally ambiguous dilemmas.  More than once I actually found myself questioning the principles I had chosen to stand by.  I was engaged in the dialogue pretty much the whole time, even when speaking to side characters who didn't contribute much to the story.
I think, in the end, I just expected more from the game.  There's a lot of build up with not a lot of payoff, and a lot of things that I expected to matter just didn't matter at all in the end.  Most of the choices you make don't come back to you, longterm, in any way.  I doubt that this would be different with a different playthrough, the game is just too short.  Characters will aquire traits based on the decisions you make, but these don't seem to have any effect on subsequent dialogue or decisions.  They're badges, basically.  The opinion, admiration, and fear you get with characters through dialogue doesn't seem to affect dialogue or decisions either, and it doesn't come back to haunt you or help you later on.  Most characters don't get more than one playthough, so you don't get to follow up on their story.  As it stands, I can only get but so emotionally invested in them.
For what it is, this game can still be fun for the right kind of person, and I'm happy to support games like this as they have so much potential.  I can see myself recommending it to a few people I know, but knowing what I know now, I doubt I would have bought it for myself.

It is THE mech game if your looking for more mech and less jetpack dude (if you want the latter, may I suggest Titanfall?)
This game takes out the run&gun COD-style shootouts seen in the Titanfalls and puts you solely in the mechs. That said, there are WAY more mechs to choose from, and the amount of customizations available is staggering, making Titanfall's mech customization look like trash.
You buy (with in-game money) a mech, and then you have the ability to choose what type of, where on the mech, and how many, of several dozen weapons of different types and styles. Add cusomizable systems such as coolant (I almost typed Coolaid), radios, targeting systems, armor, paint, and cockpit props... MWO allows the player to create their ideal personalized mech, catered either for looks or for playstyle.
My favorite mech is a "Crab" that I heavily customized. I call it "WarWeasel-6" (since you can also name you're mechs!).
Oh, I named it "WarWeasel" because it looks like a weasel (not a crab) to me. The number 6 is the version: I modified it six times before it ended up "just right"!
The gameplay itself is quite fun as well, and gameplay has it's own quirks and tricks depending on what mech your using, as well as how you have modified your mech. Individual parts of the mech can be destroyed, lowering your survivability and losing the missiles that was mounted on that arm you just lost. This, however, makes for interesting builds, such as intentionally putting a lot of armor and no vital systems on one arm with the intent to use that arm as a shield, taking damage on the said arm to protect the rest of the mech from damage. As stated, you can create whatever kind of mech you want!
MechWarrior also supports clan (or faction) warfare and there are several game modes, so the game remains fun for many hours. Voice systems are also supported in-game, which is nice.
A good, free to play game for mech fans, especially if you fell in love with your Titan in Titanfall, but wanted more customizations. Unfortunately, the mechs in MWO do not have the same kind of "relateability" as Titanfall (they all have the same OS voice and no unique personalities), but the sheer number of options available to the player is almost limitless, and you often find yourself creating your own story of how your personal Battlemech/Titan/Jaeger came to be.
**A recent commentator reminded me of the Premium content in this game. While I would certainly not classify any of it as Pay-2-Win, as it does not give you an overwhelming advantage, it does give you pleasant bonuses (otherwise, it would not be worth the money).**

PGI has done well to translate a table top war game into a computer game that ticks most of the boxes of the three points above (Robots, FPS, & Teams).
The game still has flaws and there is a lot of passionate discussion about the game mechanics. In some ways, MWO captures the feel of the Battletech Universe with movement speeds, Battlemech actions/reactions, weapon systems, general technology. However, in others, MWO is still finding its feet with the change from one skill system to another, the tweaking & retweaking of Battlemech quirks, etc. That aside MWO has the possibility of being an excellent addition to Battletech

If you grew up playing Wolfenstein, Doom, Quake, Duke Nukem, etc., then you’re going to love this game. This is simple, fun, fast Gameplay.

- I would have liked to have seen more enemies from the original games. I know they have a lot but I would have liked to have seen more.

This game is kind of a guilty pleasure for me. I just completed it on normal difficulty and I honestly can't believe that it got released with all the problems the game mechanics have. Everything you can possibly imagine that could be wrong with a first person shooter is done in this game. There is a rail section where you are in the back seat of a vehicle being shot at with no way to dodge or duck. If you start the mission with anything below 100% health, (meaning you have to complete the previous mission with 100% health) than you might as well reload an older save file and start from a previous mission. There is a sewer level where the water rises, but if you stay underwater too long, you lose health. The problem is that the damage taken for lack of oxygen while being under water is accumulative, meaning that if you begin losing health after being underwater for 10 seconds, and you emerge for air after 9 seconds, going back under the water (which is required) will start to hurt you after being submerged for only 1 second. The game finally concludes with what I can only describe as one of the worst escort missions in FPS history. The only good thing I can think to say is that there were no timed missions.
Well, the game's not all bad. Let's talk about what they did right. First, the game is short, (a good thing in this case). Second, there is a very convenient quick save and quick load feature, so no check point system. The down side to that is that you will be using the quick save/load feature constantly; sometimes over a dozen times just to get past one corner where soldiers are waiting to ambush you. There is absolutely no skill involved in this game what-so-ever. It is simply a matter of getting past an area, gaining a little bit of advancement, quicksaving, and repeating as you gradually progress little by little. The graphics, while terrible by today's standards and not very good for the standards of its release date, do a very effective job in recreating an oppressive, post-war soviet atmosphere. The game attempted to be accurate by implementing a critical hit system, which means that you can have 100% health, but one bullet in the right spot, (heart, head, ect.) can take it down to almost 0%. And trust me, there is an ocean of bullets flying at you. You'll find that this system works in your favor also as using your sniper weapon, (the most crucial firearm in the game) and zooming in for headshots is the most effective way to kill your enemies. It's a trial and error system that will have you dying A LOT!
So why am I recommending this game? One reason: The price. I got this game for two dollars on sale. For that price it was worth it. Do not pay a dollar more for this game. Deep inside of me, there is a perverse, masochistic streak that takes some sick pleasure in an occasional bad game, much like many people find watching a campy, low-budget movie entertaining. Also, I promise you will enjoy the cutscenes. Trust me on this. They are the most poorly translated, horrendously voice-acted cutscenes you will ever see in your life time. I enjoyed them immensely. If you can find this game for a dollar or two on sale, and you have nothing better to do, give it a try.

That is, until I spent five hours straight playing through the story and lost all my lives fighting the final boss. I thought "oh man, I was close do beating it, I guess I'll have to replay the level." WRONG. YOU NEED TO REPLAY THE WHOLE GAME. Five hours LOST. Maybe someday I will replay this, but for now this on top of all of the other problems makes it not worth playing to me.
For those wondering the problems (made worse by the fact you have to restart the game if you lose your 3-4 lives):
-Horrible controls, your car does not like you and will do all it can to go the wrong way or just flip over in front of enemies
-Bad physics, my car has flipped over or gotten stuck in corners or flown off of cliffs for no reason, most of the time costing me a life
-Overpowered enemies, I played on normal difficulty and the enemies with missiles (they were everywhere) killed me in a few hits even with the extra health upgrade
-Timed missions, every primary objective had a timer that in the games own words would result in a "game over" if not met. Bite Size Review - Renegade Ops
The Good:
- Explosions (they look great and the game pretty much has every enemy die this way)
- Comic Book Style Cutscense and Story Beats Look good and fit the content matter
- GI Joe Style Voice Acting
- Each player character has different abilities that can be upgraded
- The Upgrade System adds much need replayability
The Bad:
- The story overall is very average (there is an evil guy, go kill him, that is really it)
- The player characters are not voiced and really have no personality of their own
- The game is relatively short, I got about 6 hours out of it (with the base game and it's expansion combined)
- On the easiest difficulty the game removes any ability to use to upgrade system
- Timed Objectives, The game will after a while force the player to complete the objectives it deems necessary even if the player is doing side objectives (sometimes these side objectives can not be completed after you go and deal with the timed objective because the game then moves onto the next objective)
The Verdict:
This game was a decent amount of mindless fun. You drive around like a twin stick shooter with your car and mounted machine gun shooting at bad guys. The bad guys blow up in spectacular fashion and really do make you feel like you are living out an episode of GI Joe or something like that. I will say though that the story was very average or even below in some spots as the main plot of it was take down the bad guy with a few twists thrown in but not much else. I would definitely reccommend this game for around $5 or less, because even with the upgrading abilities and going for high scores and all the fun I had with this game I do feel it is a bit light on content.

This review comes with a few criteria and caveats.
- I DO recommend this controller; I've been wanting a controller that I could easily use like a mouse around my desktop for a long time, and this fills that niche perfectly. As a mouse, it even works completely outside of Steam.
- This is NOT like your Xbox controller; it has a totally different feel because of its unique physical features.
- I bought this controller on sale, and for the price I paid for it, I think it was worth it.
What I like:
- Physical feel: grip is very nice; comfortable, yet keeps your hands engaged. All the controls are reachable from the basic grip, and though some buttons are a bit awkward*, prolonged use shouldn't hurt your hands (A complaint I had about the PS controller layout that I've also heard frequently from PS players.)
- Software-side customization is great. Any control surface can be configured any number of ways (a touchpad can be set up as buttons, a thumbstick, a trackball-style mouse, etc. But also, the action buttons (ABXY) can be configured as a thumbstick. Literally, there are no limitations, and I haven't even tried Action Sets yet.)
I especially like the way the triggers are dual-stage (having an analog range, then a click) and how the soft-pull /full-pull actions can optionally do separate things, as well as how other controls (such as the thumbstick) can be programmed with dual-stage actions. (It's made movement actions like sprinting in some games MUCH simpler)
- As a mouse: on the desktop, it's nice. I can sit back with the controller and do stuff on my desktop or on the internet with less effort than an actual mouse (though for applications it won't replace an actual mouse). In games, it has variable use; it acts like a trackball, so flicking occasionally becomes necessary. Sensitivity is fully adjustable (as well as friction, so it could respond like a regular touchpad if desired), but sometimes nothing beats simply having a right thumbstick. (There are some games I still prefer my Xbox controller for.)
- With the wide range of control and emulation options comes - very wide - game support. A LOT of games work with the Steam controller; even some that totally shouldn't (I just recently bought Star Wars: Rogue Squadron for nostalgia reasons and, while there was a built-in predefined keyboard control setup it read from the controller that didn't reflect the software Controller Configuration at all, after some in-game control tweaks, I was using it comfortably.)
- Physical responsiveness: I haven't noticed any mentionable difference in wired vs wireless use, and the thumbstick, triggers, and touchpads are all very precise. I especially noticed this in driving games where I'd used an Xbox controller heavily; the thumbstick and triggers responded better than the Xbox controller's; I can get more out of their analog range. (I.E. steering in NFS Shift / Project CARS is a bit tricky with an Xbox thumbstick as even with a precise deadzone, the wheel can jump around. With the Steam controller's thumbstick, steering is noticeably easier to manage.)
What I don't like:
- The On-Screen Keyboard. It's conceptually a nice feature, but it often comes up when I don't want it to (sometimes inside a game when it shouldn't... this is dependent on the controller configuration, though, so only certain games will have this problem.) and it's not easy to type with, even once you're accustomed to it.
I have a bluetooth keyboard for when I'm not close to my computer, and I'd recommend pairing this controller with one for those who wish to "control their PC from their couch."
- *Physical feel: The one drawback of the controller's layout I feel is that some buttons *are* a little awkward to get to. the ABXY buttons can be a challenge when you're using the touchpads. The underside flaps sort-of make up for this, but it's still just a little weird. Like I said though, it hasn't caused me any physical pain, so there's that.
- Learning curve: well, it's steep. That should be obvious, because there simply isn't a controller like this out there, so it will feel unique. That also means there aren't really any games out there designed with this kind of controller in mind. I've noticed a lot of downvoting reviews seem to point to this specifically; it's a weird setup. You may not adjust to it. If you don't, you probably won't like this controller. Is that really a reason to downvote such a well-designed product? No. Like any other controller, it's simply not for everyone.
This is also the reason I bought this controller on sale; I was going to splurge and get another Xbox controller with some customization, then I saw this on sale and thought, "Well, I'll try this instead." I ALSO had already spent some time studying the controller's design and watching videos of it being operated and tried to imagine what it would be like to actually hold it in my hands. I have to say that I was pleasantly surprised; it feels a lot better than I thought it would based on my observations before purchasing. But despite that, yes, it is a unique layout that WILL take getting used to for actual gameplay.
Last thoughts:
Could I recommend this for competitive play? No. But 99% of competitive players aren't using controllers for anything. They're using tools that give them the most precise control of their game, and no controller will do that anyway. I use controllers for casual gaming, puzzle and driving games, and such. And for that, the Steam controller is great.
** This won't replace your keyboard and mouse, but it is a fun alternative to other controllers. **
Dear Valve: I would REALLY LIKE to see an attachable mini keyboard for the Steam controller. It would make typing much easier, and I wouldn't mind paying an extra $10-20 for it.
I also would like to see (maybe an "advanced" version of the Steam controller?) that features the ability to physically swap parts (so I could swap a touchpad for a thumbstick, or vice versa. Maybe swap the thumbstick for more buttons, etc.) WIth how many other things that were already done right with this, this is just one other thing it feels like it needs.
