I love this game, it really does channel the magic of knockabout old-school shooters.  The world is a delighfully hammy, over-the-top version  of now, with a scenery-chewing super-villain hell bent on exploding the world.  Only your team of 4 mercs (and Gordon Freeman with Antlions for some reason) in their various vehicles can stop hime.
Played from the top-down, each buggy, jeep and tank poerslides across the screen, controlled by a responsive twin-stick control scheme.  You can be powersliding across the screen, unleashing hell behind you and then fire off superweapons to bring down a zepelin.  Occasionally the action takes to the air via assault chopper.
The game's best played in co-op, each of you causing everything on the screen to explode, competing for power-ups, and upgarding your vehicles in new and interesting ways.
It's highly recommended.  You can drop in for 20 minutes of fun, or blast through one of the campaigns over an evening or two.  It's plenty challenging, and never outstays it's welcome.  Make sure you have a gamepad for true enjoyment!

By far one of the best dual stick shooters of all time. This game has it all, over the top story that doesn't take itself too seriously (won't go into detail), arcade style gameplay with modernized mechanics, a cast of seven characters (including Gordon Freeman!), a simple to understand yet challenging scoring system, leaderboards, three difficulty modes (casual, normal, hardcore - I'll touch on this soon), splitscreen co-op, and online multiplayer.
The maps in this game are huge and consist of many different environments and they are filled with a variety of enemies, structures, bosses, scripted events, and firepower upgrades/side weapons (who doesn't love upgrades?). Also, there is a leveling system. Each character drives a different vehicle which not only has unique abilities (which you can upgrade before a mission with points earned by leveling up), but handles differently as well. From APCs that feel heavy to nimble buggies.
I have to mention that this game is simple to get into but hard to master. Some people criticise the controls in regards to the way the physics work, but aside from some rare issues (in which you can get stuck) the controls are just right, and the physics are there for a reason! They are indeed there to hinder you and give you the feel that you're a reckless renegade speeding in a hunk of metal, but you CAN master the controls! The real issue here is somewhat of a steep learning curve. I find that the real game is hidden underneath the hardcore difficulty. That's when you start feeling like a renegade, it's just you (and up to three friends if playing multiplayer) versus a madman and his seemingly endless army - what are the odds? You'll have to tighten up your manouvering and your aim, and memorize stages in order to succeed. This is when the scoring also feels most rewarding.
The negatives for this game consist in more or less minor things such as: not being able to skip in-game cutsceenes, certain points of the map in which you can get stuck (these are rare occurances), and crashes (most notably the ava_main crash which I find infuriating because it effectively ruins the game).

I succumbed to curiosity and bought one today. I've only spent 1.5 hours in game with it so far but I am pretty happy with it. As a primarily PC gamer who turned up late to the console party and never really got comfortable with dual analogue, this is a great option for those games that feel clumsy with a keyboard and mouse. No longer am I drawing hopeless circles around the head of the guy I'm trying to shoot, nor do I find myself staring at my feet quite so often. The controller looks odd but it's suprisingly comfortable. Those big fat grips help to put your hands in the right place to use the touch pads and I have no trouble reaching the buttons even though I have small hands. The AA battery situation isn't ideal - I'd much prefer a plug-in-recharge - but it is still workable. With more familiarity and the huge amount of customisation at my disposal I am confident that this controller will get plenty of use.
My only real problems are with the (a) haptic feedback and the (b) usb dock.
(a) The haptic feedback seems to be all noise with no tactile feedback - perhaps my hands are just too battered to feel it but I have found no use for it so far. It appears to try and mimic a rumble function sometimes too and the sound is... not good - like a large fly desperately trying to escape from an upturned plastic cup.
(b)  The micro USB port on the range extension dock is too small to accept the supplied micro USB cable (or any of the other micro USB cables I own). The supplied cable fits perfectly into the controller and the wireless USB dongle works just fine when plugged directly into the computer but I am unable to utilise the range extender.
I believe valve are on to a good thing here but a little more refinement is needed.

First of all, the Steam Controller is
a replacement for your mouse and keyboard or your Xbox/Playstation controller, it instead a compliment to your "arsenal" when it comes to control schemes and setups. Instead of thinking of this as a replacement, think of it as a middleground between precision and comfort. It doesn't beat out a keyboard and mouse when it comes to precision and it doesn't beat a controller for some games, at least initially. With the unlimited configurations that can be set up, the limit is not the controller, but simply how hard you are willing to get the perfect setup for
.
Please note, that this controller is not for everyone. The controller has unparalleled customization which is a blessing for me, but for others, it could be a curse. While you can get presets from the community, this is only the tip of the iceberg. This controller is mainly for tinkerers, who love trying to get that optimal setup and constantly testing and customizing their setup, improving their experience as they go.
In addition to this, you do need to get acclimated to the controller, which may keep some people from using it, but once you get used to the controler, it gives way to a wholly unique control scheme that is well worth getting used to.
The Steam Controller does have many strengths, though. The paddles for a start, open up a lot of options for new setups and control schemes. You can bind relatively hard to reach buttons to the paddles which really drives home the idea of comfort. In addition to the paddles, the controller has gyro controls (like the WiiU gamepad) this has many uses including fine tuning for aiming in FPS and steering in racing games.
I have found that the Steam Controller works very well for certain genres of games and decently for others with little to no setup time. With these games, the Steam Controller is easily better than controller or keyboard+mouse. These games are the following:
-The Witcher 2 + 3
-Metal Gear Solid V The Phantom Pain
-DMC Devil May Cry
-Metal Gear Rising: Revengeance
-Bayonetta
-For Honor
-Assassin's Creed
-NieR: Automata
-Middle Earth: Shadow of Mordor
With these games, you can do everything that a controller does, but have more mouse-like movement for your camera, without sacraficing any comfort, which makes everything much easier and pleasant to play.
-FEZ
-Nidhogg
-Rayman Origins
-Strider
-Inside
-Shovel Knight
-Ori and the Blind Forest
-Speedrunners
All of these work very well because of the D-Pad/Trackpad on the left side of the controller. With this, you can simply slide your finger across the trackpad to move, instead of the typical joystick controls on most controllers. It gives some unparalleled comfort once you get used to it initially.
-Borderlands 2
The built in aim assist for BL2 can really help you get accustomed to FPS on the Steam Controller.
-Project Cars
With the gyro steer, you can sort of get the feeling of a steering wheel on a budget. The haptics in the controller create a switch-like HD rumble in the controller, so you feel every bump in the road, and every pebble. Gear shifting with the paddles is also amazing.
-Super Mario Galaxy
If you can get your hands on an entirely
copy of Super Mario Galaxy, I would wholeheartedly reccomend this on the Steam Controller. You can use the gyro controls built into the controller to move around the cursor, as well as the standard controller feel for a Nintendo game.
In conclusion, the Steam Controller is an impressive piece of hardware that has near unlimited versatility that is only limited by how far you are willing to go. You can play just about anything on this thing, but you will have to put in the work for some stuff to get a great experience.
Has a steep learning curve, but once you get the hang of it the controller is second to none, and can be used to control the desktop

I love the Steam Controller and every gamer should have one in the tool kit. I game with various other input devices as well depending on what the situation calls for including mouse and keyboard, but the Steam Controller is just right for certain situations. The customizability of it is awesome. Battery life is excellent, pick up a 4 pack of Eneloops and a charger and you are set.
It's great in VR for VorpX gaming, since it can be set up to control both the game and VorpX at the same time as well as running other non-native VR software like Second Life that requires mouse input. Too bad the Vive controllers don't have the same level of customization options, especially considering the price of those. The Steam Controller wireless makes it great for standing/pseudo room scale use in VR when Vive wands are not supported. Wish there was a version with Lighthouse tracking though just to keep track of it.
I've had no problems in recent times using it with non-Steam stuff, just adding whatever to the Steam library and launching through that gets it working and saves the customized input assignments. For example, to run an Oculus only game on the Vive with Steam Controller input, add a new Steam library entry, set that to launch ReVive, then launch the Oculus application directly through ReVive. Steam Controller overlay and profile carries over.
The Steam Controller trackpad does a decent job of replacing a mouse for more casual scenarios like a game of Civ and is much more ergonomically friendly for long gaming sessions than mouse/keyboard. Trackpad as mouse takes a little getting used to, but soon becomes second nature. The grip buttons underneath are fantastic, I seriously wish console controller makers would steal that idea.
There's a bit of a learning curve to the software to customize things, and frustratingly not all buttons work as mode shifts. It can be slow to customize a game and get things like mouse sensitivity right, and then memorize all the input assignments, but it pays off for certain situations. It shines for playing casual mouse/keyboard games, or when you need a highly configurable input device, as the mode shifting allows you quick access to a lot more functions than a traditional game pad. For example, a heavily modded game that you would normally prefer to play with a controller, but needs additional keyboard assignments to operate mod functions, the Steam Controller solves that problem nicely.
The one main thing stopping this from being a perfect input device for me is the lack of a second thumb stick. I would happily pay for a deluxe model with extra features like that. Keep the trackpad for mouse functions, and add another stick for a truly customizable console controller replacement. I know early prototypes had no sticks at all, and the Valve trackpad is awesome (except on the Vive controllers for locomotion) but thumb sticks are simply better for certain applications. Yes the Valve trackpad is a wonderful invention, it can often replace a mouse, but it can't truly replace a stick. Sorry guys.
So the Steam Controller unfortunately cannot entirely replace a good Xbox or Playstation controller for PC gaming. You lose the haptic feedback of native console controller support in a game too, as it doesn't pick that up. It also cannot match mouse/keyboard for super precise style FPS gaming. But it is sometimes the best input device for the situation, just don't expect it to be your main or only gaming input device.
So definitely buy it and use it when the situation calls for it, but do not expect it to entirely replace a twin stick console controller or mouse/keyboard. Think of it more like a HOTAS or wheel and pedals set, sometimes they might gather dust but when you need it, you will be very happy to have it.

Alright, for a long time, I couldn't really play MWO as my old laptop just wasn't up to the task of running the game with the graphics and speed I would like. Now I've have a much more powerful laptop on hand, I can run this game flawlessly at medium graphics, so it's about time I get a review down.
MWO, for those of you who don't know, is set in the BattleTech universe, which to simply put it is Game of Thrones in Space. In a bit more detail, it currently focuses on the factions of the Inner Sphere fending off the invading clans, though at the time of this review, that is due to change anytime soon with a new plot focus. You are a MechWarrior Pilot operating one of the titanular BattleMechs, large, powerful war machines that dominate the battlegrounds of the Inner Sphere in this conflict.
Now, this game has only recently got me into BattleTech, but this game does a great job at making you feel like your in a mighty 'Mech. Utalising missiles, cannons and lasers in several different 'Mechs to eliminate enemy targets in several gamemodes and maps. You have a great selection of the 'Mechs ranging from the fast lights to the lumbering Assault mechs. Or ranging from the humble Locust and Cidana 'Mechs to the famous Atlas and my personal favourite, the iconic Timber Wolf.
Now, you may think this is your typical MMO Shooter Game like World of Tanks, War Thunder or other games of the like, but you would be wrong in terms of gameplay.
Normally, you can quite easily operate alone, sure, it can be a pain, but it's a viable stregety in something like WoT. Not in MWO. The moment you try and play smart and go it alone is the moment you sign your own death warrant. That was kinda the death of me on numerous occassions.
There are two reasons for this, the damage system and the players themselves. First of all, there is no special abilities or penetration values which when coupled with the fact that all 'Mechs can carry weapons of similar power (meaning your Lights can carry some powerful weapons or your Heavies lots of very light weapons) AND the fact that destroying certain modules will kill the 'Mech before the whole thing is totaled means means that even a light 'Mech can bring down an Heavy or Assault. That means that all 'Mechs are viable at taking down targets along with their expected uses. Sure, a single Heavy will slaughter a Light most of the time, but it's more common than you think. As for the second reason, most players in these games are, well, to be quite harsh, a bit dumb or cowardly. Sorry, it's a hard truth I have to get out.
Not in this game, MWO players are at the very least not cowards, and if they see an oppitunity to take down a lone or weak player, they WILL take it. Even if it means their destruction. Once more than one Mech is on you, it's game over, as you are often overwealmed even in the toughest mechs. Sticking together is not only increasing your chance of survival, but can also apply bonuses with ECM and anti missile defence. In short, going alone is normally suicidal. More than once have I tried to be the smart guy only to run into three enemy players or have two enemies see me flanking alone and chase me down.
Sticking together aside, the game requires you to think on positioning, how best to support your team, well timed pushes and managing damage on your 'Mech. It makes it challenging. But makes you feel like a badass when you do well.
Now, in between fights, you can purchase new mechs, customise them with new weapons, skills and all that as you would expect. The loadout system for the 'Mechs in particular is very much like Elite: Dangerous, allowing you to tweak and swap round entire weapon and armor configurations for your personal tastes.
The interface is however... well, not bad. But certainly could be better. Having to sell stuff is a little cyptic at first before it becomes obvious. 'Mech's can't be quickly selected and sent into battle and often you have to go through more menus then you should to get to the places you want. There is a lack of decent tutorials which makes matters worse. Once you figure it all out though, it's fairly straight forward. Just wish it was... refined.
As for the core gameplay, you have your standard quickplay, but you can also join a unit and join in Faction Gameplay, supporting your choosen faction in the wars over the Inner Sphere. This requires you to bring in several mechs into a battle and can be alot of fun... but you also need alot more cooperation. More than any other game of it's type. I urge you to link up with some mates or unit, even for quick play. There is a new competive play mode around, but it's literally a recent addition as of a few days ago.
In either case, you have five modes to choose from and several maps via vote. However, although measures are in place to allow you to get a multiplayer if you don't get the vote you want, some maps are vastly more popular than others, same with the modes to a lesser extent. There isn't really enough maps around aswell to help matters.
The microtransactions... are also a little overpriced for what you are getting. Granted the rest of the game is free but for what you can get, it's not great. If you do decide to spend, just stick to the lower end transactions, you will be happier for it.
Despite some issues, the game is stable and runs well, and it already has me addicted to it as much as WoT has. As such, if you are willing to play a bit more dumb than normal and can deal with the interface and such, this is a solid game with a lot of promise in the feature, especially with the additional content coming soon.
So, if you computer can run it and you like 'Mechs, look no further.

I started playing this game almost a decade ago, long before it ever made it to Steam.
The forums are still teeming with activity (300 people active right now!) and you'll still find people hosting really cool builds and gamemodes for other players to enjoy. Yeah, the active server list is pretty small, but the community is active enough and it's always had its fair share of fantastic builders.
The Steam News feed for this game doesn't appear to update anymore for whatever reason, but if you check the forums you'll find that the creator of the game (Badspot) still posts very frequently and there are still occasional bugfix updates. He's said himself that if people are still playing Blockland, the master server will never go down.
The modding community for this game is huge and modded servers make up a majority of what you'll play on. Modding this game is incredibly simple-- the community has created a very intuitive mod manager for installing your own collection of mods locally, and the game itself will download any additional content needed whenever you join a server. Yes, the old Return to Blockland mod manager is dead, but a new communally-developed mod manager has taken its place now.
This game is a bit more mature and polished than Roblox, which is targeted towards a much younger audience. If you enjoy playing with Legos you'll enjoy blockland. Yes, the control scheme is pretty wonky. Yes, the game is pretty dated. Yes, the community is pretty small.
But is it a great game?
Oh yeah.

I'm kind of a misfit fan when it comes to Battletech/Mechwarrior. I only grew up with MW4:Mercenaries and the MechAssault games as well as only being partially familiar to the lore. But it was something that immediately fascinated me. I've been on and off with MWO though so while not a lot of time put into it I have spot checked quite a few parts in its development.
- The Graphics are pretty much exactly what the game needs and offers a game that runs very well. The game has a certain scale to it where nitty, gritty ultra realistic textures aren't needed and combat vfx are of utmost importance. They put the work into where it needed to be. +1
-  Mechlab is quite enjoyable and (when you've got the Cbills) provides a lot of freedom with some reasonable limitations per mech. +1
- Very, very.....very generic gameplay. It holds me over for a couple of rounds and then my interest is lost. -1
- Typical free to play grind after your first mech purchase - 1
- The overall visual design of the game is just kind of so so. Some mechs got a really good revamp to their design, others look absolutely atrocious (im looking at you bushwacker). Really needed some better work in this area. 0
- Sound design is good for the most part, just a few tweaks and it would be great. Good feel for most of the weapons. +1
- Rather lousy interface for any part of the game; tends to always be crowded and noisy and not laid out conveniently. -1
- Desperately needs some interesting gamemodes and maps. -2
- Game has okay balance, but some gameplay aspects make certain strategies easy to exploit despite providing a decent counter. Damage is rather all over the place though and can make no sense at times. -1
Score: -3
Overall I can't recommend it. It's just bland, and basically fills the gap for Battletech/Mechwarrior. Just don't invest money in it.

I don't regret buying one. It's been really fun to play around with, and everyone who comes to my house wants to try it and think it's real fun. However if you want a controller to actually play games with, don't buy this.
The setup is very easy, battery life great. Buttons and and feel have their pros and cons, but that makes or breaks it is of course the touchpad. It's essentially the touchpad from a laptop/media keyboard fitted on a controller which you control with your thumb.
Playing games that work well with a normal controller like Witcher 3 or Hotline Miami is impossible. It's hard to explain, but in these games you use the right stick to control the camera, and the touchpad ends up being way too sensitive and very tiring to hold steady.
Playing FPS games is very difficult. I gave it a solid try in Doom, Wolfenstein and a bit of CS:GO, but all it really did was make me appreciate using a normal controller for these types of games - something that I normally would never consider. There is a case to be made for the combining the touchpad with the motion controller, but I find this to be very awkward to use, and I am not really motivated to be waving the controller in front of me during my entire play session. Even if I did dedicate myself to get good at it, I can't imagine it being better than a normal controller.
What I was maybe most excited about was playing games like Civilizations and City Skylines, games that have no controller support at all. These games are somewhat playable with the Steam controller, but they are very slow and awkward. So slow and awkward that I'd rather not play anything at all. In fact using a Logitech K400 to play them is better, but even that's not enjoyable.
If some people like the Steam Controller then I am happy for them ,and I am very happy to see dedication to controller use and big picture mode from Valve. However I do not like it myself, and I honestly have hard time even imagining how a person can enjoy using it. One can always argue that I just need more time to get used to it, but if I don't like it after the 10+ hours I spent on it, and no one I know who has tried likes it, then I can in no way recommend it.

A game that, once, held great potential; now totally left in the dirt by an apathetic developer.
I understand that after time Hartman would have wanted to move onto new projects, but in its current state the game feels almost incomplete. The removal of terrains/maps, and interiors seemed like a great step forward. A fantastic opportunity for the team to focus more on improving the base game, and not be held back by older, and poorly aging game elements.
Unfortunately, this simply was not the case.
Many of the things proposed, or promised by the devs themselves, simply never came to fruition.
Vehicle physics were never improved,
A proper tool to make bricks was never produced,
And the updates went from small slithers of content into a rare bug fix.
While, yes, some content was added, none of it worked to freshen up the experience, or bring in exciting new elements.
And with the game's main mode of sharing modifications and add-ons now entirely redundant/non-existant, it's now even more difficult for a (remarkably toxic) community to bond together, and share content.
I want to recommend this game, as it was a personal favourite once-upon-a-time, but it's now a poorly managed mess.

Review:
Pros:
+ Combat is absolutely brillaint.
+ Gameplay feels smooth.
+ Things despawn at a very slow rate. For example: You can set a helicopter down at one end of the map. Run to another end and back and find it right where you left it.

Cons:

- Entire game is essentially a copy of Radical's: "The Incredible Hulk. Ultimate Destruction."
- Very gory, and violent. (If you dislike, or are disturbed by gore.)

So I decided to visit the Deus Ex series, starting with Human Revolution.
First of all, I'm gonna say it now - Human Revolution is good. It's a solid game that knows what it wants to be and follows that.
You're playing as Adam Jensen - a chief of security at Sarif Industries - a bio-tech corporation. Sarif's lead scientist, Megan Reed (also your girlfriend) is about to make a breakthrough in human augmentation tech and is about to go to DC and defend her work in the Congress and you are supposed to protect her and her team. Of course everything goes wrong as Unknown Assailants break into the building, kiddnap Megan's team and leave you to die. Your boss decides to save you by making you into one of the most augmented people on the planet and boom! True, you never asked for this. Deal with it. The story itself will take you around the globe and is all-in-all pretty thrilling, but somewhat predictable.
As for graphics I can't really say anything wrong about the visuals, even if the golden tint get's tiresome after some time, you'll get used to it. Although I exprienced some stutters and occasional lip desynch during conversations, I'm going to blame my laptop for that, since it's not exactly a cutting edge machine. UI is as it should be - it conveys critical information, without obstructing half of the screen. You have your health and energy, your quickbar and a mini-map.
Now coming to gameplay there are 2 main styles you can play - "pacifist" (quatation marks intended, you'll still be brutalizing people by knocing them out, although I'm sure people on the internet will prove me wrong) or No Mercy Guns Blazin'. It is important to note that the game FEELS like a stealth game and is much easier when you decide to go sneaking around. That is not to say that you can't go in like a wrecking ball, but personally I had much more satisfaction evading my enemies. The gunplay is satisfying - every gun has its own "feel" to it and you can upgreade them to a degree. There is also a hacking minigame which you will spend a lot of time playing. It is not bad, so don't worry, but without investing points into hacking stuff you will have a hard time and many areas will be locked for you.
Now... boss fights. Yes, there are boss fights. They vary in quality. From the infamous "I can take 50 headshots and live" first boss to the last one which is honestly some kind of a joke (any boss, let alone final one should be a challange in their own right... the last boss failed to be a challange. No exploits, you can defeat him very easily with propper augments and armaments.) Personally I think that the 2 middle boss fights (2nd and 3rd) were the best. They presented a challange, without being obviously over- or under-powered.
As for the RPG aspect you gain experience points which are then converted into Praxis points which you can spend to upgreade or unlock new augmentations, ranging from more inventory space (that one being pretty much mandatory) to things like dermal plating or cloaking. Praxis points can also be bought at LIMB clinics but if you want to do that you better save some money because they stand at whooping 5k per point. You will also engage certain characters in what can be descirbed as "Dialog Battle". These were one of the best conversations in the game where you will need to take a stance to persuade your opponent to your point of view. They are much easier with CASIE social augment but can be beaten without it.
Overall the game stands firmly on its two legs (be they augmented or not). It is a solid shooter and stealth game. I never asked for this Deus Ex. But it's a game that got me to love the universe.

A fast, frantic arena shooter that demands as much from you as it does from your hardware. Rated from a single player perspective.
Pros:
Game mechanics compliment the mobile, arena combat gameplay.
Thumping soundtrack drives the action during the battles.
Satisfying viseral thrill with weapons and context sensitive kills.
Level design that's both visually striking and creative in terms of hidden powerups.
Surprisingly interesting lore drops for those interested in the lore.
Doom Guy finally gets a personality.
Cons:
Very demanding on hardware for optimal performance. Check your specs.
The core experience starts to get repetitive during the last levels.
The story isn't going to rival any decent modern FPS narratives.
Mehs:
Suit and weapon upgrades don't feel like they add much to the gameplay (Most don't change the standard engagement strategy or offer new options).
Would Recommend To:
Fans of Doom or any of the 90s/2000s arena shooters (Quake, Unreal Tournament, etc) who have a solid rig. Any FPS fans who feel like cover mechanics ruined the genre. Fans of twitchy dark and violent games. Anyone looking for a benchmark game that also plans to play the game after the tests are run.
